I got this thinking it'd be a quick, throwaway AAA game to distract me, but I did not expect to enjoy it as much as I did.
The stealth itself is really good. One thing I'm pretty sick of in stealth games are all of cheap gimmicky abilities like Dishonored's warp that take a lot of the tension out of sneaking around. In Thourf, the most you have to work with is the Thief Vision that highlights collectables, important objects, and enemies. It's also got limited use in the form of a bar, so it's not as powerful as say the Detective Visor in the Batman Arkham series. No, the rest of the time, you have gadget arrows, a blackjack, and some smoke bombs to get you into trouble, out of trouble, or past it, and none of them seem particularly game-breaking for any playstyle.
One particular feature I really like that seems to be divisive is Garrett's full range of animations, especially in regards to picking up loot. It's very immersive and helps enhance the feeling of being a thief rifling through desks and containers, pocketing all of the valubles while praying the guard next to you doesn't turn around. To me, it feels satisfying to snag individual pieces or cut a painting out of a frame, but also adds an element of danger when you have to do it in places where you can get spotted, as opposed to games that just let you mash E to instantly pick up anything you see.
You get money for all loot you steal which can then be spent on gadgets, items, and upgrades for Garrett. The economy is set up much in a way that you can't really get everything you want, and start having to make choices later in the game on how much you want to spend on stealth-friendly or combat-friendly items. I appreciate that over games that let you get everything and play any way you want.
Non open world levels are set out really well. There are lots of alternate paths and lots of loot to pick up, but I never felt like there were too many paths that broke the game. You are still forced to have to sneak around enemies if you want to make progress or get extra money.
The open world is a mixed bag. The big positive comes in the form of being able to sneak into peoples' houses and rooms to nab valuables, and there are plenty of places to do so. It gives the feeling of being a real thief, especially when going into the many, many side mission and mini-mission buildings.
Outside the actual fun gameplay and stunning visuals, though, there are serious rough spots. The biggest problem I have is with actually navigating the open world. It's fine in concept, but there are some serious problems I can't gloss over. They are:
1) Transitions between subsections of the world are not marked 90% of the time. I've had moments where I'm just running around for pretty inexcusable amounts of time before I found out that to get to the next zone, I had to find a well-hidden beam to shoot a rope arrow into to climb up into a hidden window to get to the next zone. That, or having to walk up to some crates that don't seem all that important until you rub your face against them so you can hit E to have Garrett contextually squeeze through them. Keep in mind, this is with mission trackers with waypoints on, but the waypoints only tell you where in the city the objective is without marking transition zones.
2) The world is confusingly laid out, you are constantly forced to sneak around patrols, and the map is often unhelpful. This results in probably the majority of your time spent slowly skulking around in transit through the world.
3) There's no sort of fast travel. I wasn't joking when I said there were tons of side missions in the game. And it's a huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to have to navigate back and forth past guards every time you go to and from these quests.
The plot is wholly unentertaining with characters that are either uninteresting or incredibly forgettable (literally, too. People kept saying the names of very important characters whose faces, voices, and importance I could not remember). The plot is pretty lame, too, mostly involving Garrett feeling guilt over the disappearance of a woman who regularly admonishes in the opening parts of the game.
There's also a pretty lame throwaway horror mission in an asylum. I'm guessing it's supposed to emulate the Shalebridge Cradle mission from Thief 3, but it mostly comes off as an overly-long pop-scare museum. After spending an eternity, I got tired of it and just plowed through it, killing everyone I could.
Beyond the negatives, though, this game is a surprisingly good gem that fans of stealth gameplay should check out.

you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Ah, the joys of Far Cry 4.
Being my first game in the Far Cry series, and one of the first real open world shooters I've played, Far Cry 4 really was a new experience for me, and a good one at that, still sitting near the top of my 'favorite games' list. First off, the visuals are truly beautiful. As much as it murders my framerate to do so, I can't help but get to a high point, turn the settings up to Ultra, and just look down at the landscape. But as many of us know, graphics don't make a game good. Luckily, FC4 doesn't disappoint when it comes to gameplay.
I do have some pet peeves with this game, like the reused animations from FC3, but overall it takes everything from its predecessors and polishes it to a shine. The guns are responsive and each feels very unique, surprising with such a wide variety to choose from. There's also the satisfying feeling of exploding an enemy vehicle with some well-placed mines or C4. Wingsuiting is probably the most fun way to get around in any video game to date. Not only that, there's also co-op! While it's not perfect, I'd be lying if I said I hadn't had fun messing around with a friend in tuk-tuks, or shooting rockets out of the back of a truck.
The story is good, although there are definitely better ones out there. You're a man named Ajay looking to spread his mother's ashes in her home country, Kyrat. When you enter, you realize quickly that the country is run by a flamboyant dictator named Pagan Min. In true Far Cry fashion, you decide that the best way to improve this country is to grab some guns and ravage the countryside, blowing up everything in sight. Jokes aside, there are some interesting characters and entertaining moments throughout the story mode that I'll leave you to discover for yourself.
9/10, definitely worth $60.

Playerbase is practically dead as far as I can tell, at least on the North American servers there seemed to only be a few servers running at anypoint on a Thursday evening around 8 PM when you would think servers would be at their peak for the day as most people get off work.
You can hop between servers but that will raise your ping quite a bit if it is significantly outside of your region.
The graphics however while not being anything exceptional do tend to be some of the better visuals you would find in a free to play game. Though I will say that the sound design to this game is comically bad and the running sound effects on any surface are just terrible. Combat arms has consistently better mastered sound design for gods sake.
The combat is smooth and the animations are all quite strong as well, so from a gameplay perspective it is pretty solid, and there is a wide variety of weapons to buy (Though they do expire so you would have to grind A LOT as far as I can tell unless you want to spend money).
Lot of gun customization.
So as far as quality and content I would give the game an 8 out of 10 or so compared to other free to play shooters.
I however simply cannot recommend it though because the player base is so small and I don't see this game having any kind of longevity because the peak players for the last 30 days did not exceed 450 and it has been steadily declining since its release.
Quite a shame because the game does quite a few things well, and it had a lot of potential to be a strong choice on the free to play market.
Which as far as I can tell, is slowly beginning to phase out in general as people get tired of free to play games and how much it takes to progress without spending actual money.

They Bleed Pixels marked my second try at a current gen hardcore platformer.  To preface my review, I must say that I am not a young gamer anymore, and these types of games pose a huge difficulty for me.  Honestly, I was never very good at video games, and I'm not even sure why I torture myself.  I suppose I couldn't resist satisfying my curiosity after suffering through about 30% of Super Meat Boy, seeing how this game looks much more interesting, with more visual appeal and a better sound track.  To cut to the chase, this game is HARD!!  I died several hundred times on a few of the levels, and yes, it was infuriating at times, but not b/c it required pixel perfect precision like SMB, but rather b/c what I needed to accomplish always seemed just slightly out of reach of my rickety old hands.  The game does allow you do make your own checkpoints once your blood meter fills up, having killed enough enemies, and it is a joy to perform simple combos and find different ways to kill your foes.  Just know that there will be times you will want to throw your controller (try not to hit your big shiny flatscreen), blame the controls for your screw-ups, and you will curse this game repeatedly.  The levels are lengthy; so it's not so much a continuous stream of bite-sized levels like MeatBoy, it's more akin to Electronic Super Joy in that regards, but not quite as unforgiving.  The squids are a horribly infuriating, cheap enemy, and at times, the knife wielding ninjas (?) can seem a bit unfair, but if you're into hardcore ultra-difficult platformers, they will probably seem like standard affair.  One cool aspect is that there are several bonus levels that you can unlock, and I believe one of them was unlocked by default.  I didn't do the Ponycorn bonus content; I chose one of the others that I unlocked and that was enough for me.  I really liked the game, but it's very stressful for me to play, so I had no intention of doing all of the bonus stuff.  Some of the artwork that you can unlock is very good, too.  Unless you're a completionist, you may want to check online to see which slots unlcok which art pieces, b/c the styles vary and I found that the photorealistic ones were more preferable to my taste.  Now, I will nto spoil the ending, but just be warned that it is rather anti-climactic.  This game is more about the journey than the destination, and it was definitely worth the few dollars I paid to buy this game on sale.  Hopefully it won't take most people the 31 hours it took me to complete it.  As angry as the game made me, my eagerness to see new levels kept me pushing through, b/c the art style is really interesting, and far more preferable to Super Meat Boy or Electronic SuperJoy.

First impressions: Fighting status bars, grinding materials (with zero danger involved). Criptic menus with zero explanations, no active pause.
And then comes pure nonsense - no option to send more than one guy to scavenge... One would think: "well, going of to scavenge is pretty dangerous. We should stay together!". But no. You can only send one guy at a time.
This makes you not only waste time while only one guy hauls ♥♥♥♥♥on of metal, screws, wood and whatnot, but also makes it potentially more dangerous...
Game presents itself as to be a game about "survival", but it fact it is simply fighting "status bars", that are ever going down.
Forcing you to only have one guy have to haul all the crap you need to progress makes it artificially longer, because while one guy does the job, the other two are draining resources. Resources this one guy will have to haul.
I loved the idea of survival of civilians in a warzone. This is something that HAD to be explored, as it had a great potential to show that war isn't fun. But while war isn't fun, babysitting bunch of lazy bums, who refuse to go out and scavenge isn't fun as well.

I want to recommend this game for it's "artistic value" but the game isn't short enough to ride purely on it's artistic value the way something like Pony Island or The Stanley Parable is.

The skill quests are inane and omnipresent; they pop up about 3-4 times in the early tutorial games and move about as slowly as they possibly can.  The campaign option is rather deep, but as you must play with pre-selected decks - some of which are the WORST decks known to man and ones that no decent player would ever have put together - the simple joy of playing is lost to the endless frustration of ill-conceived deck construction.  Even if you consider the campaign simply an extended tutorial ... the only thing it will teach you is that some decks are worthless.
It is free, so it has that going for it.  Sit this one out and wait for Arena to pop up, or better yet just find a good game shop to hang out instead.  You'll have more fun with a penny deck than the monstrosities Magic Duels compels you to play with.

In a game like this, the strength of the writing is the ultimate criteria by which to judge. And it delivers with stunning success.
Everything about how this game is written is fantastic. There is rapier wit to spare in the clever dialogue, narrative and general premise, the characters are written exceptionally well, and the descriptive writing makes the absense of visuals a moot point; your imagination, from the visual cues indicated, is the most effective tool.
The story is quickly paced and never stagnates. Exposition is kept to a minimum and you make decisions frequently and often. Speaking of decisions, the choices you make in this game DO influence so much about the story and the characters and how everything ends. It feels like this could be your story, though the protagonist is probably a good deal more clever than you.
It's just an absolute riot, a delight to read, and you're guaranteed at minimum 2 hours on a single playthrough, and if you see those achievements you can tell there are MANY directions you can take the game. I'm gonna go for a replay soon enough!
For this pricepoint? It's an absolute steal. Highest recommendations.

Like most peeps here, I got this game in one of the Humble Bundles. Boy am I glad I only spent a few cents on this ...
TLDR version: No, just no.
The "Size does matter, give me the long one" version:
Cibele is a game that tells the story of Nina by means of written text, voiced-over dialogues and FMVs.
First, let's get this out of the way: if you are expecting a FMV-heavy game you will be sorely disappointed. There are 4 short movies, including the opening movie where you just see Nina sitting at her computer. So basically there are
where anything worthwhile happens. If all you care about are the movies, just look at the trailers above (not all stuff in the trailers is in the FMVs by the way) or check Youtube.
So there are 3 relevant FMVs, each showing you how the story progresses. The developer even has the guts to refer to these as "acts". Trust me, their definition of an "act" does not match your and everyone else's definition at all.
Hell, you know what, my morning consisted of several acts as well! First I got out of bed, that was act 1. Then I put on some clothes, that was act 2. No wait, let's call it an act per piece of clothing. I'll even count each sock as a different act, now I'm truly thinking as Star Maid Games. It's 10:14 in the morning and I'm already at act 162! My day feels a lot more epic all of a sudden.
The
itself is atrocious. You stare at a virtual desktop of the protagonist Nina, who is the typical 19 year old teenage girl ... which means it is impossible not to get an immediate disliking to her unless you are a 19yo teenage girl yourself.
This desktop-staring is actually the best part of the entire "game", just because you can get in touch with your most voyeuristic side. Snooping through a handful of her folders, all filled with the standard duckface pictures, mindless conversations or (brace yourself) teenage poetry.
I told you you would get a disliking to her, didn't I?
When you are done with snooping around the desktop (which takes about a minute for each act, mind you), it's time to move on to the main part of the "game": for the story to progress, you have to play the most boring, annoying MMO in existence. Mindless clicking on enemies until a boss appears, which you have to repeat three times for each "act". So fun!
Scroll up this page now. Go ahead, scroll up, I'll wait here. See the marketing talk about "A richly illustrated and scored game world to explore called Valtameri, with multiple maps"? Yep, that's the horrible MMO they are talking about. There is nothing to explore in this stupid mini-game, everything is the same. The "richly illustrated and scored" parts are not entirely true either by the way. And the fact that you have to play this mini-game 3 times for all 3 acts, each time with a different and even more annoying map is definitely not a plus of the game! You know what, without the MMO-part I might even recommend the game for $0.15 !
One thing I have to hand to the developers, at least they realized the MMO is boring and they tried to give you something to read during the MMO-parts by means of scripted e-mails (or the occasional photograph) that arrive once in a while.
Those e-mails are not interesting of course, just the typical "haven't seen you around lately" or "OMG Jason has the hots for you" drivel, all single line gossip. You can respond, but the response is always scripted as well and you don't even get to pick any options (if this is ever implemented, may I suggest as standard reply: "I don't care, don't ever contact me again").
That is true for everything actually:
, there is never anything to pick from. You are basically on a rail and have little other option but to witness and be an accomplice to the atrocities on your screen, unless you want to alt+F4 and end your misery prematurily (I'm not going to lie to you, I have been tempted by this last option several times during my play-through, I'm not joking. The MMO mini-game is
boring).
The
then … During you fantastic adventures in Valtameri (note: if have ever before played an actual computer game, that should read: "during the annoying and longwinded clicking about in Valtameri") you hear our protagonist Nina and a boy called Ichi chatter about relationships. During the course of the "acts" they get more intimate and the budding releationship heats up. This is not a spoiler, I only repeat the marketing blip above ... although it does really tell you 90% of the story.
The remainder of the story is pretty obvious and whoever plays this probably can tell how it is going to end well in advance. I mean, attractive older guy flirts with pretty average nerdy girl online, pressing her to send him some risque photographs and wants to meet up ...
Protip: ignore the marketing talk, the FMVs and handful of photographs in the game do not show any nudity.
So, a predictable story told by means of 3 FMVs and an absolutely boring and uninteresting mini-game that needs to be played to move the story forward. I kept playing on in the hope that the game would surprise me at some point, that something interesting would happen ... but it didn't. If I knew that in advance, I would have given up 30 seconds into the MMO in "act 1".
What abouts the
? Like I said earlier, there are only a few of them. Their quality is good (and so is the sound of the game b.t.w.) Crispy video without too many artifacts. Video directing is alright as well, although the camerawork is very static (then again, there are about 10 minutes of footage in the game so we can hardly expect anything too exotic). From technical point of view, no complaints.
The
on the other hand is wooden and the dialogue unnatural. This is of course
pitfall of games centered around FMVs: the typical "it looks like the actors never read the script in advance or care about it" syndrome. A combination of underpaid actors with little real-life experience, a script that is not interesting riddled with bad lines and too little time for the actors to get into their role. Yes, Cibele also suffers from this typical FMV-game syndrome.
Finally, the entire game is incredible
. I finished it in 48 minutes, including a 5 minute break to get a drink (actually, I hoped that the MMO would play itself even if I didn’t do anything, but that is not how it worked). I have zero intention to replay it or even leave it on my hard drive.
: I understand what the developer was trying to pull of, but it does not work here. The game is just too short for this sort of story, everything feels rushed and the player does not get enough time to bond with any of the characters. Taking away even any illusion of choice from the player is the nail in the coffin. If the developer wanted to express her personal experiences, this type of medium was not a good choice.
Besides, storytelling now relies entirely on playing a mind-numbingly boring mini-game, which just ruins any redeeming qualities that the game might otherwise have had, as that mini-game takes up 75% of the playtime.
Taking everything above in mind, I strongly recommend you not to spend any money on this game. Ignore the SJW reviews. Just because a game has a female lead and centers around relationships does not mean that a game is good (yes Wired, IGN and Vice, I'm looking at you).
Star Maid Games, just make a strip poker game featuring Nina and call it quits. This was a joke b.t.w.

In my experience, the best MOBA/shooter hybrid to date. The typical "Nexus" is replaced with a gigantic guardian that you guard/empower, then seige the enemy guardian with. Towers are replaced with summoned creatures that you protect/kill to empower your guardian for a seige on the enemy guardian. 3 diverse maps that make full use of obstacles and elevation for dynamic battles. The map also gets smaller/altered from the guardians battling during the middle-phase of the game for a faster paced end-game. You can enjoy the short length of each game instead of worrying about having enough time to dedicate it to finishing a single game (approx. 20 min). The gameplay is like GW2 on steroids, full with colorful characters and dynamic objectives. As a MOBA without creeps/farming, it is able to focus on the more 'fun' aspect, the team-based PVP. Graphics don't seem to demanding so it's great. This is the only game review I've ever given - a testimonry to how incredible the gmae is.

I've been playing this game on Windows since one of the first waves of keys in the closed beta and feel obligated to give it a review, now that it has finally released. (Don't let the playtime fool you; the game was available in the windows store and by invitation long before release.)
Do NOT believe anyone telling you this is a copy of Overwatch. It was announced quite a bit before Overwatch and plays very differently. In fact:
The game is fast and elegant. Most heroes have a mobility trick of some sort and everyone can perform a quick dash in addition to sprinting and jumping. There is a lot of verticality and positioning involved in every fight and the maps are designed to encourage clever outplays.
The game is skill based. Don't expect to in and be good at it. However, the learning curve is not to steep and some heroes, like Knossos, are easy enough to start out with. Don't play Tripp though. She is mediocre in high level play and often stomps in low level play because her skill floor is at rock bottom and new players lack the coordination to deal with her. If you get too used to stomping beginners with her, you will find that you haven't learned a lot by the time you play against veterans and will get destroyed.
The heroes are unique. When the game was first announced, Motiga was boasting that each hero would appeal to players of different genres and while they don't deviate this heavily in acutal play, they really all play in a very unique manner. This is further amplified by the many builds available to each hero with a total of 3072 combinations per hero. Many of them provide wonderful synergies and let you modify your playstyle drastically.
Of course, gameplay isn't everything. If it looks bad, people won't want to play it.
This game has a gorgeous art style. You have probably seen it in the pictures up top anyway but let me tell you: It doesn't get old. Everything looks lovingly hand made, the effects are vibrant and it really stands out in the industry.
Some people are complaining about performance issues but I really can't talk about that, since it runs perfectly fine on my PC.
Now if the game cost $40, I would recommend you watch a gameplay video or two, make sure your account balance - $40 is still enough to feed your kids and then buy it.
Luckily it's free. Unless your PC can't run it, you have no excuse not to try it.

TL;DR: Poi was an extremely fun 3D Platformer since the day it popped up on Early Access and, thanks to constant support, is really turning into something special.

A throwback to the N64/PSX days, but without being slavish to the exact design of one specific title, (the oddly named) Poi is a classic styled 3D Platformer where you play as a boy or girl explorer in a land of airships and magical islands who's tasked with finding medallions lost by an old man. The Old Man's Airship, and the sky around it, acts as your "hub" - you use the giant compass onboard to aim at an island and then set course to travel to that level. Polykid has been regularly adding in new Levels since launching this on EA too.
Also of note, in the immediate airspace around the ship, there are a few floating points of interest; when this popped up on EA, there was just one guy with a cannon who could send you to challenge courses. Since then, the devs at Polykid have added Snowland, home to some delightful penguins, as well as a second explorer girl who will give you tips and pop up in levels for a game of hide n' seek.
Once on the ground, your explorer controls fast and precisely. You're able to do a Super Mario 64-style triple jump (NOT jumping three times in the air), a backflip jump, a roll, a rolling jump, wall- and triangle-jumps, etc. They control really well; it's very responsive and they transition between animations - like going from running to balancing on a beam, climbing on a ladder or grabbing a ledge - super quickly and smoothly. Like a great classic 3D Platformer, it's a joy just to move around in these levels with these characters. Beyond the platforming, you have a few gadgets that can be purchased from the Old Man, like a telescope or a shovel. They're nothing earth shattering, but they add a little bit more to the levels, and help drive home that sense that you're exploring these locales for items and points of interest.
The levels are large, wide and totally open - this is not modern-style super linear "3D Platforming" like Mario 3D World or Ratchet & Clank. No Point A to Point B, follow the path, "nothing to see over here"-nonsense. Go wherever you want, explore! You don't even have fall damage, because that would just get in the way. Find medallions even if they're not for the mission you've selected! Hit switches you find to open up a new portion of the level! There's a lot of verticality to the levels, for lots of climbing opportunities. There are also stage hazards like moving platforms, bounce ropes, climbing walls, etc. The way everything's laid out, it's all just very engaging to traverse.
When the game launched, there were no enemies, so it was purely just a platforming challenge (barring the occasional rolling boulders or electrified gears-on-ropes). Since then though, the devs have started populating the levels with simple little baddies and NPC's, so levels are even better now. They're starting to feel less barren and more of full of life in general. The enemies are extremely simple to take out - without any combat moves, you just jump on their head - but they add to the experience all the same.
--
The whole game feels great, is super charming & whimsical, and is just plain fun - everything a great 3D Platformer should be! It may not have the looks of something like Yooka Laylee, but it definitely deserves your attention if you're a fan of the genre, especially for this price. If you're worried about it feeling incomplete or not ever getting finished due to it's status in Early Access, I wouldn't worry about it - there's plenty here already to entertain for hours, and as I've said before, Polykid has been updating this pretty regularly. There's a sense of progression in place already and it's clear there's an endgoal in sight (literally; one of the updates has introduced a mysterious island with 4 locked doors that we'll eventually gain access to through a future update).

Pick this up; it's an absolute joy to play that you're guaranteed to have fun with!

Poi is a 3-D platformer that has you exploring various worlds looking for things to collect.
The main goal of the game is to collect medallions in each level. Instead of free roam, each level has you select a medallion to go for which can alter how the level is designed. An example is the Crystal Cavern level where the first medallion you collect will turn on the lights and power, which will cause all future medallions to be in a lit cavern with running machinery. Each level has six medallions to find, where four of them are in unique areas sometimes requiring you to solve a puzzle, while two others just require you to either collect 100 coins or 7 keys to make them appear. Each medallion will record how long it takes you to collect it, and this time can be used to compete with other players to see who can collect them the fastest.
Collecting coins during levels lets you buy explorer tools and unlock challenge levels. Tools include a shovel that lets you collect fossils found in levels, and a compass that will show important objects in a level. Challenges are just short levels that have a unique set of obstacles and just requires you to reach the medallion at the end of the level. There are no coins or anything else in challenge levels, but competing with other players for the shortest time is what will bring you back to them.
Your character is very simple, who can easily run and jump around. There isn’t anything special about walking and running, but jumping comes in a variety of styles. Your standard jump can be extended by double jumps, and jumping in succession after hitting the ground first will cause future jumps to go even higher. Wall jumping is also present, where you can jump back and forth between two walls that are fairly close to each other.

Quite possibly one of the easiest games that you can buy, it is an excellent choice if you don’t want much of a challenge. However, it may actually be too easy even if that is what you’re looking for.
Your progress is always being saved and most medallions and challenge levels only take a few minutes to complete.
Even the hardest medallions and challenge levels require very little skill, so the only thing that hardcore gamers will like is speedrunning through levels to become number one on the highscores.
Just the art style alone makes it clear that it is a game that children will enjoy. On top of that, the lack of difficulty also makes it a perfect game for younger ones to play.
Collecting most medallions and playing through the challenge levels will take you between 1-2 hours. Finding everything in each world can make the game last a few more hours, while speedrunning medallions and competing for high scores can make the game last even longer.

The settings menu is very simple; with basic volume sliders, graphical options, and camera sensitivity. While it does show controls you aren’t able to change them, but the game is simple enough that it isn’t a problem.
Poi has simple cartoony graphics and runs well on any modern computer. Loading into the hub and levels happens almost instantly so you never have to sit and wait to play.
The level selection hub and levels all have their own unique music to listen to. There are characters in the game but there is no voice acting of any kind.
You will be controlling your character in third person while you are exploring levels. The camera can be freely moved around as you explore and can also be zoomed in and out, but it will sometimes be controlled automatically in some areas and may cause the camera to be in a bad location. Jumping can be a little odd at times, especially when you are in areas with walls and slippery slopes. This is especially noticeable when you miss a platform or something and as long as you simply touch something, you regain the ability to do a double jump.
The mechanics of the game appear to be complete, which means it's just content that needs to be added. There will be additional explorer tools that can eventually be bought in the store, allowing for more things to be collected in the levels. New worlds and challenge levels will also come in future updates.

I grew up playing many of the collect-athon platformer series including Super Mario, Donkey Kong, Banjo-Kazooie, Jak and Daxter, and many others. You very rarely see games like them these days which is a shame. While there are still many platformers of all kinds being made, Poi is probably the only current one in 3-D that focuses on exploration and collecting objects. Unfortunately, there are big things keeping it from being as enjoyable as the classics.
The main thing is that it is simply too easy and simple. Most medallions only take a few minutes at most to reach, and the paths and "puzzles" needed to reach them barely require much thought. Being easy is one thing, but the game is riddled with tons of hints on top of that. There's even an item you can buy that will show you where most stuff is hidden, making exploration almost pointless. Combat is non-existant(which isn't a necessity) and you will almost never die in the game. Even if you do happen to die, checkpoints are located right before "hard" areas so you're right back at the spot.
The older games had tons of other mechanics besides jumping around and gathering items, which is pretty much the only thing to do in Poi. It's not that collecting items is boring, but having them do something or have meaning is very important. Collecting coins lets you unlock challenge levels and buy explorer tools, but you can buy everything very quickly and coins become pointless afterwards. It would be nice to see more of what was in platformers of the past.
When I think about it, just a single level from a classic 3-D platformer, such as the Bob-omb Battlefield from Super Mario 64, had more depth and entertainment than the whole of what currently exists in Poi, and that is saying something. The first star that you go after requires you to climb a mountain and defeat a boss, all the while you are; exploring a battlefield that has a variety of enemies, cannons that shoot you into the sky, wing caps that let you fly, secret areas to find, rolling balls that need to be avoided on the climb up, and more. Yet in Poi, the first medallion just requires you to barely travel into the level and simply flip a switch, which causes platforms to move and you're already at the medallion.
Poi currently costs 15 dollars on Steam, and is likely to increase as it nears completion. This is a lot of money for the amount of content currently available in Poi, and if you're looking for a game with some kind of difficulty or depth, then it definitely isn't worth your money.
As there is very little story, there is no problem at all to get involved in the game while it is still being developed. It is very unlikely that your progress in the game will be reset, and if anything the time highscores on each level will be reset if big changes are ever made.
You should only consider buying Poi if you're looking for a simple platformer game and don't want much else.

When it came out, it received mixed reviews but my impression is that it was due to the high expectations. Nonetheless, Thief brand was of the most popular ten/fifteen years ago and somehow the trademark of stealth gameplay, before Agent 47 or Sam Fisher entered the stage.
However, this is a solid game. Tthe gameplay reminds the older version, but it is more linear (casual gamers will appreciate) and less challenging (basically you will ignore some piece of equipment in favour of others). You can improve some stats/gear/perks but I did not sense a huge difference during the walkthrough. Management of inventory is basically useless, while achievements (things to steal and collect) represent the true spirit of the title. The choice to switch to an open world map (even if divided into sectors) is appropriate and it could be better exploited. The main story plot is dull, characters motivation is somehow obscure as some line of dialogue result puzzling. In particular, some villains has potential (yeah, I am thinking about general Hunter) but they are too shallowly characterised. Honestly, I didn't care too much about them and I concentrated more on the loot. If the main story is dull, environments are beautifully crafted with a unique steampunk style. The most similar game one can imagine is Dishonored but Thief plays much better with lights and colours. Besides, in comparison to the Arkane Studios title, Thief is much more stealth-oriented. If you want to persevere to sort things out by combat, please forget this title. Even the rare boss fights are a matter of quickness and subtlety.

A minimalist game where you start off with a map with three stations: one circle, one square and one triangle. At each station you have people wanting to go to one of the other stations: some wanting to go to the circle, some to the square, and some to the triangle. You connect the stations by drawing a line between them and a train starts running back and forth along it. Problem solved... until another station randomly pops up on the map and you have to connect that as well.
As the game goes along more stations pop up and the number of different shapes of stations increase. To combat this you are given more train lines; more trains; more carriages and so on. You have to decide how best to connect all the randomly placed stations with the resources you are given, but eventually you'll get overwhelmed trying to get the right passengers to the right type of station and one of the stations gets too many passengers waiting at it and it's game over. It's all a question of how long you can last and how many passengers you can deliver.
It might be a nice little time waster for some people, but I think that the random placement of stations pretty much cancels out most differences between the different maps you're given to play on, and I don't see much fun in trying to connect a bunch of circle stations, that have all randomly appeared adjacent to each other, to the network when nobody at a circle station wants to go to another circle station.

I think it speaks a lot for the quality of 'Choice of the Deathless' when you consider that I bought it before it became available on steam when it was available for android devices. And here I am, having bought it
. Quite simply, Choice of the Deathless is one of the finest games from developer 'Choice of Games' and it's all thanks to the creative, imaginative world so beautifully crafted by Max Gladstone.
Now, I understand that the prospect of a text only, choose your own adventure game on Steam sounds mad, especially considering the current age of gaming, where titles are often harshly, and mostly unfairly, judged by how they look and how impressive their visuals are. I also understand that this game simply isn't for everyone. But I think this game is worth a shot.
Set in a universe where lawyers use magic known as craft to negotiate contracts, aid demonic clients and even fight for their life, the concept of Max Gladstone's world itself is very interesting, although you could claim it's nothing entirely new. With masterful worldbuilding, witty dialogue and exceptional imagery, the world of 'Choice of the Deathless' comes alive and lures you in. As your character is flung from choice to choice, you'll definitely find a few favorite characters along the way as they are all packed with personality and life.
And of course, while the game doesn't offer you much physical character customisation, the way the story is written pretty much allows you to simply just imagine your character in the story. That is the key to enjoying this game, imagination.
If I had any complaints, it would have to be that the game is largely linear. The main story path never deviates that much on repeat playthroughs with the exception of one or two minor details. But the choices you are given lead to a surprising amount of flexibility. By the end of each playthrough you'll have crafted a  mostly unique story each and every time.
So while the idea of a text only, choose your own adventure game being released on steam seems a bit mad, at the end of the day you'd be hardpressed to find a better example of the choose your own adventure genre out there and for an exceptionally low price, it really is hard to say no to 'Choice of the Deathless'.

Ah yes, yet another zombie game. The brainless corpses are being featured in more and more games, to the point where there isn't much freshness left. So... does this Death Road to Canada manage to bring a new spin on the walking dead? Surprisingly, yes.
The playstyle is nothing new and will be imediately fammiliar to every Oregon Trail (and Organ Trail) fan. You control a group of survivers on their way to Canada, where everything is better... well at least people aren't being eaten alive (and even if they are - free healthcare!) The story is not that complicated and very barebone. All you have to know is that the world is populated by zombies and that Canada is 15 driving days away.
You start out with two survivers, which you can freely customize. There is quite a lot of different options and everybody can make something to suit their needs. If you're feeling up to it, you can also try rare character mode, where most of the companions you encounter are replaced with people with all sort of special abilities. I'm 8 hours into the game and I'm still often running into new companions, so there is quite a decent variety there. Once you've selected the options you like, you can hit start and be off on your journey.
Every character has different attributes, which aren't visible imediately. Instead, you discover them over time by performing different tasks that require that perticular skill. Another thing you have to keep track of are supplies. You have to gather food, fuel, meds and three types of ammo. If you run out of any of the first two, you're basicly screwed since morale also plays a big part in the game.
There are two parts to the game. The first one is presented by different encounters, where you get to pick what you want to do in a specific situation. Attributes play a huge rule here, as they can be the difference between loosing half of your supplies and beating the bandits in a flexing competition. There are quite a lot of different random events and while you can evade sometimes prevent the negative outcome, this isn't always the case. This means you can sometimes loose a big hunk of supplies (expecialy if you run out of fuel) and even members of the group, which can get quite annoying. Sure, a bit of randomness is welcome, however to much of it can make you feel salty when everything goes to hell.
The second part of the game consists of exploring of areas, populated by zombies. These include different types of missions, such as sieges and scavenging missions, to name a few. They get harder and harder over time and the same holds for the number of zombies, which can sometimes reach over 100 corpses at a time. This means that sometimes it's better to avoid them instead of trying to kill them, since they just keep on coming. Fortunately, there is quite a lot of different weapons and this does help to keep things interesting.
From the graphics standpoint, the game looks decent but nothing special. The pixelated graphics do help it run smoothly even on older systems and integrated graphic cards, which is a big plus if your computer is a bit outdated.
Another thing I'd point out is the soundtrack. Some of the reviewers stated that they got annoyed by it after a couple of hours, but I'm still loving it - It just fits so well.
Conclusion:
Initialy, I've had a bit of a hard time deciding wheather I should recommend Death Road to Canada or not. Mostly because it isn't that cheap (you could argue 15$ is cheap) and there is a lot of randomness that can often screw you over. In the end however, I've decided to put my recommendation on it. I've had quite a lot of fun playing and every run I made seemed unique. While I still haven't managed to finish the game on normal mode, I've still had my share of fun. You know what they say - Sometimes the journey is more important than the destination.
Final Rating: 7.8/10

I love this game, but to clear the air as a disclaimer, I am COMPLETE FURRY TRASH so what I'm going to say will be probably preetty biased.
The fact of the matter though is that the game itself is pretty impressive, especially in terms of, specifically, furry visual novel projects. The english translation is decent, the story is good, and the characters are wholly likeable. The competition for best boy in this game is definitely real, and finding the path to all good endings is, for the most part satisfying.
My biggest gripe about the game is that the characters, especially the protagonist himself, follow specific tropes and stereotypes that define them. These traits are subverted or played upon a few times at most, but let's be real- it's a game about unreasonably attractive cat man spirits and that's why you're playing the game in the first place, right?
The most impressive factors to this game, to me, is the consistent, strong art style as well as the awesome character design. The three cats are designed each quite beautifully, balanced well with their personalities and stories, and the art for particular scenes is of notable quality (so yes, gay eye candy. Which you probably should be prepared for if you're playing this game). While this doesn't completely bleed over to the small cast of guest characters that appear, they're written well enough to fit the mold of the world, which in itself is cute and kind of fun.
As a follower of pretty much all things furry and creative, I'm happy to see a game tackle a furry dating sim with as much ambition and talent that I haven't seen from asian creators since the mid 2000's with the Morenatsu project, and I would definitely love to see and support more games like this in the future.

Poi I feel is a reminder of variety in platforming that has seemingly been lost sight of since the console days of the playstation and N64 days. There's a lot of heart in the game, and in it's current state it has some good moments to offer. While I feel certain area's are traversed, let alone finished far too quickly, there is a good sense of flow for each area to travel to. I do have a minor complaint with the feel of jumping, especially concerning interacting with other surfaces, as it feels so sudden and with so much weight, it almost goes against the light jump before it. Complaints aside, I would recommend Poi even in it's early access state. If the kid in you isn't dead just yet, you'll feel right at home with the familiar design elements from the back then days.

Poi is great revisiting of classic 3D platforming from the 90's era. The overall feel of the game is not unlike that of Super Mario 64 however this game controls significantly more smoothly. On the subject of Mario 64, the jumping mechanics come mostly from that game, but with the added double jump for an extra layer of precision added to your platforming. The worlds are all fun to explore, and, to add a little icing to this cake, the game rewards said exploration with its experience system used to progress the game. Your goal in the game is to become a master explorer by leveling up your character by exploring levels, finding collectables, and completing miniature challenge levels. The main collectable of the game being Explorer Medals, which there are six of per level and worth 100 EXP apiece. Getting these explorer medals is done by completing missions within the levels, but, on top of these, there are also hidden fossils that you can dig up for 50 EXP apiece, treasure chests with many coins hidden within little secret caves in the levels, and several points of interest to be found within each level that are worth 25 EXP for finding them. EXP is, of course, used to increase your explorer level, and, as your level increases, your mentor will allow you to enter more dangerous levels within the game. Unlike most platformers, your common coin collectable actually serves a purpose beyond collecting them for the sake of collecting them as they allow you to purchase explorer tools and can be spent to unlock miniature one-off challenge levels such as going down a huge slide where you need to collect seven keys or reach the explorer medal at the end of a series of falling platforms. As for problems I currently see, I hope future levels have more hazards within them. With the exception of the fourth level, Crystal Caverns, I didn't really find the main levels to be too threatening. On top of this, I feel as though the main character will ready a wall jump no matter what angle you jump towards a wall at which prompts some saves from falling that, really, should NOT have happened (Particularly when following up this wall jump with the aforementioned double jump). Another thing, while this isn't necessarily a complaint, is that I hope that the explorer tools can be more incorporated into the levels more. Among the three explorer tools currently within the game, I only found myself using the shovel with any form of frequency. Overall, this game shows a great deal of promise as a return to 3d platformers of old, and I looked forward to future versions of this game. As this early access version stands, I'd give it an 8/10
Pros:
Fun, explorable levels
EXP system promotes not just collecting the medals, but also finding secrets, and rewards exploration
Mini challenge levels are all enjoyable
Coins have a purpose beyond a collectable for the sake of a collectable
Controls like a dream for the most part
Cons:
Lack of difficulty
Tools could be more incorporated into the levels
Wall jump feels broken
This game is everything it promises to be. Well worth it.

Poi is a very fun platformer in the same vein as the late 90s/ early 2000s platformers. I expected the levels to be a lot shorter, but it's much more fleshed out than I thought. This game is hopefully the beginning of the 3D platforming renaissance I've been looking forward to for so long. You'll be retreading territory several times in each level to get all the collectables, but it's done in a tasteful way with mutliple paths through the levels. The collectables don't overstay their welcome, while still having a good amount to collect. If anything, I think the purchasble item prices need a buff. The "overworld" is also fun to explore, even if you don't spend all that much time there. Controlls are intuitive and some moves that aren't explicity explained come naturally. The graphics may not work for some peoples' tastes, but I like it. The music and sound effects are also very nice.
My biggest gripe is that only a couple medallions can be collected while being able to coninue in the level. Some medallions (the 100 coin one in particular) can be picked up with the option to continue, but others force you to the overworld. I understand that this is to facilitate barriers, but if I can see three medallions in my current area (100 coin, keys, and objective), I'd like to pick up all of them in one go.
Pros
+Level design
+Music
+Graphics
+Controlls (finally a game that's not super floaty!)
+Fun challenges beyond the core gameplay
+Reasonable camera - I don't find myself fighting it like in so many other games
Cons
-Multiple objectives in the same area can't all be collected at the same time
-Some people may not like retreading old ground, though I'm completely fine with this implementation
-Doesn't play nice with antivirus programs yet

This game promises us to take us back to the golden age of platformers, and it does, in a way. Remember when platforms like Mario 64 and Banjo-Kazooie became popular, and how every company tried to capture a piece of that market? Ty the Tasmanian Tiger and Vexx. Remember licensed platformers after popular TV shows?
Do you remember their clunky, floaty controls that glitched out and got stuck in the wall?
What about the camera that you could never get to point where you want, and clipped through the world half the time?
Or how their haphazard "cartoony" art style made it difficult to platform because the flat shading made it hard to perceive depth?
What about when they tried to turn on fancy realistic shadow, but then you couldn't tell where you would land, so they just made your character have both a realistic shadow, and a dot shadow under you?
How about when they just copied another game's levels directly, because they didn't have any ideas of their own? Except it somehow looks worse than the original, despite the near-15-year difference between them. No? Because none of those old games did that, and yet Poi did.
Poi brought me back to the golden age of platformers, by reminded me that these existed, and that they were not good games. And neither is Poi.

I wanted to leave a positive review as a huge fan of the original Thief games, because I'm seeing a lot of negativity that I don't think makes any sense.
I'd like to start off by addressing some of the main complaints people have, and give my opinion as to why I think they aren't valid.
Not sure why people have been complaining that Boss Fights exist in this game. The first Thief ended with a boss fight that had you sneak around and not interact with the Boss itself. As well as the 3rd game where you avoided the boss while walking around the city, again never really wanting to come into direct contact. I don't believe the 2nd game had one, but I might be remembering wrong.
This game handled boss fights (There are only 2 by the way) the exact same way. Less creatively, but still in character. For the first boss fight, you had the option to attack them in a sneaky way, or completely avoid them by just making your way out. The 2nd fight was handled the same way. Stealth, avoiding contact. I don't see why any fan of the original would bring this up, as the games all needed to have a climax. I'm just happy they were all stealth-related.
All Thief games had a tint of paranormal/sci-fi stuff that started coming into play the more you went through them. I won't argue that I feel this entry had the weakest version of those. The original 3 games got super exciting when all that started, where as this game had me scratching my head a little bit throughout. The story was ok, but not great, sometimes things didn't make too much sense. There's one guy who plays the role of a villain, and he manages to follow you everywhere throughout the game, with little explanation as to why and how. It feels like a bit of a forced antagonist.
Some complained that there are action scenes where you are detected and have to run away from enemies, Call of Duty-esque even if you remained undetected the entire mission. I only remember two or three throughout the game, and although I enjoyed them, I can see how they stray from the original stealthy feel of the game a little bit, but I wouldn't really let that put me off playing the game. They only last a few seconds, and although cliche, are really not that bad.
The gameplay itself is actually a lot of fun. I heard so many bad things about this game before going into it, and was fully expecting it to be nowhere near as good as the original Thief games, but I reserved my judgement until actually playing it. The gameplay was surprisingly faithful. There was a lot of darkness to hide in, and you had most of your original equipment, including stuff like water arrows to put out flames, and ropes arrows to attach to wooden beams. The game even introduced cheaper arrows that don't have pointy heads, so that you don't need to waste expensive broadhead arrows when interacting with the environment. Cool stuff! The shop system still existed, which gave you incentive to look through houses, drawers and seek out secret rooms to loot everything.
One thing I loved about the first 2 games was how useful moss arrows were. I felt like there were a lot of loud surfaces you had to traverse, and so they came in handy a lot of the times. This game and the previous one, although had the same mechanics for noise, didn't utilise it as much.
I actually thought the combat was an improvement over the previous 3 games. IF you happen to be detected, you only have your club to defend yourself with as opposed to a sword/knife in the previous games. I'm happy they got rid of it as it simplifies your inventory slightly by removing something that was pretty useless, seeing as this is a stealth series.
In the previous game, if you were detected, you would just mash the left mouse button, wildly swing your weapon and try to just move around while avoiding enemy attacks. It was messy and not fun. In this game, you have a dodge button to avoid attacks, and then click to attack back. It's more simplistic, but doesn't feel as messy. Still, most of the times you will be outnumbered, or enemies will have armour that just pressures you to run away, which is how it should be.
In this game, knocking out enemies while stealthy plays an animation that takes a few seconds, as you slowly lay their body on the ground to not make noise. In the old games, you clicked and they instantly fell to the ground. This is great, because in this game you are at more of a disadvantage if you try to knock everyone out. You aren't a fighter, but a thief. The most "canon" way for the franchise was to ghost your way through the game, leaving everyone untouched.
Just a quick mention that the sounds and music sound great and on par with the original games in my opinion. Nice to listen to with headphones.
I felt that you always had multiple ways to approach areas in the game, just like the original Thiefs.
Finally, the part that infuriated me. The worst thing about the entire game. The hub world and traveling back and forth within it. The third game in the series introduced The City. A Hub world that was alive, with civilians and guards, and you could explore and find some hidden loot. In order to go to the next mission, you had to walk to that area within the Hub world and then start it. I wasn't a fan, even in the third game. They brought it back here, and in my opinion the city itself is way more fun to traverse. It's bigger, more complex and allows you to run on rooftops easily, shoot ropes to climb, crawl through tunnels etc. The one awful flaw, was going from one section of the hub world to the next.
The City is divided into sections, and so if you want to go from Section A to B, you have to find for example, a little crawlspace between some boxes. Not too big of a deal. But some areas are only accessed through say, ONE small window ontop of a building. So everytime you want to go from Area B to C, you need to climb this building. Uhh... which one was it. That one? Open the window, Mash E to pry it open. Nope, wrong window, turn back around, Mash E again. Ok that's the right window, Open it up, go through a building, Open another Window, ah now you're finally in Area C. It's so bad, and really took me out of the experience every single time I wanted to continue through the game. I don't want to navigate a maze!
So to conclude, I think this game gets way too much hate. Again, I really loved the original Thief games, yet I still thoroughly enjoyed this. Apart from the minor Story complaints, and awful Hub world navigation, I think this game is a lot of fun. And I think that if you are a fan of the original Thief games, or a fan of Stealth games in general, definitely pick this up and give it a spin! It's a very long game if you take you time to explore and do side missions, the main missions give you options and are fun, and I think it's quite faithful to the series! Recommended

This is an excellent game. From what I've read, people hate this game for two reasons: Either they were expecting the game to be Dishonored or Metal Gear Solid, or they are nostalgic freaks that prefer the 1st and 2nd game.
I've never played Dishonored, but I've played MGS. This is not a tactical stealth action game; it's a stealth game with a focus on stealing from shadows. Your character can be quite unscrupulous and steals from everyone regardless of wealth. If you are looking for a more action oriented game, or one where you play a potential hero, look elsewhere.
However, what this game does, it does well. The gameplay is excellent and rewards being a thief. You are not capable in combat, so you must be as stealthy as possible, and the game gives you multiple ways to achieve your goal, telling you whether you prefer sneaking through like a ghost, taking advantage of the environment, or just knocking folks out.
The story is decent. You play the master thief Garret. You and a rival botched a job a year ago, and you have no memory of what happened in that year. You've gained the ability to focus, allowing you to easily find loot, equipment, alternate routes, and guards. You follow the clues solving the mystery of what happened and your role in the over-arching plot line.
Note that this game is linear. While there are some side missions in a hub-world, the game is not a sandbox. Also note that the game does not allow you to climb over everything like in assassin's creed. You have to work in the area you're given to play in.

Before I begin, Id like to preface this by saying that this is a first impression of Alpha gameplay, and subject to change.
I'm very excited for this game, and the potential it holds. Its a very pretty, pretty game: the lighting and colors are beautiful. The audio is on point, the music just loud enough to hear, but not loud enough to cover whats going on. I enjoy the design style, and i personally quite like the double jump and dodge maneuvers implemented in the gameplay.
I have two issues with the game.
Firstly, I expected more. The trailer had multiple maps, while the release on has one, and a small one at that. As well, I got turned around quite a bit, and I still have trouble locating one of the weapons consistently. The trailer also promised vehicles, of which there are none, and 9 weapons, of which I can count 5 or 6. I understand that this is an Alpha release, but Im just somewhat dissapointed.
My other issue is with one of the weapons, the Cerberus launcher. To me, it seems like it is too overpowered, or at least, overused. I personally prefer the Violator, especially its grenade launcher. While playing with bots, all of them use the Cerberus to the point of ridiculousness, and the actual servers provided me with too much lag to get a proper approximation of what they were like.
All of these issues can, and I hope will be, fixed by later patches of the game, and I am excited to see what the future holds for this game.
UPDATE:
I must say, after playing another match or two, my opinion of the game has vastly improved, on top of my already high opinion. My new favorite weapon, the Stingray, is immensly satisfying to kill with, especially with its secondary fire. I would also like to amend my previous statement about the Cerberus, as now that Ive figured out how to dodge, I can avoid the rockets for the most part and retaliate with the Stingray before they can get off a second shot.
Im a little dissapointed that this map doesnt allow us to use the Falcon very much, as its scoped zoom is almost useless in this close quarters map. As well, i would still have liked to see a couple more weapons, but perhaps on a larger map, as another weapon would make this one feel too cluttered.
While playing Squad mode, I quite enjoyed the little markers that would tell you where your teamates recently died, as it made it easier to find the nests of enemies the bots inevitably formed.
I still have some concerns.
Firstly, the fact that you cannot change settings or options while in game is incredibly frustrating, and lead to me having to quit matches to change my graphics settings far too many times. As well, the framrerate can tank, which is annoying to say the least.
Also, the lack of weapon names in the controls while changing keybindings frustrated me. Perhaps because of my years playing Quake, I expected to be able to see which weapon is which, so I could map them to keys accordingly, but sadly, this was not the case.
I shall update this review as my experience continues.

This game is the best "choices matter" game that I've ever played, but it's not just your choices that matter; sometimes you can't stop a midnight break-in, and the injuries that result.  Sometimes you need to choose whether to send that injured person for needed medical supplies.  Sometimes you will choose the easy pickings, and steal from those weaker than you, because you can't take from anyone else.
It will go from the happy days where you have all the wood you need to keep feeding the hungry wood burning stove in the middle of deep-freeze winter and good company in a comfy chair, to chopping up your only bed, just to make it through another night, and drinking your last trade bottle of antispetic alcohol in the misery that seizes one who has lost all hope.
Endgame tells you about those who have lived any given playthrough, both dead and alive, and how they fare after the war ends... or how they died and/or deserted you when things got so bad there was no recovery.
The DLC is worth it too; children add a lot to this game as you teach them... or ignore them because you're too busy trying to stay alive, and the War Child Charity Bundle adds tag art from the world over to existing structures ingame, where you can discover all of them in unique (and static) places (and there is an achievement for finding them all), along with a short history of who in real life created them, and where they live and do their art.
Sale price is a heck of a good bargain if you're on the fence, because the list price is worth the money for the time and content available; my 130+ hours ingame have all been spent playing different scenarios/characters, and I haven't yet completed every scenario - the one where you start with just one man is really challenging.
The community of players here have been helpful both in the forums and in terms of guides, and the devs have added a suite of tools that allows creative types to add items to the game and create our own scenarios, including custom characters.
The trailers/screencaps in the review make it look like a side-scroller game, which isn't exactly correct (it's not Metroid-vania) but also isn't incorrect (all locations are in fact larger than your screen) because the locations are largely static, excepting that game events and timing can cause certain resource depletions and some NPCs can come and go.  I'd advise finding a youtube video to see more about this characteristic if you just can't spend the $4, but there's more than enough content here to give you 20+ hours enjoyment, even if you don't like repeating scenarios.
One caution: there is no save game that doesn't "foul" you somehow.  If you leave the game at the start of a new day, your forager will come home and there will be a new random event for the night (or not), and if you leave the game during a run at night, you'll return to have to replay the preceeding day.  This aspect is one of the best implementations of "choices matter" that I have thus far seen in any game.
I have NEVER experienced a bug of any sort either during loading or play.
This is an excellent game - and I should have reviewed it much, much sooner.

A minimalist game where you start off with a map with three stations: one circle, one square and one triangle. At each station you have people wanting to go to one of the other stations: some wanting to go to the circle, some to the square, and some to the triangle. You connect the stations by drawing a line between them and a train starts running back and forth along it. Problem solved... until another station randomly pops up on the map and you have to connect that as well.
As the game goes along more stations pop up and the number of different shapes of stations increase. To combat this you are given more train lines; more trains; more carriages and so on. You have to decide how best to connect all the randomly placed stations with the resources you are given, but eventually you'll get overwhelmed trying to get the right passengers to the right type of station and one of the stations gets too many passengers waiting at it and it's game over. It's all a question of how long you can last and how many passengers you can deliver.
It might be a nice little time waster for some people, but I think that the random placement of stations pretty much cancels out most differences between the different maps you're given to play on, and I don't see much fun in trying to connect a bunch of circle stations, that have all randomly appeared adjacent to each other, to the network when nobody at a circle station wants to go to another circle station.

Death Road to Canada is a phenomenal mix of all the zombie games you have played before with Oregon Trail which makes for the most fun zombie apocalypse game in years if ever. This game strips down all of the slower moving aspects of zombie survival into a concise and streamlined re-playable experience.
The player controls randomly generated or self-generated characters on a romp from Florida to Canada in hopes to find safe haven. Along the way, resources must be scavenged, zombies must be crushed, allies need to be rescued or recruited, and hope to god the car doesn’t break down along the way.
Strengths:
•	The gameplay is just pure fun. Fast and Frantic with a bit of strategic maneuvering required when things get really hairy.
•	The RPG elements bring personality to each of the characters, and each specialization feels powerful enough to warrant a diverse group of zombie survivors. Just be sure to keep everyone as happy as possible or they might leave at the worst possible moment!
•	The random events are both funny and enjoyable, with a bit of rage inducing as well to keep things nice and balanced towards a harder difficulty.
•	Local co-op makes for a great addition, but what is even better, playing alone is just as fun. The AI allies are not just mindless drones, they will loot, replace their weapons and crack zombie skulls with precision.
•	The production values are extremely high, visuals are top notch, music is fantastic, and the UX is streamlined and easy to navigate and use. The game also tends to throw useful events your way if you happen to be SOL in a particular resource.
Weaknesses:
•	The lack of an online or four player option makes me a sad panda.
•	The pendulum of “Doing Well” to “Dead Meat” can swing extremely quickly. One moment you are doing fine, and the next day you are left with nothing because the car broke down.
Overall Death Road to Canada is the survival game I didn’t even know I needed in my life. Sometimes after playing hundreds of hours in Project Zomboid or State of Decay, it is nice to just have a bit of fun smashing zombies, collecting loots, and driving towards the Maple Leaf State. I see myself playing this game for months in hopes to unlock all of the different modes and characters, easily the best fifteen dollars spent in a long while.
