I recommend playing this game through the several solo campaigns. I found them to be interesting challenges playing a variety of decks, and it's free. The decks are essentially powerful casual decks: not competitive, but there are fun interactions. The games were relatively well balanced, and playing well was rewarding as I came back to win 2 or 3 games where I was on the brink of losing. However, don't bother playing the skill quests unless you actually don't know the rules. The reason is that you'll probably play them for the free gold, and gold is not useful. The reason gold is not useful is that the game goes sharply downhill after playing through the solo campaigns. What would you want to do next? Build a deck, right? Well, you're not really going to be able to do that. You'll have about 20 6-card packs, and a bunch of weak commons and uncommons. You're not going to have the card advantage engines that power a deck. You're not going to have enough cards that work together to build an efficient deck. The deck you build is not going to reward play skill much, and is mostly going to revolve around playing your least overcosted creatures on curve.
This might be tolerable, but the deck-building and collection exploring systems are really frustrating. Are you used to Gatherer searches, or the relatively mediocre collection manager in Hearthstone? Well those are both amazing by comparison. You can't do a card text search. They've decided what you can search for (color, creature type, specific keywords, stuff like that). Those filters can only be applied when building a deck. But you can only look at the cards that you don't own (say, to decide what kind of deck you might want to build, or which expansion to buy packs from) outside of the deck-builder. So you can't apply filters (beyond color and expansion) to the cards you don't own. You can't search for a specific card. I got excited about building my first deck, and kept trying to build one and getting repeatedly frustrated, ending up building a couple generic decks that didn't do much. I suggest skipping this part and hoping that MTG Arena is good.

Having come from a strongly Nintendo based console history I recently found myself desperately wishing for more 3D platforming games. Thankfully there has been a resurgence in that genre among indie developers. I had been somewhat patiently following the development of games like Clive and Wrench, Freeze Me, A Hat In Time and others but none of them had a release date. I searched the Steam Store for 3D platformer, but couldn't find what I was looking for. Then I decided to search YouTube for Steam 3D Platformers and Poi was one of the first entries. I noticed that I missed the Kickstarter and that it hadn't reached it's funding and I was worried that meant I would never get to play it and it looked gorgeous. I decided to try my luck searching for it on Steam and found that it was available in Early Access. I bought it immediately.
I've been burned by games before so I was cautiously optimistic as I was loading it up, but thankfully this game was everything I was hoping for. Not only is art style gorgeous, clean and bright, but the characters I've met in the games seem like they would be right at home in the best first party Nintendo games. Their animations and way of speaking appear to be heavily influenced by Zelda.
There doesn't seem to be any enemies in the game (this is no longer the case), and yet I don't miss them. This game is a 3D platformer in its purest form. All of the thrill and the challenge comes from traversing the detailed environments which have several paths just like Super Mario 64. In fact, one of the first things I thought when I began to play the game was "I have been waiting for a game like this since Mario 64." As much as I love the Mario Galaxy games and the 3D Land/World games, none of them managed to recapture the feeling that I got when playing Mario 64. Poi has managed to recreate that feeling almost perfectly.
I haven't completed the game, and it's early access so for all I know there is no end yet (I don't really know how early access works as this is the first time I've bought a game in early access) but I have faith that they will deliver one of the best 3D platforming experiences since the glory days of the N64.

THEY BLEED PIXELS - Subset Pixel Art/Platformer/Horror
Final Review: RECOMMENDED Rating 8/10
Overview: "They Bleed Pixels" is a pixel-art homage to classic horror in the form of a meticulously executed platformer. It features fast-paced skill-oriented combat and movement, beautiful pixel style cutscenes and in-game graphics, and an intriguingly dark storyline.
PROS:
-Combat feels fluid, well-paced and simple, yet complex enough to keep things interesting
-Graphics are carefully and thoughtfully designed. Beautiful scenery coupled with excellent level design makes for a great combination
-This game is difficult, and thats a good thing. It is horror themed after all
-The soundtrack is uniquely dark and upbeat. Balances well with the gameplay
-The storyline is a step above general "save-the-princess" platformers, so thats a plus
-Ingenious check-point system that puts control in the hands of the player and allows for awesome speedrun opportunities
-Well-crafted characters/enemies that stand out
-Good variety and complexity in puzzles and challenges
CONS:
-Personal gripe: Menus felt a bit cluttered and unweildy, but maybe thats just me
-Difficulty fits well in both categories I believe, some may find it off-putting
-Enemy variety can become a bit tiresome by the end
Overall "They Bleed Pixels" offers a uniquely addictive horror/platformer experience in a delightfully dark package complete with stunning visuals and a remarkably fresh style of gameplay. While there are areas to be polished (as with any game) and the difficulty of the gameplay may be too much for some, those who stick through to the end are guaranteed a rewarding experience.
Classic rage inducing side scroll platformer with combat smoothly integrated. You will die a lot but it remains enjoyable the entire time.
Challenging, yet very rewarding once you complete a level, if you are a fan of punishing old style games I would say pick this up. Very cheap and fun.

And you may be asking yourself how one game can have so much super in it. Well, the single button combat system is very reminiscent of 'Super Smash Bros' even though it's nowhere near as complex, while the level design and character controls seem to have been taken directly from 'Super Meat Boy'. And while we're talking about it, if you thought that 'Super Meat Boy' was a difficult game, then look out for this one because it's much, much, much harder. Now if that isn't the recipe for a fantastic game then I have no idea what is and quite frankly, I don't want to know.

To start: it's not a game, but an interactive ~1.5h experience about one's first online love.
And I liked it. I rarely see such natural stories, exposing insecurities, flaws or embarassing parts (but without extra exaggeration or dramatization). With that respect notes, dialogs, voice acting cutscenes were wonderful!
Sure some technical parts were suboptimal (e.g. moving in the MORPG part, and sometimes - closing windows), and it's bad why these simple UI shortcoming were not addressed. Still, they were not a deal-breaker.
(Disclaimer: I got it with Humble Narrative Bundle; for the full price of 9EUR it would be a too much for such a short thing.)

Kinda boring.  There are a lot of hints scattered around the game to give background about who the main character (Nina) is.  A lot of photos, poetry, blog posts, etc.  This was kind of interesting.  It felt like either cyber-stalking or detective work depending on how you look at it.
The main feature of Cibele is the story, which takes place in the form of chat messages, emails and phone calls with other "characters" while Nina plays an online Multiplayer game.  While messages / emails are flowing in and Ichi (Nina's romantic interst) talks on the phone with her, you play Nina's character in the game.  The game Nina plays (with you as her surrogate) is unfortunately really boring.
There are 3 boss fights.  To summon the boss, you have to attack little enemies together with Ichi.  All the while, you're reading messages and emails.  The actual boss fight is just waiting for your character to finish attacking until the boss runs away and you have to summon him again.
I'm pretty sure if you don't read the messages and emails, the game doesn't progress.  So the actual fighting is secondary to the social aspect of the game.
Overall, t's an interesting concept.  Definitely not a traditional game, and more of a movie with some interaction.  The things you do don't really matter, your character never dies, and you have no influence over how the story unfolds.  The story was kind of predictable, a couple of misfits in a virtual relationship, but it's the overall experience that i found interesting.  Reading the clues about Nina's personality in her poetry, chat logs, photos, her trail of online fingerprints.  I wouldn't recommend this to most people.

Things that are the problem with this game:
While the main character's relationship develops in the game, the characters never do. Granted, it's not like a long period of time has passed between every act, but it leaves me feeling unsatified because at the resolution, there's literally nothing left otherwise. Every character is boring and forgettable and some of them are completely dropped out of the story without any conclusions. The cutscenes are rushjobs with poor editing, missing sound effects and they begin and end abruptly. The climax appears to begin at the 4th chapter and it builds up to absolutely nothing. The ending is a laughable letdown that leaves tons of loose ends.
-

Once you've earned enough money to buy all the tools, you really don't need much anything besides a few rope, water and blunt arrows. So when you are not using the money on much anything, you don't end up caring for thieving either.
-
are plentiful but this game does absolutely nothing with them. Even the special arrows don't really function the same, except for water arrows. Rope arrows are completely contextual and serve to demonstrate just how linear these missions are. In truth, there's no reason for this to be a ''Thief'' game.
-
is entertaining enough for the first 2-3 hours, but most of the thieving comes from breaking into poor people's homes that consist of one or two rooms and are never inhabited by anyone. You steal one or two items of value from them before moving onto the next empty home. Apparently there are hundreds of valuables just lying around in this supposedly very poor and dying city. So you are guaranteed to get bored by the core purpose of this game.
-
is not a realistic approach despite the game's claims. Damage tools are too expensive and too difficult to obtain to maintain any sort of predatorial approach. You are much better off with stealthing through the game, the way this game is clearly intended to be played.

in this game are a botched, buggy mess. Review Version 0.98 GINGER BUILD
Should just re-name this to "Unreal Tournament 3.5"
If you have played Unreal Tournament in your life and you enjoyed it, then you will feel right at home, as it is basically the same thing, which is OK! After hearing about a new Combat Arena FPS coming into the works, I was really looking forward to it. Normally, I would never look into Early Access games, but for once in my life, I was actually EXITED to back this up... Hell I bought the $90 Godlike Package >_>
So lets start with the PROS:
This game plays and feels exactly how a combat arena shooter should. You have your quick side jumps, double jump, elevator jumps, rocket jumps, various weapons to pick up in combat, health pick ups, armor pick ups, power ups like Mega Health/Shield, Quad Damage, Jetpack (or Jump boots), and so on and so on. In addition to this, you have a temporary cloak ability that lasts a whole 3 seconds, but it's great to use when walking around corners that you are unsure about. And yes, Mutators are back baby!
The assortment of levels is also great. Some being brand spanking new, and some being re-vamped of classic maps, such as the good ol Deck 13 from UT making a triumphant return, or CUBE (AKA Level 7 from DOOM 2.) The addition of Steam Workshop mod support and built in map editor is also great to have, as this resulted in modders making even more classic or new maps. Having played all of them, they are ALL fun to play! ... Well expect for ONE.
The gamemodes are your standard modes, Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch, Domination, Capture the Flag, plus vehicle versions of such. I should not have to explain what those gamemodes are.
Weapon selection is as follows:
And now for the CONS.
My BIGGEST complaint about the game is the one map, EHRGEIZ. This is by far the WORST map I've ever played in any video game. Not only is it a small cell capture map with some vehicles, but combine basically no health/armor pickups at all and no cover to hide behind, the AI will spawn camp you hardcore to where it's aggravating to compete it. Most maps you can deal with the cheat/aim bot style AI but this one you simply can't. This being a "Contract" mission you will want to rip your hair out.
The AI is nice and can prove to be a good challenge... But they are VERY cheaty/aim bot at times. A good example is going onto huge maps, such as the mountain one. You can be standing on one side at the very top looking around, then the AI could be on the very bottom on the other side of the map, and be shooting AND HITTING you with the pistol. Even if you took a sniper rifle and zoom in you can just make out the bot as a tiny dot. Just like I said in the worst map ever, when the AI gets into the mech. You can spawn (behind cover,) go up the elevator to your powercell, and you would die instantly cause he would start shooting you through the one open side, while he was still sitting at his spawn, like he was following you after you spawned in.
A minor complaint, the weapons do not have a "combo" as UT did with some of their weapons, ex. The Shock Rifle from UT, or the alt fires for the rocket launcher.
Pros:
- Great graphics/gameplay/sound/music.
- Maps are a blast to play.
- Weapons feel good.
- Vehicles are fun.
- Good amount of customizations.
- MOD SUPPORT
- Achievements
Cons:
- Currently very few people playing online. (EARLY ACCESS problem I would assume.)
- Has one of the Worst f***ing maps ever, EHRGEIZ
- AI can be cheaty/aim bots.
- No Steam Cards. (As of yet)
Playing TOXIKK makes me feel like I'm playing UT... Which is why I brought up the joke about changing the name to UT 3.5, it's the next UT game!
Keep in mind that I am no professional reviewer, professional game critic, or Pro FPS player, I'm just a guy that loves to play video games.

To be completely honest, I didn't have really high expectations for a game called "Death Road to Canada." But I really love this. Zombie games have always been my forte and I love pixel graphics so this is great. It's got the classic decision-making sort of thing for survival games – you know, the whole point-and-click thing, "Should we try to help that guy or let him die?" sorta thing – and you also have to run around hordes of zombies to grab resources that you'd die without. And let it be known that this is actually quite a difficult game. I've been playing this for a decent amount of time and I have still not beaten it (I got so close to beating it then died when there was one day of driving left. ONE DAY!!!). It's also got a lot of really funny references in it. There's a rare character called "DSYP" which is a pretty funny reference to the game, "Don't♥♥♥♥♥♥Your Pants," there's a super "kawaii-desu-desu" anime character that shoots magical star beams from her wand, honestly just great. Some of the stuff the characters will say and do are also pretty funny. I also bursted out laughing when I realized that I could play as a dog when all the other characters in my group died and the dog was able to operate and drive a car and could also walk around on its hind legs and hold weapons. My one and only complaint about this game is that the soundtrack gets annoying after a while but that's really not a big deal considering you can just turn off the music.
TLDR; Really funny, enjoyable gameplay, you can actually play it multiplayer which is really neat, easy controls & appealing graphics. Highly recommend this game.

What a great little game.
You play against 3 AI oil tycoons. The aim is to make money and eventually become the Mayor of the town. The game is split into two phases.
The town phase sees you purchase and upgrade your equipment, sell diamonds, gain advantages by talking with saloon patrons, buy shares and select the next parcel of land to drill on.
The mining phase has you explore your land and drill for oil, gas and rare diamonds. You can do this in several different ways. Using humans, animal, electronics or even pot luck. As you collect oil you either need to store it or sell to one of two companies. This phase lasts between 3-12 months (usually 12) and you must sell your oil before the end of the phase.  Each block of land is random so finding the oil is different each time.
There are quite a few different upgrades that cater to whatever play style you choose.
Well worth it.

You see, this conundrum begun on a bright sunny sunday afternoon. I was Netflix n chillin', catching up on my favourite anime, Bojack Horseman, while browsing the interwebz. Could not have gone any better. While scrolling Reddit, out of the corner of my eye, I saw something. I see some familiar words. I quickly scrolled up and lo and behold, I see a post about this game being greenlit. Suddenly, I had a fuzzy feeling inside, and deep down I knew that, I can see something in this game, but I don't what it is. Was it potential? Possibly. I waited patiently, like a loyal doggo, checking if there's any dev update on Twitter, this Steam page, trying not to forget this game, and it's release date. In the end, my enthusiasm died out, and the wait has taken it's toll on me.
Some months pass, and it's already November 2017, time flies, I told myself. Things were quite good, but I had not much personal time. As a result, I had forgotten about my life online. But today, today is the day that changed everything. I was just checking Reddit, and I notice a familiar name.
And it has just been released on Steam. Then it all comes rushing back to me.
I get that same fuzzy feeling from last time, but it's greater. My inner-furry has been awoken. I rush to my computer, navigating swiftly pass open Word documents, PDF files, Firefox windows, handy text files filled with copypasta, Discord and finally reached my destination; the Steam app. My fingers raced across the keyboard, typing the game's name, and Steam, as always, knows me well enough to suggest it in the quick search results. Clicked it, hit 'Play' and waited some more for it to download. It's as if I haven't waited long enough.
After the painstaking waiting, I saw the game's icon on my desktop. It seemed as though it was gleeming, standing out from the monotonous-looking desktop. I thought to myself for a while before playing the game, was it worth waiting this long for a simple game like this? I had conflicting thoughts, and started the game, not expecting much, maybe even begining to regret my decision to dedicate this much time thinking about it. But as soon I saw the charcters in their full personality(or shall I say, fursonality) I was blown away by how cute they were. 5 seconds later, I found out that, yep, it's the furry effect that's going on, making me embrace it. I play some more, adore the characters even more, take a look at the time, and decide to say bye to my husbandos for now.
Proceeded to have some emotional & existential thoughts about how I will never meet anthro kitters or anthro anything in my life. Accepted this world is cruel and decided to find a way to express my feelings. I studied online on how to meditate. I meditated, imagining what a world with anthro creatures will be like. I researched on lucid dreaming, in an attempt to get closer to my husbandos. Feeling spiritually enlightened, I decided to write a review about this wonderful game, which was probably the easiest method to begin with. But with my last strengh of power, I typed away for ages to create a perfect review, which goes like this:
TL;DR:  found this game greenlit, forgot about it, months later, found this game, played it, loved it, got emotional, threw me into a state of depression and distress, seeked spritual enlightment, expressed feelings 10/10 would recommend this game.

Can't you see the signs that he's bad for you?!" but of course, you can't stop what's going to happen. You might think Mini Metro is a quaint artsy puzzle game, but that's wrong... it's more of a simulation roguelike. You need to make sure passengers are delivered to their stations in time, and while this task starts out simple it quickly gets trickier as you're forced to make tough decisions over how to spend your limited resources by the minute.
Gameplay progress is measured in 'weeks', and every completed week presents you with a choice of new resources such as trains with different capacity or new bridges to draw lines across water. Even though each resource can be used in multiple ways, you need to plan ahead in order to have the best possible wiggle room whenever something unexpected happens.
Even though the game has a very limited set of actions, every decision you make has a drawback of some sort, and balancing risks vs rewards must be done constantly. Making a line loop around evens out the waiting times for passengers, but makes extending it awkward or sometimes even impossible. Making a line cover every station means the train can soak up passengers easily, but the time spent letting passengers embark and disembark slows down its overall speed, and if a train gets full in just a few stations' worth of passengers the waiting times further down the line will just explode.
Mini Metro is full of knife-point decisions like that while still managing to be incredibly relaxing, and it's definitely worth a shot no matter what your taste in games is.

Poi is a 3D platformer similar to Super Mario 64 with a beautiful world and solid gameplay.
The game currently only has 2 main levels, but they're very promising!
Similarly to Mario 64, they're all filled with different types of collectibles, the medallions being the main type. To get medallions, you need to complete different types of objectives like obstacle platforming, or exploration.
By grabbing medallions, digging up fossils, or finding secret locations you gain xp and level up your character in order to gain access to the next level.
The gameplay borrows a lot of abilities from many old platformers such as double jump, timing your jump as soon as you land will give you a higher second jump, you can wall jump etc.
The controls feel very tight, which is very important for a game like this. Whenever you die, it's your fault.
There are a few "challenge" levels that you can play in addition to the main levels. Things like obstacle courses and timed challenges, they're actually very fun.
My main issue with the game was that after collecting a medallion, you're taken back to the hub world, and thus lose your progress on any other collectibles you had been collecting in the levels. I'd love the option to teleport to the hub or stay and continue clearing out the level if I'd like to.
Overall, it's a great game! I love the charming art style, great music and fun game mechanics. Recommended!

A promising start to a 3d platformer in the vein of Super Mario 64 and Banjo-Kazooie.  Right now there are two fairly simple worlds, but the foundation is there for a solid game.  You can choose to play as a boy or a girl, and after a short tutorial level you take a ship into the sky.
The sky hub world reminiscent of Zelda: Skyward Sword with various floating islands.  World selection is done by rotating the ships wheel, which takes you to a select screen like Mario 64, though like Mario 64 you can find the medals out of order.  Medals are their version of stars, keys are their version of red coins, and there is a medal for collecting 100 coins in a world.  The only downside is, like Mario 64, the game pops you out of a world each time you collect a medal.  There are no changes between "acts" like the 3D Mario games, so there isn't a compelling reason for this.  Collectibles and objectives for medals reset, so if you prefer to explore at your leisure rather than following the objective the game sets for you, you may find yourself partway through earning multiple medals as you're exploring only to have to choose one and restart the others.  I would prefer it to be more like Banjo-Kazooie and leave you in the world to keep exploring.
You can also spend time exploring to fill up the journal with locations and fossils. Doing these things gets you experience to level up, which is the way this game opens up new worlds.  In the hub world you can use coins to purchase special abilities.  There are is also a cannon in the hub world that can take you to special linear challenge stages sort of like Super Mario Sunshine.
The moves are familiar, from triple jumps to wall jumps to double jumps.  It's not quite as tight as a Mario game, but it controls well.
I recommend this game to anyone yearning for a return to the N64 platformers of old.  With time and more content, it promises to be something special.

What I liked:
-Atmosphere. Thief is a dark game by definition. The general design combines victorian age architecture and technology with a steampunk theme. The result is a very believable setting with lots of emphasis on social disparity in terms of wealth and social status. However, you as Master Thief, will make no distinctions.
-Level Design. In this game it is very, very good. Again, nice style and atmosphere, great verticality, themes and variations. The choices in design from place to place, really give an emphasis on the misery brought by poverty and sickness. The City is suffering and the design reflects that.
-Sound effects. The sounds themselves, including voice acting are good. They trully complete the experience.
-Weapons, equipment and upgrades. They are all useful, some more, some less depending on the playstyle. The availability and cost, solely depends on the difficulty setting.
-Gameplay. The stealth mechanics are good and the game itselft is not too hard. It allows for different playstyles: You can go full stealth warrior-assasin (predator), completely stealth with no violence (ghost) or adopt a more aggressive but not murderous playstyle (opportunist). Depending on how you play, the game detects that and awards you accordingly at the end of each level. Nice idea which increases replayability.
What I didn't like:
-Although not a crippling issue, sound bugs. They can ruin the immersion and are somewhat frequent. However, they seem to be less present on the last version while using the Mantle API, now defunct but still usable on AMD cards.
-The story. While the basis is not bad, it's not something special either. The problem arises due to the fact that it was rushed and thus, cut/pasted accordingly to probably meet the deadline for release? It is not very coherent and many explanations are missing. Also, due to this, it lacks depth. This is probably the main reason for which the game loses so much review score.
-Length. Although very replayable and long if you go for a full run, in my opinion it lacks a couple of chapters and some side quests, I would say 10. The two more chapters would have been great to accomodate a better stroryline with more stuff being explained directly. The extra sidequests would have been great to get you richer sooner and eventually, give you more info about the main quest or overall situation.
-DLCs. Completely lackluster. I later bought the bank heist DLC. It was obviously cut from the main game on purpose. It wouldn't have saved the game's review score even if they had included it in the main game since it's a sidequest. Thing is, that I only paid for the DLC, which frankly I don't mind since I got the game for free, it's like if I had paid the game 5 euros, but this kind of crap shouldn't be done by devs. I would have been ok if say it was a pack of 5 sidequests, maybe interconnected by a secondary stroyline, but this is too little no matter the cost. The booster packs are laughable and I'm not gonna say anything more about them.
Conclusion:
I hate the fact that I actually loved the game and due to the way it was developed and thus rated, I'm not gonna see another one anytime soon. The overall experience has been good for me, but I find it hard to justify a full retail price at release for a game developed like this. If you like stealth games AND dislike violent solutions, basically if you like roleplaying the thief with morals, this is the game for you. It enables you to play like that, like a ghost.
I hope that one day, the devs will work on another sequel, but next time, they've got to pick the storyline since the beginning, do it right and improve on the storytelling, sound engineering and overall length of the main quest and amount of gameplay. Also, they must either make good, content rich DLCs or none at all. Half-arsed solutions are trully bad and give this low quality feeling to a franchise that doesn't deserve it.

Reakktor dead on deliver what they promissed. "Frag like it's 1999."

Movement feels just like the classics (UT, Q3A). Some tweaking to the mouse settings and veterans feel at home within a handful of botmatches.

First off, I've been playing this longer then it may appear. Played quite a bit over a friends house.
The Good: The premise, characters, and setting are quirky (in a good way) and interesting.
The Bad: Almost everything else is underwhelming.
Some have compared this to the Oregon Trail. That comparison does not work in this game's favor because it has fewer features than an educational game that didn't have a lot of features in the first place. In Oregon Trail you can set your pace. In Death Road to Canada your pace is dependent on what car you have and what car you have is dependent on RNG. In Oregon Trail you can make major decisions on what path to take. In Death Road to Canada your decisions are limited to “Do you go to the bar or go to the old safe house”. In Oregon Trail you can set your rations, choose where you want to rest, and make a profit off trading. In Death Road to Canada you can't set anything like that, where you can rest is dependent on RNG, and most of the trading is worthless because obtaining items to even begin to have something to trade is RNG and there are few if any ways to profit off of trading.
Most if not all of your characters stats will be hidden until revealed. Revealing them requires making the character perform a certain action. If their stat is bad they will fail wasting your time and possibility costing you something,
Much of the game is spent scavenging or fighting zombies. The problem is combat is both bare bones and tedious. You will be using melee weapons most of the time because they are the easiest to find. Aside from weapons like the chainsaw they lack any interesting differences other than things like “X does slightly more damage than Y”. Guns (if you find them or enough ammo to make them useful) suffer from the same affliction.
Melee combat consist of swinging, waiting to recovering and doing the same thing again. Swing too much and your character will momentary get tired indicated by them sweating. Combine this with uninteresting weapons, uninteresting environments, and one note foes and the tedium really starts to set in especially during sieges.
At times (especially near the end of the game) you will be required to face sieges. During such sieges you are trapped in a building with zombies coming through the floor/ceiling and you are required to hold them off until they stop spawning. After that you have to exit through a small doorway which will usually be blocked by a good amount of zombies until you can clear enough to run past them.
Some may find this game difficult. My recommendation is to find a better game with a more interesting combat system or features in general. This game is not worth gitting gud at. The concept is good but the execution leaves much to be desired.

Its almost Magic, so it has most of the good parts of magic excepting of course the parts they got totally wrong. The way the game stacks the cards is just a joke, making it impossible to know what you or the opponent has in there confused blob of cards. Land stacking is bad, creature stacking is just unplayably bad. When assigning blockers the game also falls down, giving you a line of overlapping cards with almost no way to work out what is what. Not only that, but if you somehow do manage to assign the right things to block but run out of time, the game assigns no blockers. None, reguardless of how many you set beforehand.
PS, no card trading.
Magic is fun, this is a joke. Do not spend money on this game.

Teaches magic very well, but that's about all its got going. I've heard bad things about the multiplayer stuff, but I don't care about that. I'm more invested in the campaign.
While typically competent, sometimes the campaign decks are either very poorly put together (five colors with no unifying theme and a total of 10 basic lands) and sometimes they're specifically set up to doom you (a deck with no fliers or reach cards vs a full-flying deck). The gimmicky challenges range from confusing (A mill-contest against a deck that has no win condition) to just stupid (a marathon game with no healing at the checkpoints). There's been a few times where the only way I've won is by abusing an AI flaw. And with no way to customize the campaign decks or view them ahead of time, some campaign missions are quite simply a matter of trying again and again until you get lucky.
Overall, for MTG basic learning and simple matches to get used to the game, this is a solid program, just don't spend ANY money on it.
For actually playing a Magic The Gathering plotline? Even ignoring the poor storytelling (which, it IS very poor) this is not a satisfying campaign experience.

You get 10 points for killing enemy players or killing baby creatures. 20 points for killing adult creatures and i also believe collecting orbs aswell from the creatures. Each team gets to summon baby creatures around the map that have different abilities (healing, revealing enemy players, building gates) and you get to upgrade them to adults that have higher health and power. Overall I enjoyed this game and at less than 5$ I'd say it was worth the money. It's a relaxing game where you drill for oil and compete against three AI characters.
However there are some cons you start noticing later in the game.
- You buy upgrades but most of them still require you to purchase the upgrade during each 'level' while drilling for oil. Everything is so expensive it's basically not worth it in the actual levels themselves unless you come across a very large store of oil and need to drill through rock or increase the pipe flow. I would much prefer that those upgrades are permanent additions like with the Dowsers. It would increase replayability since you could choose different upgrade paths along the way.
- More to the point above the NPCs don't seem to buy any upgrades so despite them sometimes making 5k or under in profit per level they always have stacks of cash to blow at the share auction. I'm currently halfway through the last zone and I've seen an NPC purchase one upgrade which was the drill. Maybe they do purchase upgrades, and I've just been missing it. They just always end up having way more cash despite making way less profit consistently.
- Not enough micro-management - when the price of oil increases at Left or Right you want to sell as much of your oil as quickly as possible yet selling carts will go empty an oil rig and go to sell with a nearly empty cart instead of filling it from a silo, or emptying a rig and then filling at a silo. It gets frustrating at the end of every year when you have so many carts going to sell barely any oil and you end up with an entire upgraded silo of unsold oil.

Overall, at <$5.00 it's a good game.  However the developers could improve it by:
+having multiple save games.  Currently there are no saves other than the autosave back at town
+The stock market seems like a tacked on victory condition.  It's an incredibly annoying system.
+penalties for spillage are far too severe.  At the very least there should be options for reducing the penalty, it's not enough that you're already losing oil to the ground that you need to be losing thousands in profit?  This was set in the 19th century, there was no greenpeace-  who's fining me $8000 for a bit of spill!?!
+Allowing mod support (even if it's just an ini file to change variables such as SPILL penalties).
Those issues aside, and considering the price, it's worth a few bucks.

Turmoil is a game about investing and maximizing profit. You dig for oil, you purchase wagons to carry the oil to the store, you buy storage silos so that you can sell the oil when the price is up. All this happens in individual levels, with upgrades that carry between levels. Some levels you make it bug, and some you realize your investments were overly optimistic.
It's a single player game, but it's honestly a blast to play with a friend. You pick a number for your seed (867-5309, for example), make sure your level settings are identical, start at the same time, and then attempt to maximize your profit.
I once read a complaint that this game was not as good as "Super Motherload". So, I bought Super Motherload, and the two games aren't directly comparable, but if I had to own one or the other, I'd choose Turmoil.

Swim Out is a casual swimming themed puzzle game. I was surprised with number of hours I got out of the title; although it must be said I'm not an experienced puzzler. The puzzle mechanics are straight-forward; navigate to the end of the pool without colliding with other swimmers. There is a variety of swimmers and obstacles presented to you at reasonable pace throughout the game, and completionists can pursue bonus stars.
The UI and sound is minimalistic, and the art is pleasant, sunny, and vintage. You'd be safe muting the sound and zoning out to your own music, or using the game to occupy part of your mind while you listen a video or podcast or something. Most of the puzzles I found to be easy or only requiring minimal trial and effort, but as the game progressed, real brainteasers that required multiple moves of planning or timing (or dumb luck) became common.
In summary, it's a wholesome little casual puzzle game that might surprise you with how long it can occupy you.

In the game you snoop around on a girl's computer and I thought that sounded like a procative premise.  What will I find out about her?  Will I stumble upon some clues that lead to a mystery?  Perhaps it will have some puzzles where I must figure out her password to unlock her archives.  I always like those kinds of puzzles in adventure games.
None of that is in the game.  There is nothing to discover.  The most you see of the girl's life is a few poems and a spattering of selfies.  Instead the game almost immediately starts you on a story that would have made more sense as a short film, and in fact, the final scene requires that anyway.
There are some good things.  The writing does sound like a girl trying to sound cute.  The acting is fine.  And the art is very graphic.  I would like to see another game from the designer.  I just hope it is a little higher concept.  I'd also recommend she play Portal (1986), Digital: A Love Story, and The Road to Gehenna expansion to Talos Principle, to see what can be done with the concept of exploring other people's computers, message boards, forums, and chats.

Ok, so, this game is a bit of an oddball.
On one hand, you have an intriguing premise for a narrative game that is executed adequately.  On the other hand, you may find yourself rolling your eyes at the overall taste it leaves in your mouth.
For one, I will recommend it, but only if its on sale.  Luckily, I picked it up in the narrative humble bundle from about a month ago.  I thoroughly enjoy story-based games, but I kinda felt like I knew how this one was gonna go.  I liked the overall presentation of it.  The desktops that you have the opportunity to interact with at the start of each act help to flesh out the main character of the story.  Being a male, I found that this game gave me a very interesting perspective on young love, playing as a female protagonist.
Once completing this, I can assume that the game is based on a true story.  I would love to meet Nina, the girl whose not only the protagonist, but also the writer and director of this game.  She seemed to have an interesting vision for this that many seem to not necessarily understand.  I would also like to punch Ichi in the face.  Being the only other integral character to the game, he's hard to like.  From the second I heard him speak, I immediately disliked him, which contributed to the obvious outcome of the story.  He, being the love interest, should be more emotional and cause the player to become a bit more invested in him, yet he just comes across as whiny and obnoxious.
Lastly, the length of game is obviously short, being easily beat within an hour.  This ultimately doesn't justify the initial pricetag but some people must understand that even a small indie game like this takes money to support.
Ultimately, this game deserves a solid 7/10 for its interesting premise, down-to-earth charm, and character development.  Although it may be hindered by a horrible supporting character and a slightly lacking script (but seriously, awkward, antisocial college students talk like that), this game has endearing qualities that justify a purchase, although likely at sale price.

This game had a suprisingly strong start, showing an impressive amounts of polish and strong gameplay when it started as open beta. From that point, it basically got worse and worse.
Star Conflict is WoT in space, with huge selection of ships, great graphics and pretty enjoyable combat mechanics. Just as WoT, it's horribly grindy and developers made a few misguided decisions that made progression even harder and slower then it was at the beginning. The strongest example is the contract system: contracts are missions that pay you with reputation, that you can spend for unlocking high-grade gear for your ships. At first, they were an additional source of reputation, that you could also get just by fighting in matches. Then, it became the only source of reputation, what made unlocking good gear much harder (and slower/boring). Then, they changed the mechanism from unlocking gear, that you could then buy for every ship you own, to upgrading single pieces of equipment. I salute everyone that didn't want to barf at the sole thought of how much grinding it will get them to equip a new ship decently. And it's only one of the changes that made the grinding much more painfull then it originally was.
The game has pretty good variety when it goes to game modes and maps, which gives decent potencial for organized teams to dominate the game, maybe more then in WoT thanks to the much more dynamic battles. It also has a decent clan wars system, that can have some appeal for dedicated players. Still, the grindfest stays as the main complain that will probably make all but those with really strong will drop this game - and it really seems that since the release SC playerbase is rather getting smaller.
I invested 60 euro in the elite pilot pack, but after a month I couldn't force myself to play this game any more. So, unless you're a die-hard fan of WoT that wants a new game in similar style, or you want a somewhat-casual space shooter and won't care at all about painfully slow progression, you probably shouldn't give much time to this game (though you can always try it out for some initial fun, it's F2P after all).

The gameplay was enjoyable, I liked collecting loot, upgrading my gear (even though a lot of the upgrades were focused on combat.. I would have preferred more stealth related upgrades), etc... As a person who is quite fond of stealth in general, I still appreciated this reboot in terms of the innovations it brought, such as swoop and takedowns, and for the fact that it was a AAA game that dared to be different-but just not different enough. Thief 2014 to me represents a game with a hybrid vision which seeks to rope in players from different backgrounds, like Assassin's Creed and Dishonored, and in trying to cast a broader net to catch more fish, lost some pearls. I still love Thief as a series and hope to see a return to the classic formula in future games.

I just finished this game and I'd like to share my thoughts.
This games gets a lot of things right (and some minor things wrong). I can absolutely recommend it for people who like shooters with a story; for comparison: other recent games I liked are e.g. Borderlands, Alien:Isolation, The Talos Principle, or Firewatch. FC4 is equal to or better than those.
Overall, I liked most of the FC4 game - the graphics, the music, the sounds, the story, the humour (the Monty Python 'honey badger'!), the gameplay, and, yes, the setting, which reminded me, more often than not, of Thailand.
Positive aspects:
- Single Player Game Playing Time. With about 40-60 hours playthrough time on easy, I cannot complain - very good value for the money.
- (Mostly) well-placed checkpoints. If I fail at some point, the last checkpoint always places me near enough to easily try again. Compare this to other games where you have to walk very far or even repeat some battles. This is actually a biggie for me.
- Many different aspects integrated, such as gathering leaves, killing animals for crafting, having to do certain quests for unlocking skills, then the bell towers, the outposts, karma events - very nice, always something to do. I got sidetracked for HOURS before I finally got the mission I wanted to do ;-)
- The ability to re-do outposts and strongholds, and additional points for completing missions without raising alarms etc. I replayed some fortresses for HOURS to get it right. That was fun!
- The sneaking around reminded me of the early "Commandos" games, but in 3d and with some twists. I liked that, and in particularly that the game moved on and got harder once you were detected instead of failing (mostly, depends on the mission).
- There is an offline mode, which is very nice for when I want to play the game again in 5 years when all the servers have gone the way all things go
- The Gale homestead which gives you access to things which were tedious to get before, like flowers, the helicopter, etc. Nicely placed after 30 hours game play where this starts to get repetitive.
- The story has so many elements in them which relate to current crises in the world that it is sometimes worrysome; right down to the split in the rebels on questions of pragmatism and idiology... very nicely done.
- Local coloring is interesting as well - I looked up Shangri-La, for example, which has led me to the novel "Lost Horizon" I am reading now...
- Chain Takedown. Really fun! ;-)
Negative points:
- Unskippable/unpauseable cut scenes - an annoying, patronising decision. Wasn't able to get a part of the story due to someone being at the door during a cut scene...
- Sometimes it is not clear what to do next, i.e. where the next mission quest is. I got used to it after a while --- just explore some more --- but this could be better highlighted, say, in the map; or maybe have a mission screen, which has been completely left out.
- After about half of the game it does get a bit repetitive - despite having so many options what to do as pointed out above. However, I guess it is better for the game to be longer and a bit repetitive than too short.
- The game takes too long to reload after death.
- I had some issues with online play where I would complete a mission online and the connection fails afterwards. Upon restart, the mission has to be done again. I guess there is some weird timing bug involved.
- I have completion OCD. So I would apprecitate different "levels" of "100%" completion - such as "100% core game", "100% with side quests", etc. - so I can choose with which 100% to be satisified ;-)
- Technical Handling of DLCs is annoyingly complicated. I bought the season pass on Steam. The main menu still shows "Buy the Season Pass" although it seems (?) to be installed. Why not have a list of "installed DLCs" right in the main menu, with info on how to get to each content (it is OK that some are showing up only as quests in the game, but make this clearer in-game)
- It is very tedious to compare weapons for their functionality. There is no compare screen (as in Borderlands) so I don't experiment much with them, too annoying. That could have been handled better.
- Shangri-La, while nice in terms of story, is annoying to actually play.
Well, that's all folks.

You might think Mini Metro is a quaint artsy puzzle game, but that's wrong... it's more of a simulation roguelike. You need to make sure passengers are delivered to their stations in time, and while this task starts out simple it quickly gets trickier as you're forced to make tough decisions over how to spend your limited resources by the minute.
Gameplay progress is measured in 'weeks', and every completed week presents you with a choice of new resources such as trains with different capacity or new bridges to draw lines across water. Even though each resource can be used in multiple ways, you need to plan ahead in order to have the best possible wiggle room whenever something unexpected happens.
Even though the game has a very limited set of actions, every decision you make has a drawback of some sort, and balancing risks vs rewards must be done constantly. Making a line loop around evens out the waiting times for passengers, but makes extending it awkward or sometimes even impossible. Making a line cover every station means the train can soak up passengers easily, but the time spent letting passengers embark and disembark slows down its overall speed, and if a train gets full in just a few stations' worth of passengers the waiting times further down the line will just explode.
Mini Metro is full of knife-point decisions like that while still managing to be incredibly relaxing, and it's definitely worth a shot no matter what your taste in games is.

Mini Metro is a calming, charming minimalist puzzle game - lots of buzzwords there I know, but it's very pleasant in its simplicity. You draw lines between stations, which are denoted with shapes (triangles, squares, etc) and passengers want to go to specifically shaped stations. Gameplay therefore is optimizing your lines so square passengers aren't waiting forever to get to the square station, and so on.
Complexity is added with special stations, an increasing spawn rate of passengers and new stations (thus increasing the pressure on you) and upgrades that you get every week, from new lines, new carriages, to other, special things. There's a good variety in maps, too - not only do they have new layouts for the stations, they throw in rivers and lakes that you need to navigate around or over with your limited stock of tunnels and bridges.
It hits that sweet spot between simplicity and complexity, basically. So - extras. There's the main mode, there's an endless mode, there's Extreme mode where you can't redraw any of your lines (yikes!) and there are the daily challenges, which hand you a random map and mode and compare your score with the internet's. There's a speed setting, so you can pause the game or speed it up as needed, although it doesn't go as fast as I'd like in some of the slower levels...but then you hit places like Auckland and you play that map at the main speed because going slightly faster will drown you!
Now: Most of Mini Metro is chill, as you sort out your trains and enjoy the maps. It's a game you can meditate to as you finish levels and collect achievements.
Then you hit the second half of the achievements, where they give you crazy challenges like "you can only use two tunnels" or "every line must connect to one station". These are hard, and require total mastery of the game's mechanics as well as a little luck - but they're also a good learning curve! You realize you have to play more carefully with the first one, then slowly ramp up until you're ready to face San Francisco and Auckland. The game goes from being chill to this crazy rush where your lines must be optimized perfectly as you rush around triaging passagers with your extra lines and hoping it's enough to last until you have a high enough score.
In short: Mini Metro is a lot of fun, and the challenge is nicely optional. Check it out!

I initially dismissed this game on and shortly after launch as being another generic P2W snorefest. There are many worse F2P shooters out there, though there are better ones as well.
It's very much a twitch shooter, where reflexes and positioning are king, particularly on long-range maps when nearly everyone decides to use bolt-action sniper rifles (which, as expected, are one-shot kills - even unmodded, though the semi auto rifles will take two shots, which can be a bit of a handicap if you do not have access to a bolt action). Grinding for money is a bit on the slow side, but even the basic free m4 is identical in every way to the rented/purchased one, save for the fact you can not put attachments on it (most are tradeoffs, though you'll hardly notice the negatives, the tiny bit of extra damage some mods provide can help, and you're also stuck with the default ironsights). Rentals are fairly easy to keep up on, though you might find yourself struggling to make money beyond that if you don't play the game heavily. Interestingly, weapon attachments are permanent, but gun rentals are not. You can however buy a weapon permanently with real money. Some call this P2W, though this has no bearing on your in-game performance, merely your income (as in you don't spend any of it on renewing your rentals).
No real co-op mode (unless that defense mode is one, no one was playing it so I can't say) to speak of. There are some seemingly overwatch-inspired psychic abilities, though the speed at which kills happen these are often forgotten, doesn't help that they use some of your precious (and limited) health pool to activate. There's also a 'classic' mode that disables them entirely, so you'll always have that if you decide getting hit by a meteor with no warning (keep in mind there's a decent delay on the actual impact once it's been activated) is no fun.
EDIT: You CAN buy weapons permanently with in-game currency. Few, if any paid-for options offer any real advantage over things you can get for free. Unless you count gambling on the possibility of going into battle wearing a bikini an advantage.

TLDR: Fantastically put together, ruined by the RNG events.
One example, finally having a good run (these are rare) find some a special character to join as a 3rd addition to the team. Event pops up demanding I remove 1 character as they are not pulling their weight... yes, very fair.
I've died mostly in thanks to the RNG events that have crippled my team, supplies, stolen all food, broke my car, etc etc.
From my experience 70% of the events are out to ruin something for you, and will. Another example, I found a stack 31 of Gas while exploring which is rare since you find no more than 4 pieces in 1 exploration area on average. The very next moment the RNG even of "Bandit humanoid demands all your gas"
You see, that's not fun, all you're doing is stripping away the hard fought items the players have worked to strip from the cold dead hands of zombies and other carcasses. The mechanics of some of the events can be steered with specific skills for people, but since you can't check your members skills and most the people on your team have their skills hidden, it makes it an awesome russian RNG roulette.
The scavanging/exploring part of the game is challenging later on but a lot of fun. if you get cornered and eaten to pieces 9 times out of 10 it's your fault. Finding what you need to do to tackle the next area is a lot of the fun, but I have trouble recommending this game, as you spend 20 minutes pulling off some amazing survival stunt... Only to have the contents you came back with, ripped from you due to an "event" you have have little control over.
If there weren't so many I wouldn't complain, but just knowing you're highly likely to lose somerthing 70% of the time doesn't make you want to continue playing.
Last note, never go on foot. Those events will guarantee your death.

Death Road To Canada is an action rpg that has alot of charm and reminded me of a modern Oregon Trail game. You have some very tough decisions to make on you're journey to Canada that really effect the game and there are also some sections that have action oriented gameplay and zombies all over the place, the game can get brutal!
Don't let the cute, old school pixel style graphics fool you, it is very challenging and will keep you on you're toes at all times. The dialogue is well written, the game is very funny and random events are all very well done.
You have to manage you're group of people as you try and make it from Florida to Canada. Like Oregon Trail before it, you must manage many things, including fuel, weapons, guns and food. One aspect I love, that I mentioned above is some of the tough choices you have, which remind me of a good rpg.
Each game has been very different so far and I can see a good amount of replay value to this game. Did I mention make you're decisions wisely? Sometimes things as small as letting someone join you're group, to going to find loot and losing one or all of you're group members.
Sometimes the vehicle will break down, if one of you're characters is a mechanic they can fix it, if you get jumped by bandits you must make the decision to pass over of you're hard each food/gas/ammo to the bandits or attack them. All of the random events and choices are very welll written to and alot of the time are very hard choices that take a little while to decide what you want to pick.
You will also have to pick weither to stop and check out some houses or stores along you're way, sure it would be nice to get some more food, ammo or gas but at what cost? You might get jumped by the zombies and it could all end there. Do you check out the city or keep driving and going to the next one?
If you have a friend or family member around you can also get them to hop in at times and control one of you're gorup members. One aspect I wish this game had was coop for people that are not in the same house. Local coop is cool but boy would this be fun with friends from other countries or cities. The other aspect I had some issues with was the crashes, I had 4 or 5 crashes during my many hours on the game. And lastly, the controls for keyboard and mouse could be improved, thankfully it handles flawless with a controller.
Still the good far outweigh the bad as Death Road To Canada brings a wonderful new, zombie style take on the Oregon Trail formula and does most of it very very well. The writing is top notch, the game has a ton of charm, the gameplay is fun, you have tough choices to make and it has good replay value.  This is a game that I find really good for an hour at a time and I can see myself playing much more over the next year. A few minor issues didn't take away from  the enjoyment I had while playing this game. Each time you restart it feels like a new experience, interested to see what new things the developers add in the future.
Get ready for a hell of a ride with Death Road To Canada! Oh yeah, one last thing, never let a clown in you're vehicle if you see one on the side of the road!

Though a neat idea, and fun upfront, the game really has some major issues.  The first being a horrible UI and control scheme.  Trying to use firearms is difficult at best because it tries to control like a twin-stick, but you can't map controls for that properly.  The other major issue is the random nature of things leaves you in constant situations where you just can't win.  A seige with a bad map or a series of bad encounters and you just have to restart.  Though I appreciate rouge-likes for what they are, this one just seems to fall into a habit of screwing over the player as much as possible.  The ability to make custom characters is a nice feature, it lets you fine tune a pair of characters and can make things more enjoyable.  I feel that this game falls into the trap that many rouge-likes seem to of a lack of information as a difficulty setting.  Yes, part of that style game is not necessarily knowing what the item you just picked up does and having to learn it, but this game takes that to extremes by not knowing your character stats or abilities picking up weapons that have no durability rating or any stats at all.  A lack of information to make a decision is not a good way to set difficulties, it is just frustrating.
I saw this played on Youtube and it looked fun.  And though I enjoyed it for a few run throughs and dealt with the frustrations for a while, really after 30 minutes you're just repeating the same frustrations over and over.  Some people really like it, and good for them.  For me, I just can't keep beating my head into the brick wall of frustration and random events.

Wow is this game bad. Initially I thought the poor reviews were just due to GamerGate mens-rights activists giving the game a raw deal...but then I played it. Jesus what a terrible game. I have no idea why this game was made.
This isn't an intentionally mean statement, either. The game itself has no purpose; there's no real sense of rising or falling action and I feel like most of the strong emotions I feel towards the game and the elements within it are unintentional.
For instance, I hate both Nina and Blake. Nina is sheepish, insecure and muddling - which aren't necessarily bad traits to have, but there's never a real reason given. Blake is someone you're supposed to like until he voices his doubt, but he was a ♥♥♥♥boy throughout (ie telling her she has a nice wrack, calling everyone he knows minus Nina an idiot.) Their dialogue isn't sweet or romantic, it's ladden with forced compliments and pathetic grasps for attention.
This kind of mood isn't something I'm against - in fact, I would love a game about two people who are insecure ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who fall for each other but are too pathetic to stay connected. But that's not the game. If that was supposed to be the game, the purpose and intent isn't clear enough. Instead I'm left to slog through 72 minutes of people "flirting" like they're 13 years old and I don't even know if I'm supposed to hate them or not.
The price point of this game is ridiculous, so I thank the Lord I got it through a Humble Bundle. Even at 50% off I wouldn't buy this, so thinking about spending 8.99 on it full price turns my stomach.
Also, the concept isn't original or unique. The ending felt rushed, but I think that even if the creators took their time with it it wouldn't really grab me. Why? I've seen this story and elements of it before. There's nothing new about internet meet up movies, straight people falling in love movies or guy being confused and ♥♥♥♥ing off movies. And that's essentially what this is - a movie. The gaming component could be interesting if executed well, but it was ultimately useless. The messages from other people don't particularly paint any vivid picture of me. Nina is a teenage girl and has a weeby teenage past. She's had online friends, online crushes. What exactly makes her a character that stands out, other than her crutch of pink hair?
Overall the only positive aspect of this game to me was the MMO setting. While useless, I found it extremely pretty, if not a little buggy. But in general, this game is a waste of time, money and creator resources. Head on back to the drawing board, guys.

A big disappointment for Thief fans.
Not going to lie, my expectations for this reboot for Thief series were high. I liked all the previous Thief titles, and the team behind this reboot has a good record in regards to reboots and sequels, with Tomb Raider and Deus Ex: Human Revolution.
But I guess you just can't hit the bullseye all the time.
The beginning of Thief is promising; There is the gloomy city, guards, loot to steal and dark corners where to hide. You sneak around during the main story line and have a bunch of lighter sidequests for a change of pace. You get to upgrade your skills and equipment and acquire items that help you, such as various arrow types for your bow and such.
Then it begins to dawn to you that there is something off with this game. The farther you advance the story the more annoyed you will get. The main storyline is forgettable, the characters are shallow and even more forgettable, you don't really care for either. Not only that, but the gameplay also becomes repetitive and outright boring very quickly.
You never get to feel you are the "master thief" who uses cunning and stealth to perform outstanding acts of thievery. Instead, you constantly feel and know you are playing a game. A game of obstacle course, where you need to find the route some game-making people made for you. The levels do offer you some options on how to complete them, but still, it feels your creative space is very confined. The city is nowhere near open-world, more like a set of courses glued together with loading screens. The spots where you can climb a wall or a box, or shoot a rope arrow or where to even jump are pre-set by the level designers. It constantly breaks immersion.
This game was released in 2014, and the game it has been compared to a lot, Dishonored, was released on 2012. While not being strictly a stealth game, Dishonored still outperforms Thief in almost all aspects Thief is supposed to shine.
It saddens me to play this game. I really wanted to like it, and one can tell that a talented group of people worked on it. On technical aspect it worked alright, with some black screens here and there where you needed to restart the game and some conversation audio loops that just repeated themselves constantly. But all in all... The game was not fun, exciting, immersive or interesting. It was just.. okay and slightly annoying, I guess.
5/10

Reasonably good but unexceptional core stealth gameplay attached to an incoherent train wreck of a plot. The core characters, including the protagonist, are all unlikeable and frequently behave inexplicably.  The quiet antihero of the original games turned into a chatty jackass.
Dishonored is a better Thief reboot than this is. But if you love first person stealth gameplay, and it's on deep discount ($10, tops, ideally $5), it's probably an okay purchase.

The game when starting was AWESOME, basically the same stuff than War Thunder but with space-ships.

Thats the pretty part of the game... only when you start.
After unlocking the third or fourth ship... everything went into the grindfest:
1.PvE restricts you to 1 or 2 missions with different difficulty (easier and you dont earn nothing OR impossible and still dont earn a lot), thats why you can do party with low leveled people and take your Tier 5 ship into the first mission on easy.
2.PvP is extremely unbalanced, since you can get more than half of new players with Tier 1 ships against a team with Tier 5-6 ships.
3.The grind after a while becomes ridiculous, you go from a kinda affordable ship to one that takes WEEKS or even MONTHS to unlock, of course... you have to LV UP the ship that was BEFORE the one that you want to unlock if you want to do so.
4.Upgrades follow the same path, since this game was made for people buying memberships that gives boosts (and lets not mention the premium ships which gives an even more insane boost) so you basically have to spend real money constantly to keep the ingame currency on a stable flow, since not only upgrades becomes insanely expensive but the price of the REPAIRS that you must carry to make your ships "usable" again takes at least 60% (If not more) of the battle rewards.
5.Lag, yeah, lag, even if this game its not that demanding, there are many situations (and with many means ALL the time) which the screen gets so heavily loaded with effects, explosions and stuff, that either, you end up blind until everything goes away OR you get hard lagged and crash against a random rock floating in the scene.
6.Either or you get a incredible win streak (which means the PvP matchmaking working properly, which it never happens.) PLUS membership PLUS premium ships to keep a somewhat "stable" currency flow, or you have to go back to previous Tiers, meaning more and more grinding.
7.Faction system is worthless, since you can pay a sum of game currency and simply switch to another faction, same goes for clan wars, there is not a "real" reason of being in one.
This game is fun up to a point, after that, it just gets annoying, unless you have fun with hours and hours of grinding, rogue-like teammates that basically are kill-hoggers, which means that if the whole team gets crushed they wont care, they got their kill, DLCS and "I got the most OP premium ship in the game" players, then this is your game.
(By the way: this goes for War Thunder too, but with planes.)

I have not played the full game yet so can't speak for the story, but I bought this mainly for the claimed immersion and "art look"; and boy ! Does it deliver on both of those. The Graphic "look" and sound work together to create the immersion but its also the believability factor. Where in some games you might be able to get away with picking up some coins behind the back of a guard, here, if not done properly the guard hears even that. Guards do search and react in a believable fashion and immediately see you where you would expect them to see you. Compare for example with the interesting but flawed Battlefield Hardline where immersion was often broken because guards were just not believable in their actions and/or failed to notice the obvious. Plus your cop buddy is constantly in view of the bad guys and they never react. But here we get a believable world. I immediatly felt like I was being transported into an unusual and mysterious city where candles can be snuffed out and the edge of paintings searched for switches. Keyholes can be looked through and valuables pick pocketed from guards. I have not played the original Thief games so can't compare but noticed some Assassin's Creed like game play, for example "focus vision" is AC "Eagle vision". However these days its difficult to find out who is copying each others innovations. But it's a very different game to AC. Where AC excels in large open areas here we have (at least so far) smaller areas with a lot of packed in exploration.  Of course AC is mostly third person. Here we have full first person, but to call it a "first person AC" may be unfair as Thief has a unique approach all of its own. All in all this has to be one of the more crafted and artistic games of the last few years. Recommended.

Death Road to Canada is as the developers succinctly describe it in the Steam description, a 'randomly generated road trip simulator.' The game would also be considered to be a randomly generated zombie killing machine. The aim of the game is to lead you and acquaintances you meet along the way from Florida to Canada. This is because you have heard that Canada has been spared from the zombie apocalypse. However, as they say its the journey and not the destination that is the aim of the game.
I have had a great time reading many of the reviews that have been contributed to Steam. This is the perfect game for sharing individual experiences. As a result, I can see fan fiction becoming an enormous part of the game's community. Therefore, kudos for this not only goes to the community members for creating this wonderful content but also to the developers for designing a game perfect and worthy of it. It is truly a testimony to the quality of the final product.
The tutorial teaches you the bare minimum. For some this may be a concern but it shouldn't be. I have found that some of the best games only teach the basic mechanics needed to play. The rest is left to the player experience. If you put the time into the game you will continue to learn each time you play. This is a very good thing. This is because some of the tricks I have learned wouldn't have meant as much had they been in the tutorial and had I not learned them by myself. Some of the magic of the playing is in the learning. Therefore, the game demands that you learn more as you progress. Consequently, you may die a few times but you need to mark these down as learning experiences.
To continue with the 'learning as you go' mantra of the game it must be acknowledged that it is very challenging. For starters, the zombie AI - as stupid as zombies may seem - can be quite tough. They can swarm and they can, and will, overwhelm you. Therefore you must remain alert and vigilant at all times. You must consider if you are outnumbered and if so what your best avenue of self defense and preservation is.
Weapons can and do break. You will run out of ammunition. However, you can hold multiple weapons at any one time. It is best policy to remember the strengths and weaknesses of your characters. This is most noteworthy because the weapons that you choose to wield - when you find them - can make the game easier. There's nothing better than having the ability to go to town against a swarm and defeating them all.
If there is one potential weakness of the game its in the fact that the difficulty can spike unpredictably. However, there is a valid argument that this adds realism to the game. There is never going to be any scenario that is exactly as it seems. Swarms can occur at random intervals. As a result of this randomness some of these spikes can lead to frustrating deaths.
Generally, the game is unforgiving. Once you screw up there is very little chance for your survival. As a result of this the game is definitely one that has the potential to induce rage. An example of this rage came in my second unsuccessful attempt. I had successfully cleared a building and wanted to move on with the game. Therefore, I raced outside with my trio of seemingly hardened warriors into a swarm of the undead. I jumped in my car but of course I couldn't drive away because the vehicle was swarmed. They not only damaged the vehicle but proceeded to annihilate all of us. I could do nothing but watch in sheer terror.
One of the best features of the game is the way in which it is randomly generated. Stories and settings for individual segments of the game are randomly generated. However, they are based somewhat from the options you are provided with.
In one of my segments I visited a city and was given the choice of whether or not I wanted to visit a sports store or a house with a HELP sign. As this was early on in the game and I was only with my initial buddy I chose to go to the HELP house. I took my chances that the house would have somebody still alive that would be willing to join my team. Although I bet the sports store probably had a nicer selection of weapons and equipment that I could pick up. This strategy was of the hope that the numbers game would help more than a randomized weapon. I was proven to be correct. I acquired the extra party member and was able to adventure on.
In conclusion, the events are random. This is especially relevant considering the entirety of the game is played out within these little settings. However, it leads me to the next segment of the game that is worth noting and that is the game's buddy system.
This is one of my favorite features in the game. Hidden within the fun thrilled violence is a message about camraderie and the meaning of taking a road trip together. You have a choice at the beginning of the game whether or not you want to start with an ally. I would suggest that if you are a beginner that you do have one. If you have a second player with you then they can play the role. If not, then the computer will control them for you. Because the game has been well designed the AI does a reasonable job hacking enemies up for you.
Each ally comes with their own unique characteristics and skills that can add value to your team. Although beggars can rarely be choosers you may want to consider what type of characters you align yourself with. They can stay with you until they either die or they betray you. That's right, they can betray you. That in itself is a fascinating mechanic. If they do betray you then its game over. It's best to keep their morale high - through successful completion of events and stories - although I am uncertain as to whether or not this increases the likelihood of betrayal. I assume that it would.
A great feature of the game is that you can create a number of custom characters. You can choose to play this character and/or have one as your buddy. If you choose not to do this then they can and will pop up throughout the game. It is at this turn that you can add them as allies.
There is a risk/reward system at play in the combination of stories/events and allies. Events will pop up throughout the game that provide you with an opportunity to utilize their abilities. If they are successful then you can increase your stockpile sometimes dramatically. However, failure in any of these events can see a crucial member of your unit die. As a result you will need to carefully consider the strengths and weaknesses of your character, your current predicament and determine whether or not the potential reward is worth it. Given the unforgiving nature of the game each decision is significant.
With that said an underappreciated part of the game is in its resource management. Players must consider how many rations, medical supplies, fuel, etc. that they have at their disposal. Players must therefore weigh up the pros and cons of adding an ally. If you are running dangerously low on resources then adding a member to your team may not be the most sage of things to do.
As a result of the total combined randomness you are guaranteed a unique playthrough every time you play.
