For those that feel like reading I'll frame one of the highlights in the best and most relatable way I know how.
Sol 3
So I had to reload my save for the first time today. I don't know which engineer came up with that but it's a godsend! I've rebuilt the hab and secured constant automatic charging for my suit's battery. Yay computer programming! Next on the plan of me not dying is oxygen.
I'd filled the hab with the oxygen sent with me and was working on the best way to get my suit's bottle refilled. I setup an active vent to a pipe and a bottle refilling bracket. Everything was going smoothly until I realized I hadn't put a presure gauge on the pipe leading to my only spare O2 bottle. Moments later (you should be expecting this) the bottle exploded right over my head! The explosion threw me across the hab and tore several large holes in my suit.
With alarms blaring in my ears I shook off the shellshock and realized my suit was puking oxygen to the hab. I quickly patched that up with half a roll of duct tape (it really should be worshipped) and assessed the situation. My suit's O2 bottle was down to 300 kPa! I rushed around for a few hours trying to fashion a replacement bottle to fill with O2 before asphyxiating.
Man... what a day. I wonder what tomorrow will bring.

I feel that the game starts off really well, but the more I play the more I realize how much they don't show you. For example, the importance of building certain things next to each other. Elements that are very costly or near impossible to change.
This game demands your full effort but you can't even give it because you have to wait a whole day (literally a day) for resources to produce.
For a free to play game, I do think it's worth a go. But I do feel they set the bar just slightly out of reach. I do think having elements so that people will pay some money to the game is fair, but when you design your entire game around trying to get that, then the game will only end up being impossible or VERY easy with money. I payed $2.99 to the game for a starter pack and I felt it was fair to give the game $3. But at level 30, I'm realizing I would need to be paying in either serious time or in cash to get this game to do anything useful for me. And even with that, this game feels like it goes nowhere. You work you a$$ off to level up and it really doesn't make any difference. When you finally level up your troops, FINALLY!!!-- then you have to wait twice as f***ing long for them to cool down. WTF? Orrrr, pay gold. Games are suppose to pay off with the amount you put into them, and this game only raises the bar and gives you nothing for it.

I usually like narrative games, but I can't think of a single thing that makes this worth recommending. The story is a dull, drawn-out retelling of an event from the creator's personal life, which is generic enough to be of interest only to the author herself. Somehow, despite playing herself, the voice acting for the Nina character is terrible, though the male voice actor is only marginally better.
The few video segments get worse yet, with no emotion at all on display. That's particularly poor when you consider that the emotion of the protagonist is really the only draw in a game like this. Upon finally meeting for the first time after a long-distance courtship the two main characters couldn't show any less interest in each other if they tried. Even some small sign of their social awkwardness would have been nice, but instead they were almost robotic as they silently meet and then depart immediately again for their tryst.
Then there's the terrible poetry and pointless photography that's supposed to give you a feel for the main character's personality, but is all so pretentious that nothing real shines through.
It's barely worth mentioning the technical aspects of the game, since the narrative is all that matters, but the interface is frustratingly clunky and I had to swap to a second monitor just to play as my ultra-widescreen confused the game into placing important elements off-screen. If ever there was a game that deserved to be launched in windowed mode, this is it, but I couldn't find any kind of option menu so I assume that's impossible. These two problems just made sitting through the boring story elements even more tiresome.
All told, this feels like a poorly implemented exercise in narcissism and pretention. Special snowflake: the game. Buy "Gone Home" instead.

Terraforming your lordly turf is great fun and challenging to find your personal way of doing it. A thing I really like is how inevitably you form the lands once you get them in your hands. Each player works with the land in his own way, there is plenty to see.
Battles keep being a challenge and often have you on the edge of your seat, skill making the outcome. There is lots of stuff to learn gradually, the game keeping your pace at learning just nice. I'm really impressed by the way the battles keep to your skill level.
There are many little things that I really like about this game, especially the pace and format. I am a fan of having 20 men in a unit, with a few at once in battle, compared to some 200 or 20000 of other games. The scale in this game is something I really like.
Take what you will, I really enjoy playing this game every now and then to have a few medieval minutes. Currently not interested in it's PVP though, can't really tell anything about that.

Cibele is a game that works on paper, but not in practice.
I usually don't mind games that rely on their story rather than their gameplay, but there are so many ways in which Cibele falls flat.
In games like Firewatch, Gone Home, and The Beginner's Guide, gameplay is secondary to the story, but is nonetheless an important element. In Cibele, the gameplay is annoying, awful, and intrusive. It feels like someone took a text adventure and squeezed trashy gameplay into it. You just click on the same monster repeatedly and hope for the next bit of dialogue to make it stop.
If the dialogue was good, that'd be fine, but the story is maudlin at best and cringily obnoxious at worst. A love story only works if you like both characters - if you find them both utterly unbearable the whole thing just /doesn't work./
I got Cibele for a dollar in a Humble Bundle, and I guess that's fine, but actually paying for it is a bad call.
If someone else decided to try making a similar game with better execution, I'd be interested, but Cibele left me dissapointed and dissatisfied.

An ode to classic platformers of the past. Cross Mario64 with the aesthetics of Zelda Wind Waker, would end up with something very close to resembling Poi. If more Early Access games were in this state, steam wouldn't have such a bad name.
Starting off with a basic obstacle course to refine skills, immediately you should feel at home with the controls. All your favorite moves from Mario are here, walljumps, triplejumps, slidejumps, quickturn backflips, the works. Not only does it feel familiar but was very responsive as well. Didn't test keyboard and mouse as it's more a gamepad based game. After clearing the tutorial you progress into the main world, which currently consists of a 'hub' containing 2 full maps and an npc who sells unlockable mini challenges. All included global scoreboards for those adventurers seeking further glory. While Zelda had a boat, Poi has an airship and your character has a deployable parachute! Yes, you don't technically fly very far but effects are in place to make it feel both believable and magical.
Technically speaking, Poi should run a range of systems, supporting screen resolutions of 4k+ and toggles for godrays, depth-of-field and heat-haze, Controls were intuitive but unfortunately unable to be remapped. Probably the games biggest flaw at the moment is the lack of content, veterans could complete what it offers in under 2hrs. With that said for those 2hrs I had a smile from ear to ear, thanks to the devs for taking me back to my younger years in the best way possible. Look forward to seeing this wonderful game evolve further. Cheers folks. :)

Poi is an indie 3D platformer developed by Polykid and is currently in Early Access on Steam.
The game is very reminiscent of classic N64 platformers both in style and gameplay but this is most definitely a good thing. The hub of the game sees you on a sky ship able to visit different worlds that contain a number of different medallions to collect. If you replace stars with medallions, red coins with keys and coins with… coins you pretty much know what to expect.
Currently in the early access build there are 2 different worlds to explore both of which have 6 medallions. Cozy Canyon is a forest mountain level and Mount Magma is a lava style volcano level. While there is currently nothing super original this is most definitely one of the best 3D platformers I have played in years. After completing the 2 worlds I was left desperate for more and cannot wait for the game to reach further in development.
Early in the game you also meet a passing ship that can transport you to challenge levels that really kick the difficulty up a notch. There are also other things to do such as dig for fossils and with other detours looking to be added soon there is a bright future.
Visually the game looks like an early Dreamcast title but do not let this put you off. Steam is flooded with 2D retro platformers as the moment so to have a 3D one that captures the spirit of platformers from the N64 era so very well is an exciting prospect.
If you yearn for a N64 inspired 3D platformer the Poi is definitely an early access title worth keeping an eye on.

I haven't finished it, but I have to post this. I really like this game. The art, the concept, the combat (to an extent, I don't like having the no-damage kick being the same key as the actual attacks, it causes you to bunt when you mean to stab and the other way around), but my god is this game infuriating. I had to take a break after the second dream.
There's a section of the second dream where the level is almost (and I mean there's only a couple spaces that aren't) completely covered with slippery surfaces. This wouldn't be a problem if the mechanic wasn't absolutely broken. It maintains your velocity from the last slippery surface. Not the actual speed you're moving at when you hit the surface, not even your speed from the previous surface. The speed from the previous SLIPPERY surface. Meaning, you can drop straight down onto a slippery surface and then suddenly fly off to the side and crash into a pit of spikes.
I was relieved to get past that part, until I realized that the next section was pretty much entirely jumping from wall to wall. The obstacles in this section are Japanese lanterns, with spikes on the top and bottom. If you graze the spikes trying to get onto the side, you get hit and the knockback will probably send you to your death. Also, if you don't get your entire body on the wall, you'll fall. Meaning, if your feet are just BARELY too low by its standards, your character will decide you let you fall to your doom. Another problem with the wall-to-wall movement is the jumping. You get two jumps in this game, and the second jump isn't like a double jump, it's an actual extra jump. The kind where you can do it anytime. The problem with this, however, is that sometimes it'll count your first jump as the second jump, so you'll go out expecting to jump again, then just fall like an idiot. Then, once you think you've finally made it to the end, all those ghosts you were avoiding because aerial combat is difficult will come back to bite you in the♥♥♥♥♥with all their buddies at the end while you cry and try to smack levers.
If you take this game from a "Call of Cthulhu", "Hey let's see what insane, creative ways we can die" position, it's absolutely amazing. But if you want to actually get through it, it's still a great game, but incredibly aggravating.
This game also claims to have "full controller support", but that doesn't extend to all controllers. My controller works fine with most of the games that I've tried it with (the only other game that hasn't worked has been Watch_Dogs), but apparently this game (and probably Watch_Dogs) requires an XBOX controller. So basically, anyone who doesn't want to use a controller with uneven sticks, bubble buttons, and extra cost to get the special connector for PC is out of luck and has to use a keyboard.

I'd read this was a bit like Super Meat Boy with some combat and that it felt magical to play so I picked it up. While there is fun to be had and it looks nice, I'd only recommend it to people who love the sort of games where you die over and over again, slowly committing the game to muscle memory.
With what I played, all the game throws at you are slippery surfaces after the first level or two which does a few things, it slides you around to the extent that controlling your character becomes a challenge in itself, it makes combat incredibly cumbersome with both yourself and enemies sliding back and forth making it hard to hit them and finally, it prevents you from wall jumping. I'd think this was a great mechanic if I didn't feel it was so over used. It ended up just sapping all joy out of the game.
Combine this with a tiny flying enemy that dashes around in groups trying you hit you with them being invulnerable while dashing, which they do upon you being directly left, right up or down from their position, and you have some very difficult levels that just aren't fun to play.
It's not a bad game, I did have fun with it but rather than being one of those games that annoys you so much that you end up being addicted to getting just a little further, those two negatives being used so much ended up boring me. If you really like getting challenged and don't get bored of mechanics like that then go for it, otherwise I'd recommend avoiding it.

It pains me to say this, because ever since I was a kid i would play Magic the Gathering all day with my friends.
This is somthing that now since I've grown older have realised that as my friends grew up and moved away that Magic Duels was going to be an easy and fun way to play. Until I acctually played. I have prepaired a list of pros and cons.
PROS:
1: It is a free way to learn and engage into the Magic the Gathering world giving insite into recent lore and showing
promise.
2: Gives any player that nostalgic "magic the gathering" feel.
thats it
CONS:
1: Abandonware (there hasnt been an update in quite some time and game devs have shown lack of fixing this)
2: Pay-to-Win With the horrendous Bugs/Glitches and terriple AI you get screwed over alot leaving the only reasonable way to earn packs (which are only 6 cards instead of the normal 15 which a complete rip why not at least 9?) in Relation you are spending 1.99 for each booster, Which would be acceptable if maybe you recieved the physical copy in hand. But youre not.
3. Many bugs/glitches; many times playing youll see an action take place and wonder ,...... "was that supposed to happen". And sometimes yes you just miss one slight detail but Ive actually stopped the game and looked at every card and called friends who were avid players too to realize that the even tha ocured was a bug. That more times than not will cost you a game.
4. Online Multiplayer Issues; namely people who have taken advantage of the game. I can count about 5 games where it mysteriously ended right as I started and I was declaired the loser, costing me Rank, time, and patience.
5. AI severely op at times, even though sometimes AI can even run into issues like Mana flooding and a mana drought too. Which is cool until you see this and go from full health to 1 by a random combintaion from out of nowhere (this will happen alot more than you expect, I said ALOT more right?)
6. Story mode decks are completely and utterly boring to play, some are very fun like the multiple plainswalker decks that you use when fighting certain eldrazi and such, But other than that they lack in enthusiasm and are therefor lackluster.
All in all i dont even want to advertise this as a learning tool as the player who doesnt know would probobly become frustrated and bored before they could really grasp how cool magic is. Most of the time they will start by playing a dry campaign to earn a booster per set and when theyre done they will be at the mercy of online players for an utter boring and furiating mission to collect coins for boosters, which yield far less than there should be for the amount of work put in. Theres work to be done and its not getting there. If I see an update to the game I will adjust my review but until then I will leave this review as it stands.

I always try to be fair in reviewing a game and judge based on it's merits rather than condemn it for it's quirks or impurities. That said, I have never made a negative review because when I do despise a game, I tend to not even bother writing one.
Ignoring the fact that the game didn't have mouse control which apparently will be updated; I went into this with a 360 controller expecting a nice and easy 'Match 3' puzzle game (with a bit of Disney charm) to add to my 100%/Perfect game collection. But as it was with the movie; it's rather disappointing and a seemingly waste of time.
It may seem like a family friendly game but if your Steam account or device is not safely set up for making transactions, I recommend not letting your kids play this by themselves. I'm usually not an advocate for screaming "P2W" on F2P games but the game is riddled with micro-transactions. The game may start out very easy and have you question the need for spending actual money to progress but once you get to the higher levels, it will start throwing out horrible levels with questionably achievable goals that will either require a lot of luck or some actual cash to get you through without restarting multiple times.
Now I would have let it pass if you could 'beat' the game through persistence alone, but the game utilizes the horrid and ancient way of giving you a set amount of lives so that if you run out you're either forced to buy more or come back the day after and hope you get a heart from the daily login reward.. which of course you can then waste on one of the so 'challenging' levels.
Now I could go on for a while but it all comes down to the same thing anyway. In conclusion; I think this game would have been fair if it was sold for a one-time price with everything unlocked/unlockable through gameplay. But as it is, you would spend/waste a lot more money on trivial things just to progress through a game that honestly really isn't all that fun to begin with, let alone original. Unfortunately for my initial expectation, I don't think you can 100% this game legit without spending a ton of cash, time or contemplating self-destructive thoughts.

Death Road to Canada is as the developers succinctly describe it in the Steam description, a 'randomly generated road trip simulator.' The game would also be considered to be a randomly generated zombie killing machine. The aim of the game is to lead you and acquaintances you meet along the way from Florida to Canada. This is because you have heard that Canada has been spared from the zombie apocalypse. However, as they say its the journey and not the destination that is the aim of the game.
I have had a great time reading many of the reviews that have been contributed to Steam. This is the perfect game for sharing individual experiences. As a result, I can see fan fiction becoming an enormous part of the game's community. Therefore, kudos for this not only goes to the community members for creating this wonderful content but also to the developers for designing a game perfect and worthy of it. It is truly a testimony to the quality of the final product.
The tutorial teaches you the bare minimum. For some this may be a concern but it shouldn't be. I have found that some of the best games only teach the basic mechanics needed to play. The rest is left to the player experience. If you put the time into the game you will continue to learn each time you play. This is a very good thing. This is because some of the tricks I have learned wouldn't have meant as much had they been in the tutorial and had I not learned them by myself. Some of the magic of the playing is in the learning. Therefore, the game demands that you learn more as you progress. Consequently, you may die a few times but you need to mark these down as learning experiences.
To continue with the 'learning as you go' mantra of the game it must be acknowledged that it is very challenging. For starters, the zombie AI - as stupid as zombies may seem - can be quite tough. They can swarm and they can, and will, overwhelm you. Therefore you must remain alert and vigilant at all times. You must consider if you are outnumbered and if so what your best avenue of self defense and preservation is.
Weapons can and do break. You will run out of ammunition. However, you can hold multiple weapons at any one time. It is best policy to remember the strengths and weaknesses of your characters. This is most noteworthy because the weapons that you choose to wield - when you find them - can make the game easier. There's nothing better than having the ability to go to town against a swarm and defeating them all.
If there is one potential weakness of the game its in the fact that the difficulty can spike unpredictably. However, there is a valid argument that this adds realism to the game. There is never going to be any scenario that is exactly as it seems. Swarms can occur at random intervals. As a result of this randomness some of these spikes can lead to frustrating deaths.
Generally, the game is unforgiving. Once you screw up there is very little chance for your survival. As a result of this the game is definitely one that has the potential to induce rage. An example of this rage came in my second unsuccessful attempt. I had successfully cleared a building and wanted to move on with the game. Therefore, I raced outside with my trio of seemingly hardened warriors into a swarm of the undead. I jumped in my car but of course I couldn't drive away because the vehicle was swarmed. They not only damaged the vehicle but proceeded to annihilate all of us. I could do nothing but watch in sheer terror.
One of the best features of the game is the way in which it is randomly generated. Stories and settings for individual segments of the game are randomly generated. However, they are based somewhat from the options you are provided with.
In one of my segments I visited a city and was given the choice of whether or not I wanted to visit a sports store or a house with a HELP sign. As this was early on in the game and I was only with my initial buddy I chose to go to the HELP house. I took my chances that the house would have somebody still alive that would be willing to join my team. Although I bet the sports store probably had a nicer selection of weapons and equipment that I could pick up. This strategy was of the hope that the numbers game would help more than a randomized weapon. I was proven to be correct. I acquired the extra party member and was able to adventure on.
In conclusion, the events are random. This is especially relevant considering the entirety of the game is played out within these little settings. However, it leads me to the next segment of the game that is worth noting and that is the game's buddy system.
This is one of my favorite features in the game. Hidden within the fun thrilled violence is a message about camraderie and the meaning of taking a road trip together. You have a choice at the beginning of the game whether or not you want to start with an ally. I would suggest that if you are a beginner that you do have one. If you have a second player with you then they can play the role. If not, then the computer will control them for you. Because the game has been well designed the AI does a reasonable job hacking enemies up for you.
Each ally comes with their own unique characteristics and skills that can add value to your team. Although beggars can rarely be choosers you may want to consider what type of characters you align yourself with. They can stay with you until they either die or they betray you. That's right, they can betray you. That in itself is a fascinating mechanic. If they do betray you then its game over. It's best to keep their morale high - through successful completion of events and stories - although I am uncertain as to whether or not this increases the likelihood of betrayal. I assume that it would.
A great feature of the game is that you can create a number of custom characters. You can choose to play this character and/or have one as your buddy. If you choose not to do this then they can and will pop up throughout the game. It is at this turn that you can add them as allies.
There is a risk/reward system at play in the combination of stories/events and allies. Events will pop up throughout the game that provide you with an opportunity to utilize their abilities. If they are successful then you can increase your stockpile sometimes dramatically. However, failure in any of these events can see a crucial member of your unit die. As a result you will need to carefully consider the strengths and weaknesses of your character, your current predicament and determine whether or not the potential reward is worth it. Given the unforgiving nature of the game each decision is significant.
With that said an underappreciated part of the game is in its resource management. Players must consider how many rations, medical supplies, fuel, etc. that they have at their disposal. Players must therefore weigh up the pros and cons of adding an ally. If you are running dangerously low on resources then adding a member to your team may not be the most sage of things to do.
As a result of the total combined randomness you are guaranteed a unique playthrough every time you play.

I'm a pretty casual fan of SS13 but the BYOND engine always leaves me yearning for something more robust to get a better experience. I hear about this game and learn about the devs, if you think that Dean Hall is responsible for the mess that is DayZ Standalone do some research and do yourself a favour. This game has been alot of fun, but it def is not for everyone. I would recommend this game for people who are looking for complex problem solving and simulated space enviroments. This game would prob synergize with people who liked playing Minecraft Tekkit and Factorio, but I think this game is harder than both of those.
I hear alot of people complaining about the controls. First off, yes, the controls are not "standard" but there's a reason for it. The cycling between using both hands is intergral to the gameplay mechanics, simulating both hands allows for more complex actions that would otherwise be hard to implement if the controls were more simple like a Minecraft hotbar. Having two hands allows the combined usage of items and honestly it doesnt take that long to learn and the tutorial provided in the game quickly shows you how it works.
Next is the inventory system which is again, very close to SS13's. You have pockets or inventory slots determined by what you are wearing and at first it may be a little confusing because it is different it is not that hard to learn if you just apply a little time.
Once you learn the controls and inventory systems you can start the game. There's plenty of work to be done, between setting up power system, atmospherics, medical areas, living quarters, hydroponics, material processing rooms. You'll have you hands full and good planning is required to do it in a way that will make it work seemlessly. There are many ways to get the job done right but certainly wrong ways to do things as well. Continuing from there you have to take everything you learned from building a colony to building a ship. I haven't made it that far so I cant say much about it other than im looking forward to it. From there we have been promised to be able to go out on missions from a range of activities.
The devs have already expressed that they want modders to jump in and make stuff for the community so beyond what the devs have planned for game we can expect modders to bring even more to the table and thats really exciting.
So, if you consider yourself a problem solver and creative thinker and engineering interest you, this might be the game for you if you think you can learn the game mechanics and controls.

Pretty much your standard, run-of-the-mill open world sandbox game. If you've played a Far Cry, you've played them all. You've got your standard dictator figure, a ragtag bunch of freedom fighters, and a foreigner (you!) tossed into the mix to sort everything out.
I tend to like these open world games a lot, since there's generally a lot to do. However, at some point the storyline has to draw you back into some semblance of structure, and unfortunately its pretty lacking in Far Cry 4. Without revealing too much, the game falls back onto fairly safe, unadventurous tropes, and relies far too heavily on drug-induced psychedelic trips as proxies for actual boss fights. It's a gripe I had with Far Cry 3, and for it to still rear its head now isn't all too surprising, I suppose.
Gameplay is pretty solid. You gain experience as you go about doing quests and killing enemies, and doing so lets you unlock skills to increase your health, ride elephants, silently takedown enemies--standard levelling-up fare. At the same time, you can use the money you've gathered to unlock weapons and upgrades, although some weapons are locked until a set number of side missions have been completed. This at least sets the pacing correctly, since to be honest some of the later guns can turn you into a one-man army.
All in all, I'd say give it a try if the game was on sale. Otherwise, I can't really recommend it at full price.

I feel compelled to expand upon my initial review, since it was rather short and people found it to be not very helpful. Granted, after playing Cibele I was extremely dissatisfied. Having more distance to the thing now, I can elaborate why this game isn't for me… Oh yeah: Potential SPOILERS ahead!
Let’s start with one of my main gripes: the story. I know it is based on the experiences of the games designer. But that doesn’t mean it’s a story worth telling! The entire plot is short, foreseeable and frankly uninteresting. There is no twist and no conclusion – It just ends abruptly. Sorry, but there’s just not enough of a story here.
So in hindsight, Cibele serves only as a vehicle for the designer to share her experiences with a global audience. But I am not sure what’s her intention here. Does she want to invoke pity? Is this some sort of catharsis? Is this supposed to be a cautionary tale? Yes, these things happen. So what? Life goes on! Was this really such a traumatic event that you have to process it through this medium? What is this? “First World Problems – The Game”?
The shortcomings of the story are highlighted by the nondescript characters, which come across as bland and unappealing. This is not only due to the amateur (voice) actors that portray them, but also due to the poor and often cringe-worthy writing. For characters that are supposed to be in college, they act like 14-year olds. “Hey, I like your forum pic! Can you send me another one?” “Sure, let me just strip down to my bra and panties before I pose on my bed.” Really? Aren’t you the girl that just said how shy and self-aware she is? The one that writes poems when she's not busy playing MMO’s? Must be the genes from your mother kicking in… who apparently was a model. (I wish I was making this up…)
So what about the male love interest? “You have a nice rack!” Oh you silver-tongued devil, you! But what do you expect from a guy that follows a declaration of love with a monologue on how much relationships suck. (Not that he ever had one before.) If that doesn’t telegraph a "ONS" way in advance, I don’t know what does. But nerdy-girl is totally cool with that. “You know… whatever. So you think we could kiss when we meet?”
That is the real deal breaker here: The main protagonists are both extremely unlikable! I know they're supposed to be teenagers, but chimpanzees have more common sense than that. This just kills the immersion as I find myself antagonizing the characters due to their blatant stupidity and smugness. The game tries to deal with serious issues like first love and first sexuality but does this so ham-handedly that I could only shake my head in disbelief.
But Cibele does not only fail story- and character-wise, it also fails as a game itself. The gameplay consists of exploring the main character’s desktop and grinding in a rudimentary MMO. Want to browse through low-res photos, text files with poems or random emails? No thank you!
The MMO-part is reduced to killing random monsters until the boss appears, while listening to the infantile banter between the game’s protagonists. Even this simple game mechanic is hopelessly broken and agonizingly dull – which is kind of fitting as it seems to be a theme of the game.
The only saving grace of Cibele is the art style of the MMO parts which unfortunately is criminally under-utilized.
Bottom line: Cibele was a boring and unpleasant experience for me. It is unable to live up to its own ambitions due to its unlikable characters and its clumsy handling of a generally interesting premise.
And yes, the game is over in less than an hour! There’s just not more meat than that on this bone (no pun intended). As a matter of fact, it took me longer to write this review than to play through the game.

This game tells the story of two people who meet and start a relationship through an online MMO. The game is story driven and there is little gameplay to speak of; what is there really nails the monotony of MMO combat a little too well. I found myself really disliking my time during those segments as I do with most MMOs. Every chapter has a story bit and some time spent in the game where you kill minions until the boss shows up, then it retreats and you have to kill more minions until it shows up again to meet its fate. The gameplay is a vehicle to showcase the in game voice chat between to two main characters. I just wish they changed it up a bit to keep it fresh.
I liked the faux desktop environment interface quite a bit and how it changed between the chapters as time went on. The blog posts you find on the desktop were from the creator’s (Nina Freeman) old livejournal account, that was a cool touch. You might find, as I did, that the dialog between the two main characters is cringe worthy at times. I don’t think it’s poorly written, I think it hits very close to home if you’ve ever played online games because you've seen it or participated in it at some point.
It’s only about an hour long but I think it was a good little story that is relevant to people of a certain generation.

Only way to experience modern Magic: The Gathering with a good interface. Also the only "free to play" version of Magic that exists. Magic is a very costly game, in both Digital and Physical formats, especially Magic Online, which has an archaic interface (it launched in 2002 and has had very little visual updates). As of Amonkhet, they have decided to stop updating this game.
The biggest flaw with this game, other than it not being updated anymore, is the "6 card boosters" which is unlike anything in the real game. Boosters in any other format include 15 cards. This means building a good deck is going to take you a very long time. One good thing, if you have a DCI account, you can link it and get 2000 free gold, which will atleast give you enough rare cards and the ability to buy atleast one of each booster to unlock all the "starter" cards, instead of having to play through each story line (which an be very very time consuming and not that rewarding).
I have been playing Magic: The Gathering since 1993, and besides the physical version of the game, this is my favorite way to play. I can't recommend spending any money on this though, as like I mentioned previously, no new updates.
According to WotC, they are currently developing another game called Magic: The Gathering Arena, which is supposed to be the successor to this. What Wizards really needs to do is take this existing interface and patch Magic Online to match. Also, include "goals" in Magic online for pack bonuses and give incentive to play it alongside the physical game. Currently, Magic Online can be more expensive than playing with real cards.
Wizards was almost on to something with this game, but abandonded it. Play it if you want some magic fun, but don't want to spend a ton on cards.
Not adding new sets gives this game low value moving forward. Maye have been fun, but I stopped playing permanently once it was revealed new sets would not be added.

9/10. This is quite an addictive puzzle game. It has simple rules and a simple aesthetic. The bare-bones graphics might not be appealing at first, but I think this style was chosen deliberately to minimize any confusion or distractions from the game mechanics.The sound effects are pleasing, and can eventually accumulate into a makeshift musical score that reminds me of  early electronic artists like Kraftwerk. Gameplay is somewhat slow-paced. It does get challenging but never frantic. There is also an "Endless" mode where you never lose, but even in normal mode the game is pretty relaxing.
Some additional negatives: the menu system is poorly organized. You can find everything once you get used to it, but it should have had a more intuitive design in the first place. Also, like most puzzle games, it can get pretty repetitive. There are a few different maps, but still not a huge amount of variety.
This game is not going to blow your mind, but it's a good way to chill out and unwind for a bit.

I'll start this off by saying that I will be writing in some spoilers to the main storyline, and additionally that I really did try to enjoy this game.
I'll try to give some pros first:
The graphics are visually appealing. The game LOOKS nice.
The audio quality isn't bad.
The voice acting is pretty good
The story is...okay, I guess. At least at the beginning.
The lockpicking in this game is very, very good. It's probably the only thing I genuinely liked. I think it's better than what Bethesda did with Skyrim.
Now for the cons:
The audio quality SOUNDS nice. When it works. Regularly, there are skips in the audio files, the NPC's around you will start their voice lines and then 3 seconds later start them again, over the first one, so that one person is saying the same thing twice with a 3 second delay. Additionally, sometimes your footsteps will cut out, and being a stealth game, THAT IS NOT GOOD. You need to be able to hear how loud you are in order to effectively execute your actions in a quiet manner. Distances also screw with the volume at times, sometimes you can hear things far away, sometimes you can't, even under the same circumstances.
The gameplay:
The stealth mechanics are okay. the Swoop ability is cool, the tools you have are mostly useful. Some you will never use, some you will NEVER have enough of, and the game really doesn't always give you enough to effectively get the job done, and you have to improvise if you screw up even once and waste something.
You can't jump. That's bad.
Climbing changes your character perspective from 1st to 3rd person. They should have made the entire game 3rd person, or not included the poor climbing mechanics.
Some controls are not explained to you, such as that X will drop you down from a rope or a ladder. It did not tell me this. I had to scour the control options to find it.
Stealth DETECTION:
The birds and dogs that will alert your enemies to your presence do not work. At all. Either you kill them, or they go ballistic when you're close, even if you make no noise. It's not noise that sets them off, it's fast movement. Which wouldn't be an issue, if the game didn't tell you that it was noise that sets them off.
Interactivity detection:
Sometimes you'll need to hide bodies. Sometimes the button command to pick them up doesn't appear. You're simply standing over the corpse wondering if you can actually pick it up, unless you push the button just to try. In addition to that, sometimes the crosshairs for the bow will disappear for a few moments, and won't re-appear until you put the bow away and take it out again.
It is also extremely unclear whether or not you are able to climb something. Sometimes it'll indicate that you can climb it with streaks of white paint on the object, or scratch marks. This is not always the case and thus makes it difficult to determine what you can and cannot climb.
Let me get to the worst of it:
When I said the story was okay, I lied. The story is god-awful. I've seen what Square Enix can do, with Deus Ex and Final Fantasy, and this is utter garbage in comparison. If I didn't know who made it, I would not guess SE. This story was like dead animals talking to me. There was a massive difference in who worked on this at SE, because FF 14 had me screaming in agony or joy over different characters, where as this had me screaming in agony because I wanted to bash my head against a wall. The characters are emotionless, dead, gave me no cause to like them. The crow in the clock tower had more personality than Garret. I had no interest in pushing Garret to achieve his ultimate goal, which was confusing as hell.
Cutscenes:
Despite my FPS counter being at a steady 60-75, the cutscenes looked like they ran at about 20. Lip motion to voices was awful and poorly synced.
Here's the kicker, and my final point. This does contain spoilers for the end of the story.
At the end of the story, you walk up behind Erin and try to use the shiny rock to pull the primal energy out of her. Once you do this, it jumps to a cutscene. Between the end of the gameplay and the beginning of the cutscene, Erin has somehow gone from sitting on the ground inside an enclosed ship, to holding on to your hand over the edge of broken wood, over the ocean. What happened. I don't know.
3/10, this game is awful. It makes me sad that this is the same company that made Final Fantasy 14.

A really thought-provoking game that puts a different perspective on war. Most of us live in a world where we are sheltered from the horrors of warcrimes and don't have to fight for survival on a daily basis. When playing the game, you are in the point of view of a group of friends just trying to make it to the next day. If you want to help real people living in conditions such as this, buying the game alone helps out the charity War Child. The game offers an immersive story that develops your opinions towards the characters. The decisions you make (in day or night) could mean life or death for your people. One can only imagine the choices people are forced to make in reality when placed under these conditions. Overall, the game did a good job at making me think about life and what I truly value. One of the best games I've played.

The game is strategic oriented and heavily influenced by your management. One small decision or mishap may lead to an unfortunate outcome. The following is a quick summary of key details and what to expect since there isn't much of a tutorial to begin with and finishing a playthrough will take several tries, research, and studying the mechanics on your own.
You play as the civilians who are trapped in a city which is conflicted in time of war. You can choose a pre-set story with characters or create a customed story. Some characters have specific characterisitcs that will make survival easier. Each story begins in an abandoned place which contains rubble that needs to be cleared and loot piles and storages that need to be scavenged for materials. This place will be your civilians' home during the time of survival before help arrives at the end. In order to survive through each story, tough choices have to be made for your civilians. Time ticks as you progress through the day, whether you choose to rest your civilians or have them do jobs around the place such as building stations, crafting weapons, upgrading, cooking food, or participate in other activities around the home. Once day is over, night is when you choose to set out a civilian to go scavenge for materials from an accessible place in the city or stay at home to rest or stay guarded from night raids. Each place that is open to scavenge contains randomly generated loot and may contain civilians or armed combatants. Therefore, you have to make a choice to either raid, steal, trade or kill in order to help those at home survive. Each decision may have a consequence that may negatively impact the civilians at home.
You have to maintain the health of your civilians by balancing through starvation, depression, tiredness, and healing wounds. Each concluding day will have a changing effect on your civilians. This game will test your patience and decision making of whether to steal, kill, or help others in order to survive til the very end..either with everyone or just one left.

Far Cry 4 is a worthy successor to Far Cry 3. It repeats the same formula that made Far Cry 3 great but changes the location and its main antagonist. The main storyline is pretty straightforward and while the character of antagonist Pagan Min doesn't even come close to the originality of an insane psychopath like Vaas from the previous game, Pagan is a well written bad buy excellently voiced by veteran voice actor Troy Baker. Some allies you'll encounter during the story are also well written but others are quite bland and I felt myself not caring for them at all.
Far Cry 4 does well in the graphics department as expected, the location of Kyrat is stunningly beautiful with snowy mountain tops, lush forests and many caves, hidden temples and interesting buildings to discover throughout the massive map that you can explore. The place is littered with outposts, guard patrols, bell towers etc and like in Far Cry 3 it's your job to take them all out. This also brings up a key problem I found.
There's just too much going on to actually enjoy the beautiful surroundings. Everywhere you go you are constantly being harassed by deadly animals, guard patrols or these mini events that the game thrusts upon you whether you like it or not. Now if this is right up your alley then you'll have a blast with this game but I sometimes got a little sick of it and it prevented me from doing stuff that I wanted to do.
There's plenty of side quests to undertake but unfortunately they are boring and repetitive for the most part. Go here, kill that, go there, disable this etc. There's a distinct lack of originality here that I've unfortunately come to expect from Ubisoft. There are some additional side quests you receive from various allies you'll meet and those are for the most part okay and are actually fun to undertake but as a whole it's time for Ubisoft to come up with something new because after disabling the 20th outpost or bell tower it's just time for something new...
Guns sound and feel great in this game of course and there's plenty to collect. But why Ubisoft locked certain attachments for certain weapons until after you've nearly completed the game is beyond me and is just overall a bad decision if you ask me. Apart from that nearly all the vehicles, weapons and attachments that were in Far Cry 3 with the addition of several new ones are all here for you to enjoy.
So is Far Cry 4 a good game? Yes I would say so. Is it better than Far Cry 3? No definitely not but it does do a lot of the same so if you liked Far Cry 3 a lot then chances are you're gonna like this one too.
Lastly I need to add that while Far Cry 4 runs quite well on my Core i7 2600K and GTX 970 on mostly high to ultra settings there are several graphical options you will need to tweak in order to get a steady 60 fps. At launch there were apparently several stability issues but I think most of those were fixed with updates. I only ever crashed to desktop once or twice in the 40 hours that it took to complete the game.

If you enjoyed Far Cry 3 and want more of the same, then Far Cry 4 will satiate your cravings.  The setting is a nice change from the tropical island world of Far Cry 3.  The gun play is solid and I appreciate the attention to detail with some of the gameplay elements.  Taking enemy outposts without being detected is extremely fun, and probably what I enjoyed most about the game.  The story is pretty ridiculous, which is the point I suppose.  I didn't bother to finish the story, as I just didn't care enough.  The co-op was pretty lackluster, but that's not why I play Far Cry.  It's still inadequate to see something half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥though.
Pros:
+ Setting (absolutely beautiful open world)
+ Plenty to do in the world, although slightly tedious
+ Nice implementation of wildlife
+ Solid gun play
+ Visuals are good (2014 standards) and decently optimized (good SLI scaling as well)
Cons:
- Absurd and disengaging story that takes itself too seriously for how dumb it is
- Co-op is pointless
- The replay value is fairly low if you've played a lot of Far Cry 3
Grade: B-

The UI is an atrocity. It provides the worst experience I have ever encountered. It's as complicated and fiddly as dwarf fortress, with about 1% of its functionality. What makes this intolerable is that this game could otherwise be pretty cool.
I suppose one could get used to it, but the alternatives that provide similar experiences with significantly less frustration exist, and thus, I can't recommend it at this time.
People might argue that it's early access, or that it's complexity is more immersive (the opposite of which is the case), but that is wrong. The design is clearly inspired by another user interface atrocity: Space Station 13. SS13 had one clear advantage though: A mouse cursor to interact with things. Here, you have to use about 5 input elements - some several times - to switch to another tool and resource. This is made worse by the availability of only two active slots. It's like being severly handicapped.
This clearly demonstrates that the developer has not looked at the wisdom uncovered in interactive entertainment in the last 20 years. If you want an immersive interface, look at Dead Space. They made conscious decisions to make the otherwise annoying parts of the interface a little more standard-compliant, sacrificing tiny bits of immersion, but eliminating massively anti-immersive annoyances.
"Usability first, at all times" should be on the developers mind, after he throws the whole UI concept out the window. It needs a complete redesign. It also performs really badly compared to other systems simulations, which give the player the impression of being far more complex at the same time.
If those things are fixed, and a few features added (like circuits that aren't approximately Z3 times 100 sized, or more crazy stuff from ss13), the game could be damn fine.

Even though the game is in very early access the game still has a decent amount of content and there's in-depth stuff as well. The devs are very active and update frequently and also seem to listen to the community on Discord for example. Stationeers definitely has potential and the full version will probably be an excellent game.

I really wanted to like this game, I really did. I bought the ultimate pack to support the developers but man this has been a huge disappointment of a game.
- The "Full version" (Ultimate Pack) of the game which includes all heroes is priced $10 less than Overwatch was priced at release. Now I know this game is compared to Overwatch a lot and even though they're different in a lot of ways we can compare the MTX model for both. In Gigantic a legendary skin is about 500 rubies, (4.99 USD I believe) or 15,000 Crowns which takes about 15 hours to get. Crowns are like the in-game currency that you get for completing a match, you get around 90 per match but you get small bonuses when you level up or complete daily fate cards (challenges) which grant you around 50 crowns a piece per day. You also get 100 crowns each time you level a characters mastery stat but these bonuses don't add up to much. Now you might be thinking 15 hours for a legendary skin isn't that unreasonable, right? Well it wouldn't be except for the fact that if you go with buying skins you miss out on buying the creatures that in some cases are objectively better than the default ones or fit niche purposes during a match. Each creature is around 11,000 crowns except the guardian which is around 5-6,000. There's 6 unlockable creatures in total which adds up to about 60,000 crowns meaning it would take you 60 hours to unlock all of the creatures which should have been included with the ultimate pack making buying skins very detrimental to you unless you open up that wallet and slap down another $5 on top of your $30 you already spent on the game. On top of this the creatures that I was talking about earlier are also buyable with the premium currency, rubies meaning you can pay to get an early advantage over other people. There is no lootbox system or anything like that in this game to help you get cosmetics, your only options are to forego your creatures or open up your wallet, even if you already threw $30 at them for the ultimate pack.
- The game is incredibly unpolished. There's not even any pre-game or post-game chat meaning it's almost impossible to get a decent comp set up because you can't communicate with anyone during the champion selection screen, you just have to HOPE that your teamates will choose appropriate heroes to accommodate the situation. The levelling system uses a branching system in which you can upgrade each one of your heroes 5 skills twice with each level having 2 different upgrade choices depending on the branch you go down. There's no way to see what upgrades are available for a skill and what they lead to outside of a game so you have to go off-site to read the upgrade paths you can takes your characters skills down.
- The heroes roster is very imbalanced. Some heroes are next to useless (Vadasi) while others are insanely easy to be good with and require very little skill to use effectively. (Beckett, Tripp, Lord Knossus)
- The mechanics aren't explained well. Despite having a tutorial it leaves many mechanics unexplained. There's like 17 different status effects and the only real way to figure out what each one does outside of the couple of obvious ones is to google it, there's no in-game explanation for a majority of them.
- The game is an absolute cluster♥♥♥♥. Teamfights often devolve into flashing lights and bright explosions where you can't see anything. It's very hard to tell what's going on because the effects are so extremely exaggerated making it hard to fight with any sort of strategy.
- There is no competitive ladder. I'm not sure if there's even a hidden MMR system as I've seen very experienced players go up against total noobs and just stomp the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of them in an absolute slaughter.
- The game is unoptimized. The 6GB of RAM requirement hurts the game greatly as not everyone has a great computer. I can run the game great personally, but the reason games like CSGO and DOTA are so successful is because they can run on a toaster while this game is the complete opposite. Ontop of that there's a 60FPS cap for no apparent reason, just another thing the devs didn't fully think through.
Anyway, that's my review. I'm really, really sleepy right now so I kind of rambled a bit but I got the key points in. I'm a huge fan of the King's bounty series - the gradual progression of the main character, picking and choosing your battles amidst various locations, the feeling of slowly growing from a ragtag group with an inexperienced leader to a formidable army with a powerful commander. Somewhere around once every couple years I've come back to pick up the next game in the series, and while they've been somewhat losing their charm over time they've mostly seemed to scratch that occasional itch I have for this type of game.
Of the games in the series, Dark Side is somewhere in the middle. I find it more interesting than Warriors of the North but less interesting than the earlier entries. Many people put Armored Princess at the top of their list, but I think much of this is because the concept was still fresh back then.
However Armored Princess did do some things that the later games didn't learn from. Armored Princess was a smaller game, with fewer battles that were more carefully placed and a tighter emphasis on strategy over brute forcing, and while there were fewer total units available there was a much greater variety in the composition of enemy armies. Dark Side starts off rough for the first few hours, then gets considerably better, and then you hit a point of realizing that every new location is basically the same battle 20 times. Every battle on an elven island is the same elven army using the same tactics, every battle in a dwarven realm is the same group of creatures doing the same things. By the middle of the game, you realize that maybe 2-3 battles into a new location you've determined the strategy that works - and now you just do the same thing 20 more times. With each battle lasting 10-15 minutes, this ends up becoming a very numbing grind and you start groaning when the game says "complete this quest: destroy four more of the same armies you've already completely dominated."
Once you've figured out your tactics, even on Impossible difficulty there's really no longer any sense of risk. I play on Impossible, and while in earlier games it felt like you had to always be on your toes to keep from facing a considerable loss, in this game once I passed those difficult first 10 or so hours and acquired some key spells and units, it just became too easy. At one point I was blindly picking enemies on the map without even considering their composition, and I stumbled onto an army that was vastly stronger than any of the armies I'd been facing - like a jump from 100 level 4 creatures to 200 level 5 creatures. At first this shocked me and I found myself getting invested in the game again, thinking I'd really have to think carefully to tackle this one. However I employed the exact same strategy and ended up winning with no losses. In short, you end up becoming too overpowered too quickly, and that's when it just becomes a grind.
There are also bugs that crop up - certain quests cannot be completed, other quests will simply stop without telling you that you need to wait until later in the game, some unit abilities and spells don't work as expected, unit sound effects occasionally just stop working, and certain things will simply crash the game to the desktop. While these don't happen enough to entirely ruin the experience, there is a major sense of "forget it" that you feel when at the end of a 15 minute battle the game crashes because you tried to turn back time on a unit that had a shield in the prior round but not this round, or an assassin tried to use the murder ability on a summoned unit.
Dark Side has tons of troop types, tons of spells, lots of mechanics, plenty of tricks. However after about 2/3 into the game I just lost interest. This was at about 100 hours in, and while spending 100 hours in a game before getting bored sounds like a pretty stupid complaint, the first two King's Bounty games both carried me to the end. Warriors of the North got me about 90% through before I lost interest, and this one somewhere around 60% through before I just couldn't get invested anymore. My point is, the formula is getting stale.
So why do I recommend it? Because until that burnout point, it was fun. It was more of the same King's Bounty formula, better than Warriors of the North, and it scratched that itch for a strategy game with a sense of progression. If you just want more of the same, Dark Side is better than Warriors of the North but doesn't have that same early-experience magic of the first two titles. If you found yourself losing interest with Warriors of the North, I think you're going to burn out entirely on this one. But before you do, you'll have some fun for a chunk of time that's worth the cheap (as of writing) price of entry. However, while I don't think they're planning any more King's Bounty games, even if they did I'm pretty sure this one marks the end of my interest in the series.

I honestly can't tell if I can recommend this game or not, be it to a complete newcomer or to a King's Bounty veteran.
On one hand, the basic mechanics are still enjoyable, the graphics (while dated) remain charming, most of the music is great and the game overall has some pleasant moments. However, all of this ends up being spread over too many hours, too many fetch quest chains, too many worlds. If Armored Princess had jacked difficulty curve past the 1st island and Warriors of the North ended up being repetetive, this game takes both of these flaws and amplifies them, having one of the hardest beginnings in KB games (even for Demoness, let alone for mana-lacking Vampire or rage-based Orc) and turning into a massive slog half-way through. If you mix this with an already repetetive gameplay style, you end up with a completionist's nightmare. Throw in a handful of bugs (the game loves to crash, especially while casting certain spells), confusing quest/world design (an important NPC missing a map marker, unmarked items you have to search for on a map as large, if not bigger than Verona in AP, certain Elven map is a half-empty labirynth of paths I found obnoxious to navigate, painting-collecting quest that's not marked in your journal at all, forcing you to work through it blindly... or just read a guide) and boring, uninspired plot with paper-thin characters...
At 80 hours, I'm roughly at the 75-80% mark. All that's left for me is cleaning up a handful of locations, then going for the final gauntlet. Then maybe two more playthroughs to get the achievements for Orc and Vampire...
And yet the game's gathering digital dust on my hard disk while I'm having far more fun playing Armored Princess again.

So this game is Oregon Trail + Final Fight. It's hard, there's a lot of RNG, and it can be completely unfair at times. It's also some of the most fun I've had playing a game with permadeath in a LONG time (and I LOVE games with permadeath)!
The games are quick (probably 2 hours for a full game, obviously much less if you lose early) so losing isn't that big of a deal, there are a TON of options and encounters and characters and items and what not, so replayability is through the roof, the action portion of the game is super solid, and the writing and stylings are fantastic (and quite amusing). There are also lots of little touches here and there (like the varied font types or the special characters) that really make this game so much more then just the sum of it's parts.
Finally, I can't close this review without talking about the devs. These guys are amazing. Go check the dicussion forums. There are multiple devs answering questions, personally taking suggestions, working with people to squash bugs, listening and respondign to critism, talking about the future of the game (which apparently is going to be TONS of new content, with the devs saying something like "you keep playing and we'll keep making content"), etc. Seriously, this level of positive community interaction is just incredible and the devs deserve a LOT of kudos, love, and sales of their (totally awesome) game because of it.
So yeah, buy this game. It's silly fun, a crazy good value for the money, and the devs are rock stars. Can't recommend it enough.

Amazing game! Outstanding overall! Has an amazing open world map, which is huge. Has tons of colectables, locations, missions, side activities as you would expect from a open world game. The combat is good, the crafting system is good, the amount of diffrent weapons is good; theres just so much in this game that makes it really fun to play. The campaign missions vary and are all outstanding and contrasting in their own ways. Even the main characters such as Pagan Min are brought to life, him being the evil tyrant dictator of Kyrat. Summary:
You are going back to Kyrat to spread your mother’s ashes. Kyrat is a small Himalayan country ruined but civil war, a brutal dictator and gangs. Without spoiling anything you find yourself somehow related to the situation and you start help one of the resistance groups to take down the dictator and to bring order to the chaos. You are presented with a choice on how to go about helping which has an influence on the progression and the ending. The landscape is stunning and beautiful. You have to capture outposts and propaganda towers and hunt and skin animals in order to survive and progress through the story. The open world scenario makes you able to do a lot of stuff besides following the main story, which I find nice. The game has a bunch of cool cut scenes, and the main bad guy is wicked. You can mount vehicles, boats etc. and now (compared to FC3) you can also mount choppers and fly around. Compared to FC3 my personal opinion is that FC3 has a slightly better story and the characters in FC3 are also better and more believable than in FC4!
If you like FC3 you will also like FC4. If you haven’t played FC3 I recommend that you do that first.

From the trailer and screenshots, Thief looks like it has the potential to be a beautifully designed game with an equally beautiful story, exploring a fantasy steam-punk world torn apart at the seams by a mysterious plague (cue Dishonored storyline). After completing the main storyline and a moderate amount of side quests I can say that this game is a disappointment, certainly not worth the listed price of $29.99.
The game looks like it may be a hybrid of Dishonored and Assassin Creed until the completion of the tutorial level, then you realize it will be reminiscent of the last Red Faction game (the one that was released years ago - a linear adventure that had very critical reviews). When you have a chance to make it out of your base of operations the movement around this city section directs you to set points: there is no climbing up the side of a building so you can utilize the rooftops like other games. The theme of movement is to go to Point A to Point B with two possible routes to get there. I felt like a caged animal wanting to go back to the time of 'noclip' just to experience some sort of breathing room.
Moving from city section to another you will experience load times, be it opening a window or going through a passage, something I find even by 2014 standards disappointing. If I do need to have a load time, I would find it worth it if the homes I was looking in were the like the first room you are in at the beginning of the game. But the layout of these homes are cookie cutter, making me feel that the game developers put all their eggs in one basket, trying to have the buyer remember that first five minutes of game play.
Voice acting is decent (more of a "meh") however it removed me from the game when three characters below try sounding like a group of ten to twenty people. Case in point, I was going from Point A to Point B and found that three city guards where worried about FOUR PEASANTS protesting in front of them. The dialog was something like "There are so many of them - what should we do?!" I don't know shower-shoes, how about you shoot the two in back, with Smith and Jones running the two in front through with their swords. They are unarmed civilians with NO WEAPONS WHAT SO EVER so it shouldn't be so hard, seriously boys if The Watch (can you developers call them something else? 'The Watch' is saturated in every media outlet these days) are so brutal like this game tries having you believe, this should happen all the time.
In some games you have the option to help out the poor OR make moral choices on who not to steal from. That little detail makes a game. This game shows numerous people in poverity, begging to the character you play for help. There is no option to 'Give Coin' or do something for them. Fallout 3 had the option to aid those people for a moral reward in XP or gear, yet Thief failed to use this system. They have loads of beggers, but no way to help them.
I am nitpicking but it's because this game presents itself as a reputable game. Even without good graphics a story is what makes a game. I would happily forgive the lack of graphically wow and game play if there was a good narrative other than: "You bad, thief, but this guy...let me tell you, he's waaaaaay worse." I found myself not caring about the characters as there was no driving force behind their own story being flushed out. I wasted hours looking for documents explaining what is happening with no luck.
It doesn't matter if you spare someone's life or take it, there is no effect on the ending of the game or the world for that matter. This made me come to a sad conclusion: the only thing that Thief does well is to separate you from your money, something that you are reminded of each passing minute you play this game. If you ever want to burn a day worth of game play trying to find a good story only to not find one, this is the game for you.
BUT it can be saved...
SOLUTIONS:
-Release a major patch with more content to improved the game. Add hidden documents regarding the characters. This is a reboot and new players like myself may be curious to know what are surroundings are.
-Add crowds where there should be crowds, three or four people don't cut it. Additionally, bodies in the street set the mood for revolution.
-Adjust the sound. If I'm twenty feet away, the people yelling shouldn't sound like they're right behind me.
-Allow the player to interact with their environment. Give money to beggers and have the option to bribe The Watch and others.
-Adjust the ending or overall play experience. If the thief wants to be Robin Hood have their experience different than the thief who wants to be on 'Pimp my Hideout.'
-Don't bait us with a sequal. Give us a bit of closure.

Thief is a reboot of the classic Thief series originally developed by Looking Glass Studios, with Ion Storm developing the third game in the series and published by Eidos Interactive. Now, Edios Montreal, the people behind the Dues Ex series, and Square Enix bring their own rendition of one of the greatest stealth series of all time to the modern era, and it doesn't fulfill it's old counterparts very well...
Thief is a stealth oriented exploration game about stealing stuff and finding and completing collectible sets. Thats about it. While stealth isn't necessarily required it is encouraged by the means of challenges. I understand the criticism that has been thrown at the Thief reboot and although I do agree with most of it, I still had a fun time with it... sometimes
Visually the game is very impressive and the performance was solid all the way through. Gameplay is kinda fun and engaging with a huge arsenal of arrows to manipulate your environment. Voice Acting was okay on most characters and sidecharacters and in all honesty, I don't really like the new Garrett, they should have brought the old voice actor to reprise his role
Puzzle design was unique and just difficult enough to keep me invested in its 8-10 hour campaign. Overall the sound design was fitting and thematic however I did encounter some sound issues here and there
The difficulty customization is a fantastic addition and allows you to completely design your own playthough. Think the game is too easy and you can easily pass a level by simply knocking out all the guards? Remove knockouts with an add-on and so on...
However, the story and characters are "meh" and makes it really hard to get involved in the world. I really couldn't care less about any of the characters in the game, even Garrett!
While challenging at some parts overall the game is easy. Levels can be passed by staying in the shadows and just shooting guards in the the head with your bow and arrows or by just sneaking in behind them and knocking them out with your blackjack
Level design, while not awful, is not as expansive and varied as I would have liked and certainly not as wide and as exapnsive as the older Thief games
The main storyline takes you about 8-10 hours to complete, and good God were the animations repetitive and annoying!
Overall, the reboot to Thief is a game best experienced at its worst difficulty with all the modifiers cranked up to 11. While the story does have its moments where it pulls you in, you are mostly going to be wandering around a level searching for your next loot to steal
With its issues there is still fun to be had in the world of Thief and I would recommend it to any stealth lover out there even if it doesn't live up to the world the previous Thief games had made many years before

The original Thief was one of my favorite PC games of all time. It was unique in that it completely focused on stealth. Let's start with the good news. The developers have listened to negative feedback and dialed back on quicktime events and slo-mo nonsense. Beyond the standard spread of difficulty modes you have the option to play with customised settings, enabling purists to disable everything they feel intrudes on their game, from objective markers to entire features. Using custom difficulties, you can play Thief with campaign-spanning permadeath, quicksaves disabled, or the stipulation that being detected at all constitutes mission failure.
On a moment-by-moment level, Thief delivers on the fantasy of being Garrett as well as – if not better than – its predecessors.
Thief – the series – has been many things, but it has always been important. The history of PC games doubles as a history of great ideas, and the other thing that the original Thief games, System Shock and Deus Ex have in common is that they expanded our sense of what the medium was capable of

1, This is one of a growing crop of (mostly) indie games that seeks to broaden the horizon of gaming narratives. I am in favor of this at an intellectual level but the practical reality is this and a lot of games like it do what they are doing by sacrificing gameplay and that strikes me as being an uncomfortable compromise at best.
2. It is kind of precious that the games designer and director Nina Freeman calls this fictionalized autobiography "based on a true story" as if her love life were an event on par w/ a natural disaster or a major murder investigation or something. If this was a song, you might call it a confessional. It's a story about how she met her first boyfriend playing games online.
3. I kind of identify w/ this premise. I have been making friends w/ and meeting people online since before that was a normal thing to do.
4. Gameplay in this is you basically click on things until it is time to stop clicking on things.
5. Number 4 on its own is fine but coupled with the fact that essentially nothing you do matters one iota in how this whole business plays out means gameplay is just a chore you have to do to get through the story. This is an inherent problem w/ this type of game.
6. If your presentation is done really, really well the problem in number 5 doesn't matter. (See:
.) In
, it is not done really, really well.
7. Nina Freeman casting herself as the lead was maybe not the best choice. It adds a certain voyeuristic allure since you know many of the details are true to her life but the fact is she just does not deliver the exceptional kind of performance a two person cast demands.
8. The other actor wasn't that great either. Also, I wanted to punch him in the face due to his haircut.
9. Speaking of voyeuristic allure, you will see a whole bunch of Nina Freeman in her underwear. There is sometimes a focus on certain body parts over others. I won't say which parts exactly but I will say at no point does she zoom in on, for example, her shoulder blade.
10. Much of this story is told as a conversation between the two main characters which is had while you play a simulacrum of a patently horrendous MMORPG. All you do is click on things (see number 4) but the programmers didn't even get that right. You constantly getting stuck and will find yourself being frustrated by its pathfinding while never once being engaged by the gameplay. I guess it looks kinda cute.
11. The idea behind 10 is the conversation rather than the gameplay that is important. That's pushing your luck even if the gameplay is solid, which it's not.
12. The other thing you click on is Nina Freeman's virtual computer desktop. You can find some alluringly voyeristic pics, poetry, and chat logs. This stuff was the most interesting part of the game and fleshed out her character well. Had the game's story been told exclusively through this medium, I think it would have been much improved.
13. A lot of people who like this game are going to accuse people who don't like it of just not getting it. This is garbage. I think people who actually do get this game are going to like it even less than those who don't. It attempts to spice up a mundane story by telling it in a new and engaging way. The way it actually works out is you do a bunch of busy work to  reveal a really rather unexceptional teenage narrative in an aggravatingly slow manner. The end result neither entertained nor moved me.
