It's a very simple but very fun game where you dig for oil in a Wild West setting.
To achieve that, you first use dousers to tell if there's oil, dig an oil rig, draw the pipes to the deposits and hire wagons to sell the oil. On each level you have a time limit and compete vs other oil tycoons.
Of course, the point is to turn a profit, and the oil prices fluctuate heavily during levels. You can choose when and how much you sell, or if you store it for when the prices rise.
In between levels you bid for plots of land against your competitors, and have a chance to improve your technology to retrieve oil faster, buy gizmos that boost your dousing/exploring ability or take a loan if you're in a tight spot.
It's an extremely simple game in terms of what you can actually do, but the gameplay can get frantic real fast.
The graphics are charming and the music, relaxing.
Very recommended for management game enthusiasts.

A fun little game where you play an oil tycoon squaring off against three others in a bid to force your enemies to drink your milksha... I mean, in a bid to get the most cash by drilling for oil and to become mayor.
Bid on a parcel of land, buy your upgrades and get out there and dig for oil! The gameplay is simple and reasonably addictive, forming a mixture of careful management, guesswork and calculating risk. You send out your dowsers to look for oil in the depths of the earth. Plonk your rig where you reckon the good stuff is, and send down a pipe. But oil isn't always easy to find. Sometimes its sunk deep, or behind a partial barrier of rock. That's where the trained mole comes in, diving joyously into the earth and uncovering little bits of the map beneath you. Once you've started tapping the sweet black gold you better get some wagons moving to the buyer's depot. Better be careful though, if the oil spurts up too thick and fast you'll get fines for spillage. Or the market might crash, forcing you to store the product in silos until prices recover. It's a neat little balancing act, but never too frantic.
In between digging for oil you get returned to town to buy upgrades, grease the palms of the odd helpful official and bid for shares in becoming mayor. All good clean fun. Except oil isn't clean. It's a filthy business.
This game is good for one more turn shennanigans. However, after completing it a couple of times I can imagine you won't want to return to it for a long time. There's not overly much to it. But that's fine. The price fits the amount of gameplay you'll find in this package. I imagine you'll get a good ten hours out of it, not bad for seven pounds or so.
Any flaws? Well, it could do with a little more personality when it comes to your rivals. You don't really feel any comedy antagonism against them. They just say a few ho-hum stock phrases and politely try to outdo you. You never feel like you're in too much competition against anyone. Which is a shame. The odd pop up bit of dialogue between missions with them twirling their moustaches or brandishing their parasols at you might be amusing. The game could also do with some random events or periodic temporary mechanics to keep things from getting stale. Perhaps subsidence knocking out oil-rigs for a time until they can be shored back up. A passel of free-herders running cattle across the map. A travelling snake oil merchant giving your crew a little mystery bottle of 'pep' to move their horses faster.

But all in all Turmoil is a perfectly fine game. Nothing earth-shaking but good fun for a few idle evenings of play. It's the definition of a good 'seven out of ten' game, one I can cheerfully recommend.

Dark Side is easily the best game in the already great series for several reasons. First of all, the game has pretty much every single unit from all the previous games, allowing for unmatched army customization freedom, compared to previous games. It also introduces some new units and female variations of old units, which only makes the aforementioned advantage even more noticeable. Secondly, most of the units from the previous games received new passive and active abilities, providing most of them with unique possibilities to excel in particular tactical scenarios. All of this together results in a game that has significantly improved tactical depth compared to its predecessors, since the overal number of viable tactics and synergistic unit combinations has only increased.
As for the story and quality of writing, all I can say is that I don't play turn based strategy/tactics games for this.

I'm really enjoying this game so far - not been playing for long but already I find it quite compelling and enjoyable.
The first one was fun (of the new series - not the antiquated original) but I find myself preferring the Dark Side - it's just more fun to be bad.
Pros:
- You can play as Orc, Demoness or Vampire - all 3 have unique skills, qualities and back stories - making it an infinitely replayable game.
- A wonderful selection of armies to choose from - including those from the first game as well as demons, orcs and undead (the staple of your army - at least to begin with).
- Story is engaging if a bit simple - but I think the gameplay makes up for it.
- Turn based strategy (I know many people don't like it but this game wouldn't work if it were real-time).
- Not a resource heavy game - you can run high resolution graphics on a pretty mid-weight graphics card without any problems (well I haven't experienced any).
Cons:
- None that have made me break out in a sweat or shout obscenities at my PC.
- You need to be quite careful assessing the dangerousness of your enemies before engaging - sometimes you can feel overwhelmed if you rush in without thinking.
I have learnt to read metro maps thanks to this game.

9/10. This is quite an addictive puzzle game. It has simple rules and a simple aesthetic. The bare-bones graphics might not be appealing at first, but I think this style was chosen deliberately to minimize any confusion or distractions from the game mechanics.The sound effects are pleasing, and can eventually accumulate into a makeshift musical score that reminds me of  early electronic artists like Kraftwerk. Gameplay is somewhat slow-paced. It does get challenging but never frantic. There is also an "Endless" mode where you never lose, but even in normal mode the game is pretty relaxing.
Some additional negatives: the menu system is poorly organized. You can find everything once you get used to it, but it should have had a more intuitive design in the first place. Also, like most puzzle games, it can get pretty repetitive. There are a few different maps, but still not a huge amount of variety.
This game is not going to blow your mind, but it's a good way to chill out and unwind for a bit.

Death Road to Canada is an absolutely adorable rouge-like game, despite the amount of spewing guts, bones and limbs flying everywhere around.
Imagine for a second Faster Than Light fused with Project Zomboid, plus ridiculous amount of cute humor. Nothing vulgar or dark. Biggest insult you'll encounter in this game is Dingus (and even that is not an insult :p).
There's almost not a single conversation in-game that didn't give me a little smile.
Combat, and the whole game itself, is simple, minimalistic, non complex at all and still manages to be so addictive and amazing.
Today many games advertise on "randomly generated" marketing, but not as many manage to execute the mechanic well. Death Road to Canada is not bragging about it, yet it has one of the most impressive randomization mechanics I've ever seen in games.
When I said it has resemblance to FTL, it's not just about its replayability, but also the perfectly short campaign.
Games with replay value should be exactly like that. Short and interesting, and not have 1000s of hours per playthrough. My shortest (successful) playthorugh on normal difficulty was approximately 1.5 hours. I am yet to do the longer campaign mode, but am already eager to try it out after countless amounts of fails.
And speaking of fails, unlike many other rouge-like games, this one does not make you want to smash your keyboard againt the display when you lose. i can't quite explain why. Maybe it's the games general poistivity vibe, maybe it's because things lost are not so hard to gain. Maybe both.
And finally for someone like myself who is absolutely into retro games, this one will grab nostalgia by its weakest point. Amazing pixel art combined with great 8-bit soundtrack is a perfect formula to satisfy all the gamers dating way back from times of NES/Sega consoles.
Overall amazing. I have absolutely not a single complaint.
It's humorous, simple, minimalistic, beautiful and has got great replay value to it.
Passing a game like this is like a sin for every self respective gamer, to say the least

Gameplay is pretty much the same. Weapons are the same as well. There are towers you climb to reveal map, and camps you capture to remove hostiles, same as in FC3. You have a wingsuit, just like FC3, but unlike in FC3, the wingsuit is far more useful here, what with it being in the Hymalaias.
It may seem like negatives, but ultimately, the game is stunning. The mountains are gorgeous, and it just makes one long for a trip to Nepal or Tibet. And that is the main plus of the game.
So in short, Far Cry 4 is the same game as Far Cry 3, but in a huge location of the Hymalaias.

This game was...really, really weird.  You play as a girl, Nina, who falls in love with a boy via an MMO.  Being able to control Nina's desktop and browse her emails, look at her social media, etc. was actually a pretty unique premise that I thought was probably the best part of this game.  The story itself was reasonably engaging, but it definitely could have used some higher quality writing to convey itself.  Honestly, the main fault I have with this game was the boring gameplay.  Through the story, Nina plays the MMO while she voice chats with the object of her affection.  This MMO world is very underdeveloped and feels downright broken at some points, which causes frustration while essentially trying to get all of the conversation to trigger while your character is stuck in a corner again.
Ultimately, Cibele isn't an awful game by any means, but it probably could have used a little more development time to become something more interesting to the gaming community.
Cringe simulator

I can definitely see the reasoning for the mixed rating for this game (length of gameplay being one aspect), but it was absolutely the most real representation to get into the mind of Nina and her relationship built up with another player in an MMO. The layout of interacting with the outer game (Cibele) was absolutely perfect, imho. I thought the inner gameplay was paced well (Valtameri) to further the narrative.
I was fully engaged in the narrative, and fully recommend the game to others who enjoy narrative games involving a relationship.

I don't understand why everyone is taking a dump on this game. It may have been during earlier builds of the game when they were made, but I don't see anything wrong with it now. The people who complain about it being aimed and directed towards controllers are partially right, but there's something they missed. It doesnt brainiac to figure out that "Hey, maybe the controls are in the section labeled HOW TO PLAY". Now unless you only have half of a working brain you can go to the how to play section and see the entire list of controls on how to play on a Xbox controller AND a mouse and keyboard. The part where they rip on it is because the pop ups show Xbox controls instead of keyboard controls, but unless you need to see the button on screen for what you need to press 24/7, then you probably shouldn't be playing video games.
Now, the gameplay is pretty simple. It's like TTT in a way. One bad guy that tries to kill/stop everyone. It's really fast paced and the objectives change location constantly. Theres only one Map, but the generator changes locations and the bust changes locations along with the lever machine.
Each character has there own active and passive abilities. All the way from playing prop hunt to playing detective each character brings something cool to the table.
Cool things about the game: When you are the Rouge Agent you can press Q while looking at someone and recruit them as a Henchman; allowing you to have a partner in the game. It's especially fun is right before you die you hench the person who killed you so they can carry out your mission.
The game even adds an extra set of paranoia by making where even though the rouge agent is dead, the game still continues causing distrust to the very end of the match.
I've played it for about three hours now and have loved every second of this game. The only reason it's ripped on is because it was made by students, but it is an endless replay value game just like how TTT is.
I definitely reccomend this game.

Mini Metro is one of those hidden gems that was destined to be hidden.
The graphics are clear, crisp. The colours are used precisely and in a thought out manner. It's well animated too. The fluididty is perfect for this type of game.
As for the gameplay: The premise is simple. You have shapes dotted around the map. Those are stations. Each station will have passengers pop up, all wanting to go to a different shape station. The goal is to get them there quickly and efficently without the stations filling up.
Difficulty's added by the limited amount of trains and lines, adding new shapes and stations and also having to sometimes go through water with a limited amount of tunnels.
It's difficult, I'll say that much. I completed "Deliver xxx amount of passengers" achievements, but I never managed to complete the more difficult achievements. So, if you like becoming efficent in a single game, then this is perfect for you.
One gripe though: Everything's slightly randomized. Because of that, some runs are doomed from the start. Like for example I had to instantly spend a tunnel because the station was slightly touching the water. You can't really move the tracks, so that couldn't be done either.
Overall:
7/10

This is likely exactly what you think it is.  You are going along a path and, along the way, there are encounters both of a "choose your own adventure" kind where it's a scenario and it asks for a reaction and of a more interactive nature.  The interactive scenarios have you raiding buildings or making your way through floods of zombies.
It is a lot like Organ Trail, except there's a bit more of an exploration / combat aspect than I remember Organ Trail having (though it's been awhile since I played, so maybe I've forgotten a bit ...).  If you liked Organ Trail, you will probably like this game as well.
The game isn't overly complicated and that's part of what I enjoy.  I'm not keen on survival games where you have to micromanage your characters down to the bowel movements -- this game has just the right level of complexity, I feel, in the way it keeps track of morale, food, and health.
I definitely recommend it (edited this review because my complaints are all resolved!)

After seeing this game I really wanted to like it. The art style is really cool, and it felt like it'd be a nice break from OW. Unfortunately, it turned out to be one of the most frustrating games I've ever played. Each match is just one side or the other getting destroyed, so neither team ends up having a fun game, and the heros are so disgustingly unbalanced I'm amazed they were actually released into the final game.
These two things combine with the unfortunately long respawn time to ensure you'll spend more of the match spectating your team than actually playing, especially if you're on the team that's getting killed. And the time you are in the match is either walking around looking for something to do, or getting stuck in a 2-3v1 with no way out because every hero that isn't classified as high-mobility is only capable of moving about 2 inches during combat. Even with a dodge mechanic, you might as well be standing still.
Skill-wise the game is not much better. Despite having more skills per character on average than Overwatch, each hero feels distinctly unequipped in larger fights or back to back skirmishes, since everything is a one-shot attack with approximately .01% more effectiveness than your primary fire. And upgrading the skills during the fight is both incredibly obnoxious and unimportant, since those increases also feel negligible.
Despite these things being glaringly obvious after the first match of the game, I played several matches hoping it was just me being bad (Still a distinct possibility.) But then I loaded into a match and was unable to move, use chat, upgrade skills, or literally do anything but open the menu. So I alt-F4ed my way out of the game (There's no quit button during matches for some stupid reason) and restarted the client. Fortunately, it allowed me to join the game I'd left, and I could now play, but half the UI didn't work this time. The skill slots were empty, the health bar was stuck at full so I had no idea if I was dying, the stamina bar was stuck at full, and I couldn't upgrade any of the skills.
Overall, I've just found this game to be practically unplayable, and most certainly not with any degree of fun. Add to the fact that it runs via Arc, and I'd advise any friend who asked about this game to stay away from it.

I don't recommend this game unless it's on sale and I'll explain why.
The world, although masterfully crafted, is rather bland.  Many of the apartments that you break into, if not all of them, are just completely devoid of life.  Outside of missions specific places there is no one sleeping in a bed that you have to creep around to avoid waking, no one resting on a chair by a window watching the world fall to crap, no one eating dinner at a table.  In fact there is simply no one at all in these apartments! You loot away without a care to be quiet at all.  You're basically just looting abandoned houses.  Other than some traps that might be set up you're pretty much danger free and this makes the whole experience just an act of opening a treasure chest in any rpg/adventure game -- only now you have to root around in it and watch annoying animated repeatedly of you opening and window by mashing away at a button.
The world is segmented and the game doesn't save the state of one area when you leave it.  Any guards you took out just a moment ago will be reawoken and walking the same path just because you opened a window leading to another street or pushed aside yet another beam to squeeze through some boxes.  The annoying women standing alone by some food stand for some reason in the middle of the night, adjusting her hat over and over again, is just going to be standing there adjusting her hat again even though you clubbed her head in just a moment ago.
The story!  A big giant head full of WTF is waiting you when/if you beat this game.  The cut scene feels like it's just mashed in there with no regards to what happened beforehand and you'll understand what I mean if you make it to the end.  Which you will be treated to a very short and unsatisfying conclusion to what you've invested your time in.
There's points in the game where you can make a choice and I was hoping that it would play out somehow further into the game, have some sort of bearing as to what would happen later on.  Nope.
The treasure trunks!  I know this is just a small thing, but it was something that bothered me enough to write about it.  Why is it when I open these things, which stand about two feet tall, I'm greeted with a 4 in deep interior?  That's it, 4 inches and you hit wood?  I don't know if it's supposed to resemble a removable layer, like a tool box or fishing kit and there is more below, but I can't help but feel that's not it.  I think it was just a lazy♥♥♥♥♥design and they didn't take the time to, maybe, throw some junk texture in and make it appear that the loot your taking is sitting on a pile of crap and giving the trunk the appearance of depth.  No, instead you open up a deep looking trunk and peer in just to see a lonely cup and maybe some change sitting on some wood that's 4 inches from the top.
The sound!  What the hell was going on with the sound?  Two people would be talking and one would be really loud while the other one could barely be heard?  Thankfully I play with subtitles on otherwise I would likely have missed out on a lot of conversations.
All in all though, the game was incredibly beatiful and ran incredibly smooth.  Some parts were just wonderfully done and gave a rich experience, but I think I walk away with the feeling that this game was actually rather boring, empty and devoid of a real caring touch that could have turned it into something amazing.  Almost like all the development time was spent on the graphics and modelling and the rest was thrown in as an afterthough.

Cibele is short. You will be done with it in under an hour. It is a narrative game that doesn't have much narrative or anything interesting to stay, nor does it even manage to evoke nostalgia for the mmo player in any meaningful way.
The voice acting is poor, but tolerable.  Still, they could have tried to read the lines a couple more times to be more convincing.
The desktop interface is actually quite annoying as items pop over each other and are only closed via the tiny X in the upper right. They could have at least added a right click close... not that there was much to explore on the desktop. If you want to see this type of narrative done right, go find "Digital, A love story" instead.
Also, congrats cibele, you got me to grind in an MMO again listening to the forced dialog. The pathfinding was horrible, and I guess ichi (main male character) must be hacking since he can path right through anything to get to mobs. Overall this was 'good enough' to do what they wanted, but honestly was an opportunity squandered.
Overall this game felt lazy. I honestly though the setting was rich with opportunities for interesting things. There are lots of sources of 'guild drama' to pull from for good examples, and then to show that guild drama reaching into the game, the main tank quitting, the best DPS leaving b/c his gf left, or a girl 'hooking up' with the guild leader and kicking people from a raid spot, other dudes getting jealous and leaving / pulling half the guild to another, whatever, none of that is in this game.
I guess I'm writing this review because I thought there was really a chance for something good here, and it just ends so abruptly that it left me angry. If I thought gone home didn't do enough to justify the 10/20 dollars for it, this doesn't even deserve the 33.33 cents I payed in the humble bundle.
If you want a narrative game, try "to the moon", "her story", or "digital a love story", or even "gone home", leave this one in the junk pile.

HIT is a first-person shooter video game franchise. The series began on Microsoft Windows, and later expanded to consoles and handhelds. Several spin-off games have been released. The earlier games in the series are set primarily in World War II, including HIT , HIT 2, and HIT 3. Beginning with HIT 4: Modern HITfare, which is set in modern times, the series has shifted focus away from World War II. Modern Warfare, released November 2007, was followed by World at HIT and Modern HITfare 2. HIT Ops, released November 2010, takes place in the HIT War, while Modern HITfare 3, released November 2011, takes place in a near-future setting. Black HIT II, released November 2012, takes place mainly in the year 2025. HIT : Ghosts was released in November 2013. In May 2014, HIT Warfare was announced. In November 6, 2015, Black GIT 3 was released. The most recent game, Infinite HITfare was released on November 4, 2016.
The HIT games are published and owned by Activision. While Infinity Ward is still a developer, Treyarch and Sledgehammer Games also develop several of the titles with the release of the studios' games alternating with each other. Some games have been developed by Gray Matter Interactive, Nokia, Exakt Entertainment, Spark Unlimited, Amaze Entertainment, n-Space, Aspyr, Rebellion Developments, Ideaworks Game Studio, and nStigate Games. The games use a variety of engines, including the id Tech 3, the Treyarch NGL, and the IW engine.

I've come to like Death Road to Canada, its a neat little indie title that has had some thought put into it.  Its a nice twist on an old concept, I'd honestly say that it plays similar to faster than light, only instead of aliens you have to fight zombies. Death Road requires inventory and resource management, some on the fly environmental awareness and deciding whether or not you have the resources to recruit additional members to your group of happy, hopeful survivors. Speaking of recruitable members, you can come across a wide variety of survivors, ranging from your run of the mill pistol and crowbar toting survivor, to a Jason Vorhees lookalike and a magical anime girl, you can even recruit the occasional dog into your group. The game also has quite a few random encounters which can put your group members skills to the test. you may have to pass charisma or strenght checks or perhaps a more in depth shooting or medical skill check. The game has a quirky sense of humor that isn't for everyone, personally I find some of the jokes a little hit and miss. The game is a little pricey for what it is, with other indie titles of a similar style going for much less, would recommend waiting until Christmas or Summer when this will probably go on sale.
Positives
>Wide variety of weapons to choose from
>Suprisingly good character customisation
>Wide range of skills for your character
>A decent assortment of vehicles to find and use in your trek to Canada
>The randomly generated style of play can provide a decent challenge
>The humor is pretty good in places
>Soundtrack included in the game's files
>A pixel art style that has had some effort put into it
Negatives
>For those who have grown tired of pixel art, this may not be for you
>RNG can make the game punishingly difficult
>Sometimes the game provides you with little supplies on the early stages, amplifying the difficulty later on
>Zombie encounters are sometimes too few and far between, sometimes they occur too often
>Priced a little high for what is essentially a rather basic game (Honestly, Hotline Miami cost less than this)
Finally, I'll go on record by saying that this is perhaps the only game i've played so far where a character can be killed by stubbing their toe on a rock.

I been playing this game on and off my stream for a couple days now. I been hosting races as well. I bought this game blindly over the simple fact that the name spoke to me, and I am glad I did. With me being a huge zombie fan and actually moving to Canada in a month I just had to get it. Every run I have of this game I am smiling, laughing, or genuinely worried.
Now let's talk about the game. It's very fun! Like Oregon Trail but with the action sequences reminding me of Gauntlet or any over the top action game. I never truly feel safe, which is a good thing. Anything can happen, for example, have a lot of food? Well sorry you had a hole in your bag. Doing okay on health? Feral cats attack. The humor and randomness make this game feel unique. The game is simple and easy to learn but hard enough that I failed every run thus far. I encountered a few issues here and there but nothing game breaking, I considered it apart of the adventure.
When I first streamed this game my viewers loved it and a few purchased it. They been playing a lot and not one of them has anything really negative to say. We all made each other in the cute character creator and go on the adventure with another. It gives us stories and funny screen shots to share. We all love Death Road To Canada!

On top of that, game is pretty buggy. Latest update finally added levels that came to mobile over a year ago. But, unfortunately, it seems that nobody actually tested them and certain mechanics do not work the same way, making completing levels much, much harder. Even pouring money into the game does not guarantee that you will be able to complete them.
3/10 I do not recommend this game to anyone, even though it is technically playable.

It tickles my brain in a similar way to the best mods on Minecraft, but is even better than these due to the depth of the ingame systems (eg. atmospherics and electrical systems). Plus it is a Co-op game, and there is never a shortage of things for everyone to do (even at this early stage).
Stationeers is in early access, but in my experience the bugs have been slight and the game is extremely playable. There are certainly many new features planned before release (eg. motherships and away missions) and many usability improvements that can be implemented, however if you want to challenge yourself (and your friends) to survive and thrive in space this is a game well worth trying.
One negative I would highlight is that currently the tutorial is relatively limited and many of the mechanics are not well explained in-game, which I can see putting off many new players. Therefore, I would strongly suggest you have a look at some gameplay videos on Youtube to understand the basics, as well as some of the more complex tasks (like running an effective furnace and setting up a logic system so the solar panels automatically track the sun).

This is a "new gen" Thief, meant primarily for causal and console gamers and many long term fans of the Thief series will have issues with its simplified gameplay. Such is the trend with most contemporary A game titles. I'm a Thief fan almost since The Dark Project came out and I have mixed feelings about this one. The GUI looks terribly primitive, almost like an early temporary concept version, there are many issues with sound, guard AIs seem to be oddly insensitive to loud player's footsteps, there is very little variety of the NPCs, the mission levels are rather small and the most physically difficult tasks does the game itself for the player. The story has several unexplained plot holes. I'm mostly content with the game's setting, taking place a few hundred years after the original Thief trilogy and there are enough references to the "old Thief" world, but I hoped there would be an explanation of how another master thief Garrett (and Basso) appeared in the City. I can't go on without spoilers... The graphics are very nice (and that's probably the game's best feature) and the City looks mostly faithful to the old steampunk City, but absolute majority of its houses which you can enter (or rather break into) have strangely no NPCs inside. The City has more guards than civilian inhabitants. There are few new good ideas, like watch dogs and pet birds which you must avoid or else they will alert their owners. The system of Focus Upgrades looks like a good concept, but for the most part it  makes little difference on gameplay for an experienced stealth player.
The only thing that saves this game from being a total failure for seasoned players well experienced in the stealth genre is Custom Difficulty, which allows you to turn on/off and tune various gameplay elements - you can turn off most of the HUD assistance and indeed, some of the custom options can make the game a more challenging experience, like no kills or knockouts allowed, no healing or even no health damage allowed, no Focus ability allowed, no manual saves, etc...
VERDICT : If you are new to Thief series or stealth games in general, this may be a good introduction game to the stealth genre for you and it offers opportunity for different playstyles. If you are an experienced stealth genre fan, you never played a Thief game and would like a steampunk setting, it's worth a try and you may set the difficulty to your own liking, but it's still far from the most challenging stealth game experience out there and you may have some issues with it. If you are a hardcore fan of the original Thief trilogy, it will probably confuse and disappoint you. My recommendation of the game goes, for the most part, to the first two above mentioned groups. But I believe most of the old Thief fans will play the game out of pure curiosity anyway.
Still, I admit that after finishing the game in a violent "Predator" playstyle, I immediately started a new game on higher difficulty with no kills intended - it didn't happen to me for a long time with any game. Undeniably, it HAS some magic. And The City has many secrets to discover...

I love stealth games. Splinter cell, dishonored, anything with sneaking and hiding bodies.
This game captures some aspects of those games. It's more pure-stealth because if you're found, that's it, reload. You have limited combat skills and the game really shames you for getting caught. There are mechanics to deal with it but it just feels awful.
Upgrades are underwhelming, borderline essential tools have to be purchsed or you're stuck without options. There's no way of knowing which areas you've looted.
The guards were pretty unfairly alert on normal. Every tool had a quantity limit, so every arrow shot, every rope used costs money.
Let's discuss money! You loot things, knicknacks and baubles and you get little tiny bits of money. Big ticket items? Rare and amazing collectables? Yeah no, those dont earn you money. Those go in a display case in your base, which you rarely need to visit. Oh and looting, oh so tedious. You see a nightstand with 3 drawers? You have to open each one, in individual looting animations. It's sooooo slow.
Theif-vision is a limited resource that drains waaaay too fast, but is essential if you don't know the map/puzzles already.
The game witholds rewards for not looting every single item in a mission. One mission had over a hundred items, I missed 2. I lose that bonus. That's not fun, that's work.
You can custimize your playthroughs and challenges...if you want I guess.
The open world map is dumb. Its sidequests and police patrols. Who wants to dodge guards in the open world mode?!
TL;DR: Thief tries to do what better games do great and it falls short. Combat is bland, stealing 1000 dollars in 2 or 3 dollar chunks to buy a tool you NEED is not fun. Open world is underwhelming. Get dishonored instead.

I respect the hard work from the developers and appreciate the frequent updates, however some of the major design flaws make the gameplay more of a frustration than a mental challenge.
A few glaring flaws:
1. RNG decides how well you do. There are situations where it's absolutely impossible for you to get the city specific achievements. You can be using exactly the same strategy, and do exceptionally well/poor in different ocassions. That's unacceptable for a game that's essentially a time waster (even at maxmum speed, each game can take a long time to complete, with the first 10 mins completely boring and unnecessary).
2. The game challenges you by making the same stations appearing in close proximity - many times had  I had over 6 circles (and zero of any other kind) on the same island. At this point, it becomes a chore to manage the situation, and you wonder why the developers didn't try something more refreshing to make the game challenging.
3. The train loading optimization is poor - the simple rules the developer put together simply aren't enough. Here is an important one: a train should drop off passengers to pick up high priority passengers (those who are going to unique stations and the only way for them to arrive is through taking this one line).
4. The maxim speed in the game is way too slow, there should be way more then 2 levels of speed, I personally think the highest speed should be at least 3 to 4 times faster than the current maximum speed. This is very simple to implement, and making the game much less of a time waster. (At least giving the player control of how they would like to play the game.)
If the developers are able to make changes to address the design flaws, I would gladly change my reccomendation to positive. After all the execution of the game is quite well and the idea has a lot of potential to be a truly fun strategy/puzzle game.

This is rapidly becoming one of my most favorite games ever!
Stationeers is NOT for the casual player -- if you liked Factorio, heavily-modified Minecraft, KSP, or thought Space Engineers was too simple, this game is for you, even in Early Access!. It focuses on system design to build a functional space station (and motherships) in a challenging space setting.
PROS:
- Well thought out machine progession, automation, and design challenges
- Right balance of simulation and depth, without being too tedious
- Smooth, clean graphics let you focus on the system design
- Is hard, without being mercilessly hard or resorting to cheap random events, like space pirates.
- Lots and lots of things to play with
- Incredibly rewarding when you get a system functional; building your first auto-cycling airlock or a furnace setup, for example.
- Responsive, active developers regularly pushing updates
CONS:
- Needs a PAUSE button ASAP
- Information about machines and setups is still very sparse, but the game hasn't been out long. Take advantage of the Discord channel
- Needs a few more aesthetic options for blocks -- sloped/curved frames, ramps, etc.
Overall, I really love this game and I'm excited to see where it goes in Early Access!

So I went into this game fully expecting to love it. Within an hour, I had given up. It's a completely linear game with a cookie-cutter story and unlikable, boring characters. 'Linear' is not an inherently bad thing, but in this game it is. It's hard to feel sneaky when you know exactly where to go and know there's only one way to get there. It feels like a game of 'follow the dot.'
I was also never sure what would get me caught. I walked right in front of a guard (I'm talking 4 feet in front of him while he's looking straight at me) and he ignores me. I kind of expected a game based around stealth to at least have a more intelligent system than Skyrim.
Actually, thinking on it, Skyrim IS a better stealth game than this is. Which is not the conclusion I was expecting, but there it is. The stealth works better, the levels are less linear, and it's an overall more exciting stealth experience. And let me tell you, that says a hell of a lot more about Thief than it does about Skyrim.
Although most missions are quite linear, they are interesting and diverse. Roaming through the city between missions and the creepy Chapter 5 were the best parts of the game.

tl;dr: A roguelike zombie survival game done right.
There's many things about this game that just keep making making me tell myself "one more try" even after I've been playing it for hours. So far the only bug I've seen is when you get through a tiny space and your teamates will make an entire circle around the object so that they can get to you, that got my teamates killed many, many times.
One of my best runs so far, was with a guy named Dik, I gave him Megabuff and Warrior and tried to make him look like a biker. He had basically become a zombie master, with almost all abilities maxed out. I was 1 day from Canada, had more than 60 food and died to a molotov I threw at a group of zombies during a siege. My dog was the only one left, and even though he survived the siege, I hadn't teached him to drive a car, so I ended up losing and starting over. But I couldn't be mad at the game, because it was my fault.
Now, onto the pros and cons.
PROS:
+Randomly generated maps, survivors and personalities.
+Random events (I once got my character possessed by a demon)
+Zombies get more aggressive the more time you spend on a mission

This game has already brought me so much fun !
First off, the soundtrack :
It may not be the one you'd expect from a game depicting the fall of society and travelling in a deadly environment where you can die any day.
It's more one of an action-packed loot-and-run, inexplicable event-riddled road trip between friends (or are they?) soundtrack, holding a lot of energy and generally transmitting that "Let's freaking do it" vibe. I love it, and like listening to it outside of the game from time to time. You can also access it easily in the game files.
The graphics :
I personally like a lot good pixel art, and this one is truly good ! I don't really know what i could add, plus you can easily see for yourself. Pixels done right.
The gameplay :
Movements are fluid, there are a good choice of ways to deal with the zombies when it comes to the action part of the game, such as the classic melee weapons, pistols, shotguns, rifles. You can also sometimes manage to find molotovs, pipe bombs, grenades etc... Moreover, some characters have specific ways to (or not to!) deal with  zombies and get all that sweet loot.
Your ai teammates, if you choose to take any with you during looting missions are good at following you around, managing their stamina (as in not killing non threatening zombies) and shouldnt die stupidly too often.
The only issues i've encountered yet are some with the depths, for example when you think a zombie is farther than you vertically than it really is, and also sometimes walls "hitboxes" taking melee hits instead of zombies.
In the other part of the game, wich is managing your road trip across zombinated states toward canada, you are faced with events and a couple of choices. Theses can range to bandit attacks, zombie sieges, picking your looting location, recruiting or not the random survivors you come across along the road, and much more.
This is in my opinion the hardest part of the game, as i've lost more good men to bandits and unfortunate events than zombies, but it's not frustrating at all. You can generally move along without too much damage if your group doesnt have someone able to deal with the situation, and it generally rewards good thinking, instead of having randomly generated outcomes which you don't have control of. To summarize, choices are not always easy, but it's not frustrating either.
There is also a possibility of local coop, but having not tested it I cannot say if it's good or bad, though I'd say having that possibility is a nice plus !
Replayability :
I absolutely guarantee you won't see everyting there is to see in your first playthrough. You most likely won't win it either. There is a lot of elements, characters, items and events to discover, and also a few gamemodes available from the start. Custom characters are a nice addition, and the perks available are progressively upgraded as you play the game. Don't think they are useless from the start either.
I have yet to play the game more, but at roughly 5 hours of play I did not get bored of it for a second, so I'd say the game does have a lot of hours of fun ahead for you.
Overall one of the most fun "little" games i've played in a long time. The gameplay, immersion, music are all very good and the humor make this game unique and lovable.
Very fun and lots of replay value here!

Death Road To Canada is the essence of action roguelike gameplay: replayability, and yet simplicity with hidden layers of gameplay. While making your way to the land north of America, you'll be put into binds and situations that will force split-second decisions that can doom you. The mixture of the action gameplay along with the Oregon Trial like strategy gameplay works together rather well: as both end up enhancing the gameplay and choices of the other. And like a good roguelike: it's difficult, but manageable, forcing you to make difficult decisions that's not just there for show. It's the risk and reward mechanics that shine here: really rewarding you in pushing as far as your team can go without breaking, but punishing you heavily if you push too far.
Sure, you're going to struggle with some of the controls at first. But these are the right kind of “inaccurate” controls: controls that complement the gameplay in question. The only major problem I have with the game is the crashes (which is being addressed by the developer), and the AI can be REALLY dumb at times, getting itself killed rather easily. But if you like anything in the roguelike genre mixed with action, you'd be doing yourself a disservice by not picking up Death Road To Canada. It'll probably be on my “underrated games of the year” list, as it's not going to get the mainstream attention that it should. But you should give it your attention.

A very fun game, but not without it's faults.
While I enjoy each run I do, mostly due to the excellent soundtrack and humor, I've yet to actually reach Canada, though. Pretty much every time I get to the last day I've been stopped by an overwhelmingly huge siege of zombies in a tiny room, and my team dies pretty quickly afterwards. Not sure if the final massive wave is a set event or if I'm just unlucky, since my sample size is admittedly pretty small. It might be this game's version of Oregon Trail's river challenge, but unlike dodging rocks on a river, a siege of that size seems kinda impossible to complete.
I get that it's a survival game (which is one of the main things keeping me from becoming frustrated with bad RNG,) but I feel like the difficulty curve makes it really hard to recommend this to a general audience. If you're a results-driven person who needs to win to have fun or feel a sense of accomplishment, I think this game would be very frustrating. If you're okay with just seeing how far you can get and letting the trip ride out while enjoying some excellent music, I think you'd have a pretty good time. That said - even while I enjoy the journey, I feel like my best runs would be much more satisfying if I actually felt as if I had any chance of succeeding near the end. I have a really fun time playing, but it's sort of disappointing to have a run where you play/manage your resources well to only have the game tell you "nah, not this time, buddy."
What I'm saying is, it's a fun game, and a good way to burn some time, but could be a lot more satisfying with a rebalance patch or a casual mode. Either could make the game much more accessible, I think.

My first impression of They Bleed Pixels was a good one. I enjoyed the style, as well as the cute story that unfolded. The combat is interesting and it certainly feels satisfying to kick your enemies up in the air, in to a sawblade. Its really fun to dash to an enemy and proceed to stab stab stab like no tommorw. The music is nice and it makes me feel like I'm playing a platformer on a DOS system, which felt nostagic. It also has an interesting mechanic that allows you to create your own checkpoints. As I said my first impressions were positive, however, this game is ruined by overly twitchy controls and, in my opinion, sloppy level design.
Its really disappointing too, because I really wanted to like this game. I love the art style, and the combat is fun, but I just couldn't get past these huge faults. The game is difficult as you might guess, which is fine. I do enjoy being presented with a challenge. I enjoyed Super Meat Boy for the same reasons. The early levels of this game aren't to bad, but the further you get in the game the more it requires you to pull off precise and complex maneuvers. You'll have an extremely hard time with this, because a mere nudge of the joystick sends the main character flying across the screen. The controls are just so twitchy. Whats worse is some levels have slippery floors, so now you have to deal with slippery floors, and the overly sensitive controls. To be fair I'm using a Logitech controller, and maybe it plays different based on that, but I've never had this problem in other games.
The level design is sketchy in some places, but a majority of the levels I encountered have a long drop with a pit of spikes at the bottom. This can be frustrating because if you make a mistake, you have to watch the entire fall until you hit the spikes, which doesn't sound like much, but trust me after several deaths watching that fall will test your patience. You can't skip it either you have to wait till you die before you can start over. You are given three points of health, but 80% of the time you'll die instantly (Especially to sawblades, they knock you all over the place, draining all three points in seconds). Having that extra health usually just results in dragging out your death, and I find myself just mashing the revive button once I fall in to a pit of spikes I can't escape.
I sincerely wish I could tell you I enjoyed this game, but Those finer points just destroyed the experience for me. I wouldn't reccommend picking up this game unless its on sale and you really really like the style. Otherwise its not worth your money.

What's the difference between this game and a treadmill? Well atleast with the treadmill, I could be LOSING weight while going no where.
I normally don't get this bent out of shape over FREE games, but come on... Seriously who thought the "let's have an idle game that punishes idling" suggestion was a good idea?
Because that's what this is.
You have wait times and everything, but no auto collect so you have to check back every 5 minutes to actually get anywhere. And everything, I mean EVERYTHING has a wait time, some are just short enough to not justify shutting down the game, while others take hours or even DAYS to complete. What kills me most are the short ones because it's essentially the game just begging for your attention to stay and see them through. If you want any materials to collect, you have to be there to click on them manually once they're done, which means chopping trees, waiting and doing NOTHING for 5 minutes, getting maybe like 30 wood, and repeating.
The same applies to wounded units. They take several minutes to recoup after suffering losses in a battle, so even the battles, which might serve as a distraction mechanic between gathering periods, has a pointless down time further weighing this game down.
And while on the subject of battles.
What even is the point of the retreat mechanic?
If it's going bad enough you feel you're going to lose, you're going to have to spend that time recouping anyway, because you don't LOSE units in this game, they just get a boo-boo and need a few moments to cry it out before they're ready to go again. The only difference between retreating and just losing, is when you retreat, you get no XP for your soldiers at all. Different story if you just take the hit and deal with the recovery time you're going to get at the end of the battle ANYways. Atleast then you still get some XP for your trouble, even as minute of an ammount as it may be.
Of course all wait times can be bypassed with 1 of 2 currencies, gold and silver, the second being able to be bought WITH gold conveniently enough, and of course, gold can be obtained by shoveling real money into the system. Gold can also buy you units restricted ONLY to gold or 'crafting' which will take you the better part of the century to achieve, and also buy troop armament upgrades, so there's your token 'pay to win' aspect of course.
Overall, this game feels like it had the potential to be a fairly decent casualized 'grand stratagy' game, but the lack of any insight and direction or attempt at balance leaves it feeling really empty. Troop upgrades kill any requirement of stratagy you might need when you can just brute force every fight if you throw enough money at it, and wait times make little to no sense outside of being the hungry growls of the fearsome money-beast that lurks under the guise of "free to play" games.
Because if you actually want to make ANY progress in this game and don't have every second of your life to dedicate to it, you will need to feed it in order to get anywhere.

When I first encountered
it was via watching someone else play it. My first thoughts were “That looks really boring. Why so many lines? I don’t even like trains!” And that was that. Fast forward to present day, I was asked to review this title and at first was worried. What could I possible get out of such a simplistic game? What I got was a fun and challenging experience that reminded me to not judge a book by its cover. What this title lacks in flash and flair it makes up for with a solid and enjoyable gaming experience. While this might not be everyone’s cup of tea, if you enjoy a casual time with some challenge then definitely consider this game.
When you start things up you’re dumped right into the action. I’m not sure if there is a tutorial, I don’t think so, I had to learn via trial and error. While it was easy to pick up I would have liked there to be a tutorial or some sort of help feature just in case it’s needed. The game has no story, your goal is to create a functioning train system in the city of your choosing, there are eleven real world cities maps to play on. Each station is represented by a shape on the map, it can be a square, circle, diamond among other shapes. Passengers pop up at the stations wanting to get to another station and you have to connect the shapes with lines. Your train line can be short or long, straight but usually twisting. Each level you start with a limited amount of resources, usually always three lines; the amount of bridges and/or tunnels varies. As you connect more stations to each other you can make more passengers happy and hit milestones where you get more resources like extra lines, carriages to attach to a train to hold more people and other goodies. The challenge is that these are limited and the levels get more difficult and harder to manage the longer you play.
It’s the aforementioned rise in difficulty which makes this game fun. What starts off as simple and relaxing can turn into a disaster if you haven’t laid your tracks correctly leaving you in a panic to try and fix your lines to handle the influx of passengers. The way the cities grow is random so each time you play things will be different and you have to adjust accordingly. However, for the most part things started collapsing around 1000 passengers because of limited resources. There is also little variety in what resources are available and even with random city growth most levels tend to be a lot of the same thing since the basic strategy to the game is the same. The game does have three modes; normal, endless and extreme, which I don’t dare try. There are also daily challenges to participate in but for the most part you keep playing to try and beat your own score and try new layouts for your lines.
The graphics are very simple, however they are clean and easy to look at. There is nothing fancy going on here, the maps are based off of real world cities but even then they are still only bare bones in appearance. The stations are simple shapes and the different lines come in a variety of colors, each city has their own palette that mimics real world train line colors. The game offers a colorblind mode and a night mode, while I haven’t used these I am impressed that the developers added these features. The music in the game isn’t outstanding, but is soothing and fits well with the pacing of the game, there are also sound effects. The beeps of crowded train stations can be very useful if you become distracted elsewhere on the map.
is a great title to play casually for short bursts at a time, or even relax with endless mode. The game has Steam trading cards as well as achievements that offer a bit of challenge, some are easy to obtain while others require certain criteria be met that a player wouldn’t normally do in a level. The game can become very repetitive, however, and I personally wouldn’t mind more content or complexity. The price is decent but again, could offer more for the ten dollar price tag. Overall I recommend this title, it’s simple and fun and sometimes that’s all a game needs to be.

Before I get to what I didn’t like, I suppose I should get to what I thought was alright about this reboot. Visually speaking, it sports a solid look—from the environments to the characters, lighting, shadows, and art style. That’s not to say that it holds up in every regard visually; a lot of people don’t like Garrett’s redesign with a common complaint being his black eye liner making him look “emo,” but it’s not that hard to overlook if you don’t get caught up on it and you could even come to view it as something that makes sense given his chosen profession. The change of voice actor also didn’t really bother me, which is another hangup some people have when comparing it to its predecessors—other voices are either good or mediocre.
Of course, the audiovisual side of things is less important than the gameplay, and in that regard I found Thief to be underwhelming but (mostly) competent–from the mission design, to the sneaking mechanics, pacing, level design, etc. Unfortunately, a lot of what’s good about the game gets bogged down by various annoyances which include:
— Lots of repetitive forced animations. Grabbing loot, opening drawers and cabinets (many of which are empty and just waste your time), opening windows, enemy takedowns, etc. There’s also a long animation of Garrett moving a wooden beam out of his way that they reuse way too many times—sometimes they want you to mash X to move it and sometimes they don’t, although unlike the windows (more on those below) these are always used to section off map areas within a map or serve as a transition to a new area.
— There’s no indication as to whether or not a window leads to a lootable room within the map you’re in, or if it’s a transition to another area until after you’ve already initiated the animation; if you get the prompt to tap X it’s a lootable room, if you don’t it’s a map transition.
— I don’t believe the glow on rooms that strictly serve as loot locations goes away after you’ve cleared them and left, so you might end up going back into an empty room at some point if you don’t remember all of the places you’ve been.
— Somewhat clunky, limited movement. The context sensitive run/jump/mantle function screws up sometimes. There are areas you should be able to get to but can’t because the rope arrows only work at specific points. I understand the need to keep you caged to some extent, but there were times where I felt my options where limited when they shouldn’t have been.
— Cutscene direction and dialog was a bit stilted, the story felt like it wasn’t fully realized and the ending was kind of a mess. The only thing notable about the “Thief-taker General” is his massive bald spot and his penchant for being a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ other than that he was just a one-dimensional filler character that never amounted to much and got too much screen time.
— Awful audio mixing; sounds cut off abruptly instead of fading in and out and there are inconsistencies in how loud some sounds are compared to others.
—I understand it’s a reboot and they want to do their own thing, but I wish they had kept the Order of the Hammer in as a prominent backstory element. They only ever really indirectly refer to the Hammerites when they reference “The Old Gods” and with the brief appearance of the hammer symbolism in a specific area later in the game, outside of that it’s pretty much been taken out of the lore.
— Lastly, and perhaps most egregiously; the guards don’t indiscriminately call people taffers.
I don’t have much attachment to the original games but this one still managed to disappoint me in various ways; however, with all that being said I didn’t necessarily dislike it, it just has some glaring faults and questionable design decisions which left me feeling like it was largely wasted potential—unfinished and average in nearly every way.

TL;DR: This game is rather interesting, but turns into a monotonous grindfest within about an hour of playing (or however long you take to realize that better ships need to be grinded).
I was very intrigued by its looks and the fact that it focuses a lot on PvP, and decided to give it a shot. Unfortunately after only one PvP battle I realized, that I need a way better ship to even have the slightest chance at surviving the first 10 seconds after respawn.
For getting new ships, you have to upgrade the one you are currently using with points you can accumulate through PvP or PvE battles. Some kind of tech-tree then unlocks a new ship every time you reach a certain level of these upgrades, which makes it necessary to play each ship on the way to your dream ship for a rather long time.
After about 10-20 battles you then realize that it is always the same procedure over and over again. Find enemy, lock in on them, shoot them down or get shot down before you are able to do so. Structures floating in Space are supposed to offer some kind of tactical "hide and seek" option, but are really only in the way, as it mostly ends in head on confrontations anyways. Furthermore there will always be players in PvP that have way better equipment and/or ships than you do, and there is absolutely nothing you can do, to get to them/avoid confrontation with them (unless they leave you alone) or start in a newbie friendly environment.
Last but not least my main problem with it is that it offers quite a few options in fine tuning your ships (which is ofc a big plus) but unfortunately neither explains any of them (in fact there is hardly any tutorial, only a few missions which dont really explain anything), nor makes them accesable within a reasonable amount of time (I grinded for a full weekend for 30+ hours with doubled gains from fights you win, and made it to the T2 ships, which still were pretty bad).
If you are a hardcore gamer with a lot of free time you need to waste, this game might offer the right things for you, but if you are a casual player, you will very easily and very soon get frustrated with the monotony of not having a chance in PvP or doing the same PvE mission hundreds of times in a row...

This is a brilliant game which has a charming, minimalist art style reminiscent of the London Underground Tube map.
The controls are intuitive, both on PC and on the Android version, and the game is addictive and fun!
You are tasked with connecting an ever growing number of stations in some of the worlds most iconic cities, reprsented by simple shapes which denote the type of station. At these stations passengers will gather, their destination denoted by the shape of the passenger resembling that of station they wish to reach.
You will need to get these passengers to their destination before the station overcrowds. A progressively more difficult task as the number of stations and passengers increases.
To achieve this, you will need to carefully manage a limited number of trains, carriages, lines and bridges. These are granted to you on a weekly basis, often presented as an 'either/ or' choice.
This is where the challenge lies, becasue if any station overcrowds, it's game over.
There are a number of different levels to play, daily challenges and the developers are working on an endless mode,  last I heard. Available on PC, Android & IOS and is equally good across all.

If you're looking at buying Far Cry 4, you probably already know what the series is about. This one isn't different enough to bother explaining how it all works.
In fact, it was so similar to Far Cry 3 that I never really found myself very invested in it. The storyline is disappointing, and I found it really difficult to care about Ajay's story. Amita and Sabal, however, have a much more compelling storyline with some legimately difficult choices to make. It wasn't as simple as choices between morality, which was nice. However, there simply weren't enough choices, and not enough repercussions for those choices, to make that worthwhile, either.
Ubisoft is developing a particular habit of barely altering games and releasing another iteration a year later, which is something I believe I will no longer support. Buy Far Cry 4 on sale and it's worth it. I got it 60% off, and I feel like that price was definitely worth it, but nothing more. I will wait for a similar price for Far Cry Primal, though I am excited about the "minimalist" Far Cry experience it seems to offer.
I'd say I just barely would recommend this game to someone who has played other Far Cry games, especially Far Cry 3, but I would absolutely recommend it to someone new to the series who has no idea what these games are about. If this were my first Far Cry, I'd be amazed out of my mind. It isn't, so I'm not.

Wow... now this is an interesting game. Basically Oregon Trails with zombies and a healthy (And heavy) dose of humor that suddenly pops up in the strangest places. Just to give you an example of this seriously hard but enjoyable game, I'll just mention my best run yet.
Start off with two of my own characters, quickly recruited two more, and raided multiple places including buttville's police department.
Then a rather hard siege came. I lost one; an annoying woman who was always tlaking about getting swole who bore copper goggles and a pink mohawk. But she died. Then, we went and found some traders- it was actually just a talking, standing dog selling ammunition, very casually. After him, we went and raided a collapsed Y'all mart... and we lost two of our people in a vain attempt to loot sugar cakes and cans of nodescript meat.
And eventually, after crashing a car over a fissure in the ground and stealing an exterminator's van (Complete with giant plastic ant on the roof), I met Horse.
Majestic, fast, valiant... and completely ♥♥♥♥ing insane. Basically, he was a completely naked man who would just neigh, wore a horse mask, and ran twice as fast as other characters. And low and behold, he would become the hero of this story.
The last remaining survivor of my original group eventually diedin yet another siege, and for a long time, Horse marched on alone; charing through salvagable areas without even killing a single zombie because he could not swing a weapon. (For those are not arms, but his "Forelegs"!) But due to some loophole the devs missed, he could shoot a gun and he became wonderous with that shotgun of his.
Soon, I went and rescued a big fluffy white dog that took to Horse, and for nearly five days it was those two, riding on in several more cars (One which Horse managed to fix), having highly intelligent conversations between their barks and neighs.
Eventually, the dog died in a sewer, trying to protect her equine partner. The dog and the horse- a partnership that wasn't destined to last! But Horse eventually found another companion, a bright purple haired woman with a big pistol that did much of the talking for those last few days.
And then Canada, our last objective, came into view. Three sieges happened before, though... and good gods, fear those sieges. Especially when you're Horse.
My purple-haired companion perished halfway into the first one (Her pistol was big, but not big enough). Horse survived the second without barely a scratch, running in circles for two hours in game time to avoid the zombies.
But the final siege was twice as strong, and, two miles (I think) from his goal, Horse died as he had lived, running endlessly.
This is a wonderful, brilliant game that holds plenty of surprises. It's a bit pricey, but it's worthwhile, trust me.

When I first played King's Bounty The Legend, I was blown away. It was so much fun and I replayed it through multiple times. The game was rich with lore, humour, engaging tactics, and so much more. It represented an awesome reboot of the old Sega King's Bounty game from 1990.
King's Bounty Armoured Princess refined and perfected all that was good in King's Bounty the Legend. Crossworlds added a nice facelift of that game.
Then the franchise began to grow tired. King's Bounty Warriors of the North felt repetitive, but still had some positive parts.
This latest installment - King's Bounty: Dark Side is very very staid and tired. The game offers virtually nothing that is new: same graphics, same gameplay, same everything, more or less. Even playing with creatures of the darkside - the games supposed Unique Selling Point - has already been an option in all of the earlier King's Bounty games.
Moreover, KB:DS feels rushed and underdeveloped. The islands feel sparse and seem to have been designed with little attention to detail. The game objectives feel odd and cumbersome. It's all just tired and dull.
Really, the developers (1C: Company) need to come up with something fresh or the franchise is going to die a slow and torturous death. Their current plan of releasing poorly done expansions as sequels is frustrating and something of a slap in the face for their fan base, who love the game but want something more. I have to rate this game a thumbs down and hope that yet another bad review will signal to the developers that the next King's Bounty game cannot be yet another extension of the formula they made in 2008 (yes, 8 years ago now!) and must represent a major overhaul. Otherwise, this is probably the last KB game that I will buy, which is a shame.
So, no, KB: Dark Side is not worth buying. Save your money and hope that 1C will release King's Bounty 2 sometime in the nearish future.

Stationeers is a really fun game.  But, as it says all over in the description, and the reviews, Stationeers is a hard game.  However, its not just hard for the sake of being hard, but rather because designing complex systems is hard.  In that way, its very rewarding.
To oversimplify, if the idea of setting up complex systems (electrical, atmospheric, smelting, produciton, etc...) doesn't excite you, this is not your game.  That's fine, not everyone likes that sort of thing.  But, please don't trash a game just because it isn't your thing.
P.S.  As far as the negative UI comments go, I have to disagree.  This game would be very different if you could drag-n-drop.  I didn't like it all at first, but the complex keyboard combos really do let you play without stopping to fiddle with your mouse cursor.  Additionally, this game wouldn't be nearly as cool if it didn't have you changing batteries, cartridges, canisters, etc...  I mean the hope is that each of those things can be automated with access to better gear, and/or programed in.  However, to remove those things all together would spoil this game.

Since the game hit EA several new items have already been added and I'm excited to see where the game stands in a few months. I've already gotten my $25 out of it.

Please note: This is fairly difficult and time consuming as a single player game.
IMHO, this is the best off-world engineering and colonization game out there to date. This is half game, half simulation. Stationeers incorporates so much real world (real universe) science known to 21st century man. You are given the materials and devices but you have to put them together yourself to make actual functioning systems. You're not just placing a powersupply anywhere on a structure and expcting it to power everything attached to the structure. You have to run the wires and regulate the power. Storing power in batteries and conserving it. Making oxygen to breathe from frozen oxite or ice water, thru systems and methods you have to figure out and engineer. This game is a labor of love from real space/science people. So far, my gameplay in building a functioning and habitable base has been virtual blood, sweat and tears. After all that, I will die happy seeing that i gave birth to my child of a functioning moon base that may probably work in real life. If the developers are saying Stationeers v0.1.1062.5426 is very early access, I can't wait to see what else they will cram into this.

[This review comes from having experienced the game with a keyboard, I've since been told that using a controller makes the experience more palatable. An easier difficulty setting has also been added ]
This is a painful yet beautiful game to play.
From my point of view (and im the kind of guy that will be choosing the high difficulties on most of games) this game has an ultra challenging level design that in combination with not too refined controls make the potential nice experience of the game that can be experienced on the first levels vanish fast.
There are some other precision plataforming levels that are just plain better and, in my opinion, this game fails when trying to take too much from them.
For instance you have things like "I wanna be the guy" wich are blatantly made just for the sake of being annoying. That being his purpose you can just go into this game with no self exigence at all.
On the other hand, Super Meat Boy is an exigent game that is fair at the same time (and avoid stress masterfully because you dont lose much when dying).
This game just tries to seriously defy you but fails to make it a consistent and acceptable journey
The enemies are somewhat ok; while very interesting and challenging they dont get to the point of being overwhelming. BUT the game gets to the point of being stupid when the mechanics and the level design collide.
You need to do precise jumps when your every move will be abysmally diffrent on a minimal input diffrence. Not only that, but all the game is full of sliding platforms that apply that to its maximun, to the point of it being almost a gamble when you have to use them. Sincerely, the game would be really better if only one of these issues would have been eased a bit.
Other thing that bothers me to no end is that feature that the game has. Once you get enough points (making them bleed ofc), your character will create a checkpoint when standing still and empty the bar to get another one. Sounds cool right? well, if you are a player like me, its not. Not only the character will try to make a checkpoint every time you stand still, having to hold down to avoid this and making painful to stop for a sec to thing about your next step. Also, if it is your first playthrough you might end up creating checkpoints on very wrong places that could have been not so hard to avoid, and making reach the next safe zone a torture.
But that's not what i hate the most about that system. What I absolutely dislike the most is that the character will try to create checkpoints even where they cannot be done like sliding platforms, moving ones, or zones full with saws, that are there just for the sake of avoiding you to create one, witch is not bad, but will not stop the character from trying. This makes stoping even for one fraction of a second a very bad idea, since it will affect your movement, and in a game where your movement is already biased, thats bad news
On other note, the music is great and the art is really good (if you know what to expect of a cute-lovecraftian-pixel style) and i am really sad about not liking the gameplay because it is very evident that a lot of work was put into it to bring it to the point that it is now, but i can not agree with the choices.
Pick this one only if you are really interested on really pesky challenges (if you are a mechanical monster i want to see you speedruning this though)
Summary: this is Hardcore, but not sure if the right kind of hardcore.
PS: i will end it, because i am stubborn, but think twice before starting this game.

The different subway cars all make their own unique noise, so listening carefully you can hear individual cars accelerate, slow down, and pickup and drop off people.  As your city grows they are grow into background noise, but it's I love this little detail.

Existing symbols may periodically change to a rare or unique symbol, which can drastically change the traffic demands on your lines.
I love games that have leaderboards.  Definitely adds to the replayability.
Every level seems to be random, which is great for replayability, but I wish there was a way to share the "random seed" (or whatever method) to share the same map with a friend.
I'm not sure if there's a quick way to remove a station in the middle of the line.  You can quickly and easily ADD a station, but not remove it.  I have to drag from the end of the line, erasing all the stations, and then redrawing the line without that station, back to the end.
I'd love to see some of these metro layouts of the winning designs!
