What? A serious review about a jokey, hentai, lesbian, interplanetary space-boob story? Well, I guess somebody had to do it, right?
First off, I'm pretty new to this whole thing, both with visual novels and... whatever else you'd call this. I hear words like anime and hentai and yuri and weeaboo and a whole bunch of others, and I'm still not entirely sure what they all are exactly, but since it was short, free and because I'm a sad achievement-hunting apologist, I figured I'd give this a go. Plus hot girls in the nuddy, obviously. But I get the feeling this probably wasn't the best jumping off point for me.
The daughter of a detective and widowed father, Azure is a young (but still legal!), reclusive, loner schoolgirl who longs for more excitement in her life beyond the dull lessons of her school work and the monotony within the four walls of her bedroom. Sneaking out late one night, she finds herself happening upon a strange ring and sets in motion a bizarre sequence of events with its rightful owner that will change her life for ever.
The first problem I had with it was the way it's presented in the trailer versus how it actually is. There's no animation at all in it, only static backdrops, which most of the time won't even have any characters in it, only a fairly uninteresting scene with a text bar at the bottom of it. Something more engaging to latch on to would have gone a long way and really brought it to life. The "visual" of visual novels seems less of a priority here than the writing, at least until things get kinky.
As you probably already know by now, this is a mature title. That's right, it actually has genuine actual images of actual genuine virtual boobs at some actual point in it! The weird thing is, even though this likely isn't the case, it really feels like it was written in three different parts by three different people. Ditto for the artwork. The first part of the game's art is kinda basic but the writing at least interesting and made me want to know more about Azure and her life. The second part focuses heavily on a sex scene and goes into inordinate detail of every part in ways that it never bothers to at any point before or after, while this time it's like they can't show us enough of the characters for once. Then, in the final, brief part... well, sh*t just gets f*ckin' crazy by then.
I sort of wish it would have been either one thing or another, not an awkward mix of pieces that don't really seem to have been made of the same parts. And while I'm not exactly an expert on this kind of thing, I found the writing for the much touted lesbionics to be pretty cringey, if I'm being honest. Not because I'm a prude at all, far from it, but just because I think it could have been better and not sounded like Baby's My First Erotic Novel.
If anyone wants to check it out I guess I can't really tell them they shouldn't, but I wouldn't be able to recommend it either. It's undoubtedly building up to a bigger, paid-for sequel that I have a feeling will probably bear little resemblance to its predecessor (though I imagine it'll still find some way to shoehorn in some lesbian space antics. Probably with some zero-G boobs or something this time), but who knows, that may mean something great for it! Either way, it should probably take you no more than 40 to 50 minutes to find out whether or not this kind of thing is for you, unless you're the kind of person who'll want to lube up when the girly stuff kicks off. Though, c'mon, let's be honest, you really shouldn't need to. If you're reading this you're already travelling through the amazing world of the internet right now, and f*ck knows you can hardly swing a keyboard playing cat around without smacking into a bunch of nipples 'round here. Just do that, instead.

is a piece of embarrassingly amateur fanfic that would almost certainly have been written better by a 12 year old in the back of a notebook while sitting at the top of the bleachers avoiding the cool kids during gym class.
The main character is a classic 'Mary Sue' author wish-fulfilment avatar who without a hint of irony, and without going too far into spoiler territory, goes from clumsy schoolgirl to more or less being in charge of the universe in, quite literally, around 36 hours.
This ‘visual novel’ is written as a series of disjointed stream of consciousness vignettes and is full of clichés. It is also largely devoid of obvious editing for coherency and contains numerous abrupt leaps of tone, wild shifts in characterisation and several near complete breakdowns in logic.
Note that as a classic visual novel there are no choices to be made. Written in the Sky is simply an exercise in reading the dialogue as it is fed to you one line at a tedious time. This is a story that, without the line-by-line delivery, would take literally around three minutes to read if printed as text and therefore barely qualifies as a short story.
Background images are repetitive (there are only three or four significant locations) and these add little if anything to the story. Character images have almost exactly as much variety as shown in the representative images on the main store page, which is to say, each has perhaps two almost indistinguishable expressions.
Written in the Sky also contains what might easily be one of the worst, most clinical and unnecessarily drawn out sex scenes ever written, with lines such as "
." The single sex scene itself takes up around 25% of the novel’s total content.
Finally, if you come for the bewbs you will be sadly disappointed. There is only one scene with a single nipple, and it’s pretty tame at that. The game is very linear and simple. I almost hesitate to call it game because their is literally no challenge in the game. You have no opportunities to fail as you progress normally through the story.

Chances are most people today have experiemented with long distance relationships through social networking or online video games. Specifically in MMO's, the awkward banter and hesitant softcore compliments should basically be advertised under the ESRB rating. It is a strange, but satisfying happening that tugs at heart strings despite the lack of any sort of actual physical encounter. Cibele is a very short narrative game that highlights all of this, and transports players back into the complexities of virtual and real world relationships.
Cibele plays like a really low budget indie movie. The acting is decent and the monologue from both protagonist Nina Freeman and antagonist Blake is slow, and monotone - much like that of an awkward teenager. While the visual real-life footage maintains players engaged by following Nina in her undies and bright pink colored hair (including themes of sex and mature content), the "gameplay" is clunky and uninspired. The meta MMO where most of the narrative takes place results in single click actions. Click on one baddy and watch the character kill the baddy very slowly, all while reading texts and incoming emails which keep the conversation between Nina and Blake going. There isn't much gaming actually going on, so most of the time it feels like a nuisance overlapping the actual story at hand.
While the game does offer interesting aspects like the ability to explore Nina's desktop which includes poetry drafts and selfies, there simply isn't much here to compensate for the $8.99 price tag. Especially when considering the game runtime which is about one hour.
The overall concept of online relationships is sure to sucker-in anybody that has experienced such events (guilty), but unless this is on sale for a buck, I can't really recommend it.

I feel a bit churlish criticizing Nina Freeman's passion project, but I'm afraid I can't recommend Cibele. It's an autobiography told with three techniques: live-action video, documents on the protagonist's desktop, and a simplified, simulated MMO. Watching the videos, which are mostly shot in what looks like a teenage girl's bedroom, feels unconfortably voyeristic to me. Just as creepy is sorting through the images, documents, chat logs, and emails. I don't enjoy prying into someone else's life, so I probably missed a fair amount of content. A fully written or cinematic version of the story might have appealed more.
However, playing the imagined MMO fills in a piece of the story that can't easily be replicated some other way. Don't suppose the game to be particularly complicated; the only action is clicking on enemies to attack them. As you play, the main characters talk the way people (presumably) talk over in-game voice chat. Other characters interrupt with emails and typed chat messages. The stress of managing the demands of the game and multiple conversations must be experienced to be felt. This section of the game is very effective.
As the story progresses, the game-within-a-game's art style foreshadows and mirrors the emotions characters feel. But it's not at all clear why they are playing. Perhaps because I've never played much of this sort of game myself, but the gameplay does not strike a chord of recognition for me. Aren't there strategies besides rapid clicking? Even a few fake mechanics such as added equipment, leveling, and special attacks would sustain the illusion of an online game that would entertain players for several years.
I can't bear the game any ill-will. It's kinda interesting as an experiment. But the story just did not grab me and there's very little else.

When I purchasced this game I had this strange feeling I was going to end up refunding it but I was very wrong.
The game is very akin to Oregon Trail like many others have said with some playable sections where you loot and kill zombies taking place between all the text events. The combat isn't revolutionary but it feels good and there is more than one way to come at the zombies and it allows you the player some flexibility in your choice, something rare for a "indie zombie" game which typically are just cash grabs. The game is also brutal. Like unbelievably unforgiving when it comes to mistakes and just plain old random encounters. You might get have a full health team and then get 3 "lose health" random events in a row and have everyone die. It's not frustrating at least for me as the game is definitely designed for multiple play throughs and constant restarting. Though I would definitely not suggest this game to anyone who isn't of the mindset of "losing is fun".
There is a lot of great humor in the game as well as tons of easter eggs and pop culture references.  The events will probably begin to get repetitive at some point, but I certainly haven’t reached that point yet. You are also given extensive customization of your character as well as the ability to have a "folder" of custom characters you can meet throughout the game in addition to the ones already in.
The music is hilariously (in a good way) out of place, but it's still very well made and catchy. And even though I say it’s out of place it's by no way "awkward" it's just not what you would expect, but it still works. The pixel art is beautifully retro and the game also has a old western movie film grain over it (which you can disable if you'd like).
For things I didn't like, the controls felt atrocious for me, I just couldn't play with them. You are allowed to rebind and there is controller support, which is what I found was the best way to play. The options menu is also pretty barebones, only allowing you to change from full screen and windowed (which was stuck at one resolution) and adjusting the volume levels. I also found myself trying to move in certain locations only to find it was blocked by an invisible wall, but that was minor and probably a result of the "top down" view.
Overall though, definitely a worthy purchase for only $15. A cute little indie zombie game with a great sense of humor, a hefty amount of content and a clear amount of love in the mix as well.

Basically RNG: The Game.
Everything in this game is RNG, essential supplies is from RNG, HEALING event is RNG (WTF?), recruitment is from RNG, events are RNG (Usually never good, just RNG of which bad events you get), and the RNG in the game is designed against you.
The first layer of RNG is the crashes, if you survived that and thought you are good, don't worry, you are not, the rest of the RNG is by design.
For example, I made a healing character, had plenty of med supplies, but that character will never trigger the healing event even though people are almost dead. Then later down the road she died trying to pull her teeth out even though according to the dialog choice she use to be a dentist.
Or another example, I made a mechanic to fix cars, but the game always insist on making my healer fix the car. And of course she can't fix the car because her stats in mechanics is too low, so on top of losing the car, she's also in a bad mood, which if low enough the member will leave permanantly.
Also your main NEEDS to be an mechanic because the moment you are on foot when your car breaks down, you either get robbed of all your supply (you can choose to fight the bandits but the RNG never let me win yet), or you lose your life tripping and hurt yourself on flat road (again WTF?). And once your food is all robbed, and your healing supply is all used up, your mood drops to rock bottom, and your character automatically leave the team, even your main character. And then it's game over.
There are so many more problem with this game I just can't be bothered listing them all at this time. The game don't feel complete, interface needs some ironing out, game needs SERIOUS re-balance. And the bugs is in your face, I'm certain the only reason the game have a save feature at all is for crashes. I mean you can't save manually, and you can't leave the game and come back either, I tried and my save is gone once I re-launched the game.
Not adviced to purchase until the game is fixed.

A friend of mine summarized "This War of Mine" as "not really a game, more an emotional experience." His assessment could not be more accurate.
From a game play standpoint, "This War of Mine" mixes search and scavenge with build and survive. You'll want to avoid combat whenever possible, as few of the characters are suited to it. That's just one way the game illustrates exactly what life looks like for civilians trying to survive in a protracted combat zone. Everything about the game, from the washed-out gray graphics to the somber music and the sparse dialogue speaks to one thing: war is terrible. To truly understand what the game is trying to relate, consider the following: when making your first play-through, skip the guides. Don't ask for help. Just take the ride. It won't be easy, but it will be infinitely more rewarding, whatever the outcome.
9/10, two thumbs up. Without a doubt, one of the most brutally honest, uncompromisng and powerful emotional experiences I've had in recent memory. I'm glad I took this journey, but it is NOT for everyone.

A few years ago, while looking at my particular habits in gaming, I realized that I hate myself. There were a few datapoints that led me to this, but one of them concerned my standard mod-list for Kerbal Space Program. A few in particular added increased realism and complexity to make it really immensely aggravating, and yet I would continue loading them every time I restarted. And I have over 800 hours in KSP.
8 hours into Stationeers and it obviously scratches the same itch for hating myself.
You load up other survival-in-harsh-environment games and while it can still be tricky, it breaks it into manageable chunks for you. Not so with Stationeers, where you need a lengthy tutorial (naturally it's not in the game, gotta hit up YouTube for that) to figure out even the basic components they give you at the start if you want to perform some low level survival tasks like 'breathing'. And of course, immediately adjacent to that remedial instruction vid is the next basic one in the chain where you build a basic computer out of the ark of the covenant and unicorn foreskins.
All of that said, I quite appreciate the complexity of it. A game of 'mine ore, build entire airlock, place airlock, now you're safe" would be boring. This is deeply satisfying, for all the effort that has to go into it. And the trial and error and slow suffocation. While the UI is still in desperate need of help, there's enough to dig into even just two weeks after launch into early access that I can forsee this becoming another horrible, frustrating entries in my triple digit hours list.

Okay, my original review was a bit short on the content, and frankly low-effort, so i'm going to expand on it (Original review at the end)
In short. Stationeers is already a decently well thought out survival/building game. It's base systems, building, wiring, mining etc are well designed (except coal in space, seriously guys, wtf) and some of the choices even down to the battery management and the way things are built is a nice change and a nice fit for this kind of game..
The game is taken from a 7/10 "needs polish" standard early access experience to a 1/10 "I cant believe anyone thought this was a good idea" by the UX.
The UI itself is passable (barely) and obviously can be improved by it's time in early access. But the user experience is the worst i have ever encountered. The UX in this game is to UX design what Big Rigs: Over the Road Racing was to racing games. It is relatively easy to learn in and of itself, but why would you want to? I can learn to eat soap if i want, it wont make it any more palatable. And it is genuinely a pity. What seems to be a well thought out passion project is utterly demolished by a ham handed amateur attempt at "realism" and "immersion" through seemingly attempting to re-invent the wheel and somehow managing to end up with a triangle.
A lot of people make the claim "it's fine when you get used to it". Why would anyone want to get used to it? Literally every single aspect of your inventory is multiple clicks away, simply changing between two toolbelts (because god forbid the mining tool couldnt go in the toolbelt and have a seperate bag slot for storage) means moving your tools into your toolbelt (or on the floor if you prefer), then moving your current toolbelt to a hand, moving it to your backpack, moving the other toolbelt to your hand, equipping it, then moving through it to then equip your mining tool. It's a joke of UX design and a massive step backwards.
I hate to make game by game comparisons, but if Space Engineers, or Empyrion, or even bloody Minecraft, or any of the other build/survive games in any genre had this UX they wouldnt have gotten even 5% of the sales they have. I highly recommend staying away until you see news of either mod support being added and someone fixing what the devs seem to be implementing on purpose. Or simply staying away. I cannot recommend anyone play this game as it stands.
Original review - TL;DR
"Needs a competent UI and UX before it can call itself a "game". Currently more of a job wrapped in a game engine."

This game is pretty fun once you get the hang of it.  The "tutorial" gets you started but there are many parts of the game you have to figure out for yourself.  There are hints locked away behind some in-game currency (imo, they should be free as part of an extended tutorial).  For example there is a 'buy stocks' mini-game that doesn't explain how it works, so you might make the same mistake I did and pay $40,000 for stock that is worth 5-6k (according to the computer players) - not a mistake you'll make twice.
The gameplay is simple and as others have said, repeatative.  However if you like sim/strategy games, you'll probably enjoy it despite the repeatative nature.  Each level is random and with a little strategy you can maximize your profits, but unfortunately due to the poor tutorial, you'll waste some time/money figuring out the right way to do things.
One of my biggest gripes is there is no save system.  If you make a mistake, you can't undo it.  The game doesn't tell you this and you learn it the hard way (such as ending a level early - there is no 'repeat level' option, you just go on to the next level).  Similarly, you can't quit the game without leaving a level first (since there is no save system) which is annoying. (You can quit inbetween levels without losing progress)
For the current asking price ($10 CAD), I don't think it is worth the price.  For $5, it would be fine.  There isn't enough content and the issues described above make this a 'steam sale' game.  I can't see myself putting more than 15 hours into this (at max) since there isn't much to do beyond the campaign and daily levels.
PS: Got this game for free with another game I bought online.
Edit: I found a "?" icon in the game that explains some of the features (ie. stocks).  Unfortunately the icon is small and the game doesn't tell you its location - this would've helped avoid many mistakes.

Firstly I played KB: The Legend and Armored Princess ( with the Crossworlds expansion ) only skipping Warriors of the North so I am familiar with the series and could even call myself a fan and I will write this review with those experiences in mind.
Short version:
Pros:
1. More new content ( units, spells etc.)
2. Letting you play as a villain this time
3. Allowing you to more seriously play others races ( undead, demon and orcs )
4. Quests have been improved a bit by having limited choice and consequences here and there
Cons:
1. BUGS!! Damned it all if they didn't deliver on the bugs this time
2. A lot of the text seems to been either poorly translated or was written worse this time
3. Worse level design
4. About half the achievements don't work ( they show up ingame but don't count on steam )
5. Over long and more tedious than previous games ( at the time of writing this review I'm at almost 70 hours and I don't see a ending coming soon )
6. While some quests are a bit more interesting a lot are the same old kill this or that and now a good number of longer chain quests don't say what you have to do
Rant version:
Why guys, why did you release such a unfinished mess of a game? The previous 2 games I've played had almost none of the problems this one has. Probably what killed my enjoyment of this game the most were the bugs, I can deal with the way the series has been structured with the constant running back and forth for reinforcements and the somewhat railroaded pathway with an almost linear difficulty progression when it comes to the enemies.
BUT I cannot deal with the bugs this game has.
Actually let me make a list of the ones I've seen up till now:
1.Necromancers have false info show up when hovering with the attack cursor over a enemy
2.Some enemy ranged units will try to spend all of their action points even sometimes not attacking you
3.A lot of achievements are bugged and cannot be gotten
4.Crashes way too often compared to the previous games
5.Some actions in combat seem to freeze the game and has atleast 1 made me kill the program. Or you might have bad luck and get enemy units that freeze midway through their turn in which case you have to reload and hole that they won't repeat themselves
6.Some enemies had false difficulty rating show up ( until now only the priests of light that spawn after a certain quest )
7.In the demon world there is a dungeon with a few items behind bars, after killing the guard and opening the prison I found that they are unpickable.
8.Using the zombies ability to pass their turn to another unit can bug out if you use rage abilities. The unit which should have gotten an extra turn is passed over and a new round starts making you effectively lose a unit turn for nothing.
9.There is a quest for researching dark version of light spells. If you get the dark shroud scroll, learn it and upgrade it and then later on you hand in the echivalent scrolls for completing the quest the spell will reset in your spellbook thus wasting any crystals you used on it.
10.Somehow while having an enemy orc under blackies jealousy the spell didn't end and enemies started attacking that orc as well, something that should'nt happen normally with the spell.
11.Killed a unit under the empathy spell and I got 30 rage points for it. I don't think thats intended.
Also if the bugs weren't enough of a annoyance then I also had the pleasure of witnessing atrocious level design and pacing.
Some examples :
1. Spells seem to come far too late compared to previous games so get used to using the same 3 or 4 for 40 hours
2. Enemies seem to scale up in difficulty faster than you can keep up even with farming every available opportunity, again something the previous games did better ( IIRC in my playthrough of The Legend being meticulous meant that I never faced a enemy at a rating of deadly or higher until right at the end )
3. Crystals for learning and upgrading spells are VERY RARE ( until you can buy them ). Again another reason why you will only use very few spells for 1/3 of your playtime
4. A few quests have the nasty habit of not telling you where to find/buy this or that. This one is actually a minor complaint since they are few and the longer chain quests usually are linked more closely to progression through the game.
Actually scratch that I just found one that is tied to the main quest, is a fetch quest and doesn't say where I need to go to pick up some damned shrooms at a point in which I have access to most islands.
5. Also while having more options in how you can complete or progress quests is nice, making it so that all options except one end up in a quest failure is just insulting.
6. Aside from some new units a lot of the game seems recycled, with very few genuinely new assets and terrain ( meaning not just recolored like a lot of the ''new'' dark troops ) giving the game a very cheap feeling
7.Related to 2: After reaching and passing what seemed to be midgame and finally unlocking most abilities, medals and troop types the difficulty seemed to nose dive straight into easy and as long as keeping with the grind of easier enemies the game never seemed to recover it's challenge.
Think that's enough for now seeing as I am not done with the game yet I will probably edit and add to this review as I continue the game. It might be the worse entry yet in the series but I still like this style of gameplay and with enough time can slog through this to the end.

Addictive. 450 hours in across all the various KB games. That is a lot. So I am not saying "I played this game for 100 hours and it is crap". I sort of love them. Finished the first two but can't seem to bite the bullet and keep going on these later two (this and Warriors of the North).
I really love the King's Bounty series - it is probably the most fun, absurd, ridiculous and obtuse series out there. Choose a fighter, paladin or mage. Amass an army and send them into battles on a turn based chessboard. Cute graphics. No bugs or crashes experienced. My early army consisted of Wizards and Imps. Now I command mostly dragons that can fly around the battlefield unleashing hellfire. The series reminds me a bit of the Diablo clones where you just want to do one more battle to level up and increase your various map. They promote exploring as you can find cash, magic runes, other runes and spells. The battles can be very strategic.
450 hours in and I still like the music - found myself humming it this morning. What is wrong with me?
In the Dark Side the forces of good have done bloody war on the evil minions and the evil demons and orcs need saving. As a lady Demon Spirit Paladin class - I travel the various worlds encouraging the various leaders to "Turn to the Darkside" and support our cause. If they don't, I replace them on the throne by hook or crook.
The more positives aspects of this game:
For probably the first time in a KB game - I quite enjoyed the story telling and various chit chat.
I like some of the quirky people you meet on your travels - like the Seven Dwarves - very bad people.
You can enable cheating - but still get the achievements - cool
I came across a "Colossus" spell that when cast game me random Level 5 troops - hello Archdemons and Cyclops
I liked the Tomfoolery you could do with Blood Priestesses where I sacrificed my troops to increase some of the others. At one point I had 100 red and green dragons in reserve - at no cost!
I liked you can trick a Dragon Leader into accepting fake princesses who he then subsequently turns into the best units in the game - fearsome Dragon riders.
The negatives in this game can be reflected in one single word - Whattheheckisgoingon?
Some of the quests are diabolical. Impossible to figure out on your own. God save the Internet and special thanks and high esteem to two Steam users (Shadowcran and Siannah) who posted two fantastic guides. The developers should be thanking them for the majority of positive reviews.
The Seven Dwarves quests involves searching three different maps.
In the Island of Monteville - you need to get into the Castle. This quest involves a travelling circus, make up, a portrait, an elven outfit and a password. CONVOLUTED.
Buy these games cheap and you are virtually guaranteed 20-30 hours of fun. After that it's like running a marathon - all about your stamina.

First of all this is a phone app port! It's a casual game. A bejeweled clone. A bejeweled clone with Disney elements. Spacebar is Enter, Arrow Keys to move around, ESC to go back. Plus they remind you of the controls on nearly every page. IMO you don't need a mouse whatsoever. For a phone to PC port the game functions fairly well. The screens load nice and quickly. The graphics have also been adapted nicely that they look like they belong on the PC. Though they are also not the best of the best.
TLDR: Its a cute little game that functions well but is nothing we haven't seen before. If you want to play a casual game of bejeweled that also has Disney characters then give this a shot. It's free and honestly try it before you diss it.

I love how the minimalist graphics match so well the generic metro maps.
The game is simple, but everything is very smooth with lots of little details in the game.
The different subway cars all make their own unique noise, so listening carefully you can hear individual cars accelerate, slow down, and pickup and drop off people.  As your city grows they are grow into background noise, but it's I love this little detail.
I like how you can not only easily extend the end of the line, but you can add new stations to the middle of your rail line.  Just grab the line between two stations and drag into to a third station, voila!
Existing symbols may periodically change to a rare or unique symbol, which can drastically change the traffic demands on your lines.
I love games that have leaderboards.  Definitely adds to the replayability.
Every level seems to be random, which is great for replayability, but I wish there was a way to share the "random seed" (or whatever method) to share the same map with a friend.
I'm not sure if there's a quick way to remove a station in the middle of the line.  You can quickly and easily ADD a station, but not remove it.  I have to drag from the end of the line, erasing all the stations, and then redrawing the line without that station, back to the end.
I'd love to see some of these metro layouts of the winning designs!

I played FC1, FC2, FC3 before. In FC4 I finished all missions and cleared
almost the whole map.
In short: I enjoyed the game and recommend the purchase if you like shooter.
With my current knowledge about the game I would buy it for max. 35€ (inc. Addons).
If you don't like a repetitive gameplay you should watch a let's play first before buying.
You'll get a good looking, rather light-minded, not very challenging but enjoyable shooter.
1. Presentation (4/5):
If you like good graphics then you won't be disappointed. Objects, characters and wildlife
are well designed and the animation doesn't lack in anything. The big bad point is that the
world feels too monotonous to me. You'll see always the same colors and trees all over the map.
2. Story/Sidemissions/Objectives (2/5):
The Story okay, definitly not overwhelming and far too short. If I hadn't cleared almost the whole map
(opening chests, get the XP-Boosts, exploring points of interest), I could've be done in a few
hours. The sidemissions are too repetitive. The "drug-missions" are very well made.
Clearing the points of interest (belltowers, outposts) become boring after 10h playtime.
3. KI/Gameplay/difficulty (3/5)
Well, the gameplay is like the other FCs (2,3). The weapon-handling is simple and intuitive as always.
I'm a bit bored by the Takedowns. I killed about 75% of all enemies with Takedowns because of
the bonus-XP. To be honest: I could have used the guns but I'm an enthusiast when it comes
to fast leveling. The KI is nothing special but serves the needs. KI-bugs are rare.
The difficulty-level is definitly fair, maybe a bit too easy.
4. Characters (5/5)
That's the big winner category here. Sabal, Amita and especially the antagonist Pagan Min
are really really good. The side-mission characters are also very nice.
5. Equipment/Vehicles (4/5)
Sometimes the equipment lacks in logic (parachute, wingsuit, bait) but the game is filled
with an exciting weaponary and enough usable items to keep you entertained although it
doesn't really matter which weapons you use. The vehicles are mostly awesome, especially
the Buzzer and the Hovercraft.

I'm re-reviewing this game after completing it (twice), as my opinion of it has drastically changed after 'the long haul'.
The game starts well, sags horribly in the middle, and picks up brilliantly in the final third; it really comes to life towards the end, when the 2nd half of the map is unlocked, most of the weapons are unlocked, and things really start moving.  The initially tedious characterisations and plot do develop into a coherent whole, as the threads and twists start to make sense and provide more purpose to the action.  Gameplay is classic Far Cry (bincolars, scopes, takedowns, outposts), and
although there are complaints of "copy/paste" with the FarCry series, and the game doesn't feel quite as tactical or urgent as FarCry 2, all the series hallmarks are there.
TLDR:
If you play games till you finish them, thoroughly recommended.  If you're a quitter, you won't see the best the game has to offer.  Oh, if you're the kind of player who HAS to get 100% completion on a game... you're gonna be here for a long, long, long, long time.

One of my favourite games of all time. The setting is incredible, but even separate from the moral decisions you'll be making or whatever message you think the game creators want to get across about the nature of war and humanity, the simple fact is that the gameplay is just ridiculously good.
It is everything I want in a survival/managing/building game, you have to manage your resources, your people, and your time very carefully. It has the best of both worlds in that you’re telling multiple people what to do during the day, building up your base, and have to single-player sneak around during the night, gathering resources. There are some difficult choices, not only morally dubious ones during your nightly egresses, but also simply who you are going to send on what mission, or who deserves to sleep or eat and who doesn’t so you can better achieve your goals.
The only con for me is that after 3+ playthroughs the gameplay gets repetitive because there are not a huge amount of different locations and situations to explore. Eventually you’ve basically seen them all. I wish there were more, perhaps through DLCs, so I can keep playing this amazing game.

I've played a lot of hidden object games; some on steam, some not. This may be one of the few ones I actually replay. Definitely worht the money. The interface is good, the art is great, the sound is fine, and the story is very compelling, especially by hidden object games standards, which are often light on story.
Definitely pick this one up.

This is one of the better examples of a hidden object game, with lots of clever puzzles, high quality art and fun/fair object scenes, though it also suffers from several flaws that hold it back from becoming an unconditional classic.
Once again, you'll find yourself playing as a protagonist out to rescue a loved one from the clutches of an evil mad man as you rummage through his personal space in a vast, unsettling mansion. But while the player character is something of a smug, charmless git, the real staring centrepiece here is the villain, easily being the most exceptional and interesting I've seen in one of these games, and even compared to a lot of other types of games, too. The voice acting is still a little hammy, and the writing flirts with the overdramatic on plenty of occasions, but overall I really liked the story and thought it was a far more thoughtful, engaging narrative that's typically sorely lacking from others of the genre.
I'd probably argue that the standard of puzzles is higher than usual - and a fair bit harder too, I'd say - but more noticeably, they far outweigh the volume of actual hidden object scenes that you'll find throughout the four or so hours of the experience. As a result, I wouldn't instantly recommend this for newcomers to the now expansive pantheon of hidden object games. Though, that said, there is a complete walkthrough included in-game, and the option to skip puzzles should the need arise.
For all that I enjoyed about the game, its most glaring shortcoming is in its backtracking. Its not uncommon to have to revisit previous areas in these types of games and use newly acquired items to access new sections and pick-ups, but in those at least, they'll usually allow you to fast-travel to any location through your map with only a couple of clicks. Here, however, you have to manually click your way back room after room until you reach your destination, complete your task, then go all the way back again, and given how numerous and sprawling the play areas are, that can become an increasingly exasperating inconvenience.
For a five-year-old game you can probably find in any number of relatively inexpensive bundles, the price does seem a little bit steep, and I'd sooner suggest getting it either that way or during a sale. But if you're looking for a slightly darker, more ghoulish hidden object game with taxing puzzles and superb art, then this is definitely the place to find it.

I've played a lot of platformers, and yet playing this was a fairly new experience for me. I've never seen a platformer that combines fighting and platforming like this one does. All of the mechanics in TBP meld together to make a one-of-a-kind experience. With double jumps, dashing, ducking and wall jumping you have all the mobility to navigate the various environmental hazards in the game. The combat system is simple, but still allows for you to vanquish youre foes in a variety of gruesome ways, including cleverly utilizing the same hazards that can kill you with one wrong move. The controls are so tight that it's even possible to pull off air combat. Also, the ability to place your own checkpoints gives you a lot of power. You save youre progress, and it heals you too. Additionally, the soundtrack for this game is superb, and I'm a real sucker for that classic horror style. So, if you're a hardened platformer like me, you're really missing out if you don't own this great game.
On a side note, I'm not sure if Spooky Squid Games is planning a sequel or not, but if they are, I'll buy the hell out of it. Also, you just haven't lived until you've been murdered by a horde of flying lemons.

The control scheme is a bit awkward, and it could take a couple levels to get mostly used to. There ARE times that this game makes you want to punch a small child, but hey...it's a rage game. What do you expect? You're gonna get worked up a few times, definitely. However, most of the time, this game isn't TOO bad if you just keep trying. It's not like IWBTG as well, in the sense that it won't take you 100 attempts to get past a single section/screen. For TBP, give it around 10 tries. It's also not like IWBTG, where most obstacles come out of nowhere and are completely unpredictable at first. At most points it's difficult, but never unforgiving. In terms of platforming, the jumps are all made to be slightly tricky to quite tricky. It does a good job of blending platforming and beat-em-up. It seems that you, at almost any point in the game, are either making tricky jumps or fighting groups of enemies. There is rarely a point where you're only doing one of those for a prolonged amount of time. In all, it's a tricky but well-balanced platformer that isn't afraid to be tough, but tries its best to not bring you to the brink of ragequit. Most of the time that you get mad while playing this will not be because of the game, but because of your own mistakes. Final Score: 8.5/10

While the video ad for the most part shows the local only(!) multiplayer, the acutal singleplayer game itself is designed for mobile devices as a "toilet game" and a pure money grab. As a always, the first levels start out reasonably beatable, then after some you'll be at the mercy of lady luck to get the blocks that you need in order to beat the level, but it's still doable. After that levels become a money-grab, literally.
You'll be presented with levels, that task you with clearing all immovable blocks which you can only do if you build a combo touching them (frozen solid) or incorporating them (frozen solid with certain color inside), while still maintaining a move limit while ALSO the field is seperated with arbitrary lines, so can only get them from a certain direction  or using a combo that you need to make on the other side of the field to to clear them.  With the move limit, you often would need to clear 2 to 3 blocks with each single move which is unlikely.
That's where the special powers come in: the characters have somewhat useful special abilities, that let you overcome this near to impossible situations, yet you get only a limited amount of them. If you run out of them there's two ways to get them back: the ingame shop (real money) or waiting another day to have the chance at some chose-1-of-9-game and maybe earn one(!) charge. Charges for special abilites are shared between all the characters, so in combination with levels that require them to be used you'll be running out of them rather quickly. And should you have the audacity to be wanting to reach 3 stars in each level, that will cost you a lot, because stars are bound to score - the score is bound to the matches you make in your move limit. Special powers are not decreasing your move limit, thus making it easier to get matches. And yet the moment you surpass the requirements for a level, the game automatically ends the level, having your remaining turns clear some parts of the board at random - which can result in a higher or lower score based on luck, so you'll find yourself replaying the same level that you need to use powers on over and over again just to get screwed by some missing points at the end, because the randomness just didn't want to give them to you and left you at 2/3 stars.
So my verdict: stay away, play something else.

Great game, distinct from The Organ Trail despite the same overall concept. This is more of a frenzied sprint rather than The Organ Trail's marathon - instead of distance, you have 15 days of driving from Florida to Canada. You need gas, food, and whatever you can get your hands on. Good luck, godspeed, try not to die.
Exploring points of interest makes up a majority of the gameplay and is very action oriented. You can choose who goes out, and then the scavenging party goes of to a randomly generated SNES style action map level, very distinct from OT's EGA emulation.
Shooting zombies was the main defense in OT. While that's an option here, there's a huge emphasis on melee, knocking down enemies, and mobility - running past zombies RE style is usually your best option when scavenging. You and your buddies can die out there, you do not immediately get sent back to safety OT style after zombie contact. It actually takes being cornered or prolonged zombie contact to die, though, hence the mobility emphasis.
The only real complaint I have is that some mechanics may be initially obtuse, though you will probably be okay with this if you are a fan of rogue-likes that do similar things. For example, stats are hidden until you use them, which can be quite frustrating if you make assumptions or are gambling wildly on skills. I can't really say it's a negative as it does become more apparent over time who is good at what, or if you just make custom characters, but beware if it's your first time out!
In summary: good gameplay that's more active and engaging. Lots of game modes, easy to get in and out of, quite funny, great music, and gives me an odd River City Ransom vibe when scavenging, especially with some ai partners or better yet a second local player along.
Final note:
For the love of god, if you find a man dressed as Garfield, DO NOT TAKE HIM ALONG. AVOID, AVOID, AVOID. HE IS THE ANGEL OF DEATH AND MONDAYS.

Garbage. Graphics, gameplay, writing. Garbage all around.
The game
with Protagonist Reporter watching a 50's (local?) TV broadcast talking about a serial killer terrorizing the city, with approximately 40 (not actually stated in the report because that would sound bloody stupid - I'm estimating based on the number of bodies you discover) young attractive people disappearing over the past few months. The "only clue to what is happening is the column of the independent journalist Protagonist Reporter". Protagonist gets a congratulatory call from his editor, drawing our attention to his hideous lizard-person-wearing-skin-mask face. He then goes to meet his girlfriend, Anna, who was apparently kidnapped by the serial killer. Protagonist now has to meet him in a creepy mansion. Cue game.
You don't expect quality writing in a HOG, but I've rarely experienced so much amazingly rage-inducing dialog. I just want to grab the game by the shoulders (in... some virtual reality hackers verse in which games have personifications and shoulders. Kinda thinking that would count as assault against a disabled person though) and scream "people don't talk like that! Nobody talks like that, in real life or fiction! All you had to do was copy the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ dialog from whatever third-rate thrillers you're ripping off!" Instead, we get something that's either the result of a terrible translation, or a direct copy of someone's very first creative writing assignment, never reviewed by the teacher.
Anyways, the game. It's garbage, as noted above. Everything is sepia-ish gray, so good luck finding anything without random clicks. There's a map of the mansion, but you cannot teleport by using it, so enjoy tracking back and forth manually (the game guide has plenty of "now go back 10 screens, go right twice and forward three times" instructions). Better yet - enjoy the part of the game where you have to keep going back and forth via an unskippable 15 second elevator animation. The game barely ever allows you to be done with a section, sending you back and forth regardless of how far you've come and how long it's been since you last visited a particular room.
The game has high aspirations towards horror and jump scares. Every fourth or fifth room will have a scare-chord followed by a closeup of a corpse, artistically posed by our mysterious killer.  Protagonist is apparently asthmatic, and keeps gasping, coughing and wheezing in your ear at random times. The killers makes random appearances every few screens, standing behind flamethrowers / giant saws / rampaging pangolins you have to overcome.  When he's not on screen, he's blathering at you from the radios scattered throughout the mansion. The one positive side - you can walk away as he talks, which is kinda funny. Still, in this case the antagonist's blathering just makes the game extra tiresome, rather than motivating you to pursue him. The fact that he shows up in person constantly actually makes it all the more obvious that the game is going to schedule the final confrontation arbitrarily. (Contrast with Grim Legends and Alex Hunter, in which you're active in the pursuit of the antagonist and aren't just doing his bidding only to emerge triumphant from a confrontation he specifically arranged).
The puzzles are exactly the arbitrary series of obstacles I've described in my initial post. Practically no adventure-game-lite sections, nothing inventive or different.
To say the least, not recommended.

Good. Insanely good. Not since RCT II have I found as an addictive and mezmorizing game as Mini Metro.
At first, you think "It's a puzzle game!"  No.
And then you think "It's a sim game!" No.
And then you think "It's a strategy game!" No.
It's all three. And a logistics game too.
The beauty of the game lies in its simplicity and its elegance. No fancy graphics to chew up your computer speed. No messy noises to ruin your hearing. No time consuming constructions to build.  It basically takes you back to when strategy/sim games were simple, eloquent & easy to learn how to play... and nearly impossible to master.
Taking a few queues from SimCity, Locomotion, Railroad Tycoon & RollerCoaster Tycoon II, Mini Metro is incredibly easy to learn. A few quick rounds in London to get started, and you're off. Each level varies in complexity, challenging issues & equipment. Melbourne for example features same-speed trams that cross your map slowly. Whereas Osaka has high-speed rail links to work with. And Cairo's short car subways fill up quickly.
Part of what makes this game so great is the straightforward graphics. No frills. No gimmicks. No flashy BS to showcase a programmer's tiny little....ego. It's brilliant as it has less - and it works by being so much more.
Highly addictive. Highly recommended. And possibly in my top 5 games played of all time. (And I go back to the 1980s, kids...)

A truly wonderful game. Can be enjoyed casually (just link up your network at random) but there really are more effective strategies. Each city has a unique feel because the random features (station positions and type) may be tweaked to give different proportions of station types and proportions of stations of different types on different land masses. Also, some cities have unique features like the Osaka shinkansen (fast trains) or slightly different weekly choices.
There are basic achievements for each city, which lets you work out the basic mechanics of the game. Then there are more demanding achievements, with extra restrictions like only having tunnels on one line, and a much more demanding passenger target. These require a more efficient network since your network will start to crack under the strain well before you reach the passenger target. If the earlier incarnations of your network (when you have most opportunity for radical changes since there are not so many passengers) weren't efficient enough, then you likely won't make it (although you might if you're very lucky!).

Mini metro is a great game with a few terrible flaws.
It is a quiet puzzle solver which will appeal to people who like simple games that are hard to to master. The game sets you up as a light rail designer. Shapes appear as stations and you must connect them to move passengers around the city.  As the (in game) weeks go by you are awarded extra materials as the map slowly zooms out and adds more randomly placed stops. You must balance how many lines to employ, number of engines, tunnels, enhanced stations, and extra cars while keeping the system flowing.
Pro's
- Meditative/quiet
- Colorful, with clear and simplistic design.
- Global score boards for the competitive player
- Depth of strategy due to rogue-like components
- Easy to learn
- Appropriate for all ages
- Achievements which make you attempt new things.
- Each level has its own characteristics.
Cons
-  Rogue-like elements can render achievements impossible
- No guide or tutorial for many game elements
- You must constantly pause and over micro manage to achieve some of the higher scores/achievements. Doing so turns it from a game into work.
As noted above there is much about this game to enjoy, as long as you just play to play.  However, unlike pinball or other roguelike games, you can't achieve the highest score through pure skill.  You must constantly pause the game and make micro changes every 3-4 seconds. The game also lacks proper instructions as to how many of the elements work, which can frustrate the player. If you are an achievement hunter you may want to avoid this games as the random placement of stations and random end of the week rewards can result in making an achievement impossible.
I personally recommend the game if you can pick it up for less than $10.00.

Despite its MOBA leanings, Gigantic ultimately feels like a team based shooter. It's surely not an Overwatch clone either, because while characters with guns aim and fire like they were in an FPS, it borrows relatively high survivability from MOBAs, which leads to gameplay that tends to be more focused on attrition. The stamina system is perhaps its most unique feature, giving you a limited pool you can use to travel twice as fast as normal. This changes things drastically, as it means you can usually escape a battle even at a quarter of your health...but only if you didn't use your stamina chasing other players or weaving within the fight.
Another thing that sets gigantic apart is the great variety of playstyles of its heroes. You have archetypes straight out of Overwatch -- a sniper, a turret, a melee guy with a shield, a healing-beamer. Yet at the same time there are heroes who come straight out of MOBAs, with emphasis on crowd control, debuffs and buffs, there even a great many heroes who use only melee attacks, tanking up hits or flying across the battlefield. What makes it great is that they fit in seamlessly with the more traditional of the cast.
The game is a joy to play, having barely a trace of downtime. While it wears its inspirations on its sleeve, there's really nothing quite like it.
Beautiful artstyle, extremely fun so far, and I would highly recmmend this to anyone that likes team based games where co-ordination is required.

Srs review: There's a really easy way to sum this game up: if you think you'll like this game, I'm pretty certain you'll like it, if you think you won't then you probably won't. The running time of the whole game is about an hour (depening on how much you want to emerse yourself in the game) and gameplay is minimal. Don't be mistaken by the game's setup, there are no 2deep4u ideas at play here - the gameplay consists of clicking a faux MMO game, looking at desktop files and listening to two peole private chatting. The remarkable thing (and I really do me remarkable) is that Nina Freeman chooses to be extremely personal in the setup of the game; regardless whether or not the story is true, she uses her own selfies, her friends pictures and exposes herself (both physically and emotionally) to make a really straight forward narrative honest and engaging. The narrative never casts judgement on either character and the experience as a whole lulls you into really engaging into the fairly standard chats the two characters have.
It isn't perfect, but if you're prepared to just go with it then there's a lot to take out of Cibele. Personally, I think Star Maid Games have developed some really interesting games and this one is well worth your time.

Thief is a stealth oriented exploration game about stealing stuff and finding and completing collectible sets. Thats about it. While stealth isn't necessarily required (it's possible to shoot every target you see with your bow) it is encouraged by the means of challenges. I understand the critique that has been thrown at Thief and although i do agree with most of it, i still had a fun time with it. I should also state that i'm a new player to the Thief franchise and have never played the older classic games.
- Visually the game is very impressive with some of the best shadows i have ever seen.
- The performance was solid all the way through, with my fps going up to 150 (Averaging at about 110-120) and never dipping below 60. (I'm running an i5 @ 3.4 GHz CPU with a 1070 GPU)
- Gameplay is fun and engaging with a huge arsenal of arrows to manipulate your environment.
- Voice Acting was great on most characters and sidecharacters (especially Garrett)
- Puzzle design was unique and just difficult enough to keep me invested.
- Overall the sound design was fitting and thematic.
- The difficulty customization is a fantastic addition and allows you to completely design your own playthough. Think the game is too easy and you can easily pass a level by simply knocking out all the guards? Remove knockouts with an add-on. How about a modifier that instantly fails you when you get detected?
- The story and characters are "meh" and makes it really hard to get involved in the world.
- While challenging at some parts overall the game is easy. Levels can be passed by staying in the shadows and just shooting guards in the the head with your bow and arrows or by just sneaking in behind them and knocking them out with your blackjack (most of these problems can be fixed with the difficulty customization options though)
- Level design, while not awful, is not as expansive and varied as i would have liked (there is basically 2-3 ways to complete every level)
- The main storyline takes you about 8-10 hours to complete (while it is possible to bump your overall playtime up to around 30 hours by collecting EVERYTHING and doing every side objective.
- Enemy variety is limited (there's only 3. Yes it's a stealth game but still)
Thief is a game best experienced at its worst difficulty with all the modifiers cranked up to 11. While the story does have its moments where it pulls you in, you are mostly going to be wandering around a level searching for your next loot to steal. With its problems there is still fun to be had in the world of Thief and i would recommend it to any stealth lover out there. I would have given the game a higher rating had the story been more involved or the game been a bit more difficult but as it stands it's a solid 7.5/10

The indie market is simultaneously one of the best and the worst ideas in the gaming industry, and both for the same reason:  there are so many games.  On one hand, some of them must be good; on the other, how do you find them?  Gifted to me by my brother nearly two years ago, I find that They Bleed Pixels is a true hidden gem amongst the sands of the indie market.
First, but not foremost, the aesthetics.  As implied by its somewhat curious title, They Bleed Pixels puts itself in the vein of "new-age retro" with old-school graphics and gameplay.  Even though the game uses a modern graphics engine (Resulting in some slowdown for those playing games on a toaster like me), graphics are in the dead-simple style of something you may perhaps find on a SNES.  The game makes the interesting stylistic choices of outlining almost everything in white instead of black, and making all the platforms dead-simple in nature, likely to make the player character stand out more—and, boy, does she.  Animation for They Bleed Pixels is incredibly fluid; the amount of work put into the protagonist alone is insane (No frame count available since the sprites haven't been ripped yet, but it's definitely up there), but the enemies, too?  Factor in the lush pixel art for the comic-book-styled cutscenes, and the hugely detailed backgrounds in every stage, and it becomes evident that Spooky Squid really sweated the small stuff.
The soundtrack of the game was performed by a "DJ Finish Him," a music artist I hadn't heard of until now.  Specializing in unorthodoxy, his style relies heavily on using things never intended to be instruments as instruments.  As such, the music, while not unpleasant, has a tendency to fade into the background and go unnoticed by the player, nothing at all like the earworms from the old days of video gaming.  It did help set the atmosphere with its low, droning tunes, but I find it somewhat unfitting for a game falling into the "new-age retro" category.
Alright, on to the gameplay.  It is very easy to say things like "They Bleed Pixels is the Gothic Lolita lovechild of Super Meat Boy," but I find it better to view it as its own thing.  Self-classed as a "Lovecraftian Platformer," They Bleed Pixels combines difficult platforming alongside with deadly combat, all at a breakneck pace (Or it would be, were it not for my slowdown).  Gameplay is primarily based upon killing enemies in the most brutal ways possible, earning more points as you stab your foes to death in more ways.  Players who keep their claws soaked will find themselves rewarded with combo bonuses—and, with a ranking system and high-score table, there's definitely some incentive for the player to kill with skill instead of fighting to stay alive.  Speaking of staying alive, our poor heroine has only three hearts to her name, and there are a handful of things in the game capable of killing her instantly, so—simply as a fact of the way the game is designed—be prepared to die a couple times.  And start working on becoming emotionally immune to those heart-rending screams she gives every time she dies.  Luckily for the player, however, there is also a game mechanic that allows the player to charge up a checkpoint as they kill things and rack up points, and when fully charged, the player can stand still for a moment to drop a checkpoint anywhere they wish (Provided that something that could kill them isn't too close).
Naturally, the game has a steep learning curve; after a tutorial and a tutorial level, the player is thrown headlong into difficult challenges.  Unlike Super Meat Boy, however, the game never feels unreasonable, or like its only objective is to kill you.  Unfortunately, however, the combat begins to drop off towards the end of the game while platforming moves to center stage; with only five enemy types and no bosses, the player learns how to kill very quickly, and then maneuvering through the level becomes the main problem.  Even with this, though, the game remains tantalizingly fun and satisfying.
The plotline of the game, too, is compelling, and perhaps part of the driving force that keeps the player wanting to play.  An unnamed girl (Let's call her Claudia) looking to be about ten years of age is dropped off at Lafcadio Academy for Troubled Young Ladies, a boarding school that feels eerie and uninviting on its own without any supernatural forces.  In the library, she stumbles upon a bloody tome, and—out of curiosity, I suppose—she opens it, and in an instant its magic is upon her, turning her into a demonic claw-handed form of herself and transporting her to a curious dreamscape, in which she rampages about, slaughtering the denizens.  Whenever she wakes up from one of these curious dreams, she finds herself becoming more like the monster she dreamed she was...
The story is told through a series of nonobtrusive, skippable cutscenes between the levels of the game.  Not a word is spoken throughout the entire length of the story, and much of the game is left to the interpretation of the player; yet it seems to have some depth to it, with its dark, Lovecraftian theme.  I would say that They Bleed Pixels's story is one of its strongest suits.
Overall, They Bleed Pixels was not exactly a standard game by any measure.  It threw out conventions in just about every department, including that of the storyline department, and replaced them with things of its own invention.  Being unafraid to try something new is admirable in itself, but I would say that the experiment of They Bleed Pixels was a success as well.  There were no bosses, but the gameplay was fun anyway; the music faded into the background, but it still helped set the mood; the game had slowdown on my computer, but it did nothing to damper my experience.  I give They Bleed Pixels
.  Claudia has charmed me, and I hope I get to see her again someday.
They Bleed Pixels is a meager $10 on the Steam market—a fair price for its content (11 levels and 3 free DLC levels) already, in my opinion, but it goes on sale at times for even cheaper.  I would definitely recommend They Bleed Pixels if it's in your budget.

And I'd also like to say that from what I can tell, the dev is an upstanding, modest person who takes pride in making a good product at a fair price, listens attentively to users, and even appears to offer excellent customer support (he mentioned that the new build of the game won't run on an older Mac OS version, and offered refunds to anyone who wanted one if they were affected.  Whoever you are, you're a class act, mate.
Oh, and as a Cities Skylines fan, I can say that Mini Metro has made me a LOT better at designing roads, bus routes, and railways.  So if you want to improve your C:S skills, this game is totally worth it just for that reason.

But once it clicks, it works well for what the game is trying to do, and I've not had any trouble using it. The UI creates a limitation that you would experience in the real world that is part of the challenge you have to overcome. This is a hardcore Sim, nothing cuts corners to make it easy on you.

If you like survivle games that don't hold your hand with complex systems, Stationeers is for you.

If "Space Engineers" and "Oxygen Not Included" would have a child together, that would probably be this game and "Factorio" would probably his uncle or something like that.
If you like engineering, building stuff, playing around with basic chemicals like oxygen, CO2, Water, Ice, Metals and so on and combing that with temperature, pressure and power/electricity and have a large portion of patience and will to learn you will probably find your new favorite game.
Be warned however, the learning curve is currently rather steep you'll need a lot out outside help (Steam Guides, Forum, Youtube, etc.), a lot of patience and especially nerves sometimes coping with the complex/fiddling input system. There is a Tutorial, but it shows you only a glimpse of what's in there and In-Game ToolTips, Instruction and hints are currently sparse.
Also keep in mind this is very early access there are a lot of rough edges and sometimes crashes or smaller issues here and there. The developers seem to try to keep up to serious issues and is continuing to work on fixes, optimizations and additions. Reaction time seems good so far. It remains to be seen how this develops in the future, but if it continues like that and grows this still very rough stone will turn out to be a real diamond in this genre.
EDIT:
Some features and notes that might be intresting
- Gamestart on a Moon with Gravity or in Space (Mars planned)
- Terrain is voxel-based, allows digging and manipulation everywhere (though not as advanced as in Astroneer)
- Endless map generation (Map expands when moving near border) like in Factorio
- Complex Smelting/Refining/Manufacturing (Advanced Materials like composits need to be carefully adjusted in amount, temp and pressure, bad things can happen as well)
- Complex Gas Simulation and contrary to ONI allows multiple gases in one place
- also contrary to ONI it sometimes simulated reactions of matter, e.g. fire or explosions for example with burnable or explodeable mixtures
- Simulates Pressure incl. Overpressure, Leakages and even explosions of e.g. gas containers
- Simulates Temperature incl. Overheating and Destruction and Dying (with people)
- Ice and Gases smelt/evaporates and you can see real water as well with ice
- Conveyor System for resources and items for storage and transport
- Power Generation via Solar and Coal atm
- Complex Electricity Simulation like in ONI with high and low-capacity wires, transformers, batteries, generators, switches
- Complex Automation like Factorio/ONI already available incl. Logic Processors
- Automation also via Macro/State-Machine like scripting ingame
- First steps with Farming, Nutrients/Water are already partly available but worked on (will extend survival part)
- Can be played single with normal load/save possibilities or online (self-hosting and dedicated possible as well)

I have read many complaints about the UI, and many people including the devs defending it. I think the UI works very well, alltough it takes a while before you become fluent in using it. I dont think I would be playing this game if it had a "drag & drop" inventory system, as these games just play very differently and are not fun at all as you are just managing inventory screens and slots most of the time. With the current UI you actually feel like you are doing the stuff manually, which is very rewarding to me. Also, when you decide to break open some walls to update your wiring, pipes or vents, it looks kinda cool to see all the stuff lying on the floor and spread around. Kinda what would happen in real life when you are building/renovating something. Also, the UI requires an additional layer of planning and thinking from the players side, which I like. I highly recommend this game. I like to play it daily, but never for more than an hour or two.
Lets begin with the fact that it is free to play. In Star Conflict you pilot a space ship in approximately 10 minute matches. The matches include; Combat Recon: a deathmatch like game where two teams face off against each other and may respawn after death only as long as their captain is alive. Detonation: A capture the flag-like game where two team attempt to pick up a bomb and deliver it to enemy stations, winning when no enemy stations remain. Capture: Is a three point domination game where holding a base is worth points, so which ever team holds the most points over a duration will win. Domination: Is an elimination match, you when when you cap three enemy bases or you kill the enemy team. Hunt: Is a one moving point domination game where one of three points is active for 70 seconds during which the team who controls it earns points.
Players advance through a ranking system by earning credits (money) and synergy (xp). Players quickly gain access to three different hull types; Interceptors: Small-sized, lightly armed and shielded, agile, fast ships. Fighters: Medium-sized, heavily armed and lightly shielded ships. Frigates: Large-sized, heavily armed and shielded, slow ships. For the three hulls there are three sub-classes for every hull type. For Interceptors there are Covert Ops, Recon, ECM, each specializing in defeating a particular type of ship or performing a particular task. For Fighters there are Gunship, Tackler, Command. For Frigates there are Guard, Engineer, Long Range.
There are three factions, being a member of a particular faction will only determine who your opponents are. A player may purchase ships from any faction. Within each faction is a ship tree showing all the ships available and the path you must take to unlock them. Each faction will offer contracts that reward the player with special currencies that will allow for upgrades of specific weapons.
The game play is highly addictive. The controls are simple and intuitive. The game is enjoyable at every tier. Game servers handle latency very well. You wont get killed by the really laggy guy you never saw or not be able to hit the guy who skips all around.
For a free game that states it is a BETA, the devs keep you posted about updates and changes to the game and there are frequent updates.
My only complaint is that the player base is low, so the match making system can take 5 minutes to put you into a match during off-peak playing hours. During peak hours its usually under 30 seconds. In addition, the low player base forces the match maker to create matches that are slightly imbalanced ie everyone on the other team is more skilled than everyone on yours etc.

So, it took me an hour to play this, but I don't think this was an hour wasted. From my viewing experience, the best creators in any medium, are more likely to create great future works, if they start out with a small free project to get their name out there. In terms of Visual Novels, this was true for Without Within, Voices from the Sea, and (on steam specifically) Narcissu.
Considering the quality of the demo and the production for "No One But You", I can say this was a good first step. Learning about subtle shifts in lighting for art. Quirky dialogue that manages to be funny even without a vocal cast. Finishing with the most important lesson, learning how to use Renpy and getting a foot in the door with Sekai Project. All that made this worth making.
As for the actual quality of this hour of reading.
Pros:
A few laugh-out-loud moments with some insightful opinions on education, relationships, and the horrors of goldfish.
Cute characters that fufilled their roles and were good stepping stones.
Great writing to illustrate cultural differences and various opinions of alternate indiviudals.
Standard art with one or two nice moments.
Actually including an 18+ H-scene on steam officially. Not to mention a respectable and non-offensive one.
Actually giving you the opition to turn off above-mentioned scene.
A great understanding of Renpy, which is one of the best visual novel making engines available now. Check "Fault" if you want a preview of how far it can go.
A rollback button. Using the mousewheel always gets you too far forward or back. Yes it depends on the mouse, and yes its true for all VNs, but a one click button for going back line by line is very handy for those of use with butter fingers or crappy mice.
It's free.
Cons:
Short. Only an hour.
The stupidity of the whole plot may annoy you if you just finished a really good game. (I finished "Fault milestone 2 side above" yesterday.)
Only two characters who got designs.
An open epilogue,
As far as yuri relationships go, the enjoyment will depend on your taste. I'm open in my opinions of relationship choices, so I thought it was sweet. However, it could have been better, had more time to develop from friends to romantic, and it could attempt to add in feelings of caution and reluctance, which is added in almost any relationship narrative.
6/10 for overall enjoyment. It's enjoyable, just not enough of it. Plus, if you need an hour to kill, why not something free with two achievements. Look forward to more visual novel projects from Unwonted Studios.
Thanks for reading~RB

Fortunately, the plot picks up again after, building to the promise of an epic finale - and cue end credits. Wha....?
*shrugs*

This game may take a unique perspective on the MOBA genre offering third person action game play. The concept of summoning creatures and fighting guardians is enough to try the game. However, I feel that the game can not survive on just that concept. The game has many faults, and overall, I think the game comes up short to other online hero based games.
Hero’s need to be rebalanced as a whole. They need to find a good middle ground where all hero’s feel adequate. Some skills do not act properly due to it being calculated on server side, making these skills go in the wrong direction. The hit boxes of many skills extend beyond their indicator which can be irritating. I also think that some skills just need a complete rework/change.
Some maps are designed in such a way that it can cause clunky game play. Many objects in the game have horrible collision. Some times the characters appear half way through the ground. Other maps promote team camping on a single creature point where they don’t even have to play the objective until the end. This prolongs the game needlessly and gives bad experience to players. I only feel that one map is actually balanced.
Matchmaking seems to horrible. Doesn’t seem to take into player skill at all and often time will be matched up with level 30+ players while others are playing for their first time. Many matches are way one sided and due to hero and map problems listed above can further cause poor game play. As it stands at this moment, you should not look at in a competitive point of view.
I personally don’t mind the free to play aspect, however, as playing free it seems to be less rewarding then most free to play game in this genre. There is a quest objective that can give you bonus currency, but is tied to a RNG card packs. You can receive a card pack daily and when obtaining a higher account level. I’ve now played both the Steam version and the 18+ version (available for free download form the developer’s website) and I can safely say this is a great visual novel. I’m no expert on these types of games, and I’ve only played a few, but this one is probably the best to date.
The first thing you should know before thinking about playing is that this game deals with gay characters and themes, exclusively. So if you are really not into that, give it a pass, however if you are on the fence I’d still say give it a try, you may end up really liking it.
Without spoiling anything, this game has an interesting and well written story with multiple endings both good and bad. Excellent artwork and decent music combined with a very competent English translation. I got the impressions, based on certain word choices, this was translated by someone either from the UK or was trained in UK English. So while the translation and grammar is not perfect, it is perfectly understandable.
I was most impressed with the games glossary, which acts as a codex of terms and definitions which people not natively from or familiar with Chinese and Taiwanese culture can refer to when they don’t understand something. As someone from Canada this was particularly useful and I actually learnt quite a bit. There’s something of an educational angle to this aspect of the game, at least for people like me.
On a more personal note I’ve been playing and thinking about this game for the last two days. The story and its various endings have made me quite emotional. Nekojishi really is something special and at a price tag of free, if you have any interest in it at all you should check it out.
Note: like I said in the beginning if you would like to play the 18+ version it is available for free on the developer’s website. If you enjoy the game you are of course encouraged to make a Paypal donation to help support the developers.

So is the story at least worth seeing? No, it certainly isn't.
