Best weeabo simulator around; that moment when you finally become a 10th level CringeMaster is just utterly beautiful. The ending alone left my whole family lineage with an undying sensation of regret. The game mechanics were supberb; on par with minesweeper on Windows 95. I haven't seen acting like this since that time I found a camcorder in the trash and fimed my friends eating mexican candy....ahhhhh good times. The writing was just absolutely pulitzer worthy. Bukowski, Ginsberg, Plath, that girl on tumblr who still stuck in the Scene trend of the early 2000's, move out the way this game trumps you all. The raw emotion and complexity of each poem just touches my soul so deeply I might get a metaphysical restraining order. But Cibele is all about the dialog and boy does it get to you. Well thought out, well written, thought provoking, and the depth of two 10 year olds arguing over which power ranger is the best. Honestly, I loved how the effort into developing Nina's character. You really learn about her hobbies and interests. For example, a good deal was put into establishing her as a photography enthusiast and it really shows. She talks about her love for taking people's portraits and... well...just damn....she can easily be the next Avedon without a doubt, but what I love the most is how each photograph is purely candid in the same vain as Cartier-Bresson. It takes skill and years of experience to reach this level in the world of photography and she did it before the age of 20, just amazing. Now I know we can't all relate to ther photographic expertise but we do all have one thing in common: games. Her repertoire of games is just as refined as a potter making a vase mid way through the Pompeii incident of 79 C.E. Cibele for the most part maintains a healthy habit of playing the same MMO day and night. She is so immersed in her games that she puts off her whole future as a human being to play with the same guy....everyday. Coupled with her childlike intelligence and the common sense of a brain dead adult she makes decisions that any of us could have made. Her approach to love is completely revolutionary; there exists no philosopher to have ever consider love in the manner of which Cibele does. Heloise, Abelard, Kierkegaard, and the rest just fail in the intellectual capacity to understand and convey the meaning of love to the masses as Cibele does. In truth, Cibele is just next ontological step in art and gaming. A truly unique experience that no other game can other.
I can go on and on but I don't want to spoil anything for you guys. In fact I think I gave bit to much away so sorry. So really what ever you do just don't play this game.

I like games, which are pushing the boundaries of their medium and Cibele definitely tries something in style of Her Story and The Beginner's Guide here. You play as Nina and can inspect her files and launch applications from her desktop. The story is progressed by playing a MMORPG-style game together with another player Ichi/Blake. The two are shown in short films between their "raids" and voice-chat during their play-seesion. And I'm sure it could have worked: the artstyle is rudimentary but fitting and the voice-acting is actually pretty good. Where the game is getting off tracks is in it's story: I expected some kind of twist or parable, but this is one ordinary and, dare I say it, boring love story. Therefore I can recommend thinking about the idea of playing games inside a game to progress a "irl" story (as done in the totally underrated Bedlam for example), but I can't recommend buying it.

+Great blend of
and hack-n-slash gameplay

An indie title I encountered randomly, Death Road to Canada (DR2C) offers fantastic visuals and music. It's an absolutely fantastic game, and the devs have made it memorable and replayable.
Music and visuals are top-notch and the game has a lot of humour and personality. It seems simple at first with it's pixel art but the art itself has a charm of its own, especially when you see the varied characters you can meet (including some famous dudes). It's also super fun adding your own characters to it too. The music is both calming and exciting and never boring to listen to, and I absolutely recommend the soundtrack.
The game is a mix between choose your own adventure (CYOA) and a scavenging game. Each day it takes to get to Canada, you're given the ability to pick where you want to rest/loot and to choose what happens in a written scenario. The written scenarios are what makes this game shine more, because they are absolutely RIDICULOUS. They are so ridiculous it's hilarious, and I had fun every single time I attempted my trip to Canada. Furthermore, being able to control what you pick up in terms of loot is a nice touch, making it more interactive and up to players rather than up to RNG. However, that doesn't mean RNG isn't a factor, as towns and cities are randomly generated, as well as what you can pick up in town.
In the time I've played this game, I experienced no crashes, or any bugs or glitches to speak about. The devs are very on top of this game as well, releasing new DLC content with big updates named after anatomical parts (which I'm a big fan of). On top of fine tuning and polishing the game, each DLC update they release is FREE. That's pretty great coming from indie devs.
This game is one of the games I enjoyed playing in 2016, and into 2017. It's one of the games I remember fully enjoying then and now. Definitely check it out if you're up for an Organ Trail esque game...TO CANADA!

Where do I even begin with this game. First off ive been playing this game for about 7 years now and every playthrough ive had of it was exellent. There is alot of variety when it comes to builds. There is the obvious Light/Dark or Grey option for the game but there is also Force user builds, Ranged builds, Pure combat focused guardian, etc. I find the combat to be enjoyable (In my opinion) since its tactical and you can really plan attacks and things of that sort. Take DA:0 for example. Its pretty much the same system. You can start with 3 beginning classes: Guardian (Combat focused), Sentinel (Better skill progression), and Consular (Force powers). You then later in the game get different set of prestige classes depending on your allignment. Now, lets get to the writing of the game. This game has one of the best stories I have ever seen. You'll see once you play it for yourself. The reason I prefer this game slightly over the first is just because I prefer the darker, philosophical, grey aspects of the atmosphere and story a bit better (Kotor 1 is also one of my favorite games). Anyways, this game presents the idea that Dark is not necessarily evil and Light isnt nessesary good and you really get to see the Flaws of both sides. For example, you play as the Jedi Exile, who was exiled from the Jedi order for rusing to war to protect innocents. The Jedi were lazy and waited to "evaluate the threat". The dialouge and voice acting in this game is absolutely fantastic (Especially Kreia). For this game, you dont even need to be a fan of Star Wars. A non Star Wars fan would look at this game and just play an RPG. However a Star Wars fan would look at this and play an amazing Star Wars RPG. The reason for this is because the game is set in an era wayyy before the Movies. One flaw however, would be the cut content presented this game. Obsidian (The developers) were rushed to release this game by lucasarts, resulting in them needing to cut out content for the game. Luckily, a group of community modders managed to get into the games files and restore alot of the content that was cut. You can find the mod on the steam workshop. Anyways, hurry up and buy the game! You wont be dissapointed.

Tired of those endless drudges through gore and misery only to wind up going from day to day rooting out tins of cold baked beans? Sick and tired of having to scavenge hundreds of planks to make fences for your little survivor camp? Hacked off at seeing the same identikit survivors which stories which all blend into each other and just make you reach for the booze?
Death Road to Canada is possibly one of the most lighthearted zombie murder games I've run into in a long while, ostensibly taking it's inspiration from the Organ Trail, and FTL, you're put in charge of two survivors, and a car. Your job, should you choose to accept it, is to drive to Canada, or to die trying. Hint, you're going to die a fair few times before you get there, but that's all part of the learning experience. You can either take some random survivors in a default game setting, or you can create your own survivors, be they friends or people you want to see turned into zombie chow, and set off with your own choice of team, with the intent of picking up more friends along the way.
Combat is a little bit loose, but that's intended by design, you are after all, survivors, not trained soldiers, so you tend to waff your melee weapons in the general direction of whatever is closest to you, said weapons ranging from spatulas (no, no joke) right the way through to sledgehammers, hockeysticks, nailboards, and baseball bats. Then you've the proper shootybang stuff with revolvers, pistols, shotguns and so on. The stats of your survivor play a significant part in how many swings they'll get in before they become "winded", or in the case of firearms, just how accurate they're prone to be (shotguns you can get away with giving to anyone, other guns you'll want to be a bit more careful with).
For what could have been a fairly simple pick up and play game, there's a lot of statistical complexity under the hood, with weapons having their own "drain" on player stamina, weapons having their own fire rate, accuracy and spread, and vehicles having their own consumption rate, and durability. Characters too have their own personality traits and benefits, meaning that it's unlikely you'll run across two survivors that are exactly the same in a given playthrough, as a direct result, DRtC becomes a far stronger game than the Organ Trail and actually elevates itself up to the company of games like Death Skid Marks, which shares the same kind of irreverant humour and sense of fun about it.
This doesn't even touch on the fact there's pets you can bring into the team (Dogs and Cats, though as yet I've not been successful at grabbing either), there's choose your own adventure style events, though these are more simplistic than say, FTL, they are stat based in terms of the choices you get with differing chances of success, and depending on your survivors, you may get presented with different options from one playthrough to the next.
Death Road to Canada -could- have been a throwaway title, or something that would have been fun for a pick up and play but ultimately not something that would stand up to repeated scrutiny. I'm glad to report that this definitely is not the case, there's real longevity here, and there's a definite gem of a game here. One that has managed to emerge as another Kickstarter success (which is a bit of a rarity these days) and one the devs rightly should be quite happy about.
Verdict :
There -is- one unanswered question which I'll update my review with as time progresses, and that concerns a KS exclusive piece of content which whilst not *vast*, is game affecting. As is normal for any review I do, I do "due dilligence" on all games that go through Kickstarter, and I highlight such things because in the interests of being thorough, that's my job.
One of the reward tiers ($50) provided backers with a specific game unlock, allowing them to have the option of a kitten or puppy as a "morale booster" who would grow into a full team member over time, at the cost of an additional food drain. This would be something in the -longer term- I'd like to see added as purchasable DLC of some sort, as it would be nice to have the full game made "content complete", however, as I state above, because this game is predominantly a singleplayer experience, this isn't something that will affect players beyond their personal preference.
This element will be removed or revised as more information is made available.

I highly recommend this game. I like to play it daily, but never for more than an hour or two.
Lets begin with the fact that it is free to play. In Star Conflict you pilot a space ship in approximately 10 minute matches. The matches include; Combat Recon: a deathmatch like game where two teams face off against each other and may respawn after death only as long as their captain is alive. Detonation: A capture the flag-like game where two team attempt to pick up a bomb and deliver it to enemy stations, winning when no enemy stations remain. Capture: Is a three point domination game where holding a base is worth points, so which ever team holds the most points over a duration will win. Domination: Is an elimination match, you when when you cap three enemy bases or you kill the enemy team. Hunt: Is a one moving point domination game where one of three points is active for 70 seconds during which the team who controls it earns points.
Players advance through a ranking system by earning credits (money) and synergy (xp). Players quickly gain access to three different hull types; Interceptors: Small-sized, lightly armed and shielded, agile, fast ships. Fighters: Medium-sized, heavily armed and lightly shielded ships. Frigates: Large-sized, heavily armed and shielded, slow ships. For the three hulls there are three sub-classes for every hull type. For Interceptors there are Covert Ops, Recon, ECM, each specializing in defeating a particular type of ship or performing a particular task. For Fighters there are Gunship, Tackler, Command. For Frigates there are Guard, Engineer, Long Range.
There are three factions, being a member of a particular faction will only determine who your opponents are. A player may purchase ships from any faction. Within each faction is a ship tree showing all the ships available and the path you must take to unlock them. Each faction will offer contracts that reward the player with special currencies that will allow for upgrades of specific weapons.
The game play is highly addictive. The controls are simple and intuitive. The game is enjoyable at every tier. Game servers handle latency very well. You wont get killed by the really laggy guy you never saw or not be able to hit the guy who skips all around.
For a free game that states it is a BETA, the devs keep you posted about updates and changes to the game and there are frequent updates.
My only complaint is that the player base is low, so the match making system can take 5 minutes to put you into a match during off-peak playing hours. During peak hours its usually under 30 seconds. In addition, the low player base forces the match maker to create matches that are slightly imbalanced ie everyone on the other team is more skilled than everyone on yours etc.

As the space genre sees a resurgence, of which I am very pleased, Star Conflict fills  very welcome niche against the many other games that have cropped up so far.
At it's core, SC is basically an arcade style dogfighting game. You get the standard multiplayer gametypes, with a few interesting variations. The best of them, in my opinion, is Captains mode, where one player is randomly elected "Captain". As long as this player survives, respawns are unlimited, but as soon as they get blown to space bits, it becomes a deadly game of survival, hoping to take out the opposing teams Captain before all forces are lost.
As far as the free-to-play aspect of this game goes, it is by far one of the better examples of the genre. Effectively all you can buy with money is a lowered grind, and fancy looking ships. Generally there are always ships you can get in-game that are as powerful as the premium ships, and in some cases they're actually better. Really the only problem I have is charging to convert ship synergy (this games "XP") into free synergy, which is usable by all ships, effectively forcing you to use your new, weak ship to level itself up, thereby defeating the purpose of having excess free synergy to begin with.
Maybe it's the best space game. Maybe it'll only tide us all over till Star Citizen comes out. Either way, it's fun, and a worthwhile way to waste an afternoon.

✸Eidos Montreal już pokazał, że ma rękę do wskrzeszania kultowych serii. Po bardzo moim zdaniem udanym powrocie Deus Ex, przyszedł czas na zapowiadanego już od kilku lat Thiefa. I choć pierwsze trailery, czy fragmenty rozgrywki nie nastrajały mnie zbyt pozytywnie, to wciąż miałem nadzieję, że Thief A.D. 2014 nie zhańbi dobrego imienia cyklu. I może nie zhańbiła, ale zaszczytu też jej raczej nie przynosi.
✠Zacznę wszakże od pewnego wyjaśnienia. Przy pierwszym przechodzeniu w ogóle nie uruchamiałem w grze tak zwanego trybu koncentracji, ustawiłem sobie najwyższy poziom czujności SI, wyłączyłem celownik i na kilka dodatkowych sposobów utrudniłem rozgrywkę. Uważam przy tym, że wrzucanie do gry takich nadnaturalnych mocy dla sprawnych inaczej graczy jest przestępstwem i powinno być karane zanurzeniem prawej ręki w smole. Z drugiej strony rozumiem jednak, że będąc produktem wysokobudżetowym, nowy Thief musi się sprzedać, więc na tym kończę rejtanowskie rozdzieranie szat, bo przecież najlepiej jest, gdy i wilk syty, i owca cała.
♖A to akurat Thief ma spore szanse zagwarantować. Serio. Najnowsza produkcja Eidosu mogłaby bowiem spokojnie trafić do Sevres, jako wzorzec elastyczności dostosowania zarówno poziomu rozgrywki, jak i choćby interfejsu użytkownika. Tylu - i co najważniejsze - tak szczegółowych opcji nie znalazłem dotychczas chyba w żadnej grze akcji. Mało tego, nie jest to jedynie kosmetyka, czy kwestia gustu - praktycznie każda z tychże opcji w jakiś sposób przekłada się na na rozgrywkę i nasze jej postrzeganie.
♢Co zatem możemy zmienić? Niemal wszystko. Na górze piramidy mamy kilka ogólnie zdefiniowanych poziomów trudności, jednak zabawa zaczyna się w momencie, gdy zaczynamy do nich dodawać własne obostrzenia, takie jak wspomniany już brak koncentracji, zapisywanie gry jedynie na końcu rozdziału, czy nawet permanentną śmierć i rozpoczynanie rozgrywki od nowa. Jest tego całe mnóstwo, a każde kliknięcie skutecznie oddala nas od wizerunku "gry dla noobów". Warto tu jednak pamiętać, że nasze decyzje będą ostateczne, a samodzielnie zdefiniowanego kilkunastoma warunkami poziomu trudności nie zmienimy w trakcie rozgrywki.
❅Thief A.D. 2014 z założenia jest swoistym restartem serii. Twórcy niemal całkowicie odcięli się od kosmogonii starego świata (choć pewne echa "przeszłości" dają się zauważyć), nieco inny, bardziej realistyczny charakter ma obecna formuła steampunku, zmienił się także pod kilkoma względami główny bohater. Wciąż będący samotnikiem i wyrzutkiem, ale odniosłem wrażenie, że zdecydowanie mniej cyniczny, niż niegdyś. Zapewne dlatego brakuje mu też tej charakterystycznej, cichej charyzmy; oswojony, nie jest już tym samym Garrettem.
❈Grając w Thiefa miałem przez cały czas wrażenie, że Eidos za bardzo skupił się na detalach, jednocześnie zaniedbując rdzeń rozgrywki. Co raz oglądamy takie smaczki, jak świetne animacje dłoni podczas włamywania się do sejfów, podobać może się prosta, ale satysfakcjonująca mechanika otwierania zamków, a Miasto zachwyca formą. Cóż jednak z tego, skoro nad tym wszystkim wisi odium źle zaprojektowanej rozgrywki i momentami fatalny projekt poziomów. I tak miotałem się przez cały czas, raz po raz piejąc z zachwytu, by po chwili rzeczywistość, brutalna niczym celnie rzucona kostka brukowa, zmazała uśmiech z mojej twarzy.
✺To jest właśnie w nowym Thiefie najsmutniejsze. To dojmujące uczucie, że jest tu tak wiele rzeczy dobrych, ciekawie zaprojektowanych, czy starających się całkiem skutecznie zbudować odpowiedni nastrój, a jednocześnie większość z tych idei jest niemal z miejsca sabotowana przez spinające całość błędy koncepcyjne. Granie przy takiej sinusoidzie nastrojów nie należy z pewnością do największych przyjemności, których oczekiwałbym po naprawdę udanej grze.
✥A jak ma się do tego tak szeroko opisywana przeze mnie na początku, wyjątkowa elastyczność dostosowania rozgrywki do naszych oczekiwań? Otóż tak naprawdę, to właśnie ona uratowała ten tytuł w moich oczach. W ogóle nie mogę sobie wyobrazić konieczności grania z całym zaimplementowanym dobrodziejstwem inwentarza. I wbrew wszystkiemu nie żałuję tych kilkudziesięciu spędzonych z grą godzin, warto było dla tych chwil, kiedy naprawdę czułem ducha Miasta.

Played this gem of a match-3 on iphone for a few weeks and enjoyed it without paying a penny, though it tended to get a little tedious as levels progressed.  But it's a good family game and since my gaming rig has a touch screen I thought I'd give it a try on PC.  With an XBox-style controller in hand I fire up the game, controller recognized I proceed with gameplay - no surprises, nice.
Now time to try playing without controllers.  What? Neither mouse nor touch support under windows? (Stupifying considering how many of us gamers prefer KB & mouse over a controller!)  Controller support is just fine, but if you don't have one then you'll have to use the cursor keys to navigate the menus, as well as the actual game board.  This reminds me of early arcade games like Tetris.  Spacebar is the select/enter key.  So with no controller it's KB-only gameplay, not horrible but not 2015 either.  Hopefully touch screen and mouse support are in development as the game deserves it.
Apart for that, given the nickel & dimey nature of the game I wonder if there's going to be much of a market for this type of game on steam.  The play and graphics are pretty good, at least I thought so under iOS.  But the idea of liking it enough to splurge on perks to improve gameplay, well, it's like perpetual DLC.  This penny-bleeding model seems to work in the personal device marketplace so why not here??
Bottom line:  Unfortunately I regret installing Frozen Free Fall: Snowball Fight on PC, even with its small footprint.  It may be okay for tablets and smartphones, but not so much for a PC rig in its present form unless one has a controller (or two for multiplayer).  With mouse and/or touch support I might reinstall it and try it again.  But for now I'm putting this kiddie game to bed.

In Turmoil you play as a prospective oil tycoon, settled in an old west town, in which you compete against 3 AI in a rather short campaign by leasing land and digging for oil.
Gameplay is simple and easy although that doesn't mean there's no depth (ha!) at all in Turmoil. There's definitely an element of RNG in the game with respect to where you can strike oil. You can search for oil pockets using a couple of methods like a dowser, a mole and even a scanner. You then place your oil rig and start drilling.
There are other gameplay aspects which you also need to pay attention too. At the left and right of your screen are oil companies which you can buy your oil. You can transfer the oil to the company of your choice using horse carriages but you should know that the price of oil fluctuates constantly so you need to sell high in order to maximize profits.
You can also store oil in silos if you feel that the current price market is not up to your standard or to prevent spillages which grant hefty fines.
You also need to spend your money wisely. Improving drilling speed or getting wider and longer pipes isn't always a good. Turmoil is essentially a resource management game and as you progress through the game you'll come to understand how important it is in order to succeed.
Back in town, you can upgrade your oil digging equipment and bid against your competitors to get pieces of land. In the saloon you can also find other services like bribing for higher selling prices, or less spillage fines, getting hints about rich piece of lands and more. In order to win in Turmoil you need to be the majority shareholder of the town's stock after the mayor retires. Getting stock is sort of minigame where you the fastest person with the highest bid wins.
The artistic style of the graphics is fitting enough for the theme of the game but there's not really much detail to go around. Furthermore there are few bugs, especially with audio. Several sounds are gonna get stuck and loop endlessly which made for a quite annoying experience.
So where does this leave Turmoil? It's fun for a couple of hours but then the monotony kicks in. There's not really much to do and getting screwed over by RNG is no fun at all if you get a field with minimal oil reserves. I'll admit it is calming and relaxing but then again this doesn't seem to be the main selling point of the game. I got this as part of bundle and I did enjoy my limited time playing before I got bored. I'm only giving this game a negative recommendation for the pricing. If you enjoy the gameplay mechanics I'd suggest getting this on a discount or packed in a bundle. The game's not terrible but it's not that great either. It does have an air of browser flash game in it, the concept is interesting but the execution leaves a lot to be desired.

Brink of Consciousness: Dorian Gray Syndrome is one of the most effective horror Hidden Object Games I've ever come across. The plot opens when the main character's girlfriend is kidnapped by the twisted serial killer who has been preying on the city's beautiful young people. The main character is a reporter chronicling the case, and this has drawn the madman's attention - the only hope he has of saving his girlfriend's life is to travel to the villain's mansion and play the madman's game.
It's a solid premise for any horror story, and BoC:DGS' developers do it justice with truly solid scripting. The villain contacts the main character through the game via loudspeakers he's set up in every room of his house, pontificating about the nature of love and sacrifice, and valiantly attempting to justify all of the murders he's committed. It's all incredibly solid stuff, and along with diary pages scattered about the house informing the killer's backstory, and surprisingly a well-written journal that tracks the player's trek through the mansion, it offers one of the genre's high points, from a storytelling standpoint.
Now for the HOG criteria!
Criteria 1: To what degree do the puzzle screens look like a thrift store vomited on my monitor?
BoC does a great job of making its HOS fit within the world of the game. The whole thing is set in the dilapidated mansion of a maniac, so a certain degree of clutter is to be expected, but it never gets so stacked with random nonsense that it seems preposterous. An especially nice note is that the game is set in the 1950s, and the developers were very careful to only use period items in the hidden object screens. There aren't any digital watches lain across phonographs, or anything along those lines. Okay, there's a colour television at one point, but that's really the only anachronistic lapse.
Criteria 2: Are the searches justified by the premise/story?
Only in the barest sense. Conforming quite neatly to the industry standard, BoC has screens where the player is asked to pick up one item they actually need, along with a dozen that don't matter, for no particular reason. The screens are fair and entertaining to play, but it would have been nice to see the developers go that extra mile to ensure that they made sense within the story.
Criteria 3: How well do the various puzzles and object searches meld together to form a coherent whole?
BoC does a great job of creating a world where this kind of searching a puzzle-solving make sense. Oscar, the game's masked villain, is a baroque psychopath who enjoys toying with his prey - of course he'd construct elaborate puzzles for them to solve in his huge mansion. Even the puzzles are generally more practical than is normal for the genre. They tend to feel more like minigames and activities than actual brain-teasers - for the most part, whenever a lock needs to be picked or a chest opened, players are simply assigned a complex task to perform and then expected to follow the clear instructions on how to complete it. While it may not end up as challenging as some games, this certainly puts BoC among the most user-friendly HOGs I've encountered.
With its great setting and exceptional writing, Dorian Gray Syndrome stands apart from the HOG crowd as a title that even players unfamiliar with the genre can find extremely accessible. It's just too bad that it doesn't push the envelope in gameplay design as well, satisfying itself with utterly traditional hidden object screens. While it may not be reaching for the stars, BoC still manages to stand well above most of its contemporaries, providing a chilling adventure along with some merely solid puzzles.

Nekojishi is a great visual novel that is definitely worth playing, or reading I guess. While the appeal is niche, at least gay but into furries helps too, Nekojishi does have a good story that provides some insight into Asian culture, allowing this game to also provide a bit of a learning experience, should you choose to look into it.
As a visual novel, the actual gameplay is pretty light, limited simply to reading and making decisions to reach a happy ending. However, that's all this game needs; the main character, Liao, is the same person regardless of how you play. Your decisions throughout the story affect which passions he chooses to pursue, but we ultimately have little agency on who Liao is. There is a golden ending to aim for, and I'd honestly recommend trying to work your way to that ending without a guide, as getting there does require a combination of getting to know each of the characters pretty well and getting the right information. While said golden ending is the only one where everyone gets a happy ending, the other endings you'll be likely to see while trying to find it are also heartwarming. Multiple playthroughs are both easy and encouraged. In addition to figuring out how to get the golden ending, there are also a few tools to use that makes things easier; a fastforward button that can skip through the parts you've already read, a glossary that keeps track of terms and other such things so you can review the concepts whenever you like, and a gallery to keep track of the events you've seen and review the great artwork that accompanies this game. Said artwork is actually quite interesting. Pretty much all of the character designs seem a little different than the usual furry art, giving the characters' an attractive appearance as well as a sort of otherwordly mystique due to their slightly non standard features. That could just be the artists' own personal touches, but they fit regardless.
Overall, Nekojishi is an amazing visual novel to experience. A great cast, heartwarming story, and outstanding visual appeal all contribute to a good game worth playing.

This is a game where you command armies of troops and tactically maneuver them on a grid-based battlefield, while leveling a hero character up and customizing your approach to battle. That sounds pretty fun to me. Which is why I keep trying to like this series of games, as the original King's Bounty was such a staple of my childhood. But sadly it is a deeply flawed series, so despite some positive features, just isn't recommendable.
In (literally) the first battle you fight, the opposing army uses abilities that causes your armies to act on their own accord instead of listening to your orders. While the fight itself is easy, this is a good indicator of how the game goes. Design decisions were made that may have sounded tactically interesting, but result in a poor user experience where you often find yourself watching things unfold on-screen with little to no meaningful input on your part.
The AI is also acutely aware that while it can throw limitless hordes at you, you have a very finite force. It often makes decisions that would make no tactical sense in terms of winning the battle, but pick aware at you. Again, this may seem tactically interesting, but the end result is a lot of reloading and long trips back to recruit more soldiers.

Blake read as aromantic to me.  Particularly one who has not been exposed to the term, and is frustrated trying to express their worldview with only the alloromantic parameters to base his descriptions on.  This resonated with me a bit because I had a similar situation until I came across the term asexual to describe my experiences, it can be frustrating for both parties when one can’t put words to their goals or views on a relationship.
If this was intentional, then I applaud the inclusion, but since the ending was left to hang and not be handled, I don’t think it was. Not being handled is better than being handled poorly though. So with that in mind, this next part is a bit of a PSA, where I will attempt to do a bit of the handling that the game did not:
-Alloromantic - Someone who DOES experience romantic attraction.
-Aromantic- Someone who does NOT experience romantic atraction.
-Asexual- Someone who does NOT experience sexual attraction, allosexual is someone who DOES.
Just as there are many sub categories of allo-romantic/sexual (hetero, homo, etc.), there are many sub categories of a-romantic/sexual (grey, demi, etc.). And they are all valid ways to experience the human condition. If I read the game correctly in this regard, then it shows how a lack of visibility can hurt people in relationships. Both characters were in an allotypical space, so when Nina was expecting an alloromantic relationship to form, Blake was unable to articulate why that was something they neither wanted nor was capable of giving. I came away from this game feeling sorry for both characters.

I got this in a humble bundle.
As a engaged to a wonderful man I met on WoW, with all my heart I *wanted* to like this game. I understood going in that this would be more of a story/movie/experience than a game, and it was. I don't mind that, I like games like that for the most part, I want to be immersed and participate in the story while becoming attached to these people. I wanted that. And I will be fair, I didn't hate playing this game, but it had some major problems.
I liked:
- The computer interface and learning about the characters in indirect ways. The tidbits of her blog, pictures, chats with friends, I liked that. I felt endeared to her in these sections of random exploration because I could relate.
- The game interface was simple and I thought pretty, easy to interact with while listening to dialogue. I wish there was more to it, more nods to the gaming community and things we do while chatting/grinding in games, but it worked for what it was.
- She complained about loading screens once and I giggled.
I disliked:
- This game's major failing is it is *short*. Story games that are so short either have to introduce very few characters and spend all their time making sure you are absolutly enthralled with and attached to the few characters they do have or they have to information overload you. The first option is much better for this particular subject matter of romance, I believe. I didn't have enough time to see them become a couple, it felt very rushed and disjointed/jarring. I never had time to become invested in the romance because I didn't have time to believe in it. I never believed it would work or that he loved her or that she knew enough of him to love him. I couldn't be invested. I never cared about the other characters, they were just distracting and seemed like filler to support the main relationship, I couldn't care about them.
- The dialogue seemed at odds with itself. It seems like he was a jerk one moment and nice the next, like he desperately didn't want connections. I had no idea why he was talking to her at all and why he was dragging himself through the interaction and farce of a romance. Her dialogue was okay, she just seemed rather deluded by wanting to be wanted.
If this had been longer with more fleshed out characters, I would have appreciated that. If there are going to be more characters than just the main two, they need to be supported by connection. The relationship needs to be much more organic, we never got a sense of them other than he thinks she's cute, he's kind of a jerk who doesn't know how to interact, and she is always being acted upon, she never really acts. And then it ends and I don't know how to feel or if I feel anything about it.
Good start into experimental story telling territory, but it feels like just that: A start. Not a fully realized game, like the bare bones of a story that needs a lot more meat.

If you can look at Thief without measuring it up to its predecessors, its a fantastic game in and of itself. A reboot of a series/game for me is just another perspective on how the game CAN be compared to what it currently is...and in that respect, its always good to have variety and change whether thats good or bad, depending entirely on an individuals perspective. Things can become stale and boring if you have expectations of a product to meet the criteria at 100% and it been delivered as such...and for me, already knowing what it will be can ruin it...so instead of doing that its designed to make you think "oh, okay, this isn't what I expected" and from there, you either embrace the change, accepting that its a different challenge, a different perspective...or you completely deny its existence for not been the exact same sloop that you played the last three times. I can understand the position of die hard Thief fans though and I'm not saying anyone is wrong or right, this is just my opinion....take a minute and try to measure a game for what it is rather than what it isn't, just like Lords of the Fallen and Dark Souls III, or Overwatch and Paladins, people love to make comparisons but they never give a game a chance to shine for its own individual merits...which is really sad and one of the main reasons why games end up trampled in the gutter, even when they are actually fantastic products. Seperate it from everything else and just look at it as going into completely new territory. I myself used to be very biased about products not living up to their predecessors...Gothic, Metal Gear Solid, Max Payne, to name a few.
You have to remember that in current days, they try and cater to the interests of the more current generations rather than keeping the old ones happy, though of course not forgotten...and that quickly settles into fact when you compare how many older people vote down to younger generations going in fresh faced and bright eyed will adore it for what it is...and hey, even turn around and say the old ones were garbage. That, again, is down to the individual, which is why you should take any major bashing reviews and vice versa, with a grain of salt and give it a chance to explore yourself.
With that said, I do like this game for what it is...you are given the tools to be an assassin if you want to and don't care about score so much as wiping each level of all life...but this game is called 'Thief' for a reason, not 'Assassin'...those tools are there incase you as an individual struggle to get past certain points OR want to try something different...they give you the tools to engage each level differently IF you choose to. I myself find a thrill in leaving everything in its place, except from the coin and loot of course, leaving no stone unturned to leaving no trace of said stones tamperings for the guards to be suspicious about. Half the battle of making a game engaging is how YOU engage it, the second half is how the game engages back in response, and if you are up to the challenge of the retort. I personally stuck to every shadow, used every opportunity and left every guard untouched. Sometimes they are predictable, sometimes I found my movement space rapidly closing and my only ally, the shadow that sat between them and me...mistakes were made, i learned from them. Quickly pick the lock...open the chest, take the loot, close it again before the guard circles back around...slink back into the shadow, non the wiser...all the richer, knowing I got away with it held a certain sense of satisfaction that I didn't have to resort to bludgeoning all the guards or putting arrows in their heads so I can just skip through the level with zero challenge ...because then it would be boring.
The atmosphere was perfect for its time period, especially when you -SPOILER ALERT!- get to the Asylum, the spoops are real and when you first witness the creatures in the forgotten city...man that was so freaky. I loved those parts, they just kept making me want to play more and more. The filthy alleyways, the heavy fog in the air, the dim lighting, the grungy design gave the feeling of solitary depression....disease thick in the air.
Now I do have to agree with most, the Erin girl was pretty annoying, but it was a managable cringe at least for me...and the story was no Academy Award winner, but for what it IS, its not as bad as some people make it out to be...Thief always was an oddity, what with zombies, LITERAL ghosts and all the other things you wouldn't associate with a thief which made the series very approachable, for its uniqueness. They weren't afraid to try something new....sure it wasn't great but it is acceptable.
You have to immerse yourself into about an hour or two before things start becoming real interesting...finding secrets, snagging unique loot and collectibles, trying to come up with the story for some things, like the hidden room with a chair facing a painting with a goat-headed woman with her baps out...something for all your 'nefarious' needs?
Honestly though...if you go into this game with aggressive intent, you will spoil the core mechanics, the very IDEA of what Thief is and get bored very quickly. I'd say give it a try and take everything you read with a pinch of salt...because you could just be missing out on something you yourself may thoroughly enjoy for someone elses hate bashing. Have a good one!

The Thief series is one that's been near and dear to my heart as one of my most favorite franchises.  I still remember when the first Thief came out, it blew me away.  And then Thief 2 upped the bar.  Thief 3 had one of the scariest gaming experiences ever and it carried the franchise forward.  Thief 4 took years to come to fruition and the fan base was so eager to see the fourth installment.  When it finally did get released, excitement turned to disappointment as the game didn't meet the standards set by its predecessors.  Keep in mind, open-world games like Skyrim (which was released in 2011; Thief 4 was released in 2014) were embracing giving the gamer ultimate freedom.  Meanwhile, Thief 4 boxed the gamer into small "cells", giving more a feeling of a chlostrophobic Assassin's Creed than what we were accustomed to with Thief.  The developers shot themselves in the foot by giving us a restrictive, linear, consolitis let-down.  Now don't get me wrong, the game mechanics were enjoyable, but the knowledge that you're moving from tiny cell to tiny cell ruined the gameplay for me; that and the linear way the levels were designed.  It was disappointing, because Thief 4 should've been so much more.  I envision a world of Thief 4, much like Skyrim, a huge world where a thief could thrive and gain limitless wealth.  I hate to keep comparing Thief 4 to Skyrim, but if you look at the thief aspects available in Skyrim, it's what Thief 4 should've been.  Thief 4 is the first in the series I didn't complete, because of its flaws.  Nowadays, I get my fix with Skyrim, because it simply does everything better than Thief 4.  I still love the Thief franchise and I have high hopes that a lesson was learned and that the developers scrap the restrictive aspect of Thief and go for open world awesomeness.  It is possible, as evidenced by Skyrim.  That's what Thief players want, a large unrestricted and open world to explore, missions to complete and a game worthy of the franchise.  I can't recommend Thief 4.  Instead, I suggest you check out Thief 2 and 3, both of which should put you in the right frame of mind for the franchise.  Then, if you're still left wanting, go be a thief in Skyrim and enjoy a massive game world with gravy loot.

First off, let me not make one thing clear: I'm only a casual fan of the Thief franchise. I admire its goals but the actual implementations have as often as not left me cold. Hey, I thought the third game was the best of the series, so all you fanboys can feel free to ignore what I have to say.
With that out of the way, I have to say I was somewhat ambivalent about the fourth game. Right off the bat, I took offense to the main character's - Garret's - new look; it's terrible and every time I saw him it made me wince, what with the mascara, girdle and the mask that magically clings to his chin (really, how does it do that?). Other than that, the graphics were quite nice and between the lighting and level design the city was appropriately moody. Alas, SSAO made my machine chug so I couldn't embrace the game in its full beauty but even without it the game still looked nice. The city is appropriately gloomy, with lots of overhangs and shadowy nooks. I have to say I was disappointed that the city was just like the third-game) again divided into small neighborhoods requiring multiple immersion-breaking map-loads just to cross town. Equally disappointing was how limited my climbing options were; too often walls or crates that should have been climbable were non-interactive. It made the game feel more linear and scripted than it needed to be. The story was stock gothic, and failed to really engage me; I didn't really care about Garret, his lost girlfriend or whether or not the villains achieved their nefarious goals.
Other than that though, the gameplay was pretty good. The AI was not all I was hoping for, although as I wasn't playing on the hardest difficulty levels so perhaps I should give that a try before complaining too much. I thought the combat wasn't as deadly as it should have been; it was more a slap on the wrist than a show-stopper. Rather than avoiding combat entirely, as often as not I'd just stab a guard rather than patiently wait for him to get out of the way. This made the game feel more a generic action/stealth-title (like Splinter Cell) than part of the Thief franchise. Anyway, jumping up on a few crates was usually enough to confuse the guards into losing track of me. As expected, there were multiple ways past any obstacle, and as usual I did my best to explore every path I could find. Oddly enough, the side missions often felt more "thiefy" than the main campaign, as the former had more puzzles and requiring more three-dimensional thinking. The main missions felt dry and linear in comparison. Unlike prior iterations of the franchise, there was an almost total absence of monsters or undead, for which I was quite glad as I never liked those bits in the other games. The boss battles at the end did seem a bit out of place however.
Overall, I enjoyed Thief more than I disliked it, but not so much I am rushing to replay it (I still think the third was a better title, if only because I enjoyed zooming out to third-person mode; I wish that had been in option in this game). If anything, playing Thief 4 made me want to replay the earlier titles. It's an okay game but not exceptional; it doesn't destroy the franchise, merely puts it into maintenance mode.

Overall, I think that while the negatives offset what is genuinely quite an original HOG in more ways than one, the positives overwhelm them. I wish that there had either been less rooms/areas or more substance in the plethora of areas in the game, I think that's the major thing that lets this game down. As a huge fan of all the King's Bounty games published by 1C Company, this game was a big let down. I don't know what happened here, but the quality control was completely lacking.
After playing the first game in the series, I never hesitated to pick up the sequels on launch day. I could play these games forever. When Dark Side came out (and I had no idea it was in the works), there was a lot of negative sentiment and complaints of the game being bug ridden. I had faith in the developers, so I decided I would wait to pick it up until they had time to iron out the bugs. As the 4th (5th?) game in this series, I knew that the UI, combat systems, character development, were all very mature, so any bugs  in the game would have to be related to quests and items specific to this game, which is really just content.
After some time went by, they dropped some big patches and a "Premium Edition" for the game, and it went on sale for a large discount. I figured this was the signal that it was time to give it a go, I was excited to have another chapter in the Kings Bounty universe to explore! The reality was a little different.
There is no Kings Bounty universe to explore here. The worlds filled with secrets, quests, and story wonder are completely absent. What you get are large maps, that are distinctly Kings Bounty areas, with pretty much nothing on them. Where you'd ordinarily have criss-crossing side quests, caches of items in every cranny, buried treasures, and a wicked gauntlet of enemy mobs to navigate, there was instead long hallways full of spider eggs, and nothing else, towns filled with houses with no residents. Guards with no dialogue. Gates that don't actually open. Dead ends with nothing in them. Large open rooms with not a single monster or treasure in them. I couldn't go on.
To me, it seems like the team that worked on the other games had little to no involvement with this game. They polished the engine and the map making tools to a degree that perhaps ANYONE could use them to make a Kings Bounty game, but that's not necessarily who SHOULD make a kings bounty game. This one feels like it was made by someone's nephew, who wanted to get some experience in the video game industry, and obviously nobody at the company ever played it, because I can't imagine that it would get the seal of approval from anyone involved in the previous games. It should be called "King's Bounty: Experimenting With the Map Maker".
I hate to think that I now have to give conditional recommendations to the King's Bounty games. "Yes, try King's Bounty! Oh, except for Dark Side, that game sucks."  People don't respond to those kinds of recommendations, and if someone happens upon this series by chance and plays this game first, they certainly won't be coming back for more, and will instead miss out on the magic of the other games. That's sad. This game should not exist, and I'm sorry to have to say it.

Far Cry 4 is the repetition of the Far Cry formula that always somehow pleases us to play.
This time, instead of the confy / warmy beaches that the third title of the franchise offered us we get the snowy / windy yet full of biological diversity Kyrat mountains that are located near the Hymalaias.
Let's evaluate it:.
Graphics: 90/100 --» It is simply a Far Cry title. Gorgeous intricately detailed forests that are pleasant just to watch, I literally spent hours just watching the trees and water. Sometimes when you got a classy angle  in a water cascate you realize that the border between reality and virtuality is already minimal ( yet I believe we can reach perfection).
Story : 78/100 --» This standard is relative. I do , honestly , think that it is somehow a cliché. I think the main protagonist barely has influence in the narrative although the antagonist is ONE OF THE BEST I HAVE SEEN IN A VIDEOGAME. The class of Pagan Min is absolutely brilliant and I do think it is definitely a role model to imitate. I somehow enjoyed the dispute over control in the Golden Path between Sabal and Amita. Unfortanly I do think that the death of Ajay's mother is poorly explored and I do think , sometimes , it is a pretext so that the main narrative ( The territorial dispute over Kyrat ) can be played.

Sounds : 93/100 --» The sound design of the game is definitely brilliant and dinamic. I  , in a certain point of the game , was definitely afraid of the jungle as it's power felt enormous due to the energy it's sounds transmited. Absolutely brilliant !
Gameplay : 82/100 --» I honestly cannot give a better mark to the gameplay of Far Cry 4 because I already played the other titles of the franchise ( except Primal) and I honestly besides a thing or two it is exactly the same thing. Fine yet it is becoming boring due to the fact that it is always the same thing. One thing for sure, if I never played the other titles of the franchise certainly I would give a better score to it's gameplay.
Due to all of the factors explained above I give an overall evaluation of : 86/100

If time spent on games means or tells you anything, I have 640 hours on this game (I have several Steam accounts, three of which I bought Thief 4).
During this time, I have experienced all the not-so-fun hiccups the game has or have had, since its release day (the worst ones were corrected by the developers). At one time, which was insane, your save files would become corrupt and the game would even crash when you tried to save.
There are also (rarely) problems with guards not doing what they should, so you can't ghost some parts or chapters of the game 100%. And some chapters will give so called opportunist points, even if you do everything you can to "ghost".
Also, one piece of loot and 9 documents are missing from the game, and one of the ingame "thieving objectives" can't be done, simply because the developers missed to include it in the game.
There are also some irritating problems with overlapping and desynced dialog.
The story itself is apparently a mixed bag for some. At first, I disliked the "emo" female character Erin (a victim in too many ways), but now I can certainly like some aspects of her and feel bad for what happened to her (I don't want to spoil it). The music is good and the atmosphere and graphics is better in this game than in any other I have played. Ever.
You can play the game in three different ways: like a true, careful thief with a stealth approach, use the environment to take alternate paths or as a distraction, and to some extent you can just kill your enemies. But it isn't one of those other games where you are always free to get away with being an assassin.
You also get a lot of side missions in the game that are often fun and stimulating and you can play challenge maps to earn a good score on the leaderboard.
DLC's include an additional (but bad and boring!) challenge map, three (IMO) helpful booster packs and a must-buy: "The Bank Heist". Good to quickly get extra gold, but maybe a little too short to stand on its own as something spectacular other than just one of the "client jobs".
Overall, I definitely recommend this game. I'm buying it for the third time! (because I'm a nerd who likes to unlock all the achievements again).
It seems there are some loud mouthed haters of this game (who can't even accept positive reviews and the fact that a lot of people DO like Thief). So instead of trying to mature and tolerate that people are into different things, they spend their time on spreading hate and lies about the game, and basically telling people they are losers if they like Thief.
In any way, I aim to be objective with this review, but I'm a fan of Thief regardless. I'm not a fan of Internet bullies though.
My recommendation is to really try the game out and take it for what it is. Don't compare it to anything else. Just enjoy it!
I also highly suggest playing this on PC, because the game looks better and the controls work much better too, on PC than on console and with a controller. It's my strict opinion that Thief is and remains a PC game and porting it doesn't do it justice, even if it's good that as many as possible can play it of course.
Even if you don't have a PC (or not a good enough PC to meet the requirements), you should get your own copy of this game. And get immersed, spend some time and patience on it, because that's what it takes!
Again, I have played this game for so long, but then I also have the world record time for completing the game on the highest difficulty settings. So called Custom Master.
You have a lot of room to develop as a gamer with Thief, being able to build up your skills, patience and confidence.
Sorry for sounding like a bad salesman. I mostly just hope you make the right decision for yourself and have fun! :)

As someone, who have never played the previous Thief games, I’ve decided to give this a chance, because everyone said, that it’s bad because it’s not like the others. I thought I might enjoy it, since I don’t know what the other games were like. I did actually enjoy… some parts of the game.
Well, first of all there was a lame story hidden somewhere in the game, but I didn’t really care about it, since I was too busy running around on rooftops, stealing everyone’s s**t instead of listening to Garrett’s brooding. To be honest, I was so happy that nobody was at home, while I, as a master thief, was stealing all of their pretty pens in the middle of the night… Well, okay, this was the actual part of the game, that I happened to like, along with the side missions, even though I felt kind of bad for stealing from poor people who only had a ring. (I might be wrong, but didn’t the old Garrett steal from nobles and such?) Anyway the game is really short if you only play the main missions, since most chapters take like 40-60 minutes even with hiding, and there are only 8 chapters. After finishing the really, really bad main story you can still do whatever you want, so I was like yay, I'm so glad this is over, gotta go do some actual stealing now.
The stealth system was fine, I also liked the graphics, but sometimes the places were really confusing. I liked to explore, but I broke into the same houses a few times, because everything looked the same and it’s hard to tell if I’ve been there already or not.
The whole game is just depressing, since everyone was just standing there, whining about everything, and there wasn’t a single person in the game, who had at least one good thought. Garrett was also depressed, the girl was annoying, the guards were jerks for no reason, and the people were sad and miserable. There are good ways to make a dark game, but this is not one of them, since it became really irritating after a time.
A lot of people said it’s like Dishonored and that’s true. There is plague and such, even some chapters were similar and it had our dear old, blind Granny Rags, I mean the Queen of Beggars or something like that. My problem is, that I really don’t understand, why this game had to use the same system. In Dishonored you could do the missions however you wanted, because you were a bodyguard/assassin, but here you play as a thief, why would you act like a fighter? In my opinion, there shouldn’t be an option to just run through the map alerting everyone. Anyway there were elements from Assassin’s Creed, too, and maybe from Outlast, because they just had to make a horror chapter in a creepy asylum for whatever reason. Maybe they thought that the game is not dark enough yet, it needed more horror, because a morgue house was not enough… I am pretty sure that most people want play this game for stealth, not for running around in a haunted asylum, waiting for a jumpscare to happen.
It’s not a good game, it’s simply an okay game. I’d recommend it, since you might enjoy hiding and stealing stuff, because that was the only fun thing to do here, but anyway, get it only on sale.

I was really disappointed with this game, mostly because I felt like it had huge potential.
A lot of the good reviews for this game praised how it captured the innocence of youth and first love, especially in the weird age that our generation grew up in, with so many of us becoming involved with or just making great lifelong friends with people we only knew over the internet, particularly in gaming communities like the relationship portrayed in Cibele. This game had so much potential to really portray this unique situation that our generation dealt with, one that could really be poignant, painful, and beautiful.
I want to like Cibele but it just falls so, so short of what it could have been.
To start off with, Cibele isn't a game, it's just a story with a frankly boring point-and-click to go along with it. There are ways to make games based on true stories and still give the players choice-- I'm thinking of a free indie game I played a long time ago that portrayed a young man's story of trying to come out to his homophobic, abusive parents. You could decide to lie and hide, or to be open, and you faced different consequences every way. No matter what you chose, you still got real life snippets of the developer's life. That game (though for the life of me I don't remember what it was called) really made an impression on me and a lot of other people because the choices you made had huge effects, and those effects were emphasized by the knowledge that they were another human being's real life experiences, or plausible life experiences at the least. Cibele fails to deliver on this completely. There is no reason to be attached to the story or any of the characters.
The characters are another big deal in Cibele that really disappointed me. Ichi/Blake is just so damn unlikable and borderline abusive. Playing this game without having read any of the reviews, I was convinced that the game would end with Blake becoming super abusive and Nina realizing he was an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and then triumphing/surviving that situation. That's how blatantly horrible the character was. All he did was complain and boss Nina around. You clearly see her friends getting excited for the release of a new game in the first act, that Nina also seems excited about judging by how she readily agrees to go to a release party, and then you see Blake rag on the game and Nina begrudgingly go along with his statements. Throughout the acts her other friends constantly complain that she isn't spending enough time with them and only spending time with Blake, textbook abusive behavior on his part to alienate her from her friends and control what she likes and dislikes. Nina herself, while beautiful and charming, is terribly acted. She's passive and always sounds uninterested, and the fact that she has to strong arm Blake into visiting her made me really uncomfortable. I was also uncomfortable with how quickly she started sexting him. It's a very realistic portrayal of how a lot of young women on the internet, particularly gamers, act toward their male companions, but frankly I think it's harmful and I didn't like how the game showed this practice in a neutral/leaning toward positive light. Nina has bad self-esteem and craves approval, to the point that she wants it even from a total jerkwad like Blake, who is indecisive, moody, rude and constantly complaining. And there is no indication from the game that this is a bad or hurtful thing.
There were also SO MANY little subplots that were NEVER elaborated on, which infuriated me. In the first game you get a whiff from a friend that one of Nina's ex-flames is spreading around intimate pictures that she sent him. That is a big deal! I was upset for her and wanted to know how that would play out! And then... nothing. The little text messages you get while in the mini game with Blake never lead anywhere, which was so disappointing for me.
Overall I was really upset with this game. The characters are unlikable (and frankly abhorrent, in Blake's case), there's nothing except the storyline to keep you interested, which isn't great itself, and there was little to no continuity between the acts in regards to anything that isn't Blake and Nina's main storyline. The game felt rambling and like there was no self awareness. I felt like I was smarter than the game and that it didn't know what it was doing.
I would have liked to have seen a lot more interactivity, and if the game is going to rely solely on the narrative, I would like it to also rely on the background narratives and not just the main narrative. I think the idea of using video shots and voice acting and especially the open desktop screen was so clever and could have been so good, but too much of the intimate snapshots of Nina had no purpose. This game could have been so good and sadly it's mostly awful. Still, I hope the maker learns from this experience and is able to go on to make bigger and better things, because this was definitely a wonderful idea and a topic that could have been insanely interesting.

I don't normally review games, sorry if this is a little rough around the edges, for a short written review.
TL;DR: "You like Rouge-like games? You like funny things? Buy this, yo."
I've already spent several hours in the game, and am still far from getting bored with the game, there's so much to love.
Very Straightforward, your goal is to get from Canada, from the US (I want to say you start in Florida). However, like many things in life, the story's more about the journey, than the destination. You'll be creating your own story along the way, from choosing how to handle a roadside robbery, to kick certain members out of the group when they complain about the ride too much, to wether or not to give that seemingly pretty friendly dog a knife.
The gameplay is fairly straightforward in Death Road. The game is perma-death, meaning once you lose a character, until you start another run they're gone for good.
There are a set of skills in the game that are rolled mostly randomly for all characters, from being able to repair your car to how you handle certain weapons. These stats come into play in a variety of different way throughout the game.
Your character(s) have two three major types of weapons they can use.
1) Melee weapons. Almost all melee weapons will make you tired after repeated use, which takes a few moments before you can really start swinging at the undead spooks again. Most Melee weapons will also break after a certain period of time.
2) Guns. Totally rad. Guns are awesome in every way. Except they take from a preeeeeeeeetty limited supply of bullets. Some runs you're going to have next to no bullets, sometimes you'll have...no bullets. Later on you'll be gathering enough to reliably use them, but conserve ammo wisely.
3) Throwables, from grenades to Molotovs, these help clear a massive wave of zombies. They can also hurt your friends. Found that out the hard way.
You're charged with fighting horde after horde of the Zombie menace, scavenging for much needed food, fuel, weapons, and ammo. Each character can only take 3 bites from a zombie before they turn into some new lunch meat, so zombies can fairly consistantly pose a large threat in big enough numbers. Getting swarmed and surrounded from all sides will mean almost certain death,
Aaaahhhhhhh the music is great in this game. It's an awesome contrast from the pretty bleak situation your characters find themselves in, and its actually really enjoyable to listen to while managing your inventory, and making important choices like who should get the first bite of that candy bar.
Two major things stand out to me that I think are worth bringing up, the Humor and the Character Creator.
The Humor in Death Road is phenominal. Several moments in the game had me actually laughing out loud, atracting the unwanted attention of curious family members. One of my favorite examples of this is:
One of the events your party can experence is stopping by a campsite, and telling ghost stories to one another. However, in one of my runs, only a single character remained, but I saw the "Tell ghost stories" option was still there. Assuming it would act like I had more than one party memeber, I clicked it, and was pleasantly supprised by the special dialouge, where half-way through my character discovered he was telling his story to ghosts the entire time.
The Charactor Creator is also a huge pro in my book. You can create and save up to (roughly) 16 charactes. You can customize several things about these characters, from their looks, to their outlook on life. You can choose to take One or Two of these characters with you at the begining of the game, or instead chose to randomize your starting cast. You will rarely run into your characters you created when you encounter random people throughout the course of the game, making it a very special treat to run into that weird 12th grade teacher you chose to spend 15 minutes creating in a video game.
All in all I really, really loved the game, and highly suggest it to anyone interested in rougelikes, zombies, or even just fun in general. The game oozes quality, from the random times you'll find yourself bartering with dogs with guns to when you choose to end an argument by driving a car into a tree.

Death Road To Canada is Oregon Trail. That's all it is. It's a weird simplified Oregon Trail-esque game with modern comedy writing and wacky events in lieu of normal strategic planning and "realistic" events like injuries and diseases. Now, you may be thinking, "Isn't this just Organ Trail? Why do we need multiple games for this one extremely niche market?" First of all, why don't we need multiple games, second of all, what we've got here is a pretty solid game.
There are two phases to the game: traveling and the choices you make on the road, and scavenging for supplies on the open road. Traveling works the way any similar random game works, be it Oregon Trail or FTL or Convoy or whatever. You will find rest places or bandits or teammates on the open road, and decide who to barter with, what to trust, who to tell to COOL IT (from personal experience, there's basically never a reason to tell anyone to COOL IT, which is a shame). The scavenging, in my opinion, is where the real heart of the game lies. Here you are in full control, weaving past hordes of the undead and rummaging through any house you can find in search of food, gas, health, ammo, and the occasional weapon. Combat is a last resort, as ammo is limited and all weapons have a chance of breaking (the AI apparently did not get this memo, as it will move to smack any zombie that comes within smacking distance, even if all they have at their disposal is an old umbrella or a femur). House maps are generated from random rooms, whose floor plans defy the laws of known physics with rooms that overlap each other and lead to god knows where. It's silly. It takes getting used to.
Of course, any game following in the old footsteps of good old "terrible death is educational" will stumble onto the same problems as its predecessors: everything is left to the whims of the RNG, and the RNG hates your stupid surviving face. If your team has high morale, whoops, here's an event that drops everyone's morale. Got a surplus of food? Be a shame if some bandits were to get in your way. What's that? You have a car with gas? What do you think this is, Daytona USA? Sometimes while you're driving, characters will just argue with each other and lower their morale. Having an RNG that doesn't basically cheat certainly isn't easy, but typically there's some kind of middle ground. Super Amazing Wagon Adventure erred on the side of "too easy", though primarily that was due to gameplay being more based on skill than luck. In Death Road To Canada, the skill-based sections are enjoyable, but the luck-based ones are just a reminder to properly lubricate before making your decision.
I do have to give this game props where it's due: for a zombie game, it does a good job at making a proper zombie atmosphere. The zombies are many and travel in hordes, and there's a thick VHS film grain that covers the screen giving it a classic Romero graphic look. (And yes, it can be turned off.) The one real surprising outlier is the music, which for whatever reason is some arcadey honky-tonk that adds to the game's "quirkiness", and if that's the kinda word that makes your stomach crawl up your esophagus, you might as well look elsewhere. The whole game's about being quirky, from constant references to being "swole" to the ability to play as a car-driving dog. This here is the silly version of Organ Trail, that's the name it's made for itself and that's how I enjoy it. (I mean, enjoying is sort of a relative term. I enjoy it as long as the game allows me to enjoy it before throwing me into a ditch and stealing my♥♥♥♥♥♥)
Bottom line: this game is a game of Russian Roulette at some twisted carnival with the biggest teddy bear if you last five rounds. It's a twelve inch novelty♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and it's made of cubes because this game has a quirky pixel art style. And if you're the kind of masochistic thrill seeker who's into that stuff, then this is a fine way to spend your evening.

Death Road To Canada is a retro-style, top-down action game with light RPG elements. I've been waiting to play this game for a really long time, and so far it has lived up to my expectations. The gameplay is simple to pick up, but there is some strategy involved. The player has to strike a careful balance between avoiding zombies and looting quickly, but also killing enough zombies in a previous room so that the player doesn't get boxed into the next room.
The environments, story and characters are all randomized, so every playthrough is different, although you will visit the same locations a lot. There is enough variety in the story to keep things fresh. Replayability 10/10
The graphics are retro-style and well done. Like the rest of the game, the artwork has personality. No crazy over-the-top effects, but also not generic. It really feels like a game from 1989, not a game from 2016 pretending to be a game from 1989. Graphics 8/10
The story is randomly generated, and often surprised me with its off-beat humour. There are many, many story events that can occur, and your choices can have very dire circumstances. As much as you might want to pick the 'cool' or 'funny' or 'interesting' choice, it might be best to pick the 'safe' choice, or else your trip to Canada will be cut short! Story 8/10
The music is great! Very catchy retro-chiptune kind of stuff, mixed in with some nifty guitars. Very off-beat and full of personality. The music is light-hearted, and not moody. In some cases it doesn't seem to fit the theme of the game, but I kind of prefer that the music is so light-hearted for a game about the zombie apocalypse. Music 9/10
Overall, this game is probably the only game I'm going to play for a long time. I have almost 70 games in my Steam library, and I feel like this is the best $15 I've ever spent. Overall 9/10
Pros:
- VERY replayable. Every time you die, you want to start over again, and it doesn't feel that repetitive.
- Fun, laid back game, but with a lot of hectic gameplay moments
- Good balance of difficulty, good balance of loot
- Lots of modes to unlock
Cons:
- None
