Very promising EA game that is already a lot of fun to play. It aims to be basically first person Space Station 13, but also space engineers. There are some nicely simulated logical, electrical and gas pipe systems in place to play around with.
The UI can seem unintuitive at first since it does not use a drag and drop interface but simulates your two hands instead. When you get used to that you understand the reasons for it, You always have an unobstructed view of what is happening. The way every inventory slot is tied to a piece of equipment you can take off makes it feel very grounded and like you are actually building things with tools and materials that have a presence instead of funneling stuff out of one giant backpack.
Right now the game does not really explain much of how stuff works, so you will need to read some guides to get going.

The game is in early access, so the typical issues apply (bugs, unstable, incomplete). However, there seems to be a lot of content, the sandbox is really powerful, and the game feels incredibly rewarding as you figure stuff out on your own. The UI may turn some people off, but the developers have a good reason to set it up that way LONG TERM, it just makes less sense given the current state of the game. You get used to it after a couple hours though.
This game is NOT for casual gamers, it's pretty difficult to figure out. Don't expect to have your hand held each step of the way. Expect it to be an uphill battle. That's what makes it so fun!
Don't let the cumbersome UI intimidate you. This game has a solid foundation in place for future updates. If you like modded Minecraft or Factorio you'll find a lot of enjoyment here.

This game, in all honesty has had a bumpy start, but has progressively became better due to updates.
By "bumpy" I mean the game having all sorts of bugs and issues. (But what the hell do you expect, it's an early access game after all.)
So, what's my opinion about this game?
Well, I like it.
.... What, you're expecting more than that? Okay, fine.
The game itself is quite complex, infact, I've still not been able to really get a fully functional base out and working on my own. Now before you go off and say "well that is bad! You should be able to build a ba--" Hold on a second, I wasnt done. You see the reason I aint able to build a base isnt because the game is too "difficult" or "complex", more-over, it's because I'm an absolute bafoon, and still have issue understanding the systems SOLELY because of my lack of intelligence. Plus, I'm trying to play this game on my own, so that increases the difficulty by a bit. (Plus a game in general is more enjoyable with friends.... So if you DO plan on getting this game, be sure to get your friends to buy into it too.)
Now, let's talk about whats IN the game, and skip the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
1. Graphics, standard♥♥♥♥♥♥tbh, nothing really of note, can be a little bland on the colors, but what do you expect... it's ♥♥♥♥ing space, you expectin' a rainbow?

2 Gameplay, A ♥♥♥♥ton of boxes, and a whole lot of nothing. That's what you start out with. Quite literally you are provided with crates of supplies that will give you a "start" to your venture in building a functioning, life-sustaining, preferably not on fire, station. The entire effort is comprised of mining, building, wiring, welding, wrenching... and it goes on and on.
Your objective as I said before, is to survive. And god #$%^ing D@M does this game make you work for it. You have to literally make a working atmos (basically a system that keeps your station filled with♥♥♥♥♥♥that doesnt kill you when you breath it.) system, and a whole lot of other systems besides that, and that is AFTER you spend time gathering materials for building the main base itself. Hell, and even the machines you build to refine materials takes some work. For instance, the furnace, You think you can just plonk that down and it work straight after?
Well that's just wrong. You have to not only wire it to the main power, but have to provide a working gas solution in which to smelt your ores. (This furnace I am talking about isn't the one provided to you in the starting supplies.) Needless to say, you'll be spending countless hours refining your systems so that they are perfect, by perfect, I mean it not spew fire in your face.... (Don't ask me how to make them.. hell, I cant even make a damn AIRLOCK yet, and again, that's my stupidity.)
Although the game may appear a little frightening, I'm sure anyone can get into this game, given time, like I said earlier, friends WILL help you along a fair bit better.
3. "THE U.I!!!"
You see, for the most part, my time playing this game has been relatively O.K, I've never had much complaints to make because thus far, I've not seen much of anything. But I see quite a few people make some form of complaint about "The U.I! FIX THE U.I!" Well, I say to them: eh, your preference, but I see no problem with the current system. The system in which you access your inventory, is not drag and drop based. You just press a number from 1-5 corresponding to the place in which you stored the item you are trying to obtain, use the scroll wheel to select said item you want, then press F to put it into one of your hands, not that $^#@ing hard.
As of current, I've got not much else to say about the game. It's fun, got some complex♥♥♥♥♥♥ but there's plenty of guides to show you the way, and if you're still feelin' stuck even after the guides... Come onto the discord, plenty of people are there and will probably be able to help you. Plus that's also a place where you can file bug reports.
My personal suggestion, is that you buy this game if you are looking for a complex space game, honestly quite fun and satisfying, however, if you're looking for something "refined" and "stable", for right now I'd suggest holding off, and waiting until a later point in time...and if you come from the SS13 Crowd... well, you'll feel right at home. Remember though, bring friends, you'll have a better experience.

Technically, "Brink of Consciousness: Dorian Gray Syndrome Collector's Edition" is an excellent casual adventure Hidden Object Game (HOG).  Unike almost every other HOG in existence, the voice acting is excellent and the story very good.  The HOGs, puzzles, graphics, and gameplay, in general, are also all very good.  The only issue I've got with the game, itself, is that it needs a framerate limiter.  While I was playing it, my framerate ranged from 800 fps up to almost 4,000 fps.  It's possible, though, that that was because I played the game in a Crossover emulation bottle under Linux.  I do have two thematic problems with the game.  First, the game involves a trail of bodies from a psychopathic mass murderer.  So, it's not exactly goodness and light.  Similarly, the ending leaves me a bit ambivalent.  Things are tied up (especially after the bonus chapter).  But again, not goodness and light.
I got a total of 5.9 hours of excellent gameplay out of it (4.9 hours in the base game and another hour in the bonus chapter).  So, the current list price of almost $10 is a tad high.  If you ever find it for something around $6 or less, leap at it.  It's an excellent game.

If you do not like hidden object games: 4/10
I think that this game could be more challenging if they added achievements, otherwise there is not incentive to solve a puzzle on your own butratehr just "skip" it.

A particularly good Hidden Object/Adventure game - this one hits a happy balance of unfolding story, wandering exploration, and doors locked with baroque mechanisms all missing pieces which are hidden in unlikely places.  Dorian Gray gives us an entertaining villain, always a few steps ahead of our plucky hero and gloating at us with voluble, literate glee.  Oscar, the demented masked mastermind, is unusually coherent and interesting for the genre.
The Hidden Object scenes are nicely thematic - you won't be finding hamburgers in the toolshed, for the most part - and if the whole game is on the simple side, it keeps things busy enough to fill a few hours with solid play.  The puzzles are supple, the art is terrific, and the voice acting is very very good.  I was pleased with the detail in the art and with the whole experience.  Expect 6 or 7 hours of not-zipping-through gameplay - I left the game window open while I was afk a couple of times, thus my time stat.  I enjoyed this more than the Lonely Hearts Murders sequel.

One of the better HOGs available with a strong storyline and characterization (mainly of the villain who you regularly nearly get to interact with). The story starts as you arrive at the mansion of the serial murderer you were investigating who has responded by abducting your girlfriend. You then have to navigate your way through the mansion, which has been set up with traps and puzzles to give you a chance to save her.
The HOG scenes here are fine and I didn't have any problems, there is a reasonable challenge here, and the graphics are fine and don't get in the way. The point and click sections between also flow very well, nothing too illogical and the scenario of the madman in his own mansion means a lot of scope for puzzles and needing to scavenge and jury rig solutions to progress without it seeming odd or out of place, which helps keep immersion in the story.
One weakness here is the puzzles - not all of them - but some are not really puzzles as such, they are completely trivial solutions that are just time consuming to do all the moves, for example the rainbow puzzle which looked like it would be an extended "Towers of Hanoi" style puzzle, but just ends up being a trivial solution just a lot of shuffling all the pegs left and right repeatedly.
But apart from that one issue with some of the puzzles, otherwise this is one of the best HOGs available, so highly recommended.

"Brink of Consciousness: Dorian Gray Syndrome" is a perfectly palatable Hidden Object Game. As far as gameplay goes, there's not much to say, really. The game stays firmly within the conventions of the genre, mixing up actual hidden object sections with object combination puzzles and a handful of minigames. The way I see it, you either dislike HOGs in general, and then this one won't win you over, or you like them, in which case you'll most likely get some enjoyment out of "Dorian Gray" too. I would certainly recommend this to fans of the genre.

King's Bounty: Dark Side is a game which I thoroughly enjoyed from start to finish!
The gameplay is extremely fun with hex-based, turn-based battles at the core of it. The environment and scenery are very nice and those combined with the breathtaking music really add to the atmosphere. Once more as with several other games the music is simply stunning: the tune heard in the Elven lands, the tune heard in the Demonic lands etc are so different and captivate the land they describe perfectly.
The story if quite interesting, but it's especially the humor used throughout it which makes for a great experience.
In a way it reminded me of Overlord: the game is like a parody on the traditional 'goody goody' RPG's. It's really littered (in a positive way) with funny stuff, ranging from the obvious 'victimized' role of evil, over passwords like 'QWERTY', the names of the Beatles and the island of the Light having the shape and road structure of a big peace sign.
The amount of different units in this game is quite big and each unit has its own pro's and con's which makes for a great amount of tinkering and combining to try and get the 'best' army.
The game also has some nice features like for example upgrading items: in order to do this you actually have to fight the 'Keepers' of this item and only if you win does it get upgraded.
A minor issue with the game is the Quest log. While definitely not bad it does lack some important info at times making it unclear what has to be done to complete a given quest (in most cases such quests will advance later in the game).
Near the end of the game some quests require specific scrolls in order to be completed, however those are nowhere to be found (probably already sold during the course of the game). This is a bit 'meh' in my opinion since nothing makes those scrolls stand out in any way, thus the only way to complete those quests is in a new playthrough.
A bigger issue are crashes and bugs: in 50% of the time the game crashed when exiting to Windows. This is not an issue since I'm exiting anyway but it's annoying. During gameplay I had a sporadic crash caused by clear bugs. For example if one of your units does 100% damage (so kills all enemies) the game will crash, probably because the number '100' doesn't fit the allocated space or something. This happens quite rarely and when you 'know' it you can avoid it.
During my playthrough at one point I was not able to go to one specific island anymore, neither through sailing nor teleporting, the game would always crash. After some rummaging on forums I found out that verifying the Steam game cache magically fixes this. All of these bugs are luckily not game breaking but they should have been ironed out by now.
The advice here is to quick-save regularly so no data is lost.
It took me 98 hrs to finish the game on Normal difficulty doing all quests which could be completed which is time well spent. Note that this is the first King's Bounty which I have played, so I cannot compare to previous installments.
Overal I can say this is one of the best games I have ever played, great fun.
I'm giving it a 9 out of 10 where the one point is deducted for the bugs.

I wish there was a 'meh' recommendation.
The game is King's Bounty through and through, where they've learned from their mistakes from the first game and polished it from the Warriors of the North game, which was riddled with typos.
Yet, the Warriors of the North game was a lot better in so many ways.
Dark Side starts off pretty darn good. I love being able to play the evil for a change and actually commit horrible deeds to warriors of the light. Its charm, however, starts to run really stale as soon as you reach the 10'ish hour mark. Fetch quests are among the abominations of poor game design. Yes, no 'RPG' is complete without them and I'll look that through the fingers, but here comes Dark Side, where a fetch quest can consist up to 10-15 stages, where the player is running / teleporting back and forwards, making it an _absolute waste of your time_
It's not just 'bad' in the sense that this happens, it's 'bad' because nearly every quest is like this!
On top of that, the quest log has to be the poorest excuse of a 'log' that I've ever seen, yes, even worse than the games before this. 90% of the time, you're wandering about aimlessly, looking for an object / npc / location, only to find out you actually had to go to the shelter. A good example? A quest said: 'talk to the acolyte'. Ok, which acolyte, there's quite a few of them? Turns out to be in the shelter. 2 steps down this questline, it says 'talk to <person name>' which is the acolyte... As I said before, this isn't just 1 quest, the whole game is riddled with this nonsense.
The difficulty curve is another big peeve of mine. In Warrior Princess and Warriors of the North, the curve was somewhat acceptable. In Dark Side, you either have a series of fights you can waltz over, only to get a tough as nails hero to fight against you, or you fight through tough as nails monster packs, only to waltz over a♥♥♥♥♥♥easy hero fight. There's no rhyme or reason and you find yourself going back and forth to your shelter every so often.
I've enjoyed this game for the first 15-20 hours, then it became stale and I found myself just wanting to finish it as quickly as I could, hoping it'd get better. It only became more and more stale, no interesting dialogues, no interesting characters, just hopping from place to place. The only interesting dialogues are with the prisoners and that's about it.
On the very plus side? The game isn't riddled with obnoxious boss battles!
Bottom line, I wouldn't recommend this game if it isn't 5 euro's or your regional equivalent, but it's pretty decent if you're a fan of the series.

It is very refreshing to see concept like this as many are saying.  This is a constant battle of resources and trying to make it through the day vs. putting aside and building for the future.  It is difficult to get ahead in the game as you can easily get stuck in one resources which causes a consequential problem in another area.  Almost like an RTS or Civ series, but trying to survive only as a war struck person or group.
What is interesting is the large number of ethical questions, tied up stories and their implications to your psyche or body.  This is where they can build the product even further with more detailed stories and get lots of replayability.  You start with three people in your group - one of my guys got shot outside, the second got lethally wounded at home and died, and the third was so sad- he committed suicide.  That's realistic I must say and the game excels in that.  At the end, your goal is to survive the war and it is very difficult to get around without hurting someone or yourself.
The artistic side is fairly strong in the game as well as the screens would tell you.  So plus ad minuses:
+Realistic lifelike war survival
+Nice screen designs
+Fresh story
+Can replay heavily
+Complicated ethical and survival criteria
-Can get repetitive if playing too frequently
-Constant resource shortage
Overall I liked it and as long as you do not pay a huge amount, it is worth it.

You know what I remember the most about the Thief series? Being inventive.
. The second-last mission of the game. Making my way stealthily through a sprawling manor, taking out guards and heavily-armored security robots while grabbing as many trinkets as I could. Finding myself with only two rope arrows left and a booby-trapped room where stepping on the floor would kill me instantly. Cue me jumping like Tarzan between a pair of carefully-positioned ropes dangling from the rafters, trying to nab a set of masks while worrying about the danger beneath my feet.
There is no such moment that compares to that in 2014's
reboot. At its best, it's completely average. At its worst, it's a set of compelling ideas buried under mediocrity and subsystems you have to fight through the entire time to get some semblance of fun.
I wanted so badly to love this game. The
series is my favorite stealth series of all time, and one I've played for many years (and even reviewed on this site). There's a reason why
is often referred to as one of the "holy trinity" of late 90s video games - it's the one that defined the stealth genre, via creative and expansive level design, an extremely-memorable villain (Karras), awesome (and sarcastic) voice acting and the freedom to approach objectives as you saw fit.
That's why it's so frustrating to see something that feels like the worst excesses of console-oriented development grafted onto the skeleton of the previous titles. You can tell that there was the seed of something amazing here, but it's lost in a haze of its troubled development and conflicting plots.
In a better game, some of the elements introduced here could have been amazing. Nearby animals that alert enemies to your presence if you make a wrong move while picking a lock. A dynamic hub world that slowly opens up to you as you progress through the plot and get more tools (a la
). Feeling like Garrett has an actual presence in the gameworld as opposed to just a floating pair of hands. The use of tools at your disposal. Finding sets of collectibles, all with their own unique models. At every turn, these advancements are marred by a gallery of bugs, glitches and underwhelming aspects.
The level design in particular is shockingly bad. You can tell that this was developed for consoles first and foremost. Areas are very small compared to the previous games.
's "Life of the Party" had you go all the way from several blocks away from the Keep, inside and up through several floors without any loading whatsoever. This time around, you can barely turn a corner without having to lift up a board or fade to black while jimmying open a window. The use of hidden loading screens (especially ones tied to button-mashing prompts) kills any sense of exploration or enthusiasm. Not helping are strange access routes - instead of walking through a gate to go from Baron's Way North to Baron's Way South, I have to get to a second-storey window, pry it open so I can get in, then jimmy open another window and wait while a new area loads.
In many ways, the enemy AI feels like a regression compared to the earlier games. They used to search for you for prolonged periods of time (sometimes for several minutes before audibly telling their comrades that they were giving up), In this game, they search for a few seconds before mindlessly going back to their original patrol routes. It feels like the exact same AI from the past. The difference is that it was 2014 when they released this, and they didn't make any advancements whatsoever.
The plot itself is the worst part. You can definitely tell that it's a Frankenstein-like amalgamation between two different plots.
* The entire concept of Garrett's Focus abilities are shown in the last cutscene from the prologue, where Garrett somehow gets a piece of the Primal stuck in his eye... by looking at the Primal for a moment. And even worse, another supporting character knows this, but doesn't tell him about it until the end of the game. Yet you can buy Focus upgrades from her.
* Erin herself (who I'm fairly sure was originally supposed to be the young girl from the ending of
) is introduced as an impulsive, brash, arrogant woman who seems to have been designed just so she can be hated. The player is then expected to be sympathetic hours after her apparent "death" when she randomly shows up in visions whining about how much she hates Garrett for what he did to her. There's a reference to Erin having unresolved feelings for Garrett that isn't supported in any way by the plot.
* Garrett decides to leave his one true companion, Basso, who is injured and alone in the middle of a dangerous/exploding tower, so he can rob a giant safe. Even worse, this act is the entire lynchpin the story revolves around. The plot can't advance otherwise.
* For some reason, the game tries to have an emotional moment over
. I get the sense that the creature in question was supposed to be an actual person in an earlier plot.
* We learn midway through the game (in a blink-and-you-miss it sidestory) that the original Garrett went to Moira Asylum, hid caches throughout the place, got locked up, had a guy named the Architect trying to find him, and somehow escaped the prison but left behind his famous mechanical eye. Wait,
* The final mission is a mishmash of conflicting images, cutting from two characters standing in the middle of a closed room to one of the characters hanging onto the edge of a collapsed deck, with the wall having been blown open suddenly for no reason.
I get what they originally wanted to do. Judging from what we see in the game itself and the leaked trailer with Stephen Russell voicing Garrett, you can figure out that the original plot was an "older and wiser Garrett" story, where he loses his protege and fights to avenge her while coming to terms with a new age. Except it's been lost in a haze of muddled character motivations (Garrett is more of a kleptomaniac mechanic than an actual thief), the two faction leaders only show up to hammer their respective goals in before disappearing for long stretches of time, and the main antagonist you face throughout the game (the Thief-Taker General) feels like a laundry list of the worst villain cliches.
It's a shame, because the sidequests come close to salvaging the whole thing. Whether you're trying to steal an enchanted skull (that talks to you - seriously), robbing a fellow thief who's trying to muscle in on your territory or attempting to disrupt the black market, the side jobs and the questgivers are more animated and varied than what you find in the main storyline.
It is extremely, extremely frustrating, because the game fights you the entire way. Between the horrid map system, the underwhelming hub areas (run into an empty apartment, grab a fork and knife, leave, repeat 50 times), the loading screens and the terrible enemy AI, you'll be spending half your time just trying to navigate to where you want to go. Yeah, it looks pretty, but it's just not worth it.
And that's not even getting into the bugs. An emotional moment with Basso affirming his trust in Garrett was ruined by an NPC rambling about nothing in the background. A guard got caught on a street tile and began spinning at mach speed as the AI tried to freeze itself. Guards sound extremely close, even if they're on the other side of a market square.
At the end of the day,
is an muddled experience that is brought down by its fractured development cycle, a confusing and kitbashed plot, and a wide assortment of bugs, glitches and dodgy gameplay elements that actually keep the game from being fun.
TLDR: No stealth title should end up like this.

Stationeers is an Early Access game that seems to have loads of potential as the next microfocused, technical sim based around managing thermodynamics and power in the unforgiving vacuum of space, but right now it's in that Early Access valley where there's lots of depth to the core systems but not enough to do with them once you've got things figured out.
As it is now (12/20/2017) I'd recommend Stationeers to people that enjoy seeing the reactions of gases and thermodynamics in their survival sims, think that most survival games give the player the good stuff with too little effort, or are content fantasizing about what things could be like in a full-blown Space Station 13 scenario (this game has enough depth and room for expansion to make it a de-facto successor if it takes off).
A few things that make it stand out currently: Stationeers doesn't place too much immediate emphasis on typical survival basics like food and water. The focus is on managing your base's power and, to an even less immediate extent, having a pressurized habitat with a working airlock. If you can get those going, food and water should be no trouble. The inventory system is also represented "realistically" - that is to say, you can move things into and out of your hands from your suit pockets, and not much else. While effectively this bit makes doing simple things more of a chore than they would otherwise be, it does reward mastery of the system in a way that touches all of your interactions with the gameworld.
In world displays are cool and you're given very little information through the UI, although there is a tablet in game with more documentation.
I'd like to see more pre-loaded maps like the one in the tutorial, where we get access to a pre-built station and can see how it ticks. While it's fun to figure out how to make an airlock, the steps to getting to that first sustainable pocket base are many, extremely varied, and require lots of simultaneous activities (yikes if you're playing solo). Power management could be eased up at the beginning to make this curve gentler, like requiring less power for the starting furnaces and fabrication equipment and having the suit drain battery more slowly. These issues are fine once you've got a base with consistant power going, but tend to death spiral my solo games.
A full blown Space Station 13-like using Stationeers would be amazing. There are already many, many things that can go wrong and that's just with the pressure and thermodynamics systems in.
Lots of promise though, and an extremely active dev team leading into and beyond Early Access release. I'll be keeping an eye on this!

I wanted to wait for this review until I had played at least a couple of PvP matches and tried out most of the heroes. I have played the ‘hero shooter’ genre has it become to be known for many years, including; TF2, Plants vs. Zombies: Garden Warfare I & II, Overwatch, Paladins, Battleborn, and now this game. All have good and bad points, some more than others, and I feel Gigantic which is already worth playing has the potential to be among the best of this style of game.
I’ve seen most of the negative reviews center not on gameplay or bugs or other serious problems but on 3 things; the 6 gig minimum requirement, the requirement to use the Arc launcher, and the locked 60 FPS.
I just don’t see how anyone who games on PC today has less than 8 gigs. All of my friends have at least 8 and the majority has 16+ while I have 32. The 6 gig minimum may be a bit high compared to other games, which leads one to believe it isn’t fully optimized, but the game hardly deserves a negative review over that. I’d be annoyed if I had spent money on the game only to find my PC couldn’t run it but one should always check the requirements first and again 6 gigs in today’s PC gaming hobby is hardly an onerous requirement.
The Arc launcher is also a non-issue unless you are having legitimate technical issues with it. I have used it for other Perfect World games before and never had any insoluble problems with it. Some other Steam games have this issue as well and it shouldn’t dissuade you from enjoying this game.
The FPS issue is an odd one to be sure. I’ve heard this for cross-platform gaming to avoid data loss or something but I know it’s a big negative for some. It’s not a huge issue for me to date but of the 3 most common negative review issues this is the only one I can see being a real problem.
But on to the good and there’s a lot of good. The art style is obviously going to be subjective; the game lacks the sex appeal of Overwatch characters like Widowmaker and D.Va or Paladin champions like Lian and Ying but it does have a lot of character in its 19 heroes, and more are on the way. From the cartoon robot HK-206 to the large but playful Pakko and everyone in between the heroes of this game are packed with character. Their look, animations, abilities, and dialog make them stand out well from each other and I’ve played over half of them and enjoy them all so far.
The game involves both sides picking 5 heroes, jumping into the battle from their air ship, and getting to business! Summon creatures at specific points, fight the enemy team to control these points and generate enough energy to attack the enemy guardian while defending your own; a simple premise but great fun in practice and I love that even if you are on the defensive from the other team getting enough energy to attack your guardian you have a window of time to both protect it and defeat the enemy team. The game doesn’t hit a stalemate as if it takes too many attempts to wound the guardians or one of them is down to 1 wound remaining (they take 3 each to destroy) the battle enters a clash mode and the action gets even more hectic.
Make no mistake the game is fast and frantic. You will have to decide which skills to choose as you level up based on your playstyle and the composition of the two teams all while fighting in a battle that grows more hectic the longer the game lasts. This may be a downside to some and they do need to provide us with loadouts to make this faster and more streamlined, I really don’t want to take the time to ponder and choose a skill while in the middle of a battle, but the variability of character skills is a huge plus and adds a lot of variety and depth.
The tarot card system is cool too. The art on the cards is elegant and well done and while you want to satisfy sets to earn rubies (more on that in the business model paragraph) you can always redo easier ones to earn prestige and crowns. Prestige is used to level up your account, crowns are the standard in game currency. The cards are a mix of general and character specific ones and when you draw one to fill a vacant card slot, you can have 7 active cards at once, you choose which one of the 3 you want to work on. An elegant and fun system to encourage you to play often. You start with several cards chosen already for new players but you get that free draw right away and can fill that 7th slot easily. I believe the free card draw is reset once per day but it may be even more often than that based on my experience so far.
As for the business model it’s quite good for a F2P multiplayer game. You get a weekly hero rotation much like other games do and can unlock heroes permanently with crowns or rubies. Obviously it takes far more crowns than rubies since rubies are this game’s cash-based currency. You can also but the starter or ultimate packs to unlock 8 or all the heroes respectively and gain some free card draws, rubies and in the ultimate pack’s case, a starter pack code for a friend. I gave that code to a friend after buying the ultimate pack which I purchased after playing the game for free to test the waters before spending money. As mentioned before you can earn rubies via getting complete sets of tarot cards. Rubies not only unlock skins and heroes faster than crowns but also give you extra tarot card draws and victory boosts for PvP matches, giving you more prestige and crowns.
It’s not perfect, I do enjoy it immensely and highly recommend it but it has a few issues. The lack of skill trees out of a match is something I want fixed ASAP (add it to the hero roster like skins and skills are), loadouts of these skills are needed to make selecting them in battle faster and easier, better bots for practice matches, custom matches, more maps, guardians, and characters (currently only 4 maps and 2 guardians but 19 characters while 19 is a decent mix, you can never have enough in this type of game can you?),fixing the ingame  voice chat to have PTT, address the fullscreen issue (there’s a workaround but shouldn’t need one in this style of game), and some technical issues that have been minor annoyances in an otherwise amazing game experience. If you like this style of game and enjoy the cartoony look and feel along with a crazy battle environment and some interesting playstyles for the varied and enjoyable cast of characters you will almost certainly like Gigantic.

The story from Oscar Wilde was a critique about the hedonism, moral decline and decadence of the victorian age upper class in the empire. The Protagonist of the named story "The picture of Dorian Gray", has a portrait of himself that ages and takes the signs of his sins instead of him. Keeping Dorian Gray, vibrant, youthful and healthy, while the portrait ages, withers and disfigures... During the novell Dorian gray grows more and more restless and amoral, even at times sadistic.
This said, the story of the game has some similarities. I won't spoil you the fun to find out which that might be, the game as a HOG (Hidden Object Game) is quite pleasing to play, I encountered no bugs and nothing that made the playthrough a bad experience. It also has some creepy aspects, that make the game a nice one. But one warning, even though there is so much misery and bad stuff in the news, day to day, week after week, we all should take the critique of Oscar Wilde to heart a bit, and think about our own decadence, moralty and hedonism... it's already the same issue, that was reason for... well you get the picture, don't you?
Pro:
- Nice graphics, and very good HOG scenes, which are still challenging.
- Good Soundtrack of the game.
- A storyline which holds a lot of suspense in it, yeah this game also has some fishy moments - but they actually are bearable.
- Nice additional content (Especially the bonus chapter will give you a very rude awakening)...
Con:
- Don't expect replayability. Once you are done, you are done with the story too... due to the linear gameplay of most HOGs they are a lot like illustrated interactive novells... Not that bad, but you have to look if you like this as a fact... Like most HOGs this one is only slightly challenging.
If you are new to this kind of game, this game might be the perfect first try. Since it has no achievements it won't grief you with missing out stuff and have to go through the same story once again. Also the story isn't boring, though roaming through all those HOG-Scenes might get on your nerves, once you are done you'll appreciate the work that was invested in this little jewel. But keep in mind, this game is expensive, either try to get vouchers, bundle or buy it when it's cheap on sale. At 9,99 it's still worth it's money since this HOG actually is fun to play and gives you a little respite with girls being the protagonist of a lot of HOGs...

If you're a dedicated object-finder, then you could probably find a more choiceworthy title out there for your tastes.  If you primarily enjoy the flavour of HO games, however, but are getting a little tired of finding yet another shaving brush, ship's wheel and a compass, this may be perfect.  It's also a little bit on the short side, but there's a bonus chapter included, which brings it up to a respectable length.

I've played the original Combat Arms for almost 7 years (back in the early 2008 and stopped 3 years ago) and have heard rumors of this game being developed 4 years ago. So I've taken the time to play this game after waiting for quite some time for it. I have to say, I quite enjoy it, however there are a lot of things that annoy me. I'll list them out.
Pros:
-Plays exactly like the original, of course without the power ups
-You have iron scopes now
-Weapons customization has been improved on, similar to Blacklight Retribution, might I add
-You can now test weapons you customize before you buy them, very similar to Operation 7, but with a bigger practice range that includes several other courses I've never seen other games have before. A course for running, the ability to use and experience/experiment with powers, and see how bullets interact with material, like shooting through wood or metal and targets showing how much damage you deal. This is a REALLY nice feature that not many games have, and when they do have it, don't have this much extent to them.
-A decent variety of game modes for launch compared to the original.
-You unlock all powerups for free and they are permanent to keep.
-The pistols in this game handle insanely well compared to 90% of the other games I've ever played, great animation and sounds.
-Powers are really fluid and are quick in transitions between firing your weapons and casting them. Best (personal opinion) ability is heal while the worst is debatably the plasma mine.
-They added a mastery tree, which adds small benefits over time (depending on your level) and just like in League of Legends, can add a huge advantage for higher levels playing against lower levels. Its a mixed bag, con being a strong advantage over other lower level players and a pro is complementing your playstyle very well. Good news is that you can disable these when making a room or find plenty of rooms that have them disabled.
Cons:
-No starting female models when creating characters, this is a big issue, which I'll state in my next con. The original Combat Arms had only 3 male models to choose from on release, a year later an additional male model was added. After 3 years, female models were added onto the game, however, you could only change into a female base model by purchasing a $10 sex change item from the store. There were heros/mercs you could purchase who were female, but those were for custom stats (BTW, Mei the original (still) best waifu (I have her for perm)), which you had little control over. A little bit after the female base models were added, the infamous new mechanic was added, the nut shot, which gave the female models (whether it was a merc or base model) a huge, but unfair advantage. Sure, female models had a MUCH bigger hitbox than their male counterparts, but female models were harder to see and made it harder to aim at.
-The Nut Shot mechanic was transfered over from Combat Arms to Line of Sight. Oh god, the moment I saw this, I already knew you HAD to go buy the female model, just like the old Combat Arms, or else you'll be at a big disadvantage. Why did they add this mechanic to the original? because it was "funny", NO! its a terrible mechanic which was to get more people to buy the stupid female models from the store. Why did they bring back this mechanic to Line of Sight? Same stupid reason, they want people to BUY the female mercs to make profit. Seriously, I'd rather have bigger hitboxes while being harder to see to compensate than straight up having two spots to get one shotted from, whether it be from pure skill to aim or luck from a shotgun/stray bullet!
TL:DR A nutshot is basically a headshot, but on your stomach which has a higher chance of being hit by luck in a firefight than a headshot with luck.
-While the Iron Sights being added to the game is a real big plus, its horrendous to use and needs more polish to use. Once you buy a scope for your gun, its a world of difference in how well you aim becomes. I would recommend a scope to be the first investment you want to buy when modding your weapon for the first time before anything else.
-The fireteam (zombie version (forgot the name)) is complete crap, unless you bring a machinegun, which will be the only way to beat it, you'll have difficulty even completing the first round. Only good news is that there are ammo crates where you can pick up ammo, bad news is that it takes forever for you to refill your ammo, which you run out of rather quickly trying to mow down a few zombies. Its impossible for you to defend the objective without a decent team (rarely happens) and the map is smaller than the original game maps, how is that possible? Ammo crates are placed near zombie spawns, so you'll need at least one team mate to cover you (which, lets face it, aint happening in this chaos). You can damage the objective by accident with your powers and weapons which sucks. The original gamemode didn't have an objective that could be damage by your own weapons and had some maps where there was no objectives to defend and just survive (which would be nice if Line of Sight had one). Now this is the worst thing, if you die, you can use your diamonds (irl money used for game currecny) to respawn (by pushing space bar) while the original had the option of purchasing tokens with gp from the store to use to respawn and pushing f6 or f7 for party respawn. Line of Sight gives no warning that you're going to use Diamonds to make the purchase, thankfully you get three, ONLY THREE, you don't get anymore later, they don't refill, just three tokens to use to respawn, so I ended up using only 2 tokens by accident and have been careful about pushing space the moment I die in that mode. You do earn diamonds from logging in after two weeks, but only in small amounts while Diamonds to buy the a respawn costs about the same amount of free diamonds you get in a month (why the ♥♥♥♥ are they so costly and easy to accidentally "purchase"). All-in-all, avoid this mode at all costs, don't bother its a waste of time to even attempt it. The tokens you get are both a joke and a gift to save you from accidentally purchasing respawn tokens.
-Not a lot of weapons
I really do enjoy this game, like I said, it plays exactly like the original with some differences with shotguns, can't really quick switch with the snipers, and still has things from the old game that really shouldn't have been brought back from the old game.
Big tip: do NOT spend anything, until you get the free two weeks starter package which comes with several weapons, the M4A1, a Sniper, and an SMG. They will last you two weeks, and I suggest saving your ingame currency until your weapons are about to expire. If you completed serveral achievements, you will earn enough to make the M4A1 permanent with all the attachments permanent as well. You gain 50,000 currency just by using the "find a match" button for the first time, which will earn you half of what you'll need to make the M4A1 permanent, which is super helpful. Do not confuse your 2 week M4A1 with your training gun, the training gun has several upgradable features locked. Your training gun is basically an M4A1, which is a super upgrade from the original which was a m16, debatably weakest weapon in the game. Buying attachments for the training gun is a waste and should be reserved for purchasing attachments to weapons you buy in the store with ingame currency.
Would I recommend this game? Yes if you played the older Combat Arms, which means you're use to a lot of how this game works.
And Not really recommended to newer players, there is a lot to learn if you wanna compete in this game, if you want to have fun.
Just stick with teamdeath match, CTF, and One Man Army. Maybe search and destroy.
I'd rate this as a 7/10. A lot of work needs to be done, but the game won't last that long by the time they get around to it.

As with all the King's Bounty games, this one is excellent, but unfortunately it doesn't seem to be as well made as the others. Specifically the sound is very buggy, especially during battles and the ending is incredibly disappointing and short considering the source material and the length of the game itself.  Some missions are also bugged, with locators randomly either not showing up or refusing to go away for the rest of the game.
Collision detection is nightmarish, and the maps often have some points(especially bridges) where the pathfinding simply collapses. You can use this to your advantage when being pursued by monsters(if you don't get stuck), but since you can FLY and monsters can't that's almost never a problem. Since you'll find the majority of the power-ups in the overworld maps anyway, it's entirely possible to avoid most of the combat until your leadership, spells and war chest are so inflated from kiting that you can seriously stomp the game regardless of difficulty.
This game more than any other in the series has way too many step and fetchit quests, which eat up time and money in game by making you run around all over the place for seemingly little more than to pad the gameplay. Seriously, often you're revisiting areas that you depopulated of all opposition forever ago. In it's favor though it does include a ready means of teleportation between the lands, which you're going to use and overuse a lot.
The plot is, like most of these games, insanely stupid and funny and not very serious.
Classes are the standard fare for the series, with a warrior, mage, and paladin archetype - except they're the orc, the vampire and the succubus. I went with the vamp for the first playthrough, the mage class is always good for being able to crush half the life out of an army before the first round even really gets underway. Crystals seem to be much rarer in this game, so choose to learn only the spells you know for a fact you will use a lot.
Second playthrough will be with the succubus, which I may or may not finish depending on if which character you choose changes the gameplay significantly. Past games in the series have avoided this, but since the classes are actually characters in this version one can hope...
At this point, the game engine needs a serious update. Navigation seems primitive now, it hasn't changed since the first game - right along with the ridiculously locked camera angles. The camera itself still seems to fight you even after almost a half-dozen games have been made.
This game should be able to be ported to tablets. No joke. The graphics are pretty badly dated at this point, it's time for an overhaul.
At least this game doesn't deprive you of your special abilities in boss fights, something that was always insanely pointless and unfair in previous entries, although the powers are significantly more limited.
All in all the series continues it's slow decline since Armored Princess. Some serious improvements need to be made and better production values need to be embraced. Still highly enjoyable and definitely worth the cash for all it's little flaws.

The opening two hours of the game do an excellent job of disguising an otherwise great experience.
Things start off ok, you get to pick one of three characters, each representing one of the three games skill trees, and are then whisked off to a unique starting area. Things then go downhill for the first opening act, which acts as the games vague tutorial.
The areas are empty save for the few packs the game throws at you to show you the combat, there’s no loot, no treasures, no exploration. The dialogue is oddly stiff, and badly written in places. The combat in this section of the game also suffers, whereas in other entries of the series you’d get your companion early, and unlock the extra battle functions, in Dark Side you’re on your own, the most fun and inventive part of the combat locked away as you drudge through the battles, trying to make your way to the start of the main quest proper. It wouldn’t be a problem of note apart from the fact that it’s a fair chunk of time until things start looking up.
The first two hours are dull, confusing and badly paced.
Then it all changes, the game breaks wide open, you get the best companion the King’s Bounty series has ever had, a fresh heap of possible armies and new abilities. The maps open up into beautifully designed mini quest hubs full of battles, treasures, puzzles and interesting characters to woo, threaten and fight. This is as good as the King’s Bounty series gets, in a fresh new skin and from the point of view of the “bad guys.”
If you’ve played the series before you’ll know what to expect, and if you haven’t, and you manage to drag yourself through the games opening, you’re in for a treat.
My favorite in the series so far.

While the match propagation can be shaky, and it can crash, it isn't nearly as bad (at least as of recently) as a lot of these reviews would make you think.  It's pretty easy to just load up the game if it crashes, and re-trying to host a game a couple of times, or just switching hosts usually results in having a working game show up for everyone.
That said, this is most definitely a game you should bring friends for.  With a group, especially of people you know well, this game is an absolute blast.  The deceit and trickery involved makes for a very fun twist on standard PvP shooter play, and even for the simplicity of the execution (4 classes, 1 level), the premise itself is novel enough to provide a lot of entertainment.
So don't be put off by all the negative reviews here.  For a small game put together by a small group of enthusiasts and delivered for free, the bugs are excusable, and not experience-breaking.  And no, if you jump on by yourself, you probably won't have the best time, but bring friends and you'll have a blast.

THIS GAME CONSISTENTLY CRASHED -- there's a Steam topic (pinned) on the issue. Just know that I'm not the kind of person to make knee jerk judgement calls. Ater researching the issue, I came to the conclusion that it's not worth my time, particularly since the game came out almost 3 years old. Square Enix clearly didn't do enough QA, nor did they followup with robust post launch support. If you do some googling you'll also note that the game was caught in "development hell" and well, it shows. The initial vibe I got for the short time the game did run was that the protagonist was too dry (voice over delivery) and uninteresting vs. the Garrett of the old games from around 2000. I'll add that with antialiasing turned off, I wasn't getting 60 fps on an Ivy Bridge  PC with an original nVidia GTX Titan. The geometry of the world didn't seem complex enough to be straining with so much hardware thrown at it. To be fair, I was running the game at a 21:9 resolution but the narrow city streets limit geometry (vs. an open world experience) and I exected far better performance. In closing, it seems Square Enix merely wanted to get this game out the door and recoup some of its development costs. Do yourself a favor, save your money and don't let nostalgia hook you (like I was), this game is not worth your coin. Otherwise, Garrett will break the 4th wall and steal something -- $$$ from your own purse.

So, as a person who hasn't played the original Thief (yet), this review will be different from a lot of others. Overall, Thief is a good game. Far from perfect, but good. I'll break it down into a few categories below:
Gameplay: 7/10
At it's best, this is pure stealth joy, executed to near perfection. The shadow system, alerting system, and most of all the swoop are done amazingly. Hopping from shadow to shadow and barely keeping out of sight of guards never ceases to be exhilerating, and most of the levels are designed in such a way that they are linear but offer a multitude of paths to the objective.
Like I said earlier, the swoop is amazing. It essentially has the same function as Corvo's teleport in Dishonored, but in a much more fluid manner. The animation is perfect, and the added depth of the action still making noise when traversing noisy terrain is awesome. Levels feel immersive and stealth is almost always a multi-sense excercise
One of my favorite things is that the game actually feels alive, sucking you in. Carefuly creeping over shattered glass or having your herart rate spike when you accidentaly knock over a stary vase is exhilerating, and even though it's a minor thing the hand animations are one of my favorite parts of the game. EVERYTHING has an animation, from swiping goodies to opening drawers and windows, you truly feel like a master thief creeping about in the shadows
The gameplay isn't without problems, although many of the common ones I've hear people complain about never happened to me. However, small things like a guard getting stuck in a looping animation, while infrequient, did kill immersion for that section. Another issue I had was with hiding, as I was being chased by enemies I slid under a set of bars into the elevator that would take me to the objective, and even though I was in plain sight inside this open elevator, the enemies steadily lost vision of me until they just forgot I existed. Along with this is the hit or miss design of levels, where most are very well done and some are unforgettable, while a few are made in such a way that there is really only one viable path to the objective.
These issues do detract from the experience, but tend to be few and far between, so overall the gameplay is phenomenal
Story: 5/10
The story is pretty generic, and though it starts strong with a multitude of unanswered questions and interesting characters, it quickly degrades into a predictable mess with no real closure. Villians and allies alike don't feel like much more than cardboard cutouts, and though Garrett himself does feel a bit more connectable, his voice acting can be either appropriate or incredibly whiny. As a game focused on the stealth and atmosphere though, I can cut Thief some slack here, just be ready for a mediocre storyline that sets itself up well then quickly falls flat. Cutscenes are also poorly animated, and feel clunky and awkwardly transitioned.
Atmosphere: 10/10
This is where the game hits home. The City feels like a living, breathing organism, adaptingto whatever is going on in the main story and really drawing you in. Most levels proveide awesome locations and a good amount of extra lore for those who want to sink into it (like myself for instance). My personal favorite is the Asylum chapter, which is executed to near perfection in my humble opionion, and even though I was playing thorough in broad daylight I constantly felt on edge. Timing, ambiance, and music all are combined incredibly well, and as someone who loves playing as the stealth calss in almost any game Thief really hit the spot for me
Overall: 6.5/10
Thief as a standalone is a pretty decent game, and provides a good amount of playtime (about 8-9 hours for the main story, about 7-8 more for side objectives and completionist runs). The custom difficulty settings add a lot of replayability, especially for those who want to turn on the hardcore options, like your game instantly ending and save being deleted upon detection. Overall I would say Thief is a good buy when it's on sal for $20 or less, and is a well done stealth game with a crappy story shoehorned in.

Stationeers is a solid, Early Access game. The game comes equipped with complexity and uncertainty - a lot of it. Stationeers isn't a game designed for a casual, average, mediocore, soft player. Stationeers is designed for those who love an absolute challenge, who don't want to play a game that is simply a walk in the park. Stationeers does not hold your hand through everything, you either need to figure it out or use your knowledge/sense to determine things in the game. The game does come equipped with a tutorial, but the tutorial is there just so that you can get the basics done.
Stationeers has so much functionality that it can leave you playing for hours endlessly. The whole pressurization system is complex and realistic and will leave your mind scattered if you have barely dabbled with a pressurized system before. Everything in the game is designed to not be done with your cursor; turning on a machine is done by clicking a button that is on the actual machine; putting ores into the machine is done by actually going to the correct input slot of the machine and putting it in; the inventory system is done with the use of keys and with zero interaction with the mouse.
The inventory system is something that is actually refreshing and is not your generic, survival type inventory with dragging and dropping into slots. There is no generic right clicking of an item to craft, so long that you have the items in your inventory. There is none of what you see nowadays. It is a new take, and it's a take that requires muscle memory to get used to; people are complaining that the controls for the inventory system is unintuitive but that is because this kind of inventory system hasn't been done/hasn't been done much in games so one really doesn't know how to operate it because they don't have the muslce memory for it. And if you do disagree with what I said, I still think that the unintuitive inventory system accompanies the difficulty and complexity of Stationeers.
In Stationeers, there is full on logic. Logic circuits and logic computers. It is absolutely easy to use, the only difficulty is if you can comprehend the logic behind things. The UI for logic computers is simple and clean however, I do feel some adjustments can be made to make it a little bit more user friendly (at the time of writing this review, I suggest it but it may change in the future to be better). With the logic circuits and logic computers, you can really get creative and dive into deep logic and create amazing contramptions that are automated too. For instance, there are solar panels in the game that generate power for your base (obviously) but since the sun is always moving, so do your solar panels have to move too which requires manual labour (as you'd have to whip out your wrench and adjust the angle of the solar panels). With some logic, you can simply automate the solar panels to always change angle and face the sun to guarantee maximum generation of power from the sun.
The community for Stationeers is phenomenal. If you require any help with the game, in terms of gameplay or bugs, there is always a bunch of people willing to help kindly and friendly and respectfully in the community - on the Sub Reddit and on their official Discord. There are people in the Discord looking for others to join them on their adventures as well. The sheer amount of support is amazing. Also, on the developers side, they are always there on Discord to have a chat about the game - whether it be suggestions or bugs or anything really. The developers are truly awesome and interactive with their community that they've built up. The developers even go on Twitch streams, small streams, big streams, it doesn't matter what size of an audience the streamer has, and have a chat with them and watch them play and help them out. For instance, I witnessed Dean come onto a stream where the streamer was having problems and Dean asked for the logs to determine the problem and solution. Now what other developers really do this for their game? This shows the utter care that Rocketwerkz has for their game and for their community.
Many people are debating whether to purchase Stationeers on the simple topic:
Stationeers is made by Dean Hall, who also made DayZ, so will this game also be abadoned and never finished?
Let me simply put this out there for you people. Dean Hall was contracted by Bohemia Interactive, a game company that is well known for their ArmA series, for one year to work on DayZ. Dean was not the lead project developer/manager. Although Dean was the face for the publicity of the game, Dean was simply a person who worked under others to develop the game - he had no control over the direction and advertisement for the game. Dean, on his one year contract, worked another year passed the contract. He also had to work far away from his home and family since Bohemia is not situated in New Zealand. Dean had to also get visas, which are a pain.
He has now created his own game studio, situated in his homeland and is the lead person which means he can decide where his game and his studio wants to go while having others work under him. This allows him to build the game he wants, with his ideas. So honestly, stop debating on the said topic and debate whether you'll enjoy this type of game or not and then decide to purchase or not to purchase Stationeers.
Overall, at the time of writing this review, Stationeers is a solid Early Access game that I definitely recommend to anyone looking for a game that does not hold your hand, involves space, survival, complexity, the ability to automate things with logic, and interact with a fantastic community.

So close to good, I really tried to like it and I'm a long time fan of the franchise .  Oh and just some friendly advice.  DO NOT play this game right after a play through of Dishonored.  Because you'll end up writing a review like this  :)
To start, I can't get past the between mission level design.  Having to re run, sneak, climb the same sections of the map, over and over.  To get from your "base" back to the next mission.. every single time you complete a mission. (Imagine if Fallout or Witcher never heard of fast travel.)  I think they left it out because if you weren't  forced to re run the same parts of the map.  The game wouldn't have even been 15 hours of play time.  Speaking of which, I beat it in 20 hours and I was not trying to go fast.
I get that by not having fast travel it "encourages" you find new paths and new loot.  But it takes me a minuet to open a window, steal $5 worth of crap, then turn around and spend another min reopening that window. I guess the $$ adds up over time but you get $150-$400 per mission so why bother?
Which bring me to my next grip, the pointlessness of the side quests.. There is no point, unless its on the way to the next main mission.. You don't get a lot of coin. Some offer incentives to kill guards (Which makes no sense since Garrett starts off the game saying "don't kill anyone unless you have to").. And after completion, you get to re run back through the same pointless areas to get to your next mission.
For a Thief game there sure isn't much emphasis on money or needing much of it.  Mainly you just need "$248 space bucks for lunch, gas and tolls"... sorry wrong movie :)   Actually you need $250, that will buy you a sharpen bread knife that you'll need to cut certain painting off the wall.  Why don't you already have a sharpen bread knife being a thief you might ask?  Good question, but you do get a club.. that can't break anything.  Which kind of sums up my grip with the game.  You just need to steal enough money to buy the 2-3 tools you need to complete the game.  After that you really don't need to anymore, unless you're really want to kill everyone or put out every tourch.
Ok now for the good, the bones of the game and game play are pretty good.  The sneaking works well and the AI is either so bad its good or polished but their parents might be cousins.  I really like the main quests a lot and was sucked in at times.  But I wish there was a little more story going into it and a little more plot to carry through. They did a good job creating a fast paced, driven story that keeps it going forward.
Going in I knew Thief games have always been "Here.... game, story, fire, water, shadows, arrows...Figure it out".  In the end I really wish they'd have put out more DLC's to add to the world, fill in the blanks, add new depth.  I feel this game could have really have been much more.
But as it stands, if its $10 and you want to sneak around... and are tired of Dishonored, I guess maybe go for it.  But having just completed it, I'm rather frustrated and a little disappointed at the number of little annoyances that added up to killing the fun of playing this game.

My apologies, this is gonna be long. But Thief: The Dark Project was one of the VERY FIRST PC games that I ever played, and is one of my favorite games of all times, so I have strong feelings about this...
First off, this game would have worked sooo much better if they had simply called it a reboot of the franchise rather than a sequel. The iconic factions of the setting have disappeared or been swept away, and there's little mention of Garrett's past adventures - frankly, it works much better if I imagine it takes places centuries after the other games and the protagonist is some other Garrett that has taken on the mantle of Master Thief.
That said, the core gameplay is intact (particularly if you play at "Master" level, as I did) - hiding in the shadows; sneaking up and blackjacking unsuspecting guards; putting out torches with your water arrows and getting into hard-to-reach areas with your rope arrows; looking for alternate pathways through heavily guarded areas; throwing bottles as distractions to get past tight patrols; ever vigilant for valuable loot as well as dangerous traps - it's all there. Lockpicking and "feeling" for hidden buttons to open secret doors and hidden compartments are all fun minigames, although having to pry open windows FROM THE INSIDE is really silly. The Focus addition is okay, though I didn't use it except for spotting traps. I loved Garrett's "exhibit" in his home where he shows off all the pretty loot he's stolen; I always figured he had something like that. The mission level design is pretty good - a few chokepoints, but plenty of freedom to find your own path in between.
Unfortunately, there's a lot of little things that detract from the game. The looped dialogue is utterly atrocious - boring and repetitive and annoying. The Moira Asylum level TRIES to be the successor to Bonehoard and Shalebridge, but it's clearly trying too hard and is nowhere near as terrifying or immersive. Exploring the city (and the sidejobs) is great at first, but after a while I couldn't help wishing for a fast travel option. The main storyline is ok... but the ending is rushed and emotionally flat, and it leaves you with little sense of satisfaction or accomplishment.
I have very mixed feelings about this game. I really think if they had spent some more time ironing out its problems, it had the potential to be truly awesome. As it is, while the core of it is good and I had a blast playing it, it has too many drawbacks holding it back from greatness.

Really fun and difficult platformer with a great retro style. Retro-looking games are a dime a dozen these days (sometimes literally, depending on the Steam sale), and none of them really stand apart. But this game manages to balance retro styling and interesting and even pretty aesthetic very well. The platforming is exactly as hard as it should be. It's Super Meat Boy levels of difficulty, while still being very fun to play. It doesn't go too far like I Wanna Be the Guy or similar titles that are basically just torture platformers. The combat in this game is simple, but still very satisfying and fun, as well.
For what it's worth, the recommended specs are way off. You hardly even have any need for a video card at all if you've got a somewhat modern Intel CPU. Intel's HD Graphics can handle this game just fine. I'm sure AMD's APUs perform just as well. I can't really say "better," because there's no room for improvement. Intel's onboard graphics perform fully well.

I have a lot of experience with MOBAs, and third-person MOBAs specifically. I played Paragon competitively at Master rank for about 8 consecutive months. I played Smite at Diamond rank for about 6 months. I played Nosgoth in the top 100 for 3 months before it was shut down.
Gigantic feels different than all of them, and that is a very welcome thing. If I were to draw similarities, I would draw them between Gigantic and Nosgoth, if only for the fact that it's a very "Deathmatch" focused MOBA, unlike most others.
Let's start from the top.
Pros:
The game has plenty of combat depth and player choice when factoring in the various ability upgrades that can be aquired. Each ability can be specialized and will change the way you play the hero in question.
Hero balance seems right on point. There are ways to counter every hero you come across, and I haven't found any that I just dread playing against.
Hero design is excellent. Every hero stands apart from every other hero even when accounting for skins and I haven't seen any sexualization yet.
Movement feels quick, fluid, and rewarding, but not disorienting (which is impressive).
The bosses are stunning to watch.
The community hasn't been toxic yet. :)
------------
Neutral:
Current roster is small, which is what I expected on downloading this. This is neutral because I don't know the development cycle.
Training mode was a bit tedious, but was comprehensive.
-----------
Cons:
For how quick movement is, maps feel a little cramped.
Matches feel just a bit too short and "level ups" are a bit to quick.
Melee heroes don't feel like they have much weight behind their attacks.
My in-game name is "Sermon" and I found a guy named "DIety." I couldn't figure out how to add him as a friend. Q_Q
----------
I'd give this MOBA an 8/10. More fun than most of them, but I'd like to see how the competitive scene looks.

#1 - to quote the devs “this is a niche game”.
Now, as someone with 2,200+ hours in Soace Engineers, 99 hours in Hellion, and 45 hours in Astroneer :  I already LOVE this game.
There is no hand-holding you in this title, your solar panels won’t automatically work, YOU (and friends) MUST design a control system to make that happen.   The list can go on and on, but that’s what I love about this title, the building is similar to space engineers in that you place an object then use a tool and materials to finish the construction on that object or in the case of machines you have to wire them up.
Power Grid management - you will need to design and control the power grid!  No automatic power just because you plopped down a reactor!
Airlocks - guess what, you have to think about how to design them out.
Is this game for everyone?  I’d say no, but if you wish Space Engineers had more depth, this might be the title for you.
A word of warning:  There is no learning “curve”, it’s a cliff right now. You will have to rely on testing things out or watching YouTube/Twitch to try and figure things out. I myself have decided to pull my recording software from mothballs and may try and attempt some how-to videos to help people get started. This is one of those games where you almost need to “apprentice” under a master and then go out and teach another how to play.
Again, if your friends with me on steam or have heard me talk in my streams etc you know I love a balance of realism and gameplay, to that end the challenge of this game is the gameplay. You truely are forced to think and plan and accept the consequences of your choices and actions.
Also this is early release folks, of course there are bugs, of course your going to have to restart from scratch, that’s why you wanted early access to the game right?
Anyway, if your on the fence watch some videos on YouTube, but I personally think if you felt like space engineers wasn’t quite complicated enough on the systems side this might be a title for you to look into.

A very ambitious project in the making here, but Rocketwerkz seems to be delivering so far.  The game has full atmospherics, and simulates gases, electricity, and soon many other things.  I have several hours in other space building games but I have never seen the depth in any game that I have discovered in this game.  Sometimes I'm just left in awe at things that happen, chain reactions of catastrophic events that occured because of my failed calculations and design.  The level of detail in the brains of this game are quite astounding, there is almost too much to explain you would have to witness it for yourself.
This is a game about designing, building, automating, refining and maintaining your space stations and soon ships.  The amount of time you spend on certain aspects of designing and building your station is huge.  Wiring your electrical grid for starters, power is most likely one of the first ventures you will set off on.  Building that first solar array, learning how to lay power cable and design your electrical grid so you're not blowing wires. Installing transformers to bottleneck your power, also setting your transformers to provide your grid with enough power and so on.  The electrical alone gets very detailed and you will find yourself refining and refining more.
Piping is every bit as complex as wiring, in fact maybe more so. Creating a complex network of piping to capture gases and sending them through a filter system into a storage system.   Then plumbing in areas to refill your bottles after you seperate your gases, or to fuel your furnace with the gases you captured.  Experimenting with fueling the furnace and piping hydrogen/oxygen into it usually leads to catastrophic results for the new guy.  You can also manually feed volitiles to the furnace safer than pumping compressed gases into it, but there are several levels of advancing these systems, knowledge is the only thing holding you back.  Piping also leads into airlocks for decompressing/compressing, you will be doing a lot of plumbing once you learn the game.
Logic circuits are in the game allowing you to create your own little complicated networks of automations or practically anything you want if you have the knowledge.  There are premade logic boards for computers or you can custom build a circuit using multiple chips that have numerous features.
The overall game loop plans to have some very interesting features to come, the game as it stands right now already has a lot of content and enough to keep you busy for a long time.  You will find the user interface to be a bit cumbersome to use at first, but once you wrap your mind around it the user interface really works well in this game.
I'm just really barely scraping the surface on the description about this game, it's very deep as it stands and really provides that sense of accomplishment when you finally succeed at building something that works correctly.  You will feel attached to your station once it starts taking shape, you will find yourself standing there looking at things deciding what to do next or what systems to start designing for what reasons.  Imagine spending all of that time designing and building and once your station is refined and resourceful, then you can start building a ship and doing the same thing over once ships are in.  I personally can't wait for ships to be in. :)
From what I have read and watched Rocketwerkz plans on having away missions, friendly/hostile npcs, alien creatures, missions, and exploration.  Hopefully we see a decent amount of planets and the ability to travel to different systems in the future.  Also I would love to see the ability to create rovers to roam the planets as well. This really is a epic game in the making.

I don't review games often.  But this experience was just so bad I felt like I had to talk about it.  Cringe is a word I'd imagine most people will use to describe this game.  Unfortunately it's an experience that is nearly spoiled just to talk about it.  So I'll do my best here to explain why I didn't like it, without giving it away.
In this game you play a girl who has been investing time in an online MMO.  She begins talking to another player on the game, they begin voice chatting through the game, and from there you see how her life changes and where this "relationship" goes over the next several months.  The game leads up to an event in this relationship and to its apparent end.  Then the credits roll.  You'll likely feel unfulfilled by this.
As for the gameplay, for parts of this experience you play that MMO while the main character talks to the guy.  The gameplay is more or less a throwaway tech demo just there to give the player(you) something to do while the recorded coversation plays.
Ultimately, I found myself disappointed.  I normally like these kinds of experience games.  I enjoyed Gone Home, for example.  But this one is just so bad it's not worth your time.  It was bad enough I'll likely avoid anything released in the future by this developer.

I think an expanded version of this will be done as TWoM 2.  And it deserves it.
It is very refreshing to see concept like this as many are saying.  This is a constant battle of resources and trying to make it through the day vs. putting aside and building for the future.  It is difficult to get ahead in the game as you can easily get stuck in one resources which causes a consequential problem in another area.  Almost like an RTS or Civ series, but trying to survive only as a war struck person or group.
What is interesting is the large number of ethical questions, tied up stories and their implications to your psyche or body.  This is where they can build the product even further with more detailed stories and get lots of replayability.  You start with three people in your group - one of my guys got shot outside, the second got lethally wounded at home and died, and the third was so sad- he committed suicide.  That's realistic I must say and the game excels in that.  At the end, your goal is to survive the war and it is very difficult to get around without hurting someone or yourself.
The artistic side is fairly strong in the game as well as the screens would tell you.  So plus ad minuses:
+Realistic lifelike war survival
+Nice screen designs
+Fresh story
+Can replay heavily
+Complicated ethical and survival criteria
-Can get repetitive if playing too frequently
-Constant resource shortage
Overall I liked it and as long as you do not pay a huge amount, it is worth it.
