Magic Duels is the best way you can get into the popular card game. It's packed with enough features to make it worth more than just your time. However, the game comes with pitfalls that break the deal for experienced players. Once you feel proficient in this game, you might want to move on to Magic Online or buy real cards.
The most compelling feature in this game is the campaign. It consists of duels that do a great job at introducing you to base mechanics alongside new expansion cards. The first story in particular introduces you to each color, letting you learn the basics of MTG practically. The matches themselves play a part in telling the story. A confrontation with a group of elves in the story leads to fighting an AI that summons a large number of elves, making you feel out numbered in the duel itself. For a free game, the work put into the campaign is pleasantly surprising.
Once you're done playing as much as you can of the campaign, you can dabble with building a deck of your own. The game offers great assistance with it's Deck Wizard. The tool helps in showing you some example strategies and how they affect what cards you choose. Later on, you can move to building a deck of cards with your own strategy. Just like the campaign, deck building is made with new players in mind.
The rest of the game is quite underwhelming and leaves much to be desired. The online multiplayer isn't very reliable for instance, and it barely offers enough modes. Some of the cards you use in the campaign aren't available in any other modes. The support from the developers was never satisfying to begin with, and now it's discontinued. Despite all these flaws, I still highly recommend this game for beginners and casual MTG players.

This is a game where you fly spaceships and shoot at other spaceships. There's not much else to it. I wouldn't say this is a try F2P, but it's not much of a P2W. Especially when you get in higher ranked battles, the people who bought there way to the top are the first to go. This is a game of skill, not fancy weapons. The game itself gives you plenty of opportunities to level up quickly. The only issue I have to complain about is that the instructions in the missions do not reflect the recent updates, so you may end up spending a good amount of time on google if you wish to do the missions (which are completely optional, but they do have their rewards). In terms of combat it's pretty simple in terms of HUD readability and controls. Matchmaking is based on ship rank, so you will be fighting players of multiple different skill levels (which can be a good thing and a bad thing). If you really are that bad (when you are starting out), there are plenty of bot players that are added to both sides that give you a few free points and target practice. There is also a mode now where you can freely roam the sector (assuming you are ready to take on enemy pirates and players that may come your way). In terms of the ships, no matter what faction you choose, there are 3 basic ship classes. Recon: fast and deadly but almost no shields. Commander: good balance between weapons and shielding, moderately fast. And engineering ships: painfully slow, but extremely deadly to anything in front of it, plus high shields. So as you can see there is no "master" ship. Despite what you may see above, in actual combat you will learn quickly that all ships are equal, it's just a matter of learning what your ship was built to do. Upgrade paths can be confusing. There is no "this is level 2, this is level 3". You can mix and match almost any weapon type (assuming there is a version of that weapon for your ship class, some weapon types are only built for a specific class). You can also upgrade your shield, engine, targeting computer, and pretty much anything you can think of. You can also upgrade the entire ship using synergy. Synergy is accumulated at the end of battle (usually only when you win), and can be used to level up all components of your ship.
Short version of this review: It's addicting, it's fun. It's a nice break from other "shoot 'em up" games. And it's free. If you are really impacient, you can buy your way to fame at the cost of being humiliated due to lack of skill.

Willing to buy lvl13 Premium ship from scratch? Suck it, buy lvl3, lvl5, lvl7, lvl9 and lvl11 ships first (preferrably Premium ones, of course)! Pretty fair, ain't it?
(the idea of limiting purchaseability of paid items in F2P game is worth Economics Ig Nobel Prize, honestly)
Oh, barely forgot. You won't unlock all Steam achievements without purchasing at least one ship for real money. Ain't that cute?
2. Game mechanics.
Rocket launchers and torpedoes rule. Is your ship tough as nails? Suck it, one guided missile in your side and you're done! Lasers, ballistics guns, stealth devices, crowd control devices - nothing of it needed if you can just spam rockets.
3. Bots.
Bots everywhere. The game itself is all about quick skirmishes between small squads. Each botter present diminishes team's chances way too seriously.

While it's the very best space shooter I've ever played, it is also a huge grind-fest. The only way to make this game worth your time is if you keep up a license subscription, and take advantage of the various sales that happen about each week or so, including buying the DLCs that give permanent boosts when they are on sale. If you do this, then you’ll really enjoy the game and the grind will be tolerable, otherwise you’ll want to ship this one. So while it is indeed “Free to Play”, you won’t really get anywhere with the game or really be enjoying for long without spending some real money on it, but if you do, you’ll be rewarded with a pretty awesome game, that’s only getting better and better over time so far. The game devs are generally very responsive to the community complaints and requests. Unlike many other game companies out there, this one actually cares about the success of its game here, so it’s one worth supporting.

As a fan of the previous KB titles (as well as all the M&M's and HOMM's), I began playing Dark Side with some trepidation after reading negative reviews and comments. After 110 hours, I'm glad I was wrong.
Dark Side has some minor drawbacks -- unmarked quest items are too easy to sell/discard, quest dialogues don't appear unless you've solved the NPC's previous requests -- but in general I think this is the best of the KB titles. It solves the single most annoying thing about the previous games, the constant need to backtrack to previous realms/islands to replenish lost trooops. A teleportation system in this one makes travel a snap and there's a virtually endless supply of troops.
The scenery is the prettiest of all the KB games, and the game's a visual delight once you learn to fly. The game's major conceit works well: You're playing as the bad guy. Yet as the story unfolds, you quickly end up believing you're on the right side of things. The quests are generally more interesting than the usual bring-x-to-y tasks, and there are some when you have to remember people and places from early in the game to complete later assignments. Take notes.
Worth playing.

After having just completed this game on impossible, I really just cannot recommend it. I'm a huge fan of the King's Bounty series but I feel like 1C is just dicking us around at this point. They're releasing a bug-riddled, rehashed, mostly re-appropriated-content game. I don't mind paying for a new 'campaign' essentially since the engine is the same for the most part and they carry over most of the same units, but this is really just a case of relabeling a bunch of units and calling it a day.
If you're an absolute completist, the game isn't unplayable. You should prepare to spend most of your time running around trying to figure out where you're supposed to be going, though, since the quest log is almost useless and you have to guess most of the time where the quests or story wants you to go. Most of the land is pretty lazily designed and doesn't flow that well. There are re-used maps aplenty.
Ultimately, I just don't know if I can keep playing these half-baked games. They have such a solid engine to begin with, they could probably just let some users come up with new stuff for them and release that, but I guess they just really have no intention of caring about these releases. Such a sad fate for such a promising initial entry.

I'd recommend this as a neat, free alternative to a paid title for young kids playing on a PC rather than mobile device.
Not something I'd really bother sticking with, personally, but anyway.
But now, I'm going to address the various "criticisms" certain other reviews are claiming.
Firstly, lives refresh over time. Nobody has to pay anything. That's simply a shortcut if anyone optionally chooses to. I haven't spent a cent on the majority of "mobile games" with microtransactions (including the supposedly sinister microtransactions of Final Fantasy: All The Bravest or Candy Crush), because it refreshes without having to pay anything.
I have never had to pay to play whatsoever, it is purely there for an optional shortcut (which people DO have the right to use if they wish to).
Secondly, the claim that it's only controller support. False. I opened it *just* to see what all the fuss was about and was playing with a keyboard just fine. Arrow keys and space bar, really isn't that hard.
In conclusion, limited lives isn't anything that bad. It's called limiting play. Taking regular breaks from games should be obvious. And you also *earn* lives from playing, I literally gained two extra ones by selecting 1 square out of 9 choices (a daily play selection. You're complaining about something not being in the game when it very clearly is. And you can easily bank up lives for free as well. Again, never had to pay a cent in a free mobile game, and I highly doubt I'm going to start now.
It's rather sad when the supposed "self-entitled hardcore gamers" of this generation of gaming are actually *more* childish and immature than the kids this game was more likely designed for. Sheesh...

A fun little time waster.  Somewhere between M.U.L.E. and the old C-64 game, Oil Barons.
Each round has you buying land in an auction and then spending a season producing oil on that land.  Between rounds, you can upgrade elements to help you find and drill the oil more efficiently.  The oil wells are always randomized, and the drilling aspect is kind of clever.  The more you drill, the more information it reveals about the size of the well, but the more money you'll spend.  Placement between the two companies that buy your oil can affect how quickly you can sell it.   Suddenly Left is offering $2.00 a barrel, but your derricks are on the right.  So there's a little time management going on too.   The game is cleverly balanced, and a lot of fun.  Definitely worth the $10.

Controls: Especially Ragdoll and Interact commands are very unresponsive, and I doubt it's because my keys would be broken; as I am writing this, I have no problem with the keys R and E, the letters appear to this interface just as all the other ones.
Collectible items and missions: The game does not remember which items I picked up last time and what missions I did. If you close the game (or it crashes), you have to start all over again. You get the achievements, but the game does not remember a thing.
Houses: As far as I saw, all the houses can be entered, but it turned out that they are literally empty. Some have small toilets in the corner, but some are simply 100% empty small rooms.
Gamebreaking bugs: While bugs are a part of the game, there are some that make you relaunch the game (which feels like a quite a slow process): The menu icons not disappearing, physics bugging so that you can't walk and thus are forced to be on ragdoll all the time, dummy getting stuck into buildings, ground, etc. so bad you can't move... Those bugs are not funny.
I really, really wanted to like this, and this has lots of potential to be great. However, I did not find this enjoyable. It's a shame that this became my first refund. :(

Cibele is a short story about growing up with and falling in love via the medium of online gaming, told from the point of view of a teenage female protagonist.
Aspects of it felt invasive to play, being the twenty-something male that I am. I didn't
the experience at all. However it has made me reflect on some similar experiences I may have had in the past. On the one hand, how horrible it is to grow up in this world of modern technology coupled with vicious vanity and superficiality. But on the other hand, those bittersweet moments of confusion and vulnerability hold their own kind of
in my memory. I may not always like them, but I wouldn't trade them for someone else's. It's part of the path that has gotten me to where I am. And I think I turned out alright.
This isn't really a game with any kind of actual gameplay involved, you're just along for the incredibly awkward ride. And this isn't a game that will appeal to a vast majority of people, because it's not a game with a power fantasy in which you can escape from life. It's not really a game at all, more like a brutally honest self portrait of a girl during a very strange period of her life. One to which some people - particularly young gamers - might relate, for better or worse.
I really didn't want to recommend it at all when I came to write this review (as I've said, I didn't enjoy the experience at all) but I've had an unexpectedly deep and enjoyable few minutes in doing so.
What a strange, strange thing.

Seriously though, for what it is, Cibele is a decent enough game.
It never advertised with having a super-exciting RPG within the game, so you shouldn't expect the gameplay to be too interesting. You just click a monster, wait for it to die and then click the next one. While waiting, you can read and "answer" (meaning: literally click a button that says "Reply") to messages that Cibele's friends send her and listen to the dialogue between her and Ichi. When you've killed enough monsters, a boss appears and after defeating it, the story moves on to the next act.
The sections you spend looking through the data on her desktop earn you some more information on Nina and her social life, some poems that she wrote (which are obviously heavily influenced by what is going on inside her), cringy blog posts from when she was a 13 y/o weaboo and...well, selfies. Oh, so many selfies...
The voice acting is good, acting is alright and both the story and ending are propably really true to life, so I don't see anything 'wrong' with it.
As I already mentioned, Cibele is a narrative game, so don't expect too much gameplay-wise.
If you're into that kind of games (like e.g.
), I definitely recommend picking it up on sale or in the Humble Bundle - I personally don't think Cibele is worth the full price, seen as I only got 1.3 hours of gameplay out of it and it doesn't offer any replay value whatsoever.
Unique, interesting, sweet and very personal. A big predictable but that's not the worst thing ever. Took me about an hour and a half. If you like narative focused indy games try this.

That's realistic I must say and the game excels in that.  At the end, your goal is to survive the war and it is very difficult to get around without hurting someone or yourself.
The artistic side is fairly strong in the game as well as the screens would tell you.  So plus ad minuses:
+Realistic lifelike war survival
+Nice screen designs
+Fresh story
+Can replay heavily
+Complicated ethical and survival criteria
-Can get repetitive if playing too frequently
-Constant resource shortage
Overall I liked it and as long as you do not pay a huge amount, it is worth it.

tl;dr: Great game, now on my 'go to' games list, judging only on playable features currently implemented in the early access build (19/12/2017).
In its current state Stationeers follows a similar gameplay loop of other games in the survival + base building genre (e.g. Minecraft, Subnautica, 7 Days to Die) of resource collection, base building, expansion and repeat, with the survival aspect coming from sustaining essential resources, currently including electrical power, oxygen and jetpack fuel.
What separates Stationeers from other games of its ilk (I'm personally not a fan of Minecraft) and onto my list of regular 'go to' games, is the level of depth in which the systems and elements of the game interact with one another, reflecting one of the most interesting aspects of space exploration (the theme of the game), the complexity of the problems for surviving in space and the ingenuity of systems designed and built to solve these problems.
An example of the problems presented to the player by the game and my (the players) solution:
Problem: Need power. Solution: Build a solar panel.
Problem: Solar panel only generates power while sun is aligned. Solution: Manually adjust panel alignment using wrench.
Problem: Time constrained due to adjusting solar panel. Solution: Design and build logic + sensor system (also collect resources, build manufacturing capability, design the logic).
Both the singleplayer and multiplayer offers the same game modes, 'survival' and 'creative', which can be described as resource gathering required vs items able to be spawned on command respectively.
I've personally spent several hours designing, building and experimenting with several bases and systems within creative mode to figure out what I could potentially build in survival mode.  I have also spent several hours in survival mode, gradually expanding a 3x3 (flat) base consisting of a solar panel and battery charger into a 5x5x4 base with manufacturing capabilities and aspirations for becoming a breathable pressurised environment.  I feel this will be a game I will play for hundreds of hours and still be able to find something new to experiment with.
Mutiplayer is essentially the same game as singleplayer with other players able to help (or hinder) each other, ala co-op gameplay.  I've not yet spent a significant amount of time playing multiplayer but it feels very fitting, thematically, cooperating with others to build a base together, not to mention a great deal of fun helping one another, debating on priorities, figuring out solutions together (or challenging against one another) and just experimenting with the systems together, sometimes to explosive effect.
Based on my experiences (16+ hours) of the game so far, I feel that one of the games greatest strengths compared to others of its kind is that when faced with one of the problems the game asks of me (the player) to solve, on reflection of my solutions, not once have I felt ham-strung by 'game logic', i.e. where the only solutions defy reasonable logic, or an obvious 'single optimal choice'.
Quite often the problems presented to me (the player) are 'reasonable', i.e. governed by the laws of physics, and furthermore the decomposition of that problem into 'reasonable' sub-problems that that I (as the player) would expect to make a decision at quite often translate into a 'reasonable' game mechanic, system, or element that I can use.
In short, I felt it very rewarding experimenting and finding my own solution to each particular problem (that I'll probably redesign at some stage) and felt each solution was a meaningful learning experience of the games systems, and one step forward on a long path towards mastering the game.
On the performance side, I've experienced very few performance issues with the early access build, consistently achieving 144 fps on an Intel Core i7-6700 and GTX 1080.
The current price of $25 USD, in my opinion, is already a good price for the current feature set of the game, with additional features being planned for future updates.
The style and mechanics of the game appear to be designed for rapid development and the developers have said in previous live streams that the intention is to support modding in the future.  I confidently predict the game will be well supported by the community as well as the developers with future content for the game past its eventual final release.
I would highly recommend the game to the technically-minded (or those who aspire to be!), those interested in complex systems or the systems of space exploration, and closer to the core of it, to someone who would enjoy using their ingenuity to design, build and experiment with complex systems to solve complex problems (e.g. #1 survive!).

Oh Stationeers, how I love thee.
Were you one of those kids who while enjoying putting together Lego models, you ultimately always wanted more? I was one of those kids, I remember getting my first Technic truck. It had an engine, batteries and even this little scanner-doodad which you scanned pre-programmed barcode functions with to control your truck. The truck itself didn't last me long as I wanted to see what I could do with the parts that came with it... I digress.
Stationeers is one of those games for the curious, problem-solving gamer with a bit of love for engineering and clever (sometimes stupid) solutions for complicated (sometimes not) issues. Even more so if you have a friend with similar interest whom you can work together with, or as often happens, argue a little bit with because you know your way of setting up the smelting room is the best way. Obviously. At the moment your current goal (gameloop) is to survive on the moon, gather materials to build your moonbase and eventually expand it so you have enough room to build the pinnacle of human engineering. The most advanced, efficient and in general just perfect moonbase, where nothing can go wrong..
The game at the moment has a bit of a learning curve, there isn't too much documentation on the game yet and its many, many tools and functions. Which I personally find both challenging and fun! It took me probably close to three hours to properly set up my 8 solar panels to correctly switch between their three states (sunrise, midday & sunset) using the logic computer and two daylight sensors. (The day after I completed it the devs added function 'SolarAngle' to the daylight sensors. Thank you! Grrr!)
If you have been following this game at all and watched some of their dev streams you've probably heard them claiming that they've built the game around it having a quick turnaround on compiling new builds with updates, bugfixes, new assets and functionalities, etc. So far this seems to be a true statement, they have patched the game what seems to be almost on a daily basis. While the game itself has some rough edges here and there, there is already a ton of content within the game and it should honestly last you a fair amount of hours to have touched on everything there is. As for Early Access, I think they've done a great job with the game thus far. It definitely feels like a proper Early Access title to me, it has plenty of content, it has an interesting gameloop that's fun, they just need a bit of polish, balance and some bugtesting. Cool!
As for the community, I've been lurking a lot in the Stationeers Discord server and so far the community seems to be keen on helping out and being in general quite nice to eachother. Due to the complicated nature of this game a lot of players turn to eachother for help, tips and tricks on how to solve their issues. I haven't seen a single elitist jerk bashing on a new player because he didn't know how to properly pressurize a room or what have you. So keep that up please!
So to summarize a little bit; If you like a bit of building, crafting, gathering, surviving, (Space!) and some problem-solving. Stationeers might be the game for you.
Oh and also.. pipsi.

I am generally a calm person. I approach life's challenges with poise and restraint, taking time to casually find my way through each moment. However sometimes I come across a game that just makes me lose my f*****g s**t. In the past, it was the many iterations of Ninja Gaiden that brought about the doom of many a controller. And then there was Super Meat Boy, an exercise in frustration that I still have not fully conquered to this day. And now in the summer of 2012 I have met my new nemesis, They Bleed Pixels. And oh, what an adorable harbinger of destruction she is.
So imagine if you will a gloriously challenging platformer that demands exact finesse in the vein of the Nintendo-hard games of yore, complete with retro graphics, tight controls, and a rockin chiptune-inspired soundtrack (by DJ Finish Him no less!). That is They Bleed Pixels in a grotesquely Lovecraftian nutshell. When the young heroine is sent to a reform school she uncovers a necronomicon-esque book that fills her dreams with nightmarish horror as she is transformed into an eldritch crab-clawed zombie warrior who must cleanse the world of the undead.
All that side, what really sets They Bleed Pixels out from the crowd is the well thought out control system. Using a standard Xbox360 controller is the best way to experience the carnage, with it's tightly tuned context-sensitive actions that will keep the combos (and the blood) flying. Another nice touch is the way the save system works. By building up your combo chains and collection blood orbs, you gain energy to leave behind a "save sigil". As long as you find a safe spot with no traps or monsters nearby, you can place one almost anywhere, and whenever you die you will continue from it.
All in all the only downside to They Bleed Pixels it is that once the game is over, there's really no way to extend the fun. Hopefully Spooky Squid will someday release a level editor, as I'm sure that fans would enjoy trying their hand-- err claw, at making their own masterpieces of mayhem. Don't get me wrong though, They Bleed Pixels is still a complete experience, and very well polished at that. Fans of the genre should definitely pick it up ASAP.

A lightweight psychological thriller– with a good story and good antagonist– that takes the form of a decent hidden object puzzle game.
Brink of Consciousness: Dorian Gray Syndrome follows the story of an investigative journalist trying to save his girlfriend, as he slowly progresses through the mansion of a narcissistic serial killer, solving puzzles and collecting items along the way. During his trials he is often contacted by the antagonist: an excellently written character, who constantly balances on the brink of being comically over the top, but manages to stay threatening throughout the story– including one of the best bonus chapters (with an incredibly clever twist) in hidden object game history.
Although most of the game is spent by running around in the mansion, the monotony is often broken by some easy puzzles and a few very good hidden object scenes. And the best thing is that most of them have an actual reason within the storyline to be there, creating a more immersive atmosphere.
If you like thrillers, Dorian Gray Syndrome is definitely a good choice for you, casual genre or not. The great writing and level design make it one of the most enjoyable games of its kind.

Very well-done game with a combination of point-and-click adventure aspects and hidden object/puzzles.  Compared to some, this game focuses more on the puzzles and less on HO scenes.
The story was engagingly creepy and while not entirely original, was entertaining.  The back story was fairly formulaic but as it's fed to the player in small bits, via diary entries mostly, the somewhat predictable history of the villain did not detract from the story.  What helped this is that the game didn't bonk you in the head with information about the villain; to some extent you have to imagine the events leading up to the events of the game and to me, at least, that makes it more mysterious and creepy.  The villain manages to be both over-the-top psycho and creepy.  It's a combination that doesn't always work, but it does here.  It helps that the voice acting isn't terrible (a curse that many of these games have).
Minigame puzzles were generally challenging without being obnoxious or illogical; only a couple were somewhat tedious.  There is a convenient skip button for people that are stuck (or impatient).
Hidden object scenes were not overly challenging but did take some thought.  Graphically, scenes weren't grainy and it wasn't hard to distinguish objects from one another.  Objects are appropriately named (no searching for a "soccer ball" that turns out to be a volleyball, etc.).
All in all, this is one of the better choices for this genre of game.

This game has tought me everything I need to know to run a Oil industry, what horses to buy, and how to train moles to dig for diamonds!

EDIT: since the original review was written in a fit of rage and had tones I don't approve myself (why insult people, when sarcasm is available?) I'm rewriting the review. Cool and compassionate. Like a Buddha.
Turmoil is a drilling game with strategic elements into it: rent a land trying to get a low price for a oil-rich parcel, pay some equipment to make the work easier and more remunerative, bribe officials to get higher sell prices, then go for it, and during an arcade/strategic stage, mostly based on resources management, drill the land and get and sell as much oil as you can, for as much money you can, without spilling it.
In the short term, it all works - the arcade stage is fun enough that you can do... say 10 stages of it and enjoy it - but the game lacks stamina, and you quickly realize that the meta-game, is mostly a pretext to give the player a long term objective, and hide the repetitively of the task, which however is appropriate for a 5E tier game [note: when the original review was written, this game costed between 10 and 15E...].
The game has however also some serious balancing issues: you literally bleed money through all the campaign for drilling upgrades, to the point you will almost always be in the debt zone, where the AI doesn't seem to be touched.
The general impression I have is that the AI performs based on a quite crude algorithm (a function of the prospected amount of oil on the selected land, plus some fluctuations), and a couple of random withdrawal to give the impression of fairness.
No big deal, it doesn't matter what the developer use to give the player the impression of autonomous agents if it works, but when you spot the smoke and mirrors, is a failure AI-wise.
And then, there is the endgame... The last very drilling game is special game-wise, it seems, because all you have built through all the campaign, can be lost in a single turn through a (ludicrous in my opinion) "bidding tournament" where the lesser players are robbed of their shares (???), which are then put into a dutch action.
Short of it: 10 hours of (rather boring) campaign, and you loose the game in 5 minutes. I'm told there is a "back one turn" feature, but I suspect it doesn't work on the end game.
But that's not the best part: when you lose, the major talks to you and tell you "don't be mad, not everyone can be as successful as I am".
Now, I've been around. In the days of old, games that sneered, laughed, humiliated you for losing where all but uncommon, but this is something of the eighties i *don't* miss, especially when I have the feeling of having been cheated. It's a middle finger in the direction of the players, and alone would deserve a thumb down.
If you can forgive that, for 5E I guess is sort of "ok", but for me, it just  wasn't worth the time.

This game is one of the rare gems that elicits a genuine emotional response.
I could write at least ten pages detailing the highs and lows of everything I've done in the game. Insane antics, devastating losses and monumental achievements. But I'll just share one experience that really made the game come to life.
I started out the game being pretty beta, helping people, not stealing, etc. But eventually the scarcity of goods, the declining health and morale of my comrades and the impending winter freeze forced me into a corner and I decided I had to steal. There was a group of people camping out in an apartment complex who, though armed, guarded a trove of food and resources. In order to successfully complete the operation, lacking weapons and armor, I had decided to use my character who was a skilled scavenger.
Well, I loaded up the map, and after dodging these guys for a while, started getting a lay of the building, unlocked doors, etc. In the background, they were shooting at a homeless guy dressed in rags, laughing at him as they gunned him down. These guys were serious, but at least I didn't feel like♥♥♥♥♥♥for stealing from them anymore. For a second at least. I had wondered if these men and women were really as psychotic before everything went to♥♥♥♥♥♥or if they had decided that aggression was the only way to survive long before I had. Pretty strange playing a game that definitely sells its sense of realism where you see women with guns commit murder casually.
Soon, things went to♥♥♥♥♥♥ Patrolling enemies started noticing that I had left doors open and became suspicious. I didn't anticipate the AI being so perceptive. They stepped up their speed and numbers as they started combing the building for me. My character was not a fighter; he was selected for this mission based on carrying capacity and search speed. There was no room for error. If I was caught I would likely be killed. Without the much-needed supplies, more people would die as well.
I elected to hide in a darkened closet and wait until I had a clear break for the exit. Unfortunately, there were now at least 5 people, all armed with blades and guns, actively searching for me. After sweating bullets for a few minutes, they seemed to converge upstairs, giving me a good shot at freedom. However, I heard someone coming down the stairs. It was one of the women from before, holding a shotgun, calling out to me telling me that if I surrender they won't hurt me. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, I saw what they did to that guy, and for taking nothing but refuse from across the yard from their stronghold. The sun was coming up. She was getting closer. I couldn't fight. I had nothing but a crowbar. I was sick. It was now or never.
I waited for her to pass by my hiding place and brained her with the crowbar from behind, then ran to the exit.
Now, that's a pretty intense and interesting gameplay experience, but where I'm going with my assertion that the game is emotionally provocative comes from the consequences. Like life, it's easy to do things when you're pushed into a corner, but when you have nothing but time to think about it, that's when it all hits you. My scavenger, despite having saved his comrades, immediately fell into a deep depression, refusing to work or eat. He wasn't a soldier or a killer. He used to be a fireman. It was his job to save people. He was forced to confront himself for what he had done, even if the circumstances may have justified it. It wasn't until I had the other characters (who rightfully were grateful for his heroism) console him that he eventually pulled through the depths of his depression.
Yet, the memories would continue, his misdeeds chronicled forever in his journal, where he expressed his anger, regret and sadness over the incident, as well as his desire to stay positive so that he can continue to function as the main provider of resources.
Gotta say, that made me pretty floored.

TBP is precision platformer with "one button" (also makes use of the directional keys) brawling and combo mechanics, also notable is a checkpoint system that allows the player to choose when and where to make a save point.
The look of the game is a retro pixel feast, I personally can't say no to anything pixelated and think it looks fantastic, more than enough definition to always be able to see what is going on around you, what is a baddie and what is a goodie.
Controls are very sharp and very simple to pick up, you only have to worry about directions, attack and jump. Attacks change based on if you are holding a movement key in a direction and if you are holding or tap. All in all there's a dash, a kick, a swipe, a launcher, an air juggler, a mid-air to ground dash, and a mid-air-combo swipe. Together these combine with the combo system and the environmental hazards, that chop up you and foes with equal fervor, to make huge pools of bleeding pixels and gibs that drip and bounce all over the beautiful place.
Spending your time double jumping or wall hanging over and around a million spikes or razor discs is a joy... once you finally make it. But there's no blaming the game for your 180 deaths and 60 minutes to get through a 5 minute level (yes, I saw your screenshot, well done you). Once you've mastered the systems of movement and figured out how to chain together huge combos, the real fluidity of the game unlocks and you are free to maneuver yourself to the top of the leader-boards.
Collecting orbs or killing baddies you fill you checkpoint meter, once full you can stand still and as long as there aren't any obstructions (bad guys, razor discs) you can create a check point to return to when you die.
There are no other check points so without these you will be zapped right back to the start of the level at death. Your character does have three hearts, getting hit by a baddie or touching an obstacle will cost you one, lose em and die, drop a check point and they refill and you can move on.
It's an interesting system but you can quickly see the only real difference between this and a standard checkpoint system is that the game is telling you where you can't check point instead of where you can, also as you become good at the combo system you can make almost constant check points, but your good enough at that point you wont need to or even want to as your score is doubled when you are holding a checkpoint but don't use it. The level recap screen also gives a bonus for not using any checkpoints at all!
Some fun extras are included for every 3 out of the 100 plus achievements you unlock you can unlock a piece of artwork, some concept, some photoshop manipulation, some original art post process, all very very well done and a treat for the eyes. If you pick up the collectors edition you also get the sound track to the game on your hard drive, which is also quite good. 10 hours already I'm totally not sick of it, it's even caught in my head a bit. Especially how it slows down a little as you die again and again.
The game may be a bit short on levels but at 9.99 and with so many actual achievement achievements and competitive leader-boards it generates a lot more value. Also included are two levels that have been re-skinned by other developers/game makers with more promised on the way as coming soon.
Again, They Bleed Pixels may not be for you... Do you like cursing? Do you break things or hurt family members feelings when you get angry in a game? Even if those things are true, the elation at completing a level and meeting a goal you set for yourself (like not dying or... only dying 10 times, or beating a speed run time) is what games like this are for, and this one does it quite well.
There will be pixels!
Good controls, nice mix of acrobatic platforming and combat gameplay, leaderboards per level, creative checkpoint mechanics, bonus levels, collectibles... my only regret is not playing it sooner.

King's Bounty: Dark Side is the latest installment of the King's Bounty serie. For the first time, you will play as the bad guy. The balance of Light and Dark was disturbed. The forces of Light are close to wipe all the creatures of Dark. Players will choose one of the dark heroes- Orc warrior, Demoness paladin, or Vampire mage. The beginning of the game is specific for each of the character, but the rest of the game is the same. Players will be even able to travel to the places where other heroes start. In general, I find the story to be good.
The combat system is the same as in the previous games. In addition to sending forces to eliminate the enemy, players can cast spells or use abilities of their companion. The only change is that there is only one boss battle in the whole game, which some people may don't like.
The other thing I don't like very much is the design of quests. In many cases, players will just run back and forth from point A. For example a witch give the player a quest to bring her five ent sprouts. Now, ents are warriors of the Elven army, so player may expect to find them in one of the two Elven isles. But to which one to go? In the end, the Ent sprouts are to be found in a completely different island, where players can buy them from the local witch, if they didn't kill her previously. Some quests may not be finished at all. For example, there is another witch that wanted from me to bring her three magic scrolls. Unfortunatelly, I was not able to find one of them in the whole world, so I couldn't finish the quest. I've seen many people complained in the forums about this kind of quests. I've aldo read in the forums that some people had some of their quests bugged. Luckily, I didn't encounter this. However, I had problems with quest marks. Sometimes, after I progressed in a quest, the question mark appeared on the next location of where I should go, but the old one didn't disappear. This caused that sometimes I had two or even more question marks regarding one quest. Sometimes, the question mark was completely missing. The quest log isn't very helpful , because it only contains the introductory description and tasks what to do in order to complete the quest. Sadly, the tasks are often written in an rather unhelpful way(e.g. “Buy a puppy”, but where to buy it). Sometimes, you are given an advice how to solve the problem and where to go, sometimes you are not. One of the quest stopped upgrading after a while. So yes, there are flaws in the design. Not frustrating, but  they spoil the fun. The game even crashed a few times. Luckily, the loading times are short, so it doesn't take much time to return to the world of Teana.
One of the pros of King's Bounty is the humour. You can find references to other work of pop-culture, like Harry Potter or Lord of the Rings. Some dialogs are quite amusing. However, in some  dialogs players will be given more than one options how to answer, but it seems that whichever players choose, the result is the same. That is not very good, in my opinion.
The story is quite good and the locations are nice. Graphics is the same, which I don't find a big problem. They added a few new songs, but in my opinion, they aren't very good. There is also the problem that remained from Warriors of the North- the game seems to select a song that is not very suitable for particular situation. Many times I've heard combat songs in the world map and vice versa. In my opinion, this spoils the atmosphere a bit.
It's hard to decide whether to recommend this game. It's still fun to play, but it has its flaws. If you have played the previous games and just want another journey from King's Bounty universe and you don't mind some glitches, then you might find what are you looking for. For others: if you didn't like the previous installments, you probably won't like this one either. If you are interested in King's Bounty series but haven't played any of the games, I'd recommend you to pick The Legend or Armored Princess, which are the better ones, in my opinion. If I'd have to choose between Warriors of the North and Dark Side, I'd choose WotN, since quests in that game can be completed and it's in better technical shape than Dark Side.

Kings Bounty; Dark Side is a turn based strategy game set in a hexagonal
honeycomb battlefield.  This is the fifth game in the Kings Bounty series, and
I have found that for the most part, the game has remained unchanged from the
first game.
As a turn based strategy game, you lead troops into battle as an Orc,
a Demoness, or a Vampire on your choice of difficulty.  Strategy and tactics
are at this games core, with your decisions on what kind of troops you use, what
class you choose, and what spells you use influencing how well you do in the game.
The Orc (warrior) gives a bonus to Attack, the Vampire (mage) leans more heavily
on spells and spell power, and the Demoness (Leader) is the middle ground,
relying on both magic and numbers of troops.  Each unit or spell can synergize
with other units and spells, so you must be aware of what you are doing to excel.
There is a place for everything
This game series best and strongest feature is its combat.  It is highly
enjoyable and satisfying.  The issue I had with the game was that it is too easy.
While this game in the series starts out with a steeper learning curve in the
beginning, but it has the same problem as the other games;  mid to late game
battles are too easy with the gear provided and abilities earned.  It becomes
too simplistic and redundant.  The difficulty level does not increase as your
characters power increases.
As for the story;  it gets by, but is definitely not a strength to the
game.  In this particular game, you play as a dark side character, but spend the
majority of your time doing fetch and carry missions or reuniting lost loves;
nothing that falls in line with the darkness of your character.  This story
is the weakest one of all the series.
Graphically the game has not changed at all from previous games.  Also,
the quest log hasn't changed from previous games-listing current and completed
missions on the same log, making it next to impossible to find a particular one.
You are bombarded with a multitude of quests that do not fall in line with the
character you represent.  As to level design, you unlock different islands as you
progress, but in contrast to previous games, they made the islands larger and more
complicated, with convoluted roadways.  I don't play this game to enjoy the
scenery between levels.  By complicating the level design, it becomes more
annoying and doesn't respect the players time.  It slows the gameplay down in
a negative way.
While the combat is good, it is unchanged from previous games in the
series.  Graphically it is the same, the aesthetic is the same, the level design
has only been made worse.  The story is a waste of time.  I cannot recommend
this game, and would point you to the Kings Bounty; Armored Princess game if
you are curious to try out this gamestyle.

This game is OK.  Unfortunately, the King's Bounty series has stagnated.  They started out with a solid game, but successive iterations haven't really improved upon the original.  I only own this game because it was included with a bundle and I'm unlikely to purchase any further King's Bounty games or replay the ones I own.
The combat in this game remains among the best of any strategy game I've ever played but the questing is miserable.  Although the developers have thankfully taken the time to include the origin of each quest in the quest log, most quests in the log don't explicitly state where to go for each step (not where on the current map, or even which map).  And in terms of content, almost all of the quests are simple fetch quests that require slowly shuffling back and forth between a few locations many times or collect quests that often devolve into a pixel hunt.  Even with a flying mount and the new teleport mechanic, constantly running trivial errands is very boring indeed.
I feel like having some good voice acting might help ratchet up the fun-factor with some injections of character, but the quests in Dark Side are again text-driven.  The fun-factor is also hindered by some serious flaws with the underlying quest engine:  collect quests generally don't mark items as critical, leaving it possible to consume or destroy quest-sensitive items, quests frequently have hidden interdependencies making whatever quest you're currently on fail to update without feedback, etc.  It is shockingly easy to find oneself with quests that are impossible to finish without restarting the game anew, but who wants to replay 80 hours just to deliver some thorn spores?  Maybe a
script console and/or comprehensive wiki pages from the developer would help here.
I think that my favorite KB is Crossworlds.  On reflection, I think that the simple arena-style quest progression is what makes it so much better.  Combat and army-building are the focus points and uninspired questing is greatly abbreviated.  In contrast, I feel compelled to arm myself with pen and paper prior to sitting down with Dark Side and I hate having to do so.  1C must evolve or perish.
Love this game so far.  It's much better than Warrior of the North.

Usually I don't feel comfortable reviewing a game until I've either completed the main story, or put invested a respectable amount of time (30+ hours)... but I'm breaking my rule here, because there just isn't really much to say about Far Cry 4.
If you've played Far Cry 3, you've played Far Cry 4. The game feels almost exactly the same, and in fact I've had a real problem finding real differences beyond some slightly adjusted mechanics like throwing bait to attract animals, and a new map.
The new map is kind of a love/hate thing, because it can be both frustrating to move around, yet interesting to engage with. The map is very vertical, as opposed to the much flatter Far Cry 3 map, and this added verticality introduces some interesting gameplay choices. However, trying to get from point A to point B can be obnoxious, especially when the mountain in front of you apparently has no places to climb on.
You can throw bait to attract animals to attack outposts, but sometimes it doesn't work. The bait is a great way to bunch enemies together before throwing a grenade and making them all explode.
Uh, there's a wingsuit and it's fun to use... and the verticality of the map means that this time around, the hang-glider is kind of a legitimate way to get around.
The story is weak, with a somewhat interesting and snarky antagonist whom you keep in contact with. Your character just wants to go on vacation but then decides to become a murderer, and even then, Ajay doesn't seem to care like Jason pretended to in Far Cry 3. One minute Ajay is breathing heavily and scared of bullets, and then almost immediately you're skinning a leapord and killing tons of people in a conflict Ajay doesn't understand.
I don't know. I guess I'm enjoying my time here, but the open-world collect-a-thon games are kind of tired at this point, and Far Cry 4 doesn't do anything interesting or new, it's kind of just the same thing I've already played but with nicer graphics. On that note, the really nifty ultra settings are all very crash-prone, so beyond taking some nice screenshots, there is no reason to turn on all of the special settings unless you really want to crash to your desktop over and over again.
If you've never played a Far Cry game, you'll definitely enjoy the hell out of this game. Far Cry 4 has a lot to keep you busy, and the emergent gameplay can be very fun. Most of my best Far Cry moments were totally disconnected from missions, like rounding a corner to a Rhino stampeding through a group of dudes. Some really amusing stuff can happen.
If you've played Far Cry 3 or another game, though, it's seriously difficult to endorse this game, because you've basically already played it. It will feel too familiar, in a not-so-good way, and if you've been playing video games for the past few years you might be like me and a tad tired of the collect-a-thon open world games by this point. I just can't get behind tearing down nearly 200 propaganda posters or finding masks, I've climbed enough towers in games to reveal a map, I don't care about skinning animals to increase my inventory size... it's all just very meh.

I rarely write reviews on Steam, mostly because others can convey my opinion better than I ever could. That being said, after 100 hours + on THIEF and the mixed rating it currently sits at, I feel guilted into sharing some positive feedback for it.
I first played the game two years ago, waiting for sales as ratings were a bit scary. In the end, I'm glad I did, because after a second playthrough in order to successfully perfect THIEF, my opinion hasn't changed: this game in good.
For one, I'm rarely compelled to play any game with harsher difficulties, yet I did the whole Master/Custom for this one. Hell, I even perfected and picked clean every corner of the map.
Second, I frankly couldn't really understand the bad rap this reboot seems to have, and after perusing various reviews my conclusion would be that a lot of fans from the previous games were disappointed whereas another majority of critics stem from comparisons with Dishonored.
For the latter, I do see the parallels; the gloomy Victorian-ish setting, the wrecks of Progress and Industrialization, a gruffy man out to save a girl he cares for... I could go on like this for a while. It is my understanding that Dishonored *has* drawn heavily on the original Thief games, but to me Corvo is all about demonics powers whereas Garrett relies on his gear and his abitility to stay in the shadows. Yes, the general mechanics are more or less the same, but a Ghost/Pacifist playthrough in Dishonored is not only really easy, the AI can be really stupid and easy to fool as well. In THIEF, Ghost is also a choice among other playstyles, but it feels *right*.
Your gear is about sneaking around, hell the environment is about sneaking around. It's not just about rewarding you with low chaos for not killing everyone like in Dishonored, but to complete the game as a Master Thief is a satisfaction few games ever gave me. The map is opened, and while the South Quarter "Up 'n' Down" madness still frustrates the hell out of me, it really immerses you as the sneak thief in the night.
That being said, I haven't played the original Thief games, but I understand the deception of many fans hoping to see the old factions and setting once again. What I don't understand is flamming THIEF for what it is not, disregarding the reboot in itself and the enjoyable experience it brings. I happened to not encounter any game-breaking bugs or glitches, so I don't know if that makes me a lucky player, but as I said I did clock a lot of hours in the game.
I will admit that I'm a complete sucker for the sneak approach in any kind of games with a preference for RPGs, so if that colors my review the same way it did for others, so be it. I stand with the conviction that THIEF is a really good stealth-game, and that if it is your kind of jam, you should ignore the ratings and dive in.
I won't lenghten my review any more with the story, because I feel it is also satisfactory in itself. I did care for Erin, that I don't see as a one-dimensional character but as a chick who has seen some♥♥♥♥♥♥and has trouble garnering the approval of a man she secretly admires a great deal, and lashes out as a result. I appreciated Basso as the fun fence that do care for his favorite black-hands, and finally I empathized with Garrett's cool facade of "caring weighs you down" that he conveys in order to mask his inability to open-up after a lifetime of loneliness.
So, yeah, I liked this game. And I think a great deal of people would too, if given the chance.

Is this game like the "original" trilogy of Thief? No, it isn't. In many ways, Dishonored is more like the Thief we fell in love with. Does it mean that Thief is a bad game? No, it doesn't. Thief is a (delayed) polished game, not a gem, but a very involving first person sneaker, something very rare and very sought-after in today's gaming world.

This is a complex game, and maybe not an easy one. But it is
rewarding.
Stationeers is about building your own base including all systems and surviving the harsh environment of space (as well as surviving your own mistakes).
Whether you've managed to set up a working airlock or succeeded in making your first solar panels auto-track the sun position (for more efficient power generation!), it provides you with a unique sense of accomplishment and satisfaction only rarely found in gaming.
To give you an idea of what the above entails, you will not only need to place the basic components (such as airlock doors, vents, consoles) but also set up your wiring and design a working pipe system to support your airlock and pressurisation system. And those are just the basics.
Long-term goals include things like air filtration systems for your base, where you will need to figure out how to set up a network of vents, filters, wires and pipes (thankfully you can colour and label them though!) to keep your air breathable.
It is currently much more base building and survival than exploration, but this may change during the course of early access.
The building and systems are more complex than Space Engineers. A good comparison is thrusters. In Space Engineers, you can put a thruster on blocks, add power and you're pretty much good to go. In this game, you're installing the fuel pipelines and mixtures going to the thrusters.
Currently, there is less exploration and less external threats (like space bugs) than Space Engineers.
If Minecraft mod packs like Beastcraft or tekkit and the challenge of building complex processes appeal to you, you will probably like Stationeers. Keep in mind that those will currently have way more content available compared to Stationeers, but one is new, the other isn't. Stationeers
being designed with modding in mind though.
The game is heavily inspired by Space Station 13 mechanics, and many of the early testers were from the SS13 community. There is no rounds or similar though, and currently the game is entirely co-operative. Does not have clowns (yet).
It may have a similar aesthetic, but they are quite different in gameplay. Astroneer is fairly simple in its mechanics when compared to Stationeers, especially when it comes to base-building. Stationeers may be deceptively cute in this regard. From what I have gathered, the art style was chosen for quick iteration and ability to add content. Astroneer currently does exploration much better than Stationeers.
As of this review, the game hasn't even been out in early access for more than a week. The updates so far have been quick and responsive. The devs have clearly taken a good look at examples of early access well done (such as RimWorld and Oxygen Not Included). They are also very active on the official Discord server. If the direction and game loop change during the course of early access, I will update this review accordingly.
Do not be deterred by the inventory system. It is
to the bog-standard survival game inventory you see in countless other games these days. It may not be as accessible for newcomers and seem clunky at first, but you'll be breezing through it in no time. It is quite fast once you get the hang of it.
The game also does not do a lot of teaching in its current state, although there is a very basic tutorial. I personally enjoy finding out about mechanics and properties of items myself, but some people may be put off by the lack of hand-holding.
Performance has been fantastic so far, both in single player and multiplayer settings. Dedicated servers do have issues right now so if you're planning on playing with friends, hosting it yourself seems to be the better option right now.
Ready to jump in? If you do end up getting the game, I highly recommend joining the official Discord server. Have fun!

Stationeers is still a little rough around the edges, but that is expected for early access.
This game has huge potential and with updates coming out on the daily, it can only get better.

Stationeers is a great early access game focused on the management of systems and trying to survive in space. Inspired by the station simulator SS13, Stationeers offers the player the chance to create their very own space colony/spaceship/station and build everything, from the frames, to each individual pipe and wire. Even if you havent played SS13 (me), then you will have a great time learning each system and figuring out how to do things all while managing your stats and trying not to die.
Of course, since it's in Early Access, there is alot of bugs and alot of things that need ironing out and adjusting. However, it shows GREAT potential to be an amazingly immersive and complex game.
There has been alot of hate since the Lead Dev (Dean Hall - creater of DayZ) gained a negative reputation from the Bohemia DayZ game being unfinished and poorly created (of which he had no decision and was forced by contract). Stationeers definately does not show ANY signs of this. You can tell the developers care immensely for this game, based on their involvement in the Discord server and the constant stream of  patches and updates being applied to the game. Dean Hall also livestreams him playing and developing the game often on Twitch.
Again, since it is EA, there is issues - the big one that everyone seems to go on about is the UI. Honestly, when I first jumped into the game the UI controls were slightly confusing, but after about 30 mins I was blazing through and fully grasped how to control the UI. The UI and inventory system without doubt could do with some tinkering, but is still alot better then people make it out to be and is greater and more immersive then a drag'n'drop style menu. If you are complaining about the UI controls then you are certainly going to struggle with some of the systems in the game.
In conclusion, it's a hardcore space survival experience that you will come out of feeling 10x smarter and like you could actually survive in space (if only you had the money).
Obviously, if you dont want bugs and the potential for worlds to break, features to be removed, ect... then hang off until more patches are released.

First off it is not a bad game it just needs to change somethings. It started off fun for the first few hours as I was learning how to play and changing the landscape to maximize the best outcome for my resources. They did a really good job on that and there are some pretty cool late/end game builds for maximizing resource outcome (if only you’ll make it that far). The line battling has nothing that isn’t already in other games like this so if that’s all you’re here for then move along. Now I’ll talk about some of the things that need to change are the use of gold (real money) to progress your army. When you build your second barracks, archery range, stable, knight manor, etc you will be able to choose a new unit and this is where the game becomes frustrating. The game offers you the ability to buy the unit with gold which isn’t a problem all f2p games do stuff like this the problem is the need for those troops in order to progress in the campaign and regular missions. You are also able to acquire them from crafting them at level 21 but the resources to craft them takes days to get and all you will get is one unit for what is a weeks plus of work IF you are constantly checking up and gathering you resources. Also the PvP battles are unbalanced because of the gold (p2p) system. At the start of each battle you are offered the choice to spend a little gold to buff yourself in one way or another. You are also able to craft one of those one time buffs but if you do you are going in a negative direction of getting new troops that you will need. But aside from that I found I was being matched with players who clearly had paid for their troops because of the level they were at. I understand there will be people who do that but the problem is the fights had not been balanced and I was somehow expected to defeat an opponent who had better versions of my entire army. At the end of the day it has fun city builder/land transformation tools but the battles and PvP need to be reworked.

They Bleed Pixels is a hard game to fall in love with, but once it whispers its nightmares into your ears long enough to poison your mind to its world-view, you may find it difficult to put down. There are many comparisions to be made here to Super Meat Boy, but in the end they are superficial. While we are, perhaps, talking about similar genres, TBP is a combat platformer, and the fighting is what makes all the difference here.
Warning: you might hate it. One-button combat isn't for everyone, and it can be frustrating to learn. But it's not the fighting itself that is the brilliant part of this game. It is how the combat is integrated into the level design / savepoint / score system. Fighting is not necessarily hard - but fighting in a way that maximizes your results is. Pulling off a long combo in this game has a satisfaction to it that you won't find in many other experiences.
In the end, it's a spike-pit-jumper and a demon-juggler, and that's an alley that I am delighted to spend my time exploring. Easy to recommend, but only for the patient, the masochistic, and the exerimental.

They Bleed Pixels - Satisfaction that comes at a price
If you check on Steam it actually comes at pretty low price. But obviously I was not talking about money. I was talking about time (which equals money) but let talk more about why I came to such a conclusion.
So if you have read my previous review you probably guessed that I like this game because it is a 2D platformer.  And yes I like platformers and I was collecting them in the past when I had time to play any games. Naturally I came across this game and loved it at first sight. And why not? I watched the trailer and I saw fast paced action, lots of different moves and attacks. I loved this simplistic but beautiful art style. It also said it was inspired H.P Lovecraft which told me absolutely nothing at first but after searching online I know all I needed. Another thing that got me really excited was the number of achievements to unlock. And my friends know that I'm a achievement-junkie. But I should have read what those achievements are about. From the tags I new it wasn’t going to be easy and I was quite ready for that. So I grabbed my controller, fired up the game and focused on my TV screen...
And it didn't start by killing me in first 30 seconds of gameplay. Well, it started with some spooky pictures that told me the story. And the way it introduce the story was actually pretty nice. So after brief loading I was in the game ready to demolish my foes in many different ways. But first I had to figure out how. And it was really easy to pick up the controls. It actually guides you through different moves and actions as you encounter different enemies and game objects. The learning curve was not steep at all and I felt like I was progressing pretty well. I was not dying as often as I expected from a difficult game and that's partially because I was ready for it and tried my hardest to master timing and precision as fast as I could. And the latter is very important. And you will need a controller if you want that. And game developers recommend that too when you start the game. I ran though first few levels feeling pretty confident but I was about to see what this was really like.
As I was going further and further the game was getting harder and harder. Platforming required more and more precision and did the wall sliding. So at this point I really started having a hard time because my fingers being somewhat precise clearly weren't precise enough for the game. So I started my intense training. I tried the level again and again and I was getting better and better. And you know those games that don't have any saving points in the level. Well this is not one of them, fortunately. I'm infinitely grateful for the checkpoint system. And you can get as many checkpoints as you want as long as you collect enough points by killing the enemies in style. This is an amazing game mechanic and it allows you to place the checkpoint anywhere you want but you need to be careful to not to get killed while you're trying to find a perfect spot to save. There are some infuriating enemies that can make you want to cut the gamepad cord with you teeth but don't you worry because I found a key to dealing with any enemy. And that is staying calm. It may sound like a silly thing but it really helped me. After few stupid deaths I tried again but this time I was planning my actions just little bit and I was trying to relax a little because I felt I was clenching the controller way to hard. Apart from the enemies each level is sometimes your biggest enemy and can be really challenging just to get through. And there even are levels with almost no enemies which should make it easier but I makes it harder instead because it's harder to gain points and place a checkpoint. Unfortunately there is only one boss - the final boss. And even though I found it underwhelming to defeat I felt incredibly satisfied.
There are more things to do in this game. Collecting book pages for example that unlock art and achievements. There are also bonus levels which I found quite fun. And I plaid all the levels several times to find those pages some of which are well hidden.
So what was the price of all that satisfaction for me. Well it was 31 hours. I will need at least 10 more hours to get some more achievements I feel I can unlock.  That's for a game that doesn't have too many levels. And was it worth it? You're god damn right it was. I feel like this game was priced too low and I would paid even if it was twice as much money.
I do recommend this game. But ther are few things you should be aware of before buying.
It's insanely difficult for average player. Me, for instance. If you are not careful you will die a lot. Soundtrack is great and it is just right for this game but I can hardly hear it because I die to often. By now I have 2 levels to complete. It took overal 15 hours and not all of those hours were pleasant. Also I highly recommend a gamepad for this game.

This game is incredible, easily one of my favorites. As the description says, it's a war game where you're a refugee instead of a soldier, living in a ruined house and trying to gather enough resources to survive. It has good gathering, crafting, and combat systems - both in general, but especially impressive for an indie game. Excellent story that I can't help getting sucked into, and decent randomization so that it doesn't get too repetitive when playing through all of the various campaigns, which do have some overlap.
The only "problem" is that the gameplay is engaging & addictive (only saving at the end of the day creates a Civ-like "one... more... turn......" mentality), but the story can be pretty depressing, so I've often found myself getting sucked in and then feeling pretty down afterwards. So just be sure to play in moderation, and maybe when you're not already depressed, since guiding a makeshift family through a warzone isn't exactly uplifting.

This new installation of Thief is sadly know to be a poor sequel to the great reputations of its predecessors. I, however, disagree. But the gameplay and storyline is very compelling. It keeps you on the edge of your seat with goose bumps quite often. It pains me to see this game receive so many negative reviews when it really was a great addition to the already great series.
With all that being said, I would grant this game an overall 7 out of 10 due to the great storyline and development of the already interesting protagonist, Garrett, along with the very memorable moments I shared on several missions and cinematics that made me shiver or grit my teeth in anticipation. Highly recommend to anyone who appreciates quality stealth gameplay.

If you've gotten tired of the series and are looking for something to shake it up, this isn't that game. It does some interesting things, but from battle to battle this isn't really distinguishable from any other one.
If you're still having fun with the series and want to play more of what you've already played, this game is definitely better than Warriors of the North. I am unsure what to say about this game. Was it bad? No. Did I like it? No. I would recommend buying this if there is a sale, I just found it lacking in things that I like in these types of games. While an overall decent experience I personally found a few aspects annoying, however nothing game breaking.
Biggest thing that annoyed me, the story. It's trying very hard to be scary and a psychological mind game but in the end I just got bored of Oscar's yapping and was barely invested in saving Anna. The second big thing that I didn't like was the lack of hidden item scenes. The game seems to be mostly made up of mini game puzzles. What hidden item scenes were present in the game were very fun and I enjoyed the challenge.

The game also has no achievements or trading cards so if you're a collector it won't help you there. However, it is still worth a play through if you look past the few issues I mentioned, unless you like them then I say game on!

This game is the very definition of why I think Steam needs the ‘neutral’ button  between the recommend and not recommend option. In my opinion, it is so perfectly mediocre that I don’t really feel that great with recommending it while there are so many other more appealing representatives of the hidden object genre. On the other hand, this game does nearly nothing bad enough to deserve not being recommended.
The premise of the game can be liked. While the norm for the hidden object games is to take place in a fantasy or a supernatural reality, Brink of Consciousness has an ambition to be a psychological thriller with a visible inspiration in Saw or The Silence of the Lambs. However, what initially seems to be its advantage,  quickly proves to be a serious problem for me. While in fantasy games it can be at least partially explained (or at least the setting helps in suspending the disbelief), the hidden object mechanics do not mix particularly well with the thriller setting: a psychopathic murderer holds the protagonist’s sweetheart captive and what does our hero decide to do? Search for a celery, a rather tremendous number of clothespins and a set of false teeth (that for some strange reason have to be cleaned first). Furthermore, it really doesn’t help that the antagonist is perhaps one of the most uninspired and tedious villains in computer games I have played (even for the hidden object game standards of character complexity).
The graphics are where this game shines. While there surely are some hidden object games looking better, Dorian Gray Syndrome certainly has moments when it pleasant to look at. Still, I would like to make an argument here that the game’s setting limits the palette do the darker colors, mainly greys and browns, while other hidden object games are free to exercise a whole range of wild, vivid, acid trip colors, which is one of my favorite component of hidden object genre. Also, music is rather forgettable for the most of time.
Finally, the mechanics. The puzzles are mostly good, with maybe a few exceptions. The map shows the area of interest, but there is no quick travel available, and the hint system seems weaker than in other games of this genre: instead of showing the direction where to go, it just tells that there is nothing to do in this particular location.
In the end, I can recommend this game to the people who are tired of the fantasy settings of most of the hidden object games. Keep in mind though that, at least to me, this game quickly got boring and completing the bonus chapter was a chore – which is not a particularly great result when it takes around 4 hours to complete the game.
