Ta gra jest jednym z lepszych powodów dla których uważam że Steam, poza opcją rekomendacji bądź odradzenia konkretnej gry,  potrzebuje guzika „neutralny”. Syndrom Doriana Gray’a jest idealnie przeciętny i miałbym pewne problemy z polecaniem go innym z czystym sercem, szczególnie wiedząc że na Steamie dostępnych jest wiele ciekawszych gier z tego gatunku. Z drugiej strony Brink of Consciousness nie robi nic na tyle źle, żeby zasłużyć sobie na negatywną ocenę pod moją recenzją.
To co odróżnia „Doriana” od innych gier tego gatunku to świat w którym osadzone są wydarzenia gry. Podczas gdy tłem dla większości Hidden Object’ów zazwyczaj są światy fantasy,  twórcy Brink of Consciousness wyraźnie wzorują się thrillerami takimi jak Piła czy Milczenie Owiec. W mojej opinii wychodzi to jednak odrobinę (eufemizm) nieudolnie. Jednym z powodów takiego stanu rzeczy jest fakt że psychologiczny thriller nie miesza się najlepiej z grą typu Hidden Object.  W przypadku fantastyki można jeszcze tłumaczyć konieczność odnalezienia kilkunastu różnych przedmiotów odmiennością świata przedstawionego, jednak kiedy psychopatyczny morderca więzi ukochaną głównego bohatera a ten, zamiast popędzić jej na ratunek szuka w jednej z szaf selera, kilku spinaczy do bielizny i czaszki ( a dodać należy, że z bliżej niewytłumaczalnych przyczyn nie zadowoli się tą czaszką jeżeli wcześniej nie wyszczotkuje jej zębów), można odnieść wrażenie że sterowany przez gracza bohater ma jeszcze bardziej pomieszane pod sufitem niż psychopata z którym przychodzi mu się zmierzyć. Nie pomaga też, że wspomniany już antagonista jest irytujący i nudny jak flaki z olejem – nawet jak na standardy postaci w grach hidden object.
Grafika jest tu mocną stroną. Oczywiście jest sporo gier z tego gatunku które wyglądają lepiej, jednak „Dorian” zdecydowanie ma swoje momenty. Szkoda tylko że konwencja gry ogranicza kolory do ciemniejszych odcieni, brązów i szarości – jedną z tych rzeczy które absolutnie uwielbiam w hidden objectach są dzikie, szalone, kwasowo – odjechane palety barw. O muzyce nie można raczej powiedzieć nic szczególnego, przez większość czasu nie zwraca na siebie uwagi, a jeżeli już, to szybko się ją zapomina.
Można się też odrobinę przyczepić do mechaniki gry. Większość puzzli jest ok,  mapa pokazuje co jeszcze zostało do zrobienia ale nie pozwala na szybkie poruszanie się między lokacjami, a system podpowiedzi jest zdecydowanie gorszy niż w innych grach: zamiast wskazać kierunek w którym powinniśmy się udać, gra mówi zwyczajnie „w tym pokoju nie ma już nic do zrobienia”. Dzięki, nie wiedziałem.
Podsumowując: polecam tylko tym którzy przekatowali już każdą możliwą pozycję studia Artifex Mundi. A nawet wtedy, może lepiej poszukać czegoś innego? Końcówka gry była dla mnie straszliwie nudna, co nie świadczy o „Syndromie Doriana Graya” najlepiej, biorąc pod uwagę, że grę można skończyć w ok. 4 godziny.

Hidden Object games have kind of become my "thing" in gaming lately due to their casual nature. They are easily picked up during work breaks and I can usually complete one in a single sitting without frustration.
This game kind of stretched that for me [definitely not a bad thing]. It was quite a bit longer than many HO/P&C games are these days so I ended up getting through it in two sittings rather than one [it took me about 5 hours]. The story was engaging and inventive, although if you're looking for a realistic plot line, search elsewhere [maybe a different genre].
Gorgeous artwork and a beautiful soundtrack made this game a joy to play. The puzzles were challenging, but not overly so, including the hidden object scenes. I also really enjoyed the extra content [bonus chapter, wallpapers, concept art, soundtrack, etc.] that came with the collector's edition. The concept art especially was really interesting and I'm glad it was included.
All in all, one of the best HO games I've played since the Mystery Case Files series.

Though not quite as creepy as I hoped it would be, this hidden object game features gorgeous art, good music, moderately challenging mechanical puzzles and some above-average voice acting.  It served as a soothing complement to my afternoon tea for a whole week.  Very nice to take a break from the brain-busters and controller-smashers I usually play!
This was my first hidden object game.  If there are others at least as pretty and soothing as this one, I can see the much-maligned HOG becoming a staple of my increasingly omnivorous gaming diet.

I've played a lot of hidden object games, and Dorian Gray Syndrome is one of the better examples of the genre.  The story starts us with a young journalist, Sam Wilde, hot off an article detailing the disappearances of numerous "beautiful" people in the area. Heading out to meet his lady love for a date, he arrives at the rendezvous only to discover a note beckoning him to the home of the man behind the kidnappings. If if he wishes to see his beloved Anna again he is to come alone. Sam must now travel to Goldvale Manor to confront the demented and insane Oscar and rescue his love.  Ok, so the story is pretty cliché and hokey, but I have played many a game with worse premises than this.  Where Dorian Gray excels is in the gorgeously detailed artwork and locations, great atmosphere and enjoyable "adventure-lite" game play.
I must reiterate how beautiful and imaginative the artwork is in this game.  Each hand-drawn area features intricate detail that in a way feels almost life-like.  Even the character models are nicely rendered and don't come off as stiff and awkward as they do in other games.  A toggleable film grain filter finishes everything off with a gritty look.  Discovering the many locations and enjoying the art is reason enough to play the game.
Adventure-lite is the best way to explain the game play.  Most of the objectives and puzzles aren't too difficult to figure out, but a few may have you backtracking and running in circles for a bit.  A large number of items will find their way into your inventory, many of which may not have an obvious use or be used for quite awhile; this is something I quite enjoy in standard adventure games and don't see too often in these.
Of course, there are a handful of hidden object scenes sprinkled throughout the mansion, all nicely drawn without much clutter. The items make sense for the location and time period, something so many games fail to do. There aren't too many, but the ones present are neither frustrating nor too easy, just a pleasant diversion (if you don't mind them) as you make your way through the game.
Unlike similar HOG's, I spent a good 8 hours playing through the entire story, including bonus chapter.  Part of that may have been me taking time to enjoy the art and atmosphere.  Playing on Expert with no hints and minimal strategy guide usage helped extend my play time as well.  But the scope of the game itself feels much bigger than most and I feel like I really got my money's worth, especially since I'll be playing this one time and again.
A few things that bothered me included puzzles that are far too easy, many of which require very little thought and are often repetitive tasks once you figure out the method.  The voice acting can be a tad melodramatic, but is admittedly better than other casual games.  And Oscar tends to show up/be heard a bit too much which often pulled me out of my "adventure gamer" mode, but this is a personal gripe and others may have no problem with it.  Other than those few complaints, the game shines.
Brink of Consciousness: Dorian Gray Syndrome may not be the perfect HOG, but what it does right it does really right.  If you are a HOG aficionado, make sure to pick this one up.  As a rule, I generally don't recommend these games at anything above the $7-$8 price range, but even if you shell out the full $10, I feel you'll get your money's worth considering game length, bonus chapter and extras (soundtrack, concept art, etc.).

I wanna write this review because the game seems to have been deeply misunderstood, mainly due to the fact that mobile gamers are a different breed than pc/console gamers.
TOWN BUILDING:
For what it is (a mobile strategy game) it does an excellent job. The town management part gives more freedom than any other mobile strategy game i have ever seen. Instead of building the same pre defined slot-based setup town, you have a hex map on which you can do whatver you want and get any sort of layout you want. As you play you unlock more build space and get to build more towns and you can do stuff like dedicate a certain town to a certain type of production or unit etc.
COMBAT:
Combat is a Total war-ized version of a deck building game, in which armies advance toward each other, time during which you get to fire away some skills and some slight maneouvering. The more you advance in the game, the more control you get over the army. Again, for a mobile game, the quality is amazing. Animations are top notch (i would even go as far as to say that at times they are more fluid than actual TW games) and I find the mechanics to be exactly what the mobile platform supports.
It's a mobile game. Commanding actual TW armies in the way TW games work would be a mess. Scrolling, flanking, skills, all that would be a mess in the classic sense, I feel what they got here is the best streamlined version they could think of and for me it feels great.
OVERALL FEEL / UI
The game feels good, it feels like a quality product. You're not bombarded by ads, you're not bombarded by notifications and it doesn't feel like a chore. Compare this to Clash of clans which ends up feeling like a chore and a stress factor (is my village ok? have I been sieged? I need to collect my resources!). This is not like that. Animations are great, artwork is great, textures are great, UI looks great. No glossy bs, no flashing buttons, no "SPECIAL OFFER!!!! CLICK HERE!!!!" anywhere". The real currency tab is called "Trade". That's it
MICROTRANSACTIONS:
Yes, they exist, they're in the game, but since you did not pay for the game, it's normal. Whoever is distraught by microtransactions clearly hasn't played a mobile game before. They're common place.
IT'S A MOBILE GAME!
Yes, for the last time, it's not a PC game. It's a PC edition of a mobile game. These games are persistent. When you close them, they still run on a server, so the PC version provides another client from which you can access the game. It's not supposed to be the next Total War, it's not supposed to be Medieval TW portable. It's a spin-off. Enjoy it for what it is, look around the app stores for strategy games and you'll clearly realize it's one of the best mobile gaming has to offer as far as strategy games go.
If you're looking for a TW spin-off or a solid mobile strategy game, go for it, it's one of the best. If you're looking for a portable classic TW game look away, it's not this, not yet.

I want to like this game, I really do. It's a beautifully styled game, gorgeous sound track, real care of attention to the design of the characters. But it's a halfway house of a few genres and ends up being lesser because of it.
Want a chaotic hero shooter with cheap moves? Go play Overwatch (or better still Team Fortress 2 :D). Want a 3rd person MOBA? Go play Smite. This game is both of these things but not achieving enough of either's respective genres.
You will enter games after you've played against bots and realise that real PvP is nothing like what you've practiced against in the game or two you had to play to open up the PvP mode. Real PvP is about one team or the other having someone who thinks this is overwatch and that deaths don't matter, and from that point you'll have about 15 minutes of inevitable slippery slope sliding to a loss if you're on that persons team. 15 minutes if you're lucky, that is
Chat is broken, and unavailable before the game actually starts so strategising with strangers is impossible, and if you try you'll basically give up the only chance in the entire game to capture one of the middle control points on the map that essentially guarantee your team the slow win.
The game is presented as if you can make comebacks at any time, and if this were just a hero shooter the "clash" mechanic probably would do this. But it's not, it's a MOBA of sorts, and if you're on the losing team you're going to be down a couple of skills on your enemy by the end, and down on a couple of control points that basically give you "power" in order to give you the winning opportunity.
This game has all the right ideas, and it's had a sordid development history by all accounts, but the reality is that it's only fun until you keep getting paired with people that ultimately do the same thing each map making it a repetitive experience where very little is achieved, or until you happen to be in a match where no-one knows what they're doing and the chaos becomes entertaining.
I hope that it can solve some of its issues, though the lack of depth of the game is pretty much baked in at this point.
Edit: To answer Claudio's claims about this game....
I completely disagree that Gigantic is complex and adaptable. If the only thing that matters is team play then it is only a shadow of what other games are. TF2 requires team work, Smite requires team work, Overwatch to its detriment requires team work. Team work is vital for any team based game, but that's all that this game has, and as such you're going to see the same strategies employed over and over again. Why?
Because since it is basically one big team fight over and over again, with the location of that fight rarely changing, it will purely come down to which comp ends up being able to soak the most damage while dealing the most damage in return. It'll end up turning on the skills of a few individuals with disruptor characters instead of being about counter-play.
Take for example SMITE. If the enemy is taking a tower and they look like they've got it, then we could work as a team to counter push one of their towers. We can adapt, we can try a new on the spot strategy to mitigate our losses. This is because characters in Smite are, in general, slow. Reacting to things you're not in the vicinity of is hard.
This isn't the case in Gigantic, and as such if the enemy decides to push a different summoning point it doesn't matter, because your entire team can be there in a few seconds, plenty of time to ensure that the creature isn't destroyed.
Worse still, in SMITE progression matters. If you do good work against a tower then it is permenantly hurt, it makes it a weak point. However throwing yourself at a creature and retreating when you're starting to hurt as a team in Gigantic has almost no reward. If you aren't in a team that can overcome the enemy then you might as well just not try pushing because your efforts will not persist, and everything will be reset while you, the team pushing into enemy territory, are going to be at a disadvantage and at more risk of dying and powering up your enemy.
No, sorry, I respect that people enjoy Gigantic, it's chaotic shooter-esque fun, but it is in no way a deep or complex experience.

Okay I'm a big fan of the Far Cry series, and even cut the devs some slack with FC2. I like open world games. I like sandboxes.
Far Cry 4 is a ball. I've lost time of the amount of times I've hooted with laughter at random things just happening in this game, either alone on the PC or with mates on the consiole version. And the storyline has some intriguiing characters with some excellent voice acting. The dialogue is adult without seeming gratuitous. It feels like a grown up's game though - it's like the HBO of video games.
There's also some choices to be made that affect the story's outcome, which is a nice touch.
If you've played FC3 then it's unlikely that anything will surprise you, but there will be some tweaks and improvements that are pleasing. But if you've played FC3 then you're used to running around causing chaos, which FC4 does well and better.
That doesn't mean it's without fault. The fekkin wingsuit means that if you're trying to run and jump across a large gap, especially downwards, you can find yourself literally soaring and faceplanting in a suitably painful way. It's also just downright embarrassing during a firefight.
What's also crap is trying to loot a bad guy's body and endsing up just throwing your gun onto his still twitching corpse. That get's old. If you're anything like me you also apperciate looting a body or skinning an animal when it's still sliding down a slope to avoid having to sit through the looting or skinning animation AGAIN.
On the whole though, this game is great fun for the £11.99 or something that I paid for it on sale. It's a good 30-40 hours of storyline gameplay (if you do all the side character quests and a few of the missions to complete your craft items) and will have a fair amount of gameplay after that just exploring some of the locations that you missed, hang-gliding, wingsuiting, and dropping grenades on people from your autogyro.
If it's on sale, get it.

If you've scrolled through enough reviews to see this one, then I don't need to tell you that Stationeers is essentially 3D Space Station 13. For those of you unfamiliar with SS13, I'll explain Stationeers a bit differently. It's essentially a combination of the Tekkit modpack for Minecraft with the logic tools from LittleBigPlanet. Tools are given to you that allow you to interact with and manipulate realistically modeled atmospherics and power systems.
Stationeers is probably a pretty niche game, but it isn't inaccessible to common people. The control scheme has a difficulty curve but you'll quickly find that it really works for what the game is.
In the game's current state, difficulty mostly comes from learning the systems and making sure you don't screw up anywhere (which will happen many times). I can't recommend this game to anyone who expects a simple and easy survival game, because Stationeers is so much more than that.
If you are creative enough to realize that you can use logic computers to automate your machinery and connect light systems to indicate possible failures in the wiring, and that all sounds fun to you, then I highly recommend Stationeers.

This game's core prupose is to show you how difficult it is for people living in warzone. In this, the game delivers in spades. I can't give the developers enough praise for discussing this complex issue and putting it into a compelling game form.
From a pure gameplay mechanics point-of-view, the game is either too easy or very hard depending on how you play the first few days.
Start the game off by building a workshop, shovel and crowbar to get all the resources in your house. Only eat food food when you are starving, you can go 2 days without eating after a meal. Don't be stingy with your meds or your bandaids, if your characters are not at full health they're useless. That being said, don't hoard you meds and bandaids; trading them for componants and woods with Franko (the trader who comes to your house) especially early game, will allow you to get your buildings and upgades faster. The most important buildings to get are: (1) workshop level 2 (so you can build saw blades and axes), (2) animal trap (for steady meat generation), (3) vegetable garden (so you have infinte food but it is expensive), (4) board up to reduce the chance that your stuff gets stolen. Last tip is to get a working gun and some bullets; leave it at home when you go out at night. Your characters at home will be able to use it to scare away looters so your stuff will never be stolen.
Once you manage to get your food secure, you've pretty much won the game which is what makes the game too easy. It's also always possible to secure your food without killing or stealing anything so you can completely avoid all the moral choices or dangerous situations if you want. But if you don't build the right things at the start of the game (you decide to rush an alcohol distiller or sofa) then the game will seem impossible. (This might have been the developers intention, smart planing and preparation allow some people to easily survive?)
The one thing that could be improved are the random visits from neighbours asking for help. You help them out and get some form of reward. Most of the time the event involves one character leaving to help, forcing you to play one character down for a day (not really a big deal). Then some time later you get a small reward. The only difficult choice you have to make is when the kids come and ask for medicine or food for their sick mother. Giving food or meds actually hurts and the reward you get sucks, but your team does feels good about helping. What would make these events more exciting for the player is if the rewards for helping were higher but, there is also a chance that your character "goes to help" and instead gets mugged or scammed screwing you over. This would make the decision making process more difficult.
Overall great game! 10/10

This War of Mine gives you the choice to survive your own civilian hell, as the FPS players are constantly ignoring the plight of those not so fortunate to have an endless supply of guns, bullets, food, and autosaves. The choices you make matter in the chances of your physical survival as well as your psychological survival. The balance of these can be troublesome to manage as choices will need to make, desperate for food, medicine, and supplies, how far will you go? With options ranging from near pacifist to being your own local bandit. There are possibilities for different play styles and different playthroughs if you choose. I wrote this after my first time successfully surviving to the end of the war, and found the game to provide a consistent challenge throughout. As I learned more about how to best manage the resources in my current situation, at a good pace the game introduces new complications to keep me having to make the tough decisions on how to survive with an intact body and mind for all my people.
The Music provided a good atmosphere as well as the film grain style black and white visuals. The controls occasionally would result in unexpected pathing or moving a little off from where you clicked. The combat simulation is acceptable but somewhat awkward until you understand the quirks, but the stealth mechanics help make up for this.
Overall, I would rate this game 4 of 5 stars. Worth the time and an enjoyable thoughtful experience, but it didn't quite make me want to force my kids in front of Netflix, and tell my wife I had too office work on date night to get in an extra hour or two of playing as soon as I could.

This game is a fast-paced fps that plays a lot like call of duty. People move quickly, guns have high accuracy and low recoil, maps are (usually) small. If you've ever played 2 or 3 fps games in your life, gameplay itself isn't going to be much of a new thing for you. Sure, there's special powers, but those are far from a core aspect of the game. What really sets it apart is the ability to customize everything.
The selection of weapons is enough to have fun for a long time, but nothing too huge. However, you can really make any weapon your own with countless attachments. Attachments can make weapons behave differently, but ultimately it's always about preference and there is no right way to modify a gun because of the way it's balanced. Modding the barrel can incrase damage at the cost of accuracy and rate of fire, or vice-versa. Similarly, modding the muzzle can make it do more damage but also makes it noisier. Adding more bells and whistles to your guns will make them heavier (decreases your speed) and less portable (increases the time it takes to switch it to your secondary). You get the idea. And you can go crazy with that. You can add a sniper's scope to a pistol or an smg, if you want. It's up to you.
Some of us like to use snipers, for example, but not all of us use them the same way. If you like to constantly move from point to point to give supporting fire to your allies, you'll benefit from a default, balanced sniper build, with maybe a silencer. But if you prefer to camp in one place and engage enemies from great distances (which do exist on some maps), adding a longer barrel, a muzzle for more damage, and a super high maginification scope will give you a heavy duty, long distance death machine. Or maybe you're one of the weirdos who run around using snipers like they're battle rifles. The game's got you guys covered as well, since you can add iron sights to make it lighter, and shorten the barrel to increase its fire rate.
And speaking about customization, you can customize a lot of things about matches. You can make your own room and disable snipers, if those ♥♥♥♥ers got you sick. Or you can make a sniper-only game. And just like that, you can control lots of aspects to make the game live up to your refined taste.
But I know what you're thinking. It's a free game, right? Is it Pay2Win?
Not really. There is an interesting system for purchashing guns, where you can buy them for a certain amount of time once you unlock them. Buying even the starter guns permanently, meaning that they never expire, does indeed cost a ♥♥♥♥ton of money. But you can buy guns for a month, a couple of weeks, or just 3 days, which is much cheaper. Of course, this is annoying because you constantly need to pay to use the same gun. But it is pretty cheap. And you can do just fine with the starter guns, I've gotten loads of kills on high level players with them. Not sure if the higher tier guns are just very slightly better or if they're all balanced, but it's definetely not what I expected. Only time will tell if it will stay this way for much longer or if BlackSpot entertainment will eventually be forced to move to a different strategy to make money, but so far it's fine to me.

So, where to start, firstly this is NOT overwatch so stop comparing it, the only simularities are the hero shooter mechanics, which other games did before overwatch did and the fact that its a shooter, outside of that everything else is their own take
Gigantic likes to call itself a 3rd Person Tactical Shooter, which is fairly accurate i guess, gameplay is fairly simple, 2 teams fight to defeat the enemy teams guardian creature, this is done by inflicting 3 "wounds" to the creature, each wound takes a certain amount of damage, in order to attack the guardian you first have to gather enough power for your guardian to attack and expose the enemy guardians weak point, power is gained from killing enemies, killing enemies summons or by harvesting it from random points on the map, first team to reach full power gets to attack and the enemy team has to defend for a certain amount of time to prevent you damaging the guardian
Despite that the game still plays in a fairly tactical way, you have to try and kill the enemy team and hold points to harvest power without letting them do the same to you, some matches can be over quickly but my personal longest match was 31 minutes which is very long by shooter standards, all in all its a fun enjoyable game if you play with people willing to work as a team, playing solo can be frustrating but thats the same for any team based game
All in all its a pretty fun game, its free so give it a shot :P

This is why Thief is still the best first person stealth game, even after what people think is a debaucle in Thie4:
Thief 4 takes on a new twist in the tried and true series. When I first played it it did indeed seem like a convulted mess of a city, the game play was questionable because you couldn't "climb everything" and the story line was abrupt in the end. Well the end of the storyline I can't defend against, but the rest is HOGWASH!!
Thief 4, the newest installment, also simply known as Thief, is a brilliant game. You have to THINK like a thief in a world that is a bit more powerful than you. That means you have to use your wits, speed, memory, intelligence, tools and shadows to survive properly. You have to be able to read people to know where they are going, and throw something, make a sound somewhere else to make them go where you will not be. You have to know how to move from spot to spot without being seen, and if you are know how to get the "F" outta there!! You have to know what can be transversed by thinking that you don't have the power of a Creed loving Assassin. You got a special eye if you want to make things  bit smoother, but if you use your brain, you can use minimal or none of those skills at all, but what thief isn't good at increasing his combat to level 2 and knocking out a guard with a CRITICAL STRIKE!!!? Ask Locke Cole from Final Fantasy. The city does seem like a mess, doesn't it?? But a good thief is good on reconisense, and that means being able to know where EVERYTHING is, making a blueprint of the world around him and only using the map when absolutely necessary. And that is rare, cause you have a perfect memory, non? The tools are aquired early to get the big pieces quickly and get more money, then you cycle, rinse, wash, repeat until you have so much volume money that you can buy all the arrows you need!! Lastly, the name Thief Taker General? There is a book called "The Lies of Locke Lamora" where little orphans are trained into being thieves by a guy named the Thief Maker General, so the opposite of him is a play on words by Edios.
It's a game as sneaky as the protagonist, so get used to what you don't understand. Or you will think you were robbed from a game that is actually quite a steal in itself.

I found it very difficult to find a review that wouldn’t shut up about Thief’s superior predecessors, talking about how garbage it is compared to the previous incarnations…
…Of which I never played. I am free from the shackles of nostalgia for this particular franchise. This made it all the more annoying when I could barely find an impartial review. One one side, there’s Zero Punctuation, a well known fan of the older Thief games who lambaste it for audio editing. On the other end of the spectrum there is Rock Paper Shotgun, who enjoyed the game despite its various flaws.
I’m the type of gamer who looks at franchises as a whole package. I enjoyed all of the Fable games for different reasons. I play all the Mass Effects despite 3 being my favorite. All serial media has its ups and downs and you sometimes have to take the good with the bad.
Frankly, I am inclined to agree with the RPS side of this thing. The game is not without flaws.
I will say, the game is neither difficult nor terribly exciting. Some of this is self-imposed, like setting the difficulty to its lowest which mostly translates to simpler AI behavior. ZP actually hated this, about how guards just tend to walk six feet, stare at a box for a few seconds, walk another ten feet and stare at a clearing for a few seconds. I’m inclined to agree with this rather boring method of patrol scanning. Each area only hosts 2-3 guards (At least, so far).
There is the occasional exciting moment, like the end of Chapter 2 upon meeting the “Thief-Taker General” who sounds an alarm and all the guards (Again, just about three of them or so) are on permanent alert mode. That was probably the most fun I’ve had on the game so far, partially due to the fact that the alert status put them on unpredictable patrol paths, for the most part.
I will say the game is visually stunning. I find new desktops at least once per chapter or quest, and it has a great atmosphere that gives me a sort of Dishonored vibe, except even more dire. Dishonored’s situation was more grim story-wise but it was a more colorful game.
Every other odd complaint I have are merely petty grievances that don’t sap too much away from the game.
Having to press E three times to; 1) Activate the object, 2) Lockpick the object, and 3) Open the object with the occasional 4, 5, 6, and 7 of picking up silver forks and spoons. I just feel like there should be a catch-all, ESPECIALLY if Garrett is in full darkness at the time. I can understand if there’s a light source on you, and you don’t want to be stuck in a big ‘open’ animation but I didn’t like having to slam E for stupid reasons, like just opening a damn window.
I didn’t like the cutscene every three steps during the tutorial. I found them unnecessary as it could have just let us follow the girl around without needing a cutscene. This generally goes away once you get into the game properly. The tutorial also failed to explain certain things like jumping off ledges or actually meleeing enemies when you do get caught. I found myself being pummeled by guards before I got angry enough to look in the key bindings.
The talk of hand-holding is present in reviews and I did notice this; This is the same company that made the new Tomb Raider games. At least in TR, you are generally more active when jumping around obstacles. Here, all I have to do is press a button that goes in the general direction of where I’m going and Garrett does all the work for me. I have mixed feeling on this, as it leaves less room for stupid, glitchy failure because we don’t know when the game will mess with us and not detect a specific platform. (Took me ten minutes to do a simple puzzle in Tomb Raider for this very issue). On the other hand, it’s not very engaging.
I think it was RPS who said this game is “safely” good, as it doesn’t do too much to challenge you, or current day standard stealth mechanics. It even has the usual fare of Detect-O vision that highlights things for you (Which again, you can choose not to use or disable entirely).
I admit I do want to continue playing but it doesn’t try very hard to keep my attention and that’s a shame.
If you are as incapable of looking past a few petty flaws while wearing the nostalgia glasses like most reviewers then yes, I do not recommend this game. If you’re looking for a solid, if easy stealth game then there’s no real harm in nabbing it on sale. Or not, 30$ isn’t terribly demanding. Neither is the game, really.

The Good:
I'd recommend this to anyone who enjoyed the exploration and battles of the previous games. This game builds upon those established formulas and offers a fun experience for those who enjoyed that part of the ones that came before it.
The Bad.
The English localization is pretty bad. While very little of the dialogue is grammatically incorrect the phrasing and tone of many characters is awkward and confusing. Many conversations, especially those dealing with the evil nature of the player and their companions, come off as quite childish, almost like they were written by an 5 year old. Some of this may just be bad writing. It's hard to tell. Maybe they were aiming for dialogue that had a narmy charm to it? If so they fell slightly short.
Quest objectives are often vague and the solutions can be non-intuitive. In multiple cases I scouring a region for half an hour trying to find an item before discovering that the item in question was located in another region found later in the game. The icons for Quest Giver, Quest Objective, and Complete Quest are very hard to distinguish and often seem to be used incorrectly.
Conclusion:
I recommend the game only to people who enjoyed the previous games primarily for the battles and exploration. If quests, plot, and dialogue matter significantly to you, you'll probably be happier spending your money on something else.

As you can see by my playtime, I enjoyed this game. Almost too much. For the kind of game that it is, it's pretty much perfect. For being such a simple game, it sucked me in more than most AAA quality games have.
You play as a group of civilians that are caught amongst a civil war, and your goal is to survive the conflict. During the day, you care for your survivors' daily needs (such as eating, sleeping, dressing wounds, taking medicine) as well as improving your shelter. You are able to build a modest array of different things to help you make it through the war; a cooking table, a water collector, beds, etc. You're also able to improve your shelter's defenses, which is important, because you will be raided from time to time.
At night, you are able to scavange the town, looking for useful supplies. You will need to find materials for crafting, food, medical supplies, and other hings to help in your survival - all the while, trying to avoid the inhabitants of the place that you are raiding.
The graphical style of this game adds to the atmosphere of hardship and struggle, and so does the music (which was also excellent). Sound effects are good, and the narrative is very solid. The story somewhat takes a backseat, although you really don't need much more than "there's a civil war going on right now". You are able to piece together a timeline of events during the war via news stations on your radio, and you are able to find bits of information about the people that live in this town while you're scavenging, giving the NPC's a lot more life to them. It forces you to see them as more than just something to kill or sneak by; it makes you see them as actual human beings whose lives will be affected by your actions.
I would highly recommend this game to anyone that is considering it, it was definitely worth checking out. A very solid 10 out of 10, in my opinion.

This is one of those cases where the concept and cause actually overshadow the game and make the reviews more positive than they should be. This War of Mine simply isn't as good as its review scores. You have to separate the actual game from the exceptionally good social work and awareness the devs are doing. On the latter front, the devs deserve massive applause and praise.
But I'm not here to evaluate the social implications of a game. I'm here to evaluate the game itself. On that note, This War of Mine (TWoM) is a decent but not exceptional game.
The game takes place in the middle of a war and instead of being Rocket Roger Rambo killing everything, you're just a starving civilian (well, 3 of them to start) trying to get by. You're trying to find enough food and fuel to keep yourself alive  for another day. You're trying to not get sick, blow your brains out or get shot in the head while scavenging for supplies as the bitter winter and bitter reality of your existence set in.
The game is broken up into two parts. The first is during the day working around your ramshackle house to grow food, get clean water, board up the windows and not freeze to death. There will be people who come to your door but for the most part this is just inventory management and prioritization - do you use that water to make food, alcohol you hope to trade or just for drinking water? The second part of the game is taking one of those characters and scavenging for supplies at a location. You'll have a general idea of the danger when you go, but you won't know what you'll find until you get there...and most things that go bump in the night aren't in your favor.
So the game wants to put you in moral dilemmas like the choice between stealing someone's supplies or letting your housemate die of illness. Some starving kids come to your door - do you give them some of your meager rations or turn them away hungry? That kind of narrative and difficult choices are the crux of the game.
Before getting into the game play, I'd like to give this game serious props for the art style and music. Both are exceptional and give the game a distinctive look and sound that add to the experience. There's also a decently healthy mod community even if most of the mods are nothing more than extra characters. All of this adds value to your purchase.
At the same time, the game play can be a bit lackluster. Your interactions between characters are limited and thus you're just directing them during the day to make whatever stuff you have around to use. It's repetitive and often breaks down into nothing more than inventory management while out on your nightly raids as you're severely limited in backpack space. These characters must have alligator arms to only be able to carry so little. The constructs of such limited carrying capacity and only one person who can go on these nightly pickups enforces scarcity while building during the daytime. I understand while they are in the game - but both of them just seems entirely artifical and unnecessary.
The inventory management is bland. The combat controls aren't great. There are about 25 or so locations in the game and so replay value gets a little thin as only the supplies seem to be randomized. Like most games of this type, once you hit a particular level of supplies the game can get pretty easy.
Still, these issues can be overcome. If you like exploring like me then you'll enjoy going to a new area and wondering what is around every corner in this new building. You'll be excited to find a cache of needed medicine or food. The scarcity will force you into searching areas that you'd like to avoid. And you'll breathe a big sigh of relief when you can get that farm going to keep your guys from starving to death. So even while there are downsides, it can still be an enjoyable time. And again, the game play isn't terrible - it's just been done better elsewhere by many other games. But it's still a decent formula made stronger by the setting and music.
Before I sign off on this review, I have one major bone to pick with TWoM. The actions / reactions of the characters aren't realistic at times and that's pretty awful in a game about surviving the horors of war. I basically had one game fall apart when my own home-grown character decided to become super depressed when all he was doing is defending himself from evil bandits. It started a downward spiral that just ruined that experience for me. As someone who was once in a war zone, that's not really accurate for many people who understand that they were just protecting themselves. In a game about the realities of war, overly emotional reactions to events can be a pretty large issuee. Luckily this doesn't come up in every game and you can always try to roll play around it.
PS - Get the War Child DLC. It can add some different interactions and family units and it's for a good cause.

Firstly, I would like to clear up some of the misconceptions about the game at launch. Many of the reviews were negative because (and I totally agree) it was REALLY buggy and there were very few servers available. A few days after the release of HIT the developers came up with a patch which fixed many gameplay issues I experienced when I first played it. You cannot expect a free to play game which was just released to have dedicated servers.
As it is, the game has an attractive retro aesthetic. There are 4 classes of characters to choose from when you are in the lobby - each character with his/her own active and passive abilities. One rogue agent is selected by the game at random at the beginning of each round and each player is shown whether they are a good agent (operative) or the bad agent (rogue). The rogue is able to convert one operative into a rogue and together they must stop the operatives from completing the three missions.
The lever mission is cleverly implemented. It promotes teamwork, communication between players and reverse psychology.
As of now, there is only one map with the objectives spawning at random locations throughout the house.
This game is best played with at least 2 other friends. There is no in game communication (yet?) so a third party voice chat client is recommended.
Server making and joining is simple but I would like to see password protection on lobbies later on as the game gains popularity.

Frozen is a Disney franchise which has been used by Supervillian Studios to produce this Bejeweled clone F2P game. Frozen FF:SBF is clearly a game supposed to play on Pads/Tablet PCs. But who ever had the idea to bring it to Steam FORGOT TO INTEGRATE MOUSE CONTROLS.
That can be gamebreaking. For example when in higher levels there is a timelimit and you cannot reach a powerup in time because of the WASD & Spacebar controls. Apropos powerups: You see many at the beginning which are just for the tuorial levels. You will loose them after and get 1 powerup per each earned 75 stars. That's just ridiculous.

If you fail a level you also loose a life symbolized as a red heart. You start with 15 lives. But if they run out quickly you have to wait for your daily award and be lucky or BUY them in the store. This store is marvelous well integrated into Steam. 70 Hearts = 8.90 EUR, Powerups 1 EUR each. After click you land directly from this awful graphics in the last checkout screen of Steam. Don't click there wrong! No sane man would buy this crap even accidently. Btw who is the target group for this game I wonder. Little kids? With this incorporated perfideous microtransactions system certainly not. Grownups maybe. But only if you have enough time and nerves.
The game itself is divided into two parts: Firstly the Free Fall (FF) is the SP and used to unlock stars and characters. Something tells me that you are barely able to unlock all characters for free. It gets  harder fastly because at lvl15 there are time limits introduced like 60 secs to reach 40k points. Your lives go away like cat lives. And the three star goal is even higher.
Interesting find: The game gives you the illusion everything is random. But I figured out the starting position in each level is always the same. So it's more like a puzzle which you have to solve quickly in time. That can be useful but also shows the bad quality of surprise. The game just knows if you are unable to make any further move and then randomizes slowly the map new.

The second mode is the Snowball Fight (SBF) which is MP (haha it's just local MP. You would not have expected here any ingenius netcode). You should have unlocked all characters in SP and already know how to play this game basically. Then you are able to puzzle again and do 50 snowball fights against yourself.
So if you are still interested to checkout this partly unfair & unbalanced, perfideous microtransactions using, awful graphics & storyless masterpiece of negativity then go on.

Very interesting game I have here. I have played this all the way now and I am impressed with it. Like every game it had it's down points and good points so let's get down to them:
I enjoyed the story. It kept my interest and it really added depth that made me feel like I was playing the story of a really good book. It had it's boring points like some letters were a little boring and useless to read, but that could also be because at times I was tired and just too lazy to do the effort and read it all. Overall it kept me interested and it had quite a few twists and turns that made it good.
Graphics: Honestly I can't really complain at all. No glitches. Nothing unclear. I felt it was perfect as it is.
Gameplay: Here I wasn't all that happy but it didn't put me off. At first the controlls were a little bit too much but I soon got used to it as I got into the game. I think overall the controlls were greatly balanced, just a little much to remember at first. The game played smoothly for me and it posed quite a challenge for me. I loved puzzling out my moves and planning what to do. I actually had a few times where I had to reload my last check point to retry or improve on my plan. I had no glitches so far nor have I had any performance issues. The combat sucked though. At far end with a bow and arrow is okayish. Face-to-face battles is absolutely horrible. I would have liked something like a dagger in this case to help. THe takedowns is actually the only decent way of taking out enemies.
Loot: A LOT of loot that is well hidden at times and kinda makes you look for it. Honestly you don't need a lot of loot to get you set up. I didn't need a lot of loot to keep my inventory stocked because at points you would get free refills like arrows. I found it extremely hard to find all the loot and I did only manage to get about 53% of loot. THe unique loot is also not really of any value and a little pointless to me but maybe just maybe it had some value that I haven't discovered.
There is a lot of documents, newspapers, letters, etc that added depth to the story although you didn't need much of it to get a really good story. Maybe some of the info was a little useless and not that needed as I thought. I would recommend this game. It is loads of fun and I really think this was cash well spent. I haven't got the dlc's but the plain game without the dlc's was fine for me. I liked that you don't get to finish this game in a flash of time. It took me over 9 hours to even get to chapter 6 but that can also be time I spent planning it out and trying different ways of doing things.
Overall I would give this one a 8/10

Забагованная до ужаса: рассинхрон речи с анимацией, постоянные фризы. Графика на вышке то очень не очень, боюсь представить что там на минималке, лица и мимка не многим лучше Thief: Deadly Shadows (2004). Даже пререндер и тот страшненький.
Сюжет скучен, высосан из пальца. Персонажи не запоминаются, нет у них ни характера, ни личности, ни мотивации.
Геймплей прикольный первую первую пару часов. Уровни - пара параллельных коридоров и ответвление с бомжом-торговцем. Учитывая, что у Гаррета есть gps, а стражей обдурить проще простого (а можно просто у них за спиной пройти в тесном коридоре), прохождение - изи-бризи. Ghost стелс местами слишком замороченный, а Opportunist всегда слишком простой. В 3 их 8 уровнях мне не получилось получить Ghost исключительно из-за забагованный стражей, которые стояли на месте и теребели свой меч/арбалет, а не патрулировали местность, как им и положено.
Ассортимент оружия такой не нужен вообще, из него используется веревочная, водная, да тупая стрела. Апгрейды вообще бессмысленные. К середине игры забиваешь на исследование уровней и собирание лута, т.к. тратить награбленное не на что.
Короче, первые полтора часа думаешь "о, круто". Потом все эти одинковые сценки с окнами и баррикадами приедаются (особенно, учитывая, что они тормозят), все ловушки и головоломки решаются с помощью глаза. И оказывается, что это все, что есть в игре, больше ничего не будет, тебе еще 8 часов делать все то же самое, один в один.
Ну и да, улицы пустые, на повешенье приходит 2 человека.

If you want to satisfy your stealthy needs, this is the game for you. Leaving open doors, different walking surfaces, shadows - it all matters in this game. On top of that - the main character is just as you would expect him to be - snarky with a grim sense of humor. The beauty in this game is all the possibilities and side jobs. What you find in different houses can add so much life to your gaming experience. As for the difficulty (and this is the best part), you can customize it to all your specific needs! The game also lets you go about your own way of finishing the job. You can be full-stealth, a quiet assassin or a very, very, very angry robber.
The only thing you might find irritable at first is the amount of time you'll lose trying to find your way. And some jobs have pretty well hidden entrances.
All in all, this is an excellent stealth game. It has a dark atmosphere, clever quests and thoughtful obstacles. 10/10 would recommend!

More Far Cry.  What that means depends on how much you like far cry.  This continues the more recent formulas (those of 2 and 3) by scratching the fps rpg progress itch very strongly.  Early on you are underpowered and easily overwhelmed with a billion things to do and a billion icons on the map.  As you progress, you do the things, the icons dissapear, and you get better and better guns, bombs, ammo, snow leopard skin bullet bags, etc.
The treatment of animals has never really been worse here, you are explicitly sent by an insane fashion designer to collect rare/endangered specimens to holster more guns, more bullets, more bags for more skins, etc.  Its all 'ok' though because in kyrat nothing is 'endangered' and everything wants to kill you so killing it back first is just fine.
If you mostly just ignore things like that though and focus on the gameplay its still quite fun, theres still tons of insane over the top set-pieces, and the engine runs super smooth (except for the few times it crashes on startup in win 10).  So yeah, if you liked previous far cry games, you will like this one, potentially a lot.  If you didn't like previous far cry games, this one certainly is not going to change enough to change your mind.

Outside of that bonus, we have this lump of♥♥♥♥♥♥ Humble Bundle never feels like charity to me. Owning this game does.
Moving on from the mean-spirited preamble to the real details, the "game" took about 50 minutes to finish. That's not a very long time, but during that period I almost quit playing so I could erase it forever, from both my computer and my mind. Twice. The characters are terrible. One is a socially awkward idiot, the other a socially awkward jackass, and they identify themselves as such almost instantly. What draws these two characters together, you ask? I don't know, seemingly nothing? Maybe? But for better or worse, and for no reason, they are drawn together. Definitely for worse. You can tell after about 10 minutes, the game practically screams it at you. Moving on to the gameplay, there are parts where you can explore the girl, Nina's, computer desktop. It's an interesting concept, it lets you look through her photos, homework assigntments, emails, stuff like that. Kind of Analogue: A Hate Story-ish if Analogue: A Hate Story sucked. Her photos are nothing special, but it tries to make up for that in quantity. It may just be me, but I don't care to read the homework assignments of others. That leaves the emails, and those could be interesting, but since she doesn't seem to do anything other than do homework, ignore her real friends, and play that MMO with that guy (we'll call him Craig, because I don't remember his real name, not memorable enough, the only reason I got "Nina" was because it says it in the description of the game), there's not much content in her emails. There are parts where you "play" the MMO that they play together. I have "play" in quotes because all you do is click an enemy, watch your character attempt to walk over there for a while because of the terrible movement mechanics, watch them autohit the enemy about 15 times while the enemy just stands perfectly still doing nothing, then repeat about 30 times until you kill the final boss. All that "gameplay" while listening to Nina and Craig being awkward. Fun times *sarcastic tone*. The dialogue is all just terrible, half of it is just awkward laughing, the other half is made up of actual, albeit awkward, words. The game clunks along at a slow pace, trying to build an actual plot, but crashes to rock bottom at the end. It goes from climax to credits in about a minute, just so abrupt, it was pretty funny, but I don't want to spoil it for anyone. Not that you should buy this game. No, just look up a video of it on YouTube or something
When it ended I was left with this "Where do I go from here?" feeling. I decided to go take a shower to get the dirty feeling of having played this game off my skin, uninstall the game, then hide it from my Steam library. In closing. No! Bad! Bad game! Don't waste people's time like that!

I have just met this game a while ago, but I can tell you that this is one of the best games I have ever played.
Massive maps are, although often useless due to a low number of players, pretty epic. Some people would say "this does not even have a destructible environment", but I am asking, why would you need one? This game is about destroying the enemy team, helping your own and winning the battle, not about making a hole in an asteroid.
Star Conflict contains both PvP, in which you play with real players against real players and PvE, which is about missions where your comrades are real players and enemies are Non-Player Characters. PvP helps you gain levels at ships which you need for getting better ships and PvE gains you more money. That might look stupid at first, but it forces its players to play both PvP and PvE.
Another part is a completely different story. Ships. There are 3 races (but developers are working on new ones, I hope) which all have different ships. They are divided into classes like Frigates and Fighters, and those classes are more divided into sub-classes, like Engineering Frigate and Long Range Frigate. Every ship has its own part in the battle, that means if one team has engineers but the other doesn't, it might lead the first team to easy victory. Depends if players can use full potential of those ships and I am saying that not everyone knows how to correctly use their ships. Then there are premium ships. I think that 1/3 or 1/4 of all ships are premium, but those ships cannot be upgraded into better ships, players who invested money in this game have lesser advantage, therefore it's less pay-to-win. It's more about grinding, who plays it more, has more. Simple.
Then there is community. What can I tell you? Community is pretty friendly, although sometimes ignorant, mainly in battles. I have met two guys in a PvE mission who were doing nothing but destroying the all-time-spawning enemy ships without doing the objective. Of course, more destroyed ships and assists, more money and experience (which is called "synergy"). They didn't even complete the first of the three objectives (yes, THEY, not WE) and guess what; WE ALL didn't get a single credit (a unit of money) from it. Over 20 minutes of pointless fighting was in vain. But on the more friendly side, guys on global chat are nice. We have talked about religions, the universe, and even trees. You'll find specialists on everything there.
9/10 is my final rating.

This game redeems the King's Bounty series after the terrible Warriors of the North.
Unlike WotN, the game is a challenge, at least to me, on normal difficulty. The quests are interesting and at times amusing.  Reminds me of Armoured Princess, which from me is high praise.

At first it felt like 'wow, cool game, how could i miss this before'. But then the quests become VERY repetitive and boring, you have to walk a lot, talk a lot, fight weak enemies (if you are not playing on impossible difficulty), get some stupid items, etc. Dialogues are mostly boring too and in many quests you hear the same things from 2 or 3 different characters. Some levels are badly designed and you can't even use your flying mount there, so you walk over and over and over again. Many important landmarks or characters are not marked on your map so you have to remember everything. Becomes even more frustrating when you are looking for some quest stuff and there is no clue in the quest's description as to in what location is the item or enemy troop you need to get to.
Also it's not cool that you can't upgrade your usual version to a premium and get dlc content.
If you are a big fan of King's Bounty, you can still try to enjoy this, but I think there are better games in the series.

The worst King's Bounty game I have seen so far. It takes ages to finish, which is usually a good thing. However, in this case it takes ages because you have to run around from one island to the other...again and again.
A typicall quests looks like:
"Hello evil vampire, I would like to cooperate with you, but first you got to fetch me the following three items and kill 3 enemy heroes".
Off you go, often to a different island, where you have been before and where there is nothing left to do, just to talk to some NPC that gives you the desired item. Then you have to return to your quest giver. And you do this over and over again... walking...walking...walking...walking.
The quest log is horrible as well. It does not tell you what to do in many cases. So, if you didn't read the quest text carefully, you need to look it up on the internet. Otherwise, there is no way to re-read the quest text.
Oh, and the fights are very repetitive and unbalaced (nothing too unexpected, if you played the first two KB games. But this one felt even worse).
On the first island, the difficulty seems alright, then it becames very difficult suddenly (could be because I played the mage class). After the first few islands it then becomes too easy. All enemy groups classified as "deadly" or "invincible" are a joke. You just use your call nature spell to summon animals that did ~55.000 damage at the end of the game.
To sum it up, don't buy this game, unless you like getting frustrated.

It's a good game overall. It really is, gives almost as much enjoyment as previous iterations. So why the thumb down? Because there are issues which I'm not willing to see in future releases of this game, nor in any other games for that matter.
There are reviews saying that the developers completly ignored the community. I personally don't care if devs are listening to community or not, as long as they're good enough to release a consistent product. Which this is not. In far too many places it looks like the devs (level designers mostly) were thinking "ok, here's a draft of a level, I'll save it now and finish it some time closer to the deadline", and then never did.
First catacombs are ridiculously lined with eggs along the corridors walls, just like someone would launch a level editor and made click, click, click, click to spray them in few minutes and voila! We have a level!
On Whitehill there was not enough will to do even that, it's just a barren land with a couple of enemies and badly aligned textures.
Aralan feels deserted even thought there's no reason for that in the story, it's an Elven mainland!
Most other levels are ok, but from time to time you'll see things that strike you how someone couldn't be arsed to finish something on a decent level.
You don't release something in such a merry state, they should rather cut such unfinished content alltogether. Now it's like a lovely pie with a ball of poo on top instead of a cherry.
Then there are bugs. Not game breaking ones (I haven't had even a single in-game crash), rather little or bigger annoyances. Like inability to have an aspect-ratio correct display with sharp graphics (everything gets soft-scaled with some blurry filter), unless you switch your monitor to game's native resolution (1680x1050) without scaling, which makes things look better (but still not perfect). Or crashes when you switch resolutions (had to edit the configuration file manually). Or crash on every exit. Or some badly working spells. Etc.
The point is that it's not that the devs ignore the community. They outright abandoned the product - there were practically no meaningful patches, and probably never will be.
What annoys me most is that publisher is now probably sitting there scoffing "we released a 20% unfinished product and look how it sells! lets make the next one 60% unfinished, straight in the customers face hahaha!"
And they will charge it 30 euro, with 60% of levels being deserted whitehill lined with eggs, provided that you'll get out of washed-out main menu without a crash, to be fixed with the next patch, which will never come. And we'll buy it.
And that's why I thumb it down. To have the next King Bounty as well designed as The Legend, as bug-free as Crossworlds, and as rich as WotN.
As to what I liked: the overall story is fun, even though I don't empathise with evil scum (I'd rather be a hero). Some dialogues are ingenious, but some are childish (I guess there were several writers). There are no bosses (except the final enemy), which I never liked. There's some new beautifull music by Lind Erebros (he's a russian Paul Romero ;).
And it's generally another King's Bounty, which is never enough.
Go get it, and then thumb it down to let the devs/publishers know that they can do better.

TL;DR VERSION: 8.1/10: I don't feel that the Gold Edition is worth the $70 price tag, but Steam Sales are a great reason to go ahead and wishlist this. You might play only once, but the experience is unforgettable.
THE LONG VERSION: I entered into the Far Cry series as a solid skeptic at Far Cry 2. I was convinced that nothing could convince me to enjoy the series again because it only ever features male characters like so many other boring male-action-star titles produced by Ubisoft and it tends to be an unredeeming bug fest.
Then Far Cry 4 was on sale and I figured, "Why the hell not?" Sure, it had a few bugs related to platforming at times and it frustrated me to no end because I never had the difficulty below "Hard" ever. But once I really got into it, Ajay's story was a wild trip, the mayhem I was capable of causing was hilarious, and then I unexpectedly had the extreme satisfaction of conquering Yuma's Fortress undetected on the first try. I felt rewarded just for pulling it off, and that doesn't happen for me often in games.
In the end, I decided that Far Cry has redeemed itself as a series and then some. The gameplay was fantastic, the scenery was breath taking, the music was exotic, there were a few very meaningful choices to make, and several characters were so much fun to hate and then capture or kill. Other characters caused unexpected emotions, but they would have been stronger had the story helped me get more attached to them before certain plot climaxes.
Here's hoping that the true Far Cry 5 (not Far Cry Primal) exceeds this standard just a little and allows the player to choose between a male or female character when starting the campaign. I'll probably choose male and go "Hard" difficulty anyway, but a female character's second perspective and some notable changes in dialogue would address the issue of this game's somewhat poor replay value at such a comparitively low cost of labor.
My only serious complaint and a hefty portion of my "out of ten" reduction is that the game mechanics seemed to be missing a few basic borrowed-enemy-vehicle-disguise and friendly-NPC-summoning-to-follow innovations that have been around since Mercenaries: Playground of Destruction in 2005. That's about a decade behind the curve for this title.
It gets ludicrous at times because randomly generated events on roads are almost unavoidable and tend to distract the player from what they were really setting out to do. It gets ludicrous because you can only take one NPC soldier into combat when in reality you could just honk a horn and get a few more to pile into your car in older titles, or call in a full vehicle of allies as back-up instead of a single pawn who ends up dying instantly.
Very fun and addicting.

If you play Space Station 13 or Space Engineers, this game will feel very at home for you. It is a very systems and engineering heavy focused game based around surviving in space. Being in Early access, You are bound to run into bugs and other various frustrations, but power through them! Behind the frustration is a game filled with creativity thats also tied to productivity, and thats a feeling most creative games don't give.
The controls take some getting used to, I highly suggest rebinding them to suit your needs, because as some people may complain about a lack of drag and drop, it actually provides a more hands on experienced that allows you to manage inventory while moving and looking around.
If you hate Early access, either buy it and just wait, or wait to see how it is once it finishes EA, but I definately recommend giving it a try or watching someone's recording or stream of the game.

This game is not easy and although this should be obvious, it isn't finished yet. This game is meant to challenge you and make you think. Also, the devs are active with the community and are listening to feedback and bug reports.
A couple of notes on the concerns some people have expressed.
The UI is not intuitive at first and takes a bit to get used to but once you do, you can start flowing.
The tutorial goes through the controls but you might need to run through it a couple of times to get them down.
There isn't any documentation on how some of the systems or individual parts work. For example, there is a sensor. Until you try to build it, you don't know what kind of things it can sense (daylight, motion, and something else I can't recall right now). So there is a lot of trial and error and experimenting, but that is also a big part of the fun.
Again, keep in mind that the game isn't finished yet. They have mentioned that it's going to be at least a year before the end. The tutorial, for one, will undoubtedly change before the end.
There's no discovery or sense of accomplishment if the game tells you exactly how to build out the furnace so you can smelt steel. You can use the table with the right cartridge and see what the correct temp, pressure and ingredients for making steel. You have to figure out the method needed to accomplish that.
When you finally get your solar panels to move and track the sun through the day, that feeling is just fantastic. Trying to figure out how to wire your base correctly not only for what you need now but what you will/might need later is part of the charm.
I'm really looking forward to seeing how this game develops. Now, I get to figure out how to get an airlock working properly
TL:DR  This game is meant to be challenging. You need to use your brain to figure things out. Some of the controls take a bit to get used to but it doesn't take long to get used to them. This game is about figureing how to use and combine the various systems to survive and do what you want.
Frantic, vibrant and just a helluva good time and it's free so you can't really lose. It needs a little bit of work but I think this game is a gem that just needs a bit of polishing here and there.

--- This review might contain some spoilers! ---
So what have we got here?
Well, first of all, you should be aware that this isn't really a game. It is much more a short movie (played it through in less than an hour) offering you a tiny bit of interaction.
The story itself is about a young woman who met - and eventually fell in love with - a "handsome boy" she is playing with all the time. As the story progresses they find out they feel attracted to each other. Finally they decide to meet and discover what their relationship will bring.
Sad thing here is not the little interaction nor the low budget acting. All this might still offer an interesting experience.
Main problem with this story is... there is none! All that happens is very linear. The conflict - both (but more from his side) don't really know what to expect from their relationship - is just beginning when the story already ends.
Don't get me wrong. Probably many people (not only those who share the high interaction with other players in online MMORPO games) know this conflict.
But sadly the story fails in a broader "discussion" of this issue. This is most obvious when the story actually ends the moment it just begins. When the boy finally took the chance to visit the protagonist, they meet the first time outside the game. It leads to the predictable conflict that was prepared the scene before. So there was no big surprise. But this should be the moment when the story starts - not their end.
The movie does not offer any solution, nor does it show the conflict from another point of view. There is no progress for the progtagonists. Neither in overcoming their shared conflict (of not being together) nor in how to deal with being hurt by someone important for you (the first love).
So when the game ends, it leaves all this to you. This is pretty unsatisfying. Not because it would make you think. No, this would be actually a great effect. But more, because it does not give you any new input. You might know this problem by yourself or not. And when the ending credits are shown, you merely know that there are other people who share your type of memories.
Is that necessarily a bad thing? Not at all. But it doesn't offer you much more than this.
Don't get me wrong. The game also shares some nice moments. The voice acting is okay, gives you some authentic emotional moments. The art style is also somehow interesting (even though not amazingly great).
So, if you are up to watch a short movie where you have to make some clicks in order to continue an authentic story about first love with a sad ending, this might be an hour of gameplay for you.
If you expect a real interactive story, or would be frustrated playing a story which ends where it actually just began, better don't buy the game.

I was mystified to read some reviewers thought it the worst in the series (or maybe the "weakest"). That's not my impression at all. I think they stepped up their game significantly w/ the writing, quests, and overall sense of humor. Also, for those of you tired of playing the same old standby human and dragon units, this is the game for you. You can of course over time get a significant medley of old favorites, but I would recommend trying to stay close to the thematic choices that fit the 3 PCs: Mage (Vampire) > Undead units; Paladin (Demoness) > Demon units; Warrior (Orc) > well you get the idea. I've only played as the Mage, but I suspect I won't feel differently after playing the next 2 PCs.
More than past games, you really should have a pad of notepaper, and keep notes on where NPCs are, what they are selling, etc. A lot of times, the main clues for a quest are in dialogue only, so pay attention!
There is a massive amount of bang for the very modest buck you pay out (I'd go for the Premium Edition for the 2 new islands, 1 of which has a cool new unit). I spent a ridiculous amount of time on just 1 playthrough, and I plan on 2 more to come.
There is one particular new unit that is one of my all-time favorites: the Dragon Rider. They cost a fortune and are hard to get initially, but--at least for a small army game like the Mage/Vampire has--they were a huge part of my success mid-late game.
There are minor criticisms I might have, but that's all they are--minor. If anyone cares what I think, here they are:
1) while underground "realms" get maps, dungeons don't; that should be an easy fix going forward in the series;
2) changing the camera's perspective can be a minor pain, sometimes having to poke your horse into a wall and swivel around just to see from a different perspective;
3) the "bleed" damage is OP in this game. All it takes is some puny archer to hit your Black Knight stack and all of a sudden you're losing numbers of them from what should have been a minor wound;
4) on a similar note, I wish they would calculate damage/status effects a tad bit more "realistically"--for example, it's great that Ents take double fire damage, but why should any of the undead units take "bleed" damage? Silly.
Don't get discouraged in the early game when you seem limited in troop recruitment etc. Once the game opens up (i.e., other islands and realms), you'll soon have a dizzying number of potential quests. Final nice point: many times, there are more ways than just 1 to solve a quest.

Summary: Clearly the worst game in the series, but still a lot of fun.
Pros: Virtually identical game engine to previous KB games

The RPG elements are silly, but that's OK because they're meant to be.  If you take the plot seriously you're playing the wrong game.  However, the quests are also sometimes buggy and often ambiguous to the point where you'll probably have to consolt Google to know what to do next, which is not OK -- but not fatally so.  That's because the quests are merely an awkward contrivance to get you from one battle to the next -- which is where the game really shines.
As with each new game in the series, the basic combat engine is the same, with a handful of minor new mechanics for new spells and monsters thrown in.  You also get a new "companion" that provides a suite of new special abilities in combat.  In King's Bounty:Warriors of the North you got Valkyries; in Dark Side you get... well I'm not quite sure what it is, some kind of demon, I think.  As usual the new abilities are a mixed bag: some you'll use every combat, some you'll probably only use a couple times to see what they do and then file them away.
The thing that makes the game fun is the variety of units and spells you can use in combat.  After a few introductory campaigns, you can switch your army's "build" pretty easily at any time, which allows you to do all kinds of experiments with different tactics.  Over the course of my game, I went from an army built around a couple of super-strong core units (dragons), to one compsed almost entirely of undead melee units, to one focused on plastering the enemy from afar with ranged units.
Plus, there is huge variety of spells that can supplement or even become the focus of your tactical strategy.  Pump up the Hypnosis spell to its maximum level and use it in conjunction with your companion's Jealousy ability to turn your emeny's army against itself.  Spam the Call of Nature spell to overwhelm your enemy with a horde of summoned animals.  Make your own army effectively immortal by casting Resurrection every turn.  Or just lay into the bad guys with good old fashioned Fireballs and Lightning Bolts.  Those are just a few of the many strategies I've used with success.
The spell and unit animations are more or less the same from previous games in the franchise, but that's not a bad thing since they are, as far as I know, the state of the art.  The same can be said of the whole game, really: there's nothing new here, but until something new does come along, King's Bounty remains the best turn-based tactical combat game around.
