To say this is an MMO is an overstatement. It's more along the lines of DOTA, and smaller scale at that. There is little documentation making learning the game difficult. Selecting a faction does not lock you in. You choose and switch factions by simply changing contracts which are free and have no cooldowns associated with it.
Each faction differs in their early on ship roles, and even then the factions do not get certain ship roles. You earn synergy and credits through match making PvE or PvP. Synergy upgrades your ships, while credits gets you new ships, and modules. Through missions you earn Standards and Vouchers, these are used to purchase account/battle boosters, and module upgrades respectively.
Some aspects make me think this is a pay to win game, such as purchasing a DLC ship where it's fully upgraded, needs no repairs, and grants additional synergy rewards. However, through my play through to Rank 3 ships so far, most people opt out of the DLC. Most of the fun seems to be unlocking new ship ranks, and therefore new ship roles within a faction, and more advanced versions of the ships you are using already (more upgrade slots, etc).
The starting ships are fighters, and the roles available are Gunship, Command, and Tackler. (which are Federation, Jericho, and Free Worlds respectively). Soon after you begin to unlock Frigates and Interceptors. Frigates come in three flavors, Engineering, Guard, and Long Range. Interceptors come in Covert Ops, Recon, and ECM. As stated earlier, each faction is missing some roles, more specfically they are missing one role from each ship type. Each faction starts with one role per ship type, and gains another later on in the rankings.
Overall this is a very fun game. Match making queues can be on the order of 3-4 minutes some nights, with battles lasting a couple of minutes. I've found increasing match making from Region: US to Region: Any, works wonders. What makes it worth while is that the game is Free to Play, so the shortcomings are quite forgivable. The premium option comes in the form of purchaseable licenses using Standards, which are also purchasable with cash. The price per month can range from $10.50 down to somewhere on the order of $4 depending on the length of the license.

Star Conflict is surprising in many ways, graphically it’s stunning, rivalling some AAA titles on the market today. It’s beautifully textured, environments have been creatively designed, not to mention the ships also. But the quality of this, all in a free-to-play title, is second to none.
Everything has been carefully created here, shooting your weapons and blowing enemy ships into smithereens, causing a Star Wars-esque explosion is incredibly satisfying. Even just watching your ship trundle along through the environments is a great moment. RECOMENDED!

Star Conflict is really fantastic and comes highly recommended.
The control scheme first and foremost feels exactly like Freelancer, for those who have played it in the past.  Point the mouse and the ship follows.  The ease of control makes for some really compelling combat, thankfully, which means it's easy to grasp, but difficult to master.
Modules, special abilities, and unique weapons help every ship and every role within each ship feel unique and compelling.  There's certain to be something for every player in Star Conflict!
As for the Free to Play model, the developers are immensely generous.  Any amount of payment, including ships, is ultimately "pay to not grind".  The ships don't have any unique abilities or anything else you can't get from normal gameplay; instead, they have synergy (read: XP) bonuses so that you can transfer the XP off into a general pool, so as to level a ship you may struggle to play, or even one you don't WANT to play that may be a gate towards your preferred ship type.  Premium ammo does the exact same damage as its non-premium brother, but offers some synergy bonuses when used in combat.  And the actual purchasing of premium currency goes a long, long way.
PvE and PvP combat is available and offers a wide variety of gametypes, many of which you'll be familiar with, but have a unique twist to it when 3 dimensions are taken into account.  Sometimes challenging when you're unprepared, but always rewarding.
All in all, Star Conflict is really a fantastic and underestimated experience.  I hope that it continues well into the future, as this is one I'll be playing for some time.

At first the game might look like a perfect "pay to win" candidate, considering there are several DLC packs available unlocking ships for you. However, that's not really the case.
All ships available as part of DLC offers or to be bought with real world currency are more or less sidegrades or shortcuts. The most powerful ships however, can only be unlocked by playing the game. That's very nice and fair.
Unfortunately, you can describe the game with three words:
. And to be honest, that's sad, very sad, and also the reason why I can't really recommend this game without warning about this.
Let me explain the game in a few sentences:
You start out with the factions' basic ships. To obtain bigger ships, you'll have to earn "sync" points. With these you're able to level up ships. Once you've leveled a ship, you'll be able to unlock the next ship in the tech tree that's usually a small upgrade or a new ship fitting a different role.
In addition, you're able to upgrade parts of the ships or more specific modules that are installed on them: a primary weapon system (turrets), secondary weapon systems (typically missiles), a ship specific special ability (not upgradeable), and two support abilities. The problem: Upgrades won't transfer between tiers.
So game progress looks like this:
- Obtain a new ship.
- Invest (ingame) money, mission rewards (or real money) to level up the ship modules.
- Level up the ship to improve its power and unlock the next ship.
- Obtain a new ship and start over again.
And that's it, unfortunately. I guess I don't have to say that leveling the ships appears to take ages. While it's perfectly fine to not "finish" the progression part of the game within a week, it's really slow and tedious. Add to this the fact that the game's population isn't that high (typically 1000-3000 players online right now according to stats in the game), it happens that you'll have to wait one or two minutes to finally get into a PvE game. Queue times for PvP are usually slightly longer (sometimes 5 minutes or more).
And here's another problem: Due to the low population (and a very limited number of PvE missions), you're usually fighting with or against significantly stronger enemies. It's not uncommon to die within seconds versus a sniping frigate that's simply out of range for you. Once you're dead, you'll either have to wait 30-60 seconds (seems to depend on game mode) or till the next stage of the mission (in PvE). In addition, most mission stages take only two or three minutes, but there's a full minute of wait time between stages.
"Fortunately" there are ways to progress faster: You can buy the classic "booster" to gain more points, but you're also able to buy different ammo that will double your synergy gain. The unfair part: The costs! The initial price of the ammo module is 2 Standarts. That's not a lot. However, once unlocked it no longer shows any price. Although the module will still take 2 Standarts for every round you're playing. You won't see this unless you're paying close attention. And some of the costs... To upgrade a weapon from level 2 to level 3 you'll need something like 30,000 units of mission rewards: You'll get about 600 per mission - or buy the upgrade with real money. Do the math yourself.
And one more thing to remember: This game can only be played using keyboard and mouse. There is no controller support (neither gamepad nor joysticks). Also there seems to be a significant amount of auto-aim involved or there are really just big hitboxes. It's definitely far easier to hit enemies as it is in other games of this genre.

A seamless blend of crafting, survival, and stealth, This War of Mine shines a sober light on the dim reality of war.
Scholar Miguel Sicart proposes in his book "The Ethics of Computer Games" that video games are effectively ethical systems that permit the player to explore the consequences of actions in a restricted setting. Super Mario Bros. provides a relatively linear ethical system (i.e., jump on bad guys to win), while games like the Grand Theft Auto series incentivize particular behaviors over others (i.e., it's more fun to break the law rather than follow the law in-game).
As an ethical system, This War of Mine rises above the rest in its insistence upon a robust range of real consequences. Player characters deteriorate in hunger, fitness, illness, and mental health without constant intervention and resupply of resources. The task of finding enough materials to survive opens up possibilities of scavenging, charity, theft, murder, and starvation—all of which impact the player characters accordingly. Once I got the hang of the game, I played through four full times, each with a different ethical approach. Real war inevitably leads people to act beyond their normal capacities, and This War of Mine provides an excellent simulator for those of us fortunate enough to never experience such tragedy.
Even for veterans of the survival and crafting genres, This War of Mine poses a real challenge. The game offers a wide variety of possible structures to build, but only a thoughtful and meticulous construction path will ensure victory. The variety of characters and settings also keeps the game fresh for several playthroughs. The music entices perfectly and complements the handcrafted war-torn graphics.
This War of Mine ranks among the best games I have played. The attention to detail of both the setting and player experience makes this a worthwhile investment.

As there are thousands of reviews, I will keep this short.
Far Cry 4 is an excellent game overall.
There are too many positive aspects to list, so i'll list the negatives:
- As I discussed in my Far Cry 3 review, I do not understand the need for "trippy" events except to show the player a new type of constrained play-style. Maybe I do not understand the drug culture, but I suppose the developers wanted us to see the fun/darker side of hallucinations. Shangri-La was visually beautiful, but an annoying set of quests I would never want to play ever again. I suppose magical enemies popping randomly around the map went against my planning/fun, and at one point I just suicide ran to the bell just to finish it off.
- The story was a bit pathetic in terms of the mechanics. Helicopters did funny things when approaching the primary campaign locations. Gliders would fail if you were on a mission. You couldn't call in your buddies (V key) when you're on a mission. I had unlimited tokens to spend on the final mission. Nope, not allowed.
I really enjoyed this game and I definitely recommend it if you like open-world sandbox constant chaos.

Seeing this franchise has an old fanbase I will disclaim I have not played any of the old Thief games.
Now that the formalities are out of the way (since fans can be a bit fanatical) I want to declare this game one of my favorites of all time.
Yes, I think this game is amazing. The art style, the soundtrack, the game mechanics, even the story.
Okay I will admit the story has it's flaws, not to mention the confusing ending. But nevertheless I enjoyed playing through this game several times, trying out all te game has to offer, using all the challenges and limitations the game offers in its game mods to make it more dificult.
And I really don't care about the people who say that the game is too easy even with all the mods on. It's hard enough. It will get very frustrating if it's any harder. Besides, its not meant to be Dark Souls. And ohh yes, I know people who find Dark Souls "too easy" and "newbs lulz game". Whatever.
It was the first "stealthy"-based type game I ever played, which I later followed with others like Dishonored, Styx, Hitman etc. and I still like this one most of all because ... I don't know. Thats one of the things when I know a game is good - when you don't know exactly why you love it.
The feeling I get when im in this game is very unique. The general gloomy atmosphere, dark aestethic, the mysterious 18th sentury London world, it ties perfectly together.
And let me just say that the AIs in all of the games are pretty much the same - not great. It's NOT just Thief. I've done and seen others do things in this and other games that they should not be able to, and the AI not do the things they should. That does not make a game bad, even when the game relies on player-AI interaction like stealth games do. It is a very dificult thing to code. In fact it is the hardest thing. Even high level programmers and engineers struggle with this so don't expect a highly advanced and individually personafied sophisticated NPCs each with it's own moral and philosofical views and ideas bordering on with human intelligence. I mean come on ...
I do not own the DLC, and from what I hear it's best if you get them on sale.
I really hope they make a sequel after this franchise reboot. The game had some issues at launch, but you can safely ignore reviews from back then. Now I have no problems running the game, and there are a lot of steam sales you can grab the game on. It is definitely worth it!

The game is pretty fun while you're learning, but it gets very repetitive after you have a viable strategy (and the campaign does extend a bit too long in this regard, with very little significant additions).
If you like resource management games (and RTS with a focus on building rather than combat), you'll probably enjoy this. I had a good time, for a while.
The problem I have with it came later, in the Expert campaign. It's basically the exact same thing, but with much tougher opponents.
It started out fine, but things turned sour later on. This would be all fine, except that the game is a huge snowball. If you lose pace, you've lost. Especially at the end, when the opponents are incredibly good and pile up much more money than you do, unless you have a really good strategy.
Basically, you go through a sequence of levels. You start levels by setting up your oil pumps, carrying horses, etc. You have a fixed amount of money to do this (2000€), but can enter debt if you run out of it.
The interest in these levels is that 1) you have to find the oil and 2) you spend money to build everything. So you're trying to minimize your spendings on both finding and then extracting the oil.
You'll use the money you make on the level to buy upgrades, choosing land, getting some discounts and, later, shares (end-game).
This makes every level influence the future ones, hence the snowball.
The problem with this is that it really discourages experimentation. It's very risky to try out a new mechanic the game introduces. 1) because you have to buy pretty expensive upgrades to take advantage of them and 2) because you don't know how they work. So you're basically spending a lot of money on the
of taking advantage of a mechanic, and then have to play some levels very sub-optimally to figure out how the mechanics actually work.
Since the game is a race from beginning to end, the risk/incentive to explore is far too high.
These are actually 2 problems. In Normal mode, the game if fairly easy, and you can easily
the AI by not taking risks. In this case, it lacks incentive.
In Expert mode, they're so close to you that you would be shooting yourself in the foot by experimenting with the mechanics. It's too risky!
So yeah... Expert Mode was being harder, but close for a while. Then, when I was almost winning, the AI suddenly got incredibly good (probably by taking advantage of the new mechanics I didn't know how to use) and got to far ahead of me to do anything.
This wasn't at all what I expected. And, in a way, it's good that this happens! On the other hand, there are the problems above, where the game never presents the right opportunities for you to react to it.
In Normal mode, most of the mechanics ended up ignored. In Expert mode, you were expected to have mastered them. Without the space in-between.
If you are aware of this, you will probably be able to take advantage of the normal campaign to
. If not, well... oops.
I definitely think the game should encourage the player to try the new mechanics, even in a sandbox type of mode. But it needs to alert you to do, due to the snowball effect. If it's too late when you realize your mistakes, nothing will change.
This is all a problem because the campaign is several hours long. If it was 1 hour or so, you could experiment during the campaign. Since it's at least 3 or 4, this doesn't really work.
Anyway, that's it for my problems with the game.
Now, for the things I've found really interesting!
Between levels, you can buy upgrades, get discounts, etc. which is fairly generic, but you also have to select the land for the next level.
The map is divided into cells (though not a regular grid), in which every player (well, you and the NPCs) can bid for a given land. You can pay more to taken someone's land and this can happen quite a few times.
You don't know the value of each land, but you can get an idea by looking at the adjacent lands that have already been played by you or the NPCs. So, basically, you're trying to balance how much you spend (compared to the others)
with how much you
the land is worth! Pretty cool!
Building on this auction idea, in the end-game, you have to buy shares to become mayor of the town. Once again, every player wants to buy the shares, but the auction works differently: this time, the price goes down, and not up. But the first bidder gets the share.
This is, again, really cool! I'd actually be more interested in seeing this game being played by real people (if the campaign were shortened, I guess).
Since the price starts too high, everyone is trying to guess when other players will go for the share. Go too early and you spend too much on too little shares... wait too long and you've lost them!
I've actually come across auction related game theory in a class (just an overview, nothing very deep), so I'm probably finding this much more interested than anyone else (and myself at any other time, probably?...).
Still, it's a nice set of diversions to the main game that don't feel like pure filler. It's an interesting and
mini-game, in a sense.
Anyway, that's about it. These auctions aren't as interesting against an AI since you can more or less exploit them in subsequent playthroughs. So a multiplayer mode with a shorter, more focused campaign would be cool.

A lot of reviewers gave it rave reviews, but I do not necessarily agree with them. It's a good game, but it has some hangups. First, the jump control is not especially tight, and controlling your character on ice is unlike other games and uneccessarily frustrating. Additionally, the attack controls are unintuitive, as you have to hold towards your enemy to do damaging attacks which frequently dashes you into bad situations. While the two-button scheme would be effective, there are exactly one too many moves. It would do a lot better with a third button to access the kicks and allowing normal slashes on neutral. The hitbox on the basic slash is also very small.
While you get 3 hits before dying, the game often puts you in one-hit death situations where the life bar is irrelevant. It does this far too often. It also cheats with the checkpoint system; you are often unable to use a checkpoint even if you have one, simply because there is no solid ground or the solid ground is deliberately surrounded by buzzsaws that block your checkpoint activation.
While the gameplay is fun and a lot of the level design is very enjoyable, the game feels like it was made in the 1980s and has lots of irritating "pixel perfect" maneuvers. Also due to the limited use of the checkpoint system, it has long stretches where you cannot use a checkpoint and must run through lengthy gauntlets of obstacles.

At first the game might look like a perfect "pay to win" candidate, considering there are several DLC packs available unlocking ships for you. However, that's not really the case.
All ships available as part of DLC offers or to be bought with real world currency are more or less sidegrades or shortcuts. The most powerful ships however, can only be unlocked by playing the game. That's very nice and fair.
Unfortunately, you can describe the game with three words:
. And to be honest, that's sad, very sad, and also the reason why I can't really recommend this game without warning about this.
Let me explain the game in a few sentences:
You start out with the factions' basic ships. To obtain bigger ships, you'll have to earn "sync" points. With these you're able to level up ships. Once you've leveled a ship, you'll be able to unlock the next ship in the tech tree that's usually a small upgrade or a new ship fitting a different role.
In addition, you're able to upgrade parts of the ships or more specific modules that are installed on them: a primary weapon system (turrets), secondary weapon systems (typically missiles), a ship specific special ability (not upgradeable), and two support abilities. The problem: Upgrades won't transfer between tiers.
So game progress looks like this:
- Obtain a new ship.
- Invest (ingame) money, mission rewards (or real money) to level up the ship modules.
- Level up the ship to improve its power and unlock the next ship.
- Obtain a new ship and start over again.
And that's it, unfortunately. I guess I don't have to say that leveling the ships appears to take ages. While it's perfectly fine to not "finish" the progression part of the game within a week, it's really slow and tedious. Add to this the fact that the game's population isn't that high (typically 1000-3000 players online right now according to stats in the game), it happens that you'll have to wait one or two minutes to finally get into a PvE game. Queue times for PvP are usually slightly longer (sometimes 5 minutes or more).
And here's another problem: Due to the low population (and a very limited number of PvE missions), you're usually fighting with or against significantly stronger enemies. It's not uncommon to die within seconds versus a sniping frigate that's simply out of range for you. Once you're dead, you'll either have to wait 30-60 seconds (seems to depend on game mode) or till the next stage of the mission (in PvE). In addition, most mission stages take only two or three minutes, but there's a full minute of wait time between stages.
"Fortunately" there are ways to progress faster: You can buy the classic "booster" to gain more points, but you're also able to buy different ammo that will double your synergy gain. The unfair part: The costs! The initial price of the ammo module is 2 Standarts. That's not a lot. However, once unlocked it no longer shows any price. Although the module will still take 2 Standarts for every round you're playing. You won't see this unless you're paying close attention. And some of the costs... To upgrade a weapon from level 2 to level 3 you'll need something like 30,000 units of mission rewards: You'll get about 600 per mission - or buy the upgrade with real money. Do the math yourself.
And one more thing to remember: This game can only be played using keyboard and mouse. There is no controller support (neither gamepad nor joysticks). Also there seems to be a significant amount of auto-aim involved or there are really just big hitboxes. It's definitely far easier to hit enemies as it is in other games of this genre.

If you don't mind not progressing for a while or really having to start over several times, give it a try. You might like it. HIT is a good game. If you focus on the actual gameplay then it is a great game. If you go in expecting this game to be the best, most polished, most ambiguous game you have ever played then please leave this page and find another game. Also, if you're planning on playing this game solo or with only one other person then I suggest you find a few more friends to play it with and then come back. The whole setup for HIT doesn't really work with randoms but when you are with your friends, on LAN or talking over VOIP, it is really good.
The premise:
1 player is a rogue agent and the rest are operatives. The operatives' job is to launch a missile which requires fixing a generator, moving a statue to get its face scanned, pressing the right lever out of five (which operatives have information about) and then pressing a big button. The rogue agent's job is to stop that from happening. The rogue has the extra ability to recruit another player as a rogue too.
The 4 characters are quite simple in their mechanics but the dynamics when thrown together are very varied and certainly give HIT a major amount of replayability (I've played for 5.2 hours straight at this point).
The art design is pretty sweet, reminds me of Quantum Conundrum, and suits the game perfectly. The animations are good, character design is top-notch and the brief moments of voice work are a real surprise ("Medical license, shmedical license.") and the acapella mode makes me feel all warm and cuddly about the developers.
So let's get the bad out of the way, sadly what most of these 'reviews' are talking about:
Controller-madness: The game shows controller buttons quite often which is annoying but nowhere near the hyperbole of some other reviews.
Tricky Joining/Hosting: You have to make sure you only press ENTER once when loading in on the splash screen otherwise the server list doesn't load. Random. A little annoying. Not really a big deal (in a free game). I'm sure it's an easy fix.
Options menu: This leaves a lot to be desired but there's not much you should need to fiddle with anyway.

This is...a very interesting title.  However the flaws (outside bugs) make me wonder where it is going.
The controls are not necessarily unintuitive.  Just very unique.  And as a result they can be hard to wrap your head around for a few minutes.
They're really well done based on how the system is put together however.  I actually got used to them pretty easily.  I'm even rather surprised how much information/control they squeezed onto the buttons.  So much is practically one press away.
However there are some serious problems, bugs and flaws alike, that need addressed.
Bug: If you close the game with a build outline active, the outline will remain active and completely lock you out of building that item.  Still seeing how to get around this, short of reinstalling the game (verifying cache does not work).
Flaw: Tutorial does fail to explain a few things.  Granted a fair bit of those explanations (thus far) I could figure out on my own, but I do still recommend explaining more.  Things like how mining works and perhaps how to enable jetpack.
Bug: The state problem extends into the tutorial, and actually breaks it so you cannot get passed it if you finished it once already.  Very serious problem if you're looking for a refresher.
Flaw: On switch shortkey AND manual option.  I mean...are they both necessary?  Honestly?
All that aside thus far I'm really enthusiastic about where this game is going.  I cannot wait to see what technology and features come in the future.
TL;DR: If you are unsure about this title I'd recommend waiting a bit.  Put it on your wishlist for a while.  At least until they fix the tutorial so you can wrap your head around the controls safely.  But if you like SE definitely look into getting it.

Breakdown-
Gamplay: Almost identical to FC3s. Thought not a particularly bad thing, it feels a bit un-innovative. Karma events are a nice addition 8/10
Graphics: Gorgeous and well optimized. Even on mid-level performance PCs it can be ran on Ultra with solid framerates. 10/10
Story: Mediocre at best. Pales in comparsion to previous FC games. 5/10
Characters: Pagan Min is the most intriguing. Main protagonist & side characters are a bore. 6/10
Voice acting: Pagan Min is good. Side characters are alright. Main protagonist is abysmal. 7/10
Other: Requires f****** UPlay 0/10
Overall: 6/10
Reasoning-
If you are new to the Far Cry franchise, you will love this game. If you've played any of FC4s predecesors, you will view this as a disappiontment. I only say that because it doesn't live up to what FC2 and FC3 did best, story telling. 10 minutes into the story of FC3 and I was completely immersed. 10 minutes into FC4s story, and I was already bored. The story doesn't grip you, in any way really. The game doesn't succeed in grabbing my interest in what is happening in the story. I don't care about the Golden Path's cause, I don't relate to the main character, I don't feel compassion for the other main characters as I did in FC3...There is just nothing to grab on to here. Granted I have not played the story all the way through yet, so I hope it will get better. But the fact that I view playing the story as more of a chore than an experience is a testament to how bad it is. The most interesting character is of course Pagan Min, yet you hardly have any interaction with him after the first few hours of the game (so far, for me at least). Ajay's story is completely lacking in substance; why did he come to Kyrat? What was his life like before he traveled there? What reason does he have to help the Golden Path? The game makes no effort to explain the significance of Ajay's background, or the significance of his parents. The voice actor who plays Ajay really did a terrible job. There is no emotion delivered in the character's dialogue, so it's impossible to get a sense of how he feels in certain situations.
The gameplay is VERY similar to FC3. The are only a few new additions I've come across so far. Karma events are a welcome breath of fresh air. They have also added a neat feature where the enemy will try to re-take any outposts you've liberated. This makes the simulated civil war in the game more realistic. Auto-drive is also pretty convienent. The AI in this game seem to have super hightened senses that have no basis in reality. There have been several scenarios where I have been scouting an outpost from 100 or more yards away, take a shot with the sniper, miss, and are instanly spotted. Despite being hidden among underbrush and a wide variety of trees, the enemy immediately know the trajectory & source of an errant sniper shot. Assuming Ajay is smart enough to wear some camoflauged clothing, it'd be practically impossible to spot him through trees & underbrush from that distance. But my main issue with the gameplay is this: It's imppossible to defend against an eagle attack.
I don't have too much to say about the voice acting other than it's passable, save for Ajay, who is escpecially terrible.
Is this a bad game? No. Is this a good game? No. It's somewhere in the middle. The only way I would recommend this game is if you're getting it on sale. I would not recommend paying full price for this. The experience the game delivers isn't worth the full price. And more importantly, Ubisoft doesn't deserve it.

This game is disappointing. It feels incomplete - not because there is missing content (although, there might be after the point I stopped playing), but it just feels like the developers cared less and less as you progress through the story. The plot is pretty barebones from the start, but 22 hours into the game, I am literally running around gathering x for y for no good reason.
It's not so much that the quests are generic either (although they are). Rather, how random everything is. Often, I got some vague text like "you should find someone who knows X", without any other useful clues. I had to resort to randomly running around checking every nook and cranny of each (relatively large) world. Just Google "King's Bounty: Dark Side, where is..." The forums are filled with people getting stuck because there is no relationship between the content of some of the quests, and the things you need to do to solve it. Furthermore, the game feels "padded". There are quests that, upon completion, "humorously" reveal to you that you need to do more nonsense to complete them. That got old fast. If anything, you feel tricked.
What's good? Sadly, the things I enjoyed about the game only made me feel more disappointed because of the amount of potential wasted. The combat mecanics are of the classic similar-to-Heroes-of-Might-and-Magic persuasion. If you're into that sort of thing, it can be fun running around collecting troops for your expanding army. It can also get boring really quickly when weak enemies constantly overestimate their strength and charge at you, wasting your time. There are times where the game is genuinely funny, but those are few and far between. Most of the time, it just reads like amateurish writing.
I will admit I bought the game off the hype. I looked at the picture of Snow White, read about "Light and Dark", and though "Oh, cool, this will be a game about how members of the fairy tale community take sides, and wage war on each other". I found myself hunting for ♥♥♥♥ing dwarves on the behest of that stupid woman, only to have her disappear when I had killed them all.

A seamless blend of crafting, survival, and stealth, This War of Mine shines a sober light on the dim reality of war.
Scholar Miguel Sicart proposes in his book "The Ethics of Computer Games" that video games are effectively ethical systems that permit the player to explore the consequences of actions in a restricted setting. Super Mario Bros. provides a relatively linear ethical system (i.e., jump on bad guys to win), while games like the Grand Theft Auto series incentivize particular behaviors over others (i.e., it's more fun to break the law rather than follow the law in-game).
As an ethical system, This War of Mine rises above the rest in its insistence upon a robust range of real consequences. Player characters deteriorate in hunger, fitness, illness, and mental health without constant intervention and resupply of resources. The task of finding enough materials to survive opens up possibilities of scavenging, charity, theft, murder, and starvation—all of which impact the player characters accordingly. Once I got the hang of the game, I played through four full times, each with a different ethical approach. Real war inevitably leads people to act beyond their normal capacities, and This War of Mine provides an excellent simulator for those of us fortunate enough to never experience such tragedy.
Even for veterans of the survival and crafting genres, This War of Mine poses a real challenge. The game offers a wide variety of possible structures to build, but only a thoughtful and meticulous construction path will ensure victory. The variety of characters and settings also keeps the game fresh for several playthroughs. The music entices perfectly and complements the handcrafted war-torn graphics.
This War of Mine ranks among the best games I have played. The attention to detail of both the setting and player experience makes this a worthwhile investment.

Fantastic action platformer that blends precision platforming with beat em up melee combat.
The level designs are great, they have a sense of vastness, but they're not too long and end while still fun. The simple melee combat adds variety and blends with the platforming, as it forces you to use the environment to your advantage to kill enemies. The challenge level is also just right. It's tight enough so that every action feels involved and precise, but you're always able to improvise.
You can play it in a lot of ways too. You can play it with infinite respawn checkpoints that you earn and place by killing enemies. For more excitement, you can try no death runs of each stage, which is a completely different experience. If you want competition, you can play for score or speed runs (the game has separate leaderboards for each).
This is one of my favorite action platformers of all time. It has massive depth, challenge, and variety. It's exciting, and has great atmosphere. Highly recommended.

If you play this game, play all endings!! It's like Nier in the sense that you don't see the true ending until you do every route.
I actually cried 100 times, I played the 18+ version, which is currently free for a limited time, you can find it on their twitter or here , just look up Nekojishi 18+ english, though obviously there is some NSFW scenes in that!
This game is surpringsly well written, the dialogue is very real, every conversation feels true and not over the top like most VNs. I cried a lot, my face hurts. I also had to play through like 10 different endings (including the bad ones) to see what would happen, even the bad endings were well written though depressing obviously. Also lot's of save slots! I had to actually look up an ending guide to get all the endings then the one true ending, which I guess is a con but the true ending made it worth the hassle by far. There's a built in glossary of all the Taiwanese culture lingo used, a gallery, and below the gallery a collection of endings you've completed. Music is actually pretty impressive and some were even very powerful and emotional. If you take the time to run every ending, there is easily 20-30 hours of gameplay, which is a lot for a free VN.
The only cons I can think of is; Some messy translations throughout the game though with some imagination you can connect the dots and figure it out for yourself. Going through the story 10+ times to get every ending was a little tedious, but if you hold Ctrl down you can skip dialogue you've already read, if it stops and ctrl doesn't work, it means you are on text you haven't read yet, which was a nice indication of new text to look at, which helped greatly seeing some major and even minute differences in choices.**minor spoiler**  I wasn't a big fan of the Nier type rushed blog/computer endings, i wish they took the time to flesh those out and make them cutscenes. TOO MUCH CRYING.

You know how most games have "Psychological Horror" as a tag because of a funny meme?

So many crap lazy VNs being sold for money and one this creative and well-designed is free... what a world.
EDIT:
The story starts off as gay cat harem antics, but the true end goes off in an unexpected direction. Probably disappointing if you were expecting a more traditional route structure with happy endings, but I thought it worked well. It took me about seven hours to fully complete, but it'll take a bit longer if you read slowly and/or don't use a walkthrough.
There is an R18 version with a few explicit scenes, which is a nice bonus, but I'd recommend reading the all-ages version as well, since those alternative scenes touch more on the emotional and romantic side of the relationships.
The translation isn't bad (certainly much more readable than the translation of the store page), but there's lots of small errors (mostly forgotten capitals and misplaced punctuation) which can get kind of distracting.
The art is great and the animated chibi cut-ins are just adorable. I'm not a big fan of the style where the main character sprites have a single facial expression and all of the emotions are just shown in the side images, but the art direction is dynamic and expressive enough that it still worked for me.
Even if you're not into furry art or bara, I'd recommend
to any VN fan interested in the setting. I knew nothing about Taiwanese folk religion before, and I appreciated having the in-game glossary so I could learn some interesting new facts. Plus if anyone asks, you can say you're just playing an educational game =P

You know how Matt Damon used his smarts to figure out that eating poop potatoes was a viable way of surviving? That's because he was
, and that's kind of what Stationeers is all about.
In order to be successful in Stationeers you will need to learn how to design, construct and maintain complex atmospheric systems, power generation/distribution/management systems, systems for refining, processing, and utilizing mined resources, agricultural systems, medical/chemical systems, just to stay alive.
To really thrive you will need to master putting it all together to create stations with stable environments and motherships     capable of enduring the harsh conditions of a moon, planet, or the vacuum of space.
At the moment the game only has a fraction of it's planned content, but all the major systems are in and what's currently available is enough to provide endless amounts of gameplay. Bugs are being taken care of in actual-real-time thanks to the amazing dev team and new content is released almost, if not, daily.
This game has been my most satisfying digital purchase in years!

Thief is a good game cursed with an unfortunate title.
Due to the revolutionary nature of the original Thief games and their status as cult classics in the gaming community making a new edition in the series was always going to be like making a new Star Wars movie. Some people were going to hate it no matter what. While the game does have its flaws; for example, people are right to point out that many of the levels don’t offer much in the way of multiple approaches or exploration, it delivers a solid experience overall. I also never experienced any of the bugs that others claim to have run into.
While there are certain segments of the game where you can afford to be a little more aggressive, much of the game does require you to be stealthy and provides you with the tools you need to get the job done. Thief is challenging without being frustrating and offers you an incentive to complete side quests and explore the levels to steal loot by rewarding you with gold that you can spend on items and equipment. In other words, you really do get the feeling that you’re a master thief. The game’s plot is slightly above average and provides enough immersion and reasons to care about the characters to keep you going.
Ignore the haters, if you’re a fan of the stealth genre this game is worth picking up. Just don’t expect anything truly ground-breaking.

Somewhat interesting at the beginning, but quickly turns into a contrived juvenile narrarative
Maybe I'm being a big cynical here, but I guess I'm not exactly the target audience for this game...

First off, do not buy this game for its normal price on steam. It is not worth AT ALL.
I'm usually very into narratives, I even disconcern gameplay if the story is good enough, but this game really is just terrible. The main reason I say this is not because of the concept of movie-like games, but because in fact, the story REALLY IS TERRIBLE. I get that it's based off a true story, an excuse some would use to make the game's monotonous tone seem understandable, and I know that it's an indie, but this game could have been improved in so many ways.
The gameplay and the abrupt ending are probably the worst things about the game. While some do not necessarily do not enjoy games purely off gameplay, this one seems laborious. Not laborious in effort, but in waste of my time. It really is just waiting 3~5 minutes for a new, irrelevant message and the constant auto clicking. The dialogue did not compensate this in any way. If you're developing a unique, potentially succesful game like this, at least make an effort to not make the gameplay annoying, clunky, and laborious.
As for the abrupt ending, that really just came off as a "f*** you, I just wasted an hour of your life AND earned money as well!" kind of statement. It left me feeling that the developer did not work as hard as they could have and that they assumed that this was enough. The game literally skips through almost a whole year in just an hour. There was PLENTY they could have added to the game, even just some short scenes concerning some of these friends you apparently have.
All in all, I thank the Humble Bundle for only letting me spend $1 on this game, since I would have been a lot more angrier if I had paid the full price. Simply put, the story was very bland and had a lot of potential, and gameplay did not even work as a neutral factor; it purposefully made the game much worse.
Cringefest. Stay away like hell.

Cibele is...not really a game? It's an experience, a story, a short (~1 hour), poignant, and unflinchingly intimate one. It's young love and sex in the internet age: kids making mistakes together, learning about themselves and each other. Exploring Nina's computer -- seeing her photos, reading her conversations and emails and poetry -- is like seeing someone naked; not in a sexual way, but stripped bare, essentially human. Hearing her talk to Ichi, sensing the mixture of hesitation and eagerness on both sides of their conversation, knowing what will come and how it will affect the girl whose shoes you've stepped into...it's an experience unlike any other I've had in gaming. I remembered what it meant to be like to be young and in love like that, willing to forego everything else in pursuit of that one person, and felt a little hint of that long-ago glow -- along with a little embarrassment and wistfulness.
So, for a straight review: it's not a game. Don't look for gameplay. But as a story -- a very raw and intimate one -- I thought my hour with Cibele was one well-spent. I am happy that I picked it up as part of a Humble Bundle, though; $9 may be a little steep of an asking price. But I'd pay $5 for the experience easily, so keep an eye out for sales!

There are some things that I really, really liked about Olympia Rising, and some things that really, really frustrated me.
First off, the good things.
Chaining together combos feels great, it makes you feel like a mighty warrior and bonus coins make the entire thing an incredible joy when the combo is over and you are rich.
The exspansive, well put together levels that I loved to explore, running around and grabbing coins, fighting things, finding treasure rooms, all of that was great. If the whole game was just these levels, I would have so much fun with them.
Keeping your extra coins when you finish a level. A small thing, but it still felt really good. The game rewarded me for taking my time with a level, exploring all the nooks and crannies, and finding all the hidden treasure. It also created hope that eventually I would get so many coins that I could skip a level entirely because I can already pay the next fee. If I ever did this, it would have been amazing.
Now, the not so good things.
Enemies That Take More Than One Hit. Now, I realize that eventually, there has to be an enemy that takes more than one hit, but this breaks the pacing of the game. Before you find an enemy, you're jumping around and racking up a huge combo, after you find the enemy the combo is over. Everytime I saw minotaur/ice warrior/lamia/wizard/turret head/thing that I couldn't kill in one hit I knew that the combo, which was the fun part, had ended. A nice work around for this would be if the higher a combo the player had, the more damage they deal. This would mean that the game rewards the player for working an Enemy That They Can't Kill In One Hit into their combo, instead of punishing them for finding it.
Terrain That Looks Like The Background. This was something I kept finding, and everytime I did it was confusing. Normally, the background is dark and what you can walk on is bright. This game has dark background, bright terrain, and darkish other terrain that you cannot jump up through. This becomes such a hassle, trying to check where you can and can't go, in moments when I'm trying to hurry because lava death is flooding the level.
Levels That Flood With Lava Death. These things were a massive cause of frustration, because of what these levels try to be. They are expansive, well put together that I would love to explore and collect all the coins, but they are on a timer. This means I cannot explore the level or I risk death, I cannot collect coins or I risk death, I cannot search for hidden treasure or I risk death, and I cannot blindly jump combo through the level just trying to finish it as fast as I can or I might not have enough coins by the end. One of two things needs to be removed from the rising levels, either the coin number or the timer. Having both turns the level into a stressful, memory game. The first run of a rising level, I told myself "I am going to lose all my bonus coins." I knew that I would win eventually, but only when I had run the level so many times that I knew exactly which way to go and where enough coins were.
Slippery, Slidey Shoes. This was a problem on two occasions, when I was pushing through a rising level, and when I was trying to avoid the next issue.
Touch Damage. I know that touch damage is a staple in videogames, that enemies are not things I should be getting near. However, I mostly only have melee and there are some enemies that don't make sense to deal touch damage, like birds that are trapped in them sized cages. The other place this becomes a problem is with bosses, because bosses can suddenly change the size and shape of their hitbox. This doesn't feel like taking damage, this feels like being robbed of a health point.
You Cannot Use Magic After A Double Jump. This sounds minor, and it is, but the thunder magic is the only way to increase melee damage and reset jump combos. When I find an enemy with two health in a jump combo, I use the thunder magic to kill it and continue the combo, unless I need to double jump to get to it in which case the combo ends.
That's mostly it, there's a few more things. The water magic felt worthless because you had to stop moving, the jumping attack was so much better than the standing attack that the standing attack felt worthless, exploring downward didn't feel good because I couldn't see what was under me and would frequently take damage because of that.
So now, the final verdict, would I recommend this game?
NO. Don't get me wrong, there's some great ideas here, the game looks nice, parts of the game feel great, but there's so many little things that just wear on the player until the game becomes unfun. I can enjoy games that are challenging, when you win then that victory felt earned, not given, but this isn't challenging. It's frustrating. If the game was challenging, the player, if they are skilled and focus, be able to beat a level on their first try. They probably won't, but the possibility should still be there. With this, there's so many death that just came from things I couldn't see, or because I got stuck on terrain when trying to jump up, or because I took damage when I turned around to attack a stationary enemy. There is good in this game, but it does not outway the game's flaws.

Overview:
Olympia Rising is a game about a hero named Iola who was killed by The Father of All Monsters, but has been reawakened and has to reach Olympus to talk to Zeus. She meets Charon, a greedy ferryman who agrees to help Iola get to Olympus, as long as she collects enough money every level.
Pros:
-Great Music
I love the music in this game. The main theme is really catchy, and gets me excited for playing the next level.
-Funny Characters
While I've only met Iola and Charon, I think some of Charon's dialogue is really funny. Sometimes I'd find myself throwing Iola into the next boss to hear Charon's next death joke.
-Fun Bosses
The bosses in this game are original and great, and while they can be hard at times, you understand why you died and you learn from it. The deaths are almost always fair and the ones that aren't are few and far between. I can't decide which boss is my favorite.
-Combo System
With each level concentrating on gathering money, the combos reward you with more money. The combos are fun to pull off.
Cons:
-Overpowered enemies
Some of the enemies, your main source of money, are incapable of being part of combos, certain enemies take 3-5 hits before you can kill them. This means you either finish your combos for the money, or ignore them.
-The Magic
The magic abilities are pretty much useless. The fire enchantment is ok for enemies you want to deal with from the distance, but the others do diddly-squat. I'd much rather use the magic for the double jumps.
While this game isn't perfect, the easy to learn gameplay, the music, and character(s?) have me coming back to play it every once in a while.
I give this game an 8.5 out of 10. Would recommend.

I initially bought this for its muted pastel 8-bit aesthetic; in that regard,
succeeds very well, its art and music absolutely superb. The coin collecting is somewhat monotonous, sure, but understandable given the mythological Grecian theme and largely balanced out by solid level design.  One might even consider this game as a hidden gem.
They would be right were it not for a handful of unforgivable errors.
The controls? Slippery. Iola moves with *way* too much momentum for the level of precision
asks out of the player; expect to consistently under/overshoot jumps or run into enemies by accident before your muscle memory begins to compensate.
The platforms themselves don't fair much better, either, frequently indistinguishable from background objects and rarely passable from below, failed chain jumps almost always traceable back to this point; two crippling design flaws at their worst.
Oh, and did I forget to mention that the hit detection feels unfairly biased?
All in all, consider this a neutral/cautious recommendation: acolytes of the platformer genre are likely to plow through the flaws and frustration factor without *too* much complaint. Everyone else? Probably not.

It's a great game. It has the pro of free-to-play, which makes it easy to get, but also the con of having to wait for construction and healing of the wounded, or pay. However, all resources can be collected in game, even silver and gold, and there is no type of resource that can only be bought with real money. The base building is combined with economy elements of surrounding building bonuses, and the terrain landscaping to avoid floods is a nice challenge. The battles are realistic and combine a variety of abilities to unlock and improve for your soldiers. The graphics are sweetly honed, not too demanding even for lower-end pcs, and you can also zoom a little.
The only negatives are that to create a new game you need a new account, that it is hard to figure out what each unit excels at, that you can't skip the tutorial -which forces you to build some inconvenient buildings-, and that you can't have two in-game windows open at the same time, to sort, e.g., your army according to the demands of a mission.
Definitely worth a try.

I really wanted to like this game, because initially it looked pretty cool in its movement and aesthetic, but there are too many imperfections for me to recommend this.
The fun ideas that Olympia Rising has (such as the chain system) are entirely undone by the multitude of pet peeves I've encountered in the span of 90 minutes. Zero button configuration and by extension being forced to use the D-Pad on an Xbox 360 controller. Camera swivel being so overdone to the point this game is one of the few that actually struck me with motion sickness. The inability to move the camera below you when you need to descend, resulting in numerous blind jumps and making the already annoying enemy placement all the more grating when exploring. The game effectively only using two buttons on the controller yet insisting to employ down + X for special abilities, which is cumbersome for quickly moving about and simultaneously dispatching more durable enemies. Progression being gated by having to collect a specific amount of coins, only to be met with a unbearably sassy skeleton ridiculing you with unwitty remarks for every level. Inconsistent hitboxes, no health bars for bosses, shrill audio cues, ...
It's a genuine shame too, because Olympia Rising isn't
and the majority of these shortcomings could've been resolved through (relatively) minor tweaks.

Imagine FTL but instead of a ship you're given a shack. Your crewmembers are replaced with civilians who constantly get sad, hungry, and sick. They will also have crippling addictions to substances(coffee and cigarettes.) Instead of blowing up enemy ships and saving a Federation you're digging through trash piles and robbing other people's homes to find food, medicine, and scrap.  Also like FTL, any instance of person-to-person combat is awkward but gives you more stuff. It will also depress the hell out of your characters which is lovely, since morality of the things you do matter more.
If you haven't played FTL, This War of Mine is about running around grabbing stuff and dealing with other sad, hungry humans  at night while trying to optimally manage the limited resources you're able to acquire during the day.
Good little game to spend a few hours on and its perspective on war as depressed starving civilians is a nice different take  instead of the usual "playing as a supersoldier" archetype of most shooters.
I recommend having some snacks handy while you play because of all the little prompts screaming "HUNGRY" on every character of every day will only increase your appetite as you progress.
This game pulls you in like very few.  Definitely has the feel of a game one plays on the phone, but it is quite compelling.  I highflying recommend it.

A personal story I would like to share is one i have kept with me and one I will remember every time i want to play again. because it only motivates me further to find moments similar to it.
SO
We were running low on food. so much so in fact, that we found ourselves contemplating stealing from inhabited places. I had sick, hungry and wounded, and our situation was only going to get worse.
Fortunatley for us, Katia, a woman who had lost touch with her parents before the war, longed to see a home without conflict. She would be willing to anything to get us through to the end, and stealing from killers was no exception.
We had already built makeshift weapons to hold off looters, but now, we were to become such. Katia took with her a knife, small enough to keep hidden, but piercing enough to put down someone whom may alter her chances of escape.
On entering the old apartment, she quickly found fortune in the cabinets, in fridges and even in the basement, as filled to the brim with rubble as it was. There was a glimmer of hope that we may make one more week, or at least be able to hold out until someone may come to aid us. But as it is in this war of mine, hope never lasts long.
Katia became greedy, and tried to climb higher into the building to find the better supplies. and it was here she was spotted. a young girl, maybe only a couple of years younger than herself, found her hiding away in the gaps of the walls.
panicked, katia attempted to run back across the collapsed corridor, with a drop that would surely destroy her. but in her path stood a burley man, wielding a shotgun that was just as menacing as he. katia was shaken, and it seemed all she would be able to do was run as he shoots her down.
But this was not the case. katia lunged at the man, before he could fire a shot, and plunged the knife into his belly. this was all it took, as he fell backwards into the pit, freeing katias exit route. as she ran home, all she could belive was that what she had done was wrong, the girls would be alone, and likely starve. there is no telling what would happen, however, if one other just like katia would return to the house.
especially, due to the fact, that katia took the shotgun from the mans now cold, dead hands as she left. there is only innocence in death, and despite katias efforts, it would soon be all but herself that would be innocent, in the house to which she retreats.

This game about building urban subway transit systems is deceptively deep. It looks at first glance like any typical, simplistic indie puzzle game, but very quickly you'll start to realize how sophisticated the game mechanics and AI actually are. The user interface, from the main menu, to the online high-score tables, to clicking-and-dragging your train tracks around the screen, are both super easy to use and very cool looking--and everything works flawlessly. The rules of the game are actually pretty complicated, and I won't go into them here--but you can start playing without much understanding of what's going on, and pick things up gradually and casually, which is a feature I always like... If you're interested in games that are super clean and cute, and easy to get started with, but then suck you into hours and hours of increasingly complex sessions, then here's one you definitely want to nab.

Delightfully peaceful and yet engaging, Mini Metro is a zen-like puzzle challenge where the goal is to move the people where they want to go by creating an elegant but capable transport network of brightly coloured lines.  The calm music belies the building tension of panic and stress as your network and city grow, more passengers appear, and your comprehensive design becomes increasingly compromised, fragile, and complicated.  And yet it's still so fun to pull the stretchy lines from one place to another, rerouting the trains and trams from one station to the next as you sink into a flow of light, geometry, and sound.  Short, simple, and yet endlessy entertaining, Mini Metro is is a game you'll be surprised to find yourself playing late into the night.

Gigantic is like a bizarre cross between League of Legends and Overwatch.
From League, you get parts of the three-lane map concept, the variety of heroes built for various roles (from snipers to pure-melee to casters to healers and so on) and the 'protect your big thing and attack their big thing' match basis.
From Overwatch comes the snarky one-liners between heroes, the instant access to your full power/attack retinue (though you can power them up to your choosing as you progress through the map) and the nobody-ever-using-chat-properly-to-communicate. Which actually doesn't matter as much as you might think.
Characters include Totally-Not-Bastion AKA HK-206, Not-Battleborns-Attikus AKA The Margrave and Every-Sniper-Character-Ever aka Imani. To say the game is a bit lacking for originality in some of it's roster would be an understatement, but it has other characters such as Griselma, Charr and Tyto the Swift who make up for it with much closer to original skill and play styles.
And hell, it's free. There's the usual weekly rotation of free characters or you can unlock them permanently in exchange for 5k, 10k or 13k in-game currency, depending on the character - which isn't super hard to gather. 5K is easily achievable in 5 or 6 matches if you play decently and keep up on your Fortune Card 'quests'.
Long story short, give it a go. It's plenty active right now and I'd hate to see another visually pleasing and original hero-based PVP game go down the crapper because everyone's too busy deciding if they'd rather take Mei or Tracer on their body-pillow to the prom.

If you ever wanted to know what Mario 3 mixed with 300 hits of blotter acid and the necronomicon looked like, this is it. Released by Spooky Squid Games, They Bleed Pixels is a controller destroyer, and may very well leave you with an aneurysm. With that being said, it’s not only one of the hardest games I’ve ever played, but one of the best. This is what pixel art is supposed to look like and sets a standard for its genre. They Bleed Pixels is a gothic styled game with a cryptic feel, and is visual rush from the moment you begin.
Starting this game puts you in a nostalgic state, and is like pressing play on your favorite 90′s B film. At first I wasn’t sure what I was in for, but when the first cut scene of pixel animation began to play I was in awe. The cryptic visuals and dark feel, combined with the pixellated brutality would have been enough for the ESRB to rate this one Mature in 1992, but these days it’s exactly what indie gamers are looking for. The soundtrack goes perfect with gameplay and if you can catch the rhythm it’s an entirely different experience in itself. Morbidly enough before each level, the loading screen features different quotes from H.P. Lovecraft, Edgar Allan Poe and other related people of the occult. All of this together puts They Bleed Pixels in another category of its own with its instant visual appeal and dark, haunting music.
You are a young girl arriving at what you are told is a boarding school, Lafcadio Academy for Troubled Young Ladies. Unprepared for the violent nightmares that plague your dreams and transport you to other worlds, you are sent onto a journey that will take you to hell and back. Worse yet, her dreams are intruding into her waking life, slowly altering her flesh into the demonic form of her night terrors. While in the library she notices a book on the top of one of the book shelf. When she goes closer she notices a drop of blood come down on her hand. Your goal is to destroy the mysterious blood-soaked book that appears to be the root of her troubles, collecting pages throughout the game. Will you be able to make it through, or will her transmutation from girl to clawed horror become complete?
The game consists of chapters and different dreams make up the levels within each of them. Instead of points you collect pints, which after collecting a certain amount filling your power bar allowing you to not only save but replenish your health at the same time. Super Meatboy-esq, your dead corpse is left behind as a reminder of your past failures and attempts to complete each seemingly impossible level. They Bleed Pixels focuses on close up melee, utilizing the monstrous claws given to you in the beginning of the game. Different button sequences make up each strike or move allowing for combo hits awarded by extra “pints.” At the end of each dream you are given a report card, sticking with the boarding school theme. You are ranked based on lives lost, how many pints of blood you have collected, highest combo and how many pages of the spell book you have found.
They Bleed Pixels has an extras section in the main menu that includes bonus levels that are unlocked by completing each dream. You also are given badges with a manifold of different things to accomplish similar to the achievement system on XBox360 or Steam. The extras section also includes an art gallery with several pictures by different artists that you are able to unlock by beating each chapter. And of course, just incase you didn’t get everything you could out of the cut scene when you first saw it, the extras also offers a video section.
Games like They Bleed Pixels are fun no matter what or when you play them. The attack on your senses is endless from the moment you begin to the moment you end. Everything comes together perfectly from the story line to gameplay to the intense soundtrack and pixel art, They Bleed Pixels is another essential in any gamers library.

I honestly don't understand the hate this game receives.  The original series (Thief: The Dark Project and Thief 2: The Metal Age) are far-and-away my favorite games of all time, and I both played and level edited for them both heavily back when they first came out.  While this reboot of the series is certainly no Thief or Thief 2 in terms of its storyline, characters, or memorable factions (can you really top Hammerites, Pagans, and Mechanists?), I still think it is a good game and actually signicantly improves on the stealth gameplay in the original series, lockpicking mechanic, and really takes the open world hub aspect of Thief 3 and fleshes it out to a much more satisfying extent.  The graphics are gorgeous even years after launch, and even though there are areas the game could have been better mechanically in addition to the aspects already mentioned, if you're looking for a modern stealth experience I'd say there's nothing that holds a candle to this new Thief.
Add: In comparison to Dishonored, it's a different game and people who make the comparison without clarifying their thoughts are being disingenous and, frankly, not very critical in their thoughts. After playing through the entire Thief: Gold game and most of the Metal Age (lost my save progress about 75% of the way through, currently replaying it), I was sad to hear the negative/mixed reviews about this game. But regardless, it's still a Thief game so I went into it with an open mind. Upon starting a new game, I modified it as much as possible to resemble the original series. Such as no Focus (still don't really know what that is), no minimap (except for free roaming), no loot glint, Master difficulty, no waypoint, and of course, I do not knock out any guards/people, unless I absolutely have to. I also run away from combat rather than engaging in it. And honestly I'm enjoying the game. The maps of the missions may not be as open as those of the previous games, but there are still multiple points of entry, still secrets, still shadows to hide in, pockets to pick... just like the original games. Another one of the major changes to this game is the narrative is much more focused.
Most of the characters aren't anything special, but one that shines is Garrett. The voice actor is different in this game, but he still does a fine job of playing the sly, sarcastic thief. However, this game isn't without its faults, I'm not suggesting it should have won any awards. I would recommend the older games over this one anyday. But for what it's worth on sale, this game definitely has some stealthy enjoyment.

I wrote a review already, but steam apparently didn't post it properly. Oh well, I'll try to give you the highlights.
Pros
+graphics
+sound
+music
+level design
+boss design
Cons
-floaty movement
-small weapon hitbox and larger enemy hitbox than the visible boundaries
-first boss is the most difficult enemy in the game...by several orders of magnitude
-coin collection as barrier to further levels
-inability to pan camera
-password system (what is this, 1990? At least it looks cool)
This game would be great for things like speed runs, but due to the coin collection, you're forced to backtrack through branching paths. Backtracking wouldn't be so bad, but you can't pan the camera. I've taken many unnecessary hits as a result of this. I think a timer system (one that ticks down per level and one that ticks up throughtout the game for speed runs) would be a much better system for this game. I beat it in about 2 hours. It's enjoyable enough, but the faults will keep me from returning to it. Don't let the first boss get you down -- difficulty wise, it should've been the final boss. The bosses would even be a ton of fun if not for the rediculous hit boxes. Between enemies having too large of a damaging hitbox and the protagonist having floaty controls, I died more times than was reasonable to what I feel is poor design. Level design, sound, and music are really great. The art style is pleasant and unique. Try to pick this game up in a sale if you're on the fence. I think it's worth $5, but the cons truely are frustrating. I may sound overly negative, but I hope the dev will be watching the comments and improve. Maybe I'll come back to it one day in the hopes this is the case. Considering the price point, I will still recommend this game as it stands.

Harrowing but fascinating narrative driven survival game.
The resource management minigame is brutal and if you try and play like a "good" person, you will likely die (tragically true). And the platform style stealth game is tight and enjoyable, mixing a timed challenge with the usual "avoid the sight of guards" trope.
The game walks a dangerous line between highlighting and trivialising the struggles of people in conflict zones but does an excellent job of making you really empathise with the people who suffer from this around the world (as much as you can from a comfy chair in a safe country).
Watch some reports on what's going on in Syria or the Ukraine before playing to really have the reality hit home.

Imagine FTL but instead of a ship you're given a shack. Your crewmembers are replaced with civilians who constantly get sad, hungry, and sick. They will also have crippling addictions to substances(coffee and cigarettes.) Instead of blowing up enemy ships and saving a Federation you're digging through trash piles and robbing other people's homes to find food, medicine, and scrap.  Also like FTL, any instance of person-to-person combat is awkward but gives you more stuff. It will also depress the hell out of your characters which is lovely, since morality of the things you do matter more.
If you haven't played FTL, This War of Mine is about running around grabbing stuff and dealing with other sad, hungry humans  at night while trying to optimally manage the limited resources you're able to acquire during the day.
Good little game to spend a few hours on and its perspective on war as depressed starving civilians is a nice different take  instead of the usual "playing as a supersoldier" archetype of most shooters.
I recommend having some snacks handy while you play because of all the little prompts screaming "HUNGRY" on every character of every day will only increase your appetite as you progress.
This game pulls you in like very few.  Definitely has the feel of a game one plays on the phone, but it is quite compelling.  I highflying recommend it.

A personal story I would like to share is one i have kept with me and one I will remember every time i want to play again. because it only motivates me further to find moments similar to it.
SO
We were running low on food. so much so in fact, that we found ourselves contemplating stealing from inhabited places. I had sick, hungry and wounded, and our situation was only going to get worse.
Fortunatley for us, Katia, a woman who had lost touch with her parents before the war, longed to see a home without conflict. She would be willing to anything to get us through to the end, and stealing from killers was no exception.
We had already built makeshift weapons to hold off looters, but now, we were to become such. Katia took with her a knife, small enough to keep hidden, but piercing enough to put down someone whom may alter her chances of escape.
On entering the old apartment, she quickly found fortune in the cabinets, in fridges and even in the basement, as filled to the brim with rubble as it was. There was a glimmer of hope that we may make one more week, or at least be able to hold out until someone may come to aid us. But as it is in this war of mine, hope never lasts long.
Katia became greedy, and tried to climb higher into the building to find the better supplies. and it was here she was spotted. a young girl, maybe only a couple of years younger than herself, found her hiding away in the gaps of the walls.
panicked, katia attempted to run back across the collapsed corridor, with a drop that would surely destroy her. but in her path stood a burley man, wielding a shotgun that was just as menacing as he. katia was shaken, and it seemed all she would be able to do was run as he shoots her down.
But this was not the case. katia lunged at the man, before he could fire a shot, and plunged the knife into his belly. this was all it took, as he fell backwards into the pit, freeing katias exit route. as she ran home, all she could belive was that what she had done was wrong, the girls would be alone, and likely starve. there is no telling what would happen, however, if one other just like katia would return to the house.
especially, due to the fact, that katia took the shotgun from the mans now cold, dead hands as she left. there is only innocence in death, and despite katias efforts, it would soon be all but herself that would be innocent, in the house to which she retreats.

MORE CARDS. MORE STRATEGY. BIGGER STORY. Collect 1,300+ earnable cards, battle in 60+ single-player campaign missions, and emerge victorious in epic online duels. Wow, that's an overstatement if I ever seen one...
Magic Duels is another incarnation of Magic the Gathering in digital form. If you don't know what MtG is, it's an insanely popular and deep fantasy card game. In comparison the digital version is extremely lacking. The campaign is ok-ish, you have some preset decks and fight several preset scenarios. Apart from that you have access to playing vs AI or vs human opponents. All would be well if not the fact that deckbuilding is heavily limited.
First thing, same as in the physical version you have different sets available in the game, but only limited number of cards from these sets are available in the game. Second thing, you have to grind your♥♥♥♥♥off to get the cards. Or buy them using real money in the store. Yes, you get some basica cards after finishing each campaign, but to be able to build some competitive decks you have to slog through many battles with just basic commons. I love MtG, I played on national level many many years ago, but Magic Duels is so limiting it's not really fun.
I liked:
* it's MtG
I disliked:
* long and boring grind before you are able to build competitive decks
Get this if:
* you have to have everything MtG in digital form
Don't get this if:
* you expect actual MtG in digital form (go for Magic Online then)
* you're ok with slow and boring grind before you can build your own decks
Surprisingly the even more limiting previous versions, called then MtG: Duels of the Planeswalkers, were more fun than this one.

They also share the unique ingame stories aspect.
You often manage to get yourself (And your friends) into unique situations that are worth telling others about, and the fact that you shared that story with someone else (in MP) just makes it so much cooler.
The UI is doing something new, instead of settling with the current formate of drag-and-drop they are keeping you in the game with a 'hand' system, in basic you use the F key for pretty much everything.. The one area where I'm maybe a bit worried is the lack of feedback from the different systems, something that seems to be by design - While you got a tablet ingame that can provide some info, I feel as if an easier way should be provided, it just feels like the game is difficult enough that 'hunting' for the information is a bit over the top.. I would for example like to see how much power my generator is creating by simply looking at it, or how much power my door is taking and so on.
Overall I recommend the game for anyone looking for something more complex that can be played with friends.
