When 99% of negative reviews are based on
, perhaps that's precisely the problem. Such a lack of accessibility for the average player is definitely hurting the game, which would otherwise be more successful simply by virtue of the complexity and quality of its existing systems and mechanics.
I was a fan of SS13, but I played it
of the bad controls. Copying a bad system has resulted in a controlscheme which is even worse...
. I cannot think of another game I've played in recent years that features controls as bad as this.
The irony here is that as a result of adhering to their rationale of "not wanting to put interfaces between you and the game (paraphrasing),"
. They certainly do for me.
After nearly 5 hours of attempting to play despite poor controls and interface, I no longer have any desire to subject myself to the frustration and tedium of fumbling with the controls just to perform simple tasks. The controls are just a barrier between the player and the game. I intend to simply wait until the controls have been improved—or even better, completely overhauled— to try the game again.
This one design decision has only lead me to a lack of faith in the developer's ability to make an
game, so I'm not really sure what to expect from them in the future. Perhaps they'll overhaul the controls, which would improve the experience immensely. It seems just as likely that they'll continue their reluctance to make concessions in design in order to improve accessibility, so they can continue to strictly adhere to their limited vision of the game. That would be a mistake, in my opinion, and consists of a big part of the recipe for a dead game.
SS13 succeeded *in spite* of its crappy controls. Don't make the same mistakes they did.
Despite my issues with the controls as listed above, there is a lot about the game that I
like.
There is quite a bit more to build and mess around with than I expected at this point. With that said, most things aren't really intuitive, so there's a lot to figure out but little to go on. Many UI elements are confusing, though the devs are already working on improving that.
There is a lot of player freedom when it comes to object placement and setup, and building works quite well. However, going back to controls...
I've encountered some issues like crashing/disconnects and some weird errors, and while such issues are fairly frequent, the devs are working to stomp them out.
From what I can tell, there is no autosave feature. So... you have to save a lot. Kind of annoying, but again, not an issue I expect to persist for very long. If another player in your game crashes, you need to re-launch the game so they can join again, because simply reloading the save doesn't work for some reason. I assume that will be fixed soon too.
I enjoy the complexity of what's already in the game. There's a lot to it, and a lot of fun to be had setting things up, getting more machines, hooking them all together and figuring out how everything works and how you can make it work for you. The foundation of a fun and rewarding game is already there, and it's pretty solid. I like what the devs are shooting for, especially the various kinds of interactions between all the bits and pieces of systems and components in the game.
There are a number of similar games which do an excellent job of handling user input and interface management without sacrificing the experience and player awareness of the environment. The developers would do well to take a loot at games like these, such as Astroneer and Subnautica. Accessibility is key.
I recommend waiting a while to see what improvements the developers make. Right now they seem to be trying to excuse away poor design by referencing vague, big-picture ideas that the average player has no stake in. Well, that and explicitly copying content and design straight from the game's biggest inspirations: SS13, Space Engineers, etc. That isn't necessarily a problem, except for the cases where having the exact same functionality just. Doesn't. Work.

Original review: "It's like sonic the hedgehog 2"
The reason I said that is partly because I replayed sonic 2 in the same week I played this game, but also because both games share a commonality in a certain raw gameplay appeal.
This game has amazingly tight controls. They're simple and intuitive - an asset somewhat spoiled by the inclusion of a pointless tutorial system followed by on-screen directions at the beginning of the first level. However, don't fear this game staying too easy for long, it gets crushingly difficult - to the point of spending tens of minutes at each obstacle.
The tight controls are complimented by amazing visual and sound direction, which make the whole experience just plain satisfying to play. Checkpoints are left by standing still when you've collected enough blood from enemies & orbs (this game's 'coin') and respawning is near instantaneous - culminating in a fluent, frustrating and fabulously eldritch experience.
I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a challenge of skill, and the good type of trial and error - in which each attempt brings you ever so closer to victory. I also recommend that, if you can, play this with a buddy and a controller, trading off when one player gets too frustrated - the competitivity and camaraderie, as well as the opportunity to take rests, will make for a more enjoyable overall experience.

What I expected to be a heartfelt and introspective look at relationships, on par with Digital: A Love Story, turned out to be a poorly written, overly simplistic and angsty tale that bordered on fan-fiction, which, given the context of the story, It very well may have begun as.
The 'gameplay' segments are absurdly simplistic with next to no polish, to the extent that they could be replicated in Scratch with very little difficulty. The 'Fully interactive desktop' that the game description touts is, in actuality, nothing more than completely banal text documents which reveal almost to no information about anything relative to the story. The epitome of meaningless side content.
The short film segments that bookend each 'chapter' sway between being boring and uninteresting (although admittedly they are at least relatively well shot) and being cringeworthy in their portrayals of budding romance between adults.
If there is one thing, however, that I could say this game has going for it, it would be the voice acting in the calls between the main character and her prospective lover. Overall they gave a somewhat believable performance that made me smile a couple of times.
Basically, this 'game' is someones final term project, wrapped up and put on steam for profit. I assume. If this is the case then fair enough it is an impressive effort for a student project but as a professional effort it falls short in too many ways to count.
Do yourself a favour and save the £6 for something competent.

Cibele doesn't feel like a game, and it shouldn't. When you're buying a narrative driven game, "game" is just a word to describe the interacions that connect your experience with the story the developer is trying to tell you. That piece of knowledge spares you from dissapointment and also helps you make the right choice.
There's no playing here. It's like living (spying) someone else's life for a couple of hours. You get to check Nina's computer, her mails and photos. You can also read her poems and check her website backups, her posts... All of that helps you understand this 19 year old girl. Then you click on the game's icon and click around making her avatar play the game as you get deeper in her story. Reading and replying her PM's in the game and checking what she's into as each chapter advances.
The story is as good as real life is. There's no romantic twist in real life, we're not playing a "Love Actually" game here, just teenage love at ii's highest. If you're playing Cibele right there are a lot of feelings involved, you should be able to get past pretty pictures and funny chatlogs.
It's also very short and it ends kind of abrutly. But hey! that's also how it really happened so, why lie about it when you make a game about a real life event?
I liked it and love the genre. Sometimes it's best to play a narrative game for a couple of hours than to watch a film.

The story, minimal at best, is pieced together by a boring series of clicks and extremely poor controls.  This would be fine if the story was engaging.  After the sudden ending however (seriously, you can beat this in less than 10 minutes), you'll discover this plot was anything but.
I don't want to attack the game too viciously as this is obviously a personal project and a deeply personal story, as minute and simplistic as it is.  In that regard, this seems more like a self-reflective piece for the author of the game, covering a clearly important part of her life.  While relatable, it just falls flat.  To me, it feels like she planned for more, but got tired of programming and designing halfway through.
My only respite is that this came with a Humble Bundle.  I would be very aggravated if I spent even a dollar on this.
Nina, while I appreciate the effort, get back to the drawing board.  Or stick to independent film.

It's not a bad game but it's horribly scripted. All FPS games are scripted to some extent but this one is extreme. For example I have to get from the ground to a rooftop. From where I'm standing I can see many possible paths to the roof but only one path matters and that's the one that's hard-coded into the game. I may want to jump on a box on the left, then onto a fence, and then leap and grab the roof and pull myself up. Unfortunately, I can't jump on the box on the left because it's not highlighted and I can't interact with it. It registers as too high although it's identical to the box on the right. I CAN jump on the right box however and then find other things I can interact with to get to the roof. It's frustrating being unable to interact with 95% of the items on screen because the developer has left me only one way to do any particular thing. I can spin my wheels forever and never get anywhere until I find that magical formula that was the intended path.
The entire game is like that. Parts are fun and their storytelling is nice but the limited nature of the interface made me lose interest every time another game came out. You should judge on whether the strictest form of linear game appeals to you. If it doesn't, they you won't like this at all because it's among the most linear I've ever played.

This game offers a two mode game similar to Campaign and Battle in Total war, but remade as "mini-town building" and "mini-tactical battles". Think a slow moving yet somewhat compact version of a Total War with other feature in mind. I find myself doing more landscaping and "town planning" by hex buildings -  This aspect is quite new but interesting because it gives something to explore for new players who come sign-up (although from this point, maybe people decide whether the game is their style or really hate how it does not feel like Total War).
For battles, don't expect to see huge army stacks in epic battle. But quick skirmish with smaller "army groups" but with upgradeable and persistent soldier units. If you like a bit of RPG-element of improving stats and selecting which one to focus (although, there are not too many to worry about).
If you dislike the trend of "freemium" games nowadays by any type and aspect, please beware of the "time limiter" of progress of both the town building and unit management for battles (the replinishment). While gold can still be acquired in game, it is not plenty and if you are not the waiting type, you may have to choose between paying real-life money to speed things up.
So, adjust your expectation, think more like a "small-town army" manager game - with "mobile-style freemium" limits to action. If you can do this, then Total War Battles: Kingdom is a quick-fix game you can have on computer and take with you if you so feel attached to your hex town and warbands of upgradable units. It can still be likeable depending on your initial expectation.

This is a pretty neat little 2D action-platformer game! The main focus here is definitely the combat, but it's designed in a way that feels pretty platformer-y as well. Killing an enemy gives you your two jumps back (reminds me of Dustforce in a way) and chaining enemies together using these extra jumps nets you more coins per enemy. The goal of each stage is to make it to the end with a certain amount of coins in tow, and the further the game progresses, the higher this number goes, and the longer the stages get. The end result is, unfortuntaely, a difficulty curve based mainly around level length, though each new world gives you an extra heart so you can survive a bit longer. Health pickups are more than sufficient, and tend to be very useful, as avoiding damage in this game is no easy feat. I never found myself having trouble getting enough coins either, if I searched around the level a little bit I ended up having more than enough. Coins can carry into the next level, too, but are lost if you die - I can see this making for some interesting speedrunning strats, certainly. I feel like this could be a pretty good speedrunning game, really, it's fast-paced and pretty challenging though never unfair. If I had to lodge a few other minor complaints, it *is* a bit short, but the game's not particularly expensive anyways. The wall jump also feels a little wonky at times (primarily around thinner platforms). I also found the music to not really fit, it's pretty forgettable and pretty minimal most of the time. Nothing huge though and I did enjoy my time with this game, as brief as it was. Will probably replay it at some point though!

Stationeers is off to a great start!  I've been in the early access trap more than a couple times, I can safely say Stationeers has rolled out in great shape!

I'm definitely looking forward to seeing where this game goes.  Already off to a great start, and new things coming every day.  I'm 14 hours into my current station, and there's more work to be done!

This game is a Tactical RPG, with an affection system with several female members.
The main problem with this game is that the heart of the gameplay, the tactical fighting is incredibly boring. Each battle is set on a board delimited with squares (which is usually the norm) and each character has "combo tiles" linked with them. That means that if another character is staying in one of those, you can chain both characters and possibly chain skills which become even better skills. Sounds cool actually right? Well in theory yes... but since all characters have different combo tiles, you are pretty much forced to move the team in a certain way to combo, even if the positioning makes no sense. The combo system being the heart of the game, you can't really win without and essentially all battles will turn into a move A to that space, move B there so they can combo, so C has to be there and D there etc... It made the game horribly repetitive even for a TRPG and I abandoned after a few hours...

The goal is to prevent a missile launch by completing three objectives, while each round one of the players is secretly working against the others, with the goal of sabotaging their efforts and even killing them off one by one.
I could have seen this game being really popular, I could see this game become a "hit" but now that the launch has been so terrible I don't think it ever will be.  Its a small game, so if you have some friends I recommend you try the game I am sure that if you get it to work you and your friends will be able to have a good deal of fun. So I've edited this review four times and here are my final thoughts about Gigantic. It's new, so the content is very lackluster, but don't let that deceive you, because for what they are lacking. Gigantic makes up with a lot of new features and interesting mechanics in a MOBA. In terms of games I'd say it's a cross between Smite and something along the lines of Battleborn/Overwatch.
You have two titan things that basically attack each other and by doing objectives around the map you earn points for your titan and once you have earned 100 your titan goes rampage mode and you get the opportunity to attack the enemies titan. Each titan has 3 health bars and when they're all gone you win. There are some other mechanics to the game, but those can be learned from playing the game.
I haven't played long, but I am really enjoying it because I'm going through a rough patch in games and can't seem to find something to catch my interest; since all the genres I want to play have♥♥♥♥♥♥games or because I won't be able to play a something I want till 2018. Gigantic is unique, it's original and can keep someones attention for quite some time. The fast pase style makes it enjoyable and allows you to play a MOBA like TDM mode. Because of the way the game is set up I feel you could be doing literally anything at any given time and you'd be benefitting your team. For example while the enemy titan is down, you could be attacking other players and allowing your carries to nail on it more, you could be increasing the strength of your own nodes, or you could be attacking an enemies nodes to deny them some needed power.
Overall the game is 7/10 for me, I'll redo the score when I see a larger increase of playable people and maybe a different map, because I've only rolled one and I know for a fact there is more.

***Note, I do want to keep the review as spoiler-free as possible, so do read this at your own risk.. at least hopefully that I don't screw up***
****Also, unless you're not an achievement hunter, do keep in mind that you can't be able to unlock achievements, if you imported your save file from the non-Steam version, to Steam, so ye****
*****Another note, it's best to play the game as blind as possible, and to play the clean version first, before the 18+ version... unless you're a sneaky rebel*****
Ahh yes! I've been waiting for this game to be released for 1 full year! And now that it's officially now released on Steam, I'm able to play it! Well, except a bit before, I played the 18+ version for a bit, so... ye. But yeah, it's officially on Steam now! I was genuinely afraid that it got lost in the depths of Greenlight, overlooked, but it still stands <3
But anyways, enough rambling; let's go review it... at least from the experience of playing the game in the non-Steam 18+ download, and the demo.
I know that after playing the demo before, it was pretty bare-bones as heck. There was sound, but it lacked background music, and the character portraits, mostly never change, aside from the botton corner, beside the dialog bar, for the characters other than the character you play as; Lin Tian-Liao. But now, in the official release, a TON of things were added into the game, such as the character portraits sometimes moving, having a few different portraits for each character, so you're not looking at the same portrait of the character for the entire game, more emotes for the character mugshots, the camera zooming in and moving, to make it feel a bit more engaging and fun to watch, especially when paired with certain sound effects. Heck, background music is now given this time. Though, to be fair, the demo mostly demonstrated the dialog of the game, and the translations of the game, so I couldn't complain too much on the demo.
Now, on the game's story, and its general gameplay; you play as Lin Tian-Liao, a college student who can suddenly see three "furry-beast men" spirits/gods; a tiger, a leopard, and a leopard cat. The story, well, Liao sees the three cats, they ask him things, and want to do something for Liao, depending on the spirit/god you go for. Each of the tigers you will choose to help, or go and hang out with, will increase your bond with them. Well, at least being a romance visual novel, that's how it'll usually go, right? But yeah, each of the three cats do have their own distinct personality and appearance, along with their reasons with what they want you for, and are cute in their own way.(At least not them typical anime girls you see in almost every visual novels nowadays this time, haha) :3
Being an artist myself, I do love myself some nice artstyles in games, and Nekojishi is mainly no exception. The anime style of visual novels isn't anything new, but being of anime furries, or Kemono as they call it, is kind of an interesting sight to see, instead of the usual anime. Not to diss on them anime styles, I love myself some anime(because I'm a ♥♥♥♥ing weeb), but the Kemono style is more fresher to see than the usual nowadays, since kemono games, or Kemono in general, are comparatively rare.
The most interesting part of the game, is that it gives a description of some things that are said in the game, mostly about the history, description, and other interesting trivia about Taiwanese and Chinese culture. Kind of a nice touch for the game, especially to learn more about the above cultures, that are even lesser-known. Now while I did say it's the most interesting part of the game, there's not a lot to say about it, unfortunately. Nothing new, much like the Kemono style, but it's a very interesting thing to have to just learn about the Chinese/Taiwanese cultures.
Despite many ups of the game, the game isn't exactly really that complex in its way of its relationship/bonding with the cats, especially compared to Doki Doki Literature Club. However, it's not really something to overlook, being generally cute of a game to play, and still that you can feel some bits of change for the cats, on the choices you make. Again, nothing complex, but still simple enough to understand the game, but has some moments where it's still interesting, cute and likeable.
The translation of the game, isn't really so perfect, but is still readable to understand what is being said. It's very obvious in the English translation(the game can allow you to change the language ingame, so yee), with a few spelling errors here and there. Once again, not really a problem, since there won't be any words that have too much errors to be unreadable.
Overall, while I haven't played many kinds of visual novels nowadays, I find this visual novel game to be very interesting of its genre, and also a great visual novel game to play; it's cute, funny, and enjoyable! Just do be prepared for them adorable beast men... especially if you do try to play the 18+ version~ (which can be downloaded from their offical website. Don't worry too much if the 18+ version brings you to the store page of the game, the 18+ version is still free, don't worry; since the payment is meant as a form of donation, if you enjoyed the 18+ version :>)

I have to admit that I feel guilty writing a bad review for an indie game. It must take a great deal of effort to manage to pull one off, and I hate to bash those efforts, however I have to be honest...
I saw the trailer of the game and was immediately intrigued by the game's prospects - considering that I had gone through a somewhat similar (but at the same time very much different) experience myself.
[Concept]
As you start the game you are presented with the computer's desktop from which you can navigate around some of your files and ultimately open up the game within which the story mostly revolves. As soon as you enter the game, you get a call request from Ichi. From there on you play together and the story (and their relationship) progresses from thereon.
The recipe is pretty much the same: you are presented with the desktop, you optionally check some files, play the game in order to get the story going, you get a small cutscene and the game fast-forwards a bit and the story repeats itself. You are presented with the desktop...
[Programming]
If memory serves me right, the programming was done by a single person, however I don't think that this is an excuse for how unpleasant the end-result was. Starting off with the OS, you would instantly feel better that you don't really use that in real life. Clicking on directories and pictures opens them up in new tabs all over the screen. There is no consistency as to where these windows open - and you cannot drag the windows around. So you can easily end up with windows over each other or elsewhere. You cannot navigate from one photo to the other without opening the file with a click, closing it and moving on the next one. A lot of unnecessary mouse movement and clicking for a relatively simple task. If you decide to open up all the files at once and then going through them you may end up with the images not opening up (a cap on the maximum number of open windows or bug?) or sometimes downright impossible since windows may show up over the directory.
These are just some minor annoyances with what presents itself as on OS. However it gets much worse when you 'play' the game itself. All you have to do is move around, attack random targets (and get Ichi to help you) until the boss appears. You land a couple of hits on it, it disappears, and you repeat the cycle until eventually you defeat it. This could have worked out Ok, but in my opinion it was really dragging and annoying. I am aware the that the 'game' itself isn't the main aspect of the game, but that doesn't really excuse. I have played Dear Esther, and for a game in which all you do is walk, I thought it was an amazing experience (even though it got its fair share of hate from others). The character movement is clumsy, the terrain is ragged and can lead to unpleasant collisions and the AI is just horrible. Ichi can defeat the game's terrain and move around in places which I cannot. Ichi also sometimes just runs off the screen and later reappears near you. The attack animations are mind-numbingly repetetive that even simply clicking to attack the enemies feels like a chore. When I finally get the boss to appear, given how fed up I would have already been at this point, I just click as fast as I can possibly can to attack it. However clicking rapidly slows down the game and mouse movement (I don't think this is intentional) and most of the time the character just moves around to the cursor position instead of attacking the boss. All in all, I'm not even sure I was really dealing damage to the boss or if it was set to just self-destruct on its own. That is how pointless I felt to the game (...not to mention Ichi's positive remarks about how well you play the game... it made me feel like I wanted to hit myself).
[Graphics]
Moving on... I don't really think I can complain here. The game doesn't really focus on visual effects or such, but presents aesthetically pleasing graphics. The 'game' is actually really beautiful for an abstract form of game genre. The desktop itself is also relatively well laid out. I think two minor aspects that could have used more polish would be the menu buttons and how the subtitles appear on top of the game.
[Audio]
I'm pretty sure I'm wrong here but I can only recall one song being present. Regardless, the main theme song was pretty haunting and an excellent choice for the game in my opinion.
[Story]
This is where I still struggle. On one hand it presents a life and love experience through online games and user interaction - which is what the game really presents itself as being about. A little bonus would be that through the files scattered on the desktop, you can get some backstory about the character. The mail and chat messages seem as compulsory to get the story going forward, and are very distracting from playing the 'game'. The story starts off well in my opinion but then as the game fast-forwards and the whole tone of the game changes you end up feeling like you missed out on something important which has really changed the relationship atmosphere.
, the cutscene was way too dry, acted out and bereft of any emotions, which is really an anti-climax considering that the players have been investing their time just for the narrative and emotional attachment with the characters in the game.
All in all, considering the points mentioned above, it felt like the game set out to share a life experience but somehow got lost along the way. In the end you end up 'playing' a game which is both repetitive and boring just to get the story moving. You are then presented with a developing relationship that starts off fine and then ends up being too superficial and surreal, while near the end the user is left wondering why
but it really feels as if the player missed out. I honestly cannot recommend this game.
@Nina - if you are reading this, I'm sorry for leaving a negative review. Thank you for sharing your experience with us, and if any of it is true and based on your real life, then I suppose I'm also sorry for what you've been through. Note that I am not bashing the experience itself, but rather how it has been presented to others. I still congratulate you for the efforts you've put into this and the little bonus info (found on the desktop files) about Cibele / you.

I've never thought "this is not a game" before, but I guess there's a first time for everything. There is zero choice, and little-to-no meaningful interactivity. You move an avatar around and click on things, but there's no compelling reason to do any of it, to the point where a kinetic novel format would probably serve the story better. Or maybe a website with pre-existing game logs? Usually even "not a game" games have a little more exploration than "do this to advance story", and "do this to advance story" games have something more engaging in the time between cutscenes.
I also get that this is based on real life, but I didn't find the story all that interesting or well-paced. I expected a little more than "will this pink-haired weeb find true love in an MMO", but it seemed like the end was supposed to be a twist instead of the most likely outcome. There wasn't even much conflict, except as inconsequential flavour text. I know it's a commentary on how little you know about someone from their selective online presence, but that also stops you from caring too much about the characters.
The art is cute, and the game inside the game would be fun if you could actually do something.
I got this for cheap in a Humble Bundle, so I'm not out anything, but I still can't recommend it as a game. As a mixed-media story, it's fine, but still nothing remarkable.

I really wanted to like this game, I honestly did. I thought the premise had some promise. I knew there was likely to be some kind of twist towards the end, probably that the guy was a catfish or something (I won't say here whether there was or not just in case anyone actually cares).
I love narrative games. I loved Gone Home to bits and recommended it to everyone I knew. But this?
GAMEPLAY:
This has about the same amount of gameplay as Gone Home, but it feels like much less, and not just because it's only half the length. Half the game is spent clicking through files on this girls desktop, and the other half is spent playing a game that feels like someone tried to recreate Diablo in Adobe Flash as their first programming project. And it controls really badly. How they managed to muck up the simple act of clicking I'll never know - it lags like hell and just makes everything really frustrating. There is no depth to the game within the game whatsoever. Enemies cannot hurt you. There is no loot or customizability. You just click. Click on enemies. When the boss appears click on it. You don't even have to click more than once. Just give it a tap and you'll kill it 'till it's dead. There are no powerups, experience points, or special attacks. Just clicking.
STORY:
This is apparently based on an experience the writer (and lead actress) actually had. The problem is that it isn't an interesting experience. It's something that happens all the time and honestly wasn't even made that special by it happening online. The ending is disappointing. The acting is stilted and unconvincing, and the writing is mediocre at best.
OVERALL:
A genuine 0/10. It's not offensively bad, it simply has no redeeming qualities whatsoever and is a complete waste of time. It's only an hour long at most (I spent ~70 minutes because I used up some time complaining to a friend about it) and not a single minute of that hour is worthwhile.
Don't buy this game. If you get it in a bundle, don't redeem it. If you're given it as a gift, don't accept it. If somehow it ends up in your library, don't download it. If somehow it gets downloaded anyway, don't play it. I can think of absolutely no reason that anyone, for any reason, should play this game for any length of time whatsoever.

It's not so much of a game than an interactive narrative experience. If you're looking for something like a role-playing game or a dating sim, you're going to be disappointed. If anything, this is more like an indie drama film with buttons. I guess the best way to understand it is to first understand where the developer is coming from. Nina Freeman is known mostly for making autobiographical vignette games. She's more focused on painting a portrait of the characters she portrays than a traditional "gaming" experience.
The game is about Nina, a college student who spends most of her time online playing an MMO called
. She goes on runs with her friend Blake, who goes by "Ichi" online. Their avatars (who adorably look like Samus from
and Pearl from
) grind against mobs until they defeat the boss of each map. During the experience, however, you are given an extremely intimate look into her life. You're allowed to browse her computer as she would, looking through her messages and personal photos. While you're online, you're treated to long voice chats with Blake, and you get to watch how their relationship develops.
It's really easy to see why this game has a hard time finding its audience. The "gameplay" is extremely limited; you don't really have a choice in any of the interaction you have with Blake. You kind of just watch and wait to see what happens. There isn't even really combat (maybe this is a nod to how boring MMOs can be). Clicking on an enemy auto-attacks it until it dies. The rest of the time, you're kind of just waiting for message replies to move the plot forward.
I think most of the people who've played this game feel like she's taking a stance on what love is/should be. I've read many comments on how "it's her fault for trusting him" or that "she's stupid for falling in love" and other similar sentiments. I've even seen ideas that she's spreading some "Social Justice Warrior" or "feminist" propaganda, but I really doubt that's the idea here. I think this is just exactly what it shows on the surface: it's an honest retelling of Nina's first love and heartbreak. That's it. There's no heroes or villains, it's just two awkward people who've never been in relationships and have a go at it.
If I were to choose one thing I love about the game, it's the aesthetic design choices. Everything is drawn incredibly cute, and the photos and poems shared feel deeply personal. It's almost perverse how closely you're able to observe Nina's life, and honestly, it kind of made me feel uncomfortable, as if I was spying on her. The thing I hate most about it, though, is that it's both short and long. The entire playthrough was less than an hour, but felt tedious and slow-paced. There's not much to distract you while you're waiting for Nina and Blake's story to develop. Most of their performances are played through audio, so you're not getting much visual feedback other than clicking on little monsters or checking her messages. I doubt many people will want to play it more than once. It's a consumable experience that's heartfelt, but can't leave more of a lasting impression than a movie can. If you like it when games can be replayable over and over again, I'm not sure you'll get that kind of vibe from this.
Honestly, though, I can't say that I don't like it. I can connect to it, and I can see why both of them made the kind of choices they did. I was an awkward guy growing up in high school, and most of the romantic interactions I had with other girls was through talking over the phone or online. I've made some of the same mistakes they did, and I don't think there's anything wrong with it. If you think she's trying to make herself look like a "special snowflake" or that she's "pretentious" or some other weird judgment, you're probably thinking too hard. She's just telling stories.

The game itself is a simple visual novel with a sweet if short story that revolves around Azure, the likeable and awkward loner with no friends and an uncaring father. After one late night stroll leads to an unfortunate incident she gets flung into a love story that can alter the shape of the very solar system and the lives of billions of people.
But hold on there, it’s not all doom and gloom or epic romps of cosmic tomfoolery. This tale focuses on the blossoming love between the two main, and pretty much only, characters. Whilst not being the best story I have read it is by no means the worse and clocking in at about an hour you might enjoy it a little. There are a few laughs, some sadness and an adult scene that may or may not be your cup of tea (but that parts optional).
So if you like anime, visual novels or just have a spare hour to fill then this might be perfect for you. And clocking in at the low low price of free there isn’t much to complain about.

But this relatively simple system is perfect because it emphasizes the beauty of this game: the skill of the pilots. Dodging missiles and running down scouts is a feeling that I have never felt before in a game. It gives you an amazing feeling of success as you bob and weave through enemy lines with your fellow pilots, and when you pull off a maneuver, you feel like a badass. But the learning curve is certainly there, as most of your enjoyment will focus on how well you can pilot your craft. There are threemodes (that come to mind), the standard death match, team death match, and commander. Deathmatch, it's just your regular deathmatch, nothing special. Same for team, no real innovation (again, focus on combat) Commander is where the real fun begins. This mode is based on destroying the enemies commander while protecting yours, as when the commander is gone, you no longer can respawn. This creates some real tension as, even if your commander is gone, because of the enormous focus on combat, it is possible to turn the battle around. Overall, this is a very fun game with beautiful aesthetics and a solid combat system. And it's free, so, try it out when you have the time.

This is a review from the standpoint of a lifelong King's Bounty fan. And by that I mean a person who played the original King's Bounty game in 1990 too.
Before I start analyzing, I must tell you something. A single play-through of this game, doing all quests and fights, will take you over 100 hours. I am not joking. I am dead serious. If you want to do a no-loss play-through and are forced to repeat some battles, or better yet, you play impossible (meaning each fight takes a long time), you will be looking at 150+ hours of gameplay. Know what you're jumping into. This is 150 hours for 18-21€.
There are already a few reviews in. Before I start, I will state the obvious: King's Bounty, in all of its installments, is basically a single player Heroes of Might and Magic game (regardless of the fact that King's Bounty actually pre-dates HOMM). Opinions are divided, and I will tell you why: because some people are missing the point of this game. Everyone is so preoccupied in expecting an upgrade to King's Bounty: Armored Princess and Crossworlds, that they fail to expand their view and realize what the developers have been thinking. While I am not in their heads, I can see quite well what they did, and it is simple: they gave us 3 different play-styles, which you can mold YOUR WAY and have them do the stuff YOUR WAY. This is what's important to me: a game letting me do stuff MY WAY, and not forcing my hand through a plethora of corridors and bottlenecks.
People on the 1C forums have been complaining that they were forced to play the humans for 3 games in a row since time immemorial. So many wished to start with different races: be it the elves, the demons, the undead or the orcs. Now that we got a game that allows us to do it, people suddenly shift their opinion and start complaining about lack of troop variety in early game, or complain about no-loss victories.
I myself am an avid Impossible/No-loss King's Bounty player. While I take pleasure in having such a play-through, it is not the only way to play the game - hence the play-style remark. Orcs are supposed to be numerous, and with adrenaline boosting their attack and skills, they can trounce an enemy before they suffer big losses. Demons have high Hit Points troops, but as a whole, they lack healing and resurrection capabilities, until you find means to do so. Undead can also form swarms, but it is their mobility that makes them great. A single vampire, switched to a bat can kite the enemies for a millenia, while the Vampire Wizard hero, regenerating lots of Mana per turn, destroys them with spells. Never ever miss the general idea of all King's Bounty games - they allow you to get creative. So be creative - don't just jump to conclusions. Never forget that all the games up intil KBWOTN had the classes working with the same race. Here you have races tied to classes. This alone separates KBDS from any other installent till now, and I think it works well. Never forget that when the game opens up, you can still do your own thing and get your favorite line-up. Nobody stops you from doing so.
Having cleared this out, let's analyze the components of the game itself.
- Main Menu: nothing different from other King's Bounty games. There is also a 3D option, but I don't suggest you play the game in 3D for a long time.
- Graphics: a very slight upgrade over other King's Bounty games. Some textures are clearer, and some troop models look better. Then again, not by much.
- Sound: the soundtrack of King's Bounty has always been its strong side. It has different themes, mostly orchestral with opera motives. 1C has always promoted a captivating soundtrack, and they provide it in this game as well.
- Gameplay: this has always been the strong suit of all KB games. You can mix and match line-ups, get creative, and reap rewards. You also have 3 different heroes to do it with. This allows for hundreds of hours of fun.
- Price: 18EUR is a very good price for this game. I always judge the price of a game harshly: I expect a 3 to 1 return at the very least. This means that to me, every 3 hours of game time cost 1 euro. I can easily expect dumping over 100 hours in this game, so I am quite all right with the price. There are so many games on steam that don't even make the 1:1 cut, it is terrible.
- Day 1 DLC: while I don't support this practice, if people were smart enough to research the game, they should have bought the early access. I agree that nobody is forced into doing so, and I would like to set your souls at ease, that the game is perfectly playable without it. The extra item, which people have been fussing about, doesn't really do much, it gets easily outdated, and must be swapped for a better one - so you are not missing a whole lot.
- Bugs: yes, they are still present. The release is actually still quite buggy, but there are no gamebreaking bugs. If you can't start the game, try to work around it: update your video card drivers, try it on another system and so on. There is always a reason for everything. If you haven't found it, you haven't looked into it well enough.
Conclusion:
- KBDS is a good game, at a good price, providing lots of hours of enjoyment. Don't ever get this wrong.
- KBDS is based on what the fans on the forums have been complaining about: getting to play the other races in the game. Don't ever get this wrong.
- KBDS allows you to get creative just as much as KBAP and KBCW did. Don't ever get this wrong.
- KBDS is based on different playstyles, and as such it separates itself from the KBAP version of the game.
- KBDS still allows for Impossible/No-loss play-throughs, if you are willing to invest the time to do one. A no-loss play-through was never easy in any of the previous KB games. Same here. It is doable and I will prove it in the end.
- If you are still unsure, visit the King's BOunty forums for extra info:
With a view of all this game would give to you, I will most certainly recommend it to people who:
- like strategy games from the HOMM genre
- liked the other King's Bounty installments
- like to get creative in a strategy game
- like to challenge themselves
- like to squeeze maximum potential from a game
If you are not one of this gamers, then KBDS is not for you.

This game has to be one of my favorite MOBA style games to date. Their claim that Gigantic is a strategic game is what drew me to try it and that strategic gameplay is what is keeping me playing it.
There is so much depth to the combat, leveling, and team composition, yet it feels natural and simple. This "Strategic Hero Shooter" concept was really delivered on a very high level. This game feels more strategic in a non-ranked environment than something like high level tournament Overwatch play.
The way they designed the whole Guardian system as a sort of "Nexus" is fantastically executed and creates some intense gameplay. One of my favorite moments in the game so far was when we were down 80-90 Power and clutched 2 kills in a team fight over a summoned creature to wound the enemy Guardian to win.
I've had incredibly close games and blowouts throughout my time in the game, but every match feels fun and rewarding (even the 4v5 I played).
This game is incredibly well polished and I am excited to see where it goes from here.
TL;DR - Have you played a ton of League of Legends, Smite, HotS, Overwatch, or any other hero based game?
Do you feel like they don't have a lot of depth or that they get repetitive over time?
Gigantic might just be the game for you!

after playing almost 60 hours on one playthrough, finding almost everything i can, it is probably the first time in a long while i have found a game that has be entertaining, intriguing and with some fun to it.
A young man sent to Kyrat by request of his dead mother to scatter her ashes in Kyrat, he arrives in Kyrat but discovers that it is a lot more complicated than it looks judging by what is about to happen on that mini-bus you travel in on.... the rest is of your fate.
There is a lot of Indian culture in this game, you encounter a number of characters, including;
a potential re-embodiment of an old god of Kyrat.
two potential leaders with different paths to the same aim.
two foreigners who show you what local product can do in bright colors!
a half insane gun mad priest with a past.
an annoying man as the voice of freedom.
a sterotypical american hero.
a dictator with a indivisible grasp of reality and insanity.
With the graphics at full settings i can get on average a 60 fps, but when you got it all at full settings you can see the landscape for all it's glory and it is something to see.
the characters look mostly likelife, except the hair which is usually an issue i see frequently on these types of games.
audio is good, however i really don't like the radio in the background when in vehicles, i mean if it had a varied or longer audio stream that remains uninterrupted like GTA SA had, it would be better. but as it is, it is rather irritating sometimes listening to it.
The objectives are varied but these side quests are something of a grind as it were, luckily it is all over pretty quickly, same could be said for finding things on the Kyrati map, posters, loot, wheels and such. it can be quite time consuming, same with map control.
The overall impact ofthe game is fun, but if you were to play the missions out with minimal skills met in health and healing along with some fairly good weapons, you could complete the story within a number of hours at most.
One bit of the game that was interesting was the arena and the npc contact. in mainstream gaming i have seen this partial nudity maybe 2 or 3 times at most (with the npc contact). As for the arena itself, it is something else, endless mode is a lot of fun but can get boring and grinding after an extended amount of time.
There are however a number of issues i have seen, mostly objects and fights suddenly disappearing. one moment i have a machine gun mounted truck nearby, the next thing happens when something completes, the truck is just gone, same if i land near somewhere, other times i just see objects appearing out of nowhere.
Another issue and a fairly big one is the reloading of a checkpoint when you were killed, it does not load up exactly where you were or what you were doing, instead it reloads and all your previous efforts minus objectives are reset. So for example, if you are in the middle of doing something important, the towers are out and a number of enemies and then you are discovered and killed, it resets back to a point where you have just completed the objective but the towers are active and all the goons are back, even those you killed earlier.
So in the end do i give it a thumbs up? sure.
As for UPlay? that is up to you if you risk it or not.

I am a huge fan of the original Thief trilogy.  They are some of my favorite games, and in particular, I feel that Thief 3: Deadly Shadows is an absolute masterpiece.  This game is only decent at best if you are just looking for a stealth game.  But as a Thief game, it is pretty disappointing.  I don't know why, but they seemed to simply remove everything that was central to the story of the original games.
-Story is weak and gets very bizarre and confusing.
-No Hammerites.
-No Pagans.
-No Keepers.
-No funny conversations between guards.  Actually, not really any funny parts of any kind.
-No use of the word "Taff."
-Garrett gets super-powers fueled by opium.
-Gameplay gets repetetive.
-The brothel level is basically porn (which is why many team members quit).
-The game doesn't have the fantasy/medieval setting the other three had.
-The City feels cramped and depressing.  Everywhere you go feels like a trashed back alley and it looks like buildings are stacked on top of each other.
-You may rob buildings in the city only ONCE PER GAME.
-The guards in the city have the exact same conversations over and over again, starting them over only about five seconds after they finished.
-The Game crashes randomly.
-Key elements of the plot are left unexplained or only barely explained.
-The whole game looks somber and dreary.
-Lots of hard drive space.

This game is unique in the fact that it puts you in the middle of an eastern european war.. but playing the role of a group of civilians instead of soldiers. Although there is action to be had, the main focus is an emotionally choice driven experience, in which you are concentrating on not starving to death or succumbing to illness and the bitter winters as well as making nightly scavenging raids.
You are running low on food and have no medicine, but one of your dear friends is dying of illness, you go out on a scavaging mission and come across an old house. You manage to make entry and find food, medicine and supplies. But when you go to leave you stumble across the occupants, an elderly frail and frightened couple also struggling to survive. They beg you not to take their supplies...
Do you loot the place and leave them to die? Do you kill them and end their upcoming misery? Or do you leave and risk another night in which your friends may very well not make it?
These are the kinds of decisions that need to be made in this game. Its an epic experience.
Oh and i forgot, the soundtrack is absolutely brilliant.

Games focusing on the fate of civilians in a war-torn country are certainly not everyday fare. And yet, This War of Mine, where your goal is to protect a group of fragile humans from violence, starvation and emotional trauma, manages to portray its setting through masterful interactive storytelling.
The world, characters and narrative are emotionally impactful, with an unusual but fitting artistic style to match. The events of the fictional conflict are believable and memorable. Overall, the dense atmosphere is the game's strongest selling point.
Of course, the game is not without its flaws. From a purely mechanical perspective, the slow-paced realtime gameplay is not very complex and becomes tedious after a few replays. This is especially the case when trying to play optimally, and after reading wikis or consuming other metagaming information. So try to resist the urge.
That being said, those first few runs where you are still struggling and strongly attached to your surviors are more than worth it. A great game, and an excellent example of the breadth of experiences this medium has to offer.

First of all, I would like to say I am a fan of the King's Bounty series and Darkside is not a bad game. Actually, it has the potential to be one of its best installments. The key word being "potential".
Unfortunately, I cannot possibly recommend buying it to anyone. After one month participating in the early access program, I logged 400+ hours playing and testing it. I posted several suggestions in the forum and took part in several other discussions posted by others. The developers gave us, non-russian speaking customers, almost ZERO feedback. All we got were sporadic monosyllabic posts about technical issues. They posted no information about patches and/or the work that was being done.
They pushed back the release date 5 days without warning us - let alone telling us why they did it. After these 5 days there was a cosmetic 10 meg patch and that was it. The product was out.
As it happens, the game they put in the market bears very little difference from the beta version I started playing one month ago. There are huge empty areas, very little or imprecise information about several quests, many balance issues, unclear tooltips, and possibly a number of minor/major bugs. In short, it is NOT a finished product. I expect (and hope) there will be future patches to change all this. But, unless you want to buy an unfinished product,  I would wait a few months to buy it on sale.

Great little story about someone being awakened to see spirits, who just happen to be 3 felines (tiger, clouded leopard and leopard cat) who each want you to help them out. What do you decide? Very cutely written, a proper translation (not that common for Chinese titles) with only the minor error here and there they hopefully fix up, and quite the lenght. +Visually great. While the big portraits only have 2 stances, they do have many emotions in the little icon next to the text, and the CGI's are amazing. Only unlocked 4 of a lot more this run, so you know there's plenty to come back for.
+Story was pretty good up until the end, but maybe that's just the plot I've chosen.
+Many choices to make. So expect that 5 hours from run #1 to extend to quite a few more with re-runs.
+Relaxing music that never bothers and helps set the mood or give an upbeat while playing.
+Absolutely totally free!
-While I like the music, same can't be said for the SFX effects. While most make sense (telephone ringing, knocking on door etc.) there's some really annoying ones like the "ding" or thunder each line when they fight which are grating.
-No real way to set auto-speed that I found, and if you missed something the text will continue going reading the log. You need to remember stopping auto-play, then read the log, then auto-play again which isn't too friendly.
-The ending as mentioned, though that can just be the choices I made.
-A few typo's or grammer errors here and there. Nothing too noticable.

I would highly recommend this game to anyone as a poignant and thought-provoking experience. It really lends a new perspective to experience war as a normal person just trying to survive rather than a godlike human war machine wreaking havoc.
That said, I would not describe it as an enjoyable game in the slightest. It is a depressing view of something utterly awful that should never have existed, and if you get anything of value out of the game it will leave you miserable. But it will also leave you a better person than you were before.

A unique approach to survival well made to the most part.Some issues keep it from being phenomenal unfortunately.The game needs more content to justify its full price tag which is high in my opinion.However on sale pick it up without a second thought as i did you won't regret it even if you are not a survival addict like me.
Now to the point:
Pros
-Brilliant idea and many unique mechanisms that work very well together
-Captures the war feeling
-Smart inventory system that saves the player from tedious micro management
-Looting never felt so great and rewarding
-Excellent graphics and character animations give the real feel of their presence and the dark war atmoshpere
-Stealth is a very fun approach and going unoticed without killing is really fun
-Character sympathy system gives a realistic approach to players decisions
Cons
-Short,even the <write my own story> game choice which can be adjusted up to 80 days is short for a survival game and contradicts the potential this game has to offer.Biggest flaw in my opinion.
-Nice stories but not that many to interact with,could have more
-Same and few locations which become dull after a while.Needed more locations and the random level generation of each one would skyrocket the game's value.
-Could have more characters
-Autosaving system is a mess.No ability to save the game manually and when you leave the game you will probaly lose your day's progress
-Unbalanced in many aspects,because of the short content it demotivates the player to use advanced crafting choices
-Very limited communication system
-Some places like the church and military outpost keep restocking the supplies which seems like a bug so it is prety much over once you get control of these places.No more challenge.
-(Questionable)It's either the game too easy or i am a survival pro
Conclusion
A great game which could have been a survival fans dream with some adjustments.I will give an idea of how i would like it to be.First at least 100 days in game time.I would like 6 to 12 months to be honest.Communication system should give more choices and the ability to talk to characters that you encounter while scavenging(beside traders).Characters should get influenced and behave differently due to the isolation or the possible events that transpire.More characters which could have more special perks which would give much more depth to the gameplay.I would like to see animals,dogs especially that would scout and sniff guarded places and give more challenge.At the point where a boat becomes available i would like it to transport you to a new map with brand new locations let you take all your important stuff with you.This would add double gameplay time on itself.Combat and stealth are very basic but could be better especially the gunplay.Ability to save manually the game and thats prety much all.I am writing all this because i really enjoyed the game and i was frustrated when it ended so fast on my first playthrough.This game has great potential and it will be  a shame if we don't see a sequel or a new dlc.

Alright. I've seen a lot of reviews, both here on Steam and on the internet, about how Eidos stole the Thief IP and a bunch of BS about how they've ruined Ion Storm's game franchise.
Let's set some facts straight.
1. Eidos has always had the rights to the Thief IP. Eidos Interactive published the first 3 games and publishers typically retain the IP rights of games, not the developer, since they are the ones spending all the money to make it.
2. The developer of the first 2 games was Looking Glass Studios and was a contracted company of Eidos. Looking Glass was folded into Ion Storm when problems arose between Eidos and Looking Glass and Eidos shutdown LG. Most of the LG employees following Warren Spector to Ion Storm.
3. Ion Storm developed Thief: Deadly Shadows. It was published, again, by Eidos. Ion Storm was shutdown by Eidos shortly after T:DS was released in preparation of Takeover bids. Eidos was bought out by SCi a couple months later.
4. Eidos was bought by Square Enix in 2009, and folded into Square Enix Europe and switched from production to development. Eidos then developed the reboot of Thief.
So, is the game any good? Like so many games the answer is: "Maybe. What do you look for in a game?"
Parts of the game feel very natural and smooth. Slipping through the shadows and snatching coin purses off of unaware gaurds felt amazing, and the music provides perfect ambience to the levels without being overbearing. Still, other parts, namely combat and the fact that you can't jump when you want the way you want, feels very poorly done. As this is a tactical stealth game in which you play a sneak thief who dies very quickly when attacked by guards, you shouldn't be in combat, so perhaps the poor combat mechanics can be forgiven. Still, there are many people who will simply say, "To hell with stealth, let's bash some brains." More glaring, however, is that you can only jump in specific ways as part of the "free running" mechanic, and trying to jump from roof to roof is very ungainly because you have to run for a short while at a perfect 180 degree angled roof edge to 180 degree angled roof edge. No catty-corner jumps for Garrett. I was hoping for a more "Mirror's Edge" experience than this, and I've missed roofs after jumping from a ledge or simply dropped from the edge and fallen to my death so many times. So, so many times.
This was an issue for me simply because I grew up playing games that rewarded you for exploring every virtual inch of a level with alternat routes, hidden passageways and awesome loot. The levels in the reboot are very linear, and if you follow the obvious routes then you likely won't have any problems with the free-running jumps. That, I suppose, is a plus. If you want to see if you can get to that one roof in the corner, then you're probably going to go splat.
As I said above, the music is great. The sound effects, however, feel like a let down. I have all the original Theif games, and the sound effects were way better in the older games. You could tell where people were in other rooms, how far from or close to you they were even through walls and sometimes floors/ceilings. Foot steps of guards walking away from you actually had receding volume and vice versa when they were coming towards you. It feels much more ambiguous in this game. You can tell someone's in the next room but they sound the same distance on the far end of the room as they do right on the other side of the door. I suppose it's just the way things are nowadays.
The visuals are pretty impressive. The way the fog swirls and drifts, how rain glows in the light, the deep darkness of the shadows, the way leaves skitter and signs sway in the wind all makes the game feel alive. You'll quickly lose yourself in the game, the immersion is certianly a plus in my book.
In regards to graphic settings, you need a GTX 670 or better to get the most out of this game. The fog and particle effects are not kind to lesser cards. With a GTX 670 you should get 30-60FPS @ 1080p even with the settings maxed, though there will occasionally be dips under 20, especially when you're moving out of the shadows while looking at a flame.
The story, is somewhat of a mixed bag. While the plot of the game is interesting, you don't really have any effect upon it. It's a linear thing that feels as if it's tacked on, and possibly was.
Overall, it's a good game. It's not the best, and it has it's frustrating moments, but it should be enjoyable if you keep in mind a few things:
Don't try to jump from/to non-obvious platforms.
Always peek around corners/through keyholes to figure out where someone is.
You are not a combat machine. You are more fragile than glass.
Don't leave doors/containers open, you will be caught quickly.

I'm in two minds about this. I mean, it's free, so it's not just a cynical cash-grab like the crap excreted by the Sakura series developers. It was released on Steam with the option of having its adult content preserved completely (although someone will undoubtably complain about that and it'll be censored eventually, just like Everlasting Summer) which I feel is a step forward for mature adult content in Steam games. But there are other issues.
It's not a game, or even a visual novel- by the definitions of the genre it's a 'kinetic novel', basically a VN with no choices, just a linear story. Now, I have no problem with this; one of my favourite stories ever (Planetarian ~the reverie of a little planet~) is a kinetic novel. Kinetic novels can tell wonderful stories with the aid of visuals, sound and music to accompany the text that can convey more depth and details than, say a movie. Unfortunately, Written in the Sky doesn't do this. It's a
kinetic novel, extremely short, poorly paced, a mess of nonsensical cliches, and despite having this big, important backstory (and big events hinted at in the future in the stinger at the end),
An alien bimbo comes to Earth, an irritating bratty schoolgirl (who we're assured is
eighteen years old despite being tiny, having no breasts or hair "down there" at all, having a childlike face and dressing like a little girl even though she's supposedly in high school) accidentally steals a powerful artifact from her through sheer dopey cluelessness, the two have an uncensored lesbian sex scene and fly off to get married in space. That's pretty much the whole thing.
The main character, Azure, is quite the most annoying little bint a VN has ever forced me to embody. She's bratty, self-centred, lazy, insufferable, boring and while the writer attempts to make her a bit more interesting by detailing how her policeman father forced her to learn detective stuff ever since she was a child, this never ends up meaning
She's a terrible,
character and every moment I had to spend in her headspace was sheer agony. Sierra did the "weird alien bimbo" routine, mistaking school for a prison and thinking that people on TV broadcasts have actually been physically digitised and transported into the screens because ha ha ha that's so funny she's so clueless. She's a completely flat character, utterly bereft of personality, and the fact that this marks an
over Azure's irritating childish brattiness is actually kind of sad. The only other character of note in the story is Azure's dad, who doesn't even rate a character model and who basically exists to be the long-suffering butt monkey (he spends half the game being ticked off by Azure's uselessness and the other half with his mind swapped with that of their pet goldfish, then his only daughter disappears forever without even saying goodbye).
Technically speaking, the game's nothing to write home about. The sprites for Azure and Sierra are OK, in a generic sort of fashion, but they have very few variants (I don't think they even had more than 1 pose, only different expressions). Backgrounds are awful, oversaturated and murky, but frankly who cares. Music is so bland and generic I didn't even notice it, there were no sound effects. The lesbian sex scene (which, let's be honest, is the only reason anyone would play the game) was probably the highlight of the entire game- quite hot, not overlong, and the CGs were pretty good too, but while you can use the middle mouse button to hide the text boxes to see the CGs clearly, this isn't conveyed anywhere in the game (and is highly non-standard in visual novels) and I only found out thanks to someone else's review. I still think it's to the game's credit that they managed to get this content onto Steam (especially since, despite their protestations, Azure is BLATANTLY underage, or at least nothing like the 18 she claims to be) and it provided at least some payoff for putting up with the boring, insufferable story.
Ultimately, Written in the Sky is a really bad kinetic novel, with uncensored lesbian sex and the fact that it's free as its only saving graces. You might as well play it for the 2 free achievements and a quick fap, but once you're done go and play Everlasting Summer instead- a full-length, epic, gorgeously-illustrated and brilliantly-written multi-pathed visual novel ALSO available on Steam for free (which also has uncensored love scenes once you download the right patch). Or go play Sunrider, an epic free tactical RPG/VN hybrid which kicks this game to the curb. They'll show you what a REAL free VN can be like.
Oh, and I just realised what this reminds me of.
Between the bratty, whiny, self-centeredness, the out-of-nowhere romance with a nonhuman leading her to undeservedly be treated like something massively special, and the ending where she abandons her only family without a second thought, Azure is the loli Bella Swan.

I never played any of the Far Cry games prior to 4. I was gifted FC3 about the same time I purchased 4 and was told it didn't really matter which to play. I ignored FC3 and dove into FC4. The world is amazingly huge and fun to play around in. That's about where it stops for me. I played through the storyline for a while and wasn't really impressed with it. I don't really think the game needs a storyline since the grounds for the story just don't make any sense at all. The gun play is fun and when you can get a buddy into the game it's got promise. But, I was playing on the hardest mode and just found the game way too easy to kill things. I never felt that I was in any real danger or that the enemy might actually kill me. My character was essentially a huge bullet sponge and the reinforcement system needs tweaking. I'd love to play this more if we could get it far harder.
When playing in multiplayer mode, we also noticed that fighting with enemies was way way way too easy. We also had issues with vehicles simply not showing to the other player. We have a mission to destroy a convoy, well the other person can see it so they can follow it while driving nor can the shoot it if riding as a passenger.
I wouldn't recommend this game just because hard mode is really easy mode. I couldn't imagine playing it on an easier mode than hard. I wish they would release some updates for the game and make it harder. I really feel that this was a wasted purchase.

Welcome to Kyrat! Ubisoft has really outdone themselves in the visuals department because this game looks
The world of Far Cry 4 is massive and beautiful in every corner, not to mention very alive and dangerous. From the tenacious Royal Army to the merciless predators of the wild (those effing eagles, man..), Far Cry 4 will keep you on your toes... Well, at least in the first 10 hours or so.
Standard AAA games praising aside, Far Cry 4 is definitely not that far cry from it's previous predecessor. In fact, players from the previous game (which is excellent FYI) will notice from the start how Kyrat is very similar to Rook Island in a way, just with different settings and a lot more snow. There's the standard takedown moves, radio towers (bell towers, in this case) to climb, outposts to liberate and standard treasure hunting for collectibles. Don't get  me wrong, it's fun doing those but it does get boring when you're doing the same thing for hours.
Compared to Far Cry 3, the story here is mediocre at best and plus, the ending is absolutely anticlimatic, i.e. HORRIBLE, but I do prefer Ajay more rather than Jason since he's not that whiny. The plot starts with Ajay Ghale, first time in Kyrat, to fulfill his mother's final wish that is to spread her ashes at "Lakshmana", wherever or
that is. Of course, nothing goes smoothly in the harsh world of Kyrat, he founds himself captured by the story main antagonist, Pagan Min. After a few explosive scenes later, Ajay founds himself fighting for the rebel group, Golden Path, to free Kyrat.
I think the biggest problem in Far Cry 4 for me is that there's just "too much of a good thing that it's bad". There's plenty of things to do in Kyrat but mostly it's the same thing over and over again. The collectibles are also not that impressive and only serves to explain a little bit about Kyrat's history and counts toward the 100% completion rate.
Despite all the negative points I've listed for the game, Far Cry 4 is definitely an enjoyable experience as a whole, both in terms of gameplay and visuals. If you like Far Cry 3, then you're probably gonna enjoy this one as well. As for me, Far Cry 4 goes highly recommended!

Somewhere in 1C Software's offices in Moscow, there's some sad little gnome locked in a cage with a computer, cranking out sequels to 2008's King's Bounty: The Legend. If you've played any of the previous titles mentioned, you know exactly what to expect from this game: There's just nothing new or fresh to it, everything looks and feels like you've seen and played it before - because you have. Almost 30 hours in, I just can't bring myself to continue playing. It's just so incredibly dull. Been there, done that. Yes, King's Bounty: The Legend was great. But with each installment, each failure to actually add something new and exciting, I liked the series less and less. What were small annoyances in The Legend (the chaotic quest log, the useless maps, the horrible path finding, the inflexible camera, the small battlefields or the down-time due to travelling and restocking) have  by now become major issues for me.
Please, 1C, set that sad little gnome free, hire some talented programmers and give us something really new for a change. A true sequel for once, not the same game with a new logo again.

The player can pick his/her surname/nickname (but not first name) and pick from between three characters.  Female being a demoness in a g-string.  Males being an aloof vampire and a very likable orc.  The choice seems to make no difference other than cosmectically, as you can use the other characters skills in combat, and you only see your troops in combat not your main character.
You do, however, travel in the real time world as your character and encounter mob groups like in Dofus or many other turn based games over the years that most of you are probably more familiar with than I am.  So far, despite what I read in reviews prior to purchasing the game the story is quite amusing.  It's very light and does not take itself seriously at all.  It's no Shakespeare, and it's definitely not Gloria Steinem, (fantasy games almost always equal big chested males and big chested women) so don't expect otherwise. Especially since this one doesn't even take itself seriously storywise.)  Speaking of stories, don't expect voice overs.  It's clicking on dialogue.  The dialogue is amusing (to me.) However, don't expect big budget stuff. I don't recall a single cut scene.
The game is basically you buy, pick up items that turn into, or you just run across units that you use  to fight for you.  You can also use some hero powers each combat round to turn your mana into damage, healing etc. depending on your powers, and some other ones based on "rage".  The three characters can use each other's rage powers, and I believe everyone accesses the same skill trees so again your hero choice should be cosmetic?
I will be posting in the future when I regain my patience and redo the hours I've lost in gameplay. Twice.

Turmoil is a rather simple and pretty casual oil drilling simulator.
The core concept is solid enough. You drill for oil and sell it for maximum profit. This is fun for the first few levels, but the game gets extremely repetitive way too quickly. The gameplay is just too simple to be very engaging and the maps don't have enough variation.
Having every player drill oil on their own map is a huge missed opportunity. The game would have been much more enjoyable if everyone was competing for the same resources. Instead, the only real interaction between opponents are the two auction systems, neither of which is particularly enjoyable.
Turmoil starts out fun enough, but it gets repetitive and tedious way too quickly. It's not a terrible game by any means, but I still didn't find it compelling enough to recommend.
I did finish the campaign, despite the fact I was getting very bored towards the end. This does unlock the harder expert mode, but by then I was definitely done with the game.
The good:
- Solid core concept
- Nice simple art style
The bad:
- Extremely repetitive
- Campaign is way too easy
- Poorly balanced upgrades
- Poor wagon AI
- The auction systems are rather annoying
The ugly:
- No proper 16:10 resolution support
