155hrs+ and I dont recommend the game? I do, but with reservation! Read on!
TL;DR:
the game if you like complex construction games, have the money to spare and are willing to jump very early on the Rocketwerkz vehicle for a voyage into the unknown. Be aware that you buy a pig in a poke. A fancy one, though! You get your money worth of gameplay! But be ready to dig community guides. No solid ingame handholding (yet).
because the game is still in its infancy, rather lowish on content, Multiplayer is (still) unstable and new content releases are unannounced. Also theres no development roadmap whatsoever. Its probably not (yet) ready for Joe Average.
is that the Rocketwerkz team is super transparent about the development! While working they are also on Discord and dont hesitate to answer even the most critical questions! Kudos, gentlebeings!
Also they are responsive and reflective about input from the community! Most bugs in the release week got squashed fantastically fast. Even during the Xmas holidays we see patches. But we also get to the point where some bugs cant be hammered out that fast.
Overall Stationeers seems to be pretty stable for the broad majority. I had only 1 crash during 155hrs.
is a solid foundation for what can become a fantastic game. The current implemented systems are mining/refining/building/crafting, power and cabeling, gasworks/atmospherics and piping, logic circuits and the basics for greenhouse stuff. On the paper thats not much content yet, but the different systems already offer a nice, deep complexity. A few bits and t.its are already available in creative but not yet implemented in survival (e.g. weapons and motherships).
However, shipping the game into Early Access without manual, or at least a wiki, was a big mistake. A no-go, because even basic gameplay info might have changed the early impressions for a lot of players.
that still keep me sticking to not recommending the game to the broad majority are the lack of a roadmap, the performance question and the lack of a modding API.
So you can build, but there needs to be more... The developers made clear that they have more content waiting but want to stabilize the core gameplay. That makes sense, but isnt a good decision when you are already into Early Access, where Joe Average is judging based on what he has in his hands. (This is also reflected by the current sale numbers.)

In a slightly exaggerated manner: EA customers demand "playability" and want a constant sugar rush injected by fast releases of candy (read: "Update NAOW!"). The one good thing I can say about Space Engineers is that Keen Software perfected that formula during their alpha-phase with their weekly "candy" releases. Sugar rush vs. complains about imperfections. Think about it.
We have to wait and see how Rocketwerkz will handle their updates/releases during the next weeks! For some this will make or break the game!
is something I worry about. How will Rocketwerkz make basic/mid-sized bases and more possible without killing even a GTX 1060 to under 40fps? Its already eating CPU cyles like cookie monster eats cookies.
All "survival/construction" games suffer the same performance problems by having tons of dynamic content that kills GPU draw calls and has somehow to be synced over networks. Pretty much the black magic of game design!
Stationeers is still mostly at the beginning, granted, but dont let us fool ourselves again, ok? We where sold by Keen, that Space Engineers will be performant somewhen-ish. And today, years later, we know its not gonna happen. Same goes for Ark, Minecraft, 7DTD and other demanding surival games. Dont underestimate that task - its tough! But then Factorio managed to handle 200 players in a multiplayer test? There might be hope? But we simply cant know, and shouldnt lie to ourselves about this!
Fortunatly Rocketwerkz is also not falling into the overpromissing pit, and made clear that they try to to raise performance and max online players as good as possible. But this will still be a long way. Unless a little trick suddenly kicks in a nice dose of performance...
Dean Hall worked for Bohemia and their Arma-series ships with a powerful editor, scripting- and modding capability. Mount & Blade was an underground hit years before it reached Steam and had a huge modding community, because they build realised and showcased all gameplay with their integrated modding API. It seems Stationeers missed to learn this lessons to give players the creative power to make this game bigger than it is right from the beginning! What a loss!
Personally I think you should have a look at some vids and decide yourself. The UI/inventory-handling is definatly "different/unique" and not ergonomic. I wouldnt call it terrible but also will never call it "handy", hehe. Its definatly not worth to start a hamster riot about it. Its a design decision by the developers, so be it...
I think that Stationeers has arrived in Early Access a tad to soon, which might rake in some avoidable negative reviews.
At least a basic wiki should be mandatory for proper EA-playability.
Im satisfied with my purchase despite some concerns. Hope you make a good decision for yourself, too!

TL;DR: Very good platformer with a story that is told in a very cryptic way using comic-like panels with no dialogue.  Frustratingly hard but awesome combat and puzzles.
Rest of the review:
They Bleed Pixels is about as awesome as a 2D platformer can get.  It has good music, retro sound effects, lots of pixel blood, and danger around every corner.  It also has smooth controls and combat that feels satisfying.
The combat involves learning which moves to use on which enemies and how and where to strike those enemies.  The moves include kicking, stabbing, and launching.  You can kick enemies into the air to either juggle them or launch them into environmental dangers.  Your moves also allow you to jump, double jump, slide, slam, and rush through obstacles in each level.  You can hit enemies into other enemies and use enemies as part of level-based puzzles.
The controls are fairly simple and very comfortable.  You do not need a gamepad.  The movement on keyboard isn't much different from a gamepad, but I frequently chose to use my Xbox 360 controller due to the joystick being a lot more controllable than WASD keys, allowing me to more easily control the character's left and right movement speed.
The game features a lot of blood in pixel art form.  I like the style of this game and welcome the blood, but blood shouldn't make or break this game.  The only reason I mention it is I feel that some people may wonder why the blood effect exists.  It isn't realistic, it just looks cool when you impale enemies.
The visuals of the game are very eye-catchy and fun in my opinion.  The player character is lovable due mostly to the cutesy art style.  The pixel art is animated fairly well.
Sound production quality is pretty high. The music, though I hardly remember it since I didn't listen to much of it, is very good.
I got this game outside of Steam and later got a Steam copy, so don't take the lack of time investment as a sign of how long the game will last.  It is a lengthy game that I never actually completed.

They Bleed Pixels is a really rad little game. A platformer/brawler hybrid inspired by the many works of H.P. Lovecraft where you stab, kick, launch, and combo your way through eldritch abominations, TPB stars a young girl thrust into a strange and unusual dreamworld adventure every night after discovering a ritual book used by the headmaster of the Troubled Youth's school she is attending. It really is an absolute blast to play, combining elements of a brawler or fighting game such kicks, stabs, launching enemies into the air for air combos, and guard breaking with platforming reminiscient of games like Super Meat Boy, producing all the creative possibilities that combination can yield. The enemies and the environment are out to get you, but you can turn back on them just as easily. If you need a good platformer fix, or want a thrilling, Lovecraftian beat 'em up with challenge to match, absolutely pick up this game.
An excellent game! Every punishing death hurts  so good, and combat feels so fluid and satisfying, you should definitely grab this gem ;)

First off , this game bears potential to be remarkable. That however , fails to keep up the motivation long enough to endure its biggest downside. of the 78 hours i played , 90% of the time were spent in battle. Not "ever changing", challenging battles , that make you curious for more though. It is the same , boring strategy of the same long battle over and over trough the whole game, one hundred times fold. one fight may take 10-20 minutes , the number of fights between the bits of storry parts grow from just 3 to monstrous 15+ , and with monsters getting more hp and numbers, its only getting longer , but hardly more challenging or refreshing in any way. Further more , unless you paid for the DLC for a nice cut down of battle durations, you will likely end up forced to grind for materials - which are needed to craft the newer weapons and skills , because they can NOT be bought from the shop just like that. Unless you want to run around with your lvl 1 sword trough the whole game , you'll be forced to go repeat some dozen times of the battles you're sick and tired of anyways. Note also , that with those 78 hours i did not grind , because the addons came with a sale package.   At first , i was motivated to make no use of them , however... the frustration with the sheer amount of time spent doing boring, long and repetetive battles ended up changing my mind. Note also , that after nearly 80 hours , i have about 20 more hours of gameplay ahead. If this game is played without resorting to DLC weapons , you're in for 120-140 hours of torture. about 14 hours of those are enjoyable content with storry and challenging boss fights. All the rest feels like a horrible content stretching mess , meant to make people pay extra money for DLC packages with proper weapons.
While i can't possibly know, wether you will not enjoy this extreemly unballanced ratio of mental torture and occasional fanservice,  i can say for sure that i did not. For a game heavily relying on time spent in tactical battle , it lacks tactical variety.

I haven't experienced any bugs or performance issues while playing on PC that has 4core CPU, 2GB GPU and 8GB of memory.
Graphics are not photorealistic, rather minimalistic but game looks esteticly pleasing. Sometimes there is too many special effects. The UI is realy clean and easy to read.
I think the music is very good and I wouldn't change a single thing about it.
When it comes to gameplay it feels realy fun and it's very unique experience that i have never encounterd in any other game. Gameplay is dynamic, brings elements of startegy by allowing to hire minions (in place of towers in MOBA), they can heal your team, show your opponents on the map or block the entrance shaping the map in the different way.
The fights are quite fun and the number of participants varies based on the map and time of the game.
You lvl ip in match quickly, what is a bit frustrating when you are new to the game and you don't now what abilities to choose. The respawn time is also quite short so you don't have to feel badly for it, or see your team getting whooped while all you can do is sit for 60s.
One of the biggest flaws of this game is lack of content with only 3 maps and 21 characters.
For first 5-10 levels you usually play only on 1 map that's quite boring, but if you can get past this your will experience maps that change based on your "bases" health bars.
Unlocking the characters or new skins might feel like a grind but it's not worse than in other F2P games.
Also unlocking all charcters by buying Ultimate pack for 30€ is very good value.
I think the game is worth checking out, not everyone will love it, and not everyone will found present content to be enough. I really like how te game is different with the win condition, number of options you can build your charcter, and the dynamic combat. There are some intense moments but at the same time I feel really relaxed while playing it (I'm filthy casual after all).
And the developers have a lot of updates planned so the game will be getting only better and better.

This game is intresting. It does a lot of things that I haven't seen in other MOBAs. Stanima management is neat addition that allows dodging, jumping, and sprinting are really fun. Another feature is turning the "Nexus" into a strong monster and offers new gameplay to keep combat intresting. It forces the teams to fight at key moments.
The main goal of the game is to score enough points (killing towers and other players) so you have a shot at a earning a match point. 3 match points wins the game. One thing I like about this game is dying isn't as punishing as other MOBAs. You still have to wait a period of time (10 seconds at most) but then you can easily launch back into the game. You don't lose money because there is none and falling behind in levels doesn't ruin your character. While death gives the other team closer to the match point you can prevent them from scoring. In a way it allows the losing team to catch up. Once the match point is scored the game has a soft reset, like a start of a new round. Both teams must work their way up to earn a new point. This is a great way to pace the game.
With any team based PvP game the most frustrating elements are often the people. Big reason why I don't play games like Overwatch or MOBAs. All it takes to ruin the fun is one bad teammate or fighting against a strong team. This isn't Gigantic's fault because it comes with the genre. I feel that Gigantic did a great job in reducing this frustration through it's mechanics.
One thing I absolutely love is being able to pick your heros in advance before matchmaking. So often do I want to play one hero and get locked out because my computer wasn't fast enough. Also being able to practice all the heroes in training mode is highly appreciated. This works in Gigantic's favor because you can try it before you dump your hard earn coin on a hero.
If I had any complaints it would be a lack of content (don't blame it since it came out). Map rotation seems to be stuck on one map which gets old fast. Need to create a new account and uses an external launcher even with steam which causes some confusion. The menus look identical to Overwatch and Blizzard's
app. The tutorial is kinda confusing and many of the mechanics are not explained in game.
Overall it has the right amount of complexity, fun, and uniqueness.

Ok I don't ever do these, but in a sea of MOBA style games it's hard to pick out the ones that really shine. Enter Gigantic.
This game is fast, whimsical, and just plain fun! The art style is excellently creative, certainly enhanced by how well optimized it is graphically. The animations are so fluid and beautiful you cant help but to grin every time you get launched off your airship to begin a match or respawn. The voice acting is hilarious and unique, and each of the characters are iconic and gorgeous. You easily get lost contemplating each ones story while browsing through the skins and skills, (which are absurdly cheap and easy to earn by industry comparison to Gigantics peers.)
Gameplay is excellently slick. The default control mapping is intuitive and responsive. The skills fit the personality of the characters and strategies are easily modified on the fly with the leveling system. Damage output needs to be looked into with some of the heros but that could simply be my builds and come with more practice. The gameplay is chalk full of objectives and goals rotating and changing, directly reacting to a teams performance. The creature system is a novel replacement for the typical MOBA lane tower of dullness. Instead the creatures have abilities and are vital to your teams stratagy and direction of the match. The gigantic godlike team creatures are excellent motivators and call out match objectives in their omnipotent voices, thereby amping up the immersion level every time they command you forward. All of this combined washes away the framework of the calculated mathimatical coldness of modern MOBAs and smooths out those harsh edges of power gaming, creating a gameplay experience akin to a hot bowl of creamy tomato soup and a grilled cheese sandwich. It is that satifying, really.
Overall I am extremely impressed. I do not write reviews, but this game is such a breath of fresh air. A mastery of a genre that many are coming up short trying to pioneer. I am happy to say I expect to be playing this exciting work of art for years to come. Excellent job Motiga, and sorry to hear about your troubles in this breathtaking games creation. However nothing good ever came from little sacrifice. Congratulations on a huge success and I hope my words help others experience a greatly valuable contribution to the art of gaming. Thank you.

A few days before the release of a game I've been excited for, I always get this restless feeling and I have no apetite for any of the games in my library. So I always start to wonder through the Steam store aimlessly, seeing if anything tickles my fancy.
I then stumbled upon Mini Metro. I had seen it before, but never thought much of it. This time, I decided to pick it up (at 40% discount) after watching some of the reviews on youtube again. Boy, does this game tickle that "too excited about an upcoming release that I don't want to play any of my current games"-spot perfectly!
I started it up, played through the tutorial and 2 hours later I decided I really had to turn it off and prepare for bed (it was 2AM at this time). Today, I decided to show the girlfriend this wonderful new puzzle game and an hour later she's apparently left the house and I'm still clicking and dragging away to make sure that every passenger gets to it's destination before they get too angry.
The gameplay is simple: connect the shapes (stations) so that the passengers get to their destination as fast as possible.
The longer passengers have to wait, the angrier they get. Combine this with the RNG nature of the shapes, the upgrades/resources you get and the ever growing city population that wants to travel by metro, and you've got a chaotic and challenging puzzle game that's oddly relaxing at the same time.
The game has daily challenges (with leaderboards) for repeated gameplay, a bunch of different maps with different gameplay elements to make sure you don't get bored too easily.

King's Bounty: Dark Side (Early Access Version)
So, what´s the Dark Side all about? Mainly it´s a bit of a fresh take storywise (and therefore also regarding your troops), since you don´t play another boring good guy hero, but finally you can help the forces of darkness, which are being overwhelmed by their enemies, the supposedly heroes. Poor orc babies are slaughtered by mean elves, century old vampires are cowardly destroyed by slimy vampire hunters and the beautiful demons are driven from their lava pools by ugly human paladins.
So far so good or rather dark, now what´s in it, beside a real refreshing background story?
Firstly the engine is the same as in the other games of the series, so are many basic gameplay mechanisms. Therefore this game propably won´t appeal to people who are complaining about that KB series just repeats itself.
Also the "choosing" of your heroes race and class, is not as free as the marketing may claim. Basically you have your orc warrior, your Demoness "paladin" and your vampire sorcerer. Though they not only differentiate in their main skill tree, but also partly in story and even the companions you can get. So while you don´t have real free customization, the replayability is as good as never before imo.
Naturally there are also new rage skills, new units (some are real new units, some are variations of existing ones, for example the human traitors), many new item sets etc. A handy new feature is your own "base", where you have an amount of dark basic troops and a teleportation ability, which eliminates some grinding and extra ways. Furthermore you can and have to improve the base, steadily opening new options.
Since the game is still early access there are still some bugs in it, some unbalanced things and some quests which lack proper description (but knowing the series, maybe the last part will stay that way ;) ). Overall though i had a quite good and stable experience in my 30+ hours.
Conclusio: for fans of the series and/or for fans of a bit more dark (but extremly funny imo) scenario this game is a clear recommendation, for critics who want something totally new, this won´t be it.

Avalanche is a really fun casual game with that addictive "one more go" flavour. The aim is simply to get your little "marshmellow" ever higher. You do this by scaling "wall" jumping, jet-packing, etc. off of falling blocks. After every step climb you will face a "boss". Enemies are vanquished by jumping on their heads as are the bosses. Snakes, birds, dragons, octopuss(what is the plural of octopuss? Octopie? Octo♥♥♥♥♥s? OO ) block your path. The rising lava from below pushes you ever upwards least you be burnt alive.
You also get a large number of power-ups, open new power-up slots to carry more than one ability and gather coins to spend on bonuses, challenges, and cosmetic items. These add to the replay value.
This is ultimately a casual game but proves addictive and gives a real sense of achievement the higher you get. The bragging rights of a high score or a pimped out "marshmellow" are where it is at.
I recommend this if you are looking for an addictive quick blast of fun that you can play between bouts of more intensive gaming. This is also a game that the whole family can play and challenge one another for the highest score.
Last but not least I love the sound the rising lava makes.

Someone needs to inform the developer that although shooters can be played with a controller, the VAST majority of PC gamers prefer using KB+M (for good reason). I've seen a lot of bad reviews of this game from people approaching it as a pc game, This is not a pc game, it is a mobile game you can play on your pc. Taken from this perspective, I find it to be a very enjoyable game. I started playing it on my phone for a week before downloading it and it only improved the experience. I can't tell if there is more detail or I can just see more detail but it adds to the enjoyment, and battles are easier to manage. I found this game while looking for something new to try on my phone for free. I ended up downloading it on my pc because it was so enjoyable.
Despite what others say, it is not a pay to win game. Duels are the only competative aspect and while your opponent may choose to spend money in order to gain special troops, the advantage this conveys is countered by proper troop placement or some extra xp upgrades. There is always a chance to be outmatched in a duel but they aren't crucial to progress in the game. If duels seem unfair, winning a few single player battles will bring up the level, quality, and number of your own troops to give you better chances in multiplayer battles.
The other big complaint I've seen is the timed construction aspect. Once again, this is a mobile game you can play on your pc, not a pc game. The appeal to this is that you can play on your phone or tablet when you are away from home and play the same game from the same point at home.
TLDR : It's a mobile game you can play on your pc; set your expectations accordingly and you won't be disappointed.

Firstly, I'd like to say that I am no hardcore fan of the series, although I truly enjoyed Thief 3, despite its flaws. This iteration in the series is much more polished in terms of visuals (textures, models, especially animations), but far inferior story- and gameplay-wise and has a few bugs - not game-breaking, but still noticeable (I'll elaborate below). The game itself is really linear (apart from the mission hub), which stands in striking contrast to the previous games. The main character isn't memorable. Non-guard NPCs are basically placeholders - after they say their lines they walk around in silence, acknowledging Garrett's presence just by looking at him (take his appearance into account). If you block their path they simply try to walk through you with obviously poor results. To enter most interiors or to get through to another area, you have to mash the 'use' button repeatedly, to let the game load the data I suppose. Why, though? The repeated animation is useless and annoying. To me, this would be of no importance, if the core gameplay met the expectations. I played on Master difficulty (hardest) with additional crutches to enjoy the game better, but the guards were still broken. The key part of a stealth game is broken. That's unacceptable. Let me develop this topic:
Guards' flaws:
1. Most game-breaking bug: they stop following their normal patrol routes. I simply don't know how, but I've read that saving/loading may cause this. If the guard has a pause on his patrol route, he may somehow refuse to resume his patrol. I've noticed that many times, sometimes it helped me, but mostly it annoyed me, cause I tried to play ghost and be unnoticed at all times, even avoiding taking them down with the blackjack. That would be possible if they had their scripts/AI written well. Sometimes saving/loading again fixed this issue, but not always. This should not happen in such a big-budget game.
2. Blind as hell until they acknowledge you, then they are perfect at seeing you from thrice the distance, from which you'd be unnoticed had they been not alarmed, even if looking straight at you.
3. 5-second memory - if you get caught, they will go after you, but once you disappear from their sight for a couple seconds, they stand in one place, looking around or go back to their patrol routes, being mildly alarmed. After some time, they simply forget any threat was around there. Hiding in a one-entrance room was never that easy.
4. Fighting - I know it's a stealth game, but bear with me - if you get into a fight with a single guard armed with a sword (not a crossbow), it's stupidly easy to avoid every hit he aims at you. The time-window to press the dodge key is so big that anyone is able to avoid each and every attack with just a single click of a button. After each attack the guard recovers his strength for a second or two and attacks again. It's so pointless. In a stealth game it should be very hard to survive a fight.
5. Sleeping guards are a joke - they wake up from a bad step in glass or a failed lockpicking try (sure, I suppose Garrett makes such noise when he misses a pin), but ignore a fight two metres away, even with the other guard shouting. What?!
6. Some guards are looking at loot to steal on their patrol routes, yet refuse to acknowledge the fact that at some point in time it has been stolen and they are looking at an empty counter. Come on, really?
Given that the game is meant to be a reboot, a fresh start of the series, a step in the right direction, a demo of what's to come, I am afraid that's the last Thief for me. Pretty graphics on the outside, but the insides are far below expectations of a modern stealth game. Fools' gold. And this game came out AFTER Deus Ex: Human Revolution and Dishonored...

This War of Mine is a really good game that encourages players to make moral decisions while in the midst of a life or death situation in order to survive. You can either just look at this as only a game and play it like so or actually imagine yourself as one of the survivors and really think through the moral decisions you have to make in order to surive. You scavenge (or steal) food, scraps and whatever you can find to get through the day as well as arm yourself with weapons and fortify your home to protect yourself and the rest of the survivors from robbers/bandits (and even soldiers when you go out looking for scavenging). Add the DLC with little children with you and it makes moral decisions much more complicated.
All in all, it is a realistic game that tackles the reality of people who are in the middle of a war zone. I for one truly reflected on the struggles of those who live in countries that are at war.
So again, you can either see this as just a game or you can imagine yourself as one of the survivors. It's all up to you. I still highly recommend this.

This game is an intense simulation of what it's like to survive (or not) as a civilion during wartime.  It forces you to make some difficult decisions about what you'd be willing to do to preserve yourself and others, and does it all with a perfectly gritty art style, strong character writing, and really well constructed gameplay.  The game consists of a day/night cycle.  During the day, you'll be working around the house, taking care of your fellow survivors, and making improvements where you can to make life easier.  At night, you can send someone out to scavenge, while others sleep/guard the house. First, I must say that I thought I was going to really like this game, but after multiple matches I started to see the problems with it.
First off I noticed significant lag spikes while playing PVP matches, so obviously I turned all the graphical options down to the minimum, that didn't help. For a game with such simple textures this should not be a problem. This wasn't due to bad internet connecion as it only happened when the screen started to fill up with things such as explosions or other players. This was a big problem in matches as I could not effectively aim.
Secondly the pacing of the game is too fast at times then too slow moments later. There are characters that basically teleport across the screen making them extremely hard to target (the lag spikes weren't helping either). The stamina bar also depletes much too fast, making it very innefective at escaping combat. This leads to the next problem...
Thirdly, the only way you are able to ensure you win a fight is by making sure you start it with more people or more total HP. There are no items you can collect to improve your character further to make them stand any chance of winning a 1v2, once you have all your upgrades you are stuck there and can't improve or change your stats. This wouldn't be as much of a problem if most people aren't able to fully upgrade by the end of the match, but I tend to get there about 2/3 through along with most of the other players which makes the rest of the match basically whoever groups up the most wins.
If the above things are improved on I feel this game could be a very good casual MOBA. It is a lot easier to get into than SMITE or DOTA 2 which have quite steep learning curves. The art style is very nice and the new concepts brought to the game, such as the ability to choose what type of "towers" to build and the fights between the guardians make it a unique one to play.

Most of the problems people mention with this game seem to me to be intentional.
- The dialogue is very awkward.  The characters don't sound like they're out of a Hollywood movie or a blockbuster game.  They aren't supposed to.  Instead, it sounds a lot like an actual voice chat; movie or game dialogue usually is very succinct and to-the-point, while Cibele's meanders much like real conversations.  Overall, the dialogue sounds pretty much like the awkward conversations I had when I was 19.
- Likewise, the characters are not 100% likeable, but they aren't supposed to be.  I did kind of want to reach into the computer and slap some sense into Nina sometimes, but that's easy for me to say now; when I was 19, I was every bit as insecure and self-deprecating in real life as Nina and Blake are in Cibele.
- And, yes, the story is pretty predictable.  If you read the description of the game, you'll probably think, "Oh, I know how that story ends," and you'll probably be right.  That said, I got a lot out of it seeing it from a third-party point of view.  It's one thing to know what'll probably happen; it's another to actually watch it happen without being one of the people involved.
- Cibele is more of a visual novel than a game.  There is a gameplay element to it, and you can poke around a bit on Nina's computer to get glimpses into other parts of her life, but you should approach this more as a movie that you have to interact with rather than as a game where you make your own choices.
- The pseudo-MMO is very simple and repetitive.  However, I think this is essential to the storytelling.  You don't want a complex game here, because that would distract from the story.  Also, when you play an MMO for a while, you get to the point where even a very involved game starts to feel a little repetitive and you can sort of do it on autopilot; the game-within-a-game captures that, where it feels a little grindy and you don't bat an eyelash at checking email and carrying on a conversation with the game being just sort of something you're doing in the background.  (That said, the pathfinding really does suck; it's the top thing I'd change about this game.)
- The ending is a little abrupt.  I think it's supposed to be, though:
Do I wish I had more insight into Nina's life after the end of the story?  Of course.  That's because I like the character, though, and would like to know more about her; not because I think knowing is essential to the story.
There is one significant negative about the game: the price.  It's a really short game for the money.  On the other hand, I think it's more fair to compare the price to that of a movie or a play rather than a computer game; when viewed in that light, it's a little more reasonable.  That said, the comparatively high cost is why I don't go to many movies or plays--I'd rather spend the money on a computer game that I can play a lot more of.  If you feel the same way, Cibele will be too expensive for you.
Overall, I really enjoyed Cibele.  However, your expectations for this game will dramatically affect your perception of it.  Cibele asks you to have empathy for a character in a way that most games do not, and it requires you to infer a lot about the characters.  If you like indie art films, and you have had a long-distance "it's complicated" kind of relationship, you'll probably like Cibele.  Otherwise, you probably won't.

Before recently I likely would have honestly recommended this game. After all, I've spent over 500 hours on it in complete earnest. The Magic the Gathering Duels of the Planeswalkers series was envisioned as a way to teach new players how to play the game and ease them into getting into Magic the Gathering proper. This iteration, Magic Duels had a really rough start, as the developer Stainless Games has a long track history of screw-ups when it comes to MtG games. Many bugs plagued the game and a long promised update did not come out until far, far after its originally scheduled date.
Magic the Gathering Online, or MTGO, is a bug-riddled archaic mess that requires players to spend money on digital cards that can vanish at any time, and is by far not newbie friendly or user friendly by any stretch of the imagination. The previous Magic the Gathering: Duels of the Planeswalkers games do not have certain elements that are essential to learning the game, such as the upkeep step, Planeswalker card type and mana pool. In comparison, Magic Duels should have been the perfect game to play if you want to just pick up the game and learn how to play or sneak in a few games whenever you have the chance.
Unfortunately several bugs still remained and while after a long time Magic Duels finally had a mana pool added as well as the Planeswalker card type for the first time in the DotP series. What's more, each update was free and included a story mode giving players the gist of the story of the new block. Quite frankly, this should have been almost perfect for what it was. New updates allowed the game to stay fresh and allowed players to basically test drive most of the cards from the new set.
However, a couple of days ago as of the time of this writing Wizards of the Coast, the creators of Magic the Gathering, announced unceremoniously there would be no further additional content updates for Magic Duels. This game at a time when players were excited to see the new physical MtG set release and anticipated seeing a new update for Magic Duels as well as had happened for the previous four sets. Wizards has a new digital product in the works and said that having it and Duels around at the same time would have been unnecessary. Furthermore, they did not specify if or how Duels players could move onto this new game or the future of this new game but it is extremely obvious that they will never add any new cards to Magic Duels, much less fix any bugs or add any new features. In one fell swoop they not only decided to cut support for their so-called Hearthstone competitor but destroy any and all confidence players may have placed in Wizards' digital products.
Essentially what we have here is another game intended to teach players how to play Magic the Gathering using what is at the time of this writing the newest but will soon be outdated Magic the Gathering cards. If a players is going to learn how to play Magic using old cards they may as well learn using more powerful and arguably fun cards and pre-constructed decks. Magic Duels' biggest advantage, playing with the newest cards, has basically been stripped out entirely with Wizards' latest decision.
I love Magic. I spent tons of hours on this game because I not only love the game itself but because it allowed me to sneak in games whenever I was lucky enough to find time in my hilariously busy schedule. I got to play with the newest cards for free and while the changes between physical Magic and Duels were many, I still had a lot of fun (whenever I wasn't playing against TurboFog or Superfriends decks, that is). I did not spend money on this game to buy the in-game currency but plenty of people did, unfortunately and now they have nothing to show for it.
So basically, if you want to learn to play Magic, don't play Magic Duels. Use the Wizards Store Locator located on the main Magic the Gathering site to find a game store that will teach you for free how to play and even give you free physical cards. If you either cannot find a convenient location, want to play/practice by yourself whenever you have time, or just want to kick back and play Magic whenever the opportunity presents itself, I highly recommend you check out the previous Magic 2012, 2013 and 2014 Duels of the Planeswalker titles instead. While the original Duels of the Planeswalkers is still playable players do not have full control over deck composition and end up with massive decks that lack any rhyme, reason or consistency. Magic 2015 is incredibly grindy and still expects you to be able to find people to play against, which most likely is just not going to happen. I personally recommend Magic 2014 as the premier MtG game of choice.
But please don't be turned off by Wizards' actions in regards to their digital products. Magic the Gathering really is arguably the best trading card game in the world, and it's been around for as long as it has for good reason. Give Magic a chance, whether in physical form at a game store or with a friend or in digital form with previous Duels of the Planeswalkers games, but whatever you do don't pick up Magic with Magic Duels. It's simply a waste of your time at this point. I simply will never trust Wizards with another digital product. After all, once bitten, twice shy.

Ok I feel like after some time and money I put in this game already, I have to write a review.
When I first saw this game, which was in early April of 2017, I thought: Wow, this looks just like another F2P-Shooter that gets boring fast and is unbalanced. I think that is what most of you guys out there think. But hear me out, I actually would like to convince you that Line of Sight is one of the best F2P-Shooters out there.
First of, Gameplay. Line of Sight features typical Shooter Game Modes like CTF, TDM or Domination. But the Gameplay is spiced up a bit in LoS. You get to use "Superpowers", so called ESP and Psionics. The first give you small bonuses like faster sprint or a medkit, while Psionics let you use Fireballs and Satellite Strikes. These Powers really make every round and moment of gameplay unique and also encourage you to experiment with them. Overall you can say that these powers are balanced, as you unlock them all while leveling up your soldier and there are also Game Modes, called Classic, where these powers are disabled.
Next up is the currency system, which is the most important factor in a F2P Game. In LoS you earn GP while playing, leveling up, getting achievements and doing missions. Basically, you earn them for everything. All of the Guns in the Game and most characters can be bought with GP. Even though many people complain that the gun prices are very high, I can not support that argument. Sure, if you only gain 200-300 GP per match, 216.000 GP for a permanent gun sounds a lot. But as I said, you can get GP from all sort of sources. So overall, F2P-Currency is balanced...
Then there are Gems, currency that u get ahold of if you either pay real cash, or log in daily. In the first 3 days of playing LoS you will get 50 Gems per log in. After that, the cycle so to speak, changes. You will still earn gems, but less. Overall, you can get a total of 248 Gems per month. This is exactly how much you would get if you pay 2.50 Dollars. You can buy various Camos or, after some months, even a character/weapon. But Gems are mainly used for cosmetic redesigns.
Another important factor would also be, that there are servers for nearly every country or time zone, so you will definitly find a server where your ping is low.
Also, Line of Sight gets updated regularly. So new content is always on its way.
Overall, I can highly recommend Line of Sight. It is a great shooter, that rewards dedication and skill.
TL;DR Game is great, balanced. No P2W-. Currency is fair, prices aswell. Recommended

Building elaborate systems, taking into account temperature and atmosphere and energy, so many opportunities for things to go wrong. Great sense of accomplishment when you get things working. If you like Factorio and modpacks for Minecraft like Feed the Beast, this game may appeal to you.
Currently has all the bugs and friction you would expect of a game just into early access, so if you don't have patience for that then consider waiting.

Stationeers is complex.
From managing systems to filter oxygen, to just handling the wiring of the airlock. The game is not "easy".
The game however is beautiful. The simplistic art direction and simple yet complex models, create a nice setting for you go out and get yourself killed in.
One of the core goals of the developers were to keep you in game, with your hands on everything, every system and you can really see it by how the game handles a few tasks.

There is real promise here. If you are not into space simulation games I have no idea how to convince you of that. The developer is a real fan of the genre and is straight ripping content from other space sims like SS13 to get the job done, which is fine and dandy.
Now then, the game is currently surprisingly functional but content dry. That's about all there is to say about it, besides the fact that it's a voxel-based atmospheric simulation game set in vacuo. You build bases, you pressurize them, you program logic circuits to automate systems and to maintain a healthy base and spaceships to travel from instance to instance exploring.
That all being said and the genre having been described, Dean Rocket Hall is right up there with the most infamous in the gaming industry. He has failed to deliver spectacularly on 3 overwhelmingly successful (in terms of gross revenue) projects, which are:
-DayZ mod (sold to Bohemia),
-DayZ (worked for Bohemia for 2 years, then bailed. Bohemia technically is the one letting this rot in development hell)
-and ION (a huge space epic. We got one trailer, a bunch of hype, and then nothing ever again.)
Stationeers is ION reborn, in Dean's own words. He also announced yet another project less than 24 hours before the steam Early Access release of Stationeers.
Are his motives suspect? Yes.
Does this game have a lot of potential right now? Yes.
Will it ever be finished? Who knows. Dean says he's committed to one year at least. (There's been one year of closed alpha already)
Does it have an active development team / community? Yes, there is a huge discord group already with all 15 developers actively participating.
If you have $20 of disposable income right now it's a must by. The potential is simply too great to miss out on the hype. If you don't, you should absolutely instead spend your recreational funds on alcohol or bussy, because there are way better things to be doing than cashing in on a space sim that could go to the moon or off a cliff by the end of 2018.

The game is still pretty rough, but its updating frequently. If you like complicated sandbox games (espesially in space) - you should totally give it a try. But if you afraid of the EA titles - wait untill the full release.

for space games. If the game is set in space, that alone is enough to catch my attention. Granted, I haven't personally felt many great space games come out in recent times. I played a fair bit of Space Engineers, but ran into far too many issues with lag and bugs for it to be an enjoyable experience. Kerbal Space Program has to be on a top 5 list of my all time favorite games, even if I haven't played a crap ton of it. It was incredibly well done. Because of my love for space, Stationeers has instantly caught my eye.
I actually found out about Stationeers because I randomly decided to look up Dean Hall's twitter. I knew he moved on from DayZ to form his own company RocketWerkz. I was curious what game they were currently working on, as they had previously made Out of Ammo which I wanted so bad but don't have VR for. I digress, Dean Hall is the main man behind this game and that certainly piqued my interest. A lot of people who were fans of DayZ felt betrayed by the man leaving. I never felt that one bit, so I trusted him with this game as it is now his own company and his own rules.
I saw the game grow over time with that eternal "Soon™" release date. About 2 months ago I stopped following it as closely, and finally the game has been released. I followed Stationeers on twitter as this point both to follow it and of course for a chance at the giveaway. I did not receieve the game throught that, but I thought it was fantastic that they gave away so many keys.
The devs of this game have clearly been dedicated and constantly working on it. Every time I had tuned into the dev streams, some new thing was added or something. It was very refreshing to see that Dean and his team were working so diligantly on the game for so long, and will continue to do so. This seems to be a game that even Dean himself has clearly stated to be niche. He has discouraged people that are skeptical from purchasing the game, and I hope people don't buy the game solely based on this review.
A clear
point that this game has is a great community so far. Popping into the discord to see what people are chatting about can always be fun and entertaining. The devs are also there and typically reading the chat if not joining in on regular discussions. The team is very open to suggestions and a lot of this game has been built from some community help if I'm not mistaken. It's great to see that the devs are taking feedback seriously and are working on the game to make it much better. There is a great interaction between the devs to the community, as many questions are answered, and not in any vague way. It was refreshing to be able to talk to a developer of the game and get a straight answer to my questions. They also mention that they want the game to follow similar development paths as successful early access games, which is a great idea.
I think the best thing that Dean and the team can do for this game is constantly be engaged with community and ensure that all issues are addressed. Their openness with the community is amazing as it is and it should continue. On a side note, I would love to see some discord moderators so the devs don't have to dedicate any time to filtering out some of the nonsense and rule breaking that occurs in some channels. It would also be nice to the #screenshots be strict screenshots only in my opinion, or the discussion should regard only the screenshots shown.
Oh boy, I was so excited to launch this game. It's a super small file size and there's nothing better than buying a game and within minutes be able to play it. Thanks guys for such a small size! Also, shout out to this game for
. The volume is actually at a reasonable level, and no music or sound effects shatter your ear drums on loadup. (I'm looking at you CSGO) The settings are plentiful and all very useful.
A 10/10 for me. I think they chose a perfect art style for this game. It's not too load bearing as I mentioned before, as I maintain consistent FPS rates. It's a beautiful looking game as well, the lighting is so amazing, and all the in game machines and items look great. I hope they do update and make minor color changes or something to the different motherboards/circuits and whatnot. In survival you start with a bunch of chips for your tablet, but they all look the same and there's no labelling unless you drop them from your inventory which feels a little clunky to me. I could also be doing something wrong.
Definitely fun for me. I think it takes a certain type of person for it to be fun though, and even mentioned before, it is a niche game. It's expected that some people may not enjoy the complex systems and everything you need to do to prepare them.
I skipped the tutorial because I'm an idiot, and went right into survival. I was pressing random keys and just completely messing everything up. Some keys feel like that they should be changed and what not, but that's the beauty, this game has so many rebindable keys. I will personally be using my mouse for rotations of objects though, as it feels incredibly clunky to rotate objects with moving your hand off your mouse. I luckily have 12 side mouse buttons so I have the option to rebind a lot here.
Just wiring up machines and powering them on to see what they do is absolutely fascinating. It took me a while to figure out how to get the solar panel to work. (You need to put glass on it!) It also took me a while to figure out I was putting my walls on backwards. I have yet to create an airlock though, which is quite exciting. I want to get a functioning airlock. Which I would have by now, but
Just kidding, I think it exploded and flew away. I then created a fabricator and had no idea what to do with it. It's all about the excitement of new systems and what they can do. There is so much this game can provide, even with how minimal it is.
I think if you actually play the survival mode, and you haven't been following the devs streams and you don't constantly ask for help, there's dozens of hours of pure gameplay here for you. My only complaints so far are just a seeming lack of basic controls and whatnot. The inventory at first feels clunky, and continues to do so, but I like the idea of it.
I swear if anyone else says something about the tutorial being too little, I'm going to lose my mind. They don't want to spoon feed you every answer and detail of the game. Plus, it's early access damnit. They have better things to do.
In space, no one can hear you. In this game, there's next to no sounds that I know of so far. The mining drill, the welding torch, and pretty much all the tools make a muffled sound, but beyond that it's almost depressing how quiet it is. I know that's how space works, but even some music would be nice. For now I'll be playing my own music in the background, as I'm sure there are some sound plans in the future. This game made me take a break from PC gaming.
After watching my other beloved stealth series, Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell, turn to hell, I was desperately wishing the same wasn't true for Thief. I desperately wanted to play this game and find out that all the negative reviews were inaccurate, and that the few positive reviews that claimed all the haters were just playing on the easy difficulty. I desperately wanted to believe that cranking up all the difficulty settings and removing all the visual aids would actually matter. But everything the haters said came to be the truth. In a great stealth game, patience is essential for perfection and spending 3 hours on one mission is completely acceptable if it leads to that 100% stealth rating. In a great stealth game, like the older Thiefs or Splinter Cell 1-4, the more slow and careful I am, the more fun I am having and the more immersed I am.
In this game, the longer you take, the more ugly flaws you realize in the mission design and it kills the stealth experience. Guards are literally on a non-stop patrol loop, repeating the exact same actions and phrases over and over without ever throwing something new at you. Everything looks and sounds great at first glance, the lighting is undeniabely good, but at a closer look it is never that impressive. How can a master thief like Garrett not be able to do anything about a store that is "closed"? A "closed" sign should be a signal that I can go inside and steal stuff, but not in this game. The only places that are accessible have a great big orb shining on them so you'll have no problem finding where to go. It is horrible level design.
I wanted to get immersed into this game with my ridiculously powerful PC but I was never able to, and because there are no good stealth titles coming anytime soon, I decided to sell my rig and take a break from gaming. All because of this garbage modern rehash of a legendary stealth series, just like what happened to Splinter Cell. It should be a crime for these AAA developers to make sh***ty games, put a coat of fancy graphics on, and than slap on the name of a legendary series just to trick people into buying!!!! Maybe one day they will get it right...

I beat it in an hour and it's... OK? I guess? It's not really a game so much as a movie with some still shots and text you take in. The bulk of the game, when you're not looking at the pictures and such, is this in-game MMO where you play while this dude hits on you. However, there's no HP or levelling up or anything, so it's basically just a cookie clicker game with some occasionally very cringy dialogue.
I don't want to say too much as the game's so plot-driven, but the guy the main character falls for is so unlikable, she has this pointless relationship and then the game just suddenly ends. So the girl wastes a lot of her time on some jerk, gets used and then there's absolutely no closure. Maybe that's the point? The girl is definitely cute in a nerdy way, which might seem like a pointless or shallow thing to bring up but really, a lot of this game is looking at selfies she took so if for some reason you really don't like how she looks, you've been warned.
I dunno, there's a certain interesting element of voyeurism to the early half of the game (the first 15 minutes!) where you're poking through her things, getting to know who she is and was, and how she got to this point in her life. But a lot of this game is playing the MMO and listening to the whiny dude and neither of them are interesting or likable. If you got it in a bundle or as a gift, I'd say sure, play it, it's too short to really be a big regret. But I wouldn't spend $10 on it, so that's why I gotta give this the thumbs down.

Hey remember when you were fresh out of high school and you thought you were good at writing poetry? And you know that feeling you get ten years later when you realise you were terrible at poetry and everything else, because you were young and stupid? That's pretty much the experience this game provides.
I appreciate that this game is likely deeply personal for the dev, and I think it has a lot of potential, but something just fell short in the execution of this story. It failed to communicate any real depth or purpose. I don’t know if I’m just an unromantic cynic, but the “love interest” is immediately unlikeable, and I struggled to empathise with him, or the protagonist for wanting to regularly speak to him. Both characters were so annoyingly insecure in constantly seeking the other’s validation that I had to force myself to finish it ("I'm not hot, you are!" "No, you are!" ad nauseam). I suppose this is a story of naiveté, and as such maybe I shouldn’t be so harsh, but it was difficult to engage with any of the characters, and they were really the focal point of the game.
Props to the interesting unpolished style and an attempt (albeit a somewhat vapid attempt) at featuring the experience of being a female gamer in an online community. I should also note that the acting, while certainly amateur, felt very genuine, and added to the overall experience.
I wish I could recommend it, but it just isn't developed enough as a narrative or as a game for me to suggest anyone pay for it. Especially at that price.

For a game that prides itself on combining platforming with hack-and-slash elements with full controller support, They Bleed Pixels does an absolutely terrible job at focusing on consistent battle mechanics with responsive and intuitive controls. There is one attack button, where the type of attack changes based on the direction you are holding or how long you hold down the button.
This would be fine if the game didn't require such tight controls, akin to Super Meat Boy, and did not entice you to perform better due to the combo meter looming above your head. There is simply no way to precisely control your character's actions.
Have you ever experienced the dreaded "No way, I totally pressed that button at the right time! Why didn't it respond?" syndrome? They Bleed Pixels practically embodies that phenomenon, time and time again.

Really short version: a climber with nice soundtrack, cute graphics, advancement mechanics that will make you keep coming for more, even if you don't really like the genre (like myself). 7.5/10
Slightly longer version: what is a climber? Here, you hop from one block to the next on your way up with a few interesting and clever power ups. These power ups cost money game and the only way to get more is to play more. Vicious and fun cycle!
Deeper thoughts (if you're interested): I found the talkative NPCs to have a good sense of humor (the cloud-like characters). The items' descriptions also share this humorous approach and kind of suit the game's visuals, with 2d sprites colorfully printed. You can see someone put a good few hours and a lot of elbow grease into making those funny animations. Lots of poses to draw!
The level design changes slightly as you progress higher and higher, with faster bottom-screen-killing-cloud/lava/gama rays, different looking blocks and enemies that throw different stuff at you that becomes more and more difficult to dodge and to fall on top of (that's how you kill them, much like in Mario World).
All in all, considering I don't REALLY like this sort of game (i got it from Humble Bundle's Monthly), it caught me by surprise and i found it thoroughly enjoyable. It's worth 5US$, in my opinion. More than that? If you're a fan of climbers and need your daily dose, then sure, 10 bucks could be worth it.
Note: "Mr. Gionder, you played less than 10 hours! You can't have had a thorough look at it with just 10h!". I'd answer that statement like this: i played this game with a critic's eye, since i don't find it amusing to play for hours on end. So i payed closer attention to the game's quality and detail instead of its playability as an actual "player". Believe me when i say: 5h would be enough.

On this review I give this game a thumbs up and heres why.
On starting the game you are given a tutorial in which describes the usage of the abilities in the game which I found quite handy, and it's not even a boring Tutorial!
After the tutorial you get put into the menu's which look super confusing with all of the information on the screen, the game does have a feature to help label where things are however I did find it super easy to get lost amoungst all of the tabs and features.
Scrolling through the menues I did find a lot of features I look for in a game, this game contains features such as; Massive amounts of customization for both characters and weapons, Clan system, shop, Random Crates(Raffles), advanced character stats and daily missions. From the menues it took me a while to find how to join a game and once I joined a quick match it put me in a game with 1 other person, however it took sooooo long to find players that I had to use the server browser to find a match.
While playing a good few matches and leveled up I found that the game is really REALLY fun and addictive! The community is really social and serious about the game while still having fun and a laugh while playing. It's a very fast paced combat game so prepare to die a lot but if you play right you'll also kill a lot. The game isn't too hard to play, I found myself getting multi kills on my 3rd or 4th game.
One of the major downsides that I seen in the game was shown when I leveled up and unlocked new weapons and abilities, yes they were unlocked but THEY ONLY LAST ABOUT 2 WEEKS BEFORE YOU NEED TO PAY FOR THEM (Some ingame cash, some real cash). This I found very unfair because it limits what people can do on the game before having to pay for things. The thing that ticks me off about this is Is I want to be able to use a weapon I have earned without me having to pay for it.
A lot of people label this game a "Pay To Win" however putting aside the flaw above this is IN NO WAY A PAY TO WIN GAME. On this game you'll win depending on skills, teamwork and motivation, NOT WEAPONS. Yes it is greedy of the Game devs to put in usage limits on their weapons before having to buy them again but that does not mean this is a pay to win game.
In this game theres no over-powered weapons or underpowered weapons because the full game is in a way Over-powered but thats the type of fast paced game it's supposed to be. If you hate games that a few bullets result in your death or kill then this probably isn't the game for you.
Con's;
Free weapon usage limit
Complicated menues
Pro's;
Tutorial
Features
Customization
Community
Addictive and fun
Balanced fairness
Free To Play

I am so glad that devs from Japan have decided to release more of their games to the PC market. This is one game in the Generations series and is a prequel to the first game in the series. However you can jump into this game regardless if you have played any games in the series.
The graphics are just beautiful and vibrant on PC, it has full controller support but I do not recommend using it. The game is simple enough that even a console convert like me prefered playing it with the M & K.
The main reason is using the controller in the battle scenes is just plain awkward and frustrating to say the least. The game is very grinding natured so if you prefer to just run through in a linear way I would suggest Kingdoms of Amalur or something like that. This is a Japaneese RPG thru and through, so prepare to grind a lot.
One real downside to the game is the sheer lack of varied arenas, they use only a handfull for all of the battles which is sad. So if your are thinking mid way in a battle man I seen this before, you have.
That said it is still worth it to pick it up, though I would when in a sale or featured game. While it is a quality made game I still feel the $20 + price tag is to high given the ridiculous cost of the DLC. That high price of the DLC is a bad trademark of the entire series to be honest.
All in all I give the game a solid 7.5/10 I have to make a few points off for the lack of variance in the battle arenas, thee awkward camera controll, and the high cost of the DLC and game.

Let me start by saying that I gave this game a thumbs down, but if you can pick it up for like fifteen bucks or less and you're in desperate need of a stealth game, you could do worse.  It's not an awful game.  There are parts of it that I really enjoyed, but so much of the main story is just godawful.
And that's really the main problem with Thief, the reboot/revival of the classic Thief franchise.  The story is just terrible.  It's Mass Effect 3 ending bad, but the entire main plot is like that.
It starts out innocently enough.  You and your friend/mentee Erin are tasked with breaking into the manor of Baron Northcrest and stealing something.  The game isn't terribly specific, and it doesn't matter as things quickly go horribly wrong.  Erin is presumably dead and Garrett shortly finds out that he was away for a year.  This is the first sign that the writing in the game is both lazy and terrible.  Garrett finds out that he was gone for a year and doesn't even act remotely surprised.  He just kind of shrugs off what, in a well-written game, would be a major revelation.  I'm also fairly certain I saw a newspaper that said the Northcrest manor breakin was a day earlier, which might mean that certain elements of the story were changed later and they were just too lazy to re-record dialogue.  Who knows?
Regardless, the first few missions in the game are perfectly adequate, at least for the most part.  Being a Thief game, what I want is to stealthily infiltrate places and loot them.  The early missions generally provide you with an item you need to steal and a place to steal it from, and that's fine.  Some of the side missions are actually really good.  The highlight was a task to break into the home of a clockmaker who went crazy and turned his house into a giant puzzle.  More of that, please.  Perhaps ironically, the best level in the game was the DLC bank heist.  That, my friends, is what a Thief game should be.  Here's a heavily fortified building filled with swag.  Loot the hell out of it.  Why the game didn't feature more levels like that is just baffling.
Back to the story...it sucks.  Not only does it suck, but it's totally nonsensical.  The ending is godawful as well.  As long as this game is and as much as it stresses its (awful) story, the final cut-scene is about ten seconds long and gives absolutely no sense of conclusion.  It felt like they ran out of money and just didn't have time to do the final cut-scene.  Had the game focused less on story, that would have been fine.  But it doesn't.
The gameplay, though, is generally okay.  It's not amazing, but it works well enough.  You have an icon that tells you when you're visible or when you're exposed and there's another icon that appears over the heads of guards that lets you know when you're about to be seen.  It doesn't reinvent the wheel, but it's functional.  There are occasional frustrations with the AI (basically every time you try to distract a guard with a bottle a different guard goes to investigate it, which given that you can only hold one bottle a time is annoying as all hell), but overall the gameplay is fine.  It's no Dishonored, but still fun enough at times.
Visually, the game has a nice atmosphere.  Certain levels show it off better than others, but the game looks good for when it was released.  The character models suck, though, and the animations don't do much for me either.  Still, you spend most of your time hiding in the shadows and watching enemies from a distance, so the atmosphere tends to win out over the crappy models.
I was actually thinking about giving this the thumbs up after the fifth mission, but the sixth mission is about forty-three hours long and wears the hell out of its welcome, and the final two missions are just generally terrible, mostly because they are so intertwined with the story.  For that, it gets the thumbs down.  It's a game with some all right mecanics but just godawful writing and a nonsensical, lazy story.

Tried it up to level 3, and so far it's a very good class-based space shooter. The action is fast and furious, and you really have to use your various abilities to stay alive. For your starting fighter, this includes cloaking yourself and weakening and slowing targets. The frigates are much more slow and resilient, carry drones and can repair allied shields. The last class which I just gained access to is an infiltrator which can deliver a mad burst of damage and move extremely fast to take unprotected control points.
There are 15 levels of spaceships. Like in World of Tanks there are also premium ships only accessible with real money currency - I don't know if they're over-powerful (i.e. pay-to-win) or not. However I've not seen pay-to-win elements in the rest of the game: even "gold ammo" which in World of Tanks is more powerful, is only the equivalent of an XP boost here. This seems to indicate that they carefully avoided unfairness for non-paying players. I had rather good results in the battles I joined even with the basic non-upgraded ship, also a good sign.
Last interesting details: there are coop PvE battles that are as easy to hop into as the PvP ones. Also, the game is always giving you new missions, which serves as tutorial and gives a good initial income boost.

The gameplay is fun and the depth of strategy for each charater is notable because the talent system allows thousands (literally) of talent combinations.  The abilities characters have make a lot of abilities combo worthy, and a lot of talents for abilities that make the abilities serve team combos and planned compositions.  For example, an ablity that does extra damage to burning enemies might be terrible one game, but in a game with allied heroes that have burn inflicting attacks it can be devastating.
That said there are some heroes that only have a few builds that make sense largely because some of the talents need some balancing.  With monthly updates planned, I expect that overtime a lot of the balance issues will work themselves out as they do in most MOBA style games.  I would also criticize the lack of a chat for the hero selection lobby, and would argue that there needs to be some sort of draft mechanic so that teams can think about what the other team will be playing.  I would particularly suggest this because one hero in particular can shutdown a team a ranged heros on his own.
There is one more convenience factor that I would like to see added, and that is the ability to view talent trees without having to be in a match.  However, after a few rounds, you get the hang of the talents for a hero, so it's not that big of a deal, but it would make learning a hero much easier.
At the end of the day, it's free to play, so I suggest at least trying it.  Despite similarities to Battleborn and Overwatch, this is game definitely has a uniqueness that sets this game apart from those games.  Battleborn suffered from some really terrible map design and extreme pay to win mechanics, which this game does not. The maps (though few) are fairly balanced and allow multiple strategies for attack, and the combat is fast fluid and much more like the feel of Overwatch in terms of fluidness, but with more interupt abilties than you would see in Overwatch and a talent system that creates match progression that is non-existent in Overwatch.  It's like mixing the fast fluid ability action of Overwatch with the progression of a MOBA.

This War of Mine is a really good game that encourages players to make moral decisions while in the midst of a life or death situation in order to survive. You can either just look at this as only a game and play it like so or actually imagine yourself as one of the survivors and really think through the moral decisions you have to make in order to surive. You scavenge (or steal) food, scraps and whatever you can find to get through the day as well as arm yourself with weapons and fortify your home to protect yourself and the rest of the survivors from robbers/bandits (and even soldiers when you go out looking for scavenging). Add the DLC with little children with you and it makes moral decisions much more complicated.
All in all, it is a realistic game that tackles the reality of people who are in the middle of a war zone. I for one truly reflected on the struggles of those who live in countries that are at war.
So again, you can either see this as just a game or you can imagine yourself as one of the survivors. It's all up to you. I still highly recommend this.

This game is an intense simulation of what it's like to survive (or not) as a civilion during wartime.  It forces you to make some difficult decisions about what you'd be willing to do to preserve yourself and others, and does it all with a perfectly gritty art style, strong character writing, and really well constructed gameplay.  The game consists of a day/night cycle.  During the day, you'll be working around the house, taking care of your fellow survivors, and making improvements where you can to make life easier.  At night, you can send someone out to scavenge, while others sleep/guard the house.  It really ratchets up the tension, leaving your only guard sick, depressed and sleep deprived - but you need to go for food otherwise you'll all starve.

The game has a day and night cycle. Day time your inside your house were you can fortify it for protection, be involved with random events, produce items, and take care of your characters. Night time you can choose one of your characters to go out and hunt for items. You can choose which location they go to but there different risks and benefits along with threats.
This game is brutal and pulls no punches.
Let's say all four of your characters are exhausted from too many nights awake. They are becoming sad and unproductive. In desperation you let them all sleep through the night. Big mistake, your people get raided that night and the character with the most Backpack space (who you normally send out at night to collect supplies) gets injured.
That would be fine but you gave the last of your pain meds to some kids who came to the door that day and you were planning on collecting bandages in a few days. You let the character rest during the day hoping for the best.
When night falls you put one of your characters on watch afraid that you will be raided again. You send the another to a high risk location because you have already raided the low risk locations for meds. You let the last one and injured one sleep through the night. You don't find what you need and have to do this a couple of nights in a row. You alternate between the three uninjured characters but you pick the one character with the second highest Backpack space the most to go out at night. That character becomes so exhausted that their movement speed slows. They get caught by a enemy and die.
You now have three people; one who is very badly hurt at this point from lack of proper aids. You have no food and limited supplies. Do you risk someone else to get medical supplies or do you prioritize food? Your characters are sad and tired. If someone else dies your other characters will slip completely into depressed and become unresponsive.

For a narrative game, Cibele doesn’t have a particularly compelling narrative. Though the synopsis is interesting, the execution feels rushed. Rather, the game’s biggest strength is probably how real it can feel; anyone who was a weeb in the late 2000s would be hard pressed not to find familiarity in the badly drawn fan art, blog archives, and chat logs which litter Nina’s desktop, as well as the supporting cast which makes its appearance through the chat windows of her MMO of choice. It’s disappointing, then, that this sense of authenticity is at times let down by the strained dialogue and bad acting of the two main characters, with the added bonus of amateur cinematography in the live action cut scenes.
Despite its downsides, Cibele’s short length keeps it from overstaying its welcome and makes it worth a play through if you’re interested in a short interactive experience and can relate to the setting it sincerely and successfully manages to recreate. Wait for a sale, though.

It certainly has a future, but at the same time, the current state of the game is troubling -- especially given this is apparently after a year of development. When folks say that the UI is atrotious, they aren't wrong -- the unintuitive, complex inventory management will leave you fumbling your tools, rather than excitedly whipping out a wrench or whatever you need in-the-moment.
Unfortunately, though, it's worse than that. It feels like the devs keep too much of the systems in their heads, instead of communicating it to the player -- For example, being in the sun too long will cause your welder to explode (effectively ending your game, if you're playing solo). That the welder thus needs to be left somewhere out of the sun isn't communicated to the player, even after such an event -- indeed, players seem to think that it's a bug, until someone tells them otherwise on the official discord (or something similar).
Issues like this are making the game inaccessible. Complexity and accessibility aren't antonyms -- But, unfortunately, finding both takes an awful lot of careful design.
I'll keep this review updated as time goes on.
EDIT: A minor update: Yeah, obviously the welder issue was fixed. And that's good, of course. But it's early days, and remains to be seen if/how the devs tackle the accessibility issue.
