The UI is poorly designed.  moving inventory around is pretty annoying.  I gue that it's supposed to keep you immersed in the experience, and you constantly have to swap hands (as I suppose a real astronaut would) but it's just not fun in a game, and ends up taking way more effort than it's worth.
There are some pretty big elements missing, and it's hard to figure out what your supposed to do, or how things have to be designed to function. Trying to get a game off the ground is currently a nightmare.  Maybe after some experimentation, (abort, retry, fail...) the player might get things sorted, but it's damn frustrating, and further compounded by certain limitations. You have to journey far from your base to gather fuel (Coal. What's a fossil fuel doing in space? Who can say!) but your base doesn't render if you're more than 30 feet away, which means you could be looking at it and NOT SEE IT. Good luck finding your way back.  Should probably include a beacon or something with all that starting stuff that you'll struggle to know what to do with.
Also, there's a HUD, but it's never explained, and what any of it means is anyone's guess. I gues there's hunger and thirst...or something, but there's no indication when you need to worry about it, and by time you get warning about it, (or was I out of air, again, who knows!) you're already dead.  And just as a final kick in the nuts, there doesn't seem to actually be death!  You just fall asleep, the world slowly (VERY slowly) fades to black, and...that's it.  No respawn, no game over, nothing.  You just have to manually exit the game.
Now there are some cool ideas here, and no, this isn't some EA cash-grab, ignore the raging trolls.  Someone obviously put a lot of effort into this game.  It's just not there yet.  It should have had a few months more development time before release.  Hopefully the devs take these opening days of reviews to heart, and hammer out the initial user experience.  If so, this could become quite the gem, but right now, it's just a rock. (Again, apparently laced with coal, SOMEHOW)

I saw a twitch streamer play this game for 15 minutes and immediately jumped on Steam to grab it. This feels like the game I've been waiting for. The complexity of the "engineering" is on par with the expectations created by other games like Space Engineer and modded Minecraft.
Obviously, at such an early development stage, you can't expect a full, working game with all the bells and whistles. The UI is extremely clunky and horrifyingly difficult to get used to, I kept randomly getting blown up for no apparent reason (or really, no reason given), it took 4 tries for my friend to be able to connect to my game. The game crashed twice, and for some reason exited to the main menu once for no reason either.
There's also a complete lack of any soundscape - you'll find yourself wondering if your sound is still working until you weld something, because there's no breathing, footsteps, ambiance music, nothing. The silence is deafening.
The placement of items, especially pipes and wires, is awkward and needs some work. And, space management is an issue, partially due to the aformentioned UI horrors. It seems throwing stuff on the ground is probably your best bet - even the devs do that on their own streams, so definitely it needs work.
HOWEVER, all those failures in design are excusable - this is an UNSTABLE ALPHA GAME, if you think you can just waltz in and get your money's worth, you need to rethink your expectations of early access games. This game has a whole lot of potential and hopefully is on its way to the top of my favourites list of games to play for relaxation - in replacement of Minecraft which has become dull and repetitive.
I recommend this game to anyone that appreciates the complexity in designing a base with wires, cables, pipes, ducts, airlocks, power management, processing, air management... ALL THE THINGS.

This game was released to the public far too early, and could perhaps be due to financial desperation. Like most games, it has potential, but it has a long way to cover, and so the $25 is much too steep for its current build which doesn't offer much.
It has issues with content (not surprising this early in development) but it also has issues with stability. Its controls are likewise very counter-intuitive and much too complicated. I feel the developers got used to them over time, but for a new player, it takes a while to wrap your head around.
Being in (extremely) early access, the game is definitely missing polish, so we're not gonna count that, but it begs to have more of a solid foundation before really getting mass feedback from fans. I feel it will be a niche game for a while.

In it's current state, the game is quite glitchy. It is by no means unplayable, but a lot of guesswork goes into why certain things are happening in the game.
Random explosions some times occur for no apparent reason. Even if your suit is all smashed up, or life support battery is empty, you can still survive.
Despite that, I haven't had this much fun in a very long time. It is the first time I have actually grouped up with a bunch of randoms from North America to sit and chat on discord and build a base with on a private server. It was incredibly enjoyable, and we decided to do it again some other day.
The complexity associated with everything is incredible. I get the frustration some people have with it, but it is not a cause for giving the game a negative review. It is VERY hardcore. I am SO pleasantly surprised by this, because I was afraid that the difficulty would be dumbed down for the majority of the audience.
However, it took us about 5 hours to build an airlock, and we still couldn't get it to work. Not because of bugs, but simply because we don't know how to configure the damn thing.
Here's what makes this game a masterpiece, in my opinion; Every goal that you make for yourself, be it making a power system, airlock, manufacturing plant, etc... It all brings with it a lot of problems. And each of these problems have to be solved like a puzzle. It becomes a game of optimization and min-maxing to the extreme. In group play, we decided for our next play session, to each dedicate their individual tablet for a specific task, and then put them somewhere so they were accessible for everyone. I applaud the developers for doing this.
I'm not a fanboy. I would crap all over this game if I thought it was bad. In it's current state, it can be frustrating/confusing/rigid, but you'd be stupid to not see the insane potential of this game. This could easily end up beating Space Engineers, and rival Factorio.

Do you believe yourself to be an edgy person?
Or think you enjoy dabbling in gothic and horror themes?
Perhaps you just hear people call you crazy or insane all the time.
If any of the above apply to you They Bleed Pixels will poke at those boundaries with blood soaked pincers then mercilessly snap them in half before kicking them into a buzzsaw.
You might ask why, and the answer lies in the brutal level design and tight control scheme, where if you make the slightest mistake you'll likely die, and continue to die until you become a master of They Bleed Pixels or put the game away. Your thumbs will hurt, your arms will ache, your eyes will dry out and you'll keep playing. Because you'll remember finishing the last level, or earning the last checkpoint, and the immense satisfaction it gave your taxed brainpan. And all along the way the beautiful thumping music and the moody melodies will cradle your mind, and tell you, you may be alone in this asylum experience, and assure you you're near death when you're on your last heart, but it'll become a foothold for your sanity; an ill omen nudging you on like a horrible friend offering you cocaine, a friend second only to the checkpoint sigil.
The simple pixilated plot is more than is needed for the charming 32-bit looking game, but it's just one more facet that drives you on, deeper into madness. How does the girl rid herself of this evil book? Any other questions you may have become irreverent as her only goal night after night, to stop having these nightmares, becomes your own, death after eldritch death.
They Bleed Pixels is an experience worth the blood, fury, madness, sweat, despair, blisters, blood pressure, headache, tears, time, deaths, poison, cancer, money, hearattacks, nightmares, eldricsghdfndstldngngnnnn

A pretty simple action platformer where your goal is to go up as far as you can climbing the falling platforms (and avoiding the rising lava below). Pretty much no story, decent graphics/animations and music. Seems pretty polished, seems like it could have been a Gameboy Advance type of game.
While climbing up the falling platforms (which stack up to form a tower), you'll want to collect gold and power-ups that you can find from chests that randomly arrive on the falling platforms. Each power-up you have allows you to take one extra hit (like in Mario, you lose the powerup but still live). You start out with one power-up slot but can collect more slots to a maximum of four power-ups active at a time.
It feels like a lot of power-ups add minor/side benefits rather than powerful upgrades that ensure a longer run. There are several power-ups that I avoided unless I didn't have alternatives and needed the extra health. Ones that make you bounce automatically (like the pogo stick and bunny ears) eat up your jump inputs if you don't use the jump button while you're touching the ground. The main thing that will improve your progress is your platforming skill.
You earn coins by defeating enemies and collecting coins that are sometimes on the falling blocks. You lose all of those coins when you die so it's very important to dump out everything at banks when they spawn. However, at the end of each run you gain coins based on distance travelled and any challenges/missions you complete. You spend coins in the out-of-game shop to buy decor (cosmetics), Passes (the checkpoint system that lets you start at a higher altitude), or Badges (that let you start runs with power-ups), or in the in-game shop falling platform for power-ups.
In addition to the lava, enemies spawn that try to ruin your day. Most can be dispatched with a well-placed jump on the head but you'll have to keep an eye out for projectiles. However, by far my biggest threat was the falling platforms. One unluckily timed jump can easily lead to death by being crushed.
It can get annoying when I'm trying to ascend to the top of a block to find that another block is going to land on top of it as I land. I check the sky before I start the jump but I don't have the reaction time to change my mind once I commit so it's just a point of frustration in a 'I can't do anything about it' type of way. To avoid that type of thing I have to keep my eyes glued to the edges of the screen (for blocks and enemies) rather than focus on my character. It's something that some people might not be able/want/are good at doing, but it's pretty much a required skill to make good progress in this game.
I would have liked a casual mode that converted instadeath platforms into something weaker like two hits worth of damage. Instantly dying and starting over because of unfortunate positioning and block placement wasn't really my type of fun.
To make things more fun (and consistent) for me I saved up for the Extra Slot Badge (Start with extra power-up slot for 15g which meant I could take an extra hit), Outlast (Extra life for 2x enemy rate), and Repel (1/2 enemy rate) badges. The extra slot was useful when being hit by enemies and the outlast was useful when being crushed by falling objects. Eventually I ended up replacing Outlast because dying once often just snowballed to dying multiple times (because you lose all power-ups in your slots) and you can buy the extra lives at in-game shops if you're lucky and had the coin.
If you enjoy platforming (especially vertical platforming like in certain games' escape sequences) you should give it a try. Avalanche takes this slice out of other platformers and makes a full arcadey game out of it.

Launched today and all of these issues remain, game is most likely abandoned (due to being a school project with no monitization, not like I blame them for abandoning it) so I'd just save yourself the download time and ignore it.
HIT is essentially a combination of many ideas, mainly ones from an old Garry's mod game mode called "Trouble in Terrorist Town" and a source game called "The Ship". The general idea is that a group of people are all seemingly trying to accomplish a goal, only one (or more) of them are traitors and you must find and kill them. It's a really old (and fun) concept, and HIT mostly succeeds except for some major issues.
Lack of people playing, and a incredibly gimped keyboard/mouse support.
Obviously the first issue is seemingly easy to fix, and it's a free game so with a bit of publicity people just might start playing in large enough numbers for a much more in-depth review to be possible, but as of writing I can only go off of what I was given.
The second is actually bizzare to me, unlike games like Dark Souls which were designed for a console with no intention of becoming a PC port, this game seems to ONLY have been made for the PC, which begs the question why a controller is almost required? The menu doesn't respond to PC input that well, and the keyboard seems to only be used for imputting names.
Now, the real reason I can't recommend the game comes from the fact it is terrifyingly unoptimized. Load times are long enough to convince you the game has crashed (which the game frequently does, I've spent barely any time with it and only got 1 stable play test) and the options basically give you a resolution setting and your choice of "High" "Medium" or "Low".
All in all with updates, bug fixes, optimizations and UI improvements I'd easily see myself playing a game like this, but as of right now it's just a mess.

So Total War Battles: KINGDOM is a mobile game that you CAN play on PC.
And the mobile game design is integral to this game. Basically this is an
Gather resources, build and upgrade buildings, recruit units and play missions/battles. This gameplay happens over the course of days. Time walls and cooldowns take a lot of time, and the reason for it is...
A. To reinforce habitual gaming (rather than binge gaming), so the player keeps coming back
B. And to play against the player's patience and need for immediacy, so that they pay real money to get 'gold' and speed up progress.
And the game REALLY wants your money, like all games of this type. I quickly hit a wall in which to progress I had to spend perhaps another week gathering the resources in order to upgrade buildings over the courses of more hours so that I can get units that aren't trash and can continue fighting battles fairly.
The sad fact is that the game is
to being fun and interesting, but it's just stuck in a mobile time-sink design.

1- GENERAL
Thief is a stealth action game that I've bought in a sale when I was playing Dishonored. I thought it was alike... well, it is, but is not as good as it could be.
As the title suggests the game is based in stealing stuff, but we do it with no purpose. We are not Robin Hood, we just steal... maybe that's the purpose, but I think all this theft could have a meaning. It has not.
The game goes in Victorian London, now ruled by a tyrant for some reason. After the opening scene we spend most of our gameplay trying to explained what happened then and after that. Not much of a plot, but it seems all the story is kinda weak. The voice acting and character building was not very good also.

2- GAMEPLAY
But the game is about stealing and stealth, and in that aspect it's great. We are often confronted with hard sections where it seems impossible to go through without being noticed by the guards. So most of the times I just knock them or put an arrow on their heads. The game is very difficult, and even on normal it was clearly hard for me to go through. Despite that, the AI is bad, with some bugs that I've learn to exploit. That does not ruin the fun.
The game is not open world though, and we have a lot of loading screens between sections. That takes some of the immersion, since some of those could take up to 10 seconds on my laptop.
The controls are just frustrating, since we never know how to do something. Sometimes we are able to do an action just jumping, others we have to press a determined button...
The graphics are good, and I have no problems running the game in medium setup, that helps a lot.
The score mechanism gives the game some replay ability, but I warn that I do not know how can someone go through the game unnoticed. Well, maybe I'm just bad.

3- CONCLUSION
I've enjoyed the game, but I've never have that feeling of immersion. I've quit before the ending also. The problem was that I was always comparing the game to dishonored, and he always lost. If you are able to ignore the bad story and the loading screens you will have a rather good stealth game where you will love to steal everything. But I've noticed the €29.99 price tag, and even knowing that the game is on sale a lot of times, it's annoying that the producers keep it at so high prices, it's just unreal and that's the reason I thumbed it down.

Can I be blunt here? I played the original Thief games years ago. I liked them, though I never finished them. I played Thief 2014 a couple of months after it came out. I liked it and actually completed it. I won't be recommending though, due to the unavoidable issues that the game has, especially in the narrative, characterisation and level design department.
It may be an unpopular opinion, but Thief 2014 is at least better than Thief Deadly Shadows. Of course, it isn't in the same league or plane of existence as the originals by Looking Glass but honestly, it isn't the worst Thief game. What I found playing it back in 2014 was that it felt like an upgrade to Deadly Shadows, improving on that game's shoddy performance issues which make it downright awful to even be able to play today.
But lets get down to the nitty gritty review of this, quite frankly, utterly conventional reboot of a classic franchise. The large swathes of hate for this game came from, once again, unrealistic expectations being piled upon it. My only expectation was for it to be better than Thief 3 and I got that... by the fact that Thief 2014 is practically just a graphical update and can actually run on most PCs. It looks fairly nice for a console port from the new generation of consoles, though since the colour scheme is, well, nonexistent save grey, darker grey and pitch black, it isn't much of a marvel to look at by any means.
The story and characters are so bland I can't even remember their names or any of their motivations. The rebooted version of Garrett is, quite simply, insulting to even the most passing of Thief fans. I kinda liked him in as the smug sarky social pariah he was portrayed as in the originals (and to a certain extent in Deadly Shadows) but I wasn't going to parade him through the streets as an shining exemplar to being a great game character. However, in Thief 2014, he's been boiled down to the barest minimum; gruff, unimaginative semi-violent white-guy no.2million. A Batman figure, pratically, dragging along the spunky sidekick girl apprentice for missions, who overplays the 'I don't need you around anymore, Gramps' vibe far too much.
Thankfully, she is ditched from gameplay after the tutorial mission, thank God. However, the only real story thread revolves around Garrett sneaking into places to find out where she might be. That's it. She's embroiled in some kind of hilariously cliche McGuffin conspiracy plot that makes other hilariously cliche McGuffin conspiracy plots laugh out loud at it's sheer mundaneity. Overall, the plot is merely a framing device for the all the things the game feels it needs to rip off from other, better games, notably Dishonored.
Moving on from the awfully poor narrative, the game revolves around an incredibly laborious hub world to navigate around, find collectibles and engage in burglary side missions. The map given to you for navigation is horrendously unintutive to use, as from it you are not able to piece together where exactly you are in terms of elevation or whether you are inside or outside. Interior and exterior mapping isn't layered, it's it own flipping layer! It calls for some of the worst map design I've seen in years, if not ever.
Gameplay wise, it isn't all that bad. By playing the game as it's meant to be played (i.e. focus on staying in the shadows and getting to objectives by avoiding guards rather than taking them all out) is quite fun. Hardcore stealth is the best way to play and the game gives you a decent degree of customisation in order for it to feel just right as a hardcore stealth experience. There's an Iron Mode difficulty level (which doesn't allow for quicksave spamming/save scumming tactics at all) and the dumb 'Focus' ability ripped straight from AssCreed's Eagle vision, can be turned off in the options with no impact on story/level progression or collectible hunting. The wide amount of customisation options, accessed any time in either a mission or in the hub world. is welcome indeed.
Garrett has the practically the same standard yet functional equipment he had in the last games. The water arrows extinguishes torches, the moss arrows grant him a quiet floor to traverse and the noisemaker arrow distracts guards. The rope arrows this time, are used entirely contextually in only a certain place, which sucks but isn't a dealbreaker. If the levels were as open as the original levels and this feature was included, then I'd be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥but as it stands the game
Level design is strictly middle of the road. It's gone the Splinter Cell route of basically amounting to nothing more than either a corridor or a courtyard setup, together with having no more than a duo of guards to about 7 wandering around in any given areas. The cramped levels tightens the element of tension and, unlike Splinter Cell, doesn't feel quite as random when you are spotted. This game knows when Garrett is out in the open or huddled in a dark corner, and the AI respond appropriately. I'd have been ready to have gone far enough as write an angry letter to the developers or maybe held one of their kids to ransom had this been buggered up. The challenge comes from finding the right moment to move when guards aren't looking, which to me has always been the very essence of Thief as a series, it's signature element. Despite the ability to use different, un-Thief like playstyles, at its core the level design is built to highly encourage ghosting. My big gripe about the level design is by far the fact that points-of-no-return exist. It's baffling as to why they have included these, but it's no doubt a huge downer on allowing any of the missions to be enjoyable. With them, the game propels itself another 70million miles from the original games.
I'm suprised I got so many hours out of this game. It was probably because, unlike Thief 3, I was so shocked to find out it didn't just crash on startup or loop the intro cutscene half a hundred times then crash, that I kept playing not noticing the sense of shock I was feeling. Yet of course, in the grand scheme of things with the franchise, 25 hours is probably enough time to see/steal everything in just one LEVEL in the original games. I was suprised I actually finished the god-awful story. Maybe it was the promise of the game delivering a pretty good horror segment around 2/3rds of the way through and a pretty sweet race across a burning bridge of buildings close to the finale. These certainly stand out among the highlights of the story and, for the most part they were nothing but 'set dressing'.
Despite a good amount of things that it does quite decently (the ability to customise gameplay mechanics, the essense of Thief not totally lost but only hidden between the usual modern game standard ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, a really good horror level...), Thief 2014 is still a mostly unneccessary game, delivered to mostly newer gamers only to remind them that this series once existed back in the dawn of PC gaming and publishers be damned if they can't attempt to wease some life out of it yet for the new gaming generation. It's bland hubworld, lazy map design, uninspired colour palette, merely serviceable level design and truly horrible plot outweigh it's few yet significant strengths.
To sum up, Thief 2014 is only slightly better than medicore. It pales in comparison to the original games and, while the stories of the originals and Deadly Shadows weren't that brilliant, the one in the reboot drags it down to bargain bin realms of quality. However, it isn't as bad as people have said. There are far worse games out of there obviously, and worse games which ruined their franchises. To me, Thief 2014 didn't ruin the Thief series as Deadly Shadows beat it to the punch. Though I'd be a fool to deny it didn't come bloody close.

Agarest Zero: Generations of War is an amazing JRPG, and this is coming from a guy who generally doesn't like JRPG's!
Usually, traditional JRPGS just have the characters 'dancing' and standing still when 'attacking' one another, and in this game instead you are allowed to use AP (Action Points) to maneuver your party into position to attack, defend, support or counter just about anything. When you figure out how you like your party, then strategy becomes key. Characters can actually die if left alone too long without revival (and you can't get them back, really) and they each have very awesome and amusing dialogue inbetween! The game even follows a sorta-visual novel path, and allows you to make choices for the main character.
Very amusing, very challenging (easy at first, but beware later on!) and very addictive. I highly recommend this game!

There's no need to comment on the "gameplay": it's very bad and tedious, but it's not the point of the game. I still would have preferred something a bit more enjoyable. Or shorter. Because clicking boring adversaries in boring environnements (the second boss looked very good, nice design, by the way) waiting for the hidden trigger that will make the plot advance and the characters talk again was... not a good experience.
One last thing : I rolled my eyes at the end. Who quote themselves at the end of a work of fiction ? That really stuck out as unnecessary and weakly done.
All in all it breaks my heart to give a bad review to the game (especially since it's, like, my second review ever) but it failed where at least two other games  succeeded most masterfully, and for free (Digital and Emily). That was the biggest let down. I didn't think it was possible to fail with such an emotional potential.

Quote:
“Stationeers is an exceptionally complex game. By releasing the game to the community we're able to test our assumptions so far and ensure the focus of the game and our design decisions are in the right direction. This allows us to gain perspective on the game directly from our players, and factor this in as we develop new features, systems, and content.”
Approximately how long will this game be in Early Access?
“The game has been a very long time coming, developed after attempts at other games of a roughly similar nature. Basically - we're not in a rush! We have prepared a detailed roadmap of what we have planned so far but after feedback (and a dose of reality!) from our community we will announce a second phase roadmap. This means we're talking at least a year of development in Early Access. If a year seems long, consider that the longer the game is in live development, the bigger the scope of the game can grow, and the more input the community can have.”
How is the full version planned to differ from the Early Access version?
“During development of Stationeers so far we have deliberately kept the scope quite limited, both in general features, design features, content, and usability. Working with the community we expect to extend both how you play the game (such as dedicated servers, rather than directly hosting), the way you play the game (control revisions, new mechanics and features) and why you play the game (new game loops and content).”
What is the current state of the Early Access version?
“We've had a great deal of fun at the studio in the development of Stationeers. It's fully playable, and quite well optimized, for you in singleplayer or with a small group of friends in multiplayer. We consider what has been done so far as an entirely complete game loop and experience, and our work from here is about giving the game more depth. Significant work has already been done making the game robust, so even when there are bugs the game should recover reasonably gracefully.”
Will the game be priced differently during and after Early Access?
“Our current plan is to increase the price, probably substantially, when the game is fully released. However no firm decisions have been made on pricing, and none will be made without publicly discussing with the community. If you have thoughts on pricing, please get involved here or on social media!”
How are you planning on involving the Community in your development process?
“The community engagement is an integral component of our development. We only want you to buy the game if you're prepared to roll up your sleeves and give us your feedback! We are experimenting with live development through twitch live-streams. You can watch previous broadcasts on the Rocketwerkz Youtube Channel. If you want to discuss the games development directly you can join our Official Discord. Use all these methods to give suggestions, watch the game grow, and find out how we're making the game even better!”

Edit: I want to change my verdict to a positive. However,I want to clarify why I have changed my verdict. As consumers, we are thinking of ourselves as the people the product is aimed towards. What we want is the product to  evolve and become better. I believe Stationeers has a lot of potential. However, without players the game's developers can't evolve the game. Sure, they have testers. However, they know waht the game is intended to be and play it that way. Meanwhile, people like you and me like to screw around and do things that seem arbitrary. This helps reveals bugs so the developers can have a more stable game. They don't have feedback otherwise. That being said, this is a cautious recommendation depending on your preferences. Please read through my review and decide for yourself.

Ive played this game for about 20 hours now, not long enough to be a master of every mechanic, but long enough to write a review (in my opinion). This is a Niche game, the developers certainly acknowledge this in replies and forum posts. That being said, its a niche game I very much enjoy. So whats it about?
You start off on a moon with a few supply crates dusted around you. Inside are organics, building supplies and some nifty spray praint to help with decoration and orginization. Your first task is to set up a power source, without it, your suit battery is going to quickly fail and you will be left dead on the surface of the moon. Once you set up your charging station, its all systems go for the rest of the game. Eventually you will have to take care of your air supply, but dont worry, thats a bit down the line.
In the meantime, you can set up your machines, run cabeling through walls and smelt ores into ingots to get your base fully operationable. A furnace is going to be a very handy machine down the line as it allows you to mix ores together to make alloys. However dont be fooled by standard survival games, you need correct tempatures and chemical reactions to get the process started to make them. Steel is an alloy that is very useful early on
So now that Ive given you a basic rundown of what youll be doing for a bit until your base is fully set up, Ill talk about some stuff I love about this game. The interface, or lack of one.
If you want something turned on, theres a button on the side of it. If you want to charge the battery of the tool your using, you can take the battery out by looking at it and physically taking it out. If you want to smelt ore, slam it in the back of the Arc Furnace and push the button. Point is, the Devs have done their best to remove the need for interfaces or item slots. Not to say there isnt one, it would be to the point of inconvience if you didnt have some personal storage.
If your a person like me, who loves to be able to interact the world and not always be put into a GUI, you will probably love this game. If your a person who loves being able to tinker around with designs, youll probably love this game. If you dont like there being a single block for every little mechanic, and you having to build those machines your way. Youll probably love this game.
The downside of this of course, is the learning curve. It is not as impossible as some games such as EVE, but there is one there. Especially with this game being so new at this point, theres not a lot of guides out there on how some mechanics work. So some experimentation may be required.
Although strange, I do have to slightly compare this to Ark. When Ark launched, most of its core features were in the game. You could go from being naked on the beach, to getting an assault rifle, to fighting huge bosses. The core concepts were there. I get the feeling from this game as well. Not to say everything is there, this game is Early Acess right now. But I like the feeling that the core principles and mechanics of the game are in place, I feel like so many Early Access games like leaving those out, or developing the foundation of the game with input. I think that a game needs to have its foundation, what its going to be about before it comes to Early Access, or it just flops. Thats one thing I do respect about this game, so far at least.
Regarding performance, I am running fine. Haven't had any lag spikes at all, but I can't speak of multiplayer. Ive seen one or two bugs, but nothing game-breaking yet and thats to be expected. I really hope the Devs keep working on this game, I could easily see it becoming a new passion of mine.
EDIT: I did have a previous review for thumbs down as the game would not launch, found out it was my fault due to not having my drivers updated.

I've not played any of the Total War franchise before. However I can do compare this as a minor version of the Total War series in a simplifed version, mainly for the mobile gaming. You can compare this as a better version of the Stronghold Kingdoms. Well for one thing, Total War lives up to the name of complex management of battlefields. But don't expect too much management here, as it's still meant to be mobile gaming. You get to assign your flanking and foward platoons, cast a few Order skills. The city planning management is easy, but needs in depth planning on how your placement of structures in order to fully benefit its ultilisation. It's still based on the traditional hexagonal warfield gameplay. So strategising your placement is important here, as they will influences other subsiding hexagons as well. You won't be placed together with other human players, just other NPC controlled regions. So it may seems like "YOBA" gaming. But human players are still out there, during Duels.
Ignore about the reviews, saying it's a P2W game. All mobile games needs cash credits to survive. That's their marketing. However I'm very sure this game doesn't really needs those Gold in order to play. In fact the usage of Gold, is only to unlock those cosmetics stuffs for your flags or appearance of your king/queen. Yet in fact, all these cosmestics will still be unlocked as you level up. So Gold doesn't really matter here. No point spending your gold on rushing the buildings as well, since they get built very fast. Compared to Stronghold Kingdoms; where you can get to days just to build finish a building. And if you login daily, Gold will also be awarded to you. Quests also awards you with Gold.
Within two hours you can easily unlocked till Level 14. That's qutie substantial for a developed castle. Well maybe not on the resources side. For resource wised, the game has been spilt into four resources, Silvers, Food, Stone, Wood. Silvers and Wood are plenty of them in the game, and should generally earn you quite fast. Whereas for Food really depends on the seasons you are in. There will be times where the Winter has come and you have no plantation for the farm to grow on, so you have have to survive with the icy cold fishes hidden below the ice, or killing some cows and sheeps. The hard part will be getting the Stone, since getting a Stones are pretty hard; comparable that it just generates 10 Stones per 20 minutes. Therefore there are Missions for you to fight for, to earn some pretty good stash of Stones.
Generally this game would not be leaving you there hanging, waiting for buildings to get done or waiting for resources to be collected. The cooldown of the soldiers, after going through a battle is very fast. By the time you finish a battle, you are ready to collect your resources. So it's just a cycle. There are unlimited Missions, Battle Quests for you. Campaign is the next upcoming update. Each Missions has it's own difficulty as well, resulting in different payout.
For networking wise, Total War has done a good job in having the seamless synchronisation of the account. You get to play the game at home on your Steam, and on the go as you use your mobile to play the game. It maybe hard for those first time, as there seems to be no way to sign up for a Total War account. But fraid not, after you have completed your tutorial. You will actually be asked to create a Total War account. At first I was also clueless on how to create them, as I didn't want to have two accounts separately. For Duels (Humans), the networking really depends on the time of day. So far the matchmaking are mostly two levels higher/lower than your current duel level.

They Bleed Pixels is a platforming/brawling game with beautiful pixel art set in a Lovecraft-esque nightmare realm. The game's platforming is brutal, and is generally much harder than the fighting. This game is also very deep, and it has many rewards for taking extra risks.
The control in this game is pretty tight, and that's a good thing, because the platforming is completely nuts. Even the game's first level is brutal. This is not a game to play to calm down, since it will frustrate you very quickly. Not even Super Meat Boy ramped the difficulty up this quickly. That said, the game does give you the opportunity to save at many points during the levels, and you will need all the help you can get. The fighting system is very fun and rewards style. It's a nice break from the platforming.
The graphics are beautiful. I never really noticed the sound because I was so focused on the game.
This game is not for kids, and it's not for the inexperienced player. If you're looking for the satisfaction for beating a tough level, this might be your game. I'd recommend Super Meat Boy over They Bleed Pixels, though. I think SMB was better designed overall. Either way, if this sounds like fun to you (you masochist), it will definitely be worth the $10.

There are also custom user-made levels, which might lead to a better or worse experience depending on what you come across.
----
After around the 3rd dream (dreams have multiple chapters within them), difficulty starts to feel more cheap than interesting.
A good example of this is the third dream's slippery ice floors with spikes on the side of them with a small winder where you have to ascend multiple of these floors with the spikes there.
Or having enemies on slippery floors, which in turn makes it so you can't really combo them because you and the enemy will slide far apart on a slippery floor.
Or having these enemies on a slippery floor where you also can't jump, so you can only avoid the enemy by bouncing back after hitting him and being unable to combo, or risk getting hit by the enemy and pushed across the slippery slope into a spike wall.
----
It's a shame, cause the game otherwise does have good mechanics, like the save point system, and stellar graphics and sound design.
If I had to compare it to Super Meat Boy... Super Meat Boy is hard, but fair.
TBP feels hard, and unfair.
This is because the platforming challenges it goes for just seem to get cheap, possibly due to somewhat slippery movement physics that feel like I have less control than in Super Meat Boy.
----
I'd have high hopes for a second game with better level design, and perhaps better combat.

An obvious dream of any person is to run around and be so cute even the plant submits to how adorable you are. I mean, who wouldn’t want to seduce people into doing all their work for them? Well, in Mugen Souls that’s exactly what you do. Run around and seduce EVERYTHING. If you find fun in seduction this is the game for you!
But, in all seriousness, Mugen Souls is a JRPG where you have a mix of combat, exploration, and air ship battle. The controls, personally, for the keyboard aren’t the best or most comfortable so I do suggest using a controller. (I typically expect this with console games that are imported to PC). Since this is an imported game from PS3 you should expect graphics and quality to be pretty similar to the original. Since I’m a fan of many games like this (Disgea, Phantom Brave, La Pucelle, etc) this style will seem very anime.
The game follows Chou-Chou a girl who can transform into many “moe types” and by utilizing the types she will attempt take over the entire universe. Chou-Chou begins to recruit followers from each of the planets she conquers and sets off for universe domination. In the game, you get about two units from every world (for the most part), with there being seven world total, in the end having twelve characters plus Chou-Chou to battle with. However, you can only use four at a time in a party, meaning you will have to go out of your way to level other characters outside the story line. With the level cap being 9999, that number may seem ridiculously high, well it is, but the game offers easier ways to level up than just following quest lines. This takes place in another realm (Mugen Field) where the further you go in the more rewards and benefits you achieve. By doing this a player could easily get to level 100 in an hour. This isn’t required to beat the game only recommended, you don’t have to go out and hyper level if you prefer to stick to the storyline quests.
Meanwhile, there are battleship fights during the storyline you must partake in to help strengthen your warship (these can also happen in the Mugen Field). In these you are given multiple commands that your ship may do to take down the enemies. The tutorial does a better job explaining than I ever could but basically you throw things at each other until you kill something. These battles are turn based so you select your offensive and defensive commands when prompted.
For a game about seduction they do give fan service scenes to the players, however, with Steam they will be censored and keep the game’s imagery 13+. While some players may find harm in censoring the CG of the game it’s pretty standard with most games on Steam so it doesn’t terribly bother a player like myself.
Pros to Mugen Souls:
•	Costumes!
•	Tons of characters and character types
•	Great music
•	Lots of content
Cons:
•	No help screen
•	Moe Kill system can become overwhelming and complex
•	You cannot skip link attack animations
•	I still can’t really figure out the Peon Ball
•	Tons of level grinding
For my rating of Mugen Souls, I would give it a 3/5 for those into the niche JRPG games it’ll probably make you laugh or smile. If you aren’t into the anime styled games then this wouldn’t be a game for you. There’s a lot of dialogue, not as much as a visual novel though, and sometimes you get so drowned in the dialogue and can find yourself easily forgetting commands because it just went right over your head. I think that because it was originally made for the PS3 when it was transferred over it could’ve used some updates in the graphics to make it smoother, however, that would be an individual opinion for some people think it adds charm to the game.   I feel that Mugen Souls could have easily become more of a hit than it did however, with the competition being games like Disgea you can tell that there was less effort and more “lols” when making this in comparison.
If you are into JRPG games similar to the Disgea, Hyperdimensional, and other Compile Hearts titles this is for you. Otherwise, I would not recommend spending money on the game that you would shortly put down.
I, personally, would recommend this title to those that are into niche games.

Fans of the previous franchise will not see any familiar story elements, alas, not even the T word is here.
However, Thief 2014 is inspired by its older relatives when it comes to the gameplay. There is a huge respect for non-fatal ghost playstyles to be found, and I can only commend developers of a triple-A title to not go the badass action hero route.
Not all the mechanics are identical, but the ideas are there. The sense of exploration and lack of hand-holding has been toned down, which does take away from the experience, but they have nailed the flow of the gameplay. I rarely blamed the game for my failures in stealth, due to a smooth learning curve.
If you like stealth games and can get past the fact that this suffers from in-name-only reboot syndrome, it might be worthwhile.

Or maybe it's that friend who you worried about in high schol who was dating a guy way too old for her, who didn't feel pretty and now thinks she owes something to every guy. That bright, funny, self-depricating, nerdy girl who was way less of an adult than she knew. This game is painful for me. athe guy shows all these signs of being manupulative, lots of "you're not like the other girls" lanuage that is so so prevelant in gamer culture, and the protagonist is so vunerable to all of it. A very interesting game is an understatement of what is possible already. If you've played Factorio, SS13, or Astroneer I think you will find the similarities thrown about. By no means does this make the game a rip-off however; the game merges fun and hilarious scenarios with complex systems that requires hours of experience to master but only minutes to start a cataclysmic fire.
Already the game has:
- Full atmosphere simulations
- Piping of Gasses
- Logic Computers for automation
- Voxel based terrain mining and deformation
- Dynamic motherships capable of moving across multiple grids
- And Much much more
The game has just entered early access today and still has a long way to go. However, based on the dev streams and content that we have seen added every week, I feel very confident that the game will move forward at a great pace.
If you are looking for a game that punishes you for one wrong move, a game that takes the definition of 'space-sim' and robusts you over the head with it, and a game that pushes your creativity, then Stationeers is the game for you.

This game is not P2P. If you look at the hours reviewers have logged you'll notice that the only people yelling "it's pay to play" have less than 5 hours in the game. And look, jesus, the developers have to make money so obviously skins and things are going to cost. You can't have your cake and eat it too. Don't buy the premium or starter package unless you have money to burn. You can do great in the game with just the basic packages.
HitReg
The hit reg has greatly improved honestly and it's just as good as COD or CS:GO. It's a multiplayer game with players from all over the globe using different connections and pings. No game, no matter the developer, will have 100% accurate hit detection. Asking for this is absolutely ridiculous. Have I been sniping, lined up my sight on a stationary target, seen the name tag, pulled the trigger and missed completely? Yes, and it's crazy frustrating. Does it happen once per game? No. Does it happen once per every five games? Sure. Is that acceptable? Yeah, it is. I'm sorry you got killed by that one guy, truly, I am, but don't ruin the game by saying it's broken.
Hacking/"Got Rektd WTF"
A lot of this stems from people who have played COD or CS:GO or TF2. This game plays and feels differently, so don't expect the same gameplay. Search and Destroy is actually strategic instead of straight free for all (looking at you COD). Players will rush or wait for you around corners, expect that. Don't call it camping when they're defending the C4 or defending the spawn point. Don't expect a game that rewards kill-kill-die-respawn-kill-die-respawn-die-respawn behavior.  Move slowely and learn the maps. Anticipate where the enemy could be waiting for you, turn on your flashlight, blind the f*** out of them and move on. This is NOT CALL OF DUTY GET THAT WEAK S*** OUT OF HERE. Value your KAD. My biggest pet peeve is when an enemy player takes the exact same route every round of Search and Destroy and then calls me a camper because I know where he is going to be. Strategize. The flip side to this is that occasionally you do have some players that seem to have aimbotting software or something similiar. This is rare to me and most likely is less of a problem than with other platforms (looking at you again COD). Most players have learned to aim a burst of fire at head level, you should learn this too.
OVERALL, this game is a lot of fun and I've had some heart-pounding rounds of Search and Destroy/Team Survivor (the only game modes I really play). I've had some dissappointing defeats, I've let my team down, and I've seen a unbalanced game go exactly as you would expect. However, I've also saved my team at the last second, been saved by a pluckly Lvl 1 teammate, learned from more experienced players, and above all, had a great f***ng time.

This game has a great premise, cute character designs, good artwork, and music by Tenpei sato.
But, ultimately, I do not recommend it unless you are really into these sorts of games and have played everything else you can think of.
-The combat is *really* boring.  I am not even complaining about the grinding aspect of it, I play Nippon Ichi games and such.  The fights themselves are just not that interesting, and I was never motivated to level up for the sake of it.  Most fights are hugely lopsided, like if you don't one-shot an enemy it will probably one-shot you instead.  The "Moe kill" system is too complicated for its own good and doesn't make for very interesting decisions anyways.
-There are whole systems and mechanics that I never needed to pay attention to and really don't seem important to the game at all.  There's a hot spring you can use to buff your party; they spend a lot of time showing it to you and explaining it and so on, but I beat the game without ever using it.  There's also "G Up," "Fever Mode," "Blast Off," "Peon Balls" and so on, just a laundry list of things I never took advantage of and never needed to.
-The game world is tiny and yet still has lots of recycled assets.  Practically the entire story is told through dialogue boxes with animated character cut-outs, even when events are happening that should really be portrayed by machinima or cutscenes or something.  It's as if they recorded the voice-overs for a much more ambitious game and did not have the money to actually make it.
I'm disappointed overall, there was a lot of promise in the charming protagonist and the colorful cosmic-scale setting.  I'm told the sequel is better, we'll see.

Just like its demon-turned-angel character, this game has difficulty deciding what it wants to be. Which is unfortunately, as it is a good game. It tries to sell itself on its "sexyness" when in fact, it is hardly present. It tries a lot of gameplay mechanisms but does not really perfect any of them. And I guess that it unfortunately is partially reflected on its score.
So, first, contrary to what the screenshots would suggest, this game has very mild and sparse "sexy content", to the exlusion of the bath scenes that concludes each chapter. In fact, once you're past the 1st chapter, it becomes an after-thought story-wise. Maybe the result of the censorship (?), but in my case that striked a good balance.
The story is a light-hearted comedy about an egocentric goddess conquering (?) worlds by befriending the designated most powerful (and excentric) people of these planets. The characters all have funny personnalities and the comedy comes from their ridiculous exchanges as they pass each other the idiot-ball. Everyone is essentially nice and good-natured without getting dumb-good. I really liked the writing.
Gameplay wise, each world is a one-floor semi-linear map, where you travel from story-event to story-event while avoiding/fighting enemies on the path. It is similar to the Neptunias or Fairy-Fencer (same developpers). Admittely, this part can become dull, but they are short enough to avoid being tedious. The sequel improves in this sector.
The combats are turn-based. You have a team of 4 that you can move freely on the field - well at least in the limit of each character move range. As a basic, each character has access to various skills for attack, heal or support. Skill have different range and potentially area-of-effect. They are dependent on different character's attributes (attack or intelligence for example) and have different power level (damage multiplicative factors). More powerful skills will usually impose more delay on its user's next turn though.
There are many mechanisms and the general battle balance probably suffer from it. There is the "blast off", that allows to push the enemies billiard-like and is notably useful to get powerful enemies out of range. "Link-attacks" between characters in the same movement-range and successive turns. "Moe-Kill" to turn the enemies into "peons", items or get them into more-xp-hard-mode. There are many more, but those are the main ones. Most of them are explained ingame if you take the time to read.
Like in Disgaea, the game sports very-high level, very-high stats grinding, but it is only necessary for the post-game. It is also much less ridiculous than what Disgaea can be. Getting very powerful equipment only requires significant amount of gold. You get those huge amount of gold, as well as xp, in the "Mugen Field", which is actually only a gradually harder 100 fights-in-a-row. One of my main grip with this "dungeon" is the impossibility, to my knowledge, to save until completion. Given that it can take from 1h to 3h to finish, that's fairly annoying. The sequel at least offers the possibility to save on a set of floors.
For all its rough edges, I really enjoyed my time with this game.

Mugen Souls is a whacky over-the-top JRPG with free-move 3d-based combat, think tales games but turn based. The game has a very cute style going for it and a colorful cast of characters that you can customize with outfits and equipments, you can even crossdress the males!
Overall, I feel like the game is heavily underrated and underappreciated, and while not perfect, it's definitely worth a try.
As of the time of this review this is how I feel about the game(might update later):

Pros:
+ Character customization with outfits and equippables.
+ Humorous and lighthearted.
+ A lot to find, unlock, level-up and upgrade. Reach ridiculous numbers in levels, damage, etc; completionists and people who enjoy bigger numbers and progression might like this game a lot.
+ Fairly decent map designs compared to games like Fairy Fencer and Neptunia, I honestly found the maps a bit more detailed instead of re-used copypastes.
+ Pretty good and catchy OST.
+ Tutorials explain most things pretty well, make sure to pay attention though! I've certainly had less issues understanding mechanics than in Phantom Brave, for example, which received a lot of praise.
+ A lot of wonky and non-generic mechanics such as making giant balls of your servants and throwing them at enemies.
+ Haven't had any issues at all with the port so far, runs very well!
+ Good-looking aesthetics overall, cute graphics and a neat, readable UI.
+ Thankfully, there's some good guides out there for people who don't understand the mechanics.
+ Become the undisputed god(dess) of the universe as a cute anime girl!

Cons:
- Might not be for people who don't understand anime clichés.
- Unique mechanics might be clunky or not appeal to everyone.
- Forced to use link skills in battle instead of normally attacking in battle, which have needlessly long and drawn-out animations which get old quickly, these can be skipped by pressing what would be "R2" in a PS controller but this tends to make the combat feel less satisfying. IMO RPGs need fast and fluid combat...
- Not everything is fully explained, there might be some minor confusion with some things without looking them up. IE what's "ogre damage"? What's affinity damage?
- Spaceship minigame fights are a bit convoluted.
- Some minor unlockable content unavailable for dubbed voiceacting, thankfully the original undubbed can be selected.
- Generic units are initially a lot weaker than main characters unlike games like Disgaea
- Mugen Field is this game's version of the item world from Disgaea, a random dungeon with many floors that you do for power ups and exp, albeit a lot less interesting and made up mainly of just fights.

All in all, I think the game is quite decent and can be very enjoyable despite some of its flaws, so I recommend it to people who have enjoyed games like Neptunia or Disgaea and JRPGs in general, but expect a strange and different experience.

This is a linear visual novel in which you do not make choices that affect the story. It\'s simply a watch-until-the-end type of game. If you don\'t like that kind of game, or you\'re preoccupied about whether that fits your definition of \"game\" to enjoy the experience, this game is not for you.
This game doesn\'t do anything that I haven\'t seen done in other games. I like the use of live-action film being inserted; it\'s something that developers have stayed away from for a long time, but it\'s nice to see people trying it again. But live-action film games used to be a pretty big thing. And games with a \"look around on a computer\" theme are hardly new. So this isn\'t particularly an innovative game.
But it does feel like a unique experience. This game is about immersing you in the feeling of a young woman and her coming-of-age tale of first love. Nina is a nerd who feels a bit safer in the computer world, and seems to meet someone similar, and it evolves from there. Everything feels a little awkward, and a little forced -- but if you\'ve ever been in this situation, that\'s exactly how it is. I\'ve heard people actually communicate very much like the characters in the story.
The story is mostly discovered in a few different ways -- each chapter is broken into a few segments. You get a short film with live actors. You get a session of interacting with Nina\'s computer (probably most is optional -- I snooped as much as I could and ended with 75 minutes total game time btw) in which you can open her files and folders and look at her photos, read her poetry and blog posts, etc. Then you play in the MMO where most of the story takes place through listening to voice chat while you hack away at monsters. The \"gameplay\" in the MMO is just tediously clicking on mosnters and watching them die, all the while doing more important things like checking your private messages, emails, some kind of instagram-like app, and of course, listening to the voice chat. Pretty much like a real MMO.
Overall, the story was predictable and generic. I pretty much guessed the entire story from the beginning (and I hadn\'t read any reviews, just watched part of the trailer before buying the Humble Bundle) and I\'m typically horrible at guessing even the most cliche stories. But I think rather than telling a unique story, this game was about feeling, and I think that\'s where it did well.
Through most of the game, I felt a little nervous and awkward and embarrassed. Not because the game was bad but because I honestly think that was the way I was supposed to feel playing the game. If you\'ve ever been in this situation like the characters in the game, that\'s exactly how it feels. Even though I thought Ichi was ugly and annoying, I felt somehow excited for Nina to get closer to him and see if she had any nude photos of him on her computer at the beginning of each chapter.
The biggest problem I had with the game was the ending, and I think that\'s what especially ruins the game for  most people even if they were okay with it for most of the time. The ending felt very rushed and sudden. I mean, there wasn\'t much else left to even happen, so I can\'t really say how to improve it, but I felt like after all of the build-up, I didn\'t get a chance to really \'feel\' the ending because it happened too fast and without enough feeling and description involved.
Overall, I think the game was a good effort with a critical flaw in the awkwardness of the ending. Other than that, the game accomplished what it was trying to do pretty well, and I thought it was well put together. The characters were believable to me, and Nina\'s old blogs looked pretty much exactly like mine from when I was in high school, too. And I was cringing at hers the same way I cringe at mine looking back. I think that\'s the intended experience here. Overall, these first brushes with love are awkward, cringe-inducing moments to think back on, but at the same time, you feel a strange fondness for them and still recognize the way they moved you and made you feel. I think this game captures the early half of that, and because I\'m easily moved, somewhat the latter part, but I think most people won\'t feel nearly as emotional or attached the characters as me.
It\'s hard to really recommend this game for a $9 price tag. Considering the effort the developer put into it, I understand the price tag. But as a consumer, you can get so much more value from many other games for less than $9. It\'s a bit of a shame, really. I think if you can get it for less, definitely go for it and try it out, especially if you like linear visual novels and raw slice-of-life type stuff that\'s more about sharing feelings than it is about telling a never-happens-in-real-life story.
I wish I could choose a medium rating for the game. I think that this game doesn\'t deserve a thumbs down, but I think for $9 for a short game with a bad ending, it\'s hard to justify a thumbs up, too. Hopefully you will read the review and decide for yourself, rather than going by the thumb, and I\'ll give it a \"yes\" because I think the game deserves praise for its effort at least.

is a game about online gaming, community, love and the complexities of virtual/real-life relationships. It’s close to being a visual novel or movie, but interestingly enough has what resembles an MMORPG that the player interacts with and plays in. The game starts the player on the PC desktop of the protagonist Nina Freeman. From there you can read her blog files, see selfies, poetry drafts for her university courses or boot Valtameri, the aforementioned MMORPG.

Nina is a girl that is passionate about many things: anime, photography and gaming among them. Inevitably she is drawn to an online game where she becomes part of a sort of clan, led by a male user by the screenname of Ichi. Nina, under the username Cibele, interacts with the other users and her friends via IM. Voice-acted sound clips progress the plot while the player is destroying monsters online in Valtameri.
This game utilizes the modern minimalist art style coupled with soft, ambient synth music. While perhaps not the most original of styles, it is effective in giving the game a strong emotional charge.
As you can see by my playtime, I finished this game in just over an hour. I was by no means rushing. The base retail price is $8.99, which is a bit staggering for an hour-long commentary game. If it goes on sale for 90% off, get it. I got it in a Humble Bundle for $1, so I am not complaining by any means, but if games were priced by average hours of enjoyment, this one would be ~900% overpriced.
The story was wonderful and I really enjoyed it, but the ending is dissatisfying, feels somewhat rushed and sorta comes out of nowhere, though it is plausible I guess. All in all, it’s a great archetype for how a story game should be presented and if the developer were to make another piece I would strongly consider buying it.
The game is recommended for mature audiences. It deals with topics such as sex and college party life. Some of the content is very suggestive, but nothing heavier than PG-13.

Whatever you do, do NOT buy or play this.
I\'ll just comment the game description of this pos...
\"3 full acts.\"
You call those loosely connected fragments of \"story\" \"acts\"? \"X months later\" doesn\'t mean it is a new act.
\"Based on a true story.\"
There is a reason Hollywood takes an \"artistic freedom\" when basing something on a true story, making it larger than life in some way. This is a story about life, and life is boring. And this is really boring way of telling a story that isn\'t in any way interesting or larger than life and even makes it lesser than life.
\"Multiple short films offer an intimate glimpse into Nina\'s life.\"
Not really. What we get are incoherent glimpses of, well, nothing. My friends and I made more coherent short films in junior high, but we knew better than to share them with the world. If the glimpses we get are intimate, then most status updates on Facebook are TMI.
\"A richly illustrated and scored game world to explore called Valtameri, with multiple maps.\"
Wow. Where to start...
The pink corral-like map is sort of logical when it comes to where you character can move. The ... artsy(?) map is just a hodgepodge of things you can and can not walk on. The lava level looks like it should be easy to move around on, but the collision detection is very off, making your character start to walk in a completely other direction than the one you clicked.
The character AI is so bad, and not so bad it is good, bud so it is good and then gets bad again. Your character get stuck against walls trying to walk in whichever direction the AI thinks it should move to reach the enemy you clicked. The \"bosses\" oftenly goes out of reach, but they don\'t leave the screen until their health is dropped enough, so you can move to another place in the map and fight them there. Or you could just let Ichi fight them, as his character can walk through walls, and if he goes off screen he will re-appear from the other direction.
\"A fully interactive desktop that changes over the course of the game, offering a glimpse into Nina\'s life outside of her online game.\"
As stated earlier this isn\'t made larger than life, it\'s life made more boring. How much does your desktop change over the course of a few months? Not much, I guess. And the changes between the \"acts\" are few, and they don\'t contribute to anything. You learn that Nina has virtually no life outside the game, and whatever info we get is confused and unimportant if not distracting from the \"story\".
If you want a better thing to do, then go to YouTube and watch the screaming goat version of the Game of Thrones theme. It\'s more entertaining and only a minute long.

Overall it\'s alright for a short game; it\'s not worth $10.
2 Major Cons:
1. Most of the story you\'re in a game hack/slashing enemies. You actually get kind of into it -- however it aggrevates the crap out of you because of the horrible pathing and overall clunkiness of the gameplay. It\'s not the beef of the game - but it should still be enjoyable and effortless to play a little simple game while interacting with everything else happening.
2. The game ends abruptly, however there\'s a line in the ending that makes you assume there might be more to the story. There isn\'t. While I\'m satisfied with the story, there could definately be a bit of a continuation or more of a look into how the protagonist deals with the ending.
The characters are real and relatable, even the friends you only interact with through IM. The UI is pleasant and tells a lot about the girl\'s personality. The acting is kind of awkward, but it works for the characters.
If you bought this in the Humble Bundle like I did - it\'s worth an hour or 2 of playthrough. Not worth the $10 though, considering the only part you actually play is so poorly executed.

They Bleed Pixels feels like a mix of Super Meat Boy and Battletoads, a tough-as-nails trap-infested 2D platformer that will test both your reflexes and your sanity. Individual levels are lengthy and well-designed, with a unique checkpoint system helping lessen some of the frustration of dying in tough spots. There's also a somewhat clunky combat system that comes across as a bit obtuse early on but gets better with use. Controls are mostly tight and responsive as they should be in this type of game, however at times it feels as though there's a slight yet noticeable input delay when it comes to jumping. It's something I eventually adapted to and didn't notice at all after playing for a long stretch, but it was a nuisance early on. The game also features a quirky gothic aesthetic style and Lovecraft-influenced story, as well as a surprisingly fantastic soundtrack.
If you aren't a fan of difficult 2D platformers that are capable of pushing your patience, it's probably best to pass on They Bleed Pixels. But if you don't mind a rewarding challenge that provides both pleasure and pain, it's worth giving a shot.

Did you think Super Meat Boy was too easy? Do you hate yourself? Do you enjoy the thought of kicking nightmare creatures into buzzsaws? If you answered yes to any of these questions, They Bleed Pixels might just be the game for you! It's a super tight 2D Platformer with satisfyingly infuriating level design.

I've been finding it hard to continue to play since the characters and story either so bland or so over the top that it is difficult to care. I find myself dreading any 'events', but then also found myself starting to dread the combat since it was becoming so repetative.
After reading other reviews it seems like at some point this game will take a sharp turn with the difficulty and tactics, but if you are looking for a great story and a great combat system right off the bat, I would maybe look elsewhere, or at least remember to stay away from using the DLC gained items until you need them.

Now, I love rpg's and I grew up on turn based combat, but this game is severely lacking. You basically move from dot to dot on a map with very little variation. Each dot either represents a fight, a village or event. Oh, and I guess there are some quest dots you enter into that just contain the above. There's a solid amount of customization, but it doesn't seem to serve much purpose. In almost 10 hours there hasn't been one fight that required any effort.
Then there's the story itself. It feels like it could be interesting, if the characters weren't so cookie cutter and bland. You push through the drawn out fights to get to an event and you get terrible dialogue and hardly any real background on the story. Now I know 10 hours isn't enough to see the whole story, but it's more than enough to get the feel for the game.
So if you like repetitive battles, boring characters and ZERO exploration, this is for you. Everyone else should find something else.
Overall-4/10

I'm a bit hesitant to thumbs this up. Yes, it's fun, addicting and keeps you coming back for more. If you've watched 10 seconds of footage of this game, you'll know what the game is about: jumping on top of falling blocks while avoiding enemies and a rising floor of lava.
This may sound tough, and it certainly is: while controls are decent, you're never really safe from being crushed. And with the blocks falling pretty randomly, some runs will be harder than others. The coins, treasures, power-ups, shops and banks really spice up the game. On the aesthetics, all is great as well: cute 16-bit era graphics and a great soundtrack.
The main disadvantage is the fact that this is a roguelike (or roguelite, if you will). You've only got one life and the coins you collect by climbing, achievements and banking serve to buy other items that will make future runs more doable. However, since a block can crush and instantly kill you roughly every moment, the boss battles are in a way the easier part of the game. And okay, the game is never boring and plays fast enough to have that "one more run!!!" feel, but in the end this game really only has one level. A good one, certainly...but I'm not sure how much I'd pay for it if I didn't got it in a humble bundle.

Pros:
- Great character design - at the time of writing there are 19 characters all of which have unique & fun gameplay styles
- Very fluid gameplay with simple to understand mechanics but complex enough to allow for advanced team strategies.
- Extremely well done animations. The rampage of both gigantic creatures is awesome to watch.
- Execellent level design with varied, dynamic maps.
- The best queuing system I've ever seen - you can pick up to 5 preferred heroes before queuing and you will get to play one of your choices.
- Short queue times even though the playerbase is still relatively small.
- I've experienced zero frame drops (gtx 1070) and no noticable lag in the 8+ hours i've played at the time of writing.
- It's very easy to pick up (mostly down ato a very well done, simple yet breif tutorial)
- The game favours prolonged engagements (there are no 1 hit kill abilities like you find in Overwatch) this game allows for a lot of outplay potential for more experienced players.
- Clean, simple, modern UI (similar to Overwatch's)
- Free to play but has option of a reasonably priced hero pack which unlocks all heros forever (similar to Smite's God pack) so you're not forced into microtransactions to unlock them.
- Very well designed challenge/reward system in the form of reward cards - best reward system I've come across in any game so far.
- Playing in a team allowed us to try multiple stategies with different characters and was really fun to play through the game with varying styles working together to get the objectives. Promotes great team play. If you prefer to play on your own though, there are assassin like characters perfect for that too.
Cons:
- A few balancing issues i've come across so far however i honestly can't say i've played enough of the game yet to properly know if there are vaiable counters in the game or not.
- Heated battles over objectives often there's so much going on you have no idea what's happening as there are effects going off everywhere. But tbh, this is pretty fun when it does happen!
- It has it's own seperate laucher which is iritating but honestly no where near as bad as others are making out. People are massively overeacting to this in other reviews.
- Plays best in a premade team and so far it appears matchmaking doesn't account for this? Played yesterday and didn't lose a single match in about 3 hours of playing as had a full 5 man premade - We were matched against people who clearly weren't premade and I can't imagine it was enjoyable for them as we won many games without even suffering a wound on our creature.
- No ingame UI editor (unless im just being blind). I'd love this feature as i find the map to be very small and difficult to see which friendly is which on the map.
- At the time of writing there is no league system - could be planned for future
- Post game summary screen offers very little feedback on the gameplay. While I like the ist of achievements the secondary screen only offers kills, assists, deaths and damage to the guardian rounded to the nearest K. I'd love to see hero damage and heal stats added to this screen so i can better judge how well im performing on characters and what i could better pick to help the team next time instead. Also, there's an effiecy rating given to every play that i have no clue what it means as there's no explanation of how its calculated anywhere that I can find.
All in all this is a brilliant game that is extremely well polished and fun to play. Don't expect to go into this and be brilliant at it game one; it takes a little learning of the characters and the best tactics in game before you'll start performing well, but its well worth it. Very fun to play and can't wait to see all the improvements the devs have planned for an already great game.

To me, this game is awfully bad. The only point that I find quite interesting is the art, and it is the one that decided me to buy the game.
So basically, Agarest Zero takes some element of the classic turn-based RPG and some other of the average heroic fantasy Visual Novel in order to offer its content ; in the same way as Kamidori Alchemy Meister for instance. (Alas, Agarest is well worse than this one…)
At the moment, I didn't play much but for what I have played… not once have I had fun.
So, firstly, the RPG aspect of the game :
— The turn-based gameplay is interesting with it's mechanics but most of the strategic part of the game is left behind by the fact that the fights are heavily gear-reliant.
— The battles are repetitive ; if the few first one can make you think about some strategies, you quickly make one or two that will work in most occasions. In the end, the lack of diversity and the massive amount of “long” battles transforms the battle in some sort of torture sessions.
— The character creation is too confusing. Firstly, you have to choose between three classes (warrior, battle mage, sorcerer) which is quite understandable even if nothing tells you what these classes are really about. Next… you have to choose five cards that will determine the weapon you'll use and your stats growth. So… for the weapons, you have two icons on each card so you can more or less guess what weapon you will be given. Now for the stats… NOTHING actually tells you what these cards does. In other words, if running countless tries to get the char you want is your thing… this game is for you. Otherwise… well… Good luck.
Secondly, the VN aspect :
— The story is quite common for what I have seen. Basically, it's just a way to put the game in context but chances are you won't find it more than just average. It's not bad but we have seen way much elaborated stories in the RPG genre.
— As I said earlier, the art is well drawn. Backgrounds are well detailed and the fact that characters are not fixed during dialogs makes the game in itsel a bit more living.
— The one thing that I hated: the affection system. It… follows absolutely no logical rule. For example, I made some choice with a character, that got me +1 in affection with this one BUT on the other hand, I got -1 with another one that was not even here and that had nothing to do with this choice. It's as if it were totally random…
I'll probably update this review later if I progress in the game but for now, if you are seeking a JRPG/VN game, I could only recommand you to search elsewhere.
