Having a hankering for a RPG I ended up picking up this title to scratch the urge. Am I disappointed? Yes.
The storyline is bland and generic and offers nothing intriguing or exciting to the player. At this stage I barely know what my goal is (other than looking after Mimel and picking up more (female) characters to add to my party) and I've no desire to find out. The parts that talk about the storyline are tedious and bland at best and ultimately unfulfilling for the player. A solid RPG should have the player wanting to know what the next twist in the game is; Agarest fails to deliver on that aspect. Considering playing on feels like a chore that I want to avoid doing at all costs.
The tutorial barely gives you the bare bones of combat which is simple enough to pick up despite being poorly mapped, and the character creation part is totally left uninformed. The player absolutely doesn't know what to do without the help of a guide and to be honest I have no idea what on earth I picked for the MC, Sieg. Combat gets boring and repetitive quickly. If you're a player who dislikes grinding there's no worry as you're forced to grind and play through fights just to get anywhere on the map.
Speaking of characters, the characters of the game are bland, dull and boring with predictable, mundane personalities. There's a womaniser without a hint of charm, a little mysterious childish girl and then there's the MC who is the equivalent of bread without butter. The voice acting and somewhat pretty character designs aren't enough to carry the personalityless characters through with the bland script. Another part of the game which is a little more fun is the dating aspect where you woo the ladies you pick up for your party. However, Fire Emblem: Awakening offers the same kind of game as Agarest but with a better script, a easier to follow plot and interesting characters.
For the most part, Agarest has a lacklustre script and a poor combat system which ultimately lets the full game down. A much more interesting story with more engaging characters is the minimum this game would need to carry it through with the current combat system. The pixel graphics are somewhat charming, at the very least.
My overall opinion? I wish I could refund this game and would do so in a heart beat if I was able to.

The Agarest Senki/Agarest War series was always a little out of my comfort zone when it came to RPGs, mostly due to the strategy involved in the fights. Thankfully, they made it easy to figure who to place where to maximize your combo efficiency in battle, plus learning new Secret Arts through trial and error has been a blast!
This is technically the first game in the series, chronologically, but the second game to have been made. This one is a lot more forgiving than the first by means of getting the True Ending, as there are only two generations, so a lot of the original content from the first game that you had to be forced to do to get the True Ending has been streamlined for the second; giving you a lot more time to enjoy the story at a more natural pace.
My one little problem lies in the fact that they seem to reuse character designs and even come close to reusing names as well; namely, the character "Alice" is extremely close if not identical to "Ellis" in name and design both, right down to having a larva as a bodyguard. Sieghart also appears to be in close relation to the main characters of the first game, not to mention a few of the female leads seem to be borrowed concepts, as well. All that aside, however, I greatly recommend this game to everyone, especially if you want to enjoy something a little different in your RPG library!

Up front: Game's not terrible. Big ol' Candy Crush ripoff sloppily ported from mobile, has a versus mode if you want to set the kids at each other's throats. If you want that, go for it.
The rest of the story: this is one of the weirder slapdash mobile ports I've seen. Usually people make you use the mouse like it was finger for swipe controls, but this game is, as far as I can tell, entirely mouse-free. Thank god it's a slow, plan-your-moves based title and not Bejeweled, eh? The big problem is it's got a f2p energy system which can also be asked to charge you for bonus powerups, lives, the works. Straight up the only thing that separates this from a Candy Crush or the like is the license. It's not amazing, but if you're the sort who plugs away at those because "hey, it's free" and are willing to put up with the occasional recharge cooldown or what-not, go for it. I'm not.
(Also there's some other technical fiddliness. It doesn't fit on my screen. The lives counter is cut off, I had to go into the cash shop to actually find out how many I had left.)
Just play Bejeweled!

As for Multi-player, I can't even connect to the servers. Isn't that swell?

So I\'ve just finished playing Cibele and I must say that is not a bad experience at all, but as a game it needs to be polished in general. At first I was expecting a novela/thriller kind of story but I didn\'t expected to be an autobiographical real life simulator(literally) presented as an interactive game. The story itself it\'s very ordinary and common \"playing\"(or pretend like you do) as a 19 year old teen addicted to an online game, but it\'s what makes this game particular and interesting.
The presentation of Cibele is alright, the computer content it seemed legit to me, although I encountered some visual problems with the levels on the online game(third level). The soundtrack was okay and I liked the acting.
Mainly, needs more interactivity to give the player more capacity of action and more immersion, it just lacks of it. The game focuses on it\'s story events but although it was predictable(what makes the game boring  for a lot of people) it\'s not storytelling, it\'s a real world story and life can be predictable sometimes.
The game lets you discover some aspects  and interactions of the main character\'s life but it doesn\'t serve you at the game so this feature it\'s made(I think) for those who apreciate the small details at games and for good presentation purposes ,Cibele doesn\'t have any puzzles or challenges.
The mechanics inside the online game are very basic and alright(at some points) and one of the main problems here, in my opinion, is the \"combat system\". I mean I can understand that it\'s a game with basic mechanics but I think this part could be a lot more improved and it would be acceptable but it\'s how it is, very repetitive and dull. You can\'t take any damage either, what makes the combat pointless. It made me think how this pair of teens were spending time here and not on a chat website.
I had a dilemma whether recommend Cibele or not because it\'s not a polished game, but I\'ve seen some effort putt into this game. Besides ,the topic itself it\'s a very common problem nowadays, a lot of naive/young/adult people give a lot of trust to strangers on the internet and many are badly affected by this. So in conclussion try it, it\'s a peculiar life simulator that shows some relatable aspects and details about life making it a good experience, but it could have been better executed and more playable.

I was hoping that the port to PC would make this game better but it turns out that if you polish a turd, it's still a turd.
Mugen Souls tries very, very hard to be deep and interesting but it ends up as a pile of game systems and mechanics that don't mesh together at all. G-Castle Battles are like playing rock-paper-scissors except if you lose enough times you get a Game Over. The Moe Kill system and Chou-Chou's Form Change could have been interesting but there are so many affinities that at any given time you're about 100% likely to be in the wrong form to actually perform a Moe Kill. The Blast-Off system seems to work once for the tutorial and then the rest of the time, you do so little damage to anything with knockback that there's no point, so I have no clue why they even introduce it at the beginning of the game. Creating your own custom units makes sense for a strategy RPG where you're allowed to have many units out at once but you can only have 4 characters in your party and your party has already filled with clearly superior story characters by the time you get out of the first couple of chapters or so, so that's another pointless system. And Mugen Field is a pathetic attempt to ape Disgaea's Item World that somehow manages to miss everything about Item World that makes it fun.
In short, Mugen Souls is (still) irredeemably bad, regardless of how it was censored for Western release. It's just another bad JRPG trying to ride on moe.

In a nutshell, this is an unattractive game, featuring obtuse mechanics that are poorly explained.
While I have no issues with grind-heavy games, (I'm a veteran of the Disgaea series) or with fanservice-heavy games (I'm a fan of the Hyperdimension Neptunia series), this one just fails, due to the inability to properly explain the mechanics of the moe kill system (beyond the very most basic aspects).
Given that the moe kill system is presented as very important, I would have expected it to be presented in greater detail, particularly since no other game uses something like this, to my knowledge.
Add in some rather ugly and low resolution character models and less than ideal controls, along with a camera that pretty much defaults to the worst angle possible in any situation, and I just can't be bothered to try and dig deeper and find out why this game is so highly rated.
I'm sad, because I wanted to like this title, I really did. But I'm giving up on it quickly, because I feel like even at ten dollars (bought during Steam Summer Sale 2016) I overpaid. I'd rather get a refund now, as opposed to being upset later.

Before I start I also, own this for PS3 and have raced many more hours there. In my opinion this is a fairly good game. It's has a unique style to it not seen elsewhere. What Mugen souls is, is a turn based tactical RPG. While other Tactical RPGs may have areas designated for special field effects, this game uses circles and crystal-like objects to designate them. These can be broken for a variety of more effects and bonuses. The game allows you hit enemies around like hockey pucks on an ice rink. The initial concepts can seem overwhelming at first but aren't extremely difficult to learn. The hardest thing to learn in this game for me was the Moe Kill system. This is a system where you can use the main characters personaility type along with some phrases to turn enemies into loyal subjects or "Peons" as the game puts it. What makes this difficult is there is no guide or help in game to tell you what phrases match with the 7 personailities or what ones are effective against the other. The game could of had a library where as you use phrases and test out the moe system it unlocks and lets you know what is and isn't effective. I personally am a big fan of NISA and own many of there games, one of the biggest draws for me personally is with this game you can create your own custom characters. While Disgaea has some nice color palette swaps, in this game you can go in and actually alter and dress up your characters. I recommend this game for anyone who is a fan of long grindy RPG games.
In regards to the censorship. I did some research and appearantly this game is in fact censored. They removed a bathining mini game where you wash the female characters in game. For me personally I could care less about it. Quite a few characters look underage and I don't really want to see them nude anyways. The title recieved what would be considered an M rating in Japan and a T rating here. The censorship does not just end with this mini game though, the translations of certian characters have been toned down as the team felt they were too vulgar for this type of game. Personally I found most of the characters dull and lacking of common sense. That compiled with the underage look of several of the female cast makes the story rather lack-luster and obviously pandering to a niche. The censorship in no way really effects the game or takes away from it.
My final thoughts are if you look past the story and characters what you have left is a decent tactical RPG, with some overly complicated portions. If your a fan of grindy RPGs and can look past the story and characters this is a worth-while title that will have you busy for a long time to come.

A 2D Arcade Platformer, this game is extremely simple – you are a marshmallow-like blob who can jump (including wall jump).
Your goal is to make your way up as high as you can.
Blocks contstantly fall from above and pile up at the bottom of the screen. These blocks are of variable sizes, and can be jumped off of – but will squash you if they fall on your head.
A rising tide of lava (and, later on, at higher elevations, stormclouds and eventually a sweeping laser) will pursue you upwards as well, meaning that you cannot fall too far behind the avalanche of blocks or else you will die.
In addition to the blocks, there are enemies. Some of these spawn on the blocks, such as leaping snakes and chickens (which can be killed by hopping on their heads), spiked blocks (which hurt you if you land on their heads, but can be pushed off), and super chickens (which spit rolling lava balls at you). Others can fly – there are birds which try to drop eggs on your head, flying squid which try to run into you, and dragons which spit fireballs at you. All of these can also be dispatched by hopping on their heads.
To help the player, there are chests which spawn as well. These chests can contain various powerups, which fill up red squares on the right hand side of the screen. At first, you can carry only one powerup, but as you acquire more of these squares during your climb, you can carry up to four. These powerups have highly variable abilities, from a pogo stick which makes you bounce continuously but lets you jump higher, to a teleporter which lets you go through solid objects, to ram’s horns which allow you to smash blocks above you by jumping into them twice as quickly, to a shield which absorbs multiple hits before breaking. Every time you are struck, you lose one powerup – and if you have no powerups, you die. Thus, powerups serve as a sort of life meter, and continuously collecting them (and losing them as you get hit by enemies) is a major part of the gameplay.
There are also “followers”, three static powerups which follow you around and allow you to move faster and jump higher. Each of these can be upgraded up to three times. In addition, there are green extra life mushrooms which totally aren’t ripped off from Super Mario Brothers (*cough*) which can also follow you around and allow you to respawn regardless of your method of death – you can even come back from being squashed by blocks or falling into the lava, which ordinarily kill you regardless of how many powerups you’re carrying!
Breaking up the climb are various bosses at various set points. These give you a breather from the constant platforming, and are mostly very easy to beat – indeed, they are mostly welcome breaks from the much more intense platforming gameplay present while the avalanche of blocks is ongoing.
Climbing up to 1800 feet allows you to confront the final boss, but to gain all the achievements you need to climb all the way to 3000 feet and confront several “double boss” fights, where two bosses from earlier in the game spawn at the same time and you must defeat them both.
Every time you die, you must start your climb over, but there are coins you collect over the course of the game which can be spent in a shop in order to give yourself permanent bonuses (or buy cosmetic items). These coins can allow you to start with various items, companions, or even alter the gameplay in various ways, such as increasing the rate of lava rise but doubling the number of coins which spawn. These coins can both be spent on in-game items during a climb in various shops which periodically spawn, or can be stored away in in-game banks and then spent on the out-of-game items.
There are also missions and quests which periodically drop from the sky in the form of scrolls; these missions and quests give the player coins and experience for grabbing them. Experience is used to unlock all the in-game items, while the coins are useful for the same reason as always.
So, given I have now explained EVERYTHING in the game, how IS it to play?
The reality is that it is a pure reflex platformer. While it starts off fairly slow-paced, by the time you’re trying to reach for the stars (and the last few achievements), massive numbers of blocks fall from above and huge numbers of dangerous enemies spawn constantly. The game is essentially a reflex-intensive 2D platformer with moving platforms at that point, and it is likely to take you 10 hours or so to 100% the game – and probably about half that to beat the final boss.
Ultimately, how much fun you have with this game is probably up to the kind of player you are. Do you like endless arcade-style games? Are you apt to be frustrated if your ten minute long session ends with you getting crushed below a block a hundred feet before your destination? Does a game which has no story or much variety or really much of anything but the pure straightforward platforming gameplay appeal to you?
In the end, I can’t say that I didn’t find this game interesting in a sense, but at the same time, I could never really shake a sense of cheapness – it feels like a glorified flash game. It is extremely simple, and there really isn’t much to it – it is just you trying to beat your high score and climb ever-higher in the avalanche.
If that sort of thing doesn’t appeal to you, you really probably don’t want to buy this game. If it does… well, maybe there’s something here for you.

If this were a stealth game with none of the "Thief" branding...It would only be somewhat passable. For the sake of my sanity I couldn't go into everything that is so wrong about Thief 4, but to have the nerve to reboot this series as if they could do it better and produce this generic gumbo soup of all of the worst modern video game cliches and boardroom concoctions of what would sell best, is an outrage.
First, the story. The story is a joke, not only will you probably not know whats going on but you will not care even the slightest because it is so clumbsy, so poorly stitched together, right down to improperly synced voices and cutscenes that abrutly start and end like a bad commercial. The game revolves around a girl named Erin, an immediately unlikable angsty teen girl with all of the cliches you'd expect right down to "I'm not a kid anymore". Your experience with her whenever she appears to further the story is a girl ripped straight from 2016 thrown into a bland, unimaginative historical setting, just to throw a tantrum and behave totally irrationally. You don't care for Erin, yet the game seems to think you should have this bond with her while giving you ever reason to hate her and still never bother to include any context for why shes there. Shes simply a plot device to a further a story thats is painfully dull and shallow.
Not only did Thief decide to reject the supernatural elements of the past games, but they replaced it and the lore with nothing more than a religious zealot who wants to control whatever the hell "primal" is supposed to be and rejected Resident Evil wall crawlers that behave like discount clickers from the last of us. There is no imagination in this game, there is no care or interest or love of the series that came before it. If there were, they wouldn't have systematically rejected every core tennant and game design element of those games.
You'll spend your entire adventure doing nothing else but walking up behind guards and activating a painfully repetitive takedown animation which is so popular among big budget games today. Because why would simply swing your blackjack and knock out a guard when you could wait for a command prompt to allow you to activate their TOTALLY BAD♥♥♥♥♥animation which comes coupled with a sound effect so loud you'd think stealth wasn't a priority. That is one of the most frustrating parts of Thief, the animations tied to every single action you perform, from opening a drawer to picking up a coin, every one of them is paired with this 2 second animation that slows down picking up nickels and dimes to a crawl. In previous Thieves if you were to happen upon a chest with loot, you could pick up everything in that chest in as much time as it would take you to grab a single silver cup in Thief. To add to the frustration, the same command prompt for looting is the same one that locks you into peaking around cornes. You'll find yourself more often than not peering around a desk or shutting a door while you try to loot from a desk or the purse off a guard.
Strategy is not necessary. In previous Thief games you were given a wide tool set from moss arrows, fire arrows, water arrows, noise maker arrows to rope arrows, however in Thief 4, you'll occassionally use water arrows and absolutely nothing else. There is no tactical use or requirement for any of your equipment. You'll get from the start of the game to the end with just "Press Q to TAKEDOWN", the same guards, over and over and over again. Rope arrows have even been downgraded from sensibly being used on wood surfaces to specifically designated wooden beams with a glowing blue rope tied around it to tell you, "use your rope arrow here to get to this place" which is generally just a single piece of loot or an alternate path which really doesn't change anything in terms of navigation.
The world design has gone from an realistically designed location to a video gamey linear map that simply gives you a couple of different paths that take you to the same location. You can't get lost, you can't roam, you are given the illusion of an open map while really everything is walled in and blocked off to funnel you to the end. To make matters worse, instaed of a hand drawn map that clues you in as much as Garrett knows about the location, forcing you to become involved in your surroundings and navigate by landmark, they just give you a mini map with quest markers. Despite the fact the levels are basically hallways, they still float indicators all over the screen telling you exactly where to go and exactly where you are. The map alone indicates the greatest reason why Eidos Montreal knows so little or cares so little about Thief and what it is.
They simply took a popular, respected name in the video game industry and recycled it into this generic, consolized, casualized mess of modern game cliches. At times you'll be running parkour across rooftops while things explode around you and others you'll jarringly be in 3rd person climbing up pipes and grates like Uncharted. They tried to rip off every popular modern game and stir it up into one game because they figured it would return the most profit. It's an incredibly lazy effort, in fact the ending to this game is so empty, you can literally feel the interest of the devs trail off to a roll credit because they just did not care anymore and needed to finish it for release. I could go on and on about all of the ways this game fails not only the Thief name, but game design in general. Eidos Montreal does not get it, they did not care, they cashed in on Thief and left a stain on the integrity of the series. Nothing about the game indicates fans of the series worked on this project. there is nothing about this game that indicates the developers even played the previous games.
They removed Stephen Russel, the iconic voice of Garrett and replaced him with a generic angsty male that turns this now vampiric, emaciated looking Garrett into any other bland, brooding protagonist. Their excuse for this was they needed a motion cap performance that would sync up with the acting, but nowhere in this game does that ever present as either a necessity or even a feature. There is not a single moment in this game that an actor needed to record his lines while doing motion capture work, further insult to injury, but perhaps its best Stephen Russel was not attached to this poor excuse for a Garrett.
Bottom line this is a soulless, effortless, completely awful cash grab that did not respect its IP.

If you're looking for a game that is simply about stealing stuff and evading guards, like what the trailer of this game shows, this is not the game for you. The paragraph below is basically all the things I could think of that really bothered me about Thief.
Now, since I haven't played the previous Thief games, I couldn't have expected so much of this story to be so paranormal. It's actually something I greatly disliked about the game, especially how one chapter turns it into a horror game. The ending of the game is also very disappointing and left me thinking "What the ♥♥♥♥?" The level design is very linear, at least in my experience, making sneaking around guards (or at least trying) very futile. There are too many times where areas are "Mash 'F' to move debris/open window," which makes the game feel extremely repetitive and boring (ESPECIALLY when picking things up for money, you'll get tired of that real fast). The controls are unresponsive at times which can be extremely irritating at inconvenient times.
One of my main complaints of the game is how empty it all felt. The story, as stated before, was disappointing and left mostly questions than answers. The character development was awful, you barely got to know some characters before they blatantly die (which is supposed to propel the story forward, which it didn't feel like it did). Garrett also has the personality of a brick, showing little to no emotion, which is just... ugh... The City was supposed to be lively with people roaming the streets with pouches of gold ripe for the taking (at least that's what I thought), instead, we get this empty and drab city that's populated only by people sharing secrets way too loudly inside, poor and sick people who die in one hit on the streets, civilians who do nothing but scream if they see you do anything illegal (like attacking someone, but I don't even think they react to you stealing stuff or you know, sneaking around while covered in weaponry), and guards who never respawn once you take them down until you reach the next chapter of the game.
Here are some things I liked. There's actually quite a few things to do throughout the game. There are lots of little odd jobs which are short but unique. Keep in mind I'm somebody who's got more than 2 hours on this game, unlike most of these goofballs who play the game for 30 minutes then complain how the game's pay to win because they went 0/50 in their first game.
The game is NOT PAY TO WIN, every gun is buyable with the in-game currency and every gun is viable (although there are some you'll end up liking more than others). If you want the premium currency, there's an option to do online surveys to earn it for free (it's hard, but rewarding work). Everything you can buy in the game is purely cosmetic, more specifically, you can get weapon skins, character models, and accessories with premium currency that do not affect gameplay.
Despite having graphics equal to those of The Amazing Spiderman II, it runs very smoothly and even a potato can run it. The game's never crashed on me EVER and their servers have only gone down ONCE since I started playing a couple months back.
Line of Sight is a very fun game to play, whether casually or competitively, because it's a fairly polished game that's unique. Abilities that are available to players are an interesting twist to an fps and there are modes that suit the needs of players who would rather play without superpowers.
My favorite thing about the game is the Combat Mastery system. It's very similar to Borderlands 2, where your character has three unique trees to spend points into until they reach the end of a tree that they have chosen. The perks themselves need work in terms of balancing and usefulness, but this is definitely something I enjoy about the game.
The only reasons I can say to not play this game would be the amount of bugs still present (it's easy to get stuck in objects around the map) and map balancing issues (some spawns on some maps are drastically game changing). Otherwise, the game is still fairly incomplete and progress has been made by the Blackspot team and it looks like the game isn't going anywhere anytime soon.
TL;DR You shouldn't be writing a game review if you've got less than 10 hours.

STATEMENT:
"Total War Battles: KINGDOM is very enjoyable, but has too many pay-to-win apsects"
RATING :
6 / 10
INTRODUCTION:
Very enjoyable and I just played the first 7.8 hours without a brake. However, there are quiet a few cons to it as well.
PROS :
- Easy to learn (tutorials are great)
- Free
- Has multiplayer and a friend system
- Has many types of buildings; the developers have thought about balancing these buildings prices and their purposes
- Mining is especially fun, when finding out what resource you will discover
CONS:
- Gold is extremely overpowerful as a resource, and is able to be bought
- Gold can be exhanged for every other material
- Inabilities can sometimes make the game boring
RECCOMENDATION TO CUSTOMER:
I reccomend this game as it is very enjoyable and can keep you hooked hours on end. But, be wary of this pay-to-play system (although it's exaggerated by the reviewers), and think about if your wasting Gold.
FEEDBACK TO THE DEVELOPERS & PRODUCERS:
Look, you may be looking at all of those negative reviews and feel like you get no feedback; and say "Whats the point."
But, if you make some changes (examples listed below), people may feel more optimistic about this game.
- Make Gold not able to be exhanged for other materials
- Lower the hours it takes to build things, to minutes

Really didn't enjoy this one, for three key reasons
1) It feels grindy. Upgrades and costumes are expensive enough that it takes a dozen runs to buy anything, and even then most of the upgrades you have to spend coins to activate them. The progression feels closer to a mobile game trying to get you to buy coins. If they wanted to make it so high scores wouldn't be affected by the purchasable upgrades, they should have just not had purchaseable upgrades. It's not a fun progression.
2) Whatever random algorithm that makes the blocks fall is infuriating. I feel like the game would benefit greatly if, whenever it spawned a treasure chest or a mission or an enemy, it prevented blocks from falling over that space for X seconds. As it is, it feels like every interesting gimmick, good or bad, is crushed within a second of it appearing, which just isn't fun. My best runs I didn't go for any items or treasure, simply because when I did, 99% of the time a block would appear just offscreen and crush me with zero chance to react.
3) The controls just feel wrong. I tried with a keyboard first, then a controller, and it felt floatly and difficult to handle no matter what. Over and over I was yelling at the collision detection, getting crushed by blocks I could swear I was clear of, or hitting an enemy with a jump that apparently was a low enough angle to kill me instead. And the worst was the walljump, which seemed to fire off at random times. I'd jump, hit the wall, and then immediately fly off without hitting the button again into an enemy or a brick.
I'm only so-so on arcade games in general, but the biggest issue for me is that this is a platformer that doesn't feel good/fun to control. Upgrades are a matter of taste, but wonky controls and frustrating spawning put this as a firm not recommended from me.

As with the Origional, Zero is a true work of art. The Generation system is vastly improved from the original, and the affection system adds its own level of stratagy. The gameplay, while at first glance appears simple, is, in a word, "Multi-Layered". Mastering Esoterica and Combination arts is key to not only surviving some of the most difficult battles, but also recieving some of the best items in the game. With that in mind, I would be remiss if I didn't mention the Agarest Wiki that contains truely invaluable information on the game itself.
While i love the game, I have to mention two dissapointments I have in concern to the actual game itself. First, the monster capture and combination system can be a boon to any player. If only for the Title System and the High End items you can get by using it. However, capturing monsters can be a chore sometimes, and often feels like a waste of time due to the grind required to max it out.
Second, the blacksmithing system has one infuriating element that i wish they had eliminated from the origional. That is the Random Item system that occures while smithing. On occasion, while crafting items, instead of the desired item you recieve a random craftable item instead. This still uses the materials, and after 3000 craft attempts, I only recived one item I cared about, or was useful. Instead you generally recive items that are either utterly useless, or are low level and already abundant.
As to the Steam download, it has one major glitch i was unable to remedy. Unfortunatly, there is a glich where on many characters in both conversation scenes and in the gallery, the characters images are obsucered by all the other alternate appearances being layered over eachother at the same time. This takes away from the character and story driven expreance that is essential to any JRPG.
On a possitive note, the Steam DLC is absolutly fantastic. Without it, many cassual gamers may find the baseline grind to level up and aquire both Gold and EP to be a daunting task. After purchasing the DLC it was almost like starting a new game + without ever having to have played the game.
I would recomend this series to anyone who enjoys JRPG's or RPG's in general. For a more epic experience I suggest playing the original and then loading over the completed game data to Zero.
All in all, I'd give this game a solid 9 out of 10.
As a simple footnote I would suggest that due to suggestive sexual content in this game, parental supervison is advised.

Short summary: This is an amazing turn based strategy game with unique weapons, and a huge variety of characters and unlockable skills. This game is similair to fire emblem combat system, and has a cliche but an entertaining story. There are several events, and incorporates the oh so common dating sims the japanese love as well. One of the best part of the game is without a doubt, the creation of your character, where it is a tarot card system, which randomizes your character in the vague direction you build him to be.
Synopsis: Record of Agarest War Zero is the prequel to Record of Agarest War. The tale follows Sieghart, an army commander who gains magical powers from a strange woman named Mimel. Blossoming from this setup, Record of Agarest War Zero is a slow-paced tale treading on familiar territory: the world is in danger and it's up to a small band of warriors to set things right.
Combat: Record of Agarest War Zero's shining light is combat. Moving characters into position like a chess board is a challenging undertaking, but a rewarding one. Depending on which square characters occupy, they can link to other characters to unleash joint attacks with powerful results. But it's the calculated movement of sprites into position that makes exciting battles. While the terrain is flat and backgrounds repetitive, the environment is still a non-factor like the original Agarest War. The strategic requirements of success are fulfilling for all strategy fans. (Battles dish out experience like candy, yet money feels constantly tight.)
Gameplay:  The Agarest War series is different from other strategy games is that the story is split over multiple generations. When the curtain finally closes on Sieghart's side of the story, it's his offspring with the maiden-of-highest-regard that carries on the tale into future years. You are also forced to progress along a fixed path, forced to stop at each dot along the way for a battle. These often have no bearing on the plot and are simply there to make the journey from one chapter to the next take as long as possible.(although if the battle does indeed get too tedious, pressing q will turn on auto battle. A word of advice is use it on enemies you will dominate, due to the fact that the auto A.I is not the best.)
Overall, i love this game, while it may say i only have 10 hours or so, i have the rest of the series on my ps3, with a total over 200 hours, a great game focusing on turn based strategy, and dating sim like playthrough.

Agarest Zero is the prequel to Agarest: Generations of War. People who played the old Agarest will find that a few things have changed.
Starting with the good improvements. A fast-forward option during dialogue, fully turn-based dungeons with no more analog crawling or suprise encounters, and a slightly more informative esoteric book. A simplified version of the original Agarest is build into the game, and can be unlocked if you play NG+ on hard. As long as you get True End in the Zero universe, you will unlock True End in the Agarest vanilla universe automatically. You can unlock various vanilla characters and combine them into your zero party for maximum choice.
There are bad points too. For one, there are only two generations instead of five, although unlike Leonheardt who was stuck with a sword, you will have some control over Sieghart's weapon. The True End mechanic is also different, it being dependent on relationship scores and less than a handful of crucial storyline choices. You will not unlock the true ending unless you are familiar with dating sims; it is possible to get all nine women in the group to love you maximally, but unless you get somewhere close to that you won't get the true ending. The game is faster-paced due to less generations, but not fast-paced enough to warrent repeated crapshoots on the dating sim mechanic only to find out that you fail true end again and again. If you follow the True End guide for Zero on Agarest Wiki to a tee, it is a linear process and you can unlock it. But then Sieghart/Leonis will not feel like they have any consistent preference or personality. It will just be hardcore pragmatic metagaming.
On an important tangent, this game may be a little bit less friendly to female gamers than the vanilla game, because of the much more increased emphasis on the dating sim aspect. Women-to-women conversations in this game are also more superficial than vanillla. Female gamers can consider themselves warned.
It is a game with pros and cons, but if you liked the original Agarest then you might as well get Zero because it comes with a simplified version of the original game plus the interface improvements.

There are two problematic trends at play here:
The first is to rush games out before they're ready; this is bad enough with respect to downloadable content, but with critical crashes and bugs, this is a betrayal to the consumer.  I have abandoned the attempt to finish this game after two times, as this game will erase your savegames the moment it inevitably crashes.  Do not trust the reports that the savegame bug is resolved; twice I lost my progress just before the last level and resolved the plotline on Youtube.
The second is to take a beloved saga from a time of dedication and innovcation and continue it with today's negligent simplifications.  Thief began with a terrifying ideal:  what would you do if a run-of-the-mill guard could kill you and your only recourse was to evade detection?  What if you were less powerful than everything else in your world?  NOW save the world.
The fanbase, one of the Internet's first gaming fanbases, has disbanded.  You've one chance to bring them back.  Make another game, and make it Thief.
Oh--and please release it when it's ready.

To give some perspetive, the game is based on a true story about a young girl, Nina, who meets someone on an online game (based around Final Fantasy XI), and the relationship and events that unfold over the course of a few months.
+ An incredibly realistic story that many gamers can relate to based around online / long distance dating, and meeting people through video games. I've personally had very similar experiences.
+ I found it to be very interesting to play as the perspective of the female in this game. It was a bit eye opening at how annoying it must be to constantly be flirted with by random jerks online who all seemingly want to sleep with you or get nude pics.
+ Very realistic characters. I was actually thoroughly pleased when the guy had some anxiety issues, and doubts about buying a plane ticket and flying across country to meet the girl for the first time outside the game. To me this is a cautionary tale for girls and guys alike. It's far easier to talk to people online, on the phone, or through games, and when you meet someone in real life you may find that things don't work out as well....which is actually VERY common.
+ Great dialogue, which was incredibly well written and felt very genuine. The flirting especially was very cringe-worthy at times, but it often is when starting relationships as the guy gives the girl a lot of corny yet flattering compliments.
+ I may get some hate for this, but I give this game props for looking into the \"taboo\" that is sexting and trading pics. In online environments it\'s extremely common for relationships to begin by trading pics far before you ever meet someone in real life. I also give props to the developer who shared all of these pictures to the somewhat judgemental gaming community.
+ It almost feels like you are a stalker as you browse through her computer each time looking at her pictures, reading her emails, and going through a large variety of other text documents, fanart, school work, and so on which allows you to really delve into this girl\'s personality and who she is.
+ Visually the graphics in the game look great and filled with color.
- I have mixed feelings about the ending. Not to spoil too much, the guy is a♥♥♥♥♥♥ and the ending is a bit abrupt. I wish it would have shown a bit more emotion as to what happened after...and I really wanted to know how the girl felt. I mean just as an example, it could have lead to depression and self-harm.
- Very short game, it took me about 50minutes or so to finish the game. If you choose to read through the extra content like the text logs, chat, poems, text documents, it's probably around 1.5 hours.

13 Pros, 9 cons.
Pros:
1) Overall gameplay is great.

4) Sound is great.
5) Smooth GUI / UI Menus.
6) Fast queues time. (10-30 seconds)
7) Fast loading even for a slow computer.
8) Guaranteed to play the fighter you want to play by chosing before queueing.
9) Almost every skin is unlockable through in-game currency that you gain from playing.
10) Alot of skins (Alot of cheap re-coloring but it still looks good)

13) Creatures loadout and fortune cards gives a nice little extra thing to work towards.
Cons:
1) Not enough fighters (yet)

3) Not enough maps. (3)

5) Difficult to find the patch notes (Accessable only via ARC Game launcher > Forums > Patch Notes > Post)  Should be able to be accessable through the "View Updates" button on steam (IMO)
6) Third party launcher, messes it up for alot of people, (Not me, but 80% of the negative reviews complains about it)
7) You need to re-install the game in order to play the game through the ARC launcher without starting steam first.
8) No ranked queue yet, so the game doesn't feel competitive
9) Currently, the only goals to play towards are unlocking new heroes (Unless you already spent £30 to unlock them all) or skins, which feels pointless.

I tried giving this game a chance, because a lot of people have written positive reviews about it, but I just don't feel the same.
The story is so slow-paced and it takes forever for anything interesting to happen. While the writing itself is decent, I just can't get into it. It's sci-fi themed with a mystery to solve, but the mission and the mystery just don't keep me interested enough. It doesn't help that the player doesn't know much about the setting.
What really bothers me the most about this game is the narrative on racism. The game tries to get the player to sympathize with non-human people who face racism, and yet there aren't any dark-skinned characters? How does the developer not see the irony in that? "Let's address racism in this game with fictional races, except that every single one of our characters will be white as f*ck"?
Furthermore, the character Sol is racist but everyone just accepts it. The story tries to make the player see that he isn't such a bad guy even though he's racist. Um, no, racists shouldn't be sympathized with no matter how "nice" they are otherwise. Racism isn't supposed to be funny and lighthearted. Racism in the real world gets people murdered. It isn't a f*cking joke. It makes the whole point of bringing up the problems of racism in the first place absolutely pointless.
If you don't mind these flaws, sure, give the game a chance. It's free. But personally, I just can't recommend it.

Don't get caught offguard by the graphics. Despite looking fairly simplistic, there's quite some depth to the game and the different maps. You constantly have to make strategic decisions based on the amount of bridges, lines and wagons you own to keep the stations from overflowing. On top of that, changes in acceleration and speed between the various trains and metro's make each map feel distinct.
Eventhough you will eventually get overwhelmed, the pace and simplistic graphics of Mini Metro make it a perfect last game before bedtime. It's very satisfying to see your network expand while the numbers get higher.

I'm sure we've all done it, sat fuming on a Subway/Train platform, staring at the word DELAYED thinking 'Why are these things never on time? Why are the trains always overcrowded? How hard can it be?'. Well, Mini Metro gives you a chance to find out.
Now, Mini Metro is not a simulation along the lines of Cities in Motion, you simply have to connect the 'stations' on screen in the most efficient way possible so they don't get overcrowded. At the start you have 3 lines, each with 1 carriage, to connect up the 3 starting stations. These lines can then be extended or altered to link up the new stations that randomly pop up as time progresses. At the end of each in-game week you're offered one of two upgrade, these upgrades vary but they include: another line [up to a maximum of 5], a bigger/quicker carriage for a line and, later on, bigger stations. So, you keep ferrying dots between stations as best you can until one or more stations gets so overcrowded that passengers give up and the game ends.
Style wise the games looks like a subway map with its bold coloured lines and black bordered shapes denoting stations, even the way the waiting passenger count is reminiscent of the info-giving asterisks - though a square next to the station mean you have a passengers waiting to be transported to a 'square' station and not 'Closed on Sundays'. Other UI elements are simple and/or kept hidden out of the way even though hiding them is arguably unnecessary.
The game's AI is simple but it does what it needs to, carriages only stop at stations with waiting passengers, only passengers that can be can transported at least partially to their destination are picked up and passengers will take the shortest route possible to their destination. The logic used when determining what route lines take between stations could use a little work though particularly when creating lines near the river.
In short, Mini Metro is in 'easy to learn, hard to master' territory and, after finding several hours having passed despite vowing 'just one more go', it's addictive.

Combining masocore platformer with a simple combo-driven mashy combat system should seem relatively neat when you consider how tired this young genre already is. Unfortunately, They Bleed Pixels just doesn't nail it, suffering from terrible combat control, lousy hit detection, and an I Wanna Be The Guy mentality when it comes to enemy placement and level design.
The two-button (attack and jump) approach simply doesn't work for this game. There are too many different types of attack and defensive actions all assigned to one  button. Using the wrong attack happens far too often, and large portions of every stage in the game feel like they're designed purposefully around the idea of you using the wrong attack. The way slashes and kicks are set up is entirely backwards from how one would want to actually use them. It just feels like bad design on purpose on the part of the developers.
When controls aren't the issue, lousy hit detection on the 800,000,000 buzzsaws you'll see (and moving spike pillars later) in the game will be a constant thorn in your side. It's especially bad when the game is asking you to navigate tight corridors and make pixel-perfect wall jumps anytime a stationary or moving buzzsaw is around.
Your patience will likely be worn thin by the final 4-5 stages of the game and how positively ludicrous the stage designs and enemy and trap placement are. It stops being challenging in a satisfying manner and starts feeling really mean-spirited and unreasonable on an I Wanna Be The Guy level, especially given how terrible the controls are.
Play something better. Like Pid.
(I also have NO IDEA how I earned "The End Immortal" achievement. I died 219 times on the final stage.)

A good solid enjoyable visual novel game. I've paid for games I enjoyed far less than this free one.
The writing and worldbuilding are well done, and the characters are interesting. The artwork and soundtrack are both enjoyable too. The story takes place on a ship in space, and there are enough intriguing and mysterious elements in the plot to keep you attentive and engaged.
There are multiple endings to obtain too, and at the time of writing this review, several of the endings are getting their own sequel games under the umbrella title Rising Angels: Fates as part of a successful kickstarter campaign. There is also a prequel story called Rising Angels: Hope available as well.
That the developers chose to make this game freely available is quite generous, because this is an enjoyable visual novel that could have easily justified a modest price tag in its own right.

I just finished my first playthrough (about 7 hours) and what a ride. There was exploration, espionage, intrigue, drama and just a hint of romance that made Rising Angels: Reborn quite the satisfying experience. The intro song was enjoyable as well and I will definitely be looking into buying it.
I must admit, I was hesitant to play Rising Angels as I am not one for sci fi/space games. But the space theme-while prominent to the story- was really more of a backdrop to a story about the human (and alien in this case) condition. It's a story about who we are, who we want to be, morals and ethics. About balancing emotions with duty, and trusting in others. Politics come into play, and at the end of the day our heroine Natalie has some big decisions to make.
As far as decisions go however, there are not that many to make. From my first playthrough I'd estimate I made about 5 choices in 7 hours of game play. I do feel there were more points in the story where user choice would have been appropriate-but obviously that means more writing for the devs in an already fairly lengthy (but enjoyable) visual novel. Even though I didn't have that much control over the story, I was still able to immerse myself and empathize with Natalie and the rest of the characters. While not kinetic, Rising Angels is simply more novel than interactive experience, and that's ok.
Oh, I had an experience though, I had a few. I balked at the obnoxiousness of some characters, smirked as Natalie put them in their place, smiled at the sunny dispositions of some, and glowered at the creepiness of others. I experienced frustration and tension, dread and relief. I almost (almost!) got misty eyed at some parts. Overall, the characters had depth and I became invested in them, and the mission.
I did have a few qualms with the game, but nothing major. Overall I enjoyed the story and the adventure it took me on, and the characters I met. The few cons I have are lack of choices, a few spelling/grammer errors that made some sentences confusing, and a few points in the story where the writing/situations didn't make sense.
The primary example of this for me is

There were also some points where I felt like the characters were late to the party, figuring out stuff I had already or finally confirming my suspicions. Also there were some poorly timed humor attempts
. But no writing is perfect and overall I enjoyed the story and the characters.
Rising Angels: Reborn is a refreshing visual novel experience, especially if you are looking for something different than the plethora of school life romance otomes out there. I will definitely be replaying to explore the other paths, collect all the CGs, and learn more about the characters. Apparently it is part of a series so I will be checking into the other games as well. While I do that I suggest giving this one a go!
ps: I didn't find out 'till after playing that it's yuri romance only. The romance (at least from my playthrough) is so understated that you could interpret it as close friendship or one sided if you prefer. If you usually don't play girlxgirl romance please still give this a try as it was an amazing story!

This game is horrible.  The pace is slow, resources are limited (unless you pay), there is limited tactical flexibility, and the battles results are quite unrealistic.  It is just not fun to play compared to the stand-alone games in the Total War series.
The Good:
- Graphics and music are not bad.
- It does actually work on iPad and Windows laptop.
The Bad:
- The server is often unavailable and you cannot complete combat missions.
- Server repeatedly disconnected me during duels resulting in an immediate loss.
- The battle mechanics are simple and unbalanced.  There is no tactical flexibility.
- Battles are boring after the first few.
- Terrain and weather have no impact on battles.
- Even if the enemy is down to a handful of troops and you have overwhelming numbers, you will still lose if the server disconnects.
- There is a limited technology tree.  Unit advancement is very slow.
- The water flooding issue in spring was just plain annoying.
The Ugly:
- The game basically requires you to stay logged in all the time.  If you only log in once per day, your resources cap after about 1 hour and there is not much to do after about 10 minutes of game play.  After several weeks, I have made limited progress – two castles and a few units.
- The game also strongly encourages (really requires) you to duel; and every time, I have been pitted against a total mismatch – someone whose level is far above mine.
- Unit match-up results make no sense when fighting the AI.  Cavalry charge crossbowmen or archers…and somehow are all killed in the melee and not with missile weapons.  That seriously makes no sense.
Total War Battles: SHOGUN was essentially a series of puzzles, solved through creative use of various units.  KINGDOMS is just an attempt to get you to pay for fleeting power-ups and resources on a recurring basis.  I recommend that you stick with the previous installments of Total War: Medieval, Shogun 2, or Empire specifically.

Although 0.0 hours are shown on the last 2 weeks of my profile listed here, I've played this game on my iPhone everyday, several times a day, for about a month.  The i5 processor on the laptop (I'm using to type this review with) does not work as well. Too much lag.  But my phone plays this game very nicely (iPhone 6plus).  However, the play time does not appear to transfer over.  This game is, as other players have already noted, is geared more towards a phone or tablet. It's terrific for down time away from home.  It is a free download. However, the money this game generates for the company is by selling "gold" which can be used to advance your position rapidly. That's ok with me.  I like to work slowly and later decide to make a purchase with these type games.  Because I loved the Total war games that were published, I wanted to give this game a try.  First thing I noticed was the lack of instructions and no user manual that I could find. So starting off was mostly trial and error.  That was a little irksome, but I continued because I was still enjoying the experience.  I did find a forum on line that gave suggestions for play based on the authors' experience.  I used them to improve my game.  So, here's my first complaint about this game (1) Why the secrecy on play.  There may be players out there that like the challenge of exploring the unknown, but I find it tedious making the same mistake over and over again, not really knowing what I'm doing. The instructions offered are pitifully brief. I would have found it more interesting having a basic manual that showed what did what.  Like the classic PC games did.  The strategy can still be left up to me, but at least I wouldn't be fumbling around. I am sure there are players who do enjoy that approach.  I don't.
Now, in spite of the initial trial and error period, I still found this game very interesting and started following the advice of the online forums.  As I said, I found myself playing this game every day, several times a day.  I was enjoying the process of slowly building my Kingdom.  This leads up to my final complaint: (2)  So, as I said, I'm slowly building up my Kingdom with farms, roads, castles, houses, blacksmiths, etc, and just got to the point of having 4 towns in 4 regions.  This was a long time in the making.  Then, I log in after an update today and find 2 of those towns completely destroyed.  No explanation.  Instead, there were 2 large large patches of icons, each indicating 'ruins' where the building once stood.  This, in short,♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off.  No aspect of the game gave me a hint of this coming.  OK, again, maybe there are those who take this in stride and take up the challenge, but I personally play games on my iPhone for immediate comfort and gratification. There may be others out there, like me, who are not looking for unexpected massive tragedies, and very challenging play.  I just want to expand my own Kingdom at my own pace.  It would be nice if the publishers of these games would provide options to cover varying degrees of game difficulty for different target markets.
That being said, I wish there was a choice for the above recommendation beyond "YES" "NO" if I recommend this game.  I would definitely recommend this game for those serious players who enjoy the challenges this game offers.  I wouldn't  for the vanilla players like me.  It's a shame.  I was really starting to enjoy this game.  I'm curious about the statistics of the purchases made by this game's players (of "gold").  If there is any correlation to time span played vs purchases. Strange little game, very much down the puzzle / time management line, but a little hands-off-ish for the latter.
The graphics are minimal, but on purpose - the authentic line-plan aesthetics really work in favor of this one, and are rather compelling, really. It probably hits some familiarity-nerve, it's instantly recognizable to probably anyone who has ever commuted by train, subway, tram or whatever.
Of course, it also runs really well - that is not a surprise. What could be more unexpected is that it has quite an amount of depth, especially in the variation between the cities, and how much this changes the pace of the game, including which additional supplies you get and/or can select from week by week. On top of that, there are some additional "mode" options that can amplify the experience. There is, of course, also an endless mode to play, to really exhaust what can be done on a map.
For replayability (and the somewhat competitive people) it comes with stats and leaderboards, and even has a "Daily Challenge" mode with a specific game seed per day that everyone gets exactly ONE go at.
If you've played other puzzle / optimizing games (and had fun doing so), you might like this one. If you're a commuter or have a soft spot for trains - even if you don't see actual trains in this one - you might also like it for the sheer style (take a look at the screenshots to find out).
Summary:
It's a simple game that does a few things very good, and doesn't attempt to do other things at all - there is no economy in this game, no multiplayer, no storyline, no overarching progression system, persistent upgrades or anything. The system that governs which "passenger" goes to which "station", and what route they take is relatively simplistic, and every "week" of playtime you get a few more "resources" (trains, tunnels, lines) to improve and expand your metro net.
While it doesn't have a story, the slowly expanding playing field together with the graphics style go well together in creating a sense of authenticity, and a sense of expansion. In a very abstract way, this game conveys a sense of growth like few others, every single session.

By flipping the script and focusing on civilians trapped in a war torn city, 11 bit studios has created a more humanized and poignant type of war game. The game will run you through a range of emotions from starvation induced desperation, to the guilt and rationalization of a thief, to the heartwarming joy of a rare display of camaraderie among neighbors.
Much like the citizens trapped in this war, you won't receive any guidance on how best to survive. Controls are very simple and intuitive, allowing the challenge to come from how you manage resources and respond to events. My chief complaint toward this phenomenal game is that it can be too slow at times, making me wish there were a fast forward button.
A couple tips: Don't spoil the experience by looking up guides until completing at least one playthrough on your own; overcoming adversity is part of the fun. Alt+Tab consistently crashed the game for me, test it on your system after the start of a new day (when saves occur).
Like a microcosm of the split, warring factions of the city, the civilians have also fractured into small, wary, tribe-like groups. Some are willing to trade with you while others will shoot you on sight. The small group that you watch over consists of one to four people depending on which scenario you play. These are drawn from a modest collection of realistic characters. Each has a backstory and reason for being in the city when the fighting began. Don't mistake this for a heavily text driven narrative kind of game. It uses just enough text to set the stage and then lets you experience and create your own stories.
There is a realistic but sometimes burdensome level of variation in how useful each character is. They all have one unique talent that they excel at as well as some hidden general competency statistics. The imbalance among them can make some playthroughs significantly tougher than others. Overall, the game will test you mightily as you learn the ropes but actually became too easy once I had discovered enough ways to boost my efficiency.
Playing as nonviolently as I could limited my combat experience but when I did fight, I found it to be awkward. It is largely dependent on your equipment and whether you get the drop on your opponent, rather than any player skill.
One cool tool that the developers use to feed you information without breaking immersion is the radio. It can give you updates on the war's status, tips on what goods are able to be bartered at a higher price due to scarcity, weather forecasts and more. Winter is the most brutal period to make it through and you will want to know when it is coming.
This game's muted color palate and heavy use of black is what I would call subtly beautiful. It effectively communicates the grimness of the setting. A sketchy, pencil-like visual effect lends a hand drawn quality to its 3D animation. I'd also like to highlight the differences in how each character moves and holds themselves. Their personalities are imbued into their movements in a way that I don't recall seeing very often in video games.
Adding to the atmosphere is a mostly downbeat soundtrack reminiscent of The Last of Us. It has character without becoming too busy for the mood it is trying to set. I like the music, but there are few enough tracks that repetition eventually began to wear on me. The soundtrack is included as a free DLC.
I would like to encourage anyone who buys and likes the game to pick up the War Child Charity DLC. It only adds a little artwork to the game but 100% of the proceeds go to charity. You can choose to pay 1$, 10$ or 20$ for it. I skipped The Little Ones DLC but its recent price drop makes it more enticing.
A final note on game length: My first playthrough took 13.5 hours, the second lasted 11.5 hours, and my final two took a combined 10.8 hours. The final one was a custom scenario designed to be shortened by the optional Anniversary Edition ending attached to the "Epilogue: Exodus" achievement (an annoyingly difficult to accomplish task during regular play, but still fun to experience once).
Just not my kind of game and also crashed about every 25 to 30 minutes for me.

I haven't played this game long, but i've gotten decently far and I can already say that this is an underrated gem.
I was actually reluctant to buy this considering how little attention it was getting as silly as it sounds, because the trailer was trying too hard to do the adult swim anti-humour bit and didn't show too much gameplay. I thought since that only a total of 28 people have reviewed it (upon time of buying) that it was just a small forgettable indie game that didn't have much lasting appeal or grabbing power. I finally bought it on sale, yet I would recommend it full price.
The music and graphics for this game are the first thing that stand out- catchy and gorgeous. The gameplay's grasp on you as the player probably won't be immediate though... I started out the game frustrated and bored. The tutorial only gives you the basics (which is enough, although it doesn't have any music for some reason, making me worry the rest of the game would be just as silent) and after that you're thrown into the game, which is painfully slow to start off. The game will also be shockingly hard when you first start playing as well, making every death a "god damn it, do I really have to start over from the slow bit again?".
The gameplay summed up shortly: It's that one level from yoshi's island where you have to vertically climb a tower of falling blocks, only it's the entire game with much more depth. When you first start out, you will get squished. Many times. The lava will probably never kill you, because it starts out slow as molasses unless you get the risk badge. You will never be able to actually land on those damn birds that fly at you, and sometimes you might be able to sneak in a snake kill, but more often than not you'll miscalculate your jump and land right beside them, killing you instantly. Manage to get to the first boss? It will be a tedious test of patience until you finally start to do some risky moves, which will in turn make you end up dead and sending you down to the bottom again.
Yes, this game isn't a forgiving teacher. But don't hit that refund button just yet- it gets better. I got a hang of the game surprisingly fast, and it's secret amount of depth blindsided me. You'll start learning how to surf, and how to get combos to squeeze out as many coins as possible. You'll actually start to remember that the screen wraps and learn how to use it to your advantage. You'll learn how to kill the bosses quickly. You might even make it to space, or the moon once or twice.
I do have some minor complaints with the game though, but nothing gamebreaking. Sometimes you can get an absolute terrible roll of RNG where blocks just do not stack at all how you want them to and it just never ends, making you die after a good run or make you restart at the beginning of one so you can actually progress. Walljumping feels responsive most of the times, but sometimes when you're trying to chain it, it's the most frustrating thing in the world. And for the love of god, I hate how shops work. I'm trying to run up away from the advancing wall of death and I accidentally jump on one of the shop chests, wasting my money. And if it's a deposit/withdrawl chest, I might hit my head on a ceiling and deposit multiple times. I would gladly rather press an action button to buy something than have to jump on it, even if it's some sort of badge that I have to equip to balance it out. Also, some challenges are lamely bugged, allowing you to cheat- the chest one in particular, you can just use a bank over and over to cheat it rather than actually get chests in one run.
I'm not sure how long this game is before looping, and I'm not sure if the flash game was just as good as this, but I'd say those things aside it's absolutely worth your money. If you're on the fence, maybe wait on sale, but otherwise you won't regret full price.

Avalanche 2 is a roguelike platformer where you try to get as high as you can by climbing falling (Tetris) blocks. There's only one big level splitted into segments and most of the fun comes from the smartphone game style of quests - you always get three random tasks with a small reward. Those tasks are about collecting coins, climbing, "surfing" (climbing on blocks that haven't fallen on ground yet) etc. Also, there's a in-game shop where you can buy hats, upgrades and level segment skips (you don't have to start always from bottom).
- Entertaining gameplay, offering hours of addictive fun for fans of roguelike genre.
- Powerups will test your skill since some of those aren't just pure stat boosts, they may also change your controls (ex. bunny hop powerup).
- Co-op mode.
- Nice graphics style.
- Some bosses are too easy.
- You might get bored fast if you don't like repeating the same level over and over.

This is a relatively solid platformer with some interesting quirks. It is somewhat similiar to Super Meat Boy...but that isn't entirely right. It shares SMB's percision, tight controls, and OCD for making the exactly right move at the exactly right time. You also get a parade of your deaths, though not in the same way. Conversely, TBP is more complex, due to its larger range of moves, and less focused on long stretches of hair tearing, due to it's more lenient save mechanism (the difficulty is still pretty brutal though). Similarly, the stages are longer, but the game is shorter. For replay value, there are over 150 achievements, and three (soon 4) bonus levels. Notably, the achievements actually do things (unlock art, most of which is pretty nice). Visuals are nice and simple, with some very cool effects. The music is nice too, if chippy.
Overall, I enjoy this one, and would recommend it.

By flipping the script and focusing on civilians trapped in a war torn city, 11 bit studios has created a more humanized and poignant type of war game. The game will run you through a range of emotions from starvation induced desperation, to the guilt and rationalization of a thief, to the heartwarming joy of a rare display of camaraderie among neighbors.
Much like the citizens trapped in this war, you won't receive any guidance on how best to survive. Controls are very simple and intuitive, allowing the challenge to come from how you manage resources and respond to events. My chief complaint toward this phenomenal game is that it can be too slow at times, making me wish there were a fast forward button.
A couple tips: Don't spoil the experience by looking up guides until completing at least one playthrough on your own; overcoming adversity is part of the fun. Alt+Tab consistently crashed the game for me, test it on your system after the start of a new day (when saves occur).
Like a microcosm of the split, warring factions of the city, the civilians have also fractured into small, wary, tribe-like groups. Some are willing to trade with you while others will shoot you on sight. The small group that you watch over consists of one to four people depending on which scenario you play. These are drawn from a modest collection of realistic characters. Each has a backstory and reason for being in the city when the fighting began. Don't mistake this for a heavily text driven narrative kind of game. It uses just enough text to set the stage and then lets you experience and create your own stories.
There is a realistic but sometimes burdensome level of variation in how useful each character is. They all have one unique talent that they excel at as well as some hidden general competency statistics. The imbalance among them can make some playthroughs significantly tougher than others. Overall, the game will test you mightily as you learn the ropes but actually became too easy once I had discovered enough ways to boost my efficiency.
Playing as nonviolently as I could limited my combat experience but when I did fight, I found it to be awkward. It is largely dependent on your equipment and whether you get the drop on your opponent, rather than any player skill.
One cool tool that the developers use to feed you information without breaking immersion is the radio. It can give you updates on the war's status, tips on what goods are able to be bartered at a higher price due to scarcity, weather forecasts and more. Winter is the most brutal period to make it through and you will want to know when it is coming.
This game's muted color palate and heavy use of black is what I would call subtly beautiful. It effectively communicates the grimness of the setting. A sketchy, pencil-like visual effect lends a hand drawn quality to its 3D animation. I'd also like to highlight the differences in how each character moves and holds themselves. Their personalities are imbued into their movements in a way that I don't recall seeing very often in video games.
Adding to the atmosphere is a mostly downbeat soundtrack reminiscent of The Last of Us. It has character without becoming too busy for the mood it is trying to set. I like the music, but there are few enough tracks that repetition eventually began to wear on me. The soundtrack is included as a free DLC.
I would like to encourage anyone who buys and likes the game to pick up the War Child Charity DLC. It only adds a little artwork to the game but 100% of the proceeds go to charity. You can choose to pay 1$, 10$ or 20$ for it. I skipped The Little Ones DLC but its recent price drop makes it more enticing.
A final note on game length: My first playthrough took 13.5 hours, the second lasted 11.5 hours, and my final two took a combined 10.8 hours. The final one was a custom scenario designed to be shortened by the optional Anniversary Edition ending attached to the "Epilogue: Exodus" achievement (an annoyingly difficult to accomplish task during regular play, but still fun to experience once).
Just not my kind of game and also crashed about every 25 to 30 minutes for me.

Overall I had a lot of fun playing this game, but it makes me a little bugged that it could be better.
The fact that you have to play the Easy mode campaign first to unlock the advanced AI is pretty frustrating, cause there is no challenge in the first 8 hours of game. It could easily kill the game for you.

OMG this game is not great. Or maybe it\'s just not for me. It\'s almost literally a girl\'s journal in interactive form, detailing the time a guy lied and tried to use her for a one night stand. So she made a game about it. Not that it\'s a bad story, just an unremarkable one. Tragically common. Horrifyingly predictable. It\'s quite unfortunate that this story exists. But it\'s also nothing to get really worked up over, unless you are the protagonist. And we\'re kept from \"being\" the protagonist of this game. Our actions, our words, our replies, all predetermined. Which is fine, but it pushes us away from feeling like Nina is an avatar. Instead, I felt much more like a Voyer. Peering through the personal files and pictures of a girl who accidentally forgot to log out of her computer when stepping away. It gave me the feeling like I was gonna be cought snooping through the private messages and photos. But what it lacks and quality it makes up for in sincerity. The dialogue is a little \"too\" natural. Using words like \"u\'r hawt\" instead of anything that\'ll wind up written in an angsty teenager\'s quote under their photo in the yearbook. But this genuine dialogue also makes it difficult to look at the relationship as understandable. Instead, it makes us pitty Nina for the horrible mistake we know she\'s going to make. It makes me view her as weak or unintelligent. Like a lamb that needs to be protected. As a result, feminists will hate this game simply because it paints our female protagonist as a damsel who cannot protect or control herself but instead rellies on men to be her confidence. This makes it a little hard to watch. Another thing to feel guilty for.
TL:DR
Game is real, too real. No well thought out dialogue, just internet banter. Story is predictable and nothing special. I really wish I had better things to say about this game. I hope Nina remakes this game in several years after learning to write narrative and dialogue a little better. I felt nothing.

The developers are also quite active and are listening.
