OK - so I have played through most of the game and I have loved it, but I have lots of ideas on how it can be even better.
First off, should you buy this game? YES - absolutely. Easy to learn but plenty of depth too. You will be hooked on this game quickly, the power ups and money making are a very addictive strategy scenario.
OK, so here are the observations I have that could probably be improved to take the game from excellent to amazing:
* The game eventually becomes too repetitive after you beat the normal and expert mode.
* The expert mode didn't seem much different to me. It probably needs more changes to keep it interesting.
* The natural gas part of the game doesn't seem to quite come together at least for me. It's super expensive to get all the upgrades and lay the pipe need to use it. It's a neat idea, but it can be entirely skipped and you still win the game. To me, the game should be set up so that you need to take advantage of this in order to win. It seemed really hard to take advantage of this the way it was intended.
* The computer seems really dumb when it comes to the stock buying mechanic. I was able to buy up stock quite easily without being stopped by the CPU. By the fourth round I had had an insurmountable stock lead. The computer should be MUCH more aggressive when it comes to buying stock.
* The moles part of the game sounds interesting, but to me they just didn't seem to be worth the money or provide much benefit. You can basically just skip this and easily win. They dig up diamonds, but beyond that they didn't seem helpful.
*It would be great if you could do multiplayer local or over internet with a split screen. I would LOVE to play the game that way against a friend.
This is wonderful game for $6-$10 and I fully recommend it. It becomes repetitive and not quite so interesting after about 10 hours of gameplay, but this could be improved by the developers if they make some adjustments. It is just a bit too easy to win the game, and I wish the game would have been balanced to make we work harder to win.

A really interesting game.
Pros:
*You can shape the land however you want it. Initially everyone starts with the same map but the way you want to shape it's completely up to you.
*The game has premium currency but everything that's available for it you can craft from the free resources as well,once you spent a week or two it wont be a big problem to craft what you need.
*You can have multiple armies to fight while one is healing after a fight.
*PvP is ingame but you don't lose anything except your pvp rank if you lose a fight so you won't lose all your progress by someone butchering you while you're asleep or away.
*The game is still under development and adding new features to the game which is a nice thing.
*Multiplatform game so you can continue your game from your tablet/phone anywhere you are if you have an internet connection
*There are plenty of ways to generate premium currency in game by actively playing
Cons:
* No key bindings to use unit abilities in battles so everything has to be done by mouse clicking
* There are a lot of guides and videos explaining the in depth mechanics of the game but some things really should be better explained in the game itself without having someone to look it up.
* There's an ingame "friends" feature that currently is kind of useless if your friend doesn't buy gold(you get 3% bonus gold if a friend purchases some premium currency) and it's also limited to only 5 friends max.
* At this moment it may be an online game but it has 0 social aspects since it has no chat/guild features so you have no way to communicate with anyone ingame
* The unit stats are unknown until you build one which can be frustrating but i believe it will be fixed soon,the game was just released after all

Not too sure what to write here so heres a recipe for Pancakes instead
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

Awesome game. After buying so much during the steam sale, I ended up playing this for free instead...
You fly combat spaceships and shoot at other spaceships with lasers and missiles and try to outrun them around asteroids. How could it not be fun? The controls are quite good and pilot skill is very well reflected in combat. The free to play model doesn't really hurt gameplay - it's ridiculously expensive when you want to get perks, but if you don't, you're never at a real disadvantage in a battle. Besides, you get grouped with other players near the same rank so that your opponents are never out of your reach.
The problem I had with the game is that you can only play in team modes - team deathmatch, domination (capture and hold flags), bomb - usually around 10 vs 10. Sometimes you'll end up on a team that's too strong and win by an incredible margin, and often it'll be the opposite. Your individual performance can help your team but sometimes you can have the game of a lifetime and still badly lose because you got unbalanced teams. It can get really frustrating and is the reason I stopped playing.

This has been the first Thief game I've played in the series that I got around to beating and with that being said; I can see why this game has a lot of hate. The game truly struggles with a story since the story is pretty much inconsistent, jumpy and overall hard to follow and get invested in. Gameplay wise, it's kind of a mixed bag since I did enjoy some parts and I despised others. The A.I at times were really brain dead compared to previous Stealth Action games that I've played (Mainly Dishonored and Splinter Cell.) and overall just weren't that much of a challenge to get around. You can level up your gear/buy new items with Gold you steal around the city or gain from completeing levels/sidemissions but I barely spent my gold on the upgrades since I never really felt that most the upgrades were nescessary with how easy things are in this game. I'm actaully kinda sad this game isn't as good as it could've been since the level design and atmosphere at times were quite lovely to run around in and it had potiential to create a world that could've held a more interesting story than what we got instead.
I don't truly dislike this game as much as other people do since I did found some value out of it but I won't recommend it if you are in the market for a really good stealth action game or a good story driven experience.
TL;DR - Mediocre Story
- Average/Mediocre Gameplay
- Beautiful Game enviroments and Level designs
- Offers upgrade system that can be useful, but I never found the need to upgrade my gear much
- A.I can be braindead at times
Overall, I would only invest a few bucks in this game if you are interested in the atmosphere of the game and don't mind a horrendous story and average/sometimes mediocre gameplay.

If you want to understand the history of this game and the strength of feeling against it then you should know that  when it first came out it cost £10, it was not marked as early access and it had massive issues like escape key insta-quits the game and it would lock up for 30 seconds at a time and not respond to input then randomly walk you about when it "came back". You also could only play one of the three classes. (An issue, which like some others was working in the Desura version).
I have updated the review as the devs have massively lowered the price and fixed some of the bugs.
REVIEW STARTS:
This game is fairly cheap but it is also not very good. I really get the impression that the developer(s) are not fans of the roguelike genre. I don't imagine them enjoying their own game, I think they are just "pushing it out there" to make money.
One of the most fundamental problems with the game is that the controls are arbitrary and the way you do things is not consistent. In a normal roguelike, attempting to move into the space occupied by a thing (called "bumping") activates a default action: thus, bumping into a door attempts to open it, bumping a monster attacks it. In this game, bumping into a monster will attack it but doors you have to turn to face them and then press the action button (space by default). You can use the mouse to click on a monster to attack it (allowing you to attack diagonally) but you can't click on doors to open them. You can use the keyboard to move around but you can't use the mouse to click and move. You have to use the mouse to take things from chests.
The bottom line is that whether you prefer to play roguelike games with a mouse or with a keyboard you are forced to use both. If you just used keyboard you wouldn't be able to take anything out of chests and wouldn't be able to attack monsters diagonally (which is do-able but makes the game harder). If you just use mouse, well, you can't even move.
I mean come on guys, basic things like escape should close windows and enter should accept them. Do you guys not play PC games at all?
If you ignore the problems with the controls, or they get fixed, and all the various bugs get fixed you aren't left with a _terrible_ game, but it is shallow, boring, and possibly unbalanced. There are better roguelikes on steam that you could be playing, and lots of free ones not on steam.

A competitive hero shooter with amazing visuals, animations, & characters, and really unique mechanics.
Every minor objective builds your team's rampage meter, and the first team to fill their meter gets a rampage, which makes the enemy team's GIANT MONSTER become temporarily vulnerable to attack. This cycle repeats until one team's monster has been significantly damaged enough to be killed, which ends the game.
It creates a really cool gameplay loop of mini-races to fill your rampage meter (they're both emptied as soon as one gets filled), followed by frantic attack/defense encounters on the vulnerable monster. Spiced up with some minor tower-defense mechanics of planting/upgrading little monsters in certain locations on the map that can do different things and collect power for you (which also fills the rampage meter), and you've got yourself a game that never gets boring.
Highly recommended!

Ok, you are probably wondering why this is a first impressions video instead of my usual review, but after an hour of trying to play, I felt that I had to refund this game. It’s actually the first time I have ever refunded anything on Steam. So, I am sorry for this being a first impression, but I felt I needed to post this anyway.
The graphics portray the game as an old filmstrip type of movie, which was nice, but I could have done without the black splotches popping up all the time. I really like the art style, and colour pallet that the game uses, and the story sounds interesting, but don’t be fooled by how nice the game looks, it seems like a very early access version right now, and has quite a few issues!
When I first launched the game, Avast for some reason flagged and deleted the executable for BUDDY, and I had to re-verify the game through Steam and disable Avast to launch it. That wasn’t a huge deal since false positives happen, but still, it was an inconvenience. Yes, I know Avast isn't that great, but this is the first time it has ever deleted ANY of my Steam games. My reasons for refunding though are due to the gameplay issues. There are multiple bugs and glitches I experienced, and the controls are horrible.
About the controls, for keyboard you use ASD and arrow keys, but neither W or spacebar work for jumping. You HAVE to use the arrow keys. To interact with objects, only left control button works, and not the right control. There is no way to change any game settings or keybindings at all. Using the keyboard was horribly clunky feeling to use, so I tried a Steam controller, and while it does work much better, you will have to use a special customization unless you like jumping with Y for some strange reason…
Poor controls aside, the actual jumping is so painfully slow. In a few parts so far, you have to do things quickly, so there is a bit of pressure on timing.
So yea, BUDDY is a $15 full release game, and while the audio and visuals are great, there are too many other issues that need to be addressed.
Again guys, I’m sorry about the first impression rant here, and I was really hoping to do a full review, but uhh, I just couldn’t continue playing.

Cibele is an indie FMV/interactive story title that was released in November 2015, being developed by Star Maid Games. The game is based on a true story, of a girl named Nina, who starts an online “relationship” with a man who she meets whilst playing a game called Valtameri. Those of you who have played online games such as Worlds of Warcraft will probably be able to relate to this game a lot, as there are always those two people in your guild who acted like this.
The gameplay in Cibele is simple. You are a girl who is playing the video game Valtameri. The gameplay in that game is simple, and you have no chance of dying, you simply click to move and attack the enemies, that is it. There is no hidden agenda here; it’s just a method in which the story can progress. You are in a voice call with your friend, Blake, after every so many kills of monsters, the dialogue will progress into the story more. Between each chapter, you get a real life cut scene featuring the two involved. This game should be considered only for mature audience and should not be played when young eyes can see your screen.  Whilst you are in the world of Valtameri, you have other options to explore, such as the instant messenger which adds a little more background and depth to the story. Outside of the game, you can dig around Nina’s computer, reading emails, looking at pictures, reading her blog, etc. This all adds to the immersion of the game allowing you to get into the mind of this young lady.
Whilst the graphics aren’t really a main focal point in Cibele, I did find the art style extremely pleasing to look at, it has a very clean look, and the animations of everything in the game is near enough perfect.  On top of the really nice looking graphics, the game is fully voice acted, in the parts where you would expect it, so the voice chat, using something like TeamSpeak or Ventrilo, it really sounds like you are there with them as you listen. The cut scenes do have any sound effects or voice acting in though, I think this is to add to the effect of the story that things are often different between people when they meet in real life after coming together online. That’s how I took it anyway.
There isn’t any difficulty level here, you will finish the game, and it only takes about an hour to do, and that is with reading blogs, checking out emails etc. I don’t think there would be any replay ability since the story seems pretty linear, so I wouldn’t say it’s worth a second play through.
I did notice a slight stutter/frame drop at times when playing, this appeared to happen when new enemies entered the screen, which I found strange given that my rig is able to handle much more taxing games than this. I was able to play on 1440p though, so all resolutions were tight and crisp.  Keyboard and mouse will be needed to play.
To sum up, Cibele is an interesting title, that can be picked up for £5,99, I for one think that is a fair price for what is on offer, and the high standard of production values that have gone into this game. Some of you may get a nostalgia hit with the story, whilst others may actually enjoy the gameplay of the game in Cibele, but I can certainly say it is worth the full marked up price for an hour’s enjoyment.
1) Stay away
2) Not Recommended

Cibele is first and foremost a narrative experience. It's an intimate story about a young woman and a young man who meet on the internet and let their emotions take the reins. It pulls you into a hazy, narrow view of life as seen by one in lust, excited by the possibilities the social internet can provide.
The experience plays out in three ways. You explore Nina's computer, her personal photos and files and chat logs. You play Valtameri, a stylish analog to Final Fantasy XI. You also watch short FMV sequences featuring Nina, these generally occuring between the Valtameri sessions.
I found the desktop exploration to be interesting and, in many cases, a bit lewd. The information available is never too abundant as to feel exhausting to explore but often conjures other uncomfortable emotions as it is very clear that this is a young woman's personal space.
The gameplay in Valtameri is as simple as clicking an enemy and watching Nina autoattack but I felt the dead simple mindless play worked very well with the conversations that come over play sessions. It was an accurate microcosm of the idle play of hands that accompanies the social interaction in many MMOs. The conversations feel raw and real, revealing people that are young and hungry but uncertain.
The FMV sequences are well shot and emphasize the biggest shared trait amongst the game's three pillars: Discomfort. The close angles and voyeuristic tone of many of the scenes, again, are evocative of a carefree eagerness stoked by a connection online that is just as erotic and personal as it is public and volatile.
Saying much more about it I fear would spoil the experience. If you'd like a personal story with a heavy emphasis on raw emotion and just a dash of idle clicking I feel you could get enjoyment out of Cibele. It will only take you one or two sittings and is well worth that time.

The short and reductive version – A slightly more depressing and uncomfortable but interactive version of the YouTube series “The Guild” by Felicia Day.
The slightly more detailed version – You as play the developer of this game or perhaps a character.. maybe some summation of possibly real experiences of the human Nina Freeman. The main interface is that of her desktop. A bit of a homebody, she has a number of online friends mostly gained from the game she plays online. Which I think a lot of people can relate to in the modern world. The game shes plays from what I can surmise is a fairly dull and repetitive MMO; But that game is mostly a vehicle to deliver and give atmosphere to the conversations she has with her friends.
I found myself surprisingly engaged with the conversations she was having. While simultaneously feeling VERY uncomfortable as if I had invaded someones privacy against their will; against MY will. Which I think is by design. I don't want to really say the degree to which these relationships go or how many there are but I think if you've heard anything about this game through the grapevine you can probably guess pretty accurately what happens. However, I think its pretty unique of way of telling this specific story.
I find that these sorts of experimental kind of 'artsy fartsy' games usually overstay their welcome as in; The hook has penetrated, enraptured you and then made you wait to hear its secrets. But this one feels like it 'under'stays its welcome. I feel like it ends a bit abruptly.
The comparison to 'Her Story' is easy but accurate. In all honesty, this tells a different story about something else entirely. After playing both, I like Her Story overall a bit better but because Cibele made me feel uncomfortable that maybe hits a little closer to home than I'd like to admit and in ways that Her Story did not. It is uniquely different.

This War of Mine is a game developed by
. The game focuses on war however you are not a badass soldier, your a weak helpless civillian caught in the conflict.
The gameplay is simple at the start however it can easily branch off, you have a shelter to take refuge in this is where you'll craft, defend and sleep in until the war is over. At night its more hard, you choose where to scavenge and anything can happen to your survivor. Crafting is also simple you can craft chairs, musical instruments, weapons, defenses and everything basic to survive the conflict.
Combat feels smooth and simple, select a weapon weather it be your own bear hands or a simple handgun, click to take cover and fire away.
The survivor part of the game is like the sims, they all have basic needs and if you fail to meet their needs they will become sad, hungry and will eventually die. If a survivor dies it will have a knock-on effect to all of the other survivors, they will mourn one's death for a while and then eventually get back to facing the harsh realities of war.
The soundtrack is also beautiful. The calm relaxing tunes when you are managing your items at base is truley, relaxing. And the intensity of the soundtrack when you are scavenging at night makes the game look feel alot more cinematic.
To sum this game up, its a calm relaxing ride at times, sad experiences and intese situations all put together and it blends extremley well. I really want to invest more time into this game and I'm sure I will.

Great Game!  For it's simplicity it's very entertaining.  Campaign took about 6 hours from start to finish. Started the Second Game, now knowing what to do, beat my Rivals and was Elected Mayor in about 6 hours.
For $9.99, a game with a campaign that lasts at least 6 hours is a pretty good deal and well worth the price.
I really hope the devs add onto this game, with additional Campaigns/Modes to make this game even greater than it already is.  Because as of now, the only replay factor after completing the original Campaign is to try and get the Steam Achievements, if you are into that sort of thing.
As for the Single Mode, to me it's not enough to keep you playing the game.
The Mechanics of the game worked well, the only issue that I experienced while playing was the cursor on my screen seemed off from where my mouse cursor was.  This only happened occasionally and really isn't that big of a deal, it didn't break the game or make it unplayable at all.
The game is very entertaining and if you are someone like me, it is very easy to get sucked in and want to keep playing it until you beat the Campaign.  Don't be surprised if after starting the game, 6 - 10 hours have went by before you realize it.  At some point things will start feeling as if you are repeating the same thing over and over, but the Devs did do a Good Job at trying to mix things up, with the Auctions for the Land, the Upgrades to your Machinery, the Change of Environment of the land your drilling in (Some may be more rocky than others, contain more oil/natural gas than other and may or may not contain a Diamond).
To me, other than trying to get all the Steam Achievements, there is no replayablity for this game at the moment.
Overall, the game is definately worth paying $9.99 for and is enjoyable.  If they were to add onto the game, with more gamemodes / Additional Campaigns I would be willing to pay more for the game.

Small little indie puzzle game where you control a spaceship that you have to customize and rebuild in different configurations in order to complete puzzles and maneuver through the levels.

Belated review. This indie physics-based puzzle game is pretty fun. Your goal is to navigate a spaceship to the end of a level. Sure, it sounds easy enough, but there are always obstacles in your way. The main hook of the gameplay is mixing and matching parts on your spaceship in order to solve physics-based puzzles in each level (pushing and pulling objects, smashing through things, etc). I found the controls to be a bit touchy at times and wasn't a huge fan of the ship-building interface, but overall, there's not much bad to say about this game. Just go into it without any grand expectations. It's pretty laid back and is a nice way to kill a few hours. There are also a number of advanced levels available, in addition to the main story chapters, for those looking for a bit more challenge.

I don't recommend this. Most of the play time goes to putting your ship together for one 15 second puzzle, then spending another 5 minutes rebuilding it to make it past the next. Then again, it's probably more of a kid's "stick round peg into round hole" game.
It's intersting for the concept alone but the clunkiness of implementation is sometimes frustrating.

Nice music and visuals, and interesting gameplay. Most of the time it's functional, but you'll find the occasional glitch, mostly clipping issues. Still worth checking out if you want to experience a different type of 2D platformer.

Bob Came in Pieces is a lovely, casual physics-based puzzle game that features a story mode with 14 chapters where you main goal is to collect all the missing ship parts you have lost during a crash with a meteor. To solve the puzzles you have to combine certain parts and attach them to one of the 8 sockets on your ship.
Additionally the game features 10+1 really challenging and cool VR missions (heavily inspired by the VR missions in Metal Gear Solid) where you have to solve some really crazy puzzles with a pre-defined set of ship parts.
In both the adventure and the VR mode the timer can be toggled on/off so it's up to you if you play the game the casual way and explore the levels or go for gold and try to beat the clock to get a silver or gold medal and the respective Steam achievement.
The replayability depends on whether you're into time-attack or not. Either way i can highly recommend this game so make sure to get it (when it's on sale)!

A stylish & difficult physics puzzler somewhat in the vein of Gravitron. I love the Lego-like ability to build and modify your ship with newly found parts.

Star Conflict... the description of "World of Tanks in Space" works pretty well to describe it. While it lacks the intricacy of research and training crew that World of Tanks does, it still has a very similar experience grind that many other Free-to-Play games have used (Mechwarrior Online comes to mind.)
You spend time working your way through the tiers of each faction, factions you can change if you have enough credit earned from fights, each tier more powerful than the last. You have four basic types available to you ranging from small Covert Ops ships, intended for sneaky hit-and-runs against specific targets, to larger frigates that are there for longer range support with repair abilities.
The game looks absolutely stunning overall, with great dynamic lighting effects that I would have never expected from a DirectX9-based game. Effects are easily recognizable as well, giving you an easy way of knowing what is coming at you and what is going out.
The UI is serviceable. It lacks a certain flavor that would compliment the theme of the game, going fo ra simple "MMO" styled hot-button interface for extra utilities that your ship may have that dominates the bottom of the screen. The targeting cursor, or the mouse in combat, can also get lost in the middle of combat as well. Since the cursor is a a little too minimalist, and the HDR causes the screen to flash white violently at times, it becomes far too difficult to figure out just where your turrets are aiming.
Audio is alright. Voice acting is pretty poor, with quality on par with a modding team that doesn't quite have the experience needed to pull off something believable. "We have lost our commander!" comes out as someone just fresh from high-school trying to pretend to be in a position of authority with no believable emotion what-so-ever. They try to emphasize a lot, and in the end they sound pretty silly and cringe-worthy.
On the case of balance, low-tier equipment seems to do pretty well against anyone you'd get matched up with, but as you start pushing to higher tiered fights, the discrepancy between earnable ships and paid for or "Premium" ships starts becoming readily apparent. Ships purchased by "Gold Standards" with premium status have higher base stats than their earnable counter-parts and also manage to avoid the costs of repairs. Equipment purchased with "Gold Standards" also gives a top tier benefit that one must grind for with a specific faction to get, allowing people who pay cash to not only have a better core ship, but better equipment compared to the rest of their competitors.
The game's currency rate seems a bit strange. After checking the math, it comes to about 300 "Gold Standards" per US$1 which translates to $2.20 for the cheapest premium ship, $27.50 for one of the most expensive ships, $10 for a single month "license" that grants you increased chances for loot if you win a battle (which in turn grants credits and rare equipment), or $48 for a six-month "license" for loot as well.
While the licenses are less expensive than that of a standard MMORPG or MMO game in any right, everything else seems to tack on as extras. Cosmetics also cost roughly US$0.05 each depending on their type, certain equipment to mount on your ships also add to the cost, and really feels like the entire game is based on either trying to pull as much money out of you as it can for mid-tier (as that's where most players are), or nickel and diming you to death for cosmetic design.
Overall, the game can be fun, but the mid-tier combat is very much dominated by that of people who have either (rightfully) earned their equipment, or purchased it all, with premium ships looking more flashy than that of their earnable counterparts. This sets up a sense of each fight being unfair, regardless of the skill involved.
If you can tolerate the mid-field tendency for pay-to-win behaviors, and hopefully push to "end-game" tiers, then you'll have a great time with this game, but if you're sensitive to the possibility of buying out a win by equipment advantages, it may not be for you.

Gigantic pretends it does something unique, but under the hood it's nothing but a standard MOBA. The Guardians are your nexus, they don't participate in the game at all. They stand in your base and when one team powers theirs up (by killing enemy turrets and players), it flies forward and stuns the enemy guardian, exposing a weakpoint for players to walk up and attack (also note that the defending players in this encounter can't do anything to harm or hinder the opposing giant). It's functionally identical to every other MOBA that has you pushing down lanes and breaking towers to kill the nexus, except in this one there are no minions and players of either team can re-build downed towers. It's designed around a gimmick that doesn't exist, or just didn't make it in because the devs went bankrupt before it was ready for release.
I can't speak for the character design or balance or the game's merits as a standard MOBA because I didn't give it time, I uninstalled when I realized that it lured me in on false promises and the whole gimmick literally boils down to the nexus model being a giant monster (which isn't even a new concept, other games have done the same thing.) In the end it's just a standard arena shooter/MOBA hybrid that tries to do the same thing Battleborn did.
Not recommended primarily because it pitches itself as something it's not, I don't know if it's actually a bad game. There's a piece of promo material somewhere that says "Gigantic isn't a 5v5 game, it's a 6v6 game!" insinuating that the giant monsters have some actual agency, but in practice they're nothing but turrets.

You wake up on your back after allegedly falling off a cliff (!), get sluggishly to your feet, and casually stroll - not hobble or anything - along barely-existent paths which quickly give way to walking down steep waterfalls and all other manner of unfeasibly agile nonsense. Even crocodiles don't phase our intrepid wanderer: he simply walks right over them, before proceeding to walk across the surface of the body of water it is inhabiting. All hail the new Messiah, reborn after riding his ♥♥♥♥ing bicycle off a ♥♥♥♥ing cliff.
It wasn't long before, on my first playthrough, I got stuck in-between a waterwheel and some stairs I was foolishly trying to access. On my second playthrough, I worked out I wasn't supposed to climb said stairs at all, and instead found a cunningly-hidden path behind the building in question. Not long after this, I made the mistake of accidentally pressing the left mouse button, and magically found myself back at the beginning of the game.
That's quite enough shenanigans for THIS Messiah, I'm afraid. The game's menus might be difficult to negotiate, but I can still manage to find a "Quit" button when I need one.
If you've ever wondered why people defend other walking sims, just play one of those games - just about any of them, really - then play this one. You'll quickly work out what the others do right (i.e. at least SOME things), versus what this one does right (absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing NOTHING, apart from some decent graphics which the "devs" themselves aren't attributable to anyway). No vision, no imagination; not even an earnest-if-misguided attempt to create an atmospheric experience with minimal resources. Not even a vaguely passable "tech" demo, with remotely comprehensible level design. Feral chimpanzees could presumably "flip assets" with better results.
Avoid at all costs. Especially the one they're still asking on the Store page, two-and-a-half years after release. (Five dollars? Haha, nice one, fellas...good to see you at least have a sense of humour...)

I was ready to dismiss this game solely based on the Free-to-play business model. In my past experience I have found F2P games to be fleeting, grind-y experiences that while accessible to more people end up being sort of empty, vacuous.. FUN but usually not that great of a time. The free-to-play model generally suggests that rewards are withheld and satisfaction not guaranteed. ----
I used to collect, use to being the operative phrase, MTG cards. I was involved with going to the local card shop and searching through planeswalkers and specific creature sub types to try and build control or token decks. I probably spent more time building ♥♥♥♥♥♥ decks than actually playing. In High School and in the Air Force were the only times I had a group of people that I played with at any mild regularity.
This game still falls under some traps the Free-to-play business model presents. However, This might be the least egregious I've ever seen them implemented.
If you've read this far, but can't bear me any longer, the game is good. I like it -- And it's free.
is a digital, free-to-play version of the Magic: The Gathering card game.
There are a ton of features within this game. First off, there is only a singular in-game currency. Which to my knowledge is ostensibly unheard of in the free-to play model. The game has Solo vs AI with 3 difficulty options, 1v1 online with friends or ranked  match. As well as Two Headed Giant style matches aka 2v2. There are also multiple single player campaigns to play for free which unlock additional starter decks. These often help you learn new techniques and types of strategies as there is often new terminology introduced fairly regularly. It's nice to be able to zoom in and read what each ability does precisely before making a move. Not to mention the Skill Quests which act as a hyper tutorial which also provide some in-game currency as a reward.
All activities stay for repeated campaign wins and matches with friends pay out rewards to use for buying booster packs or cosmetics when deck building.
The deck building is also quite robust. You can do it all on your own or use the deck wizard to aid you by selecting an archetype and it will take cards you have unlocked through the campaigns or booster packs to help  you fill out the deck to have the best chance of actually playing with the selected strategy.
As you may expect the game being digital has it's disadvantages and advantages.

I will echo others and start by saying this is more of an interactive story than a game. And yet one of the coolest experiences I've had playing a game in a long time.
The best way I can describe the experience is that it was video game poetry, and I loved it. I really enjoyed the execution of the gameplay. The "in game" portions accurately captured the rote boredom and social multitasking that happens when playing an MMO. And the desktop navigation portions made me feel like I got to know both the public and private sides of Nina.
Though I'm a male, the story line resonated with my experiences growing up playing games and I am grateful to have been given a view into how women navigate video game/cyber culture. It was a nice moment to reflect on how though much of our love of these hobbies is shared, the way we experience and interact can be very different.
If this sounds interesting to you, then Cibele is definitely worth your time and $. Thanks to Nina for making this game and sharing a piece of her life with us, we are the better for it.

A few things before I begin; I would describe my experience with this game as negative but it is my hope that Cibele will have a positive impact on the medium of video games. A review marked as 'negative' probably wouldn't help this game reach any kind of success, so for the sake of trying to be helpful I'll settle with the blue thumb. I wouldn't recommend this game to anyone I didn't know personally or anyone at all really.
I don't feel great recommending anything to anyone but I can confidently say that if you don't see any value in games as an artform then there's probably nothing here for you. If you do however, you might derive some enjoying in seeing what Cibele has to offer. Whether or not you'll walk away from it positively or negatively is unknown to me.
-
Cibele follows the age old rule of three rather strictly;  there are three different sections of gameplay, the story is told in three different acts and the bosses go down after the third time you fight them.
The first of these is the virtual desktop of Nina, the protagonist. It's littered with folders filled with various pictures and documents of a personal nature. I often felt a sense of voyeurism, and sometimes dread, looking through Nina's files. The content isn't graphic or even scandalous. Quite the opposite actually. It's a mix of selfies, poetry, photography, chat logs and archives of old blog posts. Some might call it "cringy" but this isn't where my problems lie. My issues stem from those last two items, the chatlogs and blog posts. The awkward ramblings of a teenage girl resonate with me more than I'd like to assume. I'm not one to look back fondly on the things I've said, made or done. Seeing bits of myself and the way I used to think and express myself online in these files brought on a feeling that most would describe as disgust. I didn't like looking at them.
These do not need to be opened or looked at to progress but they provide a nice amount of context to the kind of person Nina is and was. These files also fill in the gaps between the time skips that occur throughout the story.
The second third is the MMO game-within-a-game you play called Valtameri. It's definitely the most "game-y" of the three parts of Cibele and, unfortunately, it isn't very good. But that's not the purpose of it. Valtameri is an almost insulting distillation of what MMO gameplay eventually becomes, a means to socialize with other people. A virtual space to hangout in. Valtameri is a crude facsimile of one half of the MMO experience, actually playing the game. Its actually kind of hard to believe that anyone could enjoy actually playing this game due to it's lack of depth or substance.
It does convey its point rather effectively though. It's the method by which Nina and her object of desire, Blake, interact and speak to each other through. These portions mostly focus on the social aspect of MMOs as the true focus is not the game but the conversations being had, both text and actual voiced dialogue. It's an aspect of these kinds of games I'm turned off by. I played over 50 hours of TERA recently on the least populated server in an attempt to isolate myself from anyone else who might be playing. There was once a time when I embraced and enjoyed the social features of an MMO and the idle chatter in these portions felt oh so familiar. These are fond memories mind you, but I experienced them with people whose names I hardly remember. I don't really like thinking about these sorts of things.
The third and final side of Cibele are the FMV cutscenes. Most of them are short, interstitial videos that bridge the gap between acts but there are a couple of longer scenes that add to the story. They do a good enough job of establishing the mood and vibe in the moments following and preceding the acts. The quality is a bit... poor but I think they're shot and framed rather well.
At this point I hope I've made it clear that I didn't have a great time with Cibele. Most of this negativity is from my own personal experiences and how I view them now. Obviously your mileage may vary for a lot of the content but even in the case of the things Cibele does that you can look at objectively I have a hard time justifying them as anything other than decent at best.
Despite my distaste for it, I can recognize and appreciate the risks it takes. The autobiographical nature of the story is something that is not often seen in games. When it is, it's usually in games that are available for free and distributed by more personal means. The fact that Cibele is something you can buy with actual money on a rather large distribution platform with such high visibility fills me with a bit of hope. A hope that games of such a personal nature can reach an audience and experience some modicum of success and a hope that it will eventually inspire someone to create something greater. I don't like this game very much but I'm very glad it exists.

I wanted to like Cibele, but it just felt more like a diary entry than a game or even a short film. It's an interesting idea, but It just didn't make for a very compelling experience by the end. I guess I was looking for some interesting twist that was never going to come.
I think the problem was that this story will only really resonate with someone who has been through a similar experience, but if they have, this telling isn't really any more interesting than the experience they've already had. It's sort of a catch-22. It feels (and clearly is) very personal, but personal in kind of a bland way.
I do appreciate the chances Nina Freeman takes with her games, they all feel like potentially fascinating experiments. I just don't think this particular experiment was one of them.
2015 has been a good year for coming of age games. This is up there with them.

I would have to say that it’s a charming VN, first and foremost, and would probably deserved some of my money for all the effort and writing put into it. Mind, it isn’t enough to warrant being called a masterpiece, but I would most definitely recommend this to people looking for a good VN.
There are five endings, with only the dying ones being particularly bad (and even then, it’s on the grey; it’s a morality issue/reflection). It’s not so hard to get ‘100%’ or what counts for it (completing the gallery since there are no achievements, and probably seeing all the endings) since the choices are obvious but at the same time impactful; they’re not the dreary and mindless ‘pick A for this ending and pick B for this ending’ kind we’re sometimes saddled with and you do have to put some effort into thinking what choice would get you where you want. Mostly, though, there are many choices where it’s hard to say which was the ‘right’ choice - the whole thing deals with differing views of morality and who to trust.
In summary, the art is simple (not overtly beautiful, but not ugly; somewhere above passable), the music is agreeable (didn’t really stand out, but I think it did the work justice), the writing is well done (if a tad uncreative at some parts, but it is pretty well-written and gives you much to think about), and the decision points are the exact thing you want out of a Visual Novel (especially with how the decisions reflect on you as a person and your personal take on what should be done, encompassing morality, authority, loyalty, et al.).
I can say I enjoyed going through this. I’d give it a solid 7/10 overall, but about an 8/10 where it matters (for the genre).

In the past, I had kept away from visual novels, expecting them to be a creepy waste of time and money.   However, this one was free and I figured I had less to lose by giving it a shot.  I'll be vague to avoid spoiling story!
I was hoping for an interesting story.  In my opinion, it delivered!  I also had extremely low expectations for gameplay, but it exceeded those expectations with some rare opportunities to choose the protagonist's response which could alter the story in some interesting ways.  After trying most of those options and triggering many things, I was further amused.
In hindsight, I think I had previously become jaded about games/stories offering story choices, particularly games that had hyped the importantce of choices but failed to deliver both choice and importance (I'M LOOKIN' AT YOU, FABLE.)  For me, this story has rekindled an interest, and I'll find out whether or not I regret that interest later.
To me, the three main drawbacks of this title are that parts of the story can feel a little forced, sometimes the behavior of the military characters can feel immersion-breaking, and in some cases there were typos and incorrect words used.  Taking the whole work into consideration, those faults seemed quite trivial and forgivable (and frankly my english isn't perfect either.)
Final notes:
-Once inside the game, the "Data" button can offer some backstory/worldbuilding.
-During my replays, I never noticed the "skip" settings doing anything when I changed them, but I may just be confused about them.
I would recommend Rising Angels: Reborn, though probably not to kids considering the story can get pretty dark.

I rarely if ever write reviews, but I have played many VNs in my life (both Hentai and Non-H, hehe) so, upon stumbling on one that puts many +$15 visual novels to shame, I simply couldn't let this slip....
-Story 10/10
''Whom do you trust? And whom you shouldn't trust?'' This is a very mature topic in an even more mature story. So if you expect the choices to answer this question to be as Black and White as the ''Side with the Rebels against the Evil Tyrant, or side with the Evil Tyrant to crush the Rebels.'', then move along; you won't like this VN. But if you like plot full of mystery and doubt, betrayal and friendship, where one single wrong choice could end up dooming everything you care about and you like to feel the jarring tension and drama, then you'll love this work.
-Art 7/10
OK, this score is a bit viased; for a VN with so many endorphins-releasing situations, moments of sheer shock and fear.... I seriously expected more CGs of them, not just a black screen with the text. I know the most pivotal of them have CGs, but you can count those with one hand and there many, many more events that deserved a CG.
As for what Art Style and Quality over all, this VN has better art than many paid VNs; I'd give it a 10 in here.
-Sound 10/10
The BGMs tend to be quite quiet and inconspicious when nothing of importance is happening, but when something big happens.... Well, the soundtrack kicks in just in the right way (to the point you might find yourself jumping in your seat if you favor headphones). All of the music is beautiful and perdfectly crafted for whatever events are taking place, and that's simply perfect. Love the opening soundtrack, too.
-Characters 11/10
This review is viased too; I love monster girls in all their shapes (Monster Musume be praised! And Okayado-sensei's previous hentai works too, heheh) so, to have a REAL GOOD STORY, one that's not about silly romantic comedy or pointless fanservice, in a setting with monster girls on it is golden.
Going into the specifics, a good Female Protagonist (that isn't oversexualized), a Ditzy Dojikko Dragon with confidence issues, a Tsundere Ojou-sama Kitsune, a Lazy but Lovely Wolf Girl and a Cold and Harsh Elf spelled epicness to me. But, each of the characters is much, much deeper than just their physical traits; each of them feels and acts like a real living being; with virtues and faults, issues and traumas, and with unique and interesting personalities; characters you can relate to. (Such a thing is so rare these days).
-Lenght 10/10
At first I thought this was too short (beat in on 3 hours, and got the True End in just two tries) and I was about to complain about it. Then, I saw that Kickstarter page with a fully-funded sequel, and all my complains vanished and were replaced by the desire of it being released soon. If it's as epic as this one, I'll get it even if I have to pay.
So, to sum up, if you're looking for a fanservice-packed romantic comedy, with lots of bouncing bewbs, panty shots and Gainaxing, then look elsewhere (try NekoPara, which is quite good in all the aforementioned, specially the last two). But, if you are looking for an epic drama filled with emotions and anxiety, then by all means, get this VN.

After getting a computer upgrade and finally being able to play this game, I am incredibly disappointed in what I've experienced.
First of all is the story and writing. Well aside from the very intriguing intro movie that sets up the Big Bad, Pagan Min, and one of his three main cronies, the game very quickly goes south in story telling. Your protagonist is supposedly a descendent of Kyrat natives, but was raised in the United States living some life that the game never really takes the time to mention. For all intents and purposes, Ajay has no backstory beyond 'lives on America' and 'mother died and wanted ashes spread on some hill in Kyrat'.
Apparently living in America automatically makes people like Ajay into instant super warriors and killing machines with no training. The 'good' guys 'rescue' Ajay and almost immediately drop him into a desperate escape from about two dozen guys - all on his own - armed with just a huge knife. Nothing comes out of Ajay's mouth to remark on his situation, leaving me wondering if I'm really just controlling a seasoned serial killer that some American cop is losing sleep over stateside.
You're probably thinking: are all FPS protagonists basically that, though? Well they more or less wind up that way, but given that Far Cry 3 showed Jason going from spoilt rich kid scared of pirates to full-blown psychotic murderer, I was expecting something in the spirit of that kind of characterisation in Far Cry 4. Instead we got a protagonist with basically no character beyond the player's whims, which just feels lazy.
On the topic of lazy, we reach the gameplay. It's basically the same as Far Cry 3. Same skills, Same guns (more or less). Same kinds of vehicles (the pilotable helictoper is a waste of time). The only thing different is the difficulty. Overall the game is stupidly easy, with powerful weapons and items that would take a while to get in Far Cry 3 being acquireable in the first few hours of Far Cry 4. I had the wingsuit in less than five hours. I had taken two out of the four fortresses in seven hours. The rest of the time I wasted trying to get to the third fortress - only to find that the game will instakill/relocate you to keep you out of the Northern section of the mission. I did do some story missions, but I just don't feel invested in the plight of the other characters. They're all caught up in some civil war and are going on about low morale and how Pagan Min's army is tough - completely ignoring the fact that I've been curbstomping them and liberating outposts and radiotowers and two fortresses since I got here.
There's not really anything in FC4 that FC3 doesn't do much better. You're better off playing FC3 instead, and then playing Blood Dragon if you want something different - because you're not going to find anything interesting in FC4. Do stupid minigames? Collect pointless junk? Try to force yourself to appreciate the most boring storyline in the series? No thanks. I'll stick with Far Cry 2, or Far Cry 3 + Blood Dragon. Hell, Far Cry 3's co-op mode is pretty kickass. You'll have more fun that way.

Massive space battles with customizable ships. Lots of fun, simple to get into, increased depth the longer you play. Good game.
While some people will always complain about the grind and the buy-to-win in a free-to-play game, the developers managed an interesting balance in those topics.
Don't get me wrong, there is some grind. But when compared to other free-to-play tittles, it's not that much.

As for the win-to-play that often puts off people in free to play games, I have to disagree with whoever thinks this about Star Conflict.  Ships are divided into tiers, and each tier can have 2 to 4 ships of each class, with increasing effectiveness. Battles match-making is also divided into tiers. This means that when you get to rank 3 (the last of tier 1), if you are any good you will be owning battles like a boss. But as soon as you get to tier 2, a whole new world of ships, more effective, with better pilots, and more ships modules(skills), you will be like the little fish in the pond of sharks.... again. That is, untill you get the best ships in that tier as well. Same happends when you jump from tier 2 to 3, and from 3 to 4, and so on.
This leads to some people thinking they are dying because the other player has a premium ship.
Wrong.
While premium ships do have a very slight advantage in their stats, most of the time it's irrelevant. A good pilot is born from experience. Of course, premium ship owners are usually good pilots. Often only play with that ship and become very good with it.
But the slightly better stats will only make a slight difference in a 1 on 1, with 2 very good pilots. Any premium ship gets utterly destroyed with a simple 2 to 1. And lets face it:
If you and your team can't do a 2 to 1 in a 10 vs 10 battle, then you deserve to loose against him.
Finally, ships tend to get more effective as tiers go up, and pilots also become better with experience. This leads to the tactical side of the batlles to become more apparent as you go up, as well as taking longer to get decided.
The different ship classes are also well done, with each having it's own specific role.
In the end, and considering there is nothing of the kind in recent game releases, together with the competent work Gaijin did with Star Conflict, this game is mandatory to any spaceship combat fan.

TL;DR:
I'm really enjoying it, somehow it feels like a mix of Paragon and Battlerite.
- You don't have the typical MOBA creep farming, hence why it feels like Battleborn.
- You have a similar, fluid targetting system to Paragon.
- It's not nearly as overwhelming as other MOBAs. Little-to-no punishment compared to other games like Dota.
A few negatives to begin:
!!! There are some REALLY buggy mechanics. I mean, frustratingly♥♥♥♥♥♥mechanics. For example, playing Wu and using his second jump to escape can sometimes result in you spinning/jumping into an invisible wall. It's actually ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and is the most annoying thing, hence why I don't play many of the melee classes.
- The artstyle can be distracting while in chaotic team fights. For example, if you play a Summoner, you might find it hard to keep track of your summoned 'pets' as well as your ability cooldowns and what's happening in front of you.
- Dodging mechanic - I honestly feel it's needless. I find that dodging is more problematic than just running away to be honest. I haven't found any situations yet where I can say "Wow, that dodge saved my life". Instead, I can honestly say "The ♥♥♥♥? Where'd my stamina go?" since I realise I accidentally dodged and lost a quarter of the stamina i could have used to run & jump out of a sticky situation. (I realized 5 minutes after posting that you can change the keybinding for dodging in the options menu - didn't see it before)
- It's VERY chaotic for your first few games. As for advice, I'd say stick to a hero that fits your playstyle: if you like shooting people and dealing damage, pick a shooter and stick to that choice for a while to learn the mechanics of the game.
- The practise mode is a good idea, it helped me to decide early on which role I'd prefer to stick with. Very helpful for new and experienced players.
- Lastly, I feel that summoners are extremely underpowered when compared to other roles like assassins. Let's take Griselma (summoner) and Tripp (assassin) as our examples. Griselma's damage output - as a RANGED character - is dire compared with even a support's damage output (like Vadasi). Over 5 seconds, I've found that with Griselma, I am dealing about 300-400 damage. Let's take the situation where my summoned 'pets' (or hands) have been killed, which actually puts your RMB skill on cooldown and thus unusable and limiting your damage. Compare this with Tripp - being in combat for 5 seconds, you'd have killed your target and already escaped behind your team. That's kinda insane considering Griselma is meant to be a damage dealing summoner. Yes, you can build for utility - buffing teammates and zoning the enemy - but once your hands are dead, you're worthless, might as well be a meatshield for your support. *BUT THIS WILL PROBABLY CHANGE IN A FEW BALANCING PATCHES TO COME (hopefully)*
The positives:
+ Unique graphics. Very nice to jump in and have this TF2 nostalgic feel. I'm personally a fan of this artstyle since it's cartoonish and reminds me of that.
+ Overall balancing is acceptable this early on. My first 'expensive' hero was Vadasi, and honestly her playstyle is so different from most other heroes that I had to 'main' her for several hours before I could comfortably find two builds that work. You'll also find that a hero that comes under a certain role, like Vadasi being a 'healer', can actually be more flexible. You can build damage for Vadasi, heal on the side and mostly focus on your damage output which actually benefits your team moreso in certain situations.
+ Map design. It's actually quite well-made. How the map changes in the 'Clash' stage brings more variety to the map design; there might only be 3 or so maps available, but the fact that some literally change in the second half of a match makes it feel like two maps in one. Very nice to have this.
+ I feel like the Ultimate pack is actually quite a good deal. £24 to unlock all heroes (and future ones, which is good), 10 level boosters (which is decent) and a friend code that gives them all these benefits. That friend code makes this pack basically worth it. Quite a good deal to be honest.
-> Comapring the size of my negatives to the size of my positives, you'll probably wonder why I'm recommending it. It's not for everyone, same can be said about most games with cartoon graphics and an emphasis on skill-based PvP. The third-person might not even be for everyone either. It's enjoyable to win and lose, which for me is what wins me over in any MOBA. That's how I get better, if I lose but enjoy it in solo queue, I'm gonna play again and get better over time. What makes it enjoyable is all the variety from the hero builds to the map changes in the 'Clash' phase and all the parkour you can begin to deploy in-game.
-> From a PC gamer's perspective, I feel like it needs a ranked system, or a competitive scene since the overall feel of the game so far is nowhere near as punishing as other MOBAs like Dota. The Devs HAVE SAID that they'd focus on the competitive scene if the community wants it, which shows the Devs are listening to the community - very good for a MOBA (and any game...).
-> I must also say that the Arc Client isn't very good. However, I don't feel this should detract much from the game's potential.

This game took away everything from the original Thief games that makes it unique and a challenge.
Having a hard time navigating Victorian London? Good thing Garrett has a GPS-like minimap and objective markers everywhere.
Wanna jump over this pesky table and climb those boxes over there to avoid guards? Nope. Jumping and climbing only work in context sensitive areas.
Ledge too high to climb and don't feel like walking to find stairs? Too bad! Rope arrows are now 500% more context sensitive!
Looking for a gripping story? Go fish.
Devs said in an interview ""we want you to play as a thief, but we don't want to force you to play as a thief." Quick reminder in case you forgot the series' title - THIEF. Garrett now has expert assassin/combat skills.
Good thing we can see his hands moving, though, don't know how we ever survived without some visual feedback to remind us what we just did.

A really fantastic interactive short-story. I found it to be a very cohesive experience that combined light gameplay, FMV and an interactive desktop. The acting in both the FMV and the voiceover felt very real and the desktop elements helped flesh-out the protagonist's life. Although the gameplay is very light, the experience of playing the MMORPG felt pretty authentic in its attempt to balance the social and gameplay elements. The point of this game is its narrative and the gameplay serves that end well.
Some reviewers have stressed that if you haven't had a similar experience to the protagonist the game may not speak to you. I disagree. I found the experience quite moving. Ultimately, it's a coming-of-age story that contains universal themes, albeit one that is set around the social world of MMORPGs. Despite not having a similar experience with an MMORPG or an online relationship, I had no problem realting to the characters and theme.
Overall, a very moving and cohesive experience that I would highly reccomend for fans of narrative focused games.

I liked this a lot. It feels like a piece of interactive fiction almost more than it does a game, but it's multimedia in a way that I haven't encountered in interactive fiction before; a minigame, a series of short films, poetry and photography and illustration all wrapped up in a desktop you get to explore at your own pace. I liked that the characters were three-dimensional in their personalities despite being minimally-written; I felt for Blake almost as much as for Nina by the end of Cibele. The art style is beautiful, and I loved the soundtrack, which helped.
This wasn't what I expected, I don't think, and it took me a little while to get into the rhythm of a game that propels itself along mainly without input from its player. But I liked it, and it'll stick with me, and I would recommend it if you like beautifully-drawn little vignettes of human beings in all their imperfections.

Imagine you are a normal citizen of a slavic country that had just erupted into war on the streets you grew up on. With no options, you seek shelter from the bitter weather with two complete strangers and decide to work together to survive. You have no idea how to do anything. You are already wounded, and with very little supplies to go on, all you can do is hold on. You scavenge up what you can and try to scrape by for just one more night so that your new friends might scavenge up some bandages for you. You live in fear every night because the guards you left might not be enough to repel the looters. You are constantly given the choice to help those in need and maintain your humanity, or devolve into a heartless survivalist and raid the homes of the innocent for much needed supplies. When you encounter more dangerous groups of survivors, you must learn to fight on your feet because any wrong move in the heat of things could spell the end for you. Even when you return with a good haul, you have a growing sense of dread that your group might not all make it.
My advice is if you think you'd like a game that is emotionally harrowing and mechanically very simple, don't hesitate to get This War of Mine. Don't look up any guides, don't watch any playthroughs, just jump in.
This game is best enjoyed when you know nothing about it going in. The story that you weave in the way you choose to approach tough decisions will be a great reflection of yourself. I highly recommend asking what This War of Mine was like for your friends, because you'll be surprised how many different ways you can play this game.

The core mechanic comes from reconfiguring your ship in-level with the pieces you have found to solve the puzzles that strew the levels.  For instance, you might need to build an arm-like extension to prod a boulder out of your way, or need rockets on one side to propel you quickly through a guantlet.
There's also the requisite speedruns for when you are finished.
I enjoy collecting things in games and building/configuring them, but personally, I like my puzzles less physics-based.
This game, however, does both fairly well and is worth a look.

This game is a visually appealing mix of the MOBA and TPS genre. Although only a few classical MOBA elements are present, the game plays around key points (which are, gameplay-wise, similar to towers), and the goal is to bring down the enemy team's boss creature by damaging its weak spot, which is only available for a short time frame in every few minutes. The gameplay is pretty fast-paced, the movement and FOV are both satisfying, the art style is simply stunning. The game plays fast, and unfortunately that's not always for the better. Maps are rather small, and key points are close to each other, so moving around feels a bit too quick. Abilities are diverse, yet I don't feel they are well thought through or balanced. Sometimes the game doesn't even explain what a specific ability of stat (like shield) is good for, or what percentage some values convert to. Animations are beautiful, but could be so intense, that battles become effect fests where the only visible things are the health bars you're chasing down. All in all I like the overall feel of the game, but the execution needs way more polishing before we can call this a must title. Worth a try, just don't expect it to be your daily driver. Feels like a better and definitely faster version of Paladins.

I really wanted to like this game. I like roguelikes, and this is a modern, nice-looking one that seems to have the right level of complexity. I've tried to play it a number of times over the years and I always bounce off immediately. The interface is bad. It doesn't know what the game wants to be. It lets you move your character from tile to tile with the arrows like any other roguelike, but most things you do in the game require you to use the mouse.
There's an option to perform certain tasks, like attack enemies and open doors, with the arrow keys, but (a) it's insane that attacking enemies by walking into them isn't the default, this is a ROGUELIKE, and (b) activating items by walking into them doesn't feel natural. I accidentally activate items I don't want to. Just give me a use key.
The game description says "Classic Roguelike gameplay with the sweet, refreshing taste of point-and-click interfaces. No longer must you press CTRL-ALT-SHIFT-x to drink a potion." But this isn't any better. It's the interface of an action RPG without the action. Just give me intuitive, well-designed menus that I can access with the keyboard, or god forbid, a controller! Being able to do most (but not all) things you need to do with the keyboard but then having to click the mouse to pick up an item, dismiss a dialog box, or access your inventory is incredibly frustrating.
I'd recommend Fatal Labyrinth over this. It's $2 cheaper, and despite coming out 2 decades earlier, it feels a lot better to play than this game. Arrow keys or D-Pad plus three buttons. Your inventory is nicely arranged by item type. It's a little basic, but it doesn't feel like the mutant offspring of a roguelike and an ARPG.

== Medium Length Review ==
Hi folks!
This is my review to "Dungeons of Dredmor" ("DOD") . So what's this game about?
In short, it is a classic, turn-based hack 'n' slay RPG / dungeon crawler with retro-style, pixelated graphics.
The main story is as simplistic as it is uninspired: You are the hero ( or heroine) who has to slay the evil king who is in charge of the (also evil) dungeons and you shall bring an end to its (ever-so evil) reign of evil.
In order to do that, you first decide which kind of class or class-combination you want to play. After choosing the corresponding skills, you are ready to go and you start at the first of (up to) 15 dungeon levels.
The dungeon levels of the game are arranged in a semi-random order, meaning that they are generated differently each time you play the game, though certain elements stay the same which you will recognize pretty fast.
In order to fight of your evil opponents, you can resort to melee attacks, ranged attacks with throwing or shooting weapons or you can finally resort to magic attacks of different kinds. Since - of course - the enemies get tougher with every level, you will need to look out for all kinds of loot after slaying the enemies, use the built-in crafting system or buy new stuff in the "shops" where you can also sell your outdated gear.
That pretty much covers the basic gameplay. Suffice it to say that the dungeon is not only covered with enemies, but also with deadly traps and some (very tiny) puzzles. You can optionally also take on side-quests which will reward you with some extra loot like a special unique weapon.
Depending on the initial difficulty setting you have chosen, you will be able to save the game and reload your save game after dying or your character will be permanently erased,  once killed. Also, you can choose whether you will be able to return to earlier levels by "going back up" (which helps a lot) or you will be forced to play the game "rogue-like" (which is much tougher).
So now let's have a closer look at the good and bad aspects of the game. Let's start with the good ones:
1) There are many classes to choose from and each class has different skills you can choose.
2) The general mood of the game is funny. You will find a *lot* of references to other titles,
movies, etc. etc. in the game and if you like this kind of "nerdy humor" (which I do), you will probably find that this is one of the best aspects of the game.
3) The crafting system is quite okay (though needlessly cumbersome to use).
4) There are a lot of mods for the game which you can use to blow some fresh wind through the dusty dungeon if you get tired of the original game.
So, why did I not recommend this game, you might ask?
So let's look at the things I did not like about this game:
1) The game is extremely repetitive. I know - that is to be expected for a turn-based game and I do not mind that, but combined with the fact that most of the time the full extent of "strategy" you have to use to overcome your enemies is just to click on them for a melee attack, that gets boring way too fast.
2) If you want to play the game on a higher difficulty level, be warned: Once permanent death is turned on, it can get very frustrating. Although the general difficulty seems to be okay, you sometimes end up being killed "out of the blue" after playing straight for hours without ever losing more than a quarter of your health points before. The problem is that once you get to realize you are in trouble this time, it is almost too late. If you chose a sub-optimal combination of classes and skills, you will not be able to run away from the fight and will simply be battered to death by your enemies. Yes, you could argue that this is only a problem if you play on higher difficulty settings, but it is also worth to consider this when looking at the next point:
3) A single "run" thought the dungeon (at 15 levels) takes way too long - especially when playing this game rogue-like. If you are playing carefully (mind pain point 2) and you collect a lot of loot, then you are in for a lot of tedious inventory management and walking back and forth. A complete run at lower difficulties may cost you up to 20 hours, not to mention higher difficulty settings. So now imagine your frustration of carefully grinding for 20 or even more hours just to fall victim to a stupid trap + enemy combination...
4) A lot of the in-game mechanics are not explained very well or are not explained at all (also not in the tutorial). This can lead to very frustrating moments in the game when you have just activated a new skill (with just an ominous explanation text to it which gives no real clue on what it truly does) and then finally realize that you do not know how to use it. The game gives you no kind of explanation or hints whatsoever.  I played one run with rogue-class, buying a skill which seemingly "revealed all hidden items" which never had any kind of effect during may play-through at all, although it was activated. This pain point might sound trivial, but if you choose the wrong classes / skills, your "hero" will be pathetic up to the bitter end.
5) There is no real skill tree. Skills of one category can only be activated linearly, meaning you cannot activate the last skill in the "tree" without having activated all others first. The problem is that many skills sound much better than they actually are, and - which is even more unnerving - you sometimes have to activate three or even four useless skills just to get a decent one.
6) The final boss / bosses of the game can be very challenging if you do not prepare for the final fight from the very start. I will not spoil this for you, but suffice it to say that some classes will have a *very* hard time beating the boss, even if they have been maxed out. Also suffice it to say that the final boss can deal out a lot of more damage with single hits than any other enemy can, so be warned!
7) This point weighs most heavily for me: The combat system is too simplistic. If you play with a fighter or rogue-class, then all you ever do is hack and slay. There is almost no kind of strategy whatsoever required to progress through the game as long as you collect the strongest gear and do not let yourself get surrounded by too many enemies at a time. Since all enemies behave somewhat identical with only little exceptions (some enemies can indeed use ranged attacks against you - imagine that!), that makes the game too boring way too fast.
8) (Auto-)Saving and Loading takes surprisingly long.
9) During my 20-hour play-through, the game crashed multiple times for no apparent reason.
10) The soundtrack of the game gets boring very quickly. There are too few songs and the music is way to repetitive.
So what is the verdict?
DOD is - all in all - a mediocre game. It is not "bad" but it certainly isn't good or great either. It makes me wish that steam would offer a third, "neutral" recommendation.
But since it doesn't, I am forced to not recommend this game. The retro-style artwork and humor of the game is good, but it cannot make up for the boring and tedious game play. In any case you should not be required to look up how skills work in a wiki to get a basic understanding of them.
If you are heavily interested in mods, this game might be for you, after all, but I cannot really consider this fact in this review of the basic game.
Play it. Now.

The problem with naming a game after a beloved series is that it will inevitably be compared to that series' best version. It happened with DMC: Devil May Cry, and it happened here.
On it's own this game isn't that bad. It's biggest problem is that it feels like it was made on a factory line with a checklist. Standard love interest, check. Standard villain, check. Standard gameplay, check. Standard weapons and gear, check. Nothing in this game really makes it stand out from the crowd. In Thief 2 you had huge sprawling levels you could get lost in with tons of secrets to find if you were observant and clever enough.
One thing that I really noticed was that rope arrows in this game only worked at very specific points. If you fired a rope arrow anywhere else it would just be a waste of time and arrows. In Thief 2 you could fire one of those suckers anywhere and climb up even if it led nowhere. It encouraged exploring outside the linear hallways and streets.
TL:DR version. Not the worst game, but there are better stealth games out there.

To start with, the reason I decided to write a review: The game has a rather good, almost beautiful, swimming animation, even for sideways and backwards swimming. This is something I've seen done badly in quite some games, including AAA titles.
Sadly, you only get to see this swimming when you jump in the sea
- The swimming animation, as mentioned above
- I had a turtle as a steed (though it did not move)
- Tedious, feels like you are walking way too slow.
- Story: non-existent. It says you fell from a clif while cycling, and your bike broke, yet there is no bike, and nobody who fell like that would walk for 30 minutes to a boat, which just happened to be there. Especially, since it felt like I was lost the entire game, not knowing where to go, searching for the way which actually lead somewhere.
- Music: very loud. ominous, made me feel like something was going to jump-scare me, which didn't happen (luckily).
- Sound effects: barely any, only an obnoxious waterfall, which was distance triggered, and the sea. There might have been some softer ones, but I couldn't hear them, because I had my volume turned way down, because of the music.
- Settings: They suck. Game resorts to it's defaults every time, which means it sets the graphics to something weird, which makes it near impossible to get it right. It also sets my language to German everytime on start-up, since I had to force close it first time (due to the graphics, I couldn't click continue) and it was on German then. And of course, as is normal with this quality of games: no sound or music volume settings.
- Physics: Bad, you jump way too high, and you can walk up wet steep hills.
- Graphics: Mediocre, which is bad for a game that is basically a graphics showcase. Mind you, I had my settings on Ultra. I encountered plants so thin, you couldn't see them from the side, doors which looked painted on, and some other oddities.
- Environmental interaction: little to none, the birds and deer scare off, and the croc snaps at you (but doesn't do anything, I went on to jump on it)
