First off, let me start by saying that while I did not enjoy this, that does not mean it is a bad game. I got this in the humble bundle and the mechanics are fresh and interesting, it has cute graphics and makes for a neat little 'puzzle' game. Not to mention  the sound design is very well done.
For me, however, the game felt more like a chore than a pleasure. It wasn't hard, by all accounts it was incredibly easy, but even though it only took me a little more than 4 hours to complete about halfway through I just felt incredibly bored. You should  get this if you enjoy 'trial and error' gameplay, but unfortunately I couldn't bring myself to enjoy it and came out feeling dissapointed.
The main mechanic of the game is finding someone who is going to die, and then repeating the day from checkpoints you can set yourself. This is amusing at first, but after a while grows repetitive. Most deaths can be stopped in two or three repeats if you are astute, and there are a few that only take one. two of the puzzles seemed difficult at first, but by simply 'going through the motions'  I found that they weren't. You really need to just remember to use all of your abilities everywhere you can and then you are done.
At many times the menu can be unintuitive,  At one point you find a recipe to make a 'hungry skull'. at the time, I had no idea how to read or even access this recipe (later turned out it was a pin on the map), but managed to solve the 'puzzle' easily anyway. The storyline is interesting at first but it isn't long before the 'twist' becomes painfully obvious. While I liked the premise, there just wasn't much meat to it, and nothing to really keep me interested.   Some elements also seemed kind of silly, like the masks people wore trying to chase you.
also, the ending is extremely lackluster and felt uninspired.

All in all this is only barely a negative review. I would rate it 4.5/10.

There is only one reason I can think of to recommend Far Cry 4, and that's if you're low on sleeping aids and need something to lull you into a blissful slumber. The game is boring as hell, for the pure and simple fact that the designers just weren't thinking about all the game breaking mistakes they made that cause it to be an easy cake walk where you simply slog your way through the motions.
Let me explain how the process of Far Cry works. What typically happens in a Far Cry game is that you are given the options to complete missions, find loot, and use it to buy weapons and upgrades. Alternatively you can activate towers in order to make the weapons in the game free. How liberating towers works (or rather how it's supposed to work) is that you travel to a tower, fight off a dozen enemies guarding it, figure out a way up the tower, get to the top, and press a button. After which you are rewarded with free loot at the top for you to scavenge.
This was a fun and interesting challenge in Far Cry 3 because you actually had to do all those steps I just mentioned in order to activate them. But for some brain scouring reason, Farcry 4 just gives you a personal gyro-copter right off the bat. They're just lying around for you to get in and pilot at the start of the game.
So here's how the game play of Farcry 4 goes: You turn the game on, get to the first outpost, find a gyro-copter and then you win. Because after that I never, EVER encountered a single challenge in the game.
The towers you liberate are supposed to be challenging obstacles that makes you weigh the benefits of spending money on weapons, or overcoming the challenge of activating the towers to unlock them for free. But where is the challenge now? I have a gyro-copter. Now I can just fly to the top of the things, press the button and fly to the next. There are seventeen in total and I had liberated ten of them this way within the first twenty minutes.
So now that almost all the weapons in the game were free and the loot at the top was mine for the easy taking ten times in a row, the only thing I had to worry about spending my money on was upgrades for the weapons. And let me tell you, once you fully upgrade the sniper rifle you may as well just shut the game off, because you already won. Now all you have to do is slog through the chore of winning.
Liberating camps is easy as hell when you can just pick enemies off from a continent away, and most of the actual in game missions can be completed from a distance as well. Occasionally you have to fight a ground battle, but the enemies are so interchangeable and predictable that I was picking them off with the starting, non-upgraded shotgun and got by just fine.
An exploration game just isn't fun when you can just fly to each destination undisturbed, and a shooting game isn't fun when you're basically just lay in a beach chair picking people off from the next town over. Sure you could limit your self to not using the copter or the sniper rifle, but why on earth would you hand the player those things and then say "Just don't use them if you want to have fun?"
It was particularly hilarious when I was given "Tail the target" missions. "Oh, bet you won't be able to keep up with this guy as he's weaving and bobbing around dicey roads" the game said as I rolled my eyes and just followed him high above in my helicopter, waiting for him to stop his stupid car. I was then supposed to eliminate him and the guards surrounding him in order to obtain a blood diamond. So naturally I parked my copter a good sniping distance away and easily picked them off one by one like cardboard ducks at a carnival, after which I parked my copter outside the cave I was supposed to enter.
"Okay, now get the blood diamond. Good, now take it back to the dealer. UUH-OOH! We just spawned six bad guys outside your cave! Bet you can't fight your way through them!", the game said as I rolled my eyes, got back in my gyro-copter and made my way to the buyer, looking down at the enemies shaking their fists at me pathetically as I flew away in safety.
And then the game had the audacity to give me a mission where my destination was a league away. In that instance I was apparently supposed to trek through the wilderness and tundra to get there, but again, my handy dandy personal copter was sitting right there, so I just had my self some coffee while I held the forward button for twenty minutes until I got there and hilariously noticed from above an elaborate rock climbing set up I was apparently supposed to have use in order to get up there. You gave me a helicopter you guys! Stop pretending that I'm ever going to get somewhere any way else.
The unbelievably short sighted design decisions in Far Cry 4 made everything that was fun and challenging in Far Cry 3 a complete waste of time. When you have to go out of your way not to use what they gave you in order to have fun, you're just playing a broken game. If you have Far Cry 3 and loved it, I say just play that again. Don't bother with this broken, boring slog.

This is not really a game, it's an interactive story.
The choices you have are very limited (didn't count but probably around 20 until reaching an ending) but can have a huge impact, especially near the end. So feel free to (quick)save if you want to explore all paths (though you can just skip to the next decision whenever you want to).
Is it worth your time? For me it was, but it certainly depends on what you like.
The focus on the game is less on action, but rather on characters and their relationships (e.g. girl-on-girl romance :D) as well as exploring the unknown and building all kinds of suspense in a sci-fi space ship environment.
The music was nice: versatile and fitting. The race concept
Don't let the supposedly cute manga/anime look fool you, the initially light-hearted story becomes actually rather mature and thrilling, because unlike most movies or series (I guess you could compare it a bit with Star Trek or Andromeda), this has multiple endings, allowing twists which can be good, bad or something inbetween and there are several dilemas that have no "right" answer.

First of all, this is not your usual game of 'doing things', this is a Visual Novel, which means that you will, most of the time, be reading, getting filled with the atmosphere of the game and at some points making decisions about which path the protagonist will take.
I like to read, and that's what it took me like 5 hours to finish my first run of the game, so you can finish it in one sit.
I really liked the theme and the story of the game, but it feels too linear, maybe it could gain in depth with more choices, specially in the first stages. Later on, you will be able to do much more important choices that will change the ending of the game.
The art is nice, although it may feel a bit too repetitive, as does the music, but you can always turn it down and concentrate more on the text, which is what this games are about.
TL;DR:
If you like reading and Visual Games, chances are that you will like this game.

is a short Visual Novel, inspired by the popular VN Everlasting Summer, about the main cast of Semyon and the girls gathering together for a New Year's celebration. Just like in Everlasting Summer, there are character routes for each girl.
The VN displays the warm theme of the New Year spirit extremely well; you get the joyous experiences of gift-giving, launching firecrackers, and of course, snow. Because of this, Frosty Kiss is best played during the New Year. Also, the writing is quite detailed and well-paced, making the VN enjoyable.
The background artworks are quite appealing and comfortable; I like how the style is reminiscent of the backgrounds in Everlasting Summer. Although most of the character art is borrowed from Everlasting Summer, the different appearances are a welcome change and fits with the winter theme. The game also offers some nice guitar soundtracks.
Despite this, there are some minor drawbacks, such as minor translation and word choice errors (i.e. "Go get a warm") and the fact that the soundtracks do not fade in and out; however, because this is such a short game, these drawbacks do not affect much of the overall gameplay.
In conclusion, Frosty Kiss is overall a nice, short, and easily completable Visual Novel for fans of Everlasting Summer.

Pixel Puzzle franchise. Recommended for those who literally like to put puzzles together, and I do mean piece by piece.
Pixel Puzzles 2: Space
Features space and all things related: planets, nebulae, astronaunts, satellites, space craft. There is even an introductary puzzle of the space shuttle found on the main screen. 24 puzzles in all ranging from 60 pieces to 350 pieces, with some odd shaped and space themed puzzle pieces (arrows, stars, rockets). All the puzzles can be seen in the picture gallery once the puzzle is solved. The game grid is floating spheres so the player can choose any puzzle they want without constraint.
Puzzles: 60 piece - 5, 112 piece - 6, 153 piece- 6, 220 piece - 6, and 350 piece - 1.
The game board is surrounded by space where the puzzle pieces float and MOVE. The pieces also must be rotated to gain the correct orientation (like in a physical puzzle.) Fortunately there is an option for the player to choose the correct orientation permenantly (or until such time as the player chooses to turn it off). I recommend having this feature on for the 220 piece and 350 piece puzzles due to the size of the pieces.
Best feature of this game: The Launch. In this game a spaceman bounces about trying to flag down a space craft.  During the puzzle phase if the player uses no hints and builds the rocket from the floating capsules among the puzzle pieces the rocket will launch.  If the rockets launches, at the end of the puzzle the rocket will return to pick up the bouncing astronaut.
NOTE: There is a launch achievement attached to ever puzzle, making every puzzle solved actually worth 2 achievements: one to solve and one to pick up the astronaut.
However, if the player choses, the floating capsules can be used as hints. Simply put a capsule in one of the three tiny landers to launch them for the hint.  The first lander (left to right) is "ghost". This power-up shows the puzzle picture for approximately 10 seconds. The second lander (L to R) will cause the selected puzzle to gain the correct orientation (unless the player rotates the piece). The third lander (L to R) shows exactly where that piece belongs in the puzzle, edge or middle.
Other functions can be found in a side vertical menu including: a tray to hold the pieces, shuffle the pieces, zoom in on the puzzle board, and changing the puzzle board's background color.
There 55 achievements and trading cards available.

The Raiden series are always well-regarded shmups but they don't tend to do anything revolutionary. They're well made and good score attack fun but they don't redefine the genre like say, Ikaruga did. Raiden III continues this tradition. Unfortunately, the PC conversion of this game is not particularly good, very strange indeed when you consider that it originally ran on PC-based arcade hardware. It's locked at 640x480 resolution with scalable windowed options available and while it still looks OK, it's dated resolution shows. It also does support controllers but not natively and you'll have to manually do all the bindings in the separate configuration utility. There's no online play or online leaderboards either. That said, this game will run on a potato and plays great with the keyboard so it's perfect for low powered laptops and the like.
It's an exact recreation of 2005's original arcade game, including local co-op and with some additional features that originally came in the PS2 version, such as Boss Rush and Score Attack. You also can save replays and some high-level play from what I presume the developers comes pre-loaded.
The core Raiden games are good but don't feature as advanced a scoring system as the Raiden Fighters series, nor do they have multiple ships you can select. You get one standard ship with bombs and a few different weapons you can pick up during play. It's not complicated but the simplicity is where the core Raiden games shine. They're good shmups that anyone can pick up and play and get good at with a minimal amount of practice. Even if you're a casual player, there's a lot to like here.
Personally, given that this is only one game and a weak conversion, I think it's too expensive at full price but on sale, it's a no brainer. If you're looking to spend $10, I'd recommend Raiden Legacy (which is not on Steam sadly but is on GOG and Green Man Gaming), which is a very well put together collection of several past Raiden titles. Raiden IV Overkill is also apparently a much better (though more expensive) PC version but I have not played it at time of writing.

Sounds disarmingly simple? As your interconected railway gets more and more passengers youu must fight to make it as efficient as possible - as if a single station becomes conjested, your metro is closed and that's game over.
To summarise, Mini Metro is a beautifully simple, easy to understand game that you can pick up for barely anything. It's basically Train Simulator for people who don't actualy care about rtrains and just want a caual, intuative, endlessly replayable puzzle game. That was interesting. This is a game where you experience the online life of a nerdy 19 year-old girl, discovering romance, love, and sex. In the game, you can look through photos and text files on her desktop and you'll play her favorite MMO and listen to conversations between her and her crush. It's also quite short.
If that sounds interesting to you, you should probably just play it right now. As for my take...
The game was surprisingly jarring, though I don't mean that in a necessarily bad way. You really do feel like you're looking into the personal life of a teenage\young adult girl. I never lived that life, but I think I've come away with a better understanding of what life was like for someone like Nina. The game is separated into acts. The first part of each is browsing files on Nina's desktop. This did feel kind of voyeuristic, especially looking at the kinds of pictures that she'd taken of herself, though other files like poems and blog posts were generally more comfortable to read. There's a lot of text to take in at once. As one who's never been good at following TV and movies, this was a bit difficult, but ultimately rewarding. The real meat of the game is experienced in the sequences taking place within the world of the fictional MMO Valtameri, where you play as Nina's character, Cibele. There isn't a lot to the gameplay and it's thankfully never difficult or confusing, but it really just serves as a backdrop for the in-game voice chat between Nina and her crush, known as "ichi", as well as some live IM feeds. This is where the story plays out. At first, the talk feels kind of bland and stereotypical, but over time Nina and ichi open up and really develop an interesting relationship. It becomes quite an awkward saga, which perfectly fits these characters. Between acts, there are a few short live-action scenes showing what Nina does after each session.
Overall, I found it to be a rather unique experience. It succeeded in telling a very personal story and putting you in the shoes of young Nina. It's well written, well acted, and well paced. It certainly delivers on the themes it promises and comes across as a fairly natural. A great way to spend a couple hours, especially if you enjoy narrative games.
Still, I have some issues, though they're pretty minor. The desktop doesn't quite feel like a real desktop. Everything opens with a single click and you can't drag windows around. I think a couple UI additions could make the game's setting feel more genuine. While the in-game sequences are great, I feel like they could have been more fleshed out. The conversation is often rather superficial, though it's likely that this could be intentional and an accurate depiction of the relationship. The in-game sections can be a tad frustrating due to some questionable pathing, but it never really impedes progress or kills the pacing. The ending is kind of abrupt, but it's also pretty appropriate. Aside from that, I suppose some of the texts feel unnecessary and don't really do much for the overall experience. I guess I just wanted a bit more from the game, though that's not such a bad thing.
I was quite enthralled with Cibele while it lasted. If you're the sort of person who likes artsy, weird, or otherwise non-traditional games, I would whole-heartedly recommend this. For anyone else, I'd urge you to give it a try if you find the subject matter or premise intriguing.

Cibele is a narrative experience about the story of Nina and Blake, two people that met and iniated a relationship through a MMO.
The story is presented from Nina's point of view. You will interact with her computer desktop where you will find many photos, exchanged emails and texts, chat logs and so on. It feels eerily personal and voyeuristic, like you are really looking through another person's life and personal thoughts and situations.
You progress through the story by playing through a MMO game. There isn't much to that game itself, just clicking mobs  and bosses until they die( aahahah, to be fair that does capture what you end up doing in many many mmos).  Nina goes on raids with Blake, while talking to him through voice chat , and that's where their relationship grows. You also can text with some of Nina's friends as well.
As you go on, the desktop will change and will have new texts, new photos , etc, that will reflect Nina's state of mind and relationships. You can see how her herself changes throughout, as well as her friends. The relation ship of Nina and Blake  also develops at a steady pace, starting from some slight flirts to more deep conversations and then even talks of a deeper relationship. The dialog feels quite realistic and natural (well, it ressonated with my awkward teenager years at least) The very personal point of views keeps the plot quite engaging, it really feels like looking into someone else's life, personality and fears.
For people who like narrative experiences like The Begginer's Guide, I definitely recommend it.

This is a story driven game, and so it absolutely crashes and burns when the story doesn't hold up the game at all. The story is incredibly short, but less "short and sweet" and more "well, where's the rest of it?". It understays its welcome, and having such a short story means that the characters are not given time to grow at all.
The relationship between the two main characters is the main focus, but the player isn't shown any of that development. Instead, the two characters talk, one of them delivering extremely creepy dialogue that wouldn't be out of place in a stalker movie, and then there's a time skip, and then another section starts and they're somehow magically closer to each other. The sudden transition from friends to "I love you" is jarring and really poorly paced.
And speaking of which, the sections where most of the story is delivered is in an MMO within the game itself (gameception!). The main problem of this is that this segment is so incredibly poorly programmed. The pathing around is practically broken, which makes the "combat" frustrating when your character gets stuck on a piece of terrain. There's only ONE combat animation per character (and the character with an arm cannon doesn't use it to attack, but rolls up into a ball and glows instead?). This can be forgiven if the story being delivered was decent, but as stated above, it's not. These MMO segments quickly become a chore, since the story won't progress until certain markers are met. The three different MMO segments are basically just palette swaps of each other, and don't hold the player's attention at all.
The game seems to rely entirely on the underwear cutscenes to draw attention and sales. The way it plays out, it seems like the developers wanted to make a short movie rather than a game, but decided a game would sell better. They say it takes 1.5 - 2 hours to complete, but I finished everything in 50 minutes. This game really would have benefitted a lot more from another hour or so of content, with more time to develop the characters. Instead, it immediately jumps out of the gate and falls flat right on its face. "Based on a true story" doesn't excuse the story and characters from being lifeless.
There's no replay value, the story is just boring, the gameplay is frustrating to non-existent. I requested and got a refund. Definitely not worth the launch price of $7.64. Definitely not worth the full price of $8.99. Definitely not worth your time.

Turmoil was released on June 2nd of 2016. The game was developed and published by Dutch indie developer Gamious. Turmoil is a simulation game biased on 19th century oil rush. The game originally released on windows only but has since been ported to OSX and Linux.
The main goal of the game is to become mayor beating out the other 3 oil tycoons of the city. This is done by competing in auctions for parts of the city but you need money for the auctions and this is where the oil comes in.
The main gameplay in turmoil is spent drilling for oil. Each round in turmoil consists of a calendar year where you have to make as much profit on the land. Prior to each round you have to bid on the land that you’ll be using for the year and in later levels you also have to do a stock auction where a percent of the city goes up for sale.
Once you’re out in the fields and drilling there’s really 3 main elements to the game. You have to find oil, drill for that oil, and transport it and sell it. Each element and timing is super important to having a good season. Each round usually starts out with you looking for oil usually by using dowsers who will indicate if there’s an oil patch beneath them. Usually there fairly accurate but sometimes I’ll have one find oil and I just can’t figure out where it is.
Now that you found oil it’s time to setup an oil rig and drill down. Your unable to see what’s in the ground until you drill so you have to guess where you think the oil patch is, usually its directly beneath a dowser. As you play though the game your able to upgrade your ability to look for oil beneath the soil with moles and eventually a scanner.

After your pumping oil you have to ether store it or sell it. If the oil rigs capacity goes over a certain amount the oil will spill and you’ll get a fine at the end of the year. In order to transport the oil, you have to have horses and wagons move it ether to your storage facility or to the right or left company. As the year progresses the value of oil from each company is constantly changing so your goal is to sell the oil when the prices are high and store it when the prices are low in order to maximize your profits.
At the end of each year your taken back to the town where your able upgrade pretty much every element of the oil drilling process. You can increase the maximum number of horses you can and how much they can carry or you can upgrade the pipes your oil rigs use In order to pump oil faster.
Additionally, in town your able to head to the bar and make deals with various people that will affect how the next year’s oil drilling will go. For instance, you can bribe the companies that buy your oil to keep their oil value above a certain level for the year, or you can bribe a city official to have your oil spillage fines waved for the year.
As you progress in the game your taken though 4 areas that each have their own additions to the game’s gameplay. For instance, in the second area the desert you’ll be introduced to rocks under the ground that can’t be drilled though unless you get a certain upgrade. These areas keep the game fresh and also raise the difficulty as you play.
Turmoil is a blast to play, the way the game evolves as you upgrade your gear each year makes the game really satisfying and makes you feel like you’re making real progress from year to year. Looking for hidden oil pockets couldn’t be more fun. The game’s campaign can be beaten in about 2 hours, however the game has a lot of replay value and you can easy lose track of time playing it when your really getting into it.
Graphically turmoil’s minimalist and clean look makes the game look incredible especially on large screens. The games simple graphics make all the colors just pop making the game a delight to look at.
Turmoil’s sound might be the weakest part of this game with most of the soundtrack consisting of a steel string guitar playing old west sounding music but that’s not to say it’s bad. The music does fit the game and is nice and calm when works well with this type of game it’s just very forgettable and not something I’d seek out to listen to.
Overall Turmoil is an extremely solid simulation game that has easy to pick up and play game play that keeps me coming back. The Campaign as you play it really makes you feel like your progressing year by year thanks to the games upgrade system. The gameplay it’s self is a blast with enough things to balance and strategy to the game keeps it extremely engaging and fun to play. Turmoil is without a doubt worth checking out if your into simulation games.

I have played over 500 hrs (or so Steam says; it must include time the compurter is active even though I am not).
The game is okay, but not great. Now that I have occuppied all six territories, I am not sure what would motivate me to play again. There is not much variation in the game; gather resources, update buildings and/or units then go fight a couple of battles, then repeat. The battles are boring, the waiting for some some buildings and upgrades are boring and the battles do not come close to representing medieval warefare.
The game starts out stating that it is 915AD.
The English did not have longbows in the 10th century. The Welsh may have had longbows that early. They certainly did by the time of the Anglo-Norman invasion during the later part of the 11th century. Edward I (kind of England 1272 - 1307is generally regarded as being the one who introduced the use of the longbow into the English forces.
There were no knights in England prior to the Norman invasion in 1066. While the Thegns and Ceorls rode to the battle on horseback, they dismounted to fight.
I have no idea what composite bows are suppose to represent.
Crossbows and longbows have similar ranges and impact (killing power) but longbows have a much higher rate of fire yet in the game, they seem to fire at the same or nearly the same rate.
Longbowmen took years to train while crossbowmen took an half an hour at most to instruct, yet in the game you have to pay real money or spend an eternity to make crafts to acquire a crossbowman, while a longbowman is available immediately.
Javelin men usually only carried two javelins which were expended as a preliminary to a melee charge. Yet in the game, they have an unlimited number of javelins to throw. The effective range of a Javelin was about 20 meters while the effective range of a longbow and crossbow was in excess of 100 meters, yet in the game they have essentially equal range to the archery units.
Spearmen vs mounted knights, this is an absurdity. Until the advent of pikes and halberds, the knights were the kings of the battlefield. Prior to the battle of Sterling Bridge, there was no significant battle in which a knightless force defeated a force with knights. Pikes and halbards were effective against knights but the Pike did not come into common use until the later half of the 13th century and the halberd about 100 years later.
Knights should be extremely expensive and rare and virtually industructable. Longbows and crossbows could bring down a knight, but mostly they brought down their horse and knight was trampled by one of his peers or foes.  It took years to train a knight. They started training at the age of seven as a page. After seven years, the page would become a squire and after another seven years the squire might become a knight. An exceptional squire might become a knight as early as age 18. however, not all pages became squires and not all squires became knights.
So if the game is to be about England and you want knights, longbowman, and pikes, the it need to be set in the middle 13th century, no the 10th centry.

Avencast is a B-list ARPG that actually manages to surpass expectations in some aspects beyond what you'd originally expect.
Starting off rather well, the game attempts to teach you all the different aspects in which this game differentiates itself from other ARPGs. You've got loads of combos to get by the end of the game, and a multi-type dodge system to boot, and that's not to talk about the summoning types, and the two-branch leveling system. All those are very decent except for the part where you need not bother with half those skills as long as you get the other more powerful types, and those are the ones you'll need since the game doesn't go easy on you as you progress through it, with the finale being quite difficult with hordes of enemies jumping on you at a time.
The graphics are, I'll admit, mediocre at best, then again, I never got the appeal of great graphics with a bad game, so the gameplay is what took my focus, and the graphics never really annoyed me seeing as how some of it was atmospheric and aesthetically pleasing at times...rare times.
The soundtrack is repetitve to the point of extreme annoyance by the end of the game since most of it is level based and the tracks repeat over and over considering how long the level is. The SFX is nice though, with great sound effects for all the different spells and monsters to help you differentiate between everything.
The story is the weakest point of the entire game. With bad storytelling, shoddy voiceacting, and a bad script, the game fails greatly in that regard. Hence why I called it B-list.
Overall, I ONLY reccomend Avencast to any serious ARPG addict like myself with a love for gaming masochism and one who feels rewarded by discovering games like this that are seriously diamonds in the rough. Avencast is for those that get what ARPGs are all about and don't mind anything else as long as they get their fix, and it provides the fix well, especially with a surprisingly climactic ending boss fight!

Viking Squad is a solid beat em-up, that I really wish had... more.
To start off with the pros, the fighting is fun. Beating stuff up... is fun and satisfying. So considering this is a beat-em up, that's a major plus.
The art is great, which is always a plus.
There are also some neat bosses, the first boss actually has you having to hide behind things that fall from the cieling to avoid getting hit my a water wave bent on your destruction.
However, the cons were pretty apparant after awhile, and I felt this game has some missed potential.
The most major things, I feel the game is too expensive and short
The game took me and a friend 3 hours to beat.  That was completing every level and counting some deaths. Comparing the game to Castle Crashers which had a lot more play time for a singular playthrough.
This can be oversighted if you just buy the game on sale or if the value proposition is different for you.
But I also feel this game had a lot of missed potential.
For example, at one point during a level there's a merchant who sells a weapon you can buy only on that level, a mid-game merchant is pretty neat! You would think there'd be more... but that's it. That's the only case of a merchant who is in a level rather than the small hub zone. It just makes me wonder why they didn't do more of that. There's also cases where you can carry something to a point to get into a secret level, which is pretty neat! But that also only happens a few times.
Finally, I felt the bosses got progressively worse. I actually found the first boss to be the best boss. The other bosses were just underwhelming, ESPECIALLY the fourth boss. Who took about 20 seconds to beat and was super super simple. The final boss was also very meh.
Basically, if you really want a solid beat em up, but nothing amazing, go ahead and get this. You won't be blown away and it'll likely be a game you finish in one sitting if you're playing with someone.
The game is still fun for sure, and considering how few beat-em ups come out these days I would still reccomend it if you're a fan of the genre.

Well, I downloaded this little gem out of pure curiosity not knowing what to expect. Have to admit, I don't do many Visual Novels. They aren't really "games" in the same since most people think of when hearing the word. If anything, I always think of them as "Interactive Picture Books". Which I don't think if a bad thing, I may not have played many Visual Novels, but I have played enough to where I can say that I know a good one from a bad one. And I've played bad ones. And this... is not one of them. It's a fantastic story actually, that kept me going all the way to the end in one sitting. I didn't stop till the it was over, and it was a very well done V.N. With some very miner grammar mistakes here and there, but to be honest, I don't think there is a single one I've read that didn't have at least a couple grammar errors. They did stick out, but nothing that really pulled me out of the story enough to be much of a bother. The story it's self is far from original, but that's not really a bad thing as long as it's told well. And this one is told very well. Honestly surprised a V.N. that is a free download would be this good. It actually reads more like a science fiction book than the more classic romanticized stories I typically come across when looking at these kind of "games". It's actually pretty refreshing to see one done in this way.
The characters in this V.N. are all pretty colorful people. Maybe a bit stereotypical. but honestly there is nothing wrong with using classic stereotype characters, like the tsundere girl who act's superior to everyone, as long as these characters are used in the right way. And I personally believe they are here. Every character, be the a stereotype or not, fits into their respective role perfectly. Anyone who is a fan of Visual Novels, would probably like this one. I'm not even all that big on these kind of things, but I like it quite a lot. One of the best I've read even. And I wish the creators the best of luck in their efforts to make a sequel, cause I do want to know how the story ends with everyone in the story.
Having said all that, the main issue I think anyone who already knows what to expect from a V.N. is going to have is the reader's ability to direct the flow of the story. Or rather the lack there of. It's kind of an important part of any V.N. to have reader choices that have a large part in controlling where and how events will happen, be they for better or worse. This story, as much as I like it, is a lot more linear than what I would like it to be. However I did read from the makers of this novel's kick starter that they plan to fix this in the next installment of the story, which I would love to read by the way. Giving readers more power over the protagonists actions and building or breaking relationships between your crew members. With that in mind, I do believe that is a worth while effort to support them in their kick starter, and help bring the next chapter to life. Those are my thoughts on this Novel, and my hopes for the next one.

Dungeons of Dredmore is a unique and funny turn based RPG with roguelite elements like permadeath, procedurally generated levels and loot, and a tile based movement system.
Instead of choosing a class to play as, you choose 7 skills out of the over 50 available (much more in the workshop) and each time you gain a level, you can level up one of the skills you chose.  Each level you get to decide if it would be better for you to gain passive or active ability from, for example: Swords, Vampirism, Alchemy, Magical Law, Battle Geology, Perception, or Demonologist.  All of the skills themselves have a real identity, and combining 7 skills gives each character a real uniqueness.  This uniqueness coming from character creation is both why I like randomizing skill selection and why I like to play with permadeath, learning new characters can be as fun as maxing out a long lived one.
Calling the gameplay turn based is accurate but might give the impression that it is slower than it is.  For example you can click any tile on the screen to take as many turns as you need to move there, and fighting monsters using attacks and skills on hotkeys feels natural.  On your turn you can move to a new tile or use a spell or attack, then any visible enemies will take their action before its back to you.
The humor is on point, the core gameplay loop is satisfying, and the customizability is deep.  This is a game you can find yourself getting immersed in and coming back to again and again.

edit REMINDER: YOU HAVE TO NAME THE EXPANSION PACK.
This is easily one of the two greatest roguelikes ever made - the other being Tales of Maj'Eyal - and it will hold a special place in my heart for all time. As you progress through Dredmor's lair, you will be consistently driven to bemusement, bafflement, and BRUTAL PLAYER DEATH in equal measure. And since the player death is so brutal, this game is therefore exceedingly funny and weird. It is one of the funniest games of all time in any genre. Oh, sure, the game's mechanics are perfectly functional and easy to learn, but the presentation - the sheer experience, the horror that creeps into your mind crying, "that did what?! who would think of this? why would they think of this?" - will likely cause a few existential deaths onscreen and off. Existential damage is actually a damage type that some abilities and monsters can inflict.
Seriously, though, pay close attention: most of the sprite animations have few frames... except, for some reason, monster deaths. Sure, you may be a little weirded out by what the monster is, but then you take a moment to really watch it die.
These developers were completely out of their gourds. I once got an achievement for somehow crashing the game, and another for getting killed during the tutorial, and of course one of my very first achievements was for dying on the first level with an identical build twice in a row. Your basic diggle is a small, yellow floppy bird with a rubbery drill instead of a beak, and you can collect achievements for getting killed by each of almost every species of diggle in the game. I will not speak of Thrusty. When you try to quit the game, the Unreal Tournament-esque (?!?!?!) announcer (...?)  will occasionally plead with you in his gravelly voice, saying, "Please don't go. The diggles need you. They look up to you." The same voice that, minutes prior, was yelling "YOU NEED MORE MANA! DRINK MORE BOOZE!" Also, you have to name the expansion pack.
The Steam Workshop content is full of great stuff, too! However, I strongly recommend spending a lot of time with the vanilla+DLC version before installing any mods. Some mods certainly approximate the devs' particular brand of insanity, but even now sometimes I have more fun without using any mods. And, yes, I bought the game when it came out and I still play now and again - and, when I do, it's "one more turn" all night.
And, no, I have never killed Dredmor, that son of a ♥♥♥♥♥.
Dig, dig, diggle.

After visiting Japan, fighting undeads, observing birds and watching anime, you're going to space! Pixel Puzzles: Space is a jigsaw game, based on the universe, planets, astronauts and everything that can go to space.
You have to build pictures by assembling pieces that are floating in space, which is the core of the game. However, now, you can choose any puzzle instead of waiting to unlock them: meaning that you can begin by the 350 pieces one and finish by the easier ones of 60 pieces.
To make your job a little easier, you can use bonus: see the whole picture for a few minutes, rotate the piece or show the right place. But how to unlock them? Floating with the pieces, you'll find parts of a rocket. Put one of them on the bonus you want to use and launch it. However, using the bonus will prevent you to launch a bigger rocket and to unlock the puzzle launch achievement. In other words, if you're an achievement hunter and using bonus in every puzzle, you'll have to do them twice. At least one of them will have to be done that way as achievements for launching the bonus are also included.
While the feature above is the main novelty of the game, with the freedom of choosing any puzzle, I have to speak about the little astronaut bouncing around. He's not annoying (he doesn't speak) but some people are bored to see him - contrary to me that managed to forget him at each puzzle. You can take him and make him bounce from an higher height, until you hear him scream and crash on the ground, dead.
My only little problem is that while trying to place a piece and rotating it too quickly is sending it back to the floating sky. Besides, for the pieces that are doing the outline, they're also often send back to it. While they're placed correctly, you can see them move a little during the process. If you try to place them at that exact place, it's like the game is considering that place as the floating sky. It's annoying after a while as the best way to begin the puzzle is to find a maximum of the outline pieces.
I loved the pictures in it: they're really varied - planets (Earth or not), deep space, astronauts, shuttles launching, satellites, anything that is related to space and that can make a beautiful view. The soundtrack itself is very faithful to the theme.
However, I noticed that on my laptop, the game was lagging a lot while on my desktop, it worked perfectly fine. I don't know why however and I will not try to find the answer as I finished the game on the desktop.
Pixel Puzzles: Space had an hard launch because of the bugs tied to the launch achievements and to puzzles not resetting. However, these are fixed. I waited for that to make a review (and to finish the game). Else I was ready to post a positive review about it.
Pixel Puzzles: Space is easily one of my favorites in the series, with Japan. Developers did a nice job. If you have any patience and loves jigsaw games, you can buy this one without problems. You have 25 nice pictures with the ultimate challenge of not using any bonus (that's the first game where I didn't rely on the bonus, apart for the achievements related to them).

I'm actually writing this review because I am thoroughly impressed with the developers. They had done many bug fixing patches but I encountered one they missed. I asked them to please look into it and see if another patch was needed. That very same day, they released another patch just to fix the issue I had found. So they not only keep track of the discussion board on a regular basis, but they also listen to us and fix things promptly.
I've always enjoyed their jigsaw puzzle games and Space is just as fun as the rest. While you're playing, there are little mechanical cylinders floating all around (in the same floaty space as your puzzle pieces). There are 3 little spacecrafts at the bottom of the screen and you can place a cylinder in one of them to get a hint. Since there are so many cylinders, you can use many hints, if need be. The first little rocket will show you the picture again for a few seconds so you can make a game plan. (hit the letter G to launch it). The second little rocket will show you where in the puzzle the piece you're holding goes - so pick up a piece and hit the space bar. The last little rocket rotates your puzzle piece to the correct angle. So pick up a piece and hit ctrl. (I think I got that right). Also, I believe there is an option to set all the pieces to the correct angle to begin with if you dislike rotating them. So... after you put a cylinder into a little rocket and hit the correct key to gain that hint, the rocket will blast up and off your screen - but will reappear again right away so you can use that hint again.
Now for the fun part. If you don't use a single cylinder for any hints, you can build the BIG rocket, all the way to the left of the screen. It requires every single cylinder to complete - thus why you can't use hints. If you're not planning on using any hints or you find you're almost done with the puzzle and haven't used any cylinders, then build that huge rocket (with each cylinder added, you can see it take shape) and it will blast off when completed. Okay, it's very cool looking but why are we doing this exactly? Because when you finish your puzzle, a shuttle will come down and land perfectly straight - which gives you a "launch puzzle" achievement along with the "complete puzzle" achievement. Two achievements for the price of one. As long as you don't use any hints.
Lastly, if you're feeling morbid and twisted, you can grab onto the spaceman jumping around, drag him all the way to the top of the screen, and drop him. He will splat and you'll have a nice little bloody mess to stare at while you're working away on your puzzle. I did it once to see what it was like but it was just a little too ooky for me. I mean, I was trying to relax with a cool puzzle and nifty space music - so killing the poor spaceman and then getting to stare at my handywork kinda broke the mood I was going for. :p
In closing: This is a very enjoyable jigsaw puzzle game made by developers who care and listen to us. I recommend this game wholeheartedly.

Ok, let's start from the start.
I didn't finish this game. Nor do I have the intention of finishing it. But, I believe it has potential. So I thought I'd give it my 2 cents instead of just forgetting about it.
And there will be spoilers. But really, if you're interested enough to want to avoid spoilers before deciding whether or not you're going to play it, just play it. It's fairly short, and it's not terrible.
This game is a visual novel. A kinectic novel, technically, as there aren't any choises(atleast up to the point at which I played). So all you will do is read and look at images. This vn doesn't have any voice acting, but it's free so that's expected.
When you first open the game, you're given three options.
Play Written in the Sky, suffering through eternal existence and ending all your suffering. I picked Play Written in the Sky. I don't think I'll come back to try the other options.
Then, the next thing I did was open the settings. It's the minimum you'd expect out of a vn, nothing is missing there(except for, maybe, resolution, but you won't need that in a vn).
Then I got into the actual game. Before you start playing, you're presented with a "enable +18 content" prompt, which is interesting given Steam usually doesn't allow any porn into itself.       Anyways, I enabled it because I though "eh, might as well see all that the game has to offer".
Now, how's the game? Not bad, but I wouldn't say it's good either.
The main character is a female angsty teenager named Azure, with an absent father and a dead mother. And the problems start here.
Her father is a detective, so it makes sense that he's absent, but he forces detective training upon her, and that made her not find anything else enjoyable somehow(she doesn't like tv, books, the usual "girly" stuff, videogames, etc) which makes it quite hard to relate to her. Though, you can see why she would be an angsty teen who skips class and♥♥♥♥♥♥ I won't hold that against the writters of this. Though, there's one difference between her and the perceived average angsty teen. She doesn't hate her father(or doesn't appear to, anyways). That could be because he's the only person, so that makes sense.
And then there's her mother. She was shot and killed by someone who held a grudge against her father, and sure up to that point it's all well and good, but once Azure mentions her mother died once she was a toddler she shoves it aside and goes on about something else, as if it meant very little to her, which makes it even harder to relate to her. You could argue that she doesn't remember anything about her mother, but having one of your parents missing in your life should bring anyone alot of pain, even if they didn't meet said parent. You could also argue that she's in denial, but she shouldn't be aware of the reader and her being in denial within her own thoughts without tormenting herself while doing it doesn't sound like something that a person would, or even could do.
Then Azure ends up running into Sienna, an alien that really is just a human that is maybe different but it isn't really explained how so. Azure puts on a ring and then she has to marry Sienna, for reasons. And those reasons are explained pretty well in the game, but I'm too lazy to put all of them here.
Now, Sienna is from Mars, but she's half Martian and half Marsian, and there's a war going on between the two which is part of why she needed to marry someone in the first place. Because she is half martian half marsian, the marriage doesn't need to be between her and a martian, and the do address why pretty well in the game. Aparently the ring was stoled to instigate that war, after it brought peace for some time to the two("alien mating ring stolen by the FBI during an intergalactic peace conference") through political marriages. Now, the motive of starting another war wasn't explained in the portion of the game that I played, but I hope it is afterwards.
Azure accepts throwing her life away to marry with Sienna. Her justification for it is that her life is boring, and sure that's fine, but she completly disregards her father, which is why I'm not sure about whether or not she hates him.
And then they ♥♥♥♥. Now, only god knows how old Sienna is, and Azure is 18 years old, even though she doesn't look like it, so no problem there. Nothing against yuri, I love me some yuri, but it doesn't feel right. It feels like a complete afterthought, completly tacked on and desnecessary.
And that's where I stopped. I'm sorry if loli on ♥♥♥♥♥ monster muffin mashing is your thing, but it just doesn't seem right to me.
There's a quick rundown of the parts of the story I remember and why they work or why they don't.
Now, to the visuals.
They're ok.
The characters are pretty well drawn, and some of the backgrounds are good.
But only some of the backgrounds.
BECAUSE alot of them are half drawn and half 3d.
Now, at first I didn't notice, which means it was working. But then it got to a scene where it only used 3d, and even though it was dark, you could still see it, and it only went downwards from there.
All that said, what could have been done better?
Make her father a businessman who wanted a son to take up on business once he got too old, so he forces his business stuff upon her, even thought she doesn't want anything to do with it. That should make her situation more relatable, although it would lose the uniqueness that the detective thing brings.
Make her mourn her mothers death. That should help with creating more empathy towards her.
Remove the ♥♥♥♥ing. Make Azure younger and keep it innocent. They can still marry, but please no ♥♥♥♥ing.
And please for the love of Christ, don't use 3d backgrounds on a vn, but if you're going to do it anyways, make the background very detailed, with lots of gradients, then put lots of filters on the image to make it not contrast with the characters too much.
Or just take real pictures and put filters on them. Katawa Shoujo did it, and it worked well enough.
But the key here is how it contrasts with the characters. The visuals should be consistent, that creates immersion and makes the overall experience more enjoyable. And mixing 2d drawings with 3d graphics is pretty hard to work out. It's not impossible, and as I said, at times it worked out, but the backgrounds will need alot of work before they fit in with the characters.

I have nearly 500 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.
One Hour Reviews - Game 15
Avencast
Purchase Date: 3/14/2015
I got this game for free thanks to a promotion from Bundle Stars.  I'm grateful I didn't have to pay anything for this, because this means the only thing I wasted was an hour of my life.
I'll start with the few things that I didn't hate about this game.  The graphics were a little dated, but not bad.  Avencast provides some level of customization options which cover the basic configuration options, along with a handful of more advanced options.
The opening of the game begins with a nifty cutscene explaning the story.  I liked the art style used in the opening sequence.  The game explains how you are a young boy with an aptitude for magic, who is raised by an old mage before being sent to the Academy of Avencast to continue his studies.
After the cutscene ends, the game begins inside of a classroom, and it turns out the boy is kind of a dumbass who is sleeping in class and gets scolded at by his teacher before being kicked out of class.  So now I get to explore the academy after the game tells me to pick up a staff and head out.
As I explore I meet a few of the other instructors, whose personalities seem to either be 'bumbling' or '♥♥♥♥♥♥♥'.  I'm quickly piled up with various little quests, mostly involving killing little critters.
The voice acting wasn't terrible, but it wasn't very good either.  But something was really odd in the way the voices were recorded.  It's like the developers were trying to add some kind of echo effect, which I'm guessing was supposed to emulate what a voice would sound like in the halls of a castle.  It just sounded off to me.
I soon was introduced to my first bit of combat.  It's become clear to me very quickly that this game wants to focus on the combat, and not so much the story.  Maybe that comes later.  But for now I am busy fighting imps.  The combat is really basic to start with, and involves 2 things.  The right mouse button shoots purple orbs, until you run out of mana.  The left mouse button swings the staff.  So basically combat strategy involves dodging attacks by double-tapping movement keys, while using either of these 2 types of attacks to take out enemies.
Once you level up, you do get the oppportunity to spend skill points to get new spells.  One annoyance about the level up process is there is no 'commit' after spending your points.  I ended up spending all of my points on attributes before realizing I had to spend these same points to get spells as well.  Unfortunately the points are instantly spent so there's no take-backsies, unless you want to reload the game.
I would have probably found these annoyances a little easier to deal with, except for one problem.  I absolutely hated the control scheme in this game.  If your game has multiple control schemes, and one of them is named "Expert Controls", it most likely means you're doing it wrong.  There was absolutely no need for the controls to be this cumbersome.
You have 3 choices of control schemes, Easy Control, Expert Control, and Follow camera.  I found easy control and follow camera to be fairly similar.  In these modes, the camera stays pinned to your back.  Moving the mouse will then move the camera as your character turns.  But the problem with this control mode is that the mouse pointer stays pinned to the center of the screen.  So if you need to hit the icons on the left of the screen to bring up your inventory, you have to hold down the middle mouse button.
Expert control is even worse.  In this mode, the mouse moves the mouse pointer without the character turning.  To move the camera, the middle mouse button has to be used.  This doesn't sound bad, but in combat, it's very trying to coordinate pointing the camera while trying to independently move your character.  In the end I wished they had just made this a first person game, or looked to some other game for some better ideas on controls.
The best way to sum up Avencast is to imagine taking the world of Harry Potter, then stripping out any trace of it's charm and warmth.  Then add a bunch of uninspired characters giving out boring quests, along with a bunch of combat, a few puzzles, and top that all off with a control scheme that serves as a far bigger villian than the actual bad guys.
Even for free I couldn't recommend this.

I can heartily recommend this game. It has a lot of subtle little things that make it very easy to process the information in the game. For example: the visualization of oil flow / efficiency, how dowsers tell you all the patches have been tapped, how wagons are marked with the colors of left or right inc etc. Most people won't even think about this, but imho it is why the game plays so well.
I am never overwhelmed by information or too much to micromanage.
I have only one minor negative - some of the things you can do in the game are never explicitly explained to you and (at least for me) not everything is self evident from the game play. For example, you are never told that drilling a pipe has a start-cost, so one long pipe is cheaper than several segments totalling the same length. I would prefer new mechanics to be explicitly explained rather than discovered during play (especially since each area only has four 'rounds of play'). I'm halfway area 3, and I still haven't figured out precisely how to use gas to boost prices. And I only know it's possible because a) I saw the dev stream a game where he did it (I just don't recall how precisely) and b) it's mentioned in one of the mayor's tips. But is never simply explained (unless I missed something). I think game rules should not be discovered in a tip envelope.
But that shouldn't be too hard to rectify with a few more screen shots or a brief tutorial. And other than that, awesome game, seriously.
The campaign is fun, and you'll probably play it a few times before you're done. Then you will probably start playing specific levels or even replay them to better your score. You can enter the same seed again and again and you will get the exact same soil composition every time. If you don't like that sort of 'grind', there won't be too much replay value in this game (but I do, so for me there is).

Let's start with the TLDR: This is a decent game, but buy it during a sale.
Avencast starts out light and whimsical (think Harry Potter) but quickly takes on a more Diablo tone. The story goes in a few unexpected directions which was nice, though there are some cliches.
The gameplay is ok, but not amazing. You have the ability to roll away from attacks, but you have to stand still to cast spells. Spells are cast using a combination of WASD and left/right click, which for the most part works. There are a few times you'll mess up the combo (say to avoid an attack) and either cast the wrong spell or use a basic attack instead, but it likely won't mean your death. You can select 8 or so combinations to be visible in the UI so you don't have to memorize them, and you can hotkey 4 spells. There's 3 skill trees to advance in, depending on if you want a more ranged/melee/pet build and you're able to pick from them all.
I highly suggest setting the camera to "follow" mode, as the default mode seems a bit odd. The camera in general is my biggest complaint as you can't change the Y-axis at all, but that's really just an annoyance.
Avencast has a fair amount of puzzles scattered throughout, and you have to pay attention to quest/item text if you want to get past several of them. The bosses are decently designed and have a lot of health, so the big fights will take a while.
The game is relatively short for a RPG - doing all the side quests that I could find put me at under 20 hours. It's not an epic title by any means, but overall Avencast is decent. I got it free during a giveaway, but I'd say it's worth a few dollars - just wait for a sale and pick it up cheap.

My first impression after playing Gigantic for just a few hours:
One of the best f2p games I've played so far.
Pros:
+ Fast-paced "Action MOBA"
+ Beautiful cel shading graphics
+ Gameplay feels very smooth and fluid
+ Nice character design
+ Atmospherical, not too dominant music
+ Haven't seen any hackers so far
Cons:
- Gathering ingame currency takes quite some time
- Only a handful of maps so far
- Some champs feel a bit unbalanced
- No way to report AFKers or other misbehaviour
So, after playing this game for a few hours, I can say that it has many perks of a good full price game. Also, I can understand why the developers didn't want to give up on the game back in 2016. It is a lot of fun to play, and even though it has some minor discomforts, it's definitely worth trying.
First of all, let's talk about its appearance. The game's graphics look kinda minimalistic due to its cel shading optics. At the same time, it is colourful, yet not too colourful. Both of which compliment the very fast and fluid gameplay. When a thousand effects and lights flash on the screen during a teamfight, it's nice to keep the environment down to the simple, yet appealing look. Also, the game's own soundtrack is pleasant to listen to and not too dominant.
At the same time, the teamfights over the game's few objectives can become pretty flashy and chaotic, especially if you play one of the melee characters. But thanks to the very precise and intuitive controls, you never have a feeling of really losing control over your character in battle. In general, fighting in Gigantic feels very smooth and is fun to do, even as a melee.
Now, maybe the term MOBA might suggest the implementation of lanes and creeps to you, but there are none. Well, not directly. The tactical aspect of the game derives from the winning condition of having to wound the enemy guardian three times and, in order to be able to do so, collect enough Power beforehand. This is done mainly by summoning creatures on certain spots, improving them, destroying enemy creatures and, of course, killing enemy players. You don't have to push or freeze minion waves, get last hits on creeps for gold or whatever. You can just summon a useful creep in a strategic spot and concentrate on how and where the next fight will be, which is simple and fun. Also, every character has an individual Talent Tree, which allows the player to choose from different abilities for each of the heroes' skill at each level up. This way, almost every character can be played in completely different ways (you can play The Margrave as full tank, hard smashing DPS, or something in between, for example).
There are actually just a few downsides that I experienced so far in this game.
One of them is that some champs feel just a lot stronger than others (Tripp, Pakko, Beckett...), so it still needs a bit of balancing. Also, there are not too many maps to play on at the moment, namely just three. But that hasn't bothered us too much, since the different team comps and different ways to build your "base" provide enough variety to let each game have the potential to be fun and interesting. The only real "problem" we've experienced so far is the non-existing possibilty to report hackers or AFKers. If someone accepts a match and then just stays afk in base instead of actually playing, there's literally nothing you can do about it. No votekick, no report, nothing. Luckily, the amount of players who happen to do so are not a big problem. You'll find yourself being annoyed about the teammate who won't attack the open wound or defend the spot a lot more often than about an actual afk. But people who don't know how to use the minimap are a problem in any game that has one, I guess.
EDIT: The devs posted an instruction on how to report hackers etc. on the game's Discussion page on Steam, so there's that at least.
On the whole, I'd recommend at least trying Gigantic to anyone who has fun playing 3rd person shooters and/or MOBAs or RPGs. This free to play game does a lot of things right that some full priced titles don't. It's fast, fun and addictive.

Yeah, I only got 2 hours of playtime in this game, but two hours is all yah really need with MOBA's, at least with me, as first impressions are everything. In short, I'm quite impressed!
Pros:
-Game looks REALLY nice. I love the artstyle and overall cartoony vibe.
-Combat is pretty smooth, and since characters have a lot of speed to them, melee characters don't get insta-wrecked by ranged characters.
-The game actually feels like a BATTLE ARENA. Unlike LoL, DOTA, Smite, etc., the main objective is to essentially beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥outta yer enemies till you get enough points for your guardian to mount an attack on the enemy guardian. Doing this three times wins you the match.
-The game is fairly engaging in terms of MOBA combat. It's all action based and in third person, so it doesn't really get boring unless the match drags overlong
Cons:
-Games can end in like, 5 minutes, if yer team is stupid.
-Games can also last stupidly long, because of how the pushes work. It can egg a match on for WAY too long.

Neutral:

Does it look like Castle Crashers? Yes. Does it feel like Castle Crashers? No.
This game offers very similar atmosphere to CC, but after spending few hours of gameplay, I counted 3 major parts that makes Viking Squad different.
1. Viking Squad is LANE-BASED.
In CC you could just run around in circles and it was somewhat difficult to calculate the hit radius. Lane-based mechanics in Viking Squad makes the game more strategic, making it feel close to turn based strategy combat.
2. Levelup progress.
In CC, you could only gain experience pts by constant fighthing. Viking Squad has a bit different system in rank-ups. The stats upgrades are based on the loot which you gather from adventures. The same loot is used in home to buy/unlock everything you've found before.
3. Graphics.
The art comparison is not even close to properly compare. Castle Crashers was first made in 2008 and the graphics are mostly well performed animations. The art is very childish and cartoonic, but can't blame it for its age. Viking Squad is one of those games with moving images. Games with this kind are usually easier to make, but the art quality in VS is insanely high detailed! Clearly a lot of time and effort was spent in the art alone. It still has the same cartoonic 2D look but you don't find many games with high 2D details such as this anymore.

Every character has a different play style in this game and the combat depth is decently deep.  You'll need more than mashing buttons if you're going to make it to the late game.
The gameplay goes as follows.
1) Go through a level bashing as many enemies as possible
2) Survive and bring back treasure/loot to upgrade your character stats, and buy gear
3) Use money to buy potions and keys for treasure chests (any unspent loot is disgarded)
4) Set sail to go through another level
You're given the opportunity to go back to camp with your loot and money at the end of each stage, any unused loot you disgard before your next run.
Controls feel great and 3 players is just enough to keep things chaotic but managable. The game scales with the amount of players you've got.
There's light puzzles in the world that you need to figure out that give you pretty cool rewards.  They're clever but not too hard. Some hidden stuff in the world too, you just have to pay attention and experiment.
Drop in, drop out multiplayer offline and online (Note, you join an online game when they finish a section of a stage).
You only have one revive in multiplayer where your partner needs to get to you before the valkyrie gets you.
There's a new game + that has its own content not accessible in normal mode.
I've primarily been playing it solo by choice and occassionally hop online.

I thought this game was a bit slow at times, a bit too easy at times, and a bit too aribtrary at times. Yet, without a doubt, a few things are certain in my mind: This is a beautiful game with beautiful artwork and an absolutely *beautiful* story. The last thing I thought I would be doing is crying in this game, however I did.
First, this game is inherently intriguing because of its concept: You're in this enormous mansion with devilish servants that kill off guests simultaneously. Everything's multi-threaded. You have the ability to rewind back to the beginning of the day. That's interesting and that is potential.
However, I do admit that it gets a bit drawn out and overwhelming at times. The mansion is, well, humongous. Finishing one portion of the mansion, feeling proud, then unlocking an entirely new and unknown area can be a bit daunting. I didn't often find myself excited to go exploring this new area. Perhaps it's the bleekness that I'm discovering someone dying, or perhaps it's the dauntingness of starting from scratch in a new area where you don't know the rooms, the layouts, and the players nor their movements. However, it's good casual fun with the servants often giving more than enough hints if you stalk them around and listen into their conversations.
The real part that surprised me is the story. I ended the game with the revelation that I really, genuinely, cared about the characters and their past and their story. I loved each and every one of their unique personalities, and above all: I love the main character. The antagonist and protagonist colors this story into a heart-wrenching and truly inspirational message in the end. I truly didn't think I'd leave this game having learned life lessons, but I think I did from this game.
To summarize my opinion: The gameplay is engine revving up for this game: It's unique and quickly gets your attention, yet dries up fairly quickly. The story, however, is the smooth drift onwards. The ending? That's the reward and final destination. It's a beautiful, beautiful ending.

Overal though, it's a witty, fun experience and one I'd highly recommend to anyone who is a fan of the genre.

The Sexy Brutale is an isometric, puzzle/mystery game where you work with a fun time rewind mechanic which lets you relive the events of a 12 hour cycle in order to stop the grotesque murders of the guests of the titular casino. The mystery is intriguing and has a satisfying payoff as you clue yourself about the deadly circumstances afoot. Stopping the murders are fairly simple once you piece things together as you relive the day piecing together clues by following different guests, guards and even ghosts.
The game is fun but lacks polish, especially with the audio design. The music is great(even if there are a lot of jarring cuts to it during gameplay) and the setting is incredibly garrish and lavish and it really sells the experience for me.
There are a few performance hiccups, but this isn't a twitch shooter so it can be excused.
It is a fun 6-7 hours if you can pick it up on a sale.

9.5/10 TLDR: This is a minimalist and highly abstract transport simulator that can be understood in minutes but addicting for hours. Strongly recommended for patient people age 5+ who love observing, analyzing, and optimizing systems.
Pros:
+ game encourages one to search for new solutions as editing anything costs nothing in-game
+ ability to view & save a GIF replay of the current map with all the lines and stations
+ sleek interface helps one concentrate
+ practically infinite replayability
+ nostalgic feeling if one has visited some of the cities
+ suitable for all age groups
+ no learning curve beyond the basic controls
Cons:
- patience required as a new change could take minutes to reflect at the system level in late-game
- control over the spacings between trains of the same line requires micromanagement
- normal timed mode can be stressful
- really easy to lose track of real-world time in endless mode
- some achievements are not sufficiently challenging
- regular price of $10 seems a bit high considering the scope of the game, but this would be a steal during any sale
Tips:
* hold & drag a line segment between stations A-B back to station A to delete that line segment
* think about the frequency of the shapes - use the unique ones as hubs or at least connect them with a dedicated line
* minimize river tunnels to get more capacity upgrades
* in timed mode, drag-and-drop trains from anywhere to temporarily relieve any failing stations
* in endless mode, simply ignore some stations at the edge of the map, esp. if they are 3 or more circles in a row

Cibele is a short affair that has you browsing Nina's desktop over the course of several months. You can read emails, view archived posts from her blog, and look at pictures. This all helps give a sense of the kind of person you're playing as, and I highly recommend exploring the desktop before launching the MMO every time you can. It helps give a sense of what's going on outside of Nina's conversations with her internet boyfriend. Some of it is cute, some of it is a bit sad.
In the MMO, you mostly talk to Ichi while mindlessly clicking away at enemies. The conversations are not terribly romantic considering the subject matter, but the awkward exchanges really ring true to me as someone who is also very introverted and has had an online relationship. There's also other players who will try to chat with you while you talk to Ichi, and you're free to engage or ignore them as you please.
I hesitate to say much more for fear of spoilers. The things you've heard about how this game explores relationships in the digital age, that's all there. There's also a lot of almost cringe-inducingly nostalgic details sprinkled throughout that feel very true to life. I felt feelings with this game.

I recieved this game as a gift from my cousin.
It's a game with a message we've seen many tims before. War is bad. Nevermind the people in the game are essentially sheep, lacking any reedeeming values aside from "fast runner" "good cook" "can barter". It's all about the "feels" for characters that are essentially robots, who need the player to help them come to terms with the reality they find themselves in.
The actual gameplay is little better than a mediocre survivor. Anyone with survival game experience and a good location/character roll is going to do just fine, if not thrive. Despite the game's claim of forcing "hard" decisions, it generally comes down to saying "no" to helping Johny carry his brother home, or deciding whether to steal from the local hospital as opposed to starving to death. I mean, you don't have to steal, you could go to sniper alley and got shot at instead, because, you know, that's what an actual person trying to survive would do. Choices!  The "experience" is going to come down to your mentality as a person, and if you're not a huggy care bear, you probably won't bat an eye when someone in your group dies or you go to rob the old couple down the street (who get along just fine without all thier food by the way). There just isn't that much reason to get invested in anyone, and the characters themselves tend to react very little to thier circumstances.
Ultimately, its the fact that this a game that ruins its message. Games are meant to entertain, and be won, to which morality often takes a back seat. In a game, no one suffers as a result of your actions, and if your characters die you can just reroll. If anything it downplays the whole point of expereinceing the cost of war, and just frustrates people who are tired of the anti-war propaganda.
