I definitely recommend Frosty Kiss to anyone that enjoyed their experiences in Everlasting Summer. Frosty Kiss is filled with small things that make your memories from Everlasting Summer come back; memories of those blissful days in Sovynok when everything was so simple, yet so complicated. And most importantly memories of our journies with these star-crossed strangers that we grew to love (possible pun intended there), and the memorable moments we went through with them as we began to strive less and less to find that cursed bus and more and more to just get them to accept us.
I love all the little references to the events in Sovynok and how the characters have grown as individuals, as well as a group that can share such a great treasure together. The music adds to that atmosphere and offers a laid-back vibe and the tone of every character pleasantly gives the suggestion that there will always be something to look forward to in life.
On a side note, despite going through each route I never unlocked any of the four achievements for the game. And they are all hidden achievements so I don't know what to do to unlock them. Other than that it's a very nice and simple game, certainly fulfilling, with no mazes or Yulya's coincidentally gathering supplies for the winter. (And regrettably no stargazing even though that was always a thing with Lena)

It's free, so why not give it a go? The story is very short and all the choices lead to good endings, which didn't leave me with much of a sense of accomplishment. Also the music is quite bland. You should probably play Everlasting Summer before playing this game. Other than that, it's alright.

"War is Hell" the best way to describe this game. Honestly I don't know where to begin with this one. Every steam review before mines has covered what this game entails in terms of the gameplay design and apporach. And I must say, they were very accurate.
This War of Mine is insipired by real events. You take charge of 4 random survivors each one of them has a story to tell as you try and survive a hellish situtation in a war torn city. You will have to make tough choices in this one that could overall affect your group or affect the people around you. And this game really does a solid job at making you care about the characters you control and the NPCs you interact.
The micro-management system (building stuff, ration out supplies, etc.) makes the game more strategic as well. There are times where you can go without a few days worth of food. But! And eventually, you will have to safeguard your safehouse while sending out someone to gather supplies and start taking really good care of your survivors. Stuff like takes the game to the "Thinking cap" approach. Do you ration out supplies almost everyday? Or do you wait until they become very hungry? Stuff like this will keep players on their toes.
You can also create your own "story" within this war-torn city with selected locations and characters that are either premade, modded, or created by you. The only downside is that you can't create the background. Everything is premade or modded. Which is nice I guess but that would've been a neat thing to see.
Lastly the DLC furthers enhances game as you can now select families or children. Which takes the game to incredible heights that also does a solid job.
I can go on and on with this game. Point is, This War of Mine is a well crafted game that takes players to the morality side of gaming. And it does an excellent job.
Recommend!

Now, plenty of the reviews have already discussed the beautiful, heartbreaking meaning this game holds. "This War of Mine" is a game about the civillians in a wartorn city--the side that CoD never talks about.
But, there are plenty of reviews about the amazing range of emotions this game makes you feel, so I'm going to talk game mechanics for those who care.
The game is seperated into days and nights. Days, where you rest up, eat, and recover from injuries or sickness while upgrading your base with furniture to make it feel more "homey" and tools to help you survive. Nights are where you scavenge for supplies to use during the day. You travel to one location a night and loot all available objects--rubble piles, closets, fridges, the like. Sometimes, a location will have people inhabiting it and you will have to decide whether they are a threat or a non-issue. If they are a threat, you decide whether or not to avoid them and sneak around, or to kill them. Every choice that you make has implications, and that isn't even counting the decisions you make when another civillian ends up on your doorstep.
The game uses point-and-click mechanics effectively. You click on the character you'd like to do a task, you click the task, they're off. It simplifies the actual controls to further shine a spotlight on the emotional toll this game takes on you and your characters. You spend less time learning complicated tutorials, and more time experiencing the game. There's actually no time spent on tutorials, the game throws you right in, and I personally think that's a good thing (though I'm sure others will disagree). I like that you're just thrown in to a game where the people you're trying to guide to safety were also just thrown in to a situation. It puts you on an even playing field from the very start and gives you something in common, though subtle.
After you complete your first playthrough, you gain the option to create your own custom story, with your own custom group of people and map. I like that the game forces you, on your first playthrough, to play in a non-sugar coated, completely unexpected, randomly-generated circumstance. It ensures that your first playthrough will start with confusion, then you learn throug trial and error, then become a hardened survivor (or die in the process). It makes sure that everyone that buys this game experiences the story this game was supposed to tell before letting you mess with it, but still allows customization after.
All in all, I'd say this game is a solid 9. It uses game mechanics masterfully in tandem with the emotionally heavy story this game sets out to tell to draw you in despite the simplicity. I'd say it's a must buy, even when not on sale.

This game is just so immensly fun.
The combat is fluid, fun and skillful; it's centered around a stamina system that you use or pretty much everything; abilities, sprinting, jumping. It creates rythmic battles with a greater tactical depth when combiend with the high time to kill that forces to dip in and out of battle strategically and rewards good game sense.
Every character is unique and has a dinstint playstyle, some of them which are unlike anything I've seen in pretty much any other game (Vadasi, Grismella, Wu or Ksenovia for example.). This is further amplified by the level up system that allows you to upgrade your skills. The thing, it nevefrs just give you upgrade like a couple more damage points but rather completely changes how the abilty works; for exemple by turning a bow into effectively a close range shotgun that slows people. This creates actualy build diversity that gives one character a wde variety of effective playstyles.
The artstyle is godamn gorgeous, which is the most noticeable thing. Every caracter is unique and doesn't fall into cookie-cutter presets. The maps are equally beautiful, the animation work is fluid and expressive and the particle and attack effects are reminiscent of hand-drawn traditional animation.
Buisness model is also excellent, taking a much more generous approach on the Smite type of model. Every character mus be bought, with the option to buy the game outright for 30€ and daily quest; which can be chosen between three randomly chosen ones. The main key differences are that Gigantic character are overall cheaper and that most model-changing skins can be bought for ingame gold.
Its just good all around; my only gripes are that the rocky development of the game as left the releases game a bit unpolished on some non consequencial aspects, but I'm sure this will get fixed soon.

The simplest MOBA ever (yes I know it's a third person shooter but it functions just like a MOBA), even more easy to pick up and play than Smite with no items or mana bar, max level of 10, around 25 heroes, respawn timers of about 17 seconds and matches lasting rarely longer than 20 minutes. You won't fall behind in level or or get snowballed in Gigantic, leveling up is too easy and the game always ends up on equal ground.
The graphics/fps are crisp and smooth and look amazing with bright colours and a cartoony feeling, the hitboxes and projectiles make sense, the maps are just the right size, heroes are varied enough to be interesting and the connection and player base seems ok (this review is about 3 days after release, so only expect it to drop).
The game seems fairly balanced, although some heroes have very small hitboxes due to their size and move very fast making them extremely difficult to hit them without AoE attacks. This is more of an annoyance than a game imbalanace and can be delt with if you use teamwork and play smart.
There is only one gamemode, but it does a good job of being more than 'attack the ancient' or something, requiring timed pushes when the opponents guardian is pinned and vunrable, moving though phases in which the map changes making the game feel very progressive and like a actual story mission with stakes and excitement.
The only irritating aspect is it does not unlock any heroes at all for you to use, relying on a rotation. Like Smite, you must buy them with 'crowns' (don't worry you don't have to spend any real money) Since everyone is in the same boat, rotations means you usually end up playing the same hero over and over as everyone else can only select from five heroes in a team of five (and everyone usually only has access to these rotation heroes). This is probably only a problem to do with the fact this game is so new, later on people will buy different heroes and this problem will fade somewhat.
Oh and like Ubisoft you have to get an entirely new gaming launcher called Arc with its own account and stuff, which is annoying, but not debilitating to any degree.
Some people on Steam discussions talk about connection issues and graphics problems, I live in the UK and use a gtx 520, and have not found any of these problems, but hey it's a free game so if it does not work it's not like it matters.
Overall I am very pleased with Gigantic, it knocks all other MOBA's like Dota 2 and Smite out of the park (I have not played LoL but why would I want to) just because it's easier, more fun, and more enjoyable than the cesspool of inhuman psychopaths on those other games which ruin everything.

A quite short, but extremely well done game that struggles to have a specific genre. It's mystery, but not really as the killers all wear the same masks, it's an adventure, but not exceptionally, as the mechanics are light, I guess the best classification I can give it is a story-heavy adventure / puzzler hybrid.
The story takes place in a small mansion over 12 in-game hours (which play out in 5-10 minutes total) as a series of guests meet their deaths at the hands of the hosts and you search to find out what's causing their deaths and how to prevent it. Fail, and the day repeats, succeed and you get another ability, unlocking new options and more of the mansion (along with more guests to save).
The mechanics are very simple: Look at objects of interest in the environment, pick up rare items of note (typically used to prevent a murder), and spy and listen to activity in nearby rooms - an ability that is critically important since you are unable to occupy the same room as a guest or a host (which is, frankly, a little distratcting and unnecessary - they could have had the same effect if you were simply a ghost that none of the characters noticed).
I beat the core game in under 4 hours, but I didn't mind too much. If you like, you can use your end-of-game abilities to scour the mansion to get a good understanding of where each guest and host is at any point in time (a feature also present in the very well done map screen) and collect a few collectables (which do change the ending if you get 100% of them).
The overall story turned out to be surprisingly strong and integrated well with the gameplay (no luddo-narrative dissonance here). While I would have preferred to not need to hide, it did add a certain aspect to the game. My other gripe that the game isn't really a mystery since you know the hosts are killing the guests was also something that served the end of the story as well.
The music and art style are spot on and really shine. While these are both repetitive, they add so much to the game and give it its unique character.
Overall, I recommend this game, but it's likely to be so short of a playthrough that you should probably wait for a sale.

I never played the Total War games so I don't have to contend with the usual "I love this franchaise, lets watch it get disemboweled", but having played this game I would like to play more TW games. This game is almost the usual free to play fare in that you have a city to build and it has timers. If you have played
free to play game then you know the deal.
What I like about TWB:K is that, get this, you don't recruit peasants and then turn them into soldiers! You build a barracks and BAM you get troops. Troops also don't die?! Is this even a free-to-play game!? Instead they go on a cooldown/respawn timer.
This means you can fight and fight as much as you want. Yes you read that correctly, no stamina system! This game does so many things right compared to its competitors thats its almost a full fledged game in its own right. If the town didn't have cooldown timers for building things, you would be forgiven for thinking it was a full free game like Relic Hunters.
The downvotes and negative reviews this game has do make sense however because had this game been called, Flower Patch Kingdoms it would probably have had a lot of good reviews, but as it stands, it is not a Total War game in almost any sense of the word so for people who play Total War games you really want to avoid this game.
For everyone else, this game is fun, I recommend it. With, however, a huge 'Cavet Emptor'.
This game is balanced, very balanced infact oddly too balanced infact. You can't pay for an advantage, which I like, always a fan of that but what makes this game so 'oddly balanced' is that each troop has about 3 counters to it so their is no 'best unit'. This is fine for PvP and tough skirmishes, but when you are grinding mooks for resources you can't take a break and just hammer out fights for resources.
Every fight demands your full attention because one wrong move, wrong match up, wrong ability used at the wrong time, failure to charge, you get the idea. The battles are
so grinding in itself becomes something you need to mentally take a break from. A real life stamina system as it were.
That doesn't mean the game is bad, but who is the target audience? People like me who are new to TW? Or casual gamers, whom this free2play market is usually targetted at?
If you ever wanted to get into the Total War series then this is the game for you. If you are a casual gamer, give it a try as it costs you nothing anyway and you might enjoy it. If you are a Total War veteran, download it so you can downvote it

However, upon conquering the area to my north a river suddenly appears out of nowhere and floods my original area, wiping out my roads, farms and mines.  I built dams at the source only to have them break several hours later, once again putting the entire region under water.
The wait times in this game are ridiculous.   Build a farm and it could take several days before you see any food source appear from said farm.  Build a woodcutter and it will take several days for the land to turn to dirt, for your workers to plant trees and then several more days for the trees to grow so you can chop them down for a meager reward only to repeat the cycle over and over and over.
Armies are small compared to other games in the total war series, yet you always seem to face an army that is twice as large as your own.  Your army to limited in size and if you choose to train the wrong type of soldier you're pretty much SOL until you're able to upgrade your baraccks.  However, upgrading is so tedious it'll take days, if not weeks, to get said upgrade.
If you're a glutton for punishment and love "paying to win" then this is the game for you.

Needless to say, I am disappointed.
As my enraptured fanbase knows so well, I liked Everlasting Summer a lot. It was the first actually good interactive novel I had played- which isn't actually saying much- and when I found out there was even more Everlasting Summer to uncover, I nearly p***ed myself.
Needless to say, I was disappointed.
The game serves as an ending for the players out there who wanted a bit more romance when they got the "Harem" at the very-very-VERY end of the game. I was fine with it. It wasn't a perfect ending, but I didn't need to a kiss with a girl of my choice to make me feel fulfilled. But the game is short- damn short- about fifteen minutes for me to get my first ending.
And that wouldn't be bad if the game were actually... interesting.
My biggest problems in Frosty Kiss come from the obvious lack of refinement since Everlasting Summer. Yes, it's a new team, but the text boxes are improperly shaped for their text, there's tons of grammatical errors, and the menu and choice system are absolute garbage.
The main menu, from what I've played, is inaccessible until you get to the end. You can skip with Ctrl, but you can't change any settings or load a game (but you can save a game), until you get to the end of whatever choice you made. Why? That is so stupid.
And a lot of times I might have misclicked or something, but some decisions seemed to opt me in one direction but take me in another. For one, I thought that if I dropped the firecrackers out the windows, I'd be pursuing Ulyana. No, I have to do that if I want to pursue Miku or Slavya or Lena. And in the kitchen if you look at Lena, you pursue Slavya... but if you look at Slavya, you pursue Lena. What kind of logic is that in a choice?
The endings are all very samey. Talk to X for a few lines, get a final kiss, get the "Frosty Kiss" logo. Roll credits. But, for some reason, Slavya (my personal favorite of the girls) got me the sh**tiest ending! There was a kiss, but I ended up getting crowded by the other four girls. Very intimate, touching scene there.
Frosty Kiss is there if you liked Everlasting Summer and wanted more time to flirt with the girl of your choice. Beyond that, I don't really see any substantial value for it. I personally think Everlasting Summer was nice and contained. It wasn't perfect, but everything fit in together in the end. But this is like a floppy attempt to end a specific ending of a game that was pretty okay by itself. I preferred the "Yulya" ending, anyway... well, kinda.
"Frosty Kiss" kinda sucks, but it's not wholly flawed. It's still well-drawn, the music isn't god-awful, and the dialogue is pretty meh. It gets a 5/10.

Finally a MOBA that truly hits gold in just the right areas. Gigantic is an addictive game, and here are my reasons:
Pros:
- Fluid combat which is rewarded by skills and tactics. The stamina system keeps you in check, if you just run around during combat like a maniac, you will run out of steam and you will be punished.
- Wonderful artstyle. It has that Wind Waker style rendering to the characters and they have their own charm.
- Unique and varied champions. Each has their own playstyle, so there's quite a bit of mastering with each of them.
- The gamemode is a wonderful twist to the usual MOBA one. Creatures replace the lanes and minions you would usually expect. There's never a shortage of action in the map.
- It has a lot of potential for a potential professional scene.
CONS:
- First of all, the arc launcher. Personally it doesn't bother me too much, but it would always be nicer if you could run it directly through steam.
- Still some bugs to be spotted somewhere, sometimes during victory screen your character is clipping halfway through the ground.
Overall, I recommend you pick this game up, and I hope it gets more recognition.

One of the first games I've ever bought on Steam and to this day still one of my favorites. Why? The replay value, I never get tired of playing this one. There are several options you can tweak to alter your play style, the levels are all randomly generated, plus you can choose from a long list of "professions" to change your abilities/spells with each new try you make at beating the final floor. (or at least getting farther than you got last time)
Depending on what you pick from the profession list, you can spend your time crafting plenty of neat things to help you hack and slash your way through the dungeon. Engineering is one of my favorites to have, (making bombs, chainsaws and armor that lets me survive being struck by lightning is always a plus). But there's much more to pick from than that, which always gives you something new to try each time you play. Want to make a Thief that knows Blacksmithing and can teleport? You can do that. How about a Pirate that makes acid potions you can throw on crowds of monsters but can also summon minnions to fight for you at will. Yeah, you can do that too. There are so many combinations to choose from, it keeps the game interesting for a really long time.
So yes, I recommend this game. Not just for the all the movie and game references you can find on a lot of the items or all the random jibberish the monsters will say to you, but for the sheer amount of fun I have had wandering around the dungeon looking for treasure..and usually finding a Monster Zoo..(that's an entire room FILLED with monsters..yeah.)

As someone who has played the original Rogue, as well as Moria, Angband various -Band variants like Zangband and Gumband, Pernband and Cthband, and then later games like ADOM and TOME, I have a real love for this line of gameage.  Dungeons of Dredmor is a light hearted comedic take, that is very easy to get into, and has a lot of options.  But it lacks the depth of some of those other games too.  That's fine.  It's a $5 dollar game that's more than worth the price of admission.
There's nothing in teh game that's not pushed to a humorous level.  Take the stats for example.  Gone are stats like Strength and Intelligence.  Instead we have Burliness and Caddishness.  And that's fine.  It's a fun send up of the entire RPG concept.  But I stil have to do a mental translation each time I read a name a few hours into the game.  And the jokes wear old.  There are only so many evil potatoes you can kill before the joke starts to wear a little thin.
Now I do love that you aren't locked into classes.  Choose your skills!  For my first character, who died pretty quickly, I grabbed a melee attack, missile attack, armor, shield, psionics, paranormal investigator, and perception. It's more flexible that a lot of the true roguelikes.
And make no mistake.  DoD is a true roguelike.  Many games call themselves roguelike but are't.  They might evoke one or more aspects, like permadeath, of the Rogue games, but not DoD or similar games out there.  Nope.  This is a pure Rogue descendant.
And there is a lot of versatility under the hood.

I have a soft spot for roguelites, even though I'm (generally speaking) absolutely SHÏTE at them. But they're usually a whole lotta fun. Charging into a horde of enemies, battle-axe in hand, loincloth flapping in the wind, and then getting stomped into monster sandwich spread because what kind of a fûckin' retärd doesn't wear PROPER armour when they're out savaging monsters?!
But I digress. Dungeons of Dredmor then. I like it. I won't go so far as to say that I love it, but I will just spoil this review right now and tell you: YES, I WILL RECOMMEND THIS FÛCKING SHÏT, BECAUSE IT'S A REALLY GOOD GAME.
I feel like I basically cut myself short just now, seeing as how I don't have all THAT much to talk 'bout when it comes to ol' DoD. I mean, the humour in it is nicely silly, without being overly dumb. And I do like that it's not pitching a tent in either the Bulletstorm cesspit or the Duke Nukem Forever leper colony, but the much less unappealing Monty Python-esque silly nonsense, uhh... fish factory. I dunno. I was struggling to come up with something, so I just wrote the first thing that came to mind.
Anyway! Moving on. I like that pretty much every single skill in the game is at least somewhat unique, and that they all have some measure of usefulness, even though some are pretty damn overpowered (lookin' at you, Perception (yes, that was a pun, get over it)) while some are... well... less useful (*coughs* veganism *coughs*). But anyway. The ability to mix 'n' match skills 'til your boxers squeal (because the expression "till your hearts contents" makes no göddämn fûcking sense!), so you'll have plenty of replay value.
The gameplay itself is nicely straight-forward. You typically walk around with WASD, you see an enemy, approach them, and then either bump up against 'em or click on 'em to attack. Not exactly rocket surgery, ehh? But the fact that the game is, how should I say... "step-based", I guess? Well, whatever you'd call it, it's the only hybridization of real-time and turn-based I've ever seen that actually works really well.
Those of you who've played Fatal Labyrinth on the SEGA Genesis know what I mean. To clarify, enemies can only move, attack, and do other stuff at the same time as you do, but you don't take traditional turns attacking each other. So when you attack an enemy, they'll attack you back. This makes it so that you'll ALWAYS have time to think about what to do next, but the pacing of the game doesn't necessarily suffer for it, unlike in games like Heroes of Might & Magic or XCOM.
The graphics are fairly simple and low-key, just to change the topic com-fûcking-pletely, but they have a nicely stylistic charm to them. Most pixel games generally just go for the 8-bit style out of sheer laziness, but DoD seems to take the same road as Stardew Valley or Shovel Knight, and instead have a pixelated style with plenty of details and actually nice colour palettes. Which I obviously like.
And now I'm reaching dangerously close to the final point regarding DoD: if it's such a solid game, why do I not like it more? Well, I will warn you right now that it's insanely fûcking grindtastic, and unless you play with the Smaller Floors option on, you'll be doing a fûcking retärded amount-a walking around in the game. There's also the fact that even though almost all skills are in some way useful, there are builds that WILL inevitably break the game, even on the hardest difficulty, and basically turn you into an all-powerful mega-god.
But I have to admit, DoD does a lotta things really, really, REALLY well, and since my only complaints with it are minor nuisances at most, I really can't give it that low of a grading. It's also worth noting that Dungeons of Dredmor (unlike nearly every single roguelite out there) does actually let you play on a fairly softcore difficulty level, and while I personally wish there were more options to customize the "hardness" of the game, this does make it so that even less skilled players can play it. So that's definitely a big plus.
All in all, DoD has a lotta solid points, and while it's a bit rough around the edges, it's still got a lot of charm to it, and it's definitely worth buying, even if you're normally not a huge fan of roguelite games. 8.9/10

This is a game that could have been much more than it was. I have not beaten the game but I've played enough of it to know where it's going and how I'll get there.
Avencast is an ARPG which tries to break up the right and left click ad infinitum by giving you smal lcombos to do with your spells as well as letting you put them on the function keys. for example pressing right then left, then right click performs a wide AOE blast spell if you've learned it, down then up and right click is a penetrating line shot, etc etc. Left click spells tend to be melee, right click spells ranged. Unfortuntately, for a game that focuses entiirely on magic, that's about as innovative as the magic gets. Only one of the spells I played with felt particularly "impressive" to land, though most all of them look fairly pretty. There are only 2 and a half trees of magic: One melee, primarily fire and poison based, one ranged, primarily ice and "soul" (read: "purple magic") based, and a final one based aorund summoning, but there's no real build to be done in summoning, you just pick the creatures that correspond to whether or not you're a Blood/Melee or Soul/Ranged mage.
Spells are unfortunately rather boring. On the melee side you have... horizontal swipes, AOE bashes, and a few buffs. that's about it. The higher spells in the tree simply augment the lower ones to do more damage/slightly bigger AOE/etc. The ranged tree has a freezing spell that does do damage, but hits so few creatures you're better off nuking. There's also an AOE wave attack that tends to be your bread and butter spam, and a few single target spells that are hard to use due to the AI beuing pretty good at dodging. So mostly you end up spamming the wave attack over and over. Again, for a game that prided itself on being a mage, the magic feels very underwhelming, though flashy to look at.
Combat is fast paced and full of projectiles and rushing enemies. There is no invincibility frames when being hit so a crowd of enemies can overhwelm you. Luckily the game makes you very mobile, with sidesteps and dodge rolls. Stick and move is the name of the game even as a melee mage. Despite the complaints above, the comat is actually fairly engaging. There aren't a lot of enemy types, but they are thrown at you in enough varied ways to where you need to actually pay attention. Bosses generally have a gimmic kthat needs to be overcome to kill them.
Another issue is the levelling system. The level up points you get have to be split between both 4 stats (functionally, you will want 3, as there's no reason to mix being melee or ranged, but no matter whta you are, you'll need lots of health and mana.) and learning all your spells. This often means levelling your stats feels like playing catchup to even out disparities than it does you actually getting stronger. The game is not overly difficult and levels come fairly quickly, but with no real sense of 'strength' gain outside of the first time i successfully nailed someone with Meteor of Might, it falls a bit flat again.
The story is not impressive. But let's be honest: Story is not the high point of an ARPG. Every dialog is voice acted, and to its credit, the voice acting is not terrible. The script? Not so great. But the voice acting itself is decent. Quests are your basic fetch quest variety, with a few puzzles thrown into the mix to keep you on your toes. Nothing too intense or brain burning but enough to break it up here and there. Reading is necessary. Don't expect a game thta will send you on a long magical journey, because for the most part, you will be looking at Avencast Academy for the entire game. Reminds me a bit of Dumbledore's Army and Harry Potter in a way.
All in all, I got the game on the cheap and got my money's worth. I'll probably end up beating it. It won't end up high on my recommendation list, but if you enjoy ARPGs, you'll probably enjoy this since you'll like the twitchy spammy combat, even if the levelling itself feels a bit underwhelming. If you don't enjoy ARPGs and prefer your games a bit more cerebral or involved, give this a pass. It's no Diablo or Path of Exile or even Torchlight, but it tries, and you can tell. I just wish they'd have gone the extra mile.

Hello steam subscribers I am here to write a review for this game. Before I get into the fighting♥♥♥♥♥♥spirit with this review I should tell you I am a long time Total War player and started with Shogun 1 when my balls first dropped and have played everything after that and enjoyed them thoroughly (although some more than others). Since the series has been around so long players have come to expect a certain type of game when they see the total war logo with the tiny samurai horseman logo next to the letter, you know the one I'm talking aboot ;)
WHAT IS DIFFERENT?
This game for all intents and purposes is NOT a total war game, there is no turn based campaign map instead it is real time much like a command&conquer where buildings need time to finish contructing. While there are real time tactical battles, the open ended and diverse battle maps known from the other total war titles are gone as well. This means there are no terrain advantages or disadvantages (at least I have found) during battles and the battlefield is made up of 3 lanes.
+WHAT IS BATTLE?+
Each lane has 3 slots for units, and I will illustrate how you may distribute your units among these slots by making a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ diagram with text and little symbols here
front<- [ Infantry, Cavalry, and Ranged ] [ Infantry, Cavalry, and Ranged ] [ Infantry, Cavalry, Ranged, and Siege Weapon ]
front<- [ Infantry, Cavalry, and Ranged ] [ Infantry, Cavalry, and Ranged ] [ Siege Weapon ]
front<- [ Infantry, Cavalry, and Ranged ] [ Infantry, Cavalry, and Ranged ] [ Infantry, Cavalry, Ranged, and Siege Weapon ]
As you can maybe see there is SOME depth to battles, but the meat of battles and how they are decided is military orders and unit abilities and the traditional rock paper scissors gameplay of other TW tittles. And yes, I spelled titles that way on purpose. After your units gain enough experience they can unlock special abilities with a variety of effects depending ont he unit type. Each unti has 2 choices for ability. Military orders are like general abilities but you are able to use them throughout the whole battle but they have a timer cooldown between each use, unliek unit abilities which can only be used once. So troop choice is extremely important in battles and the right combination of orders and abilities.
+WHAT IS CAMPAIGN?+
The campaign map is layed out before you like a giant deep dish pizza pie on hexagonal tiles. You can build buildings, gather the resources which are silver, stone, food, and wood *INSERT STRONGHOLD "Wood Needed" VOICE CLIP HERE*. I'm pretty sick of writing this review already so I'm going to wrap it up with the big important thign about this game.
+WHAT IS LOVE?+
This game screams IPHONE WINDOWS TABLET TIME SINK. And like most other tablet time sink the pace of this game  is extremely slowwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww

Summary: The Sexy Brutale is a time loop game. You are to prevent the deaths of several characters.  This is done by witnesses their movements, their actions, and learning what items and timing you need to preven their deaths.
Two great things about this game:
1.) There's really no penalty for mistakes.  Just rewind time!  This makes the game a very calm and engaging experience.  The controls are fairly easy.
2.) This is an easy game.  The puzzles and tricks weren't that difficult. There were just a few moments where you just try something and lo and behold it works!  if not, just rewind time and try again.
Two bad things about this game:
1.) It's a short game.  It feels like it should be longer.  Especially when I'm enjoying the art and the ambiance.
2.) In the game you prevent each death.  All throughout this game I thought, "OMG, this is gonna be so cool... I'll have to do the entire day and prevent all deaths within one day!"  As I played the game, I made exhaustive notes on how to move between locations, plan out which deaths happen and the best order in which to prevent them, and was excited to have figured it all out.  The biggest disappointment is that the game developers did not think this was the coolest thing evah!  Which if they did let you do that, it would have made this game one of the most amazing games I ever played.  Instead, it was just, "Meh.  It was good.  Short, pretty, but I'll probably have forgotten it because I didn't spend more than two days playing it."
All in all, if you like time loop games, low stress, easy functionality, a small time investment and a bit of story, this is a great game. You won't regret it.
If you prefer something more challenging, faster paced, clever in its puzzle making, and epic endings, you can give this one a pass.

I am so torn about this game.  It's woth a play, but it seems very... limited.  While interesting it just seems some elements are broken.  Not they don't work, but they are not really featured. Some of the core is broken too imo.  If you are in a room with ANYBODY else, it's supposed to be a bad thing and you need to get out of there.  However, I found myself perfering going through a room when somebdoy was there becasue while you are in the same room as them, time stops; gives you that advantage of saving time while manurving thought the mansion.  The penealty is very... amost non-exsistant.
The puzzles aren't hard, but they aren't easy.  Maybe simple?  Generally consisting of one found item to be used in one item that requires an item.

I mean, even Hitman games have a similar vibe as the day repeats everytime you "try again" but Hitman games require a lot more peices and planning.  Like I said, this game is simple. Quick review:
Pros:
-Varied builds
-Lots of loot
-Very good music
-Good graphics
-Standard hard rogue difficulty curve
-Cute mechanics like monster horde rooms
Cons:
-Very repetitive, imagine a single player only diablo
-Catastrophically bad inventory management
-Grindy as heck, even on the no grind game option (lol)
-Not very well balanced
-Surprisngly simple for a rogue game
Details:
Possibly the worst part of the game is the inventory management.  This sounds like a weird gripe, and I've played lots of games with terrible inventory management and just dealt with it, but this is definitely the worst inventory management in a game I've ever seen.  Basically you've got somewhere on the order of 1000 different item types in the game, and all can be used to craft stuff, but you can only hold onto 60ish items at a time.  Sure you have a dimensional stash that you can visit any time, but with that many item types, you'll be visiting it every 3 minutes.
Even choosing a no-crafting skills build, which seems to be the only option, its still surprisingly annoying to deal with given you need food and booze of which there's like 100 types.  So then it comes down to choosing builds that don't craft and use vampirism (no food), and don't use throwing or crossbows,  just to play the game without going insane.
Next up is the repetitiveness.  Most roguelikes have unique enemies with interesting abilities, enviromental hazards, and their own brew of general randomness to spice things up.  This game is mostly just stacking on various resistances and bonuses and dealing with your enemy's resistances and bonuses.  You look at the forums, and most build discussion is even just about choosing builds that let you stack certain stats.  This kind of munchkinery is super fun for about 15 hours or so, but it gets old really quick.  When you combine this with the fact that a floor takes about an hour (half an hour on "no grind" lol) and there's fifteen floors, and you're mostly just spamming the left mouse button, I think a lot of people will just get bored.  Even with the builds that implement some form of strategy, it's going to be the exact same strategy for any situation.
There's some major balance concerns as well, although since it's single player, you can just opt out of using the overpowered crap or choose random builds.

Dungeons of Dredmor is a rather silly rogue-like with its odd sense of humour, but one with an extreme amount of depth to it. In many ways it is extremely simple to play, with a variety of skills to choose and customize your character with, crafting of various types of items ranging from weapons to armor to consumables, and a huge roster of different enemies to fight.
Essentially the game is played by traveling room by room. There are multiple stairways which are used to changed levels, and there are also a plethora of different interactable environmental items, and you also have your personal pocket dimension which you can use to store loot.
Primarily what is really good about this game is that it is beginner friendly. While experienced players can also find enjoyment from playing Dungeons of Dredmor, one who has never really experienced what Rogue-like games has to offer will likely be the targeted audience of this game.
While other Traditional Rogue-likes will generally be more about attracted players who have already played Rogue-likes, it is rather unique to see a game like Dungeons of Dredmor which seeks to attract players from outside of it.
Hats off to this game for that!

The basics first – Rising Angels: Reborn is an anime-style visual novel. It doesn't have any gameplay as such; it tells a story through dialogues and lets you make decisions about its direction at various points, which will give you different endings. The graphics are more or less entirely still images. Backgrounds are well done, even if there aren't very many of them, so they can get a little repetitive. The character images are good as well, even though the character *designs* are very stereotypical - basically just humanoid feline alien, humanoid canine alien, angel alien, demon alien, etc. Not very creative.
So, "Do you recommend this game?", Steam asks. I really wanted to like this game, and I kind of do, but at the same time...
A VN stands or falls by its story and characters – that's basically all there is, so it has to be good. And my issue with RA:R is that the main characters are just incredibly unprofessional and emotionally unstable. The protagonist, who is some sort of military special investigator, repeatedly overlooks or fails to follow up on obvious clues and inconsistencies. The ship's executive officer keeps droning on about teamwork and regulations, yet he's also a blatant racist who continually denigrates the other members of the (predominantly non-human) crew. The navigator is a sheer megalomaniac. The ship's doctor is incompetent. No one seems able to follow a straight order and several characters are just downright corrupt or insubordinate. And even in obvious crisis situations, almost all of them keep getting sidetracked by emotional angst or just plain chatter.
The story is actually quite touching and deals with some interesting ethical and emotional issues, but it would be a lot better if it was more mature and didn't rely so much on "holding the idiot ball" (as TvTropes calls it). Even allowing for some anime "over the top"-ness, I just can't believe these people are the highly-trained officers they're supposed to be. It feels more like a secondary school class than a military crew.
But even after all that, and after literally shouting at the screen more than once when the characters did something stupid… it still did manage to hold my interest for over two hours, and by the end I was genuinely engaged in the protagonist and the choices and sacrifices she had to make.
"Do you recommend this game?" Yeah, I mean, I suppose so? I think it's a bit of a flawed gem. (Not a diamond or a ruby. Maybe a garnet or jade.) It's free and can be completed in a couple of hours, so you might as well take a look at it and see if you like it. I'll probably play it again to see a few of the other endings.

I don't normally write reviews, so bear with me.  I've only just begun playing and did a quick little run through, almost purposely losing towards the end for the sake of seeing what happens and to open the opportunity of trying it all again with more knowledge.
This game builds an atmosphere that most survival games simply can't.  This is a story that you can control as opposed to just surviving a plotline.  Half RPG, half (incredibly dark) survival game.
From what I've seen, there's plenty to do and explore.  The game has a bit of repetitiveness, but I feel that it's almost intended.  It's a sense of progress and shows the general grind to stay alive, similar to "Papers Please".  Nothing feels clunky about it and it runs very well.  The systems at play (Trading, looting, fighting) all come in different shapes ad sizes and are balanced well.  Every move you make matters, and you'll get that "What have I done" / sinking feeling when you made a mistake.  I've never felt bad for letting a character die in a video game before.
The only con I can think of for this title is that I was supposed to go out to eat with my girlfriend tonight. Not happening.
If you're on the edge about this, and it's on sale, you are straight silly to not pick it up!  I'd pay full price for it in a heartbeat.

War. But it's not the war you're used to see. You don't see the soldier glorified. You don't get to shoot the enemies. It's the civilian aspect of the war.
The game reminded me a bit of Don't Starve, it's technically 2D survival but with a hint of 3D. You get to select your characters, build your own base, try to defend your place from raiders aswell as loot, scavenge and upgrade your stuff. You beging with essentially nothing, and you need to scavenge in order to find loot. But it isn't that easy as you thought - you have a limited amount of space in your backpack, and have to choose if you're going to take materials or food. But you have to choose carefully, you'll always need something!
This War of Mine is visually appealing, with a dark vibe and sad but calm music. It helps muild an atmospthere of tradegy and pain, what the civilians feel and how they are during war time. The houses are cut in half in a 2D-like doll house style, but moving the camera around reveals it has an aspect of 3D in it, not much, but enough to make it unique in my eyes. The soldiers are portrayed as horrible who the people do not trust when they don't know who they fight for anymore.
How well the game runs; as far as I know, only problem I had was when I installed a workshop mod, but otherwise it runs smooth, constant 60fps or more, doesn't feel like it takes up much juice at all and I can easily multitask or play some other game at the same time. Computer includes 8GB ram, nvidia GTX 980 and an intel i5-4430 so it should be powerful enough to run whatever game too.
Overall the game is hard, but it's definitely worth the praise. Would recommend.

I purchased this game on a whim because, until Steam showed me a sale banner for it, somehow I'd never heard of it. Greatest decision I've made in a while.
It's a bit of a cliche to say that you wish you could forget a piece of media so you can relive it for the first time again, and while it's always been a relatable sentiment, I've never truly, *truly* lamented the fact that a fresh runthrough is over until this game. Which isn't to say that completing it leaves no room for replay - in fact, to see all of the dialog in the game you'd probably have to do quite a bit of running around and traveling through time over and over.
The puzzles are unique and inspired, but none so difficult that they become frustrating. Even collecting all 52 cards for completion's sake was something I was able to do with just some time and patience, rather than needing a walkthrough or hint like I was prepared for.
My recommendation? Play with a friend or two. Whether they're at your side or watching through a stream, I feel like this is a game that truly benefits from having a second set of eyes (and thoughts) to point out not just possible solutions but tiny details of story and design that deserves to be noticed.

This one is tricky. Not that Sexy Brutale is not a good game, but it's also rather short and expensive for that and has some gameplay and technical issues. So, ultimately you have to decide if about 5 hours are worth 20 bucks to you.
What is TSB? It's a kind of murder solving puzzle game with a time rewind feature. Your task is to save the guests in the mansion, one by one. To do so you'll have to stalk their movements, listen to their monologues/dialogues and find out how/why they die and who the murderer is. These murderers are the household staff, which you can of course also stalk and eavesdrop on. With every piece of information you can in theory get closer to preventing their deaths, as every movement and every room you have explored is cartographed in a map that can be manipulated to show where a certain character will be at a certain time. Once you have enough information, or they have died or your 12 hour day is simply up, you can just restart the day from the beginning and try again. After you have successfully saved a gues you get a new special ability that will be necessary to save the next one. Make no mistake, the game is absolutely linear as far as I know. You can't just go everywhere, because paths will be blocked and guest can't be saved without certain abilities (like talking to ghosts).
Most of these cases aren't terribly difficult and are logical, however, there are a few point in the game where I was simply left clueless as to what I'd even have to do now to continue the game. With enough exploring you can get through usually, but a hint or two here or there wouldn't have been terrible, especially since interactable objects don't always make 100% sense. Who would think about filling an object with water to water a tree? Repeatedly? And some objects are hard to see and especially 1 little detail you've maybe noticed at the start of the game can suddenly be relevant again at the end of it. Only the most important details are noted on the map, but for example what is shatterable glass and what isn't? Well, let's just say there's room for improvement. One puzzle in particular was aggravating, since the area in which it took place was just so enormous, going about it logically seemed really hard to do. For the most part though, the puzzles are fun.
So far so good, if it weren't for the terrible performance issues. In some rooms the framerate (no graphic options by the way) will simply tank hard and it shows. There's also a real performance issue when transitioning from one room to an unexplored room (on that particular day). It seems the game has to reload the assets with every restart of a day, which leads to severe issues when opening doors or trying to peek through them. The game is simply unresponsive and might even freeze for a while. An SSD MAY alleviate those problems, but frankly, an SSD should NOT be required for this game to work properly.
Another minor nitpick is the animation length, especially after starting a new day. Most animations just take forever and can't be cancelled or skipped. Yes, it looks neat, but after doing some task for the tenth time I just want my character to get it done. Since there is no running in this game and no quick travel either this can get tiresome after a while.
In the end TSB is an interesting game with some beauty flaws and no replay value whatsoever, so I'd suggest at least a 50% discount. But the experience itself is definitely worth your time, just maybe not the full price.

Of the handful of free-to-play, castle-style games I’ve tried, they have been a handful too many.  Stronghold Kingdoms was either too lonely or filled with inter-House drama.  Sparta: War of Empires was too deceptive with its trailers and required zero micro.  Kingdom Wars had too many bugs and performed too poorly.  Upon reading several negative reviews, I convinced myself internally that this game would prove no better.
Total War Battles: KINGDOM is none of any of those bad things.
KINGDOM, firstly, plays very, very smoothly and quickly.  Controls are responsive and the game doesn’t waste your time.  “But stuff takes forever to grow and collect!!”  Not my point.  When you are in-game and interacting with the world, you don’t encounter slowdowns, or annoyingly-long cutscenes, or needless exposition.  The engine is a well-oiled machine, undoubtedly.  The music is also really good, complementing the game without getting in the way.
KINGDOM’s depth really sells it, mind you.  The Realm overworld map is hex-based in style, with each space viable for manipulation: elevation, irrigation, terrain type, etc.  Building placement encourages wise structure layout.  During battles, your formation and tactics matter in equal measure. (a qualm I have is that the archers’ ranged attack acts like an ability and does not auto-fire on enemies; I assume this is done to encourage micro, but it’s more tedious than tactical)  Warfare requires very simple, but constant, micro.  It’s not too overwhelming, but also not "set and forget."
And judging by the speed at which units gain experience and upgrade, there is so, so much more to do.
“But Gold makes it pay-to-win!!”
Accept it.  There is no way around that.  The amount of PvE and personal kingdom development, and strictly optional PvP (there's almost always a PvE option to quests), however, mean there’s more than enough to do without interacting with another human online.  And the prices for most things is extremely minimal in cost.  Need a boost this battle?  Sac 3 Gold.  Desperately need that bit of Wood absolutely right now?  1 Gold for your troubles.  The costs do not murder the player’s treasury, and a variety of in-game methods offer the chance to accumulate Gold independent of any real money you spend on the game.
The game does not persistently badger you to share with your Facebook friends with annoying pop-ups every time you successfully gather grain, or pester you to buy Gold every 3 minutes.  The option is up there, quietly sitting on its own, not bugging you.  Mad props for not beating the player over their head with it.
TL;DR: Total War Battles: KINGDOM is not your average free-to-play, castle-style title.  It is indeed better than the simplistic tripe that passes on most on mobile devices or sits in the back tab of web browsers.  I would recommend people try it simply because it runs so blasted smoothly, but the profundity to the grand strategy of it all may arguably keep you hooked.

The long and the short of it is this: Thief is, quite simply, not a game I would ever recommend playing. To anyone. Do I regret playing it? Not exactly; some parts of the game were fun and enjoyable. But on a whole, I could have spent that time on a better, more worthwhile game. Dishonored and the original Thief games come to mind, and I've heard good things about Deus Ex. I have a few main reasons for disliking it this game: bad gameplay, poor level design, and low quality writing.
I found the gameplay to be severely underdeveloped, counter-intuitive, and choppy. There is no "lean" control as there is in Dishonored and Amnesia: The Dark Descent. Not only can you not perform this simple motion wherever and whenever you like in Thief, but if you're going to look around a corner you have to approach the corner and press E. Which is the action button for everything. So while you are searching a desk, you may find that Garrett gets in one of his jumpy moods and suddenly huddles behind it, peeking cautiously around the corner at...nothing. All because this feature was poorly designed. Also, counter-intuitive actions. You hold E to peek through a keyhole and press right-mouse to stop? Who thought of that awful idea? It makes sense to me that you press one button to start an action and the same button to stop it.
Also, whose idea was it to have the player spend gold on upgrades that make a task
I spent some good money on upgrading Dexterity. Does the upgrade make lockpicking easier? NO. It is more tedious, it takes longer, and it uses Focus. Bad, bad idea.
On several occasions while I played the game, I found myself unclear on what I was supposed to be doing and how I was supposed to do it. The tasks and how to accomplish them just weren't always clear, and it's not because I'm an inexperienced gamer or don't know what I'm doing, it's because the level and the sequence of events/objectives was not thoroughly developed.
Also, was anyone else frustrated by an apparent inability to use rich text in the documents?
. Couldn't you just write an italicized word
rather than *like this*? Nothing interferes with a game's immersion like seeing that kind of notation to remind you that you're not, in fact, a thief in The City during a time period similar to the 19th century; you are in fact in the 21st century, playing a disappointing game.
A note on graphics: it was excessive. I turned all of the settings all the way down on my computer, and it still crashed a good 20 times or so. I've played games with great graphics on my computer (all 3 Bioshock games, Portal 2, The Talos Principle, etc) that never made it crash; Thief could have easily been a good-looking game that didn't have a seizure every hour or so.
...Do I even need to say much on this? So much
. The dialogue was sub-par, and Erin is the most annoying, angst-filled teenage girl I've ever seen in a game. The story of the game just felt...dry.
Thief was a game that tried to be everything that Dishonored was, and fell miserably short. Dishonored benefited from a rich and immersive story, fluid and intuitive gameplay, and well-designed levels that gave the player options without confusing them; Thief had none of these in its favor. Eidos missed a great opportunity to make Thief into a fantastic reboot, and they could have done it if they had held themselves to a higher standard and taken the time to produce a quality game. Unfortunately, they didn't, and this is the result.

My advice is to try and fit as much of this game in your mouth as possible. It's fantastic.
Let's talk a little, quickly, about the lane brawling and then I'll cover the elephant in the room. I think that lane brawling is absolutely the tightest way to cram as much information on the screen as possible. Now, onto the elephant.
Castle Crashers.
This is not Castle Crashers. There are mechanical similarities, sure. But castle crashers was ultimately a game about mashing attack while laughing. This is a game about timing, cooperation, and careful resource management. Lane brawling means that the screen is far more legible and that player interaction can be a lot deeper. The characters are much more differentiated, with hitboxing and charged abilities designed to create disjoint battlefield utility.

The lane combat could turn some away and at first I wasn't sold on it. However, in my time with the game I've learned to appreciate it. In games like this (Especially, when playing coop) it can be very easy to lose track of where you are or line up attacks in the midst of complete chaos. However, the lane combat here serves to mitigate that. As long as you are in range and on the correct lane, you'll hit the enemy.
The music and SFX seem appropriate for the game, although nothing has stood out as exceptional at this point. You can viking yell though... so there's that!

Stellar visual novel, exceptionally well-written and able to fluidly transition from comedy to drama. The characters are, for the most part, engaging and well-written, and there's a lot of good to take from their interactions in general.
The choices made are consistently difficult near the end of the game, and consistent with its overall themes of morality and what it means to be a hero; combined with a good mystery that invites the user to speculate and consider what will come of it all, Rising Angels: Reborn is engaging from start to finish. Production values are for the most part all very solid, and mood music is used with great effect. The CG stills are comparatively cheaper looking next to the rest of the game, but there's nothing overtly wrong with the game and so much of it is done very well.
It's also free. So, you know, it's absolutely totally worth it. One of my favourite things I've found, will be sure to tell all my friends about it. Looking forward to more episodes!

Star Conflict a game that makes one promise, to give you an action packed space combat game. It delivers on that promise tenfold. You start out selecting one of 3 factions which for the most part is cosmetic though the Empire does well with Railguns and have a unique sniper weapon called the Decimator and The Federation performs best with Plasma Cannons and have strong supoort Drones, while the Jericho (who are big fans of space triangles) seem to work well with Laser Cannons and Long Range Missles.
Every battle is set nearby special zones located by automated recon droids which are to search for ancient civilization remains. From all over the world mercenaries come to these territories to fight for control over them. In the game this struggle is depicted with fighting for beacons that mark certain areas. Matches are designed to be for 2 teams 16 players in each. There are decent amount of game types with more being added, but you have your basic team deathmatch with respawns and one without (Thus it helps to bring more than one ship) a domination/conquest mode where you capture beacons and the longer you hold them the more defense drones they produce to help you hold them against enemy attacks, combat recon which is a fancy way of saying team deathmatch BUT each team has a Team Captain if that person dies then the team they were captain of can no longer respawn. That game mode is alot more fun than frustrating to be honest and can really make for some very good and tactical combat. The last game mode I've seen is basically sabotage, grab the floating EMP bomb and attempt to get it to one of the 3 enemy beacons and blow them up. This of course makes for some very fun cat and mouse gameplay.
Speaking of gameplay lets get into it, you fly your ship with a combination of WASD and QE for rolling your vessel, S & D allow you to strafe while the front of your ship follows the mouse. It's easy to get the hang of and fly effectively and after about an hour any sense of discomfort or disorientation is gone, flying for the most part feels fast and its easy to get into the action. Weapons feel powerful and as realistic as large laser cannons can feel. Most "Combat Sectors" or maps have a healthy amount of asteroids which will damage you if you run into but for the most part are saving graces more than anything provide cover from frigates who stay on the outskirts of furballs providing support and allowing for a quick hiding space from pursuing enemies. I recall when I was being chased down in my fighter and my pursuer launched a missle after me, I ducked behind and asteroid and watched it slam home saving my life. Quick thinking and graceful flying are definately rewarded in this game.
Now the ships you start with while good pale in comparison to the very next level, Tier 2 ships have more active modules, passive modules, ship modifcations, and weapon augmentors that take the game from being a simple arcade shooter, to strategically building your boat to maxium effectiveness. Do you build for shields being strong and resilent or armor? Do you enhance your normal weapons so they are better at thier normal damage type or do you agument them so you can handle any threat? Are you thinking of the team with active support modules or are you concerned for yourself with personal shield boosters? These options are all available to you, build your ships the way you want to play them, and the ways to play are more than varied and just as rewarding as any other.
Last but not least the premium pay for currency "Galatic Standards" are used only for short time skips when it comes to weapons or ships, the same stuff can be purchased with credits they are just better and cost a bit more than normal weapons. This game isn't pay to win at all, and I wouldn't play it if it was.
Overall I give the game and 9/10 and recommend it to anyone with a love of space combat.

The Sexy Brutale is unsupported.
The game apparently has controller detection issues. If you have multiple controllers or virtual controllers, the game forces controller mode and it does not seem to read the controllers correctly. You cannot switch back to mouse and keyboard mode so once you start the game you cannot even complete the tutorial and you are forced to kill the process via task manager.
This is a really basic bug that should have been fixed right away. However, the earliest report of this bug occurred back in April, when the game was released. So for 9 months this bug has been untouched. The dev team’s recommendation (from July) is to uninstall all other controllers to force keyboard mode. That is not a fix.
Some people seem to have no trouble using a 360 controller, or just mouse and keyboard mode. However, for me the game is unplayable without the unreasonable workaround.
Definitely not recommended.
Edit:
So after playing the game on a different system I encountered several other issues.
First, the game stuttered significantly switching rooms, something you do often.  It seems to be a loading issue but I have it installed on a SSD. Not sure what was causing the issue, but a few other players seem to have it.
There are almost no graphic settings. You can lower the resolution and set window mode. No anti-aliasing and no filtering, which was unfortunate because jagged edges are very noticeable in this game.
You can get the alternate ending before the main ending. Luckily, it is not much of a spoiler.
The game reeks of being lazy console port, which is awful because there is a decent game under the bugs and lack standard features. The Sexy Brutale borrows heavily from Majora’s Mask, though lacks the depth of story and has an unfortunately cliché ending.
Sadly, still do not recommend unless the developers can see to addressing the issues.

This is a great, if short, game.  Prevent the murders of nine guests at the Sexy Brutale casino mansion, in a total of six brutal 'cases'.  Time is on your side, because if you miss something important you can always rewind and start the 12 hour period over again.  As you spy on the comings and goings of the guests and servants, you'll get to enjoy an outstanding soundtrack and good though simple graphics.
Very little in the game was hard to figure out, so don't expect brain-wracking puzzles.  On the other hand, it can be tricky to find all the information you need to actually prevent a given murder, and it's highly enjoyable when you do finally get that missing piece of the puzzle.  New abilities are added as you save guests, keeping the pace nice and easy to learn.
In the end, you mostly play this for the alternatively amusing and terrifying story.  The gameplay is fun, at least once you get used to the control scheme (probably better to use a controller), the atmosphere is a definite plus... just don't expect to be biting your nails about how hard the game is, if that's what you enjoy.

So I wanted to take the time to write a quick review for Florensia so here it goes:
Ok, so I know that i'm only about 10 hours in on this game but I do have some positive things to say. For one, I have an EXTREMELY average laptop with an EXTREMELY average internet connection therefore resulting in laggy gameplay, shotty connectivity and a less than stellar experience when I try and do gaming for the most part. Lastly I do like the differential between the land and sea combat, both are a quick learn and seems like the customization is pretty deep, although the sea combat controls i do find a bit clunky and will get some getting used to.
I can not speak to higher end content like various bosses, raids (if they have them?) gear crafting and buffing and so on but if you are looking for a very chilled out mmorpg with questing, fishing, various combat interfaces and an overall smooth gameplay I suggest you give the game a shot. Another thing too, I do see a LOT of new players running around the game so I think Florensia coming to Steam has brought a nice influx on new players so thats a positive. Give it a shot, its not bad.

If you're looking for a deep game that has you managing armies and cities or one that is going to tell some 3 hour story well... this isn't it.
This is an "old-school" arcade game.  Essentially an homage to Atari's Asteroids and it does a very good job at it.  The basics are that you're in a ship shooting asteroids while a variety of alien ships try to destroy you.
The game offers a nice challenge in that your ship constantly moves forward.  You have a limited ability to boost and slow down however.  The game ups the challenge as well by not giving you unlimited ammo even for your basic weapon.  Your ship does have a shield that basically acts like a life.  Some ships  It is only when you don't have a shield and you are hit does the game end.
Because your weapon only has a limited amount of shots you're required to pick up ammo capsules to keep reloading your weapon.  There are also a variety of power ups that float by that  you can collect which give your weapon a different way of attacking.  They're balanced nicely in that the more powerful ones tend to go through your ammo quicker so that if you run out you lose the power up.  You're also given a limited amount of super bombs which destroy everything on the screen.
As well as weapon power ups occasionally a shield or boost recharge will appear.  The shield recharge gives you an extra life and the boost filler will refill your ability to speed up or slow down faster than waiting for it recharge.
The enemies are also of a nice variety.  Some shoot at you, others are essentially time bombs that blow up after a certain period of time, others launch a large volley of shots, etc.
At times the screen is so full of your shots, the enemy's shots, the asteroids, the ammo spheres, etc. that you get lost in it all.  And I mean that in a good way.  It's never comes across as unfair to the player.
Gold coins will also appear from destroyed enemies.  These gold coins can be used to purchase new ships which have different stats: more shields, more super bombs, etc.
The soundtrack is also pleasant to listen to.
My only real issue is that sometimes it doesn't recognize the joystick/controller.  It will still vibrate, but none of the buttons or sticks work.  It could just be something on my end, but I felt I should mention it.
TIP: If you want to make the game harder turn on auto-fire.  It keeps you from being able to conserve your ammo and makes picking up those ammo capsules even more important.

A competitive shooter/brawler akin to Paladins that has been in development since the dawn of time. The company very nearly went under during the development which would have seen the game never release, the team behind the game decided to work for free instead to deliver a game they're very proud of.
You'll love this game if:
- You like fast paced combat
- You like Third-Person over the shoulder style MOBAs
- You like having some freedom over how your hero plays. The way you level up your abilities in this game can mean you play a hero completely differently to the way someone else plays the same hero.
- You like close games with plenty of opportunity for the clutch plays.
- You like interesting and unique visual styles
Things that may turn you off:
- Hackers aren't exactly a rare occurance at the moment and there is no ingame report function.

Majora’s Mask meets Agatha Christie with a dash of HP Lovecraft in this beautifully presented murder mystery game. In The Sexy Brutale you use observational skills in order to solve puzzles and save the party guests at a masked ball, so it's probably more acurate to call this a murder prevention game. Check out my first impressions video for more in depth thoughts on gameplay.
The detailed, animation-like visuals and charming character designs fit nicely with the upbeat, toe-tapping music, but this can swiftly and smartly turn to macabre and melancholy. The Sexy Brutale has bags of atmosphere and an interesting take on puzzle solving.
It’s a nice change from the point and click style of puzzle solving which involves rubbing things on things to progress. Having now completed the game I’m a little disappointed in how basic the puzzles are and it’s a little shallow in this regard compared to something like Majora’s Mask. Perhaps giving you alternative solutions to the puzzles would have improved he gameplay as a lot of the rooms in the mansion (in which the game takes place) feel underused, as do the ‘powers’ you get from the saved guest’s masks.
What makes the game memorable is its presentation and story, which you unravel like the puzzles. It was a little predictable towards the end and the characters lacked depth but the presentation made it feel more involving and emotional.
I suffered from an annoying technical issue whilst playing; on opening doors I would often experience slow down or freezing for several seconds which wasn’t game breaking but needs to be fixed.
Still definitely worth checking out for people that like puzzle games with a twist or atmospheric games with nice art styles.

A fantastic murder mystery puzzle game with a fun art style, some fantastic characters, and a healthy dose of twists and turns throughout!  I thoroughly enjoyed the game (enough to 100% it, which is a rarity nowadays).  That takes about 10 hours to do (maybe less, if you catch on quicker than I do).  It's a tad expensive for that, but honestly, these guys deserve it for the great work.
The mechanics are easy to understand and the puzzle solving is intuitive and the gradual opening up of the mansion as you gain mechanics is very reminscent of survival horror like the early Resident Evil games.  There are a fair share of spooks and the murders are fairly grisly (if not rendered to be so explicitly, it isn't SAW).  The game itself isn't HARD, however, and the challenge is in puzzling out of solutions and executing them at the predetermined times than in any sort of quick reaction or on your feet thinking.  You're not going to die due a botched quick-time event; there's none of that here.
All and all, the game is fun and rewarding, if a bit slower paced.  It can be repetative when you're trying to figure things out or keep having to redo things in order to figure out exactly what needs to be done at what time, especially later in the game, but honestly, everything is conveyed really well regardless.  My one major complaint would have to be that for lower spec systems, the game hitches really badly when loading new rooms sometimes.  I didn't find it impossible to deal with or have it hurt my enjoyment, but I could see how it could frustrate people, so be wary, the more of the mansion that's revealed, the more the game starts to stutter/chug.
STILL, all and all a fantastic experience, and I would recommend it for mystery, horror, and puzzle fans wholeheartedly.  Also, check out the soundtrack, it is /fantastic/.

This is a great game.  The graphics are terrific and the gameplay is very intriguing.  Now diehard Thief fans may not enjoy the changes from the older style Thief games, but for those folks who are willing to keep an open mind or who are new to the Thief genre, this game is a winner.  For one thing, there are multiple ways to approach almost any situation.  If you want to get through the game completely unseen, it is possible...not easy, but possible.  If you are the aggressive type and want to go through killing everyone in sight, well...ravage away.  It is a long enough game with a large world so you feel like you have definitely gotten your money's worth if you play all the side missions.  The storyline is interesting and the dialogue is very witty in many places.  It all depends on how you play the game and what your actions are.  This Thief is not as 'dark' as some of the earlier ones and differs in mood from say Thief Gold.  I didn't see this as a negative as some other reviewers did.  This game was a breath of fresh air after playing some of the earlier games.  This is not a criticism of the earlier games...just telling you that they shouldn't be compared directly.  This version of Thief is very good on it's own.  To believe it should be a direct descendant of the earlier games is to do all of the games a disservice.  Evaluate this Thief on its own and I believe you will agree.  There is a place for the old ones and the new both in the Thief world.  Enjoy...
