I edited my review and put at the beginning the important facts I see after more hours of play. Below comes my initial review.
Here are the important facts new players (old PG players) should know:
- Better fighting rules. (Suppressing fire, easier attack when more units adjacent to attacked hexfield, etc.) Real good small things old PG players will love when they see it.
- Better overall units and stats balance. (no overpowered PzIVF2 with range 2 for example :))
- Special skills are transparent now: For good fighting units gain Iron Crosses (no effect) and brigade heroes, which give a random skill + 1 to 3 points. You see the result when hovering mouse over in detailled unit view or other GUI manifestations of these battle honours.
- Trains! Trains can move units from CITY TO CITY along rail tracks with high speed. Excellent logistics feature.
- Some units (towed guns) can switch operation mode. Mostly AT/Artillery or AT/AA mode. To be chosen every turn before using unit.
- Better (more difficult) unit upgrade system!!! You can easily upgrade within a unit type, like the sub types of PZ2, but when going to PZ3 for example, you pay full price, even if the upgrade goal is "less worth" regarding prestige. This does what was missing in other PG games: More variation in your own core army and some more older units that are still in service in your core army. That is cool!
- Good map graphics and unit sprites in full zoom mode as well as zoomed out.
- Very much detailled units that differ visually and in stats.
- Units you get from high command (prototypes in PG2) have special camouflage and slightly better stats than regulars. They can be "sold", but they do not add to the maximum of deployable units in the level, so there is a big motivation to keep them regardless what they are! Very good rule!
- Very good abstract fighting animations. Really creates a good battle feeling!
- The sounds are very very sexy. Moving units and shooting with them is wonderful. You will feel very evil :) when advancing the german army and snowball the enemy on the way with your big nasty weaponry.
- The zoomed out mode is like the PG1 stategic map view, but detailled as hell and still in-game so that you can still do everything on the map. It is a calculated zoom view by the Panzer Corps game engine and the unit strength numbers are slightly blurred than in 1:1 mode, but everything is still visible and better than a switch to strategic view. (looks like a super detailled PG1 1:1 view on a modern screen.)
- In-Game Battlefield structure and campaign tree has (unintended?!) strong reference to PG 1 & 2. Really feels like home.
After some hours of a good campaign (currently early Moscow), it just feels like the best hexfield game SSI would have made.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
First I thought it won't be as good as Panzer General 2 (German: Panzer General 3D).
- I wondered why these nice and detailled PG1 style sprites did not have many directions photographed so they would move like in PG2.
- I was afraid there wouldn't be the sexy devastating sounds of 8.8er Flak or 15cm sFh 18 when they shoot or the cool battleship artillery
- I thought the goofy looking big units on the map would bug and disturb me with time.
But it is all OK. After several hours this game is approved.
The AT sounds in general are wonderful.
The units are not goofy. They are detailled and don't have to have a seperate sprite for every direction they are facing.
It is the same damn addiction I had all these years when switching between PG1 and PG2.
Actually you forget you are playing another game and just feel that you are continuing the same game of PG1 and PG2 in another way. It is much much fun.
It will cost me damn much time of my life.
I waited with the Steam purchase until it was on discount, but now I know it is worth full price.
You don't have to be afraid. I was very very very sceptical; and the effect to really REALLY like the game came long after the 1 hour Steam refund period.
So just continue gaming and see the beauty and intelligence in that game's rules and style.
I hope this little general review is useful to anyone on the verge to purchase.

Changing my review to Not Recommend, after arguing with another reviewer about the music. He said the music was good, and I was shocked since there was only a bit of melody played over and over. I kept thinking about this, and I realized there is not a lot to like about this game, except that it is inexpensive and it works. But is that the bar that must be met for me to RECOMMEND this game? I certainly would not recommend this game to a friend. After playing this for thirty seconds, I was pretty well bored with it, and while I will certainly play it again, I would not recommend anyone get it.
Let's compare it to another asteroid clone called Maelstrom on the Macintosh computer that totally blew me away, in 1995. When I first played Maelstrom, I could not get away from the keyboard for hours. I looked forward to playing it over and over. And yet the two games are so similar, with ship upgrades, a race for higher scores, rotating and thrusting for movement... Now here it is twenty years later, and what does Bit Blaster have that Maelstrom doesn't? Plus, Maelstrom was released as free software, so you can download it even before you finish reading this review.
I am fairly certain that the majority of reviewers would be spitting mad if they had purchased the Bit Blaster game for the ten dollars that most light steam games have for a price. I do not think the overwhelming positive reviews are a good reflection of the quality of this game, except that people have very low expectations when they are getting what they see as a bargain. (And my sympathies in advance to the game author, who no doubt will read this and try to respond, as I have seen him do to other negative reviews. I do understand you put a good faith effort into creating, pricing, and supporting this game.) In hopes of being balanced here, I want to point out that there is a nine MP3 track DLC that unlocks at no cost. It is chiptune music. I initially did not notice it, and it may be interesting for people still considering a purchase.

A luke-warm positive review. Very fun MOBA gameplay at its core, marred by bugs and a HUGE lack of features (ranked matchmaking, replays, in-game voice). I wish them well at improving the problems but honestly if this is what they launch with I don't have that high of hopes at seeing this take off...
EDIT 1: It has now been two weeks since launch, and there hasn't been a single update. The pace of updates MUST increase if they want people to keep playing their game...They NEED more maps, they NEED a replay system, they NEED ranked matchmaking. I'm still having fun, but the trajectory of development does not look great right now.
EDIT 2: I really do enjoy this game, but I've been playing less and less recently. Motiga has just released the FIRST patch for the game (one month later, ONE UPDATE.), adding features which are STANDARD for a game to be released with in 2017, particularly in the free-to-play category, where competition is so harsh.
Can you imagine that this game was RELEASED with voice chat...but no push-to-talk functionality?? I mean I understand that it's cross-platform, but that is a joke. I imagine that's the same reason that it took so goddamn long to get a single update; I guess I'm just used to PC games where small updates are commonplace when they're needed. It was also released without any real ranked matchmaking...replays...custom lobbies, I could go on and on but the point is that you can't just expect players to come along for the ride as you build a functional game POST-RELEASE, and this is what Motiga has done, probably out of necessity more then anything.
At this point, I have to change my recommendation from positive to negative; the already-small community will continue to grow smaller unless something big changes, meanwhile the game has a lack of features, and the gameplay itself is still fresh and needs balancing, as shown by some of the enormous (and it could be argued, reckless) changes made in this patch.
As doom and gloom I'm being about the game, I'll probably be back to edit this again, because at it's core it is essentially a fun and distinct MOBA.

Half of them I find hard to believe in as adults capable of dressing themselves.  The main character herself is the least bad, but even her, while I find her emotional arc somewhat affecting, just systematically breaks her original image as someone who supposedly graduated first in her class and is remotely competent.  Not even the whiz she imagines herself to be at the beginning, just borderline capable of seeing things obvious as the nose on her face or taking basic operational security precautions.

You figure it out, you do it once, move on to the next. The puzzles are neat and tidy and each one tends to build on the complexity of the last in satisfying ways, and for a game so focused on the timing of things it doesn't make you sit and wait for something to happen very much at all.

Ever wondered what its like, if you could go back in time to do something differently and change the outcome of a situation? Well, The Sexy Brutale is basically a whole game about that idea.
One day, without any memory of how you got there, you find yourself in a mansion. You will realize very soon that there are some strange things going on however. The guests of the mansion are being murdered by its employees and it is your objective to save them. The gimmick here is, that once a day comes to an end, it will start over again similar to “Groundhog Day”. By repeating the same day over and over you will have to analyze the different actions that lead to a murder and find a way to manipulate the outcome. By saving a guest you unlock new abilities that will grant you access to new parts of the mansion, where new murders are waiting for you to be solved. And that is pretty much how the gameplay in The Sexy Brutale works like, it’s basically a puzzle/detective game with point and click elements.
While replaying the same day over and over might sound boring to some, I quite enjoyed solving the different murders and putting all the pieces together to understand the story behind the mansion.
Besides the gameplay itself, the game has a great looking art style with a lot of love to detail in every room. Combined with the isometric/top down view it makes the game look fairly unique. Every area of the mansion has a different soundtrack as well and in my opinion, it added a big part to the games atmosphere.
Overall, I greatly enjoyed my time with the Sexy Brutale. If you enjoy detective games and casual puzzle solving with some nice graphics on top, this is your game. I also have to add, that the price of the game without a discount is pretty steep since it can be finished in 6-9 hours, so you might want to wait for a discount or bundle here.

I'm middling on this game. Is it well designed? Yes. Is it fun? Yes, for a while. Does it have a lot of play time? Well...that depends.
Art:
Minimalistic, like a subway/tube map, with simple shapes to represent stations that simple-shaped-people are trying to get to.
Music:
Also minimalistic, with the sounds of people getting on and off the trains, adding trains or tracks, new stations popping up all represented as tones that all grow together to make a wonderfully soothing soundtrack. However, it gets really boring after a while. It's like listening to a song with only one chord for anywhere from 5 minutes to however long you play for. There also seemed to be a glitch where music from a level would continue on even after exiting that level or starting a new one.
Gameplay:
There IS a tutorial, but it's hidden. So the game essentially drops you into the action with no indication of what you're supposed to do. I didn't even know that I could delete tracks, switch trains to different tracks or detach stations from tracks until WAY late into the game. You have limited resources (bridges, train engines and train carriages being the scarcest). There are also two modes of playing: 1) the fast-paced survival mode where your game ends if your stations get too overcrowded, and resources are doled out on a "weekly" basis and 2) the endless mode where you are rewarded for the efficiency of your map, only receiving resources if you reach certain milestones of efficiency. This second mode is less stressful, but you also seem to stop receiving resources at all at some point and the game becomes stalled where you can't make your map any more efficient without resources but they don't give you anymore. Likewise, the AI is simultaneously well-designed and cruel. Your passengers will always take the shortest route to their destination, so it's easy to see which stations need a more direct route to avoid overpopulation. However, the new stations pop up at random with no hint of what kind of station or where it will be, making long-term planning impossible. Also, you will always have a TON of people wanting to go to certain stations (ex. square) but there will be only 1 or two compared to 10 or 12 circle stations at a given time. I guess this is more realistic, but it really adds some difficulty.
Overall: I recommend this game, but it quickly became boring and repetitve in endless mode, or exponentially difficult in the survival mode. Don't expect a ton of playtime out of it. Buy it on the cheap. 6/10

Most of my playtime is on my laptop, which I don't have cooked up to my internet so it's missing a hundred hours or so :P This game is a godsend of a game for me, considering it's not very hardware intensive. It'll run on just about anything modernish. For anything older... well, I'm sure there are abandonware sites with Panzer General floating around.
My memories of playing Panzer General 2 have faded in the 2 decades since I had it, so this is the first hex based game I've played in a lifetime it feel like. An overall satisfying experience, and with the editor alogn with the game you can make your own fun as well. The scenario selector is also pretty fun, although just hopping into some of the later scenarios has you waiting for quite a while while the enemy has the dozens to hundreds of it's units all act, so might want to toggle off seeing their moves if you are feeling risky.
The base game is plenty of fun, especially with the altering campaign tree, though the grand Campaign is where most people find the best parts to be. You can sink hundreds of hours in this, and will definently have your tactical mind put to the test on higher difficulties.
I would heavily recommend only going for the plethora of DLC when it is on sale, or just get the whole game and DLC on sale, as it's 100$ or more normally, and that's a big chunk of change. If you want a slightly more advanced version of this, try Order of Battle from the same company/developer. It's slightly more hardware intensive, enough so my current toaster wont run it, but features units that actually move as opposed to tokens shifting. Order of Battle also has a LOT of DLC for different scenario packs and seems to be banking on selling them to make a lot of mone, by selling campaign seperately. However, the base Order of Battle game is free, so you can see if it's up your alley with no issues!
Overall, if you are burned out on RTS', then take the general chair where you can have a slower more relaxing time, without the micromanaging of Hearts of Iron level of strategy.

**Caveat - My main genre of games are FPS and Shooters (minus super sci-fi laser themes of FPS i.e. battlefront, quake, doom)
**FPS played - CS1.6, CS:CZ, CS:GO, Battlefield(s), Crysis, Rainbow Siege, Overwatch, Insurgency & CoD(s).
First off, yes Steam launcher merely just to launch the Arc launcher which you then use to launch Gigantic is Clunky in 2017. And also yes, there are some login issues, and running issue in loading the game.
Now about the game itself;
1) beautiful art style (if you dislike stylization thn not for you)
2) mechanically interesting - movement mastery with the stamina system & skills augmentation (running, dodging, dash, super jumps, jukes, escapes); something most FPS doesn't bring to the table, Crysis 1 had this aspect more so than Overwatch. Other games CS/CoD/BF have the same movement for every player basically.
3) tug of war game mechanic - collecting power for your "ancient" to intiate attacks on the opposing team's ancient is played out by defending points that generate power & also sabotaging opponents' points, in addition to hero kills generating power. Requires more coordination with your team in what should everyone do to help with getting power.
4) hero builds - upgrade skill paths for more build varieties
The game is not Overwatch, only the art style bears resemblance. Though imo, I prefer Gigantic's (more stuff is happening on screen, which some might find too noisy to be enjoyable). A welcome addition to the shooter genre of games (not replacement to other games).

I have been playing this game for like 6-7 months by now, it was only recently added on steam. A truly fantasic game. Basically, this is World of Tanks in space.
Its absolutely PERFECT quick PVP space fights - its been many years since i saw a game of this kind. You take direct control of the ship. Absolutely no point-and-click like in EVE online, which leads to a very intense fights, fully depending on your skill. There is no auto-lock of the main weapons(of course there are guided missiles and close-range smart bombs, but rockets are very limited(from 2 to 5 per ship per match) and modules require cooldown), so it all depends on how you can track your target, which is moving fast in all 360 degrees. Piloting physics in also very advanced.
There are LOTS of modules, weapon and ship modifications, letting you create your own perfect built. You will not get acces to all slots and modules at the start, obviously, but the further you go - the more customisation you get.
Graphics look pretty awesome for a F2P game. And what is amazing is that there is absolutely NO "pay 2 win" - money only lets you unlock ships and modules a little earlier, and still not out of your tier/level.
TL;DR - A quick PVP action in space, with long PVE missions present. Great graphics, amazing skill-based combat and piloting engine, A LOT of ship/modules/weapons/mods loadouts and no "pay 2 win". HIGHLY RECCOMEND.

I've played through this game fully one time.  I hesitate to say game because it's not one.  It is a visual novel.  It has some interactive parts that let you make choices at times that may or may not influence then ending, but there is no "gameplay."  Some of them are obvious and some aren't.  All of them effect the story a little bit in what you get to read, whether it has an impact on the plot or not.  If you're looking for a sim rpg then move on.  The closest thing I can compare this to is the "choose your own path" books.  I've only gotten one ending so far, but I absolutely plan on playing through again and checking out the other paths.  If your looking for a fun story this is great.  Either way I recommend at least taking a look at.  I look forward to the sequel, and I look forward to reading the prequel Rising Angels: The Red Rose.
On a slight side note, the sequel I mentioned will take into account the complaints about "lack of interaction" and will be pushing more into gameplay with two modes: story mode and "investigation mode."  Because of this, I highly recommend reading this, even if it's not your favorite type of thing.  If you don't you'll be missing out on a lot of backstory when Rising Angels: Fates is released.

The Sexy Brutale is an extremely interesting game with a lot of good and some bad. One could say it's a flawed gem. The premise is murder investigation / prevention which makes people think that it's a puzzle game but in reality the game really has 3 parts:
1. You map the manor.
2 You map the locations and movements of all characters in the manor.
3. You map the the actions and the reasons behind the actions of all the characters in the manor (in other words you find out the story and plot).
The puzzle elements are very light after those three.
In short I recommend the game to anyone who is at all interested in this kind of games but you might want to get it on sale due to the short length
Overall
8-
Pros
+ The graphics / art style and sound are spot on
+ The concept of the game / gameplay is fresh and it's simply fun to play the game
+ The story is presented very well with few exceptions
+ The plot and sub-plots are fairly simple but good / interesting
+ The game starts with a lot of hand-holding but then stops and let's the player experience the game on their own
Cons
- Some parts of the game don't really work because the game doesn't give any hints what it wants from the player
- The game if fairly short with practically no replay value
- There are collectables but they don't really add value / valuable gaming time because collecting them feels mainly tedious

The way you can rewind time is very much like Zelda: Majora's Mask. You may follow one person, learn their movements and how they get killed, then rewind and follow someone else. You can listen to what the characters say at different moments of the day to get clues to prevent their death. Unlike a typical murder mystery, you don't need to reveal who the killer is, instead you need to prevent the death from happening.
The game is mostly linear, you prevent the murders in a specific order. When you prevent a murder you gain new powers that unlock a new area of the mansion. When you enter the new area, you have a vision of who you have to save next. You can revisit old areas to search for collectables you missed (or to just explore), but you never need to revisit an old area to prevent any of the deaths (i.e. you don't need to revisit the casino to prevent a death in the guest rooms).
You must sneak around and remain hidden from everyone, even the guests you are trying to save. You can look through keyholes to see a portion of whats happpening in the next room, or stop and listen for nearby footsteps and talking, You can also hide in a closet, this is similar to looking through a keyhole but you can see and hear the whole room and you don't have to worry if someone enters the room your in (no one ever checks the closets). If someone sees you, you just have to leave the room (your given plenty of time to do so), they don't keep chasing you once you leave. It's possible to quickly pass through areas with people in them (as opposed to waiting for them to leave the room) without any repercussions. I have no idea what happens if you just stay in a room with another character (not sure if your booted to the main menu or the day just restarts). Near the end of the game, remaining hidden can become tedius. I was expecting one of the end-game powers you receive would be invisibility, but no such luck.
The worst part, for me anyways, was the ending, I wont give away the ending, only that you don't need to peice together whats really going on, You are eventualy told everything without any test to see if you figured it out on your own (your just given few doors you need to unlock and then the antagonist begins walking you through everything), and I don't think it's possible to figure out the big secret on your own either. Once you do know the truth you can go back and see a few small clues (spoiler:
). The ending isn't horrible, but it renders everything that happened to be a bit meaningless, and I would have greatly preferred slowly piecing it all together throughout each prevented death.
Aside from my nit-picking of gameplay aspects I would have changed, and the ending, I didn't want to put the game down, and I was left wanting more.
One last thing: There is no need for the "Sexual Conent" tag to be applied to this game, "The Sexy Brutale" is the name of the mansion the game takes place in, but I didn't see any sexual content. The closest I can think of is one character talking about his disappointment with the lack of nude artwork in the library.

They clearly have no clue what made the Thief series special. I understand the necessity to streamline for a broader audience in order to finance the development of a AAA reboot. I do not understand however, how you'd plan out the reboot of a series and simply forfeit the key things that made it unique.
A typical Thief experience in the first 3 titles:
- player agency is king
- Garrett is a master thief, as in the kind of person who pulls off difficult and challenging heists
- the world is mysterious but largely consistent
- the various factions' beliefs determine the world's institutions, shape, and nature of places Garret visits
- Garrett is intelligent, witty, and cynical
- sound is the primary means of conveying stealth information to Garrett (direction and distance of footsteps, voices, etc.)
In this new Thief:
- player agency is severely hampered (contextual jumping, pre-determined spots for rope arrow, mostly linear map design)
- Garrett does not come across as a professional thief, more like an emo-batman, and the missions are way to easy and linear to require any thought or plan at all
- the world is generic, inconsistent, not plausible, and therefore boring (loot placement, decorations, outdoor design, interior design)
- there are no factions representing any kind of beliefs, the little struggle there is between factions is not shaping the world, it's just alternating who's running it
- Garrett's writing and voice acting has declined sharply from previous titles
- sound is not important at all, there is no robust sound propagation in this game, thus... Garret has a radar map
I could have enjoyed the game with all the other things that water down the experience for the sake of a broader audience: takedown mechanics, focus time, radar map instead of rough sketches, shallow side-quests, shallow character pseudo-progression, whatever rocks your AAA boat...
But a set of features does not make a good game, especially not one that needs you to feel like you're there, in a dangerous place, pulling off a heist or rescuing a friend. For that you need depth, and that has gone out the window in this game.

In Thief (2014) take the role of Garret once again in a modern first-person stealth/action game set in a fantasy steampunk world resembling the Industrial Revolution era.
Like the earlier titles dating back to 1998, you can choose how you deal with enemies although the games design focuses on stealth.  For those who want action, there are weapons available that allow direct confrontation although ammo is limited and expensive to replace limiting your skill upgrades.  Each enounter allows you to decide if you break cover and go head-to-head with the enemies, stealthly assassinate them, or remain in cover and bypass them all together.
The level design is very similar to 2004's Thief Deadly Shadows in that the game is open level based (not world) so you may choose to explore the city and steal items at will, but you must load level to level.  If you choose to do the side missions, which I personally enjoyed, you will uncover most secret areas and collectables easy enough.
The AI while deadly in numbers can be easily avoided as they tend to pat in a pre-determined pattern and if you are seen, you can easilly escape.  Melee combat with several guards on you will usually result in almost certain death.  The AI is not overly intelligent but still provide a moderate challenge although die hard fans of the series have expressed disappointment in how forgiving the AI can be.  I believe it provides a good balance.
The graphics are very immersive and look great, although the game originally ran rough upon release and was not very well optimised pushing my GTX 780ti.  It now runs much smoother without the stuttering and frame drops.
Overall I really enjoyed this game and recommend it.  I enjoyed the story and the gameplay although I would have liked to have seen an actual open world.

Mini Metro is one of those games that is just deceptively simple, and yet can be quite challenging.
It's essentially a puzzle/simulator, with really simple mechanics of 'add some trains to lines' and 'get passengers from A to B quickly'. From the get-go, that doesn't seem very hard, but this game does a good job of ramping up the difficulty. By the time you've gotten to the more difficult levels, or are trying to complete the achievement challenges, you realize you need to consider a lot of problems and juggle lots of different possible configurations of lines and trains.
The graphics and sounds in this game match the simple premise, and help to avoid distracting you from the simulation at the base of the game. I did find that this made it hard sometimes to get the game to do what you wanted, like going around a river bend rather than using up a tunnel by going through it, but overall it works well.
Definitely worth playing if you're interested in transport/management simulator games.

This game reminds me of Railroad Tycoon in that you try to lay tracks for maximum efficiency given some constraints (funds in RR, number of tracks/trains/tunnels in MM). Great gameplay and tasty design. A very addictive game.

Way too many new shapes in far off distances to where you can only use one metro to cover most if not all of them because you get such a small number of tunnels. There's a lot of tweaking that could make this game much more enjoyable and stable for long games. I feel like more focus on say 6 shapes in multiple locations instead of a ton of circles, some triangles, two squares and literally one of like 6-8 other shapes in one corner of the map would be amazing.
Super addictive, I definitely think it was worth getting the humble bundle just for this game. I get into a stressful trance, which is definitely an interesting combination.

First off, yes Steam launcher merely just to launch the Arc launcher which you then use to launch Gigantic is Clunky in 2017. And also yes, there are some login issues, and running issue in loading the game.
Now about the game itself;
1) beautiful art style (if you dislike stylization thn not for you)
2) mechanically interesting - movement mastery with the stamina system & skills augmentation (running, dodging, dash, super jumps, jukes, escapes); something most FPS doesn't bring to the table, Crysis 1 had this aspect more so than Overwatch. Other games CS/CoD/BF have the same movement for every player basically.
3) tug of war game mechanic - collecting power for your "ancient" to intiate attacks on the opposing team's ancient is played out by defending points that generate power & also sabotaging opponents' points, in addition to hero kills generating power. Requires more coordination with your team in what should everyone do to help with getting power.
4) hero builds - upgrade skill paths for more build varieties
The game is not Overwatch, only the art style bears resemblance. Though imo, I prefer Gigantic's (more stuff is happening on screen, which some might find too noisy to be enjoyable). A welcome addition to the shooter genre of games (not replacement to other games).

It's good for learning the basics and the mechanics introduced in each set if you're new to Magic.
Could increase ways to get cards or at least give more cards in each booster pack. But I guess, it's a free-to-play game and they need to make money somehow.

Pros: This game plays really well on PC. The card selection, a subset of each set released starting with Origins, is well-tuned. Earning coins for free by winning matches, and then buying packs with those coins, is nice. Having a finite amount of packs needed to own a whole set and not have extra cards you can't use is also nice. All quantities of packs are the same price per pack so there is no "penalty" or missed discount for just buying one with coins you got for free. 1P story mode is challenging and fun, and you get gold for completing each step for the first time.
Cons: The amount of coins you need to build competitive decks for online play is
. You can't buy/sell/trade anything whatsoever so you are completely at the mercy of the pack RNG, which admittedly is less random the more cards you own. It's a real mountain to climb, probably about $800 as of Amonkhet (@ approx $100 per set) if you wanted to buy the coins and then the packs outright. Older packs cost the same as newer packs. 150 coins per pack of 6 cards builds your collection very slowly if you're going the free route. The AI hits your CPU hard - be prepared to heat up your system if you have a complicated board state.
Pro / Con depending: The max number you can own of each card depends on its rarity. (You won't open "dead" cards in packs.) You can't build a deck with 4-of a rare or mythic because you can't own that many. So while your deck's consistency won't be as good as paper Magic, your opponents are also subject to the same increased variance.
TL;DR: While this is free-to-play and very much Magic the Gathering-y, you are probably going to spend a lot of coins on packs before you start enjoying anything other than the Story mode.

Avencast is pretty atypical among the action-adventure clones of Diablo but still has pretty straight-forward arcade style gameplay. The choices here are much more flexible and tactical but the casting system and the magic itself lacks the pristine polish and substance found in Magicka or Nox and there is no lightning magic (an odd developmental choice, in my opinion).
You can either choose to cast spells via an arcade style input (left, right, click... etc.) or by hotkey. I prefer arcade input myself. The story is cliche as hell but the setting is pulled off decently and worth a two-finger round of applause.
Now, the SDK provides a good deal of potential and has a very detailed and easy-to-use readme. I put together a somewhat large mod myself, overhauling the Soul Magic tree and even added more spells.
Overall, Avencast is certainly worth the asking price if you are a magic-user enthusiast like me and definitely worth it when on-sale.

Original review (thumbs down): The game features mouse and keyboard support. Technically. Because if it sees anything to make it suspect you may, MAY, have a controller plugged in, it'll auto-switch to an XBOX control scheme. "Oh, just switch it back" - no option to do so, not in the menus, not in command line. This happens even to people who never had any sort of a controller. Horrible decision, that, and it may easily leave the game completely unplayable if you happen to be one of the people this happens to.
New additions: I was one of those people this happened to, with no gamepad connected. What's worse, actually CONNECTING a gamepad also didn't help, since the game insists on "XBOX controller" and as the bottom-forward-right button on my generic one isn't actually called "RT" it refused to accept it as a substitute and I couldn't perform a vital action. While I finally figured out what was making it trip itself into thinking I had a gamepad connected (an old device that USED TO be connected still left some driver residue for quick reconnection), this is a serious issue that may prevent people from playing the game, and the developer doesn't seem to be taking it seriously (the "solution" I found offered was "make sure you have unplugged everything, and carefully scour the system for software things to disable before playing"). All it would take is adding a command line option to force the game into starting in the keyboard mode. It's not the prettiest solution, but it would work. While this issue is there, it's enough for me to hesitate in recommending getting the game strongly enough that I'm keeping it at thumbs down (I'd prefer something neutral, but that's not an option).
About the game itself: It's actually pretty neat. At its base it's a puzzle/adventure game. You run around, spy on the guests and the staff of the titular casino/mansion who are running through their day in an ever-repeating loop in which all the guests get murdered, in ones or in twos. You're unable to directly interact with any of them, so you must figure out some way to prevent the death of each guest in some indirect manner. This is usually a rather simplistic puzzle. Pick up an item, deliver it somewhere at a right time, act in a specific way according to the information you obtained by spying on the guests/staff, that sort of thing. Nothing earthshattering, but honestly it's mostly just there to structure your exploration of the mansion. And the mansion really makes itself worth exploring, as do the characters who populate it make it worth it to follow their looped days around. The execution of the looped routine is quite excellent, aided by the well-made animation (in particular, the gas masks on those butlers are surprisingly expressive), fitting music and consistently good artstyle. The story is not overly complex in its broad brushstrokes, but very, very well executed, with a lot of care and detail, and particularily with how it's ultimately tied together (deliberately avoiding spoilers). This isn't a game with much "gameplay" as such, but as an experience it's well worth having.
...if it'll let you, on account of the wacky controller issues. If I hear they got fixed, I'll change to "thumbs up".

It's been a while since I've played, and I didn't play for long when I did. There's a reason for that. I don't want to trivialize what happened.
I started an average game with an average cast. Of them, one stands out in my memory: a soccer player who could run a bit faster than everyone else and who could carry a decent amount, too. He was my first pick for forays outside. Me and him, we were able to dart in and out of places easy, make deals with other survivors, and come back home safe.
That was, until one fateful night.
We went to what we thought was an abandoned house. Bit out of sorts, shelled, but still standing nonetheless. I walked up to the front door, thinking I'd greet any survivors and possibly work out a deal with them. In retrospect, I should've been more understanding when they pursued me, and I should've ran away instead of further into the map. Hell, at the end, I drew a knife I found on them and tried to defend myself. But their shotgun blew my soccer player away.
The man I had relied on was dead.
In my mind, there was only one thing left to do: retrieve his body and bring justice to those who murdered him. I returned to a shop I had been to earlier. They sold handgun parts, but I couldn't afford them, so I killed them. I killed a man's son in front of him while he cried for me to stop. Then I killed him.
I thought.
Of course, the young man I killed would've lived longer, but I omitted that.
I started omitting a lot of things, honestly.
After going back and systematically killing every member of the offending family that murdered my soccer player, I felt I had carried out justice. But that wasn't the end to this "justice". I went to a supermarket and found dirty raiders, looters, and bandits.
I mused.

And so they died, too. For justice.
As time went on, lives ended, and round after round was chambered, this perversion of justice came to a climax. I was down to one man. All the others had died in combat, including during raids on my home carried out by the families of those I killed. Honorable deaths, all of them. None of them like my soccer player. I armed my one man with an AK and stormed a hotel that was being used as a distribution hub for human trafficking. Many died. So did I.
I could have started another playthrough. I did, actually. But not far in I realized that I had already taken all I needed to learn from this game, and that playing it further would be - pardon the expression - an
to what I had learned.
It was at the end that I realized what this game was getting at: humans can rationalize a lot. Sure, I was detached from it all. I wasn't seeing through my eyes and smelling their blood and feces. But the decisions I made - for "justice" - were inherently flawed. In putting down what i thought to be monsters, I became one myself. And to uphold a moral, I broke it beyond recognition.

What did I just witness? Firstly, this is basically a novel. There is very very little interaction. Secondly, it's incredibly poorly written. The characters are unbelievably inept and the entire adventure plays out like you would expect if you put a bunch of fifteen year old junior high school students in charge of a space ship. They all act like small children. At one point you're in a room of officers discussing who has crushes on who. It was very weird.
It's bad, it's cringeworthy, it has terrible pacing. Throughout the story most of the characters engage in extremely immature, childlike-banter. This includes when they are in serious and dangerous situations... "Oh we have a spy on board, I better take a moment out of this staff meeting to discuss how clumsy and silly our security officer is." What? The important point is that this is a school drama/relationship game. The ancient weapon plot is entirely in the background and barely relevant to what you spend most of your time doing: Gossiping with children.

I've been a fan of the series since the original Theif: The Dark Project, so I picked this up when it came out.
A big plus is the amount of customizing you can do to make the game more difficult or more easy depending on your playstyle or patience.
I played through a bit and left it alone since I wan't getting decent performance with the hardware I had. After upgrading my system, I did a Thief marathon. I played through Thief Gold, The Metal Age, Deadly Shadows, all on the hardest difficulty. In Thief 2014, I stopped at what amounts to a boss fight against the Thief-taker General. It just seemed like an annoying addition to the game that was thrown in since the game designers follow some sort of formula that must involve a boss fight. The customized settings I play on make it frustrating: No focus, hidden takedowns, no crosshair, no special arrows, no poppies, no damage, expensive equipment, slower movement, no upgrades, no killing, and no alarms.
It's not quite as bad as the Deus Ex: Human Revolution pre-patch boss fight debacle, but it's the same stupidity. DX:HR had many options for a character build and then force you through a limited options boss fight. In Thief, you can set a wide variety of options that affect what capabilities you have in your playthrough, and then you are limited in your playstyle in the boss fight. If you spend time sneaking and knocking guys out in the game, that's suddenly a useless skill on this fight since he just detects you if you get close. I know its a matter or whatching his movement patterns and picking the lock in between after cranking the wheels. I'm assuming the lockpicking was designed with console players using controllers in mind since I've read they get vibration feedback. Not so with the mouse, and with a tiny sweet spot and looking for the subtle hand movements, lock-picking is not fast. This hasn't been a problem anywhere except this boss fight. Maybe one day I'll go back to this game and finish it, or find a console command to skip this giant stinky turd they put in the middle of an otherwise good game. Even having not finished it, I still played it a fair amount. Still recommend.

Having played all the previous games, I couldn’t pass on an opportunity to try out the latest in the Thief series. This one in particular seems to have also gathered a rather bad reputation, but that didn’t really deter me from trying it out for myself. I did manage to play it all the way through the end and came to the conclusion that this game is basically a weak upgrade to Thief: Deadly Shadows with a bit of Dishonored thrown in.
Gameplay is altered a bit by the new ‘swoop’ mechanic, which allows garret to zip across short distances similar to the blink ability in Dishonored. At first this seems almost like cheating but it is counterbalanced a bit by noisy surfaces and broken glass, which give the sound effect as if you had sprinted over them.
You get the usual myriad of special arrows including the new choking and blunt arrows used for stunning opponents and remotely triggering devices and switches respectively. The rope arrow makes a return, but it’s pretty gimped and can only be used as a “key” to get to certain highlighted areas. You also get a few purchasable tools usable for unlocking areas and disabling traps. Finally there are a bunch of passive and active focus abilities that can augment Garret’s ability to stealth, pick locks, fight, and other useful thief-related things.
Playing through the game on highest difficulty, I kind of expected something akin to previous Thief games where I would be required to loot a certain percentage of the level’s treasures. Unfortunately, the new challenge system no longer requires that you meet specific requirements to complete a level. Instead, you receive bonuses for meeting certain criteria like “avoid detection” and “knock out X enemies”. The only overall requirement the game seemed to impose, even at the highest difficulty, was “don’t kill or knock out civilians”. So basically you can just zip through levels and avoid collecting any treasure if you want (not very thief-like!) Most of the upgrades are pretty useless for stealth playthroughs too as well as most of the arrows and tools.
Towards the end of the game I kind of stopped caring about looting places and picking pockets because, to me, the whole game started playing more like an action-fest than what Thief is supposed to be. Even exploring the hub areas for secrets and treasures is soured by the requirement of buying expensive rope arrows, only to find out that the loot you uncover barely covers the initial cost. This is essentially punishing the player for exploring levels, and a huge no-no for making a Thief game. The collectables system doesn’t even pay out until you’ve completed a set, further forcing the player into unnecessary debt from spending arrows to reach secret areas. The whiney female sidekick dream sequence levels didn’t do much to improve my mood either and probably could have been handled way better. Additionally, they decided that adding boss battles to Thief would be a good idea (it isn't).
Ultimately, I cannot recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of previous Thief games. If you’re completely new to the series, you probably won’t care and it’ll be another barely-memorable action game to you. Thief’s only saving grace is that it wasn’t AS bad of a game to its series as Absolution was to Hitman, but man, it’s not very far behind either.

If you are a fan of Panzer General or similar games, Panzer Corps is for you. Campaigns are decent, but the biggest deal here are THE GRAND CAMPAIGNS (unfortunately as a DLC, but if you'll buy them on other sites than Steam, it should be cheap). There are plenty of these grand campaigns because they are divided to west or east front and take place in a certain year. Although vanilla campaigns introduce a general overview of the conflicts, these grand campaigns, on the other hand, introduce more detailed and linked conflicts - for example, Stalingrad as part of GP '42 has 3/4 scenarios dedicated to this epic battle. Furthermore, you can import your core forces between the grand campaigns, so if you start at 39', in 45' your forces will be badass 5-start veterans with heroes and top-notch ritterkreuz. And trust me, you'll spend plenty of hours to reach 45' (currently I have 150+ hours and I haven't finished yet). Gameplay in GP is more dynamic - enemy actively counter attacks or renews offensive from edges of the map by bringing new forces, objectives can be more diverse than just simply capture a town.

Back in the 70's us old time gamers used to play Panzer Leader and Panzer Blitz - Avalon Hill produced table top board games for about 6-9 hours at a time, 2 hours just to get the game setup when you had 3 games combined with 3 players to make a massive battle. Pizza, beer and war! The Slitherine Panzer Corps is much like those killer strategy games but with much great features. The strategies logic by the computer is no slouch, not often do you find them easily baited into doing something stupid for you to capitalize on. Don't get me wrong 6 turn long flanking ambushes can still work but the real challenge to most of your missions is the number of turms you have to accomplish what you need, in many cases you don't have 5 or 6 turns to setup a pincer encirclement or backside flanking insert.
The units are very well balanced and the use of combined arms is rewarded with great success as it should be. Artillery cover and softening work well but unless you have air units in your mission your range is pretty limited without moving pieces into position - thus exposiing them in transport. Air units, when available are realistically limited to what they can do depending upon the weather - rain and snow making them  pretty impudent.
So who is going to get the most fun out of this series of game? Anyone who is an absolute strategist! If you like TBS or turn based strategy this a great game. The movement and reaction plays much like modern Xcom. Even if you are new to the genre of set piece TBS strategy it is very easy to learn the mechanics and a few of the strategies that work right away. The real challenge is getting your core group through each mission intact so that they gain the veterancy that makes them more OP in missions down the road. Truly, you wince when you lose a good level 13 tank that has been with you since it was a boot camp 10.
I especially like the downloadable content where the in game missions might take 3 missions to do a region and the download content lets you play that same time of war content in a much more detailed dozen or more missions. Always fun to invade Britain, who doesn't like that?
Great game for the modern strategist and us old dogs that fought the fight with carboard counters back in the day. RND was the dice we rolled baby!  Easy to stop in mid turn and take up where you left off next time. Great representation of the actual vehicles of the time, nothing seemed unbalancedthat I could find. The magic is in the way you mix up your inventory within the constraints (troop count and type of unit available at the time) and then exercise your best strategy and using them.
These graphics are not going you knock you off of your chair, but then, that's not what this is about.  Somewhat nostaligic, I think people would get a kick out of seeing how gaming used to be, back when my first computer was a Heathkit H89 and Commodore 64~

This is a great base game held back by designer wheraboosim on an incredible scale. If you enjoy rolling over things with Nazi armor, you'll have a great time. If you'd like to play as the groups that crushed the Nazis like a bug, such as the Americans, Soviets or British, you'll be fighting an enemy with many times the number of overstatted Panthers, Tigers and King Tigers than you get Shermans or T34s or Cromwells. And they'll do it while flooding the skies with more planes than you've ever seen outside of the Bagration mission.
Vastly more effort is spent on mission design and content for the Nazi campaigns. The Allied content is perfunctory at best.
The actual combat has issues too. Combat stats as reported by the game are largely lies. Your results are essentially random and incredibly spikey. A battle where you are likely to get 7 kills and no losses can flip to you losing 7 strength and the enemy losing nothing. While this is fine in large scale -- and much better designed -- operational wargames like Decisive Campaigns : Barbarossa, in games where your force count is a couple dozen at the end of the game the fate of an entire campaign can hinge on whether or not RNG decides to stuff a broom up up your rear and wiggle it around. I had one missions where I lost three units fortified on hills to enemy infantry that in the previous turn I was predicted likely to beat on the attack. Why? Because RNG hates me.
Order of Battle : WW2 is a much, much better game with much more predictable battles, a more complex game environment and a far better UI. It also doesn't descend into the unholy depths of Nazi tank wank like this game does.

Mini Metro is one of those games that is just deceptively simple, and yet can be quite challenging.
It's essentially a puzzle/simulator, with really simple mechanics of 'add some trains to lines' and 'get passengers from A to B quickly'. From the get-go, that doesn't seem very hard, but this game does a good job of ramping up the difficulty. By the time you've gotten to the more difficult levels, or are trying to complete the achievement challenges, you realize you need to consider a lot of problems and juggle lots of different possible configurations of lines and trains.
The graphics and sounds in this game match the simple premise, and help to avoid distracting you from the simulation at the base of the game. I did find that this made it hard sometimes to get the game to do what you wanted, like going around a river bend rather than using up a tunnel by going through it, but overall it works well.
Definitely worth playing if you're interested in transport/management simulator games.

Surprisingly solid low budget magic-oriented action RPG.  It feels like a mix of Diablo & NWN, except enemies don't respawn, you have direct control of your character and don't click to move.  You don't click on enemies either and must aim your spells.   Moving around using the wasd keys while moving the camera and aiming reticle with your mouse is very comfortable and fluid.  The story unfolds through cutscenes with still art, and there's full voice acting for quests and story.
There are three skill trees: Blood (close range), Soul (ranged) & Summoning magic.  You can buy skills in all three, but you use the same points from leveling up to enhance your attributes, so you have to plan somewhat.  Combat goes a bit slower than a hack & slash since it's more careful, but the game is paced so that there's never more than a few minutes without some type of action once you get past the beginning.
About 12 hours to do everything in the game.

You are given two different skill trees to draw from, one mainly dedicated to melee attacks, and the other to ranged (and a third set for summoning spells) and while you are free to invest in both, the damage of every spell in each set is governed by a separate attribute; therefore it seems most efficient to just pick one so as not to have to spread those attribute points too thin.

It's been a while since I've played, and I didn't play for long when I did. There's a reason for that. I don't want to trivialize what happened.
I started an average game with an average cast. Of them, one stands out in my memory: a soccer player who could run a bit faster than everyone else and who could carry a decent amount, too. He was my first pick for forays outside. Me and him, we were able to dart in and out of places easy, make deals with other survivors, and come back home safe.
That was, until one fateful night.
We went to what we thought was an abandoned house. Bit out of sorts, shelled, but still standing nonetheless. I walked up to the front door, thinking I'd greet any survivors and possibly work out a deal with them. In retrospect, I should've been more understanding when they pursued me, and I should've ran away instead of further into the map. Hell, at the end, I drew a knife I found on them and tried to defend myself. But their shotgun blew my soccer player away.
The man I had relied on was dead.
In my mind, there was only one thing left to do: retrieve his body and bring justice to those who murdered him. I returned to a shop I had been to earlier. They sold handgun parts, but I couldn't afford them, so I killed them. I killed a man's son in front of him while he cried for me to stop. Then I killed him.
I thought.
Of course, the young man I killed would've lived longer, but I omitted that.
I started omitting a lot of things, honestly.
After going back and systematically killing every member of the offending family that murdered my soccer player, I felt I had carried out justice. But that wasn't the end to this "justice". I went to a supermarket and found dirty raiders, looters, and bandits.
I mused.

And so they died, too. For justice.
As time went on, lives ended, and round after round was chambered, this perversion of justice came to a climax. I was down to one man. All the others had died in combat, including during raids on my home carried out by the families of those I killed. Honorable deaths, all of them. None of them like my soccer player. I armed my one man with an AK and stormed a hotel that was being used as a distribution hub for human trafficking. Many died. So did I.
I could have started another playthrough. I did, actually. But not far in I realized that I had already taken all I needed to learn from this game, and that playing it further would be - pardon the expression - an
to what I had learned.
It was at the end that I realized what this game was getting at: humans can rationalize a lot. Sure, I was detached from it all. I wasn't seeing through my eyes and smelling their blood and feces. But the decisions I made - for "justice" - were inherently flawed. In putting down what i thought to be monsters, I became one myself. And to uphold a moral, I broke it beyond recognition.
Good game.

Before I start my review, I have to say that I have played a number of Japanese Visual-Novels and have experience in the matter.
Rising Angels: Reborn. Is it a good visual novel? Yes.
To go into detail, I must say, the amount of detail in the dialogue is better than I expected from a free-to-play visual novel. The characters are believable. You feel that they are alive and that they mean something to you and not just some hollow arch-type character to move you along through the plot. The main story flows fluidly with the characters itself rather than the character-goes-here-for-the-plot type.
The music is decent. I mean, for a free-to-play, what do you expect? But, I do have some problems with some scenes in having the wrong kind of soundtrack to play in a heartwarming or first-clenching scenes. Other than that, it was okay.
But your main hook on this genre will not be the music, or the graphic (which is obviously CG drawn) or even the endings. Its the character development. You learn their history, their drive to their goal, their will. And you care for them across the story. With the amazing dialogue, I had no problem believing any of the hardships they went through together.
In the end, I was left feeling, "Wow, I wasn't expecting this good of an experience." And was satisfied with how the plot ends. I cared for the characters and even for the ones that died. It managed to enter my personal territory and made me feel sad with each hardship they go through. I want them to succeed and I cheered for them. All done without paying a single penny towards the developer. (Which made me feel sour at the end for enjoying such a good experience without paying a single penny)
You don't get a massive cliffhanger that makes you want to rip your goddamn hair off, but it leaves enough plot to settle for a sequel (which they are working on and is being funded in a kickstarter)
All in all, this was a Visual Novel worth of your 2-3 hour of spare time and definitely worth doing all the routes to all the ending. What's even great is it's free! (I wouldn't mind paying this for 5-10$ though)

The best word to describe this game is "unique". It plays like a point and click adventure, but while having pretty innovative gameplay and mechanics. Adding the lack of hand-holding throughout the game, it becomes a very memorable experience.
The big thing about The Sexy Brutale is time traveling, but in a Groundhog Day fashion. There are a lot of crimes to solve, a vast mansion full of hidden passages, and killers roaming around the place. I won't take my description any further, because part of the enjoyment comes from figuring out what is happening and how you can approach the game.
+ Graphics: although they are 3d, thanks to the perspective they play like a SNES RPG. Good stuff across the board
+ Music, and the sound loops in particular: they are perfect, and never feel repetitive
+ Character design: very charming, and some funny dialogue
+ Gruesome elements
~ It is a slow game. There is a teleport feature, highly appreciated after a while, but even that is not enough. You can get bored during your last couple hours walking throughout the mansion.
~ The map feature is really good, but it is missing blocked pathways
- Stuttering from room to room: some room transitions are smooth, and others freeze the game for a second. I guess it has to do with pre-loading different mansion chunks, but I have found moments were I can walk while the room and the transition has not even completed. I thought it was my machine, but after watching some let's-plays on yt, they have the same stuttering in some specific rooms.
- Odd control decisions: having one button for seeking and another to stop seeking, you can't WASD, so you have to right-click to move around, then left click to execute an action not available to register until you get there...
The Steam Controller "start press" and "release press" events are your friend on this one
8/10

They've taken the original Panzer General and produced a modern(-ish) version of it. More detail, more units, bigger maps, more scenarios. If you're a fan of map-based, turn-based WW2, go buy it. It's excellent.

First, ignore any review that mentions this not being like other Total War games as a negative. It is not meant to be.
It is also not pay to win, because there is no winning, and the wait times for things like growing crops and such are a few hours, perfectly reasonable for this type of game.
Now for my review. To put it briefly, good idea but needs work. The game essentially tries to combine elements of Total War, Civilization, and farmville-style games into one. The problems?
1. the Total War element, the battles, are terrible. Wayy to basic and repetetive, battle maps are too small. Not fun. Also the rewards are so minimal there is little incentive to do them.
2. There is no purpose, drive to the game. No reason to push forward and in that sense the farmville-style element of it is a little too strong.
For the above two reasons, I would not recommend this game. As I play this, I really just get the urge to play Total War or Civilizations, it does not do what it should to mesh these game types together in a way that can stand alone.

You play as a hero trying to defeat Dredmor; starting with a build of 7 skills and your wits you delve into the dungeons ready to fight whatever monsters you meet and collect a wide variety of items that can be useful (or not) in your quest. The large number of skills to pick from, as well as the insane number of stats to investigate give thee player the ability to customize their character beyond what anyone could consider rational. But thats the fun of it, after all!

Main con is its instability from time to time. Could use a bit more work on the backend but Gaslamp Games has since moved on to solely working on Clockwork Empires, so don't expect it anytime in the near future (or at all, but never say never!)

Rising Angels: Reborn is a second novel in Rising Angels series. If you wish to know more about the world and backstory you can get the first novel, Rising Angels: The Red Rose, as well as other games kind of set in same universe directly from developer's website:
I played Rising Angels: Reborn before and wrote a small review back then. Republishing it here with small changes.
---------------------
I applaud to the artist who did character sprites - he or she had to work with the relatively big cast of nine characters and did a marvellous job. Each character identified by distinct silhouette using different body shapes, poses and features like ears, horns and wings. Sprites utilize poses and body language to convey information about the person, like Zuri is almost always shown in positions that imply motion or Stan often drawn covering his mouth with his hand in a gesture subconsciously associated with lying. I think wings were superfluous for character's design - they take too much screen space and people who have wings could be easily recognized without them - but it looks like each race appearances were already defined in earlier novel drawn by another artist and it's too late to change something now.
In contrast to character sprites backgrounds look nice and clean, but also grey and unimpressive and there is too few of them, but it's understandable because most of action happens on board of a small spaceship. Game could definitely use more CGs as well; few CGs present are somewhat bland and characters appear noticeably different from their usual sprites. Also, if story takes place on a spaceship, it's almost necessary to show how this ship looks from outside, but I guess nobody in development team could do mechanical design.
Music clearly was professional - it sounded like something I could hear before in some games or movie trailers. Perhaps it was licensed from some recording studio. Any sound effects are sadly missing. Adding little sound: footsteps, gunshots, "woosh" of spaceship door would only help immersion.
The list of races itself is more what I expect to see in some Star Trek fanfic written by a schoolgirl, not standalone serious work of science fiction: generic fantasy races, angels and demons, furry people - all together in space. Just like in Star Trek, critically important ship personnel are sent with away teams to investigate dangerous planets, apparently unarmed. At least no officers were killed during planetary missions, despite all of them except one wearing red shirts.
However, even if Rising Angels series started as mere fanfic, it came a long way and Reborn deserves being distributed through Steam.

What I expected: A "locked-room" (mansion) mystery adventure, with a twist, in an interesting setting and with an excellent and colourful artstyle.
What I got: Exactly that, and a whole lot more. The game is simply captivating with its interesting characters, great soundtrack, beautiful art and interesting progression from one "murder" to another.
It's a bit reminiscent of the "No Naku Koro Ni" VN/anime series, especially Umineko, where the protagonist is trying to find a serial killer in a large mansion by reliving the events over and over again until the mystery has been solved. Especially here, when you really get attached to these interesting characters, seeing (and hearing) them get murdered over and over again as you reverse time is really interesting and a tad bit unsettling.
It is a story-centered, medium-length (some would say short) game that, granted, doesn't have huge replay value. Like with most mystery and detective games, once you learn the "jist" of the game, in this case "whodunit", and solve the simple yet memorable puzzles, you're not likely to go for a second playthrough right away. Yes, it is very difficult to replicate the experience you had the first time, but experiencing the game even once, in my opinion, is worth it.
Biggest pleasant surprises: The soundtrack. Holy moly is it good. I also got really attached to all the characters even though originally I thought they were just some masked party-goers. Only after finishing the game and "digesting it" a bit do I realise what a great job the devs did.
Main problem is: I want more. Please let there be more! There's so many interesting things you can do with this artstyle, setting and gameplay mechanic (locked-room mystery and rewinding time), so here's hoping!

The puzzles arent all that hard to solve, the hard(er) part is simply finding all the parts you need as all items have a circle around them to let you know you can interact with them in some way.

The click and hold to move does not work too well and it probably would fare better if it had a normal point and click format. However I think with a controler this complaint would no longer hold.
The graphics serve their purpose and I found myself really liking them. The only texture that I had a problem with was Bloody Girl's texture. I honesly cannot figure out wether the graphics are glitching or if thats the way the developers wanted it.
My favorite part of this game, for once, is probably the music. The music of the game is probably what influenced me to actually go out and buy it. It has this nice jazzy feel to it and it fits the tone of how the party should be, and as the murders start happening it slowly turns much darker and mysterious.
While this game was not too challanging I would still find myself recomending it for the overall tone of the game and my personal love of mystery games.

A lot of the reviews for this game seems to consist of people reading the words "Total war" followed by installing the game without further looking in to the game. they enter the game, noticing that it is NOT a total war game, followed by a negative review. I myself entered this game after looking through pictures, who developed it, and what its purpose is, and i find the game exellent for that.
First of all, its not a total war game. its a total war: battles game wich is a spin of series developed by a different team then the people making shogun, rome, etc. they where aiming to create a "click on stuff and wait" game that was designed to be a bit "more", for people like my self who enjoy more advanced games as most titles from thhis genre tend to be a bit bland.
At this the game succeeds heavily. With things such as crafting units you otherwise have to pay real money for, and battles that include a lot of real time management this game manages to stand out, and i myself finds it the best in its genre from what i've seen so far. My only hopes are that when they finally introduces the "Campaign". it will resempble something like Strongholds: kingdoms inviting cooperation with friends and true wars against other players.
To summon up my review: Try the game, and don't judge it for its in-game transactions, because there is not one game in this genre that does not have them. Its how they work and without them it wouldn't be a free game.

2023 Turkey Simulator
Point and click masterpiece.

Recommended for those are into survival- simulation, time management and high replayability value.
Note : I buy this recently, with the Anniversary Edition update included.

1. Control and Gameplay : point and click game, with some "panic system" at times. Minimum loading screen. Autosave system. Even at high res setting, it does not lag. Quite realistic and easy to learn.
2. Fun Factor : I am not quite amused by timed- management games, but it give me adequate times to think and act wisely. Will get used to quickly deciding actions in just a minute.
3. Graphic : Unique sketchy and black-and-white-ish artwork is really suited the gloomy and mellow war atmosphere. The small details is impressive, but limited variations on item designs.
4. Replayability Value : you have custom mode stories and more content could be downloaded at workshop
Nice bonus for adding a surprise free update/dlc after 3 years of release date (the anniversary mode- add new locations and npcs).
5. Sound : nothing spectacular, but the music fits the theme well.
6. Story : fresh point of view, quite uncommon to play as the victims (while usually we get used to FPS as the soldiers).
7. Value for Full Price : to support the great indie developers out there, why not? But honestly, it's quite overpriced for college student like me. And also, I am interested to pay the dlc (which 10% of it is a charity) with the price gap in sale.
Thank you for reading!

If being drawn into the unfairly destroyed lives of war victims, and tasked with making critical decisions about where and what to scavenge and craft, one day after another, has any interest to you, then here you are. Do you go for medicine today, or food? Do you need more gun parts for self-defense against bandits, or might you not get enough wood for your heater, risking freezing to death? Every day is a life or death challenge for your survivors, and it can really weigh on you.

Welcome to The Sexy Brutale, an extravagant mansion and casino where in the midst of a grand masquerade party something far more sinister is afoot. This is one of my favourite puzzle games. You play as Lafcadio Boone who is trying to prevent the murders of The Sexy Brutale's guests at the hands of the staff, but there are a few catches. First of all, the day is on a loop. The day's events replay over and over again as everyone does the exact same thing without even realizing it. That is, until you come along of course. The second catch is that you can't directly interfere with the guests or the staff. Thus you have to find more subtle ways of saving the guests' lives. This results in a really fun puzzle game where you have to piece together the day's events while manipulating objects around the mansion in order to change them. You're a bit like a detective, except instead of solving a murder you're trying to stop one. And with each guest saved you gain a new power that adds another tool to your toolbox.
The Sexy Brutale is also gorgeous. The character designs are all very distinct with unique personalities. Plus if you like seeing some interesting and appropriately dramatic deaths, then this is the game for you. The music is also worth mentioning, because not only is it fantastic it fits the game perfectly. Each section of The Sexy Brutale has its own song, and because you're trapped in a loop the song syncs with the events of that area. What results is a heart-racing experience as you scramble to save the guest's life in time while the music ramps up in the background.
The only downside is that this is a short game. This isn't necessarily a bad thing as it means it doesn't overstay is welcome, but it is something to consider. In my opinion the length is mainly due to the difficulty of the puzzles. While difficulty is subjective, especially for a puzzle game, I didn't think they were very difficult. Overall I think I had more trouble with getting my timing down than I did trying to figure out what to do. My first playthrough took about 5 hours, and I did take my time to explore beyond the main objectives.
All that said, I had so much fun with this game. Every second I spent playing was well worth it, and I highly recommend this to anyone looking for a stylish puzzle game that won't have them rage quitting over the difficulty.

Having finished all the achievements, and clocked just about 505 hours on it, I think I am done with this game.
So why the thumbs down, you ask?
I started playing because I used to be into Magic the Gathering when I was younger. The Story mode was quite decent and kept me going for some time. Not gonna lie, expanding my collection, building decks, getting to the top of the ladder,
it was all quite fun for some time. I also quite enjoyed playing coop (two headed giant) mode with my friends, despite connectivity issues.
Unfortunately, the current state of the game is something I can't honestly recommend. There are bugs that haven't been fixed for over a year, we only get half the cards from new expansions, most people disconnect right at the beginning of the match. Even the story mode which drew me into the game is a disappointment, featuring unwinnable missions due to bugs. It's not really the developer's fault, as I imagine they are terribly underpaid and underfunded.
It's a shame, cause this game could have been so much more.
Since then, I moved on to other F2P digital card games that are available on steam. Since then, I can't spark any more love for Magic Duels. In comparison, this game feels sluggish, unoptimized and has poor interface for just about everything.  It speaks volumes when one would rather use an external site for deckbuilding.
That said, having completed the last achievement for this game, it's time for me to say goodby. Not to say all those 505 hours were a waste, quite the contrary, but I sincerely hope the next digital variant of Magic the Gathering will get the required level of attention from Wizards of the Coast.
