Having been a long time player of the SSI classic Panzer General as well as its Pacific and Allied versions I was actually rather surprised I had missed this game when it first came out. But man this was certainly worth the wait.
While the graphics aren't much to write home about and the fact it doesnt run directX or OpenGL (which means the steam overlay wont be happening) (sorry folks) they do pay a lovely homage to the Graphics of Panzer General 1 and 2,Allied General and Pacific General.
while the premise is you are a new panzer group leader the story really doesn't deviate from history except in a few cirumstances where you are able to make some decisive victories which in turn will alter the campaign. Operation Sea Lion? Check, Invasion and take over of the good old US of A? Check. Taking India from the British Empire?Check being able to take Moscow from the reds before general winter arrives?Check.
Another interesting feature I have noticed so far is the inclusion of a Core Force mechanic ie you have a group of units that you carry over from scenario to scenario which means they get experience take losses etc etc which is very handy because I think some of the later scenarios if I didn't have a core force that was what it was I would have been hurting pretty badly. Multiplayer is not directly head to head but goes back to the old days of multiplayer in strat games by way of PBEM (yes there is local hot seat so you could play against a friend in person on one computer but where is the fun and anticipation in the wait for emails?The Opening of that email when you get home from work or school and see your partner finally emailed you his turn so you can now give it a look and hopefully throw his entire plan out of the water?
verdict? while yes it is every pricey once you get in to the domain of its DLC's the game is worth every penny as there are also a decent amount of modding sites on the web that contain additional scenarios,campaigns and even full conversions.

A very solid war game that has a myriad of addons. The base game has you controlling German Panzer forces through a series of scenarios that cover the war. If you complete them within a certain turn limit then the campaign branches into some "What if" scenarios.  I personally found the turn crunch my least favorite part of the game.
The unit scale seems to be maybe company level, but its not entirely clear. The distances of each hex is once again unclear.
Which is fine, the game abstracts a lot and that keeps it simple, the game maybe falling a little short of being a "hard core" wargame. But at the same time its pacing is nice, and the tactical thinker is rewarded.
I've gotten the most mileage out of the "Allied Corp" expansion though I do look forward to trying Soviet Corp when the time is right. Allied Corp, the AI is fairly scripted which makes save scumming the generals greatest weapon. The RNG is a wee bit to wild at times, and you will watch inexpilicable things happen like motorcycle troops beating tanks in open desert.
On sale this game is a total steal, and to be perfectly honest if you enjoy turn based wargames this price is worth it at full price.

Thief 2014 is a stealth based game developed by Edios Montreal and published by Square Enix. The game was released in 2014 as one of the entry titles on the next gen consoles while also being released on PS3, 360 and of course, Steam. This is the fourth instalment in the Thief series.
You take control of a thief named Garrett, and play in a first person perspective. Having only previously placed the other games in the series sparsely, I was going into this game with no real feelings about the franchise, other than I had heard great things.  The main aim of the game is to complete objectives in a stealthy manner. Each of the chapters has more than one route that you can take. Each level is also full with guards patrolling the grounds in order to try and catch you out. You are able to distract the guards in many ways, such as throwing bottles to grab their attention, blowing out candles, opening doors etc. On top of a heavy amount of guards, you also have to deal with another kind of enemy, dogs and birds. I have never seen so many birds in cages in a game before; but the idea behind it is, you have to be extra sneaky around the bird cage, or else you will startle the bird and it will start squawking – this bringing attention to yourself. I thought this was a really original idea that adds that extra level of depth to the game play.
Whilst you are sneaking around, you will find plenty of opportunities to steal items, these items are instantly converted to an amount of gold, which you can then buy extra supplies with, such as different arrows, or passive stat increases such as health. Whilst the game is a stealth based game, there may still be moments where you have to use combat; the bow and arrow aspect of the combat system works really well, with an abundance of different types of arrows to choose from, you will always have something for the specific moment. Where the game’s combat lets it down, is the melee; the controls seem really off and it essentially turns into a button mashing competition with anyone you are in a fight with. I know that combat isn’t supposed to be used in this game, but why it is there, and it should be of a decent standard if it is going to be used.  Like I said, the majority of the game play is stealth based, but a good portion of the game also uses the a parkour system; it felt like a poor man’s version of Assassin’s Creed when this was forced on me, there is actually an entire level based on this system which grew really boring very quickly.  Where this game does well though, is the really in depth stealth mechanics, making use of light and sound perfectly.
Thief was one of the first big titles to be released in the next gen market, so as expected; the graphics are of a high standard. I couldn’t quite push out a 4k resolution, but I was playing at 1440p and the is awesome. The lighting in the game is done perfectly, and as it is such a key part of the gameplay, it should be! As PC gamers will probably face more commonly now, the gameplay actually looks better than cut scenes.  Water is also a key element of the game, and that too looks really good. Animation of all characters is done superbly as well.
The game has varying levels of difficulty, the settings are chosen at the start of the game, with no option to change mid-way through your story mode, so you should choose wisely. The difficulty does take a rather high curve towards the latter stages of the game, but nothing that cannot be outweighed by the skills you have learned up to that point. The higher difficulty you pick, you will also be impaired with certain flaws too; such as enemies being more aware, and your energy bars now regenerating in between chapters.  I would have liked the option to change the difficulty on an adhoc basis, as doing it this way may encourage players to just play on the lowest difficulty and not really have any problems completing the game.
Whilst this can is often referred to as an open world, it isn’t as open world as some games such as Skyrim or Fallout. Yes there is a city in which your hide out is located in, and you are able to explore it to your hearts content in between levels, but once you explore it once, there isn’t any real need to go digging again. The base city is small, so even that doesn’t take long to look around. The game does have a couple of side quests which you can do in between chapters to, these are a good way to earn a little extra gold and to squeeze a couple more hours of content out of the story mode. As you can probably guess though, a lot of the side missions are simply fetch quests, since you are their hired thief.
The single player story mode took me just over ten hours to complete on a medium difficulty, I only did a handful of the side missions, as they did start to become very repetitive after a while, but I did take every opportunity to explore levels up and down trying to find collectables.  I felt the length of the game to be satisfying without ever feeling like I was being cut short of content at any point.  This is one of the few single player only games that I will say has a fair bit of reply ability, you can replay missions to complete challenges in them, such as finding all of the loot, or not being discovered by guards, and you could also simply replay the game on a higher difficulty and trying to finish it with the self-imposed handicaps from the start. So you can probably get roughly 20-25 hours out of Thief if you really get into it.
No major technical issues were found whilst playing; the game was running at a smooth 60 fps the entire time, with the resolution high and graphics cranked all the way up to full.  The game has full controller support, but I don’t know why you’d want to use it when the controls fit keyboard and mouse perfectly.
My conclusion is that if you go into this game just expecting a modern day stealth game, you will get a lot of enjoyment out of it. The only reviews I have seen that have put this game down, are ones which have the nostalgic connection to the series, whilst this isn’t a bad thing, it just doesn’t do this game any favours. This is just a modern day version of the game, and in my opinion, is a thrilling experience. The regular price of £19, 99 is OK, if you plan on replaying the game at least once to try out challenges or different difficulties, if you just want to see the story through, then you may just want to wait for it to drop below the £10 mark.

I really don't understand some of the criticism leveled at it, as far as I can tell you always have plenty of words to defeat the level; when I finish I don't think I have ever had less than 100 unfound words and I wouldn't be surprised if it was never less than 200 (the game tells you). If I failed a level usually all I needed was to find 1-3 of those words - hardly an impossible challenge. The review also made me expect to lose a lot of progress by randomly being dealt impossible letters - certainly I am sometimes dealt difficult letters, but the levels are what? 1 minute each?
I got this game in part because it looked like bookworm adventures (popcap), which I was fond of. I don't find it as good, but still, it has some of that charm.
One thing that may make this game much worse for many people is that it appears to be balanced for someone like me - someone with at least a moderate scrabble vocabulary. This is very different than having a good vocabulary, because it relies on using words that are in the dictionary but aren't really used. Like aas. Computer word games generally are much too easly for me because they are balanced for real vocabulary and someone with this artificial category dominates it. I can well imagine that someone who just likes anagramming and has even an excellent vocabulary but hasn't learned a bunch of the stupid 'scrabble' words would have to grind too much.
This is also very reliant on speed - which many people playing word games are not as keen on.
So: If you like fast anagramming and have a reasonable scrabble vocabulary - you will almost certainly like this. If you like word games but don't want the stress of a speed experience, steer clear. If your scrabble vocabulary is weak you might need to grind more than you want to; for you then it would depend whether you like the challenge level of the grind. A grind is only bad if you don't like the underlying activity, if you like it then it is "playing the game".
I wish I had known:
Use the keyboard, not the mouse. I think it would be impossible to play this for long with the mouse. You can access your power ups with '1', '2', '3, etc.
You can't earn stars the first time you play a level no matter how well you do. You must play it a second time against slightly stronger monsters - and often have to finish it without taking any damage.
Developers: If you develop this further it would be great to have a 4+ letter word mode. I wouldn't want this mode to necessarily be harder so it would need rebalancing, it is just a drag to slog through the three letter words every time, I would rather have a bit more time and be forced to find longer words.
Fun spelling game, though there are times when you have to go back just to gear up enough to move forward. Unless you get a lucky set of letters that you can just rock.
Ignore the haters. This game is legit.

Item management and upgrading can be the key to win a tough, close round. There is plenty of strategy even, so long as you manage your Letter/(spell) pool to your advantage. Something tells me as i get further, this will be more important than just spamming any words you see when you see them. You get different equipment and can upgrade your Hats, Robes, and Wands, each bit of equipment coming with different effects. Whats good about this though, is old equipment doesn't immediately obsolete by unlocking the newer gear, like in most fantasy games. There is strategic ways you can use their effects in a mixed set. I recommend this game to anyone who likes games like boggle, or spelling games in general, but especially to those that enjoy fantasy based games, because it also does quite well with those aspects, and ties the two together in a pretty seamless and fun manner. Quite addictive. And over 200 levels to play with tough bosses on each 10th floor. Definitely what I was hoping for out of this game. It was a great idea.

Written in the Sky is extremely short as far as visual novels go. The reader is given a look into three days of Azure's life as she goes through the daily drag of high school. It's made immediately clear that Azure, an 18(?) year old girl, dislikes school, but we're given a little insight into why - her father works long hours (present only to reprimand her for her behavior at school) and she longs for his approval or his attention. Her characterization ends there.
Azure is a truant who was raised by a single father - a world-class detective - and one day, after being scolded by her father and sneaking out of her home, she happens across a mysterious and powerful alien ring. This ring puts her in the sights of the equally mysterious and powerful Sienna - a woman who claims to be from mars. Sienna's characterization ends there.
The reader is given no agency over the development of the story and the art is nothing to really talk about - the father himself isn't even given a character sprite, even despite being a major player as far as story/character development goes. The porn is mediocre at best. The story fails to make the reader want to care about any of the characters or events. It ends on a cliffhanger - or rather, a very vague hint at things to come. If this story is a prologue to something else then it falls short of making the reader care want more, aside from handwaving everything away as "terrible things happened because militants" which itself is never really explained.
There are many more questions raised than answered, which is frustrating considering it could have been developed in many different ways. It's a worthwhile read only if you have thirty minutes to burn and really want two achievements.

Where to start...
Honestly, this is normally not the type of game I would play, let alone buy, but for some reason the premise grabbed my attention and the sale pushed me over the edge. I ended up finishing the game in one go.
It's basically a murder mystery game with a time-travel gimmick and a strangely light and comedic atmosphere, despite the very grim premise. The graphics are colorful, pretty and stylish, the music is perfectly complementary, and the writing is witty and quite good.
At some points it can be hard to figure out what to do or where to find what you need since you're given minimal direction and you're up against a ticking clock, but I feel that adds to the mystery and the mechanics encourage trial and error.
As far as replay value goes considering the relatively short length of the game, I have not yet touched it since finishing it the first go but I suppose that for the completionists among us it pays to play it multiple times (e.g. the first playthrough to figure out what to do, the second or maybe third to find all collectables). I suppose much of the dialogue may also find deeper meaning on consequetive playthroughs.
I found it a great little distraction from the more action- and fighting-oriented games.
I guess the trial and error mechanics and short length also make it quite casual-friendly, so I would also deem it suitable for those that look for a more casual gaming experience.
Tl;dr: Not a big game, but a great bang for your buck.

Mini Metro is a great game that has given me hours of fun. I bought it in a recent Humble Bundle for it specifically and after a few hours I'm comfortable giving it a thumbs up, despite the criticisms that I am now about to lay out.
My first caution is that, while the game is well designed and enjoyable, its content is a little thin for the sticker price of $10. There are 12 cities, and while there are some unique quirks between them, the only other practical difference is where the rivers are located. Most end up playing pretty close to the same way. It will still take you a while to invent and explore all the possible strategies for building your metro, but after about 10 hours I found my interest waning as there wasn't much else to spice things up. The three game modes help in this regard.
That said, what content is there makes for quite a challenge. It's a perfect example of a game that gives you a small set of tools that can be combined to make incredibly complex systems.
I also see some room for improvement with the UI. I like the game's minimalist graphics, but the interface takes this a shade too far. There were a few things that bothered me:
1. Trains/carriages are a bit hard to see, being the same color and only slightly larger than the tracks, and often obscured by other objects. It's very difficult to see where everything is at a glance. Something to help them stand out, like a black outline, would be a big help.
2. The stations have the opposite problem. They stand out well, but they're all the same color, differentiated only by shape. It's easy to lose track of where specific stations are since many look alike.
3. Some more feedback in the UI would be nice (at least in sandbox mode, if it would make things too easy on normal/expert). Perhaps some summarized info about each line, like number of passengers waiting, number of trains/carriages active, average wait time. There's a stats page that has some of this info, but it's on a separate screen several clicks away.
4. Speaking of the stats page, the minimalist design doesn't work so well there. Having to mouse over each data point to see numbers does not for easy reading make.
In conclusion, Mini Metro is a simple but deep game that plays pretty much as advertised. Perhaps a bit lacking in content for full price, but still a solid pick for anyone who likes puzzle/strategy type sims.
Edit: The more I play this game, the more I crave more features. I love the challenge but it's actually kind of frustrating how many times I think "gosh it would be nice if I could do X to make my metro more efficient", but alas, X is beyond the scope of gameplay. This really is perfect as a casual, pick-up-and-play mobile game, but if you're used to more in-depth sim type games, proceed with caution.

The medieval/steampunk setting is immersive, thanks to a great shadow usage, skilful design and gloomy colors.
The main story is quite short and "unsalted" but always great in places and background happenings. The severely intricated city, which is the mission hub, is the soul of the game.
Optional client jobs, secondary missions and break-ins are the way to actually feel the thief essence: this is a game to be explored, as every corner can hide a lever or a secret passage, and information gathering is crucial.
Game mechanics are not perfectly refined as in Dishonored, and the sound (which is of good quality) is affected by some bugs, but the sense of realism and immersion in the atmosphere of Thief is deep and catching.
88/100

First off i played this game for a very long time. Back when it was on alaplaya and after that on Pro7/Sat1. So my experience is build on at least several years.
Let's start with the Lvl-ing.
It's grindy. Not the soft type of grind, it's the hardcore one. Quests are rare after Level 40 (max is 99). You have to grind at least 60/70% every time. This means of doing the same thing over hundreds of hours to reach a higher level.
The PvE-Part of this game is boring. It enterly build of grinding. Even the quests are grinde quests and give a little amount of Exp. Sometimes it's better and faster to skip the quests and just grind.
But the grind doesn't stop at the land part. See is even worse. After level 31 you have to level 1v1 on Sea. Aoe-ing is quite hard because of the lack of melee monsters at sea. Also, the often so praised part "sea" in florensia, is more curse then blessing. Most of the skills are irrelevant cause you gonna 1v1 with the torpedo ship anyway. Also some Aoe's on sea are just copy-paste of land aoe's (wrath of earth).
PvP:
PvP is suprisingly fun in florensia. Extended wars in Droes (and other warzones) and HoW (battle arena) are quite fun and engrossing. Sadly HoW is currently inactive (for more then 1 1/2) years now. Thats pretty sad cause PvP is the only end game content florensia has.
Another bad part of pvp is the cash-side. PvP is enterly P2W. The upgrade system is pure luck and cash reliant. If you dont cash real money you will be left behind.
Money:
The prices in the Ap-Shop (cash shop) in florensia are bold. To pay atleast 20 euros for 1 single dress is common. If you buy upgrade items, success isn't guaranteed and it just feels like throwing your money out of the window.
The Publisher (GiF) and the Producer (aha):
It's a mess. Since the restart they didn't add anything new to the game (in a span of 2 years). The new dungeons are just copy paste of old one's, the marriage system is buggy, cash reliant, and destroyed most part of the pvp and deathlines are just a fantasy product. The community isn't involved in anything. There are lot's of feedback thread's in the forum but non of the feedback get's into the production, it's a farce. They pretend to care but in the end they will do what they want (even if its bad for the game)
All in all i can say if you like anime inspired games, with a heavy grind factor, a publisher that just doesn't care and are willingly to pay high amounts of money (500 euro+) to be good in pvp, this is your game. Not even sarcastic, some ppl. like to pay to be good.
The community and the game itself are quite good, it's a little one but you almost know everybody and feels just way more personal than any other mmorpg, where you are just one anonymous being amoung many others, florensia just had always the misfortune to fall into greedy hands. The desing of the weapons and some location's are quite astounding even for the old graphic's. If you like to have a personal and emotional binding, don't want to play pvp it's maybe fitting for you, but if you want to compete in pvp without paying you should look for something other

Right, so I've played this game for a rough total of 4 years, and have literally put thousands of hours into this game.
I've played without, and with microtransactions so I have knowledge from both sides.
It's a great game to play with friends, when there's a community. Unfortunately, there isn't one anymore. It's dead.
The first 15 levels are easy. But after that, everything is a grind. While grinding can be fun, gathering the same set of mobs, aoeing them, waiting 2 minutes, and repeating for hours-on-end isn't fun. And I ended up being level 95/40 (You can go up to level 99 land and 64 on sea, 2 separate types).
Sea is abysmal. The moving is flawed, everything's buggy, there's multiple, multiple clientside issues that makes it so disappointing and appalling to play. It's a notoriously disliked and hated feature of the game, trust me. You can ask any experienced player about their opinion of sea, and I guarantee you the majority of people will hate it. It's often we actually pay other people to account share and level up for us because it's that abysmal and we like to force it on someone else (It's against the rules, but that's literally simply just how bad it is).
The only attraction Land has is killing bosses, which gets boring in its own time extremely fast. Because you don't get loot of insanely cool "high level armours" at all. There's no "promising rewards" like mounts or anything impressive you see from the likes of MMO's, it's just casual armour that everyone gets ahold of. What makes it special is how well you upgrade it, and hey guess what! That's where microtransactions come into play. Because otherwise it's very, very difficult to upgrade to even +6, and after getting your item to +3 it can break without using a protection item (which is more money! Woohoo!). Oh did I mention that there's 15 upgrade levels per item? And to get one to maybe +10 alone can cost about £150's worth of microtransactions? Yeah, you tell me this game isn't a cash-grabber.
The only endgame attraction at this point is PKing, which is dead now due to the severe lack of players. Literally all anyone does after they've hit the high level now is just sit AFK in town all day waiting for a war to begin so we can have a war which lasts about 20 minutes before someone gives up. So really, you won't even get any enjoyment out of that because there's nothing to do!
The community is absolutely horrific, if you want people as clueless as a stereotypical Hillary Clinton supporter with the mental capacity of a stereotypical Donald Trump supporter who can only insult you and make excuses, then congratulations! You've found your mothership!
There's legitimately no endgame content, there is no thriving community, the promises of bugfixes haven't been met, the class balancing will never happen because there's no time spent on it. The only thing considered is microtransaction promotions, which I get are necessary. But please, make a game to complement and make use of them.
The game's economy is a joke, you've no hope of ever catching up to prices unless you spend real money or grind constantly for a month or 2 to even amount to the point of making some money. And then you have to actually grind to make it, and that'll take long enough on its own due to the economy being so damn ruined.
There's no drag to keep players in, it's difficult to pick up unless you've a friend with experience to tutor you. Nothing is clear, and a lot of translations are flawed which confuses and disorients any new player, so it's very much not friendly to new players in the slightest.
The game needs a lot of reworking, and the promises can only fall on deaf ears at this point because it's notoriously known to the current/old players that it will never happen. The promises have been made countless times, and they won't be hit.
As an Ex-QAT for this game, I can tell you that the testing system is also extremely flawed, the developers really don't have much of a clue what they're doing in the absolute slightest. Trust me, it's really not worth investing into this game at this point. Unless there was suddenly a huge influx of active players there's really no hope beyond this point.
Considering LuxPlena is supposed to be the largest server, with the most channels. I think overall there is a significantly disappointing less than 200 players in the higher bracket of levels currently active, and I do not exaggerate that at all. There are many more, but we've all long quit.
The rules also often contradict themselves, and the support team is also terrible. There's a lot of room for gray area, so you never quite know when you are and aren't breaking a rule, and you can get banned for the most stupid and simple of things.
Trust me. Look elsewhere. This is not what you want.

tl;dr below
Alright, I don't know where to start.
I've played this game (when it wasn't on steam) for longer than I'd like to admit.
Let's start with something positive:
The game doesn't require a good computer, nor does it require a mediocre one. It just requires anything that goes by the definition of a computer. I'm pretty sure you could run this game on a potato powered computer. On highest settings.
Next positive thing might be that it is free to play. So you don't need to spend any money on it, right?
Let's get to the point.
The game isn't good, like at all. Graphics are terrible (I mean, this game launched around 2005 or something and they didn't update any visuals since then).
The story is nonexistent, there are no cutscenes and no story quests, but quests always have a wall of text (with no voice over -  you can read, don't you?).
The Community (at least on german servers) is made of 33% trolls, 33% 40-year-olds and 34% unfriendly people whose only purpose is to ruin your experience/mood/day.
The gameplay consists of land combat, which, at a certain level, only consists of grinding random enemies for hours, and sea combat, which is probably the most boring thing I (and many others) have ever done. Its the same from level 1 on, no changes, no progression, just braindead killing enemies with one. single. spell. for hours.
PvP in this game is pretty much the most unbalanced thing this game has to offer. 10s stuns with no counterplay, every other stun has a 40% chance to fail, you gear up for evasion, so PvP is pretty much being lucky or getting stomped by any Noble class. (Or getting oneshot by a sniper)
In addition to that, there is something called "fusion" which adds stats to your gear (10 per piece) if you pay for it. Hands down the worst feature of the game. Rich people will just run around with 10 additional stats per piece (which you've got 5 of) and just stomp anything who's got less.
Character/Equipment progression is purely money based. Not ingame money, real money. It's pretty much impossible to upgrade your gear to an acceptable level without either spending hundreds of €/$ or farming for hundreds of hours straight (And I'm not exaggerating on that one, trust me.) Oh, and did I mention that any gear that gets you some valuable stats either costs money or tons of ingame currency? No? There you go, bud.
And don't get me started on updates/maintenances. It took the publisher aroung 6 months from first announcement that Steam was coming "soon" to actually releasing it. The relaunch back in 2015 got delayed by 4 months. Anything's prettymuch delayed or not coming at all. (I'm looking at you, fifth isle)
So what's left of the game? Pets are kinda cute, I guess.
tl;dr
If you hate yourself, communities and people in general but love braindead grinding for hours, boy do I have a game for you!
If you like a good game, with a great story, a helpful community and nice graphics, well, go play something else.

The Sexy Brutale is one part puzzle game, one part adventure game, with a bit of stealth mechanics put in for good measure. However, in a lot of ways, what brings it all together for me is the game's art design, which has the look & feel of some of the quirky, unique games that you'd find during the PS2-era, but with bit more of a modern polish to it. This isn't something that is seen very often nowadays, and it feels pretty refreshing compared to other games out there nowadays, especially considering the high quality of the menus & UI, which tend to feel like an afterthought in many other modern games.
Overall, The Sexy Brutale is an intriguing game which not only feels well made, with a great sense of visual and audio design, but also with unique and original game mechanics. I would recommend it to fans of puzzle games and adventure games, or to anybody who is just looking for something fun & unique.

It's exactly what it is advertised to be.  A "how many words can you make" game with an RPG and timing gimmick.  It's very similar to the old Bookworm Adventures game from PopCap, which is not a bad thing.
You're given a set of 10 pseudo-randomly generated tiles that you will use to make words.  Your character marches from the left of each level towards the right, stopping whenever he reaches a new enemy.  A timer starts at the same time, indicating when the enemy will attack.  A good vocabulary and decent typing speed will help you kill enemies before they can attack.  The longer your words, the more damage you'll do.
You obviously can't use the same word twice on a level (that would make beating the enemies fairly trivial).  Part of the challenge is saving the longer words that you think of for the most powerful enemies on a level so that you don't have to resort to wimpy, 3-letter attacks.
As you progress you'll earn gold and items that you use to buy upgrades to your gear.  Each piece of gear has special abilities.  One of the early unlocks is a monster guide that you can use to examine the strengths and weaknesses of the enemies on each level, helping you to choose the gear that will do the most damage to the toughest opponents.
If you get stuck (and you probably will) you can replay old levels to earn stars (which unlock more gear), and gold (which you can use to upgrade the gear you have).  It can feel a little grindy, especially at the beginning when there aren't many levels to go back and play so you end up playing the same levels 5 or 10 times to grind out gold.  The game is pretty good about generating different tile sets, though, so you'll be racing to come up with new words even on replays.
Definitely a fun game.

Oh boy oh boy, a word game with a sprinkle of dungeon crawler where I fling as many words as I can come up with at hordes of fantasy enemies! Right? Well, sort of.
First is the battle system. You get ten letter tiles per dungeon and those letters aren't used up or able to be switched out for the entire dungeon. Get a glut of consonants and not many vowels? Sucks to be you, have fun getting halfway through the dungeon and then be unable to come up with any more words. Oh, and each word can only be used once, barring plurals or verbs. So you can use the word "saw" and you can also use the words "sawed" and "saws". The length of a word determines its power and by association your ability to get through the dungeon. So a bad set of letters means you're screwed from the get-go. Not really the free-form word-slinging dungeon crawl I was expecting.
Next is the equipment system. As you ascend the tower you unlock new wands, robes, and hats with their own special abilities. Each of these is able to be upgraded as well, a necessity as you find enemies who hit harder than you can withstand or are resistant to the damage of your best wand. By itself this is fine, even welcome, but where it loses my favor is how the necessary gold needed is not even close to the amount you earn by progressing. You can re-do a previous floor for a Challenge Reward but you can only get each Reward once per floor. So sure, you can earn 3,000 gold on your first clear of a Challenge but if you go back to that same floor you get maybe 400 gold per pass. Oh, and that new wand costs 22,000. Get grinding. You can of course opt to sell the items sometimes dropped on a floor, but each one where I'm at on Floor 37 sells for either 75 or 150 gold. Yeah, really raking in the dough there.
Either of these problems alone probably wouldn't be an issue. If I could choose my words I could speed clear floors for gold and have fun doing it. If I could redo Challenge floors I could deal with the limited board. But when you combine them both you have entire floors where unless you are a human dictionary you are doomed from the get-go even after spending your time farming a colossal amount gold to upgrade your wand once. Ramming your head against enemies again and again and again.
It's not like my vocabulary is small. I write as a hobby and people seem to consider it to be pretty good. Left to my own devices I can construct a plethora of words at 72 per minute last I was officially tested. And that was just typing what was in front of my face. When I'm writing on my own I get much faster. None of that meant anything to this game though and it seemed less like it was testing my typing/writing abilities and a lot more on how many words I could pick out of a limite pool within a short time frame repeatedly.
Perhaps others will like this game more than I did, but personally I am not recommending this game. There's got to be better ones out there. The bar's not especially high.

Spellspire is a cute spell-casting game where you type as quickly as you can to string together words from a letter bank. You can use your mouse and keyboard, but the game also has full controller support,
While it's fun to test your vocabulary, the early game is quite easy even for the most inept of typists. The difficulty quickly escalates from there—no pun intended—as more powerful monsters are added to the mix that will require you to save your larger words for later. In order to contend with the growing monster threat, you can equip your character with wands, robes, and hats—everything a wizard needs to succeed. Other than those light RPG elements, there’s no leveling up or stats to manage.

Each piece of equipment can be upgraded with the gold you win from defeating monsters and completing levels.
Your base health and damage can be upgraded individually in the store, too.
You also obtains items dropped by defeated monsters that help you find words, restore your health, and inflict status effects on monsters. At first, you’re only able to hold one item at a time, but you can expand our inventory space in the shop.

Clearing the challenges that open up after you’ve cleared a stage for the first time grants you more gold and stars. These challenges consist of replaying the stage with faster, stronger monsters with the goal of walking over the finish line with full health. It’s important to note that you can take damage during a challenge so long as you use a potion before touching the star and you will still be able to retrieve it.
Stages are quick, taking no more than a couple of minutes at most. In the beginning, the levels feel a bit too easy with how quickly each level is over. As you progress, each floor will become longer and will require you to spell more words faster. However, there are elemental effects for each outfit that will factor into how much damage you do to monsters. It's somewhat turned based as you have a timer. Once the timer runs out, you will be attacked by the enemy and the timer resets.
The music is not grating, but it won’t be something you remember as it plays on a constant loop. The game’s aesthetic is cute and cartoony, which gets the job done without pushing any GPU limitations.
Just some feedback for the devs to include quality of life:
It is difficult to remember what you typed and it would be nice to see a list of words that you have already used. There is also no way to quick clear for deleting words that are already typed, forcing you to waste time by backspacing.
.Pros.

.Cons.
.Bottom Line.
While at first Spellspire may seem like a kid-friendly game, it amps up the difficulty quite quickly. You’ll need to type quickly and accurately If you expect to deal with the monsters that attack you—particularly if you hope to clear the challenges unscathed.
I recommend this game to loves of word games and puzzles, but not to anyone with a casual interest in either as this may prove to be frustrating as you ascend the tower.

Mini Metro is a great game that has given me hours of fun. I bought it in a recent Humble Bundle for it specifically and after a few hours I'm comfortable giving it a thumbs up, despite the criticisms that I am now about to lay out.
My first caution is that, while the game is well designed and enjoyable, its content is a little thin for the sticker price of $10. There are 12 cities, and while there are some unique quirks between them, the only other practical difference is where the rivers are located. Most end up playing pretty close to the same way. It will still take you a while to invent and explore all the possible strategies for building your metro, but after about 10 hours I found my interest waning as there wasn't much else to spice things up. The three game modes help in this regard.
That said, what content is there makes for quite a challenge. It's a perfect example of a game that gives you a small set of tools that can be combined to make incredibly complex systems.
I also see some room for improvement with the UI. I like the game's minimalist graphics, but the interface takes this a shade too far. There were a few things that bothered me:
1. Trains/carriages are a bit hard to see, being the same color and only slightly larger than the tracks, and often obscured by other objects. It's very difficult to see where everything is at a glance. Something to help them stand out, like a black outline, would be a big help.
2. The stations have the opposite problem. They stand out well, but they're all the same color, differentiated only by shape. It's easy to lose track of where specific stations are since many look alike.
3. Some more feedback in the UI would be nice (at least in sandbox mode, if it would make things too easy on normal/expert). Perhaps some summarized info about each line, like number of passengers waiting, number of trains/carriages active, average wait time. There's a stats page that has some of this info, but it's on a separate screen several clicks away.
4. Speaking of the stats page, the minimalist design doesn't work so well there. Having to mouse over each data point to see numbers does not for easy reading make.
In conclusion, Mini Metro is a simple but deep game that plays pretty much as advertised. Perhaps a bit lacking in content for full price, but still a solid pick for anyone who likes puzzle/strategy type sims.
Edit: The more I play this game, the more I crave more features. I love the challenge but it's actually kind of frustrating how many times I think "gosh it would be nice if I could do X to make my metro more efficient", but alas, X is beyond the scope of gameplay. This really is perfect as a casual, pick-up-and-play mobile game, but if you're used to more in-depth sim type games, proceed with caution.
